https://www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Chip pan fire
https://www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Chip pan fire
Chloe Culling
9:29pm 24 Nov 2026
Date
7.01pm - 24 November 2026
Chip pan fire
Firefighters were called to reports of a kitchen fire in Billericay this evening (Tuesday 24 November).
On arrival, crews found the kitchen smoke-logged, with damage caused by a chip pan fire.
The occupants had been using a saucepan of oil to cook chips but had left the hob switched on after cooking. Their smoke alarm alerted them when the pan began to smoke.
One of the occupants picked up the pan and placed it in the sink before turning on the tap. This caused the burning oil to flare up, resulting in burns to their hands.
After making the scene and occupants safe, firefighters visited neighbouring properties to reassure residents and also took the opportunity to check that neighbours had working smoke alarms.
Fire safety advice
Never leave a pan of cooking oil unattended, and always turn off the hob when you have finished cooking.
If a pan of oil catches fire:
Never move the pan.
Never pour water onto burning oil.
Turn off the heat if it is safe to do so.
Leave the room, close the door and call 999.
Closed
Fire
Incident number
349633
Location
Billericay

Firefighter rescues dog with its head stuck in a wall
Station Manager Antony Clement rescued a two-year-old Springer Spaniel in Takeley today after she got her head stuck in a decorative wall feature.
Antony worked to rescue the dog using small tools and she was safely reunited with her owners.
He said: “She’d managed to get her head stuck in a decorative cut out in the wall and was getting quite distressed while she was trapped. Working with her owners, we were able to chisel her out of the wall feature until she could squeeze her head back out. She was quite happy to be reunited with her owners and hopefully she won’t be getting into any more mischief.”

https://www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Smoke alarms alert neighbours to kitchen fire
Jade Saunders
5:40pm 24 Nov 2026
Do you have working smoke alarms?
Smoke alarms save lives. They can alert your family as well as your neighbours and passers by to a fire in your home if you're not in.
We recommend you have at least one working smoke alarm on every level of your home and that you test them at least once a month.
If you or someone you know doesn’t have working smoke alarms at home, please get in touch with our Service. Visit essex-fire.gov.uk/book or call 0300 303 0088.
Book a free home safety visit here
Date
12.35pm - 24 November 2026
Smoke alarms alert neighbours to kitchen fire
Firefighters are highlighting the importance of having working smoke alarms at home after neighbours called us to report a fire in Colchester today.
On arrival, crews reported the kitchen of a house was heavily smoke logged with a fire on the hob.
Firefighters put the fire out by 1pm and while in the area, they spoke to nearby residents door to door about fire safety and carried out two home safety visits.
Firefighter Chris Simson from Colchester Fire Station said: “The neighbours acted quickly to call us when they heard the smoke alarms going off and this incident shows why it’s so important we all have working smoke alarms at home. The resident wasn’t home but their smoke alarms alerted their neighbours to a fire inside.
“If you or someone you know hasn’t got working smoke alarms at home, we can fit them for free. Please book a free home  safety visit in with our team where we can give you safety advice tailored to you and your household and fit free smoke alarms if you need them.”
Closed
Fire
Incident number
349582
Location
Colchester

https://www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Crews extinguish fire at scrapyard
https://www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Crews extinguish fire at scrapyard
Dom Bowers
7:21am 20 Nov 2026
Date
6.08pm - 20 November 2026
Crews extinguish fire at scrapyard
Crews extinguished a fire at a scrapyard in Little Thurrock.
We were called to Rectory Road yesterday (Thursday 19 November) at 6.08pm and found about 80 tonnes of scrap metal alight.
About 20 firefighters tackled the fire. They extinguished it by 8.50pm and worked with site staff to break up the material and check for hotspots.
Crews left the scene at 9.30pm.
It is believed the fire was caused by a discarded battery.
Station Manager Rick Williams said: "This incident highlights how important it is to dispose of batteries properly, not in a skip or with your general rubbish.
"Batteries can ignite if they are damaged or crushed, so please take used batteries to a recycling centre or collection point."
Visit loveessex.org to find your nearest recycling facility.
Closed
Fire
Incident number
349136
Location
Rectory Road, Little Thurrock

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: Stopping knife crime: the power of intervention this Sceptre Week
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
From school workshops to carpentry qualifications, Essex Violence and Vulnerability Unit (VVU) supports young people to stay safe and build a better future.
Young people in Essex are getting support to stay safe from violence and exploitation – from gaining carpentry qualifications and having access to youth workers, to hearing first-hand about the dangers of gangs, knives and drugs.
This Sceptre Week*, Essex VVU is highlighting it’s preventative work across the country to show how projects focusing on early intervention help tackle knife crime alongside police enforcement.
Since 2019/20, knife crime across Essex has fallen by over 25%. During the same time period, the number of young people entering A&E with knife-related injuries has also fallen by more than 50%.
Positive Futures
One of the programmes Essex VVU supports is Positive Futures, delivered by ATF (Achieve Thrive Flourish) in schools in Chelmsford, Castle Point, Rochford and Southend. The programme combines sport with classroom-based workshops on risks, choices, consequences and motivation. Speakers draw on their own experiences to talk to pupils about the dangers of gangs, knife crime and drugs.
Dan, one of the speakers, describes becoming involved with the wrong people and feeling unable to ask for help.
He said: “It felt weak to ask for help. I grew up with my mum and three sisters, I felt like I should be ‘the man of the house’, I didn’t think to ask for help or even realise I could. I got involved with the wrong people, and while it was easy to get involved it was hard to walk away.”
“I got involved with the wrong people, and while it was easy to get involved it was hard to walk away. I loved sport, particularly football, and I should have just talked to my coach, got help, learnt the courage to say no – that’s what I love about Positive Futures, the fact I’m supporting these young people at risk to be that trusted adult, to talk to me and ask for help if they need it.
Through Positive Futures, Dan now offers young people someone they can talk to and ask for help.  He added: “Seeing their smiles, they find me in the corridor and tell me about their day, they’ve turned up, they’ve participated. It’s a great feeling.”
Project Work
Essex VVU works in partnership with many projects across the county that are supporting young people to stay safe, stay in education, have a safe place to meet and socialise and have access to trusted adults and mentoring, for example:
Harlow:  Rainbow Services carpentry project helps young people who have disengaged from school to gain qualifications and get support from trusted adult.
Chelmsford:  North Avenue Youth Centre’s mentoring project supports young people with identified needs.
Thurrock:  Riverview Charitable Trust runs the EmpowerHer project, which works with vulnerable young girls offering workshops to educate them and improve their mental health.
Alongside these projects, Essex VVU works with families and helps professionals recognise warning signs so support can be offered sooner. It also provides targeted help to young people who have already offended, aiming to stop their offending from continuing or escalating.
Katie, whose name has been changed, receives support through Essex VVU’s ReRoute intervention after previously getting into trouble for carrying a weapon. Workers are helping her make better decisions and understand the consequences of her actions.
She said: “If I could speak to my younger self, I’d tell her not to take the knife. I thought it would make me safer but it was stupid and actually ended up hurting me.” She added: “I’d stop and think about the consequences rather than just bulldozing through; it was stupid and I just hope it doesn’t ruin my future and what I want to do.”

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: Working with Essex Police during Sceptre Week
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
As part of Sceptre Week , the national campaign focused on tackling knife crime and serious violence, Essex Violence and Vulnerability Unit (VVU) is highlighting the wide range of work undertaken across the partnership to prevent and reduce knife crime and serious violence.
One example of this is our recent visit, alongside Essex Police, to a local secondary school.
During the visit, vape devices confiscated by the school were tested to help identify potential risks and provide insight into the products young people may be using. The activity formed part of a wider conversation around vulnerability, prevention and early intervention.
While at the school we met with staff to discuss the challenges facing young people today and the importance of recognising early warning signs of vulnerability. While vaping itself may not be directly linked to serious violence, it can sometimes indicate wider issues such as peer pressure, risk-taking behaviour, or exposure to harmful influences.
These discussions highlighted the vital role that schools and partner agencies play in identifying concerns early and providing support before issues escalate. By sharing knowledge and strengthening professional awareness, schools are better equipped to recognise when a young person may need additional guidance or intervention.
Sceptre Week is not only about enforcement. Prevention and education are key components in reducing the risk of serious violence and knife crime. Through our work with schools, communities and partner organisations, Essex VVU helps to build resilience, raise awareness of exploitation and vulnerability, and support young people to make informed, positive choices.

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: Young People’s Voices Driving Positive Change Across Essex
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
Young people across Essex are continuing to shape the work of Essex VVU, with a range of improvements delivered in direct response to feedback gathered throughout 2025. At the recent Youth Voice Day on 17 October, young people were shown how their views have influenced projects, services and investments designed to make Essex a safer place to live, learn and grow.
A key priority for Essex VVU is ensuring young people have access to opportunities, support and trusted adults. This year, 14 Youth Resources Networkers have been appointed, with one based in every district, borough and unitary authority across Essex. In addition, the VVU grants programme has funded 20 charities and community organisations to deliver activities and support locally, helping to reach more than 3,000 young people. These initiatives contribute to the VVU’s commitment to early intervention and creating positive pathways for young people.
Young people also told us they wanted better access to information, support services and safe spaces. In response, the Essex Youth Map has been expanded and promoted across the county, attracting more than 120,000 views since June 2024. Feedback has also helped shape education programmes delivered in schools, including sessions on knife crime, healthy relationships, Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG), hate crime awareness, stalking, harassment and online safety. Development is also underway for a new AI safety session to help young people understand emerging risks and opportunities in the digital world.
Creating Safe Spaces
Creating safer places and reducing the fear of crime remains a key VVU priority. Working alongside Essex Police and Community Safety Partnerships, improvements have been made in town centres and public spaces through targeted patrols, enhanced lighting, CCTV upgrades and reassurance activity. Public spaces in Chelmsford, including Central Park and Angel Meadow, have also been improved to be more welcoming and inclusive for girls, while the countywide VAWG Strategy includes commitments to improve safety on public transport.
The feedback shared by young people continues to influence how partners across Essex tackle violence and vulnerability. Through an annual investment of more than £2 million in prevention programmes, the VVU now supports initiatives that reach more than 50,000 people every year. The changes highlighted at Youth Voice Day demonstrate the importance of listening to young people and reinforce the VVU’s priorities of prevention, partnership working, community safety and creating positive opportunities to help all young people thrive.

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: And that’s a wrap: Youth Voice Day 2026
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
The 2026 Youth Voice Day was held on Saturday 17 October, and we want to thank all the young people who attended, shared their views, challenged us with their ideas and engaged in meaningful, insightful dialogue on safety in Essex.
Essex VVU ran workshops with two groups of young people, asking about their concerns in their communities, and how we can change things for the better. The young people talked eloquently about crime, safety, differences, neighbourhoods and youth violence.
Most of the young people talked about feeling safe in their neighbourhoods, which mirrors the findings we are seeing in the Essex VVU Listening Report. There was a questioning and reflective view of the benefits of social media.  As well as a sense that some platforms portray some places as unsafe, which does not always match with their everyday reality.
In the afternoon the young people were able to put questions to senior leaders across the county on topics such as personal safety, tackling violence against women and girls, county lines, knife crime and community safety. There were some great ideas about how to build safer communities – a reminder to all of us how important it is to involve young people and capture the youth voice.
We thoroughly enjoyed the day, not only hearing from our Essex young people but also catching up with the Essex VVU Youth Resource Networkers and hearing the impact they are having in their communities. The whole event was a great example of partnership working and the positive impact we can have when we all work together.
A huge thanks to everyone who attended and took part. Also, thank you to Essex Boys and Girls Clubs and Essex Council for Voluntary Youth Services for the logistics behind the scenes and making it all happen!

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: Finding space at Third Space Youth Club
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
Essex VVU Community Grants work with a wide range of amazing groups across Essex, delivering activities and support which help young people stay safe, feel supported and thrive in their local communities.
This programme responds to what young people consistently tell us matters to them – safe spaces, trusted adults and positive activities that help them feel safe and supported.
One of these amazing groups is The Third Space Youth Club in Chapel Hill, Braintree and we recently visited the Friday evening session which is funded by Essex VVU.
The Youth Club runs out of Essex County Council’s Youth Centre and on the evening we visited there were a huge range of positive activities on offer for young people to get involved with – including basketball, bracelet making, drawing, colouring, table top games, pool, and photography.
The club is really popular and 45 young people regularly attend each session, which is the maximum number the club can accommodate. The young people told us how much they love attending the club, they’ve made friends and feel it is a safe space to hang out – with some having experienced bullying at their local park.
Talking to the youth workers they told us how they are building positive relationships with those who attend the club, with more than 100 different young people having visited and engaged with the activities on offer.
It was great to see the youth club so vibrant, with high levels of energy from all the young people in attendance. Young people being kept safe, spending time with trusted adults and their friends, developing social skills and building relationships.

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: Essex VVU Community Grant Launch 2027/28
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
Community groups, charities and not for profit organisations across Essex are being invited to apply for funding of up to £35,000 to deliver projects that help young people stay safe, feel supported and thrive in their local communities.
The Essex Violence and Vulnerability Unit (VVU) has opened applications for its 2027/28 Community Grant Programme, with successful projects beginning delivery from July 2027.
The funding programme has been shaped by the voices of young people through the seventh Essex VVU and ECVYS Listening Project, which highlighted the critical role that safe spaces, trusted adults and positive activities play in helping young people feel safe and supported.
Although asking questions about safety and youth violence, the latest feedback from young people across Essex paints a positive picture of safety and resilience:
85.3% of young people say they feel safe in Essex when out with their friends , a significant increase from 65% last year .
91% have not been a victim of violent crime .
79.5% are not worried about being exploited by a gang .
Young people also shared what helps them feel safe when they are out and about. Common themes included:
Being with friends.
Staying in well-lit areas.
Using mobile phones as torches.
Access to GPS and location tracking technology.
However, alongside these practical measures, young people consistently highlighted the importance of having trusted adults to turn to and safe places where they feel welcomed, supported and understood.
The Essex VVU Community Grant Programme is designed to fund local projects that provide exactly these opportunities, ensuring young people can access support in the places where they live.
Roger Hirst, the Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner for Essex and Chair of the Violence and Vulnerability Partnership, said: “The Listening Project is an effective way to understand the views of young people when it comes to feeling safe in their local neighbourhood and wider community – there should be no no-go areas in our county. It is an opportunity to understand their perceptions about crime, so that grant funding can be targeted to support local projects where it is needed the most. Whilst it is encouraging that more young people report feeling safe in our county, the findings also reinforce the importance of trusted adults, positive relationships and safe spaces.”
“The Essex VVU Community Grant Programme is about investing in organisations that understand their communities and can respond quickly to provide the right support, at the right time. This grant programme backs youth clubs, mentoring programmes, diversionary activities and other community-based interventions. Projects that help build resilience, create opportunities and prevent harm before it occurs.”
“By engaging more young people in local projects at the earliest opportunity, there is every prospect that their concerns about crime can be addressed. It is also important to help guide those tempted by a criminal lifestyle to make more positive choices about their future. Those currently leading projects that can strike the right balance between listening to young people without judgement and offering a catalyst for change should seriously consider putting in an application.”
Projects funded through previous rounds of the programme have supported thousands of young people across Essex, providing positive activities and opportunities to develop confidence and life skills, and reduce serious violence.
The 2027/28 grants will continue to support initiatives that prevent violence, strengthen protective factors around young people and respond directly to local needs identified by communities and young people themselves.
The main criteria for the 27/28 grants include:
Applications are open from the 14 September. Closing date is 26 October 2026.
The maximum amount an organisation can apply for is £35,000.
For delivery 1 st July 2027 to 31 st December 2028 (to deliver across at least 14 of the 18 months)

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: A summer visit to Teen Talk Harwich
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
Essex VVU Community Grants works with a wide range of amazing groups across Essex, delivering activities and support which help young people stay safe, feel supported and thrive in their local communities.
This programme responds to what young people consistently tell us matters to them – safe spaces, trusted adults and positive activities that help them feel safe and supported.
One of these amazing groups is Teen Talk. Essex VVU recently visited one of Teen Talk Harwich’s summer holiday Pop In sessions, one of the activities the VVU Community Grants supports.
It was inspiring to see first-hand the difference this service is making for local young people. Teen Talk’s Pop In sessions run every Tuesday and Thursday from 12pm to 2pm during the school holidays, providing a welcoming and supportive space where young people can relax, connect and simply enjoy being themselves.
A significant number of the young people who attend the Pop In sessions are neurodivergent. All of the Teen Talk sessions are tailored to support individual needs.
During Essex VVUs visit, young people were happily drawing, playing UNO, chatting with friends and enthusiastically making, and eating, hot dogs. There was certainly no shortage of ketchup!
Alongside crafts, games and food preparation, the sessions provide invaluable opportunities to build friendships and social skills. Staff told us that for many attendees, this is the only activity they choose to come to during the holidays.
Seeing the Pop In session in action made it clear why it has been such a success. Teen Talk is providing far more than activities; it is creating a safe, supportive community where young people feel valued, understood and empowered to thrive.
VVU support for Teen Talk extends beyond the school holidays, also supporting the Teen Talk team to deliver weekly mentoring and outreach sessions for young people at two local secondary schools – Lift Academy’s Frinton Upper and Thorpe-le-Soken sites. These sessions focus on building resilience and coping strategies through mentoring, providing a trusted adult and a safe space where young people can talk through challenges and receive practical support that help young people develop the tools to navigate everyday life and manage challenges.

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: Promoting Positive Opportunities at Braintree Youth Festival
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
On 28 August, Essex Youth Service and Braintree District Council hosted a Youth Festival at Weavers Park in the heart of Braintree, bringing together local organisations and young people for a day of activities, information and engagement.
Essex Violence and Vulnerability Unit (VVU) attended the event in partnership with Braintree Rugby Club, with members of the club’s Under-16 team helping to promote the importance of young people accessing positive activities and local opportunities. Together, they highlighted how involvement in sports, youth clubs, drama groups and other community projects can help young people build confidence, develop skills and form positive connections.
Throughout the day, more than 200 information cards and keyrings were distributed, signposting young people to local activities and support. The rugby players also spoke to their peers about the Essex Map, an online tool that helps young people discover opportunities and services available in their local area, sharing their own positive experiences of being part of a team.
The VVU also gathered feedback from young people about community safety, crime concerns and how they would like to see their local areas improved. The conversations provided valuable insights that will be shared with local partners, including the council and police.
The event was a fantastic example of partnership working, with Braintree Rugby Club’s young ambassadors playing a key role in engaging their peers and promoting positive opportunities. With great weather, strong community spirit and plenty of enthusiasm, the festival was a positive celebration of the young people of Essex.

https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.title: Essex VVU/ECVYS Youth Voice Listening Project 2026 Report
https://www.essexvvu.co.uk/feed/.text:
Essex VVU is proud to deliver projects and interventions across Essex and partner with a wide range of amazing local organisations – work that makes a real difference to children, young people, families and wider communities – reducing knife crime and contributing to safer communities. A key element of our approach is listening to the experiences of young people and communities, ensuring their voices inform and shape the delivery of the Essex VVU work programme.
For the seventh consecutive year, we commissioned Essex Council for Voluntary Youth Services (ECVYS) to run a young person’s listening project to gather the views of young people on how safe they feel in their local communities, wider Essex and what could help them feel safer.
This was carried out in two parts; the first part took place through school assemblies, with Year 7 pupils. The second through face-to-face conversations in small groups through a range of local youth work provision, in a range of settings.
In total more than 5,000 young people took part in the project, keen to share their views and affect change in their communities. This report and its findings, along with other Essex VVU evaluations and learning, are used to inform the ongoing development of the overall Essex VVU programme and the wider violence reduction approach in Essex.
Because each part of Essex is different, ECVYS have created both an Essex‑wide report and local reports. This means the VVU, and others who want to keep communities safe, can understand what young people think at both a broad and local level. The report reflects the work of local youth organisations and, most importantly, the voices of young people across Essex, to whom we are very grateful.
The report can be viewed and downloaded via ECVYS website and a series of webinars are being held to run through the findings. Each presentation will cover the Essex wide picture followed by individual districts specified. The webinar links are detailed below and all run 2pm-3pm:
17th August – West (Uttlesford, Epping Forest and Harlow)
19th August – North (Colchester, Tendring and Braintree)
24th August – Mid (Maldon, Chelmsford and Brentwood)
26th August – South West (Thurrock and Basildon)
28th August – South East (Rochford, Castle Point and Southend)
Specific diary invites can be requested from Nicole@ecvys.org.uk

Neighbourhood officers and council team up for fly tipping crackdown
Leona.Murraygreen
Date
26 November 2026
Date
26 November 2026
Category
Environment
Brentwood Neighbourhood Policing Team and Brentwood Borough Council’s environmental officers are fighting back against fly tippers as part of a new operation.
The joint team is carrying out extra patrols in areas of the borough that have been affected by the illegal dumping of waste and pulling over vans for spot checks.
Domestic waste, car parts and even burnt-out vehicles have been found by the roadside, and there have been occasions where roads have been blocked by building waste.
The officers believe the secluded areas of the borough, particularly in and around Navestock, have been targeted because of their close proximity to the M25 and A12.
PC Tom Marriott of Brentwood Neighbourhood Policing Team is leading the policing side of the operation and said that he understands the concerns of local residents:
“Fly tipping causes huge amounts of disruption and damages the environment.  We have seen examples of fly tips blocking entire country lanes, leaving a trail of rubbish that takes a long time to clear, impacting everyone living locally.
“A lot of the waste is household or building waste but we have also had people dumping hazardous materials like asbestos – materials that cost the council thousands to pick up and can harm people and wildlife.
“We’re here to help the council stop fly tipping and deter those people who think it’s OK to use the district to dump waste.
“If you’re getting rid of waste, be careful about who you’re passing it to. Make sure they’re an accredited company with a waste carrier licence, which can be checked on the Environment Agency website .
“If you see an active fly tip, call 999 and we’ll try to get to it. If you spot waste, use the What3Words app to tell us the exact location, take a picture and report it to the council.”
Councillor David Worsfold, Chair of Brentwood Borough Council’s Clean & Green Committee, added: “There are an average of three fly tips every day in the borough, and it costs more than £95,000 a year for their clearing and disposal. Working together with other agencies, like Essex Police, is important to tackle the issue.
“The Council uses fixed penalty notices in addition to the existing powers of prosecution to provide additional means of enforcement.
“We recently had a successful prosecution that resulted in a prison sentence which is a stark warning that if you are found guilty of fly-tipping in Brentwood, you could face imprisonment or a fine of up to £50,000.”

Manalikah.Campbell
Date

Date

Do you know someone who goes out of their way to make a difference in our community?
The annual Civic Awards are back, and we are calling on you to nominate those individuals and organisations that are making a difference in our community.
We would like to recognise the hard work of organisations and locals, who have continued to help others and make Brentwood a better place. The Civic Awards provide an opportunity to acknowledge their dedication in going above and beyond for the community.
The Service to the Community award is open for nominations to both individuals and groups, regardless of age, and can be nominated to someone who volunteers their free time helping others, such as caring for a family member, helping others within the Borough or someone who has done something exceptional for the community.
The Lifetime Achievement award is designed to honour someone who has dedicated years to creating a lasting and positive effect on the community and deserves recognition for their accomplishments.
Mayor of Brentwood Councillor Nicky Cuthbert said, "Our communities are strengthened by the dedication, kindness and commitment of the people who quietly go above and beyond to make a difference in the lives of others. The Civic Awards provide an important opportunity to recognise and celebrate these outstanding individuals, groups and volunteers. I encourage residents to take a moment to nominate someone whose efforts deserve acknowledgement, helping us shine a spotlight on those who make Brentwood such a special place to live, work and thrive."
Anyone who lives or works in Brentwood can be nominated.
To assist the judging panel, please ensure you include as much detail as possible when nominating with examples of what the individual or group have done in the community.
The nominations close on Friday 5 February 2027 and will be considered by the panel of judges.
The awards will be presented on Friday 16 April 2027 at the Civic Dinner.
To nominate, please complete our online form on our website: https://my.brentwood.gov.uk/service/Civic_Awards_Nomination . Alternatively, please email mayors.secretary@brentwood.gov.uk to request a hard copy of the nomination form.

https://www.brentwood.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Brentwood Council launches Women's Safety Charter and marks 16 Days of Activism with community events
Manalikah.Campbell
Date
23 November 2026
Date
23 November 2026
Brentwood Borough Council is marking the international 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence campaign by highlighting its commitment to creating a safer borough for women and girls through the Women's Safety Charter and a series of community engagement events.
The annual campaign, which runs from 25 November to 10 December, shines a spotlight on violence against women and girls (VAWG) and encourages organisations, communities and individuals to take action to challenge harmful behaviours, support victims and survivors, and help create safer environments for everyone.
A key part of Brentwood's commitment is its Women's Safety Charter, which was launched to improve safety and confidence for women and girls across the borough. The Charter brings together businesses, community groups and organisations in a shared commitment to creating safer public spaces, promoting active bystander intervention and ensuring support is available when it is needed.
Participating organisations can become accredited Safe Spaces, providing visible locations where women and girls can seek assistance, while staff receive guidance and training to help them respond appropriately to concerns. The Charter also encourages residents to reflect on how their own actions can contribute to a culture in which everyone feels safe and respected.
The initiative supports the wider aims of the White Ribbon campaign, which works to prevent violence against women and girls by encouraging men and boys, alongside the wider community, to challenge harmful attitudes and behaviours and become part of the solution.
As part of the 16 Days of Activism campaign, Brentwood Borough Council and its partners will be hosting a series of community events where residents can learn more about the Women's Safety Charter, access advice and information, and find out what support is available locally.
Upcoming events:
25 November, 10am to 12pm - Unit 10, Baytree Centre, Brentwood
3 December, 10am to 12pm - Outside Marks & Spencer, Brentwood High Street
10 December, 2pm to 4pm - Unit 10, Baytree Centre, Brentwood
Representatives from organisations including Essex Police, Victim Support, Changing Pathways, Renew Counselling, Phoenix Futures, Active Essex, housing services and Essex County Fire and Rescue Service will be attending events at the Baytree Centre and Brentwood High Street throughout the campaign period.
These events will also provide opportunities for local businesses and organisations to learn more about the Charter and how they can support the council's ambition to make Brentwood a safer place for women and girls.
Councillor Dr Tim Barrett, Chair of the Housing, Health & Community Committee, said: "Everyone has the right to feel safe in their community. Through our Women's Safety Charter, we are working with local organisations and businesses to create safer spaces, encourage positive behaviours and build a culture where violence against women and girls is never tolerated.
"The 16 Days of Activism campaign provides an important opportunity to raise awareness of this issue and encourage conversations about the role we can all play in preventing violence against women and girls. I would encourage residents to come along to one of our community events to find out more about the support available and how they can get involved."
To find out more about the Women's Safety Charter or how your organisation can join, visit: www.brentwood.gov.uk/womens-safety-charter

https://www.brentwood.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Fatima Whitbread MBE awarded the Freedom of the Borough of Brentwood
https://www.brentwood.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Fatima Whitbread MBE awarded the Freedom of the Borough of Brentwood
Manalikah.Campbell
Date
13 November 2026
Date
13 November 2026
Essex Olympic medallist and campaigner Fatima Whitbread MBE has been awarded the honorary title of Freewoman of the Borough of Brentwood in recognition of her outstanding sporting achievements and her dedication to improving the lives of children in care and care leavers.
The honour was formally approved at an Extraordinary Council this week (11 November) and recognises Fatima's exceptional contribution to sport, society and the local community.
Fatima Whitbread is one of Britain's most celebrated athletes. A double Olympic medallist, World Champion and European Champion in javelin, she became the first British athlete to set a world record in a throwing event with her 77.44 metre throw at the 1986 European Championships.
Beyond her sporting achievements, Fatima has become a leading advocate for children in care and care leavers, drawing on her own experiences growing up in the care system. Through her national campaign, which is headquartered in Brentwood, she works to improve outcomes for vulnerable young people and raise awareness of the challenges many face as they transition into adulthood.
Earlier this year, Fatima led the UK's first national care summit, bringing together hundreds of representatives from health, housing, education, sport, business, the arts and technology sectors to drive positive change for children and young people in care. Her campaign continues to champion practical support through mentoring, financial education, employment opportunities and community partnerships.
Fatima has also maintained strong links with Brentwood through a number of local initiatives. These include hosting The Power of Resilience fundraising event at Brentwood School, organising the Day of Inspiration for cared-for children at King George's Playing Fields and visiting Brentwood Ursuline Convent High School to share her personal story and inspire young people.
Fatima Whitbread MBE said: “I’m deeply honoured to be made an Honorary Freewoman of the Borough of Brentwood, a place I’m proud to call home. This means a great deal to me, and I share it with everyone in our community who gives their time and heart to help children in care and young people leaving care feel they belong and have the chance to thrive.”
The Leader of Brentwood Borough Council, Councillor Barry Aspinell, added: "This honour is about more than recognising an outstanding career. It is about celebrating the positive impact Fatima has made by championing the voices of children in care and care leavers, and inspiring others to make a difference. Her work has touched communities across the country, including here in Brentwood, where her advocacy helped shape our approach to supporting care leavers and encouraged the Council to adopt the Care Leavers Pledge, strengthening the support we provide to young people as they move into adulthood. Through her campaign and community engagement, she has built strong local connections and created opportunities that make a real difference to people's lives. Awarding Fatima the Freedom of the Borough is our way of acknowledging her achievements, thanking her for her commitment, and recognising the opportunities she continues to create for others."

https://www.brentwood.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Brentwood remembers – hundreds of people show their respect at annual Remembrance Day parade
Leona.Murraygreen
Date
09 November 2026
Date
09 November 2026
Category
Community
Hundreds of people lined the streets of Brentwood on Sunday to show their respect for those who sacrificed their lives for our country at the annual Remembrance Day Parade and Service (Sunday 8 November).
The parade, superbly led by the Brentwood Imperial Youth Band, started at Brentwood Town Hall and saw members of The Royal British Legion (Brentwood Branch), Veterans, serving Armed Forces Personnel, Cadets, Scouts and Guides, and members of our public services, proudly march down Middleton Hall Lane towards the war memorial at the junction with Shenfield Road.
Following a short service led by Father Mark North, the laying of wreaths took place and two minutes of silence was respectfully observed. The parade then continued along the High Street, where the salute was taken by Deputy Lieutenant of Essex, Graham Clegg, accompanied by other dignitaries including the Mayor of Brentwood, Councillor Nicky Cuthbert and Dennis Rensch MBE of the Royal British Legion (Brentwood Branch). A service at St Thomas’ Church followed the parade.
Following the parade, the Mayor of Brentwood, Councillor Nicky Cuthbert said: “It was an honour and a privilege to lead the town in remembrance to all those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the course of defending the freedoms we have today.
"Thank you to everyone who was part of the Remembrance Sunday Parade and to all the residents who came together to pay their respects and honour the courage and sacrifice of our Armed Forces personnel of past, present and future.”
To see a video and photos of Brentwood marking Remembrance, visit the Council’s Facebook page.

https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.title: Cabinet 26 November 2026
https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.text:
Epping Forest District Council’s Cabinet has approved a new Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy, backed plans to invest in technology to support customer services and considered a range of governance and financial reports.
Opening the meeting, the Leader of the Council, Cllr Chris Whitbread, addressed concerns regarding the rejection of public questions relating to Qualis Commercial. He reaffirmed the Council’s commitment to transparency and effective scrutiny, explaining that the Council’s Constitution contains provisions designed to avoid substantial duplication of issues already considered through public meetings, and to ensure Council business remains focused on matters requiring consideration and decision.
View the agenda for Cabinet 26 November
Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy
At its meeting on 26 November 2026, Cabinet approved a new Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy 2026-2031.
The strategy sets out how the Council, and its partners will work together over the next five years to prevent homelessness, tackle rough sleeping and improve housing outcomes for residents.
Demand for homelessness support has increased in recent years, with approaches to the Council rising from 1,086 households in 2022/23 to 1,357 in 2025/26. The strategy focuses on early intervention, partnership working and increasing access to suitable accommodation to help residents at risk of homelessness.
Customer Services technology
Cabinet also approved plans to invest in a new enterprise communications platform. The technology is intended to support future improvements to customer service and help create a more joined-up experience for residents when contacting the Council.
While digital tools will play an important role in supporting services in the future, the Council remains committed to ensuring residents can access help in the way that works best for them, including through personal support and non-digital channels.
Other business
Cabinet also considered a range of governance and financial reports, including budget monitoring, risk management, and an updated debt recovery policy.

https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.title: Roding Valley Recreation Ground set for improvements
https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.text:
A new strategy setting out a long-term vision for improvements at Roding Valley Recreation Ground is set to be approved by Epping Forest District Council.
The strategy is part of a wider approach, established in the Epping Forest District Local Plan , that must manage to the Council’s legal obligations to the nearby Epping Forest Special Area of Conservation. It will help guide future investment priorities in the popular green space, delivering enhancements that improve accessibility, biodiversity and the overall visitor experience so that more people are encouraged to get outdoors closer to where they live.
Projects identified within the strategy include improvements to walking routes, new tree planting, meadow and habitat creation, upgraded entrances and signage, interpretation boards and other measures designed to make the site more welcoming and accessible for residents and visitors.
Funded through developer contributions
The enhancements will be funded through existing and future S106 developer contributions secured from new developments in the area, helping to ensure growth contributes towards investment in local green spaces and community infrastructure.
Projects will be delivered in phases as funding is received, allowing the council to bring forward improvements that support both local communities and the long-term future of the recreation ground.
Download the map showing the development areas for Roding Valley Recreation Ground (png 5MB)
Supporting communities through growth
Roding Valley Recreation Ground is a much-loved green space and an important asset for local communities in Loughton, Buckhurst Hill & Theydon Bois. It’s somewhere I visit regularly and I know from first-hand experience how important it is to local people. During the Covid-19 pandemic, it became a lifeline for many residents, providing a safe place to exercise, enjoy the outdoors and support their wellbeing during a particularly challenging time.”
This strategy gives us a clear and fundable plan for future improvements that will make the site more accessible, attractive and enjoyable for residents and visitors, while also enhancing biodiversity. It is a key component of us meeting our legal obligations to the nearby Epping Forest Special Area of Conservation to protect it for future generations.
I’m particularly pleased that these enhancements will be funded through developer contributions. This means investment from new development taking place in the local area is helping to deliver lasting benefits for our communities and ensuring that growth supports improvements to local infrastructure.”
Councillor Ken Williamson , Portfolio Holder for Shaping Our District
Working with local partners
The strategy has been developed with support from local partners including:
Loughton Town Council,
Buckhurst Hill Parish Council,
Natural England, and
Essex Wildlife Trust.
Together, they have helped shape a long-term vision for the recreation ground that balances recreation, accessibility and environmental enhancement.
The enhancement strategy forms part of the council’s wider work to invest in high-quality green spaces for residents while protecting and improving the district’s natural environment.

https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.title: Council crushes first vehicle linked to fly-tipping
https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.text:
Epping Forest District Council crushed its first vehicle linked to fly-tipping – a Ford Transit truck – on 11 November 2026, putting its commitment to get tough on fly-tipping into practice.
The seizure and subsequent crushing are an historic first for Epping Forest District Council (EFDC), a significant milestone resulting in the first-ever seizure and destruction of a vehicle used in fly-tipping and illegal waste offences in the Epping Forest district.
It is in line with renewed government guidance urging councils to destroy vehicles used in illegal dumping.
Huge fly-tip in Epping Forest
The truck was involved in a huge fly-tip where more than a tonne of construction and demolition waste was dumped on heathland in Epping Forest in January. In August the vehicle was seized after the vehicle’s driver was arrested on a separate matter.
The City of London Corporation (CoL), who own and manage the forest, recognised the truck’s connection to the original fly-tip, contacted EFDC, who have statutory powers to seize and retain vehicles.
With the help of Essex Police, the swift partnership working between the 3 organisations led to a vehicle used in fly-tipping being taken off the road for good.
Zero tolerance to fly-tipping
Crushing our first vehicle sends a clear message – fly-tipping will not be tolerated in the Epping Forest district.
This is the first time we’ve used our powers to crush a vehicle used for this crime and we will not hesitate to do it again if such selfish and criminal acts continue.
Our stance is clear – we have a zero-tolerance policy for fly-tipping and we will use all enforcement powers available, including CCTV, fines and vehicle seizures, to hold those responsible to account. Where we have evidence, we will prosecute.
This action is designed to send a strong message – fly-tipping risks not only fines of up to £5,000, but also offenders losing their vehicles.
Combatting fly-tipping requires coordinated action with many organisations including local councils, the Environment Agency, police, housing associations, landowners, and residents. My thanks go to both CoL and Essex Police for helping us achieve this historic first – we’re working together to stop these environmental criminals!
Councillor Darshan Sunger , Portfolio Holder for Environment and Regulatory Services
How to report fly-tipping
If you find fly-tipped waste, or someone in the act of fly-tipping always remember to stay safe first:
Do not confront fly-tippers: If a crime is happening right now, call 999
Do not touch or move the waste: Items may contain broken glass, syringes, asbestos, or toxic chemicals, and may contain clues to trace offenders
Report it to us: Report fly-tipping online at any time or call 01992 564000 during office hours
Fly-tipping is a selfish and criminal act
Fly-tipping is a selfish, criminal act that harms our communities and countryside, costing taxpayers thousands of pounds every year.
We all have a role to play in keeping our district clean, so I would urge residents to think about how they dispose of their waste. If you are using a private business, make sure the company is on the register of waste carriers . Don’t use a cold caller or social media ad whose offer seems to good to be true – this is often a warning sign of a rogue collector who may fly-tip your rubbish.
If your waste is dumped illegally, you could face fines and prosecution. Your waste, your responsibility. responsibly and report any incidents of fly-tipping to us.
Councillor Darshan Sunger , Portfolio Holder for Public Protection and Environment

https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.title: Epping Forest District’s 50 favourite trees revealed
https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.text:
Throughout 2026 – as part Countrycare’s 40 th anniversary celebrations – local people have been nominating their favourite trees.
These have been ranked as the new 50 Favourite Trees of Epping Forest District and were revealed in an exhibition opening at Epping Forest District Museum on 21 November.
Created by Epping Forest District Council Countrycare and Epping Forest District Museum CIO, the exhibition showcases the 50 trees nominated by members of the public, highlighting their beauty, history, wildlife value, and personal significance to local communities.
Featuring photographs and stories from across the district, the display encourages visitors to explore the area’s natural heritage and discover the special connections people have with the trees in their local landscapes.
Trees matter to us
We know the trees work very hard for us – for our health, for our wellbeing, for biodiversity and for the appearance of our towns, villages and countryside
But trees also matter to us for more personal reasons. It may be because of a historical or family connection, their location, their size or appearance.
Our residents have taken this challenge to their hearts and chosen some truly beautiful trees from across the district.
Cllr Darshan Sunger, Cabinet Member for Countrycare.
The exhibition is located in the museum’s central stairwell and runs from 21 November 2026 to 14 April 2027.
Download the 50 Favourite Trees exhibition poster (jpeg 465KB)
Epping Forest Countrycare
Countrycare was set up in 1986 offering practical help, friendly advice and clear information on the countryside, nature conservation and wildlife law in the Epping Forest District. Its aim has always been to protect, maintain and enhance the natural environment for the benefit of both local people and wildlife. This is achieved by creating and caring for habitats, improving access to the countryside and helping people better understand and value the district’s rural heritage.

NHS Essex is encouraging residents to get vaccinated by Friday 11 December to give the vaccine time to work before Christmas Day.
They are urging anyone eligible for a free flu vaccination to get it now if they have not yet had it this winter. The call comes ahead of spending time with family and friends this Christmas.
The flu vaccine can take up to 2 weeks to build protection.
Reduce your risk of serious illness
Christmas is a time when families and friends come together, and flu can spread easily through close contact. Getting vaccinated helps reduce your risk of serious illness. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to family members, including those at greater risk of becoming seriously unwell.
Older people, pregnant women and people with certain long-term health conditions are particularly at risk of serious illness from flu. Getting vaccinated helps reduce that risk.
How to get your flu vaccine
Visit NHS Essex for more information:
Flu vaccine for adults
Flu vaccine for children
Flu vaccine in pregnancy

https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.title: Council shares suicide prevention work in Parliament
https://www.eppingforestdc.gov.uk/catego.text:
Epping Forest District Council (EFDC) was invited to Westminster to share its work on suicide prevention in the workplace at a parliamentary roundtable hosted by Liz Twist MP and the British Standards Institution (BSI).
Suicide and the Workplace standard
EFDC’s Public Health Apprentice and Service Director for Communities attended the event on 12 November at Portcullis House in the House of Commons, where they presented a case study on the council’s implementation of the BS 30480 Suicide and the Workplace.
The roundtable brought together more than 60 representatives from a wide range of sectors including the NHS, construction, higher education, aviation, banking, manufacturing, retail, the armed forces and suicide prevention charities to discuss how organisations can embed the standard to better support employees affected by suicide.
From left to right – Ezra Hewing Head of Centre for London for James’ Place Charity, Fabrizio Ferrari Service Director, Communities for Epping Forest District Council, Laura Cleverley Public Health Apprentice for Epping Forest District Council, Liz Twist MP for Blaydon and Consett,
Jane Packer Head of Standards at BSI
and Anne Hayes Director of Standards Development at BSI.
Suicide prevention and postvention measures
The discussion marked the first anniversary of the publication of the British Standard and explored both the opportunities and challenges organisations face when introducing suicide prevention and postvention measures in the workplace. EFDC representatives shared learning from the council’s journey so far, including the cultural changes being developed through its Suicide and the Workplace Working Group.
Compassionate and supportive workplace culture
The council’s work began following feedback gathered from suicide awareness sessions delivered earlier this year, which highlighted that many people felt workplaces were not sufficiently prepared to support staff affected by suicide. This insight led to the council adopting BS 30480 and establishing a dedicated working group to help embed its principles across the organisation.
The working group includes colleagues from Public Health, Human Resources, Community Resilience and specialist partner organisations, all working together to create a compassionate and supportive workplace culture.
Helping to start important conversations
During the roundtable, delegates highlighted the importance of taking a sensitive, authentic and people-led approach to implementing the standard, recognising that every organisation has its own culture and challenges. Participants also discussed how introducing even small elements of the standard can help start important conversations and improve support for employees.
Epping Forest District Council hopes its experience will encourage other organisations across the district and beyond to consider adopting elements of the standard and strengthening their own approach to suicide prevention, intervention and support for people affected by suicide.

Taking place at Epping Forest District Council Offices, 323 High Street, Epping, CM16 4BZ, the evening will celebrate local businesses while supporting the invaluable work of our local hospice.
Buy your ticket to the Fashion Show at:
Epping Town Partnership Eventbrite page
Tickets cost £10, including a glass of fizz.
Local designers and businesses showcased

The catwalk will also showcase clothes from:
Coles Menswear,
Rock Theydon Bois,
Kay T Fashion,
Runkitfox,
and a fashion stall from Epping Market, alongside vintage and pre-loved fashion from St Clare Hospice.

https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Rochford District Council considering letter received today from Government
LeonaMG
Date
23 November 2026
Date
23 November 2026
The Government has directed Rochford District Council to begin the final pre-submission public consultation on its draft Local Plan on 7 December 2026.
The Minister of State for Housing and Planning, Matthew Pennycook MP, set out the intervention decision in a letter to the Leader of the Council, Cllr Adi Malviya, on 23 November 2026. According to the letter, the consultation must be on the 'option 1' version of the Plan presented to Full Council on 23 September 2026, before the changes agreed at that meeting.
The letter also directs that Rochford District Council:
Must not take any step to withdraw the Plan
Must report monthly to officials from the Ministry for Homes, Communities and Local Government on the Plan’s progress
Must progress the Plan to the end of the examination process
Can make minor modifications to the plan after the consultation, but any significant changes must be set out for consideration by the Secretary of State.
Cllr Adi Malviya, Leader of Rochford District Council, said, “Many people in our district feel strongly about the Local Plan. We are considering next steps in how we respond to this letter from the Government and will update residents in the coming days.”
Residents interested in the Local Plan can sign up to the planning e-newsletter .

https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Rochford Council launches Women's Safety Charter and marks 16 Days of Activism with community events
https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Rochford Council launches Women's Safety Charter and marks 16 Days of Activism with community events
ManalikahC
Date
23 November 2026
Date
23 November 2026
Rochford District Council is reaffirming its commitment to tackling violence against women and girls (VAWG) by launching the Women's Safety Charter and hosting a series of community engagement events as part of the international 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence campaign.
The annual campaign, which runs from 25 November to 10 December, brings together communities, organisations and public services across the world to raise awareness of violence against women and girls and encourage action to prevent it.
As part of its commitment, Rochford District Council has joined the Women's Safety Charter, a county-wide initiative designed to improve the safety of women and girls by creating safer public spaces, encouraging active bystander intervention and promoting a culture where harassment, abuse and violence are never tolerated.
The Charter brings together local authorities, businesses, community groups and partner organisations in a shared commitment to making communities safer. Through training, awareness raising and the creation of recognised Safe Spaces, the initiative aims to ensure women and girls feel supported, respected and confident when living, working and visiting places across the district.
The council's involvement in the Charter supports the wider aims of the White Ribbon movement, which encourages individuals, organisations and communities to play an active role in preventing violence against women and girls by challenging harmful attitudes and behaviours and promoting positive change.
To mark the 16 Days of Activism campaign and raise awareness of the Charter, Rochford District Council and its partners will be hosting a series of community engagement events across the district. Residents will have the opportunity to speak with local services and organisations, find out more about the support available and learn how they can help create safer communities.
Event information
25 November 2026, 2pm to 4pm -The Mill Arts & Events Centre, Rayleigh
3 December 2026, 2pm to 4pm - Clements Hall Leisure Centre, Hawkwell
10 December 2026, 10am to 12pm - Outside Star Café Pie & Mash Shop, Rayleigh High Street
Partners attending the events include Essex Police, Active Essex, Phoenix Futures,  Bar ‘n’ Bus, Sanctuary Housing, the council's Housing Options Domestic Abuse Service and Community Safety Team, as well as other local organisations working to support vulnerable residents.
Councillor Jo McPherson, Chair of Rochford District Council’s Community and Housing Committee, said: "Our neighbours, friends and families are at the heart of why this work matters. Everyone should feel safe in their everyday lives and confident that they will be listened to when they need help. Violence against women and girls has a devastating impact on individuals, families and communities. By launching the Women's Safety Charter, Rochford District Council is demonstrating its commitment to creating safer spaces, supporting those affected and working with partners to challenge the behaviours that contribute to violence and abuse.
"The 16 Days of Activism campaign is an important opportunity to raise awareness of these issues and highlight the support available locally. I encourage residents to come along to our events, meet the organisations involved and learn more about the Women's Safety Charter. We all have a part to play in creating a district where everyone feels safe, respected and supported, and I want anyone affected by violence or abuse to know that they are not alone and that help is available."
Residents are welcome to attend any of the events and speak directly with partner organisations about the support and advice available.
To find out more about the Women's Safety Charter or how your organisation can join, visit www.rochford.gov.uk/womens-safety-charter .

Data and Insights

Wed, 18/11/2026 - 11:53
Data and Insights provides access to the evidence we use to understand our places, communities and services and support informed decision-making. It brings together local and national data, council information, research, consultation and resident insight, interactive dashboards and other sources of evidence in one place.
Community Insight Dashboard
The Community Insight Dashboard brings together key data and insight about Brentwood and Rochford, helping the Council to better understand our places, communities and residents.
The dashboard draws on a range of external data sources, including ONS, health and Essex-wide data, to provide an accessible picture of our local areas. It can be used to:
explore demographic, social, economic and community characteristics;
understand how our communities are changing;
compare Brentwood and Rochford with other areas;
identify trends, inequalities and emerging issues; and
support evidence-based policy development, service planning and decision-making.
Consultation and Resident Insight
Data tells us part of the story. Understanding the views, experiences and priorities of our residents, businesses and communities provides important insight too. Through Engage With Us , you can take part in current consultations and engagement activities, find out what we have heard and see how feedback is helping to inform council decisions, services and priorities.

https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Women's Safety Charter
https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Women's Safety Charter
danielle.ward
Wed, 11/11/2026 - 16:06
Foreword from Councillor Jo McPherson (Chair of Community and Housing at Rochford District Council)
Everyone has the right to feel safe, respected and welcome in the places where they work, visit and spend time. As Chair of Community and Housing, I’m proud to support Rochford District’s Women’s Safety Charter and the shared commitment it represents.
Local businesses and organisations play a vital role in creating safer communities. By signing the Charter, you’re helping to make women’s safety a clear priority: challenging unacceptable behaviour, ensuring people know where to seek support, and creating spaces where concerns can be raised with confidence.
This toolkit offers practical guidance to help turn that commitment into action. It recognises that every organisation is different, while setting out meaningful steps that all businesses can take — from appointing a Women’s Safety Champion and training staff, to improving communication, reporting arrangements and the physical environment.
Creating lasting change takes collective effort. I encourage every business to use this toolkit, share its messages with staff and customers, and help build a Rochford District where women and girls feel safe, valued and able to thrive.
Working Together to Improve Women's Safety Across Rochford District
The Rochford District Women's Safety Charter is a community-led initiative that aims to create a network of Safe Spaces across the district while promoting positive cultural and behavioural change to improve women's safety. The Charter has been developed following local research and engagement with women and girls to better understand the experiences, behaviours and environments that can contribute to feelings of vulnerability in public spaces.
By joining the Charter, businesses and organisations can play an active role in creating a safer, more welcoming and inclusive district for women and girls.
Why Join the Women's Safety Charter?
Women and girls have told us that they want to see more Safe Places and Spaces, as well as positive changes in behaviour that help them feel safer when working, shopping, socialising and travelling throughout the district. The Women's Safety Charter works with local businesses and organisations to help deliver these changes.
Becoming a Charter member allows your organisation to:
Demonstrate a visible commitment to women's safety.
Support a district-wide initiative aimed at creating safer communities.
Help customers, visitors and employees feel welcomed and supported.
Promote a culture of respect, inclusion and accountability.
Be recognised as a business that actively supports community wellbeing
The Women's Safety Charter Pledges
Businesses and organisations signing up to the Charter are asked to commit to the following pledges:
You Will:
Allocate a nominated Charter Leader
Train all staff members to become “custodians of culture”
Clearly display campaign sticker and pledge to identify as a ‘safe space’
Clearly display media which sets expectations of behaviour, both physically and online
Signpost people who require support to the best source of help
Consider making changes to physical space to promote safety
Join the Women's Safety Charter
We are inviting businesses, organisations and community groups across Rochford District to become part of the Women's Safety Charter.
By signing the Charter, your organisation is making a public commitment to participate in the Women's Safety Charter programme, undertake the associated training, and work towards becoming a recognised Safe Space for women and girls. Charter members commit to promoting positive behaviours, supporting those who may feel vulnerable or unsafe, and helping to create safer, more welcoming spaces across Rochford District.
Sign Up
To join the Women's Safety Charter, please complete our online registration form:
Rochford Women's Safety Charter Application Form – Fill in form

https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Household Energy Payment
https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Household Energy Payment
charles.thomas
Wed, 11/11/2026 - 14:30
The Household Energy Payment is a one-off £100 payment to help eligible households in Council Tax bands A to D with their energy bills.
The government announced the payment in the Autumn Budget on 28 October 2026. We will start making payments from January 2027.
Who can get the £100 payment?
The payment is for eligible households living in a property in Council Tax bands A to D as their main home.
You can check your Council Tax band on GOV.UK or find it on your Council Tax bill.
We will publish the full eligibility criteria once we receive government guidance.
When will I receive the payment?
We will start making payments from January 2027. We will update this page when we can confirm payment dates.
Do I need to apply?
If you pay Council Tax by Direct Debit
If you are eligible and pay Council Tax by Direct Debit, we will pay the £100 directly into your bank account. You do not need to contact us or apply.
You can set up a Direct Debit online or call us on 01702 546366.
If you do not pay Council Tax by Direct Debit
You will need to apply for the payment. We will explain how to apply on this page once we receive government guidance. The quickest way to receive your payment is to set up a direct debit now, which you can do online or over the phone by calling 01702 546366.
Will there be any additional support available?
The government has provided funding for a discretionary support scheme which councils can use to help households most in need. We will publish eligibility criteria and application details once local arrangements have been agreed.
How can I avoid scams?
Only the council should contact you about claiming a Household Energy Payment.
Only share personal or bank details if you are sure you are dealing with us. If you are unsure whether a message is genuine, call us on 01702 546366 before sharing your details.

https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Temporary Change to Green Waste Collections, Commencing Monday 23 November 2026
https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Temporary Change to Green Waste Collections, Commencing Monday 23 November 2026
charles.thomas
Fri, 06/11/2026 - 12:27
Rochford District Council has agreed to launch a winter pilot scheme that will see garden waste collections move to a fortnightly schedule during the months when residents typically produce less garden waste. The decision was approved by the Environment Committee on Thursday 1 October.
The Council's waste collection service is facing increasing demands, with longer journeys to disposal sites, a growing number of homes across the district and rising operational costs placing greater pressure on existing resources.
To help address these challenges, councillors have agreed a pilot that will test whether fortnightly garden waste collections, alongside improvements to collection routes, can help the service operate more efficiently and provide a better value, while continuing to provide a reliable service for residents.
The pilot is intended to help the Council understand how the service could be delivered sustainably in the future. The findings will be used to inform future discussions about waste collection services across the district.
Residents will also have the opportunity to share their views through a district-wide consultation, which will take place as part of the pilot. Feedback from the consultation, alongside the results of the trial, will be considered by councillors before any decisions are made about the future of the service.
The results of the pilot and the feedback received through the consultation will be reported back to councillors before any consideration is given to making changes to the garden waste collection service permanent.
Q&As
1. What is Rochford District Council proposing?
The Council has approved a pilot scheme to change garden waste collections from weekly to fortnightly during the winter period which will be followed by a consultation with residents about possible permanent changes to the frequency of the service in the future.
2. Why is the Council considering this change?
Since the introduction of separate food waste collections, the weekly tonnage collected through the ‘green bin’ service has reduced significantly.
During the two years before separate food waste collections were introduced, approximately 7,000 tonnes were collected through the ‘green bin’ service between November and July. In the equivalent period following the change, tonnage fell to approximately 3,000 tonnes.
Of the 15 Councils in Greater Essex only Rochford offer a weekly collection service, all other Councils provide a fortnightly garden waste collection service .
Rochford are currently providing a free weekly garden waste service at an estimated annual cost of approximately £980,000 to the local Taxpayer.
Demand for the garden waste service in the months – October to March – is considerably less than throughout the spring and summer growing season.
Peak demand for the service is throughout the summer months, peaking generally in May, and then dropping off to a trough in February. The lower demand for the service in the 25/26 year as opposed to the two previous years reflects the introduction of the separate food collection service.
The waste collection service is facing increasing pressure from:
Longer journeys to waste disposal sites.
A growing number of homes across the district.
Rising operational costs.
The pilot will test whether fortnightly collections and improved collection routes can help the service operate more efficiently and affordably.
3. When will fortnightly collections start?
The change will start on 23 November 2026. Residents should check the website for updates or sign up for the council's online newsletter https://www.rochford.gov.uk/winter-garden-waste-pilot-approved-as-council-reviews-future-service
4. Is this a permanent change?
No. The approved pilot is intended to run for approximately four months and will cease on 29 March 2027. After this time, the normal service will resume. Y

https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.title: Rochford District Council calls for swift Government decision on Local Plan
https://www.rochford.gov.uk/rss.xml.text:
Rochford District Council calls for swift Government decision on Local Plan
AnnaB
Date
06 November 2026
Date
06 November 2026
Statement from Cllr Adi Malviya, Leader of Rochford District Council
Rochford needs an up-to-date Local Plan. Without one, the district is more exposed to speculative planning applications for development in the wrong places, without the infrastructure our communities need. Getting a plan in place is the best way to protect what makes Rochford special and to make sure new homes come with the transport systems, schools and services to support them.
We are committed to submitting our Local Plan to the Government by the deadline it has set. It was already a tight timeline to get it done by 31 December, and we requested a two-month extension to give councillors more time to read and understand the evidence, but we were on track. Since 2 October, the plan has been subject to a holding direction by the Government, meaning we cannot begin the final round of public consultation until that restriction is lifted.
We provided the evidence the Government requested in its holding direction on 7 October and trust that it is currently being reviewed.
To meet the deadline, we needed a decision by 5 November at the latest. That would have provided two weeks to prepare for the consultation - including making any necessary changes, printing materials, booking venues for consultation sessions, and organising publicity - and six weeks for residents and other consultees to have their say.
People's views matter and the plan must stand up to scrutiny. I want to be open with residents about what this delayed timetable means. Even if the Government lifts the holding direction today, to meet the current deadline the consultation would need to run over Christmas, which is far from ideal. If that happens, we will do everything we can to make it easy for people to take part during a busy time of year.
It also means the consultation would close on the same day the plan must be submitted, leaving no time for councillors to discuss the responses before submission. Every comment will still be passed to the Independent Planning Inspector, who will consider them as part of the examination.
The Government has said that there may be an opportunity to extend the deadline until March. Given that we are now so close to the wire due to the holding direction, I hope that this deadline extension will be offered when the Government does respond to the evidence we have submitted. I call upon the Government to do right by Rochford residents and provide enough time for meaningful consultation. We remain ready to move as soon as the holding direction is lifted. We will keep local people updated at every stage.
