https://www.activeessex.org/feed/.title: Nominees and distinguished guests come together to celebrate success at the Essex Activity Awards!
https://www.activeessex.org/feed/.text:
The annual Essex Activity Awards took place on Thursday 4 th December, at Hatfield Place, bringing together over 150 shortlisted nominees and invited guests to celebrate the remarkable achievements in physical activity, sport, and wellbeing across the county.
Organised by Active Essex, the annual event highlights and recognises the outstanding contributions made by individuals, communities, schools, clubs, and workplaces that inspire and promote the importance of physical activity and movement in Greater Essex.
Hosted by ITV News Presenter Charlie Frost and Paralympic Gold Medallist Danny Crates, the evening saw awards given out across several categories. While some winners were chosen by a private panel of judges, others were decided through a public vote and the Young Sports Personality of the Year award by a selection of the Active Essex #MoveWithUs Ambassadors, ensuring the community’s voice was heard.
Michelle Agyemang, who helped the Lionesses to an inspirational Euro’s title in July, was crowned Essex Sports Personality of the Year. Unable to attend the evening, in a video sent in for the evening, Michelle explained; “ It’s a great privilege to receive this award, especially as somebody that has lived in Essex all of my life. I’m grateful to God for this opportunity, and thankful to all my friends, family and teammates, this couldn’t have been done without them.”
The Unsung Hero award voted for by the public, went to Lee Clark who was recognised for his significant efforts for charity. Despite managing work, family and personal health challenges, Lee runs a mental health walking group, a litter-picking team and a charity football club. Known for the creativity of his approach, Lee gives every spare moment to helping others and to date has raised nearly £500,000 for over 70 charities.
The Inspiring Young Lives award, a new category for this year was awarded to Rosedan Breakfast and After School Club. A vibrant and multicultural club that offers inclusive daily activities, summer programmes, all delivered by nurturing staff. Rosedan helps young people build confidence, creativity and friendships, all whilst encouraging healthy and active lifestyles.
Other categories that celebrated individuals during the ceremony included Young Sports Personality of the Year, awarded to Arsenals Max Dowman, and Move With Us Champion, another new category for this year, acknowledged young people aiming to inspire those around them. The coveted Find Your Active Wellbeing award, given out as part of the Find Your Active: Move for your Mind campaign, went to Sarah Clyne who uses physical activity as a tool to improve residents mental health.
The evening also recognised groups of people striving to make a difference, with awards like Sports Club of the Year and Active Employer of the Year. The Active Education Provider of the Year shined a spotlight on an education setting prioritising sport and physical activity in its setting, with TreeTops Free School coming out as winners.
Active Essex Chair Dr William Bird MBE said: “The Essex Activity Awards shine a spotlight on the incredible energy and commitment that drives physical activity across our county. From grassroots groups to elite performers, and from schools to parks and workplaces, these awards celebrate the people and teams who work tirelessly to create opportunities for everyone. Whether it’s inspiring someone to take their first step into finding their active or coaching the stars of tomorrow, this event recognises those who make movement accessible, enjoyable, and life-changing for our communities.”

https://www.activeessex.org/feed/.title: £9.8 million secured to build stronger Essex communities and tackle inactivity
https://www.activeessex.org/feed/.text:
Significant investment from Sport England will transform lives through the power of sport and physical activity.
Almost £10 million funding has been secured to strengthen communities and tackle inequality in activity levels across Greater Essex. The investment, from Sport England, secured by Active Essex, will support the Place Partnership programme.
The Sport England funding will see £250 million of National Lottery and Exchequer funding invested in more than 90 new places across England until 2028.
The Place Partnership programme aims to:
increase physical activity
decrease physical inactivity
provide positive experiences of physical activity for children and young people
tackle inequalities in local communities
The latest investment into Greater Essex will see Castle Point, Harlow and Thurrock benefit.  Basildon, Colchester and Tendring have also received further funding support, following the work achieved through the Essex Local Delivery Pilot.
Aiming to break down the everyday barriers that prevent people from moving more and living well, this opportunity will focus on areas that need support the most, helping make physical activity a daily reality for everyone, regardless of their postcode or income.
Lisa Dodd-Mayne, Executive Director of Place at Sport England, said:
“Our recent investment into Essex reflects our continued commitment to ensure that interventions are rooted in the unique needs, cultures and priorities of local communities. Targeted investment in areas of greatest need can unlock participation and reduce health inequalities. The 3 new places in Essex, and the 3 already well on the journey, will be shining examples of how these types of approaches can drive real change locally to help create a more active, healthier nation.”
Opportunities will be co-designed with communities, in response to their specific needs. Local organisations and projects will be supported to deliver initiatives that help build capacity across the system, creating meaningful and lasting impact.
Councillor Louise McKinlay, Deputy Leader of Essex County Council and Cabinet Member for Communities, Economic Growth and Prosperity, said :
“Sport is incredibly powerful. It can literally change lives. I am very proud of the work that has been done with the Greater Essex Partnership over the past few years to support people to fulfil their potential and all through sport and being active.
“This additional funding will really help to drive the efforts of Active Essex. We know healthier people are happier people and working with our incredible local partners across the county, it will really make a difference to so many lives.”
As one of 43 Active Partnerships, which started as a legacy of the London 2012 Olympic Games, Active Essex are pioneers in place-based working. This has been expanded through the work of the Essex Local Delivery Pilot (LDP), which began in 2017.
Dr William Bird, Chair of Active Essex said:
“The success of the LDP has meant that Essex has received further funding to support three new areas. What we’ve learnt alongside our partners, is that we must create the conditions for our communities to thrive, and I have no doubt that this further investment will be capitalised on by all places in Greater Essex. Utilising learnings across the system from health and education to transport and recreation, we all have the ability to co-create physical activity opportunities for everyone.”
Across the six Place Partnerships, work has already taken place on identifying local needs. This has seen opportunities such as Essex Pedal Power, The Gunny Project on Canvey, and Rose Villa Surgery Community Garden in Basildon develop.
Find out more about Place Partnerships here: https://www.activeessex.org/place-partnerships/

https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.title: Peter Furley Obituary & Funeral Arrangements
https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.text:
Peter died peacefully at home on 13th October aged 88, with his daughter Jo and son Jon at
his side. He joined Southend Rugby club in 1955 when the home pitch was situated on the
slope in Priory Park, he also joined the Municipal College Cricket Club’s second eleven the
same year.
He originally played Flyhalf for a lower team at age 18 with his brother Michael, but
graduated to the Priors aged 24 where he played with Terry North. Aged 37 in 1974 he
became Captain of the ExA1: 4th Team. When he reached an age that he was too old to
actually play the game, aged 44 he moved on to being a referee which he did until the age of
75 and alongside that he was also a 4th official for the 1st team, he ended his active
involvement at the age of 77 and then became an avid supporter of the 1st team. He would
travel to home and away games when he could and in later years his daughter joined him
too.
He worked as an architect in London for his whole career and was very involved in the
clubhouse and later the stand design too.
His brother Roger Furley remembers one famous occasion when Roger was umpiring a
hockey game on the Old Southendian’s astro pitch, Peter was refereeing a game on the
rugby pitch on the other side of the fence and their other brother, Michael, was doing the
Priors game on the main pitch. Roger’s friend commented at the time, that the Furleys were
succeeding in ruining 84 peoples afternoon at the same time!
He had a very long and happy life for 88 years and it was only his body that gave out on him
in the end, his mind was as sharp as always even in his last hour. He will be missed dearly
by all his family and friends.
His funeral will take place at Southend Crematorium at 1pm on Friday 6th November 2026 followed by a wake at the club.
Please find below the link to the tribute page for dad, the page also contains the link for the live stream for those that cannot attend and also the address for the crematorium and details of the charity that we have chosen.
https://peterfurley.muchloved.com  “

https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.title: Ken Baynes
https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.text:
Over three hundred people attended Kens Funeral on Friday 2nd October. They included past and present members of our club as well as members of Rochford Hundred Golf club and friends and collogues from the business world and beyond. The wake at the club after was bursting at the seams.
Kenneth 'Ken' Baynes
13 August 1961 – 13 September 2026
Kenneth Baynes died peacefully on 13 September 2026, aged 65, surrounded by his family, after living with myeloma. A devoted husband to Davina and a hugely proud father to Robert and Hannah, he will be deeply missed by them and his many friends.
He was born in Cardiff, the youngest of four children, and grew up in Hitchin and Southend. He went to Westcliff High School and then Felsted, where he became Head of House and played in the school's unbeaten rugby and hockey teams. After a year in Munich, where he was named Player of the Year for Munich Rugby Club, he came home and joined Southend Rugby Club, turning down an opportunity to play first class representative rugby at London Scottish. He played for SRFC 1st XV for over three decades, and kept going until he was 51.
He worked for Barclays for 33 years, 28 of them in the dealing room trading the sterling money markets, and was highly respected in the City. Alongside his career he took on charity treks along the Great Wall of China, in the Himalayas and in Brazil, raising hundreds of thousands of pounds for The Children's Society.
He retired in 2013 and immediately sailed across the Atlantic with Charles. He then set himself new goals, becoming a single-figure golfer and a fully qualified Level 3 international ski instructor, and he loved nothing more than skiing with his family. He became Treasurer and Co-Chairman of Southend Rugby Club and was made a Life Member in 2024. He was also a proud member of Rochford Hundred Golf Club for over 20 years and was honoured to be appointed RHGC Club Captain for 2026.
Competitive, funny, generous and fiercely determined, Ken faced his illness with the same spirit he brought to everything else. In his own words: "I would rather die on my feet than live on my knees."
FUNERAL
Friday 2 October 2026, 3pm
Southend Crematorium - 285 Sutton Road, Southend-on-Sea, SS2 5PX
WAKE
Southend Rugby Club, from after the service until late
(Warners Bridge Park, Sumpters Way, Southend-on-Sea SS2 5RE)
FLOWERS/DONATIONS
No flowers, please. Ken was passionate about supporting Myeloma UK to help find a cure, and the family warmly asks that you donate to the charity in his memory.
DRESS CODE
Traditional funeral wear, with club ties for members of RHGC and SRFC

https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.title: Saxons Ready For The Challenge Ahead
https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.text:
With pre-season complete and the opening league weekend finally upon us, there is a real sense of excitement and anticipation around the Southend Rugby Club senior playing group.
The summer has brought plenty of change. We have said goodbye to some experienced players who have contributed enormously to the group, but in their place we have welcomed a number of exciting new faces.
Some arrive with valuable experience from higher levels of the game, while others represent something equally important to us — talented young players who have progressed through our own junior and academy pathway and are now ready to take their opportunities in senior rugby.
With so many new faces coming together, one of the biggest challenges throughout pre-season was always going to be how quickly we could bond as a group.
In that respect, the extended pre-season has actually worked in our favour. It has given the players more time together, both on and off the pitch, and the response has been fantastic.
Throughout the summer, the group has continually pushed and challenged one another. There has been a real desire to improve, compete and strive for excellence, with standards being driven by the players themselves as much as by the coaching team.
Now, on the eve of the first league weekend for both the Saxons and Priors , you can feel the excitement levels rising.
Pre-season is done. Now the real challenge begins.
There is plenty of potential within this group, but potential alone means very little. What has been particularly encouraging is seeing the belief, trust and understanding between the players continuing to grow.
We also know that no season is straightforward.
There will be difficult Saturdays. There will be moments when things don’t go our way and occasions when this group will have to go to the well for one another , dig deep and show exactly what it stands for.
From everything we have seen throughout pre-season, there is every reason to believe that this is a group that will keep fighting, keep working and keep pushing for each other.
As we head into the new campaign, the focus isn’t on making big predictions or looking too far ahead. It is much simpler than that.
Be better each week.
Keep learning. Keep challenging each other. Keep raising our standards and take something from every performance — whether that comes from a win or a loss.
There is a long season ahead and plenty of rugby still to be played, but there is a genuine sense of excitement about what this group could achieve together.
Now it’s time to get started.
One Club. One Direction.

Southend Rugby Football Club Announces Paul Robinson Solicitors as Main Club and Shirt Sponsor
Southend Rugby Football Club is delighted to announce the continuation with a two-year partnership with Paul Robinson Solicitors, who are once again the club's Main Club and Shirt Sponsor for the next two seasons.
The partnership marks a significant milestone for both organisations, bringing together one of Essex's most established rugby clubs with a leading law firm. The sponsorship will see the Paul Robinson Solicitors logo proudly displayed on the front of Southend RFC's playing shirts across the first XV section, while supporting the continued growth and development of rugby at every level of the club.
The agreement represents a shared commitment to community, excellence and long-term investment in local sport.
Speaking on behalf of Southend RFC,  Club Marketing Director, Nathan Strange:
"We are absolutely thrilled to once again announce Paul Robinson Solicitors as our main club and shirt sponsor. Their support is a fantastic endorsement of the direction our club is heading, both on and off the field. This partnership will play an important role in helping us continue to invest in our players, facilities and community programmes over the coming seasons. We look forward to continue building a strong and lasting relationship.
Speaking on behalf of Paul Robinson Solicitors LLP,  Senior Marketing and Business Development Executive, Imogen Ward:
“We are looking forward to supporting the Club for the next two seasons and are excited to play a part in helping the club achieve its ambitions, both on the pitch and through the positive impact it has across the wider community. Having supported the Club for more than 15 years, we are proud of the strong relationship we have built and look forward to continuing our partnership for many years to come.”
As preparations continue for the new campaign, the club is excited to unveil its new playing kit featuring the Paul Robinson Solicitors branding and looks forward to celebrating the partnership with members, supporters and the wider community at the upcoming matches.
Everyone at Southend RFC would like to thank Paul Robinson Solicitors for their confidence and support and warmly welcomes them once again into the Southend Rugby family.

Havens Hospices cared for Matt's dad over 10 years ago and, more recently, supported his mum with compassion, dignity, and kindness.
They also cared for Kev's mum in her final days, ensuring she was comfortable and surrounded by the very best care.
The care and support their families received will never be forgotten, and this challenge is Matt and Kev's way of giving something back to a charity that has meant so much to them both.
The trek to Everest Base Camp will test them physically and mentally, but they are taking on every step with the hope of raising vital funds so Havens Hospices can continue providing outstanding care to other families when they need it most.
Every donation, no matter how big or small, will make a real difference.
Thank you for supporting Matt and Kev on this journey and for helping Havens Hospices continue the incredible work they do.

https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.title: Welcome From The Director Of Rugby
https://www.southendrugby.com/news?forma.text:
Director of Rugby Welcome
A very warm welcome to Warners Bridge, the home of Southend Rugby Club.
Having been a player here for over ten years and Head Coach for the previous eight, I am incredibly proud and honoured to be appointed Director of Rugby at this fantastic club. Southend RFC has been a huge part of my life and is built on strong values, passionate people and a proud rugby tradition. It is a privilege to lead the next chapter of our journey together.
My vision is simple: One Club. One Direction.
We will continue to build a culture where standards drive performance and performance drives success. I am excited to continue the work that Josh, myself, our coaching staff, players, volunteers and management have worked so hard to establish over many years. We have built strong foundations, but there is still much more to achieve. The challenges ahead are exciting, and I look forward to seeing what this talented group of players can accomplish together.
The work starts now.
Reflecting on Last Season
The 2025/26 season was one of highs and lows but ultimately the club's most successful campaign in recent years. Our Saxons finished 4th in Regional 1, producing some outstanding performances both home and away throughout the season.
The upcoming Regional 1 campaign promises to be even more competitive. New grounds await, fresh challenges lie ahead and the return of Eton Manor will reignite a healthy rivalry that many of us have enjoyed over the years. With a young, talented squad strengthened by some exciting additions, we are looking forward to seeing how far this group can go by playing ambitious, intelligent rugby.
Our Priors finished 9th in Counties 1 Hertfordshire. While the league position only tells part of the story, the squad once again proved its importance within our rugby programme by preparing players for senior rugby. Several players stepped up to make their Saxons debuts, highlighting the strength of the development pathway we continue to build.
We're also delighted that the Priors have now returned to the Essex league structure and will compete in Essex Counties 1 this season. This is something the club has worked towards for a long time and provides an even stronger platform for player development and progression.
Developing Home-Grown Talent
One of the areas I am most proud of is the continued development of our own players.
This season has once again shown that our academy pathway is thriving. Academy players have progressed into the Priors, first-year seniors have earned Saxons debuts and several Colts have represented both the Cardinals and Bishops. These achievements are a credit to our coaching staff, the commitment of our players and the pathway we have created throughout the club.
Our ambition is simple: to provide every player with a clear route through the club, giving them the opportunity to fulfil their potential and one day represent the Saxons.
What Success Looks Like
Success isn't measured solely by league tables.
Of course we all want to win rugby matches, but true success will also be measured by the environment we create, the players we develop, the standards we uphold and the pride people feel when pulling on a Southend shirt.
We want our players to enjoy their rugby, our supporters to feel connected to the club and everyone involved to contribute to a culture that people are proud to be part of.
The People Behind the Programme
No rugby club succeeds without the people working tirelessly behind the scenes, often without recognition.
Tracey Gilson is quite simply the backbone of our playing group and affectionately known as the club's "mum". Whether she's preparing food after training and on match days for our players and visiting teams, or feeding the hundreds of Mini and Youth players, parents and supporters who come through our doors each weekend, her dedication and care never go unnoticed.
Donna Munroe and her team behind the bar are equally integral to the club, providing a warm welcome

What does it actually mean for an event to feel festive?
Beyond the Christmas jumpers, how do we create that elusive feeling of being in the Christmas spirit? We all recognise the atmosphere of Christmas when we experience it, but translating that feeling into something we can deliberately create is a different challenge altogether.
Few occasions demonstrate the relationship between atmosphere, space and experience quite like Christmas. From the music playing in the background to the little details that transform a room, it’s often the smallest touches that make an occasion feel special.
At Firstsite, creating that atmosphere starts with understanding the vision behind each event. Whether a facilitator wants to introduce a little festive magic or create something entirely their own, our approach is to listen and help bring their ideas to life.

https://firstsite.uk/feed/.text:
The Firstsite Collectors’ Group Bursary Awards scheme aims to support artists working in Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk and Cambridgeshire with their professional career development. These annual awards are made possible through the  Collectors’ Group continuing engagement and interest in contemporary visual art in the region.
Applications to the Bursary Awards scheme should demonstrate ambition, and a commitment to, or development of the applicant’s current artistic practice.
Proposals can be made to contribute towards the costs of making new artwork, purchase of equipment, research and travel, exhibition making and other forms of professional development.
To register, please fill out the form: Firstsite Collectors’ Group Bursary Awards 2026 Application Form and send it to opportunities@firstsite.uk .
In 2025, 12 winners across East Anglia were awarded £5,000 between them.
Criteria:
Firstsite Collectors’ Group Bursary Awards are open to individuals only.
Applicants must be based in Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk or Cambridgeshire.
The Collectors’ Group will consider applications for between £100 and £1,000.
Applications should be made using the Collectors’ Group Bursary Awards application form and emailing it back to opportunities@firstsite.uk .
Applications can be made as a word document or exported pdf, via a picture collage, a 5 minute (or less) raw video or audio files in response to the questions in the application form, and sent to opportunities@firstsite.uk .
The closing date for applications is 5pm, 22 November 2026. Applications received after this time will not be considered.
We are unlikely to fund a similar project that was previously awarded a bursary by the same artist in two consecutive years.
We do not fund the displaying of artwork (for example, framing, fabrication, display cases), unless it is inherent to the production of the artwork itself.
We do not fund documentaries or news-based films.
We do not fund photography intended to document the installation of shows and/or artwork, or for the purposes of portfolio development
We do not fund travel for overseas work.
If you have any questions, please get in touch at fundraising@firstsite.uk and we’ll be happy to help.
Please note due to the high number and calibre of applications we receive, applicants will be informed of the panel’s decision in January 2027.

https://firstsite.uk/feed/.title: In Conversation with Your Work: Preparing for a Portfolio Review with Larain Briggs
https://firstsite.uk/feed/.text:
How do you prepare for a portfolio review, and what can you gain from the experience?
Artist and researcher Larain Briggs shares practical guidance on selecting and presenting work, reflecting on process, and approaching review as a space for dialogue and discovery.
Briggs is a multidisciplinary artist and Doctorate in Fine Art researcher whose practice explores transformation, symbolism, and psychological inquiry through creative practice.
Understanding the Portfolio Review Process
A portfolio review can be much more than an opportunity to present work.
It can provide a space to reflect on how work is selected, presented and understood, while testing ideas and identifying new directions within a developing practice. It can also help clarify the aims of a portfolio and what it is intended to communicate.
From this perspective, the review is not simply about receiving feedback; it is an opportunity for conversation, reflection and discovery.

https://firstsite.uk/feed/.title: Catching up with Rebecca Riess, artist behind her exhibition ‘Lossless’ at Firstsite
https://firstsite.uk/feed/.text:
With ‘Lossless’ entering its final days, we spoke with multimedia artist Rebecca Riess – winner of the Firstsite Collectors’ Group Bursary Award 2025 and the artist behind the exhibition – about the thinking, making, and instinct behind the show – and how you give shape to what can’t always be seen.
The exhibition invites us to explore how we cope with the noise of the modern world through a bold and immersive series of otherworldly large-scale sculptures and installations.
Her work reflects our emotional responses to the world around us – from the overload of digital life and technological waste, the growing ecological crisis, abuse of power, and the physical and emotional ways we experience these pressures internally.
Rather than offering fixed meanings, Rebecca leaves space for interpretation, curiosity, and instinct – whether that’s reading a shape as a beak, noticing a shadow, or simply being drawn to a colour.

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: A Growing Family: Baby Chimp Born
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
A New Arrival For Our Growing Chimp Family.
In the early hours of Tuesday 3 rd November 2026, the Animal Care Team were delighted to discover female chimpanzee, Tara had given birth to a healthy baby.
We are especially excited as this is our second Chimpanzee birth of the year, following the arrival of Kiera in January. The two youngsters share a special family connection, as they are both grandchildren of the late Billy Jo, mum of Tara and Kora, and it is lovely to see another generation of her family continuing to grow here at the zoo. Kiera is, of course, very curious about the new arrival, and it is wonderful to see how well the group are getting along together.
Our Animal Care Team are keeping a close eye on mum, dad, and their new arrival, as they spend these precious early days bonding together. They are pleased to report that mum, baby and Dad Napoleon are all doing really well.
Chimpanzees are currently listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species , facing a number of threats out in the wild, from habitat loss to deforestation as well as hunting, making this birth especially important for the conservation and future of this species.
We know that visitors will be excited to catch a glimpse of our newest arrival, but we do kindly ask that all visitors keep noise to a minimum when visiting Chimpanzee Lookout to allow our new family time and space to settle.
Please keep an eye on our website and social media channels for the latest updates.

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: Advancing The Fight Against EEHV
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
Over the last decade, Colchester Zoological Society have supported pioneering research with the EAZA Elephant TAG EEHV Fund, donating £6,000 to help find and develop a cure for one of the biggest health threats facing young elephants – elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus (EEHV).
EEHV can cause severe and often fatal illness in elephants with a mortality rate of up to 80% once the infection takes hold. The acute haemorrhagic disease, EEHV-HD, sadly develops in one in every six young Asian elephants. There are also seven known species of the virus, as well as several subspecies, therefore it is imperative to understand the virus and how elephants respond to it, so that preventative measures can be taken, as well as developing treatment for those infected.
A Step in The Right Direction
The latest research shows huge advancements in the development of a vaccine, following a successful safety testing phase. A number of young Asian elephants across European zoos have since been vaccinated as part of ongoing research and nine have developed a clear antibody response against EEHV1A (a subspecies of the virus and the leading cause of most EEHV-HD infections).
The research team are now closely monitoring this group of elephants to understand how long the antibody response will last and crucially whether the vaccination provides immunity against EEHV-HD. Whilst there is still work to be done, the results represent an important milestone in the vital research to protect young elephants.
The Bigger Picture
The research has also highlighted the complexity of EEHV. There are several different subtypes capable of causing the disease, meaning that developing broader protection will be a significant part of future research. Alongside the vaccination programme scientists are investigating potential treatments for elephants that become infected, as well as exploring how antibodies from adult elephants could be used as a preventative measure against the virus. Each discovery brings scientists one step closer to understanding this devastating disease and finding better ways to protect elephants and prevent further loss.
One small step for elephants, one giant leap for conservation.
By donating to CZS, you can help us continue supporting vital projects just like this one. Donate today at www.colchesterzoologicalsociety.com/support-us/donate/

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: CZS & University of Suffolk Launch Zoo Degree
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
The University of Suffolk, in collaboration with Colchester Zoological Society (CZS), is launching a new course that will support students looking for a career in conservation and zoo management.
The BSc (Hons) Zoo Science and Management will launch in September 2027 and will combine academic learning with real-world experience. Students will work closely with the team at CZS, one of the UK’s leading conservation zoos, while developing the skills, knowledge and confidence needed to thrive in a rapidly changing sector.
Modern zoos play a critical role in wildlife conservation, scientific research and education and the new course will explore all of these areas as well as management and leadership, visitor engagement and animal behaviour. Students will also learn about the role that technology and research plays in zoos, conservation and the wider sector.
The course will be delivered in partnership with the team at CZS, with students spending approximately half their time on campus in Ipswich and the other half on site at Colchester Zoological Society.
In addition, students will have access to optional field trips, including visits to a number of UK zoos and wildlife parks to develop their knowledge and build their professional networks. In the final year, students will have the option of choosing to join a residential trip to the Umphafa Nature Reserve in South Africa which is managed by the Colchester Zoological Society.
The University of Suffolk already runs a successful Wildlife, Ecology and Conservation course and students on both courses will have the opportunity to work together to explore a broad range of topics.
Through the course, students will have access to work placements, allowing them to develop and enhance their practical experience and support their career journey.
Dr Christopher Turner, Head of Life Sciences at the University of Suffolk commented:
“This exciting new course has been developed to meet the demands of working in the zoo sector covering topics from management, tourism and education to research, conservation and animal management. Our innovative partnership with the Colchester Zoological Society will provide a unique learning experience with students spending equal time on academic learning and practical experiences, creating a solid foundation for their future career.”
Andy Moore, Director of Science, Education and Training, Colchester Zoological Society said:
“The zoo sector is changing rapidly. Today’s zoo professionals need a broad range of skills, from animal welfare and conservation science to education, sustainability, and public engagement. This degree has been designed with the future in mind, ensuring graduates are equipped to contribute meaningfully to modern zoological organisations and conservation efforts around the world. This partnership also reflects our commitment to serving our community. As a charitable organisation, we are passionate about creating opportunities for learning, skills development and career progression. By working with the University of Suffolk, we are providing a new route for local people to access higher education and gain real-world experience within a leading conservation zoo.”
Staff at Colchester Zoological Society and other wildlife organisations will be able to access a selection of modules on the BSc (Hons) Zoo Science and Management course as part of a professional CPD programme.
Find out more about studying at The University of Suffolk by visiting: www.uos.ac.uk

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: Love Not Lost: The Story of Ebby and Peru
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
Ebby and Peru have both experienced the loss of a partner but today they have found companionship in one another.
Ebby, 19, arrived from Germany in 2007 as a juvenile. Over the years, she formed close bonds with several partners, including her most recent partner Mako, until his passing this year. She is one of the easiest penguins to spot, thanks to the large black splotch on her tummy. Peru, 13, joined us from the Czech Republic in 2014, also as a juvenile. He had previously shared his life with Tequila, who sadly passed away this year.
For Humboldt Penguins these relationships can be particularly important. They are known for forming strong, long-lasting bonds and often remain with the same partner for many years. However, when a partner dies or does not return, they can go on to form a new pairing.
What started as a companionship has since developed into something more. They have now formed strong bonds, and the pair are rarely seen apart. They enjoy spending time together in their favourite spot amongst the bamboo or cosying up in their nest box.
For visitors, Ebby and Peru offer a chance to see these relationships developing first hand. Look closely when visiting the Inca Trail and you may notice the pair tucked away together, exploring their surroundings or simply sitting side by side.
These days, wherever you find Ebby, there’s a good chance that Peru is close by.
The post Love Not Lost: The Story of Ebby and Peru appeared first on Colchester Zoological Society .

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: Making a Splash: Californian Sea Lions Arrive at CZS!
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
We are incredibly excited to announce the arrival of an entirely new species here at Colchester Zoological Society – Californian Sea lions!
After months of planning and preparation, we are delighted to welcome Sofia and her four-year-old daughter Cali, who have joined us from Welsh Mountain Zoo and are now settling into their new home at CZS.
Their arrival marks an exciting new chapter as we introduce a brand-new species to our animal collection, and we are thrilled to be able to share this special moment with our visitors.
Meet Sofia and Cali
At 16 years old Sofia was born in Rotterdam Zoo and has resided at Welsh Mountain Zoo since 2012. Her daughter Cali, aged four was born at Welsh Mountain Zoo and the mother and daughter duo have now made the move to Colchester together.
Sofia and Cali have begun settling into their new surroundings and the Animal Care Team are excited to watch as their personalities develop over the coming weeks.
Californian Sea Lions are fascinating marine mammals, known for their intelligence, agility and inquisitive nature.  According to the IUCN Red List, Californian Sea Lions are currently classified as Least Concern, with populations increasing. Their arrival gives visitors the opportunity to learn more about a new species and see them for themselves at Sealion Shores here at CZS.
“We are so excited to have Sea Lions back at the zoo and to welcome Sofia and Cali to their new home. We are really looking forward to getting to know their individual personalities, building relationships with them, and discovering all the little things that make each of them unique. There is also a great anticipation around getting them back into training and creating new experiences with them. It will be a real pleasure to be a part of their journey and to share in all the memories they will make along the way.” – Kirsty Lawman, Team Leader of Sea Lion Section.
A new home for a new species!
Welcoming Sofia and Cali has also given us the opportunity to transform their new home. The habitat had been empty following the passing of our much-loved Patagonian Sea lions in March. Since then, our in-house staff have been working incredibly hard behind the scenes to revamp the area and make the relevant adaptions to accommodate our Californian Sea lions.
Come and meet our newest residents
With Sofia and Cali settling into their new home, visitors can once again enjoy seeing Sea lions in a much-loved area of the zoo. From watching them glide through the water to views from the underwater tunnel, there are plenty of opportunities to observe these fascinating animals as they explore their surroundings.
Why not come and see them for yourself?
Make sure to keep an eye on our social media channels and website for all the latest news and updates!
The post Making a Splash: Californian Sea Lions Arrive at CZS! appeared first on Colchester Zoological Society .

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: 200 Submissions, One Shared Goal
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
What if a small biological sample collected today could help wildlife decades from now?
Here at CZS, our commitment to conservation extends far beyond the present day, as we constantly look to the future to protect wildlife for generations to come. This year we have reached our 200 th submission of genetic samples to the RZSS WildGenes Biobank at Edinburgh Zoo, a major milestone in our ongoing commitment to conservation and wildlife research.
But this milestone is about much more than a number.
As the UK’s leading wildlife biobank, RZSS provides a long-term resource for scientific research by securely storing blood, tissues and other biological samples that can be used by researchers to better understand wildlife and help protect endangered species. This research also plays a vital role in monitoring and preserving genetic diversity across species, as well as helping to mitigate wildlife diseases.
With wildlife facing increasing pressures from habitat loss, disease, climate change and declining genetic diversity, having access to this biological material gives scientists a valuable resource for understanding changes in wildlife populations and exploring new ways to protect them.
For CZS, conservation takes many forms. Alongside caring for the animals at the Zoo, we are proud to support scientific research and collaborate on conservation initiatives that extend far beyond our gates.
Because protecting wildlife tomorrow starts with the work, we do today.
“We have now reached 200 submissions with Colchester Zoo providing our milestone submission. This year alone, they have contributed over 500 samples across multiple submissions playing a great role in proactive conservation. By sharing high-quality biological material from a wide range of species, institutions help us build a vital genetic resource” said Dr Cecilia Langhorne, senior biobank technician at RZSS.

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: Beneath The Surface: Advanced CT Technology comes to CZS!
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
What can you discover when you look beneath the surface?
On 27 th August, the Animal Care Team at CZS, had the opportunity to do exactly that, when Burgess Diagnostics brought their specialist mobile CT scanner to the Zoo. Several of the Zoo’s animals underwent CT scans to take a closer look at the health of some of the animals in our care. Ensuring the comfort and safety of our animals is our top priority and bringing the mobile CT unit directly to Colchester allowed us to achieve that goal.
A total of ten patients were scanned during the visit, including two aardvarks, a red panda and a sloth. The scans formed part of the teams ongoing care for the animals with certain health concerns, providing an opportunity to gather further information about their health that other diagnostics have not been able to. Scanning ten different patients across a range of species also meant that the team had to adapt their approach to each individual animal and having two vets from the International Zoo Veterinary Group (IZVG) working in tandem helped make this possible.
CT scanning allows vets to see highly detailed cross-sectional images of the body, providing information that cannot always be gained through routine veterinary examination. For animals, being able to identify what is happening beneath the surface can be particularly important.
Unlike human patients, animals are unable to communicate if something is wrong or if they are unwell. They are also adept at masking health concerns so the Animal Care team must solely rely on daily observations, body scoring, veterinary checks and advanced diagnostics to build a clearer picture.
Burgess Diagnostics’ visit also offered an insight into the specialist work that takes place behind the scenes at CZS. While visitors see the animals going about their daily lives, a dedicated Animal Care team and veterinary professionals are constantly monitoring their health and wellbeing.
“The CT scanning day was a huge success and very important for all the animals seen. It allows us to ensure the highest level of welfare is maintained and that our course of treatment for those animals is correct. It also allowed our team to experience the mobile imaging service to facilitate further visits in the future ” – Angela Matthews, Head Keeper
The visit from Burgess Diagnostics forms part of Colchester Zoological Society’s commitment to providing high standards of care, combining expert knowledge with modern technology to support the health and welfare of the animals in our care and contributing to wider species conservation programmes.

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: One Seed at a Time
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
This World Elephant Day we are shining the spotlight on our very own gentle giants  here at CZS.
Known for their impressive stature, iconic tusks and remarkable memories, elephants are amongst the world’s most extraordinary animals. But what many people don’t realise is that they also play a significant role in keeping ecosystems healthy. In the wild, elephants are nature’s gardeners, helping the grasslands and forests thrive through an incredible process called seed dispersal . Whilst travelling in the wild, elephants eat a wide variety of fruits. Many of the seeds they consume pass safely through their digestive system before being deposited in nutrient rich dung. This gives the seeds the perfect opportunity to germinate, helping new vegetation grow within the area.
Here at CZS, we have been lucky enough to witness this extraordinary process in action.
Earlier this year, our elephants enjoyed pumpkins as part of their enrichment. A few months later our keepers spotted something unexpected – pumpkin seedlings sprouting from the area their dung had been left behind. Fast forward to today and those tiny shoots have sprouted into the elephant’s very own pumpkin patch!
While our pumpkin patch may be a small example, it perfectly demonstrates the important role that elephants play in shaping ecosystems across Africa. Every seed they disperse has the potential to become food or shelter for countless other species.
At CZS, our commitment to conservation extends far beyond the zoo. Since 2010 we have provided support to the Elephant Orphanage Project in Zambia, aiming to protect and safeguard the future of wild elephant populations.
Whether it is growing a pumpkin patch or regenerating forests across Africa, elephants remind us that even the smallest seed can have the greatest impact. Why not pop along to CZS this summer! By visiting CZS, you are helping to support the conservation work that protects these remarkable animals for generations to come.
The post One Seed at a Time appeared first on Colchester Zoological Society .

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: A Flamboyant Arrival
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
All hands (and feathers) are on deck as we welcomed a sea of pink with 39 Chilean flamingos arriving from Auchingarrich Wildlife Park to join the Colchester Zoological Society family.
Since their arrival, the 39 birds have spent some time in quarantine before joining our current flock of 25 flamingos down at the lake. This is to allow our team to perform health checks on the birds to ensure that they can be mixed safely with our current residents.
Bringing the total flock to 64 birds, our Estates and Maintenance Team have been busy expanding the already existing habitat by transforming their current indoor house as well as ensuring the whole area has been fenced to accommodate the birds, with new gates being installed at the top end of the habitat. This fenced area gives the birds more space within their habitat. With the increase in flamingo numbers, visitors will now be able to enjoy their vibrant colours with the installation of better viewing access along Scoop and Go and Wrap and Roll.
On 3rd August 2026, the two separate flocks were mixed to become a ‘flamboyance’! It is hoped that these new arrivals will encourage breeding amongst the flock. The Animal Care Team will be watching and listening carefully for the pitter patters of webbed feet. It is thought that flamingo’s pair for life!
Chilean flamingos are currently listed as ‘Near Threatened’ on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species , with an estimated population of about 200,000 individuals in the wild.
Did you know… Flamingos have bristle-like tongues to filter water and food. The colouring of their pink feathers comes from the tiny shrimps that they eat!
There are many ways you can help support Chilean flamingos both here at CZS and out in the wild, from adopting the flamingos to making a donation . Even your visit to the Zoo will help to care for wildlife and wild places!

https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..title: Thank you from the UmPhafa Field Rangers!
https://www.colchesterzoologicalsociety..text:
In June, the rangers at UmPhafa Nature Reserve were lucky enough to recieve a brand new pair of Jim Green boots – perfect for the type of work undertaken on the reserve! We would like to say a big thank you to both Jim Green and the Game Ranger Association of Africa .
Here at CZS, we are dedicated to researching and conserving animal species all over the world. UmPhafa Nature Reserve , based in KwaZulu Natal, South Africa, is our fully funded and managed project that we continually support.The Reserve encompasses 6,000ha covering a 1,200 foot gradient, from the banks of the Tugela River to the top of mountains and covers a diverse range of ecosystems, including open grassland and bushveldt.
These new boots, which were sponsored by the Game Ranger Association of Africa through their Ranger Boot initiative in collaboration with Jim Green , were gratefully received by the UmPhafa Team and the Field Rangers were over joyed to recieve their pair!
UmPhafa is a charity without a commercial entity, unlike tourist-based nature reserves, who use the income from paying guests. Instead, as an education reserve, subsidised by Colchester Zoological Society, UmPhafa is able to charge guests the minimal payment to cover basics. This allows interns from all backgrounds from all over the world to visit the Reserve and experience what it is like to work alongside free-roaming wildife.
UmPhafa is focused on protecting endangered and vulnerable species such as cheetahs, wild dogs, mountain reedbuck, leopard, vultures and cranes to name a few. Unfortunately, one of the main threats faced by these species is the increase of poaching in South Africa. It is therefore vital that the Reserve is monitored 24/7 by a team of Field Rangers in all weather conditions. With such an ongoing threat on the fence line, and with the help of donations, the Reserve have been able to increase the number of Field Rangers patrolling and protecting the wilidfe that UmPhafa is home to.
The Field Rangers at UmPhafa work tirelessly to protect the wildlife on the Reserve by doing daily patrols on foot as well as monitoring the animals. They are passionate individuals that care for the nature of this world, protecting it for future generations to come.
While their new boots will help with walking the reserve, in order to fulfill their role, they also need torches, cut-resistance gloves and handy tools. Your donation could help pay for essential equipment that will ensure UmPhafa can continue the conservation battle.
Donate today and help to care for wildlife and wild places.

https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.title: These questions were at the heart of our 2026 symposium – Civil Society in a Changing Landscape
https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.text:
How can civil society respond to a changing landscape, and what will it take to build stronger communities across Greater Essex?
These questions were at the heart of our 2026 symposium, Civil Society in a Changing Landscape , held at Hatfield Place on 19 November. The event brought together members of the voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) sector, public sector leaders, health partners, funders and community representatives from across Greater Essex to explore the changes shaping civil society and consider how we can strengthen communities and shape what comes next.
Our Director of Programmes and Partnerships, Gavin Benn, opened the symposium, with Trustee Gail Cunningham hosting the day. In her opening address, A Changing Landscape , Gail reflected on A Joint Vision for Civil Society in Greater Essex and the partnerships it has helped build between ECF, local organisations and public sector partners. She highlighted the importance of better understanding the sector’s experiences and needs, which led to the commissioning of our Community Listening Project: VCSE Sector Audit 2026 .
Professor Tony Chapman of Durham University’s St Chad’s College presented the VCSE Sector Audit findings in Understanding Civil Society in Greater Essex . He explored the scale of the sector, its contribution to local communities and the pressures organisations face, including financial uncertainty, rising demand and difficulties recruiting and retaining people.
Despite these challenges, Tony was struck by the ambition and optimism of organisations across the sector. Reflecting on ECF’s ambitions, he remarked: “Your ambition is totally out of control!”
Emma de Closset, Chief Executive of UK Community Foundations, joined Gail for Greater Essex in National Context , discussing national pressures on civil society and opportunities for local collaboration. She praised the Joint Statement for Civil Society in Greater Essex as “such a wonderful innovation”, highlighting how bringing organisations together around shared goals could offer a model for other areas. She also described Greater Essex as “a real inspiration for place-based working and local convening”.
Dr Sebastien Chapleau, Community Organiser at Citizens UK, then led From Insight to Collective Action . Drawing on Citizens UK’s experience, he explored how building relationships around shared concerns can help communities strengthen their voice and influence change.
Click the photo below to see a full gallery of images from the day on Flickr.
Essex Community Foundation
Hatfield Place
After lunch, we gave attendees a first look at our #MyEssex campaign, ahead of its public launch.
The afternoon began with Resilience Through Change , as Gina Gardiner of Fatima’s UK Campaign reflected on how individuals, organisations and communities can navigate uncertainty and recognise their strengths. Maria Wilby from Refugee, Asylum and Migrant Action (RAMA) followed with Navigating Change: A Local Perspective , sharing insights into the opportunities and challenges facing organisations working directly with communities.
To close the day, ECF Trustee Maggie Desmond led Shaping What Comes Next . Drawing on the VCSE Sector Audit and the day’s discussions, she encouraged attendees to put the findings to use in their own work, involve local organisations earlier in decision-making and identify practical opportunities to work differently with others.
Thank you to everyone who joined us and contributed to the day’s discussions!

Behind Essex’s 5,200 voluntary, community and social enterprise organisations is a sector making a huge difference to local communities. But what does the evidence tell us about the challenges and opportunities shaping its future?
We’re excited to share that our Community Listening Project: VCSE Sector Audit 2026 is now available to read on our website.
Across Essex, these organisations contribute an estimated £4.6 billion in economic and social value, playing a significant role in supporting communities.
Bringing together quantitative research led by Professor Tony Chapman of Durham University and qualitative research by Hannah Fletcher, the VCSE Sector Audit draws on the experiences of organisations and public sector partners. It explores the sector’s contribution, how organisations operate across Essex, funding and financial resilience, the pressures facing staff and volunteers, and relationships with health services, public bodies and infrastructure support.

https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.title: New Fund Puts Essex Communities at the Heart of Better Health
https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.text:
In partnership with the NHS Essex Integrated Care Board (NHS Essex ICB), we have launched a new pilot fund that will explore how the NHS and the voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) sector can work more effectively together to improve health outcomes for people across Essex.
The NHS Essex Community Health Partnership Fund will focus initially on vaccine uptake, an area where some communities are harder for statutory health services to reach. Grants will support charities and community groups that already have trusted relationships with these communities to share information, build confidence in vaccinations and help more people access the protection they need.
By drawing on local knowledge, lived experience and the trust these organisations have built over many years, the pilot will test how VCSE partners can help shape health services, so they better meet the needs of the communities they serve.
The Fund focuses on vaccinations for pregnant women (whooping cough, RSV and flu), teenage girls and boys (HPV), and children (MMR). ECF will provide larger grants to organisations working across several districts, or with multiple priority groups, and small grants of up to £10,000 for grassroots organisations working locally across Essex, excluding Southend and Thurrock, with priority given to projects in Basildon, Harlow and Tendring.
Through our Future of Essex series and the development of the Joint Vision for Civil Society in Greater Essex , we partnered with NHS Essex to engage VCSE organisations and wider partners in exploring how health services can better respond to community needs. These conversations helped inform the NHS Essex Community Health Partnership Fund, highlighting the importance of involving communities in shaping services and recognising the role of local organisations in reaching people and understanding their needs.
Tom Abell, Chief Executive Officer at NHS Essex, said:
“This pilot has been a great opportunity to work with Essex Community Foundation and strengthen the partnership between NHS Essex and the voluntary, community and social enterprise sector. By working together, we can draw on the knowledge, experience and trusted relationships of local organisations to help address some of the big health challenges facing our communities.
We look forward to building on this work and continuing to strengthen our relationship with the sector to improve health and wellbeing across Essex, Southend and Thurrock.”
Caroline Taylor, Chief Executive of Essex Community Foundation, said:
“The VCSE sector must be recognised as a full and equal partner in decisions that affect the communities it serves. Local organisations understand the needs of the people they support, and their knowledge and experience should help shape how services are designed and delivered. This pilot is an opportunity to explore what genuine partnership between statutory services and the VCSE sector can look like in practice.”
The pilot will explore how grant funding can help local organisations improve vaccination awareness and uptake, while strengthening collaboration between health services and the VCSE sector. As a proof of concept for this approach, it will help NHS Essex understand what works and inform wider engagement with the sector, which is planned to launch later this year. The learning will also help shape future approaches to partnership working and the role local organisations can play in improving health services across Essex, Southend and Thurrock.
Who Can Apply?
Applications are welcome from:
Registered charities
Community and voluntary organisations
Community Interest Companies (CICs) limited by guarantee
Other not-for-profit organisations meeting ECF eligibility requirements

https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.title: The Geoffrey Sneed Engineering & STEM Scholarship Programme Reopens
https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.text:
Dr Geoffrey Sneed (pictured above) devoted his life to learning, innovation and inspiring others through science and engineering. Raised in Ilford, he showed an early aptitude for maths, physics and engineering, which shaped his academic and professional career.
After graduating from Imperial College London and completing a PhD, Geoffrey spent 15 years teaching physics, maths, chemistry and applied sciences at Ealing High School. Known for his forward-thinking approach, he helped establish one of the first purpose-built applied science laboratories in a state grammar school and developed specialist experimental equipment, with a strong focus on real-world application.
Beyond the classroom, Geoffrey held senior academic and research roles, including as a research director at the University of Surrey, as well as appointments at the Science Museum and Imperial College. In 1979, he was awarded a Churchill Fellowship to study international approaches to science education and later received the Churchill Medal at 10 Downing Street.
An inventor as well as an educator, Geoffrey created the Pulsometer, a medical chronograph watch designed to measure heart rate quickly. His work consistently reflected his belief that engineering should serve society and solve practical problems.
Inspiring young people remained central to his life. He founded the Molecule Club, introducing children to science through a musical performance that toured schools across the Midlands. Alongside this, he maintained a lifelong interest in the motor industry, writing extensively about its engineering and history.
When Geoffrey died in 2022 with no immediate family, he agreed that his estate should be used to establish a charitable fund in his name, recognising his lifelong contribution to education.
A New Opportunity for Future Engineers
This decision led to the creation of the Dr Geoffrey Sneed Engineering Scholarship , which launched in April 2026 and provides a new opportunity for academically talented students across Essex who face financial barriers to higher education. Through ongoing financial support, the scholarship enables students to focus on their studies and pursue careers in engineering and STEM, applying their knowledge for the benefit of society, values that were central to Geoffrey’s life and work.
In its first year, the programme awarded scholarships to five students, helping them progress towards higher education and future careers working in engineering and related STEM fields. Following the success of the initial round, the scholarship reopened for applications in September 2026 , with the first stage of the application process closing on 16 December 2026 .
What the Scholarship Offers
The scholarship provides financial support towards living costs while studying at university. Awards are made for an initial three-year period, with the potential for review for a fourth year, helping to ensure stability and continued support throughout a student’s degree.
Interested in Applying?
If you live in Essex, East London/Essex border, are currently studying A Levels, and plan to progress to a STEM-based degree, particularly Engineering, you may be eligible to apply.

https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.title: Discover the Programme Helping Local Charities Thrive!
https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.text:
The Thrive Programme was developed to help organisations navigate these challenges and build strong foundations for the future. Delivered in partnership with the Cranfield Trust, the programme forms part of our wider Funder Plus approach, providing support beyond grant funding through access to expertise, advice and opportunities for development. It is funded through our Thriving Third Sector Fund and Community Resilience Fund, helping us provide additional support to the organisations working at the heart of communities across Essex.
For 9 months participants have worked on their individual organisational priorities, from developing strategic and financial plans to exploring opportunities for growth and improving financial sustainability.
The seventh round of our Thrive Programme has now come to a successful close, having supported a further 11 organisations across Essex to build resilience, strengthen leadership and plan for long-term success.
Leading a charity comes with many responsibilities, from managing finances and securing funding to supporting staff, developing services and planning for the future. Finding the time and space to step back from day-to-day demands and focus on the longer-term direction of an organisation can be difficult.
This tailored support combines one-to-one consultancy projects with experienced Cranfield Trust volunteers, individual mentoring and a series of leadership workshops. Topics include change management, building effective teams, getting the most from trustees, collaboration and partnerships, and income generation.
An important part of Thrive is also bringing charity leaders together to share experiences and learn from one another. Running a small charity can sometimes feel isolating, particularly for those responsible for making important decisions and navigating challenges with limited resources. Connecting with other leaders facing similar experiences provides a valuable opportunity to exchange ideas and build lasting relationships.
The value of the programme is reflected in feedback from participants. One leader explained how Thrive had helped them develop a five-year plan for the first time, giving them a clearer understanding of their immediate priorities and how to prepare for the future. Another described gaining a new perspective on the different roles they balance as a small charity leader, and how this would help them approach their work.
Hear from the 2026 Thrive Programme participants:
Following the successful completion of this latest round, our programme panel has approved a further two years of Thrive, allowing us to continue offering this opportunity to more organisations and their leaders.
We are also developing a new Thrive Plus pilot, which will explore how we can widen the support available to VCSE organisations across Essex. More information about Thrive Plus will be shared in the new year.
As the challenges facing the voluntary sector continue to evolve, ensuring local organisations have the skills, confidence and resources to adapt is increasingly important. By investing in the people and organisations behind our communities, we can help build a stronger, more sustainable sector that is better equipped to make a lasting difference.
Take part in the next round of the Thrive Programme:
To find out more about the programme or apply for the next round, visit our Join our Thrive Programme page.
Have a question?
If you’d like to discuss the programme or find out whether it’s right for your organisation, contact Grants Officer Frankie Web Huseyin at frankie@essexcf.org.uk or call our Grants Team on 01245 355947 , who will be happy to help.

Across Essex, local organisations are finding different ways to protect the environment, care for their surroundings and create more sustainable communities. From conserving natural habitats and planting trees to developing community growing spaces, their work is helping to make a difference in local areas.
We’re taking a closer look at three organisations working to create greener spaces, connect people with nature and care for the environment.
Daws Hall Nature Reserve: Protecting Nature and Connecting People with the Countryside
As Daws Hall Nature Reserve approaches its 42nd year, it is celebrating the progress made in protecting its natural surroundings and bringing people closer to the countryside.
Through the creation and improvement of a mosaic of habitats, thousands of species have been recorded on this protected landscape. Daws Hall Nature Reserve combines practical conservation work with an extensive education programme, which has now welcomed more than 120,000 young people and thousands of adults.
These opportunities to learn about and experience the natural world help spark a lifelong connection to the countryside.
ECF has also supported Daws Hall Nature Reserve’s work, including helping to reconstruct platforms providing access to the River Stour, used by the general public and children on school trips. We have also contributed towards its environmental education programme, providing school-age children from across Essex with practical and engaging lessons on conservation, alongside supporting career development projects for young people at the reserve.
Reflecting on the work, General Manager Will Dover said:
“We continue to find sustained and renewed interest in our work, giving us inspiration for future growth.”
The Tree Action Society of Clare: Planting for the Future
The Tree Action Society of Clare (TASC) was established in 2017 following the unnecessary felling of local trees. Since then, the group has been working to increase tree canopy cover in Clare and the surrounding area, strengthen the local landscape, create green corridors and improve biodiversity.
A key part of its work is a tree propagation nursery, where locally sourced nuts, seeds and fruit are grown until they are ready to be planted in community projects, including schools and public places. The group is also particularly keen to re-establish the rare and native black poplar in the area.
With support from ECF, TASC has been developing its nursery, including work on fencing and water collection facilities. The group has also planted 11 cherry trees along Cavendish Road as people enter Clare, bringing the promise of a display of white blossom each spring.
Dr Paul Davis from TASC explained:
“TASC (The Tree Action Society of Clare) was set up in 2017 to increase tree canopy cover in Clare and the surrounding area, to enhance and strengthen our local landscape, create green corridors and improve biodiversity.”
Abberton Rural Training: Growing Together in Harwich
At Abberton Rural Training’s Harwich site, participants and volunteers have been working together to transform an outdoor space into a welcoming place to grow flowers and herbs, learn and spend time together.
The group has built raised beds and makes use of donated and recycled materials to develop the space. Manure is sourced from a local farmer, while tyres from a local supplier are given a new lease of life as planters. These practical approaches to reusing resources have helped turn what was once a blank canvas into a growing space filled with plants, herbs, raised beds and seating areas.
The space has become more than just a place to grow. It provides a social area for participants who may not have family and friends nearby, as well as a quiet outdoor space for those who want to relax and enjoy their surroundings.

https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.title: Turncole Wind Farm Community Benefit Fund Surpasses £500,000 in Grants Awarded
https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.text:
The Turncole Wind Farm Community Benefit Fund has now awarded more than £500,000 to charitable projects supporting people and communities in Burnham-on-Crouch and Southminster.
Established with Essex Community Foundation (ECF) in 2016, the Fund supports charitable projects within the parishes of Southminster and Burnham-on-Crouch that enhance the quality of life for local residents, contribute to vibrant, healthy, successful and sustainable communities, and promote community spirit and activity. Since its launch, it has supported a wide range of local organisations, helping people of all ages access support, develop new skills, improve their wellbeing and strengthen connections within their communities.
Over the past decade, grants have supported projects including advice services for local residents, activities tackling loneliness and isolation, support for young carers, opportunities for young people, family wellbeing programmes and community sports initiatives. Funding has also helped local organisations develop new services and sustain activities that continue to make a difference across the area.
Among the organisations supported is Home-Start Essex, which received funding to deliver family-focused fitness sessions, stay-and-play activities and family support groups for families in Burnham-on-Crouch and Southminster.
Nic O’Brien, Chief Executive Officer of Home-Start Essex, said: “We are so thankful for the funding that Home-Start Essex received from the Turncole Wind Farm Community Benefit Fund. It made such a difference to socially isolated families living in Southminster and Burnham-on-Crouch who were able to access Family Fitness and Fun sessions and attend our weekly Family Support Group. Families consistently reported enjoying the opportunity to try new fitness activities, increasing their weekly physical activity, greater confidence in engaging in activities with their children and a reduction in feelings of isolation. Many also noted a measurable increase in emotional resilience and personal wellbeing. This flexible and responsive use of funding maximised impact and ensured that families received timely and relevant support where it was most needed.”
The Fund has also supported Action for Family Carers, helping to establish and expand support for young carers across the rural Dengie area. Funding has enabled work in local schools, including Ormiston Rivers Academy, providing awareness activities, after-school clubs and one-to-one support for young people balancing education with caring responsibilities at home.
“Funding from the Turncole Wind Farm Community Benefit Fund helped Action for Family Carers establish and grow much-needed support for young carers across the rural Dengie area. Young carers already face pressures and responsibilities that most children their age do not, and living in a rural community can bring additional challenges, including isolation and fewer opportunities to access support.
We have reached hundreds of local young carers, including through our work at Ormiston Rivers Academy. Our support gives young carers someone they can trust to talk to, helps them feel less alone and better able to cope with the pressures of caring. The Fund’s support helped us build a service that continues to make a real and lasting difference to young carers across the Dengie today,” shared James Clarke, CEO, Action for Family Carers.
Zoe Brampton, Grants Manager, Essex Community Foundation added: “Reaching £500,000 in grantmaking is a significant milestone and reflects the lasting impact the Fund has had across Burnham-on-Crouch and Southminster over the past decade. Through the support of local projects and organisations, the Fund has helped strengthen communities, improve wellbeing and create opportunities for people across the area. It is inspiring to see the difference these grants continue to make and the positive impact they have had on local residents.”

https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.text:
Smaller charities and community groups across Essex, Hertfordshire and Suffolk now have another opportunity to apply for funding as the Saffron Community Fund has reopened for applications.
What the Fund Supports
The Saffron Community Fund focuses on projects that support elderly people, children and young people, and environmental or green causes. Applications are open to charities, not-for-profits, and volunteer groups. Each application is assessed individually to ensure funding is allocated fairly.
Priority is given to organisations based near a Saffron Building Society branch, but the fund is open to eligible groups across Essex, Hertfordshire and Suffolk that are working to make a positive difference in their local communities.
Discover if there is a branch near you – here .
Why it Matters
Since its launch, the Saffron Community Fund (SCF) has awarded over £300,000 in grants to a wide range of causes, enabling grassroots organisations to deliver essential services and projects that strengthen local communities. Established by Saffron Building Society and managed in partnership with Essex Community Foundation, the fund ensures support is distributed fairly and where it can have the greatest impact.
In 2025 Saffron Building Society  reached a major milestone, with its endowment fund at ECF surpassing £1 million, well ahead of the five-year target set in 2023.
This achievement means the Saffron Community Fund can now award around £50,000 each year to support local projects, charities, and initiatives across Essex.
Claire Hunnable, Saffron’s Community Business Partner, explains:
“Our Fund is an essential source of funding for some of the smaller charities and community groups around our branches. We have developed a unique and important working relationship with Essex Community Foundation that ensure all grant decisions made by our panel are undertaken with expert guidance from them. “Every year we are amazed by the diversity of the applications and are always delighted to be introduced to groups we may never normally have been aware of. I also have the pleasure of meeting the people behind the projects and to see the amazing work that is happening all around our communities.”
Examples of Projects Recently  Supported by the Fund:
Dance Network Association (DNA) – A dance charity supporting people living with dementia and Parkinson’s, as well as their carers, across Essex. They were awarded £5,000 towards the core running costs of the charity, helping to sustain their creative programmes and support for local people and families.
Accuro (Care Services) – A charity supporting children, young people and adults with disabilities across West Essex. They were awarded £5,000 towards the delivery of Accuro Active, a programme of activity days and outings for adults aged 19+ with SEND in Uttlesford, helping to provide opportunities for social connection, independence and community participation.
Red Kite Support – A charity supporting survivors of rape and sexual abuse across Hertfordshire and West Essex. They were awarded £10,200 towards the ongoing running costs of the organisation over two years, helping to provide a volunteer-led helpline and free trauma-informed therapy sessions for survivors.
