https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.title: NHS Essex Community Health Partnership Fund Opens for Applications
https://www.essexcommunityfoundation.org.text:
Community organisations across Essex can now apply for grants of up to £10,000 from the NHS Essex Community Health Partnership Fund to support community-led projects that encourage, enable and support greater vaccine confidence and uptake.
The NHS Essex Community Health Partnership Fund has been established by NHS Essex Integrated Care Board (ICB) and ECF. The programme is exploring how community-led approaches can help improve preventative health outcomes and increase vaccination uptake among communities where take-up of vaccines is lower than expected.
To help achieve this, the Fund is investing in local charities and community groups that often have trusted relationships with the people they support and can engage people and communities that statutory services may find more difficult to reach.
Priority Groups
Projects must work with one or more of the following priority groups:
Pregnant Women – Pertussis, RSV, Flu
Teenage Girls & Boys – HPV
Children – MMR Dose 1 & 2
Priority Areas
The Fund will consider applications from across Essex (excluding Southend and Thurrock) but priority will be given to projects working in:
Basildon
Harlow
Tendring
What Can Be Funded?
The Fund is designed to support organisations that are already working with one or more of the priority groups and have strong relationships within the communities they support. Funding is available for projects that can build on and strengthen work that is already taking place.
Grants of up to £10,000 are available for projects lasting up to 24 months.
The Advisory Panel is looking for organisations that have strong community connections and can work collaboratively to help increase vaccination uptake among Essex’s priority communities.
The Fund is looking for community-led approaches that:
Increase awareness and understanding of vaccinations
Build trust and confidence within communities
Address barriers to accessing vaccination services
Support informed decision-making
Engage communities that are underserved or less likely to engage with mainstream services
Create sustainable and collaborative approaches that can inform future delivery models
Who Can Apply?
Applications are welcome from:
Registered charities
Community and voluntary organisations
Community Interest Companies (CICs) limited by guarantee
Other not-for-profit organisations meeting ECF eligibility requirements
To read the full application guidance click here
Application Process
There are two stages to the application process.
Stage One: Expression of Interest
Organisations must first submit an Expression of Interest (EOI).
Deadline: Wednesday 25 November 2026, 5pm.
EOIs will be reviewed by the Advisory Panel and organisations demonstrating the strongest fit with the Fund’s priorities will be invited to submit a full application.
Applicants will be notified of the outcome of their EOI by Wednesday 16 December 2026.
Stage Two: Full Application
Organisations invited to the second stage will be asked to provide further information about their proposed project. Any additional questions from the Advisory Panel will be shared with applicants at this stage.
The deadline for Stage Two applications is Friday 22 January 2027.

Expression of Interest deadline: Wednesday 25 November 2026, 5pm.

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Greenstead Care: Residents’ Experiences of Care, Health and Wellbeing Report
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Today we are pleased to launch Greenstead Care: Residents’ Experiences of Care, Health and Wellbeing, a new report exploring how care, health and wellbeing are experienced in everyday life in Greenstead, Colchester.
Working in partnership with the School of Health and Social Care at the University of Essex and African Families in the UK, the Greenstead Care report brings together the experiences of local residents to show that health and wellbeing are shaped by much more than formal health services alone.
Coming as a result of a participatory co-design workshop held at the University of Essex in 2023, the project sought to understand the experiences of residents from Global Ethnic Majority backgrounds to ensure their voices are included within a distinctly participatory way. Through four community mapping workshops involving 39 participants, 13 walking interviews and eight interviews with local stakeholders, we explored the places, relationships and everyday experiences that shape health and wellbeing across Greenstead from an asset-based perspective.
One of the strongest findings to emerge from this report is that care happens everywhere; it happens through family and friendship networks, neighbours looking out for one another, community centres and libraries, parks and faith spaces and through access to local amenities. These everyday spaces and relationships form an important, but often under-recognised, part of the infrastructure that supports health and wellbeing in local communities.
In line with this, the Care report identifies five interconnected dimensions of community care practices, health and wellbeing: relationality and connectedness; embodied and emotional experiences; reciprocity and mutual aid; environmental and material conditions; and cultural and ethical experiences of care.
These dimensions prompt us to think differently about how we understand and address health inequalities in local communities. Improving health and wellbeing cannot rest solely on encouraging individuals to make healthier choices or improving access to clinical services. It also requires investment in the wider conditions that make health and wellbeing possible: accessible and welcoming places, strong social relationships, responsive local services and community infrastructure that enables people to feel connected, supported and valued.
The full report can be found here.

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Community360 Shares Macmillan Community Voices Research at National Conference
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Community360’s Development Manager, Matt Mason , recently presented findings from our Macmillan Community Voices Project at the Voluntary Sector and Volunteering Research Conference, contributing to national discussions on health inequalities and cancer care.
The conference brought together researchers, practitioners and voluntary sector organisations from across the UK to share learning and explore some of the most pressing issues facing the VCSE sector. Matt attended as part of the conference’s New Researchers Day and presented From Practice to Knowledge: Reflections on Health Inequalities from the Macmillan Community Voices Project .
The presentation highlighted how intersecting health inequalities can affect cancer care journeys, with barriers often shaped by a combination of factors including (but not limited to) ethnicity, language, socioeconomic circumstances, geography, age and cultural experiences across six cohorts . Our Partnership with Macmillan Cancer Support allows us to use our Participatory Action Research approach to  co-construct people’s experiences of cancer, allowing us to effectively communicate challenges in care journeys to decision makers and partners across the health system.
Research from the project identified a range of structural, cultural and bureaucratic barriers that can influence people’s access to care and support. The findings demonstrate the importance of designing services around individual experiences and ensuring that those most affected by health inequalities have a voice in shaping future provision.
Reflecting on the conference, Matt said:
“It was a very rewarding and stimulating experience to attend the VSVR conference, showcasing Community360’s Macmillan Community Voices Project. Across the conference, the breadth and quality of the work was inspiring to see, with practitioners and researchers coming together to tackle the big issues facing the VCSE sector, sharing knowledge from far-reaching places in the UK.
As part of the New Researchers Day, connecting with early career researchers and key members of the Voluntary Sector Studies Network provided an important touch point to discuss some key learnings around the co-constructing of intersectional health inequalities for Community360, further expanding the reach of our project.”
The event provided an excellent opportunity to showcase the impact of the Macmillan Community Voices Project, build new connections and contribute to wider conversations about reducing health inequalities and improving outcomes for people affected by cancer. Community360 is proud to see the project’s learning helping to inform research and practice on a national stage.
If you would like to know more about any of our project work, please email voices@community360.org.uk

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Trustee Annual Report Changes: SORP 2026 Briefing
Overview
The new Charity Statement of Recommended Practice (SORP) came into effect on  1 January 2026  and  applies to all accounting periods beginning on or after the 1 st  January 2026 . The changes place greater emphasis on transparency, impact reporting, financial resilience, and future planning meaning that charities really need to ensure relevant data is collected throughout the year, rather than at year end.
Key Changes
> Impact Reporting and Charitable Activities
Trustee Annual Reports must provide clearer evidence of the difference a charity is making. This means demonstrating outcomes and impact, not just activities undertaken and showing how activities contribute to charitable objectives.
You can use evidence such as:
KPIs and performance measures
Beneficiary statistics
Case studies and personal stories
Long-term social impact data
Include visuals where appropriate, such as graphs, charts and photographs.
Action:  Begin collecting impact data and case studies throughout the year.
> Reserves Reporting
There is an increased requirement for transparency around reserves so reports should include:
The charity reserves policy, its rationale and any variances from that policy.
Actual reserves held during the year.
Actions being taken to address any shortfalls or excesses.
Action:  Review reserves policies and ensure trustees can clearly explain reserve levels.
> Going Concern
Trustees will need to provide more detailed commentary on the charity’s financial sustainability and r eports should cover :
Financial resilience.
Key assumptions made by trustees.
Risks affecting future operations.
Explanations where reserves are low or zero.
Action:  Strengthen financial planning and document assumptions supporting future viability.
> Future Planning
The focus is not solely on past performance.
Reports should include:
Future priorities and strategic objectives.
Planned projects and service developments.
Expected impact of future activities.
Funding arrangements supporting future plans.
Action:  Develop clear forward-looking narratives aligned with organisational strategy.
> Volunteer Reporting
Volunteer contributions must be better recognised and all charities need to report on the nature of volunteer involvement, and the significance of volunteer contributions.
Tier 2 and Tier 3 charities should also include:
Number of volunteers.
Volunteer roles.
Volunteer hours contributed where practical.
Action:  Introduce processes to capture volunteer numbers and activity throughout the year.
> Linking Narrative and Financial Information
There is a greater expectation that financial statements and narrative reporting work together with reports needing to explain:
How funds have been spent and on what activity.
How spending contributes to charitable objectives.
How future income and reserves will support ongoing work.
Action:  Ensure reporting links financial performance directly to charitable impact.
>Environmental and Social Reporting
SORP 2026 introduced enhanced expectations around environmental, social and governance (ESG) reporting, particularly for larger charities. Areas that may be covered include: Environmental sustainability initiatives, Energy efficiency and recycling, Social responsibility and community impact, Governance and ethical decision-making.
Action:  Consider how the charity is responding to environmental and social responsibilities and begin gathering supporting evidence.
Delivering SORP in 2026
To minimise year-end pressure, charities should:
✓ Collect impact data and case studies throughout the year
✓ Review reserves policies and financial resilience
✓ Strengthen links between financial information and activities
✓ Record volunteer contributions consistently
✓ Develop clear future plans and strategic priorities
✓ Consider environmental and social reporting requirements

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Armed Forces Community Roadshow
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Our Macmillan Community Voices team was delighted to attend last week’s Armed Forces Community Roadshow, organised and hosted by Braintree District Council. Aimed at serving personnel, veterans and their families, the event provided a valuable opportunity to access a wide range of information and support, including housing, benefits, cost of living assistance, mental health services, employment support, and health and wellbeing resources.
Supported by Macmillan Cancer Support, the Macmillan Community Voices team attended as part of our ongoing work to engage with communities that experience health inequalities, which includes the veterans’ community. Through these conversations, we aim to better understand people’s lived experiences of cancer and identify ways to improve cancer care and support across Essex. Alongside meeting Cllr Richard van Dulken, Chairman of Braintree District Council, the roadshow provided a fantastic opportunity to build new connections with both members of the armed forces community and the many organisations in attendance.
The LGBTQ+ community is another group experiencing health inequalities that we have been focusing on, so we were particularly pleased to meet Fighting With Pride. The organisation was initially established to support those affected by the military’s ‘Gay Ban’, which was lifted on 12 January 2000. Prior to its removal, thousands of LGBTQ+ service personnel were dismissed or forced to leave the armed forces because of their sexuality, despite serving their country with pride. Since then, Fighting With Pride has expanded its work to support serving personnel, veterans, their families, and those leaving military service today.
If you have lived experience of cancer, either personally or as a carer, and are a member of the veteran and/or LGBTQ+ communities, we would like to hear about your experiences of cancer services.
To share your experiences, please email voices@community360.org.uk or call 01206 505250 and ask to speak to the Macmillan Community Voices team.

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Partnership, Lived Experience and Learning at the Heart of Macmillan Community Voices Workshop for the Adults with Learning Disabilities Community
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Professionals, carers, voluntary organisations and people with lived experience came together in Great Saling on 16 June 2026 for a Macmillan Community Voices (MCV) workshop focused on improving the cancer care experiences of adults with learning disabilities.
The event was the third in a series of workshops delivered by the Macmillan Community Voices team, building on feedback and insights gathered from communities across Essex. With the support of partners including Lady McAdden Breast Cancer Trust, St Helena Hospice, Essex Carers Network, Blade Education, Learning Disability Specialist Health Services, The Edmund Trust and NHS LeDeR (Learning from Lives and Deaths) representatives, the workshop explored how organisations can work together to reduce inequalities and improve cancer outcomes.
We were also delighted to welcome regional and national colleagues from Macmillan Cancer Support to the day who engaged directly with partners and contributors to ensure learning fed directly back into the work being carried out by them to support the National Cancer Plan.
Shared Findings
The day provided an opportunity to share emerging findings from the MCV project while creating space for discussion about the barriers adults with learning disabilities can face when accessing cancer screening, diagnosis, treatment and support. A recurring message throughout the event was the importance of listening to lived experience and ensuring individuals are involved in decisions about their own care.
Speakers shared examples of ongoing work to improve accessibility, awareness and support for people with learning disabilities and their carers. Topics included improving access to cancer screening, supporting conversations around serious illness and end-of-life care, promoting reasonable adjustments in healthcare settings and increasing understanding of the challenges individuals can face when navigating health services.
One of the most powerful moments of the day came through a film produced by Blade Education on behalf of Macmillan Community Voices. The video featured a parent describing the challenges of receiving a cancer diagnosis while continuing to care for her adult son with a rare syndrome, highlighting the impact cancer can have on entire families.
Gathering Key Themes
The Community360 Macmillan Community Voices team also shared key themes gathered throughout the project so far, including barriers to screening and appointments, communication challenges, limited awareness of reasonable adjustments, and concerns about people with learning disabilities not always being fully involved in decisions affecting their health and care.
Participants then joined a collaborative discussion to consider how communities, services and organisations can work together to address these issues. Conversations highlighted the need for greater awareness and training, more accessible information, stronger advocacy and continued partnership working across the health, voluntary and community sectors.
Positive Feedback
Feedback from attendees was overwhelmingly positive. Participants reported increased awareness of the health inequalities experienced by adults with learning disabilities, improved knowledge of available support services, and a greater understanding of the importance of inclusive, person-centered care. The workshop also created new connections between organisations, helping to strengthen relationships and future referral pathways.
The learning gathered will contribute to Macmillan’s national research and help shape future Community Voices activity.  It will also be shared with partner organisations to support ongoing work aimed at improving cancer experiences and outcomes for adults with learning disabilities.

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Macmillan Regional Professionals Conference
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Introduction
Last week we were honoured to attend the East of England Macmillan Professionals Conference and contribute to a panel discussion exploring how community projects such as our Macmillan Community Voices project can generate meaningful insight and translate this into real-world action to better support people affected by cancer. Alongside us on the panel were Angharad Binder, Programme Officer for the Farming Community Network and Caitlin Evans, Rural Health and Wellbeing Manager for Cambridgeshire ACRE.
Insight into Different Challenges
The panel discussion provided an interesting insight into the challenges different communities face when affected by cancer. The Farming Community Network highlighted the assumptions that are often made that farmers are wealthy and live a wonderfully privileged life, and that there is a real lack of understanding around the challenges farmers face and the realities of the workload and isolation. Cambridgeshire ACRE highlighted the barriers faced by rural communities such as transport poverty and digital exclusion. While our Macmillan Community Voices project pointed out structural inequalities including language access, culturally appropriate care. However, there were also a lot of similarities between our projects, not least the importance of building trust.
Overall the whole event was very informative with a number of other presentations throughout the day. Macmillan’s Chief Nursing Officer, Claire Taylor in their keynote speech highlighted the challenges that Macmillan Professionals face today, while celebrating the positive impact they have on people’s lives and highlighting how Macmillan are supporting the NHS Cancer Plan to improve outcomes for patients.
“What if you couldn’t hear your own diagnosis?…”
Closing the conference, there was a powerful keynote presentation from the Deaf Cancer Support project, which is delivered by Self Help UK and supported by Macmillan Cancer Support. Titled, “What if you couldn’t hear your own diagnosis?…”, the presentation vividly illustrated the significant physical, emotional and practical impact that communication barriers can have on D/deaf people throughout the cancer-care pathway when accessible communication is not provided.

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
By 2045, the number of people living with cancer in the UK will increase by 58%.
When we heard this at the national Macmillan Professionals Conference in April, it stopped us in our tracks.  Currently there are 3.5 million people living with cancer ( https://www.macmillan.org.uk/about-us/latest-news/news-and-stories/change-is-needed-3-5-million ) and Macmillan recognises that there is more to do to improve the experiences of everyone who is affected by cancer.  To consider that this number will exceed 5 million in less than two decades strengthens the resolve to encourage reflection on what will make a difference day-to-day.
Our focus, working in partnership with Macmillan Cancer Support, has been learning about and responding to health inequalities.  Speaking to hundreds of people about cancer across Essex from diverse communities from the point of screening, through to diagnosis, treatment and aftercare has only highlighted how these clinical terms and the stages associated with managing a condition, do not adequately describe the experiences of the person living with cancer.  We need to prioritise the person and remember that living with cancer has economic, social, cultural, and environmental consequences.
For example:
Economic  – when you live at a distance from your treatment centre and rely on public transport, what are the implications?  We have been told of people spending as much as £74 to get to one therapy appointment.  The financial costs and the effort to co-ordinate this are significant.  Therefore, linking to relevant support services ( https://www.macmillan.org.uk/cancer-information-and-support/get-help/financial-and-work/money-faqs ) is vital.
Social  – who can you turn to as support when your life is changing after a diagnosis?  Finding out about accessible community groups is key.  We have identified more than 60 voluntary and community organisations that specialise in cancer support in Essex and there are many, many more that work with patients and their families in diverse communities in different ways.  Many are recorded on the Cancer Care Map ( https://www.cancercaremap.org/ ) but we are regularly discovering grassroots groups stepping into this sphere need to amplify their impact.  We are working with organisations to promote what they do and seek additional resources to help more people.
Cultural  – if you have additional communication needs, how do you stay informed and access opportunities to inform your care givers of what you need?  Communication has been the most consistent and recurrent theme in our conversations across the county.  Whether that be the challenges in co-ordinating BSL interpretation with appropriate medical knowledge to join an appointment, or assumptions being made about your levels of understanding, whereby you feel you cannot voice what you need, there is space to learn more from diverse communities and make space to listen first.   ( https://www.macmillan.org.uk/cancer-information-and-support/get-help/translations-and-other-formats )
Environmental  – every person has a history, relationships and life experiences that may inform their journey on a cancer pathway.  For instance, people have shared how past trauma may impact upon their access to treatment.  Being disconnected from potential networks of support can increase isolation. Opening up conversations about what people value and benefit from when living with cancer encourages more personalised care that can help people to cope with the challenges they face – valuing their voice and responding to their own circumstances and priorities more directly.
Our work on the Macmillan Community Voices programme continues over the coming months. We are keen to hear more from people who would like to share their experiences, to speak to voluntary organisations who may need help to promote their work or find ways to support it in the future, and to share the findings of our work to inform best practice in cancer care locally.

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Macmillan Community Voices (MCV) Workshop – Exploring the experiences of people living with cancer in Essex – LGBTQIA+ communities
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Introduction
Our workshop was the first in a series being undertaken by the Macmillan Community Voices team who are working in partnership with Macmillan Cancer Support to explore  cancer care experiences of different groups in our communities. Our programme of workshops focus on groups that data demonstrates, face significant health inequalities.
This workshop engaged with clinical and community stakeholders involved in the care and support of members of the LGBTQIA+ community who have or are, receiving cancer care.  We worked with two key partners to build our programme for the day, Transpire (based in Southend) and The Outhouse (based in Colchester) who helped to ensure that content was as useful and accessible as possible.
We wanted to take learning from our discussions and from the lived experience of community members to explore what plans and strategies could be developed to improve those experiences. We also wanted to consider what was working well and positive steps taken so far.
Our Workshop Programme
C360 presented a creative case study involving a trans woman who had previously engaged with the project, using collages to explore one positive and one negative cancer-related experience. The stark contrast between the two collages demonstrated the significant impact that being listened to, understood, and supported can have on an individual’s wellbeing. LGBTQIA+ themes and feedback gathered throughout the MCV project, alongside wider insights identified across different cohort groups were also shared, helping attendees understand common barriers and experiences within these communities.
Attendees also heard presentations from Transpire and The Outhouse, which highlighted the healthcare inequalities faced by LGBTQIA+ community. Research shared by Transpire explored concerns around access to gender-affirming care, fears of seeking healthcare due to the instability of Shared Care Agreements, and experiences of invasive questioning and perceived bias. The Outhouse outlined its Trans+ Levelling Up programme,  which aims to strengthen healthcare professionals’ understanding of Trans+ health needs, particularly  in relation to cancer screening and early diagnosis. This initiative also includes community focused campaigns to help educate and empower individuals. Following a pilot, educational gaps were identified and a new training programme developed.
The session concluded with a powerful personal testimony from a member of the LGBTQIA+ community who shared their experience of a late testicular cancer diagnosis, reflecting on both the challenges they faced and the exceptional support they received from Macmillan Cancer Support during their treatment and recovery.
Attendee Participation Session
A key focus of the event was understanding the lived experiences of LGBTQIA+ individuals affected by cancer and the importance of inclusive, person-centred support. So, we encouraged attendees to consider what they could do as a community member to improve the cancer related experiences of the community and consider what the system wide challenges are that can be worked on together.
Our Learning
Feedback from attendees confirmed that the workshop was highly informative and impactful. Participants highlighted that much of the information shared was new to them and increased their understanding of the inequalities faced by LGBTQIA+ communities when accessing healthcare and cancer services. The discussions generated a strong appetite for further learning and identified several priority areas for future development and improvement.
Key Outcomes
Increased awareness of the health inequalities and barriers to care experienced by LGBTQIA+ communities.
Recognition of the need for additional education and training for professionals and organisations supporting LGBTQIA+ individuals.
Greater understanding of the importance of engaging with LGBTQIA+ people in a confidential, respectful, and inclusive manner.
Identification of gaps in current health

https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Celebrating Volunteers’ Week 2026
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Celebrating the Heart of C360: Our Volunteers
At Colchester C360, everything we do is powered by people – people who give their time and energy to make a real difference in their community. Our volunteers are not just an extra helping hand. They are at the very core of what makes C360 such an impactful organisation. Quite simply, we couldn’t do what we do without them.
Why Volunteers Matter at C360
Volunteering is important because it brings people together, strengthens communities and helps services expand their reach. Volunteers offer time and skills that can make a real and lasting difference, whether that is through practical support, companionship or sharing specialist knowledge. At the same time, volunteering can be hugely rewarding for the individual, helping people build confidence, develop new skills, make connections and gain a strong sense of purpose through giving back.
What Volunteering Looks Like
There is no single way to volunteer at C360 – and that’s exactly what makes it so amazing. Opportunities are varied and flexible which suits different interests and skills. From being a volunteer driver to being a trustee, researcher or community group leader – there’s something to suit everyone. Every role, big or small, plays a part in shaping the experience of those who walk through our doors.
A Place to Grow
Volunteering at C360 isn’t just about giving, it’s also about growing. Many of our volunteers develop new skills, boost their confidence, and even take steps toward employment or further education. We pride ourselves on creating a supportive environment where everyone feels valued and encouraged to develop at their own pace.
It’s Volunteers’ Week!
Volunteers’ Week is a UK-wide celebration of the contribution volunteers make to charities, community groups and local causes every day. Taking place from 1st to 7th June, it is a chance to recognise the time, energy and commitment from volunteers and the impact they have on their communities. It is a moment to say thank you, celebrate volunteer stories and encourage more people to get involved in meaningful community participation.
Throughout Volunteers’ Week, we are sharing our volunteers’ stories through interviews that celebrate why people choose to volunteer, the incredible work they have done since joining us, and the personal benefits they gain from volunteering.
We are also running a workforce-wide volunteer nomination scheme ahead of a volunteer celebration and awards ceremony later this month. Alongside this, we are promoting not only our own volunteer vacancies, but volunteering opportunities more widely, to highlight their potential to strengthen communities even further.
A Big Thank You
To all our volunteers: thank you. Your dedication, kindness, generosity, and enthusiasm are what drive C360 forward. You are valued more than words can express, and this week (and every week) we celebrate you.
If you’ve ever thought about getting involved, there’s never been a better time. We also offer participation via corporate volunteer and student placements.
If you have any queries please contact us  Volunteer@community360.org.uk .
We will be at the love Colchester event at Firstsite representing the importance of volunteering in Colchester on 5th June!

Step Into Something Meaningful at VolFEST 2026
Thursday 4 June 2026 | 9.30am–4pm | Chelmsford High Street
Chelmsford, Essex – Chelmsford CVS is delighted to announce the return of  VolFEST 2026 , the city’s much-loved celebration of community, volunteering and local charities, taking place on Thursday 4 June in the heart of Chelmsford High Street.
Now firmly established as a highlight of National Volunteers’ Week, VolFEST will once again bring together around 50 local charities, community groups and support services for a day filled with conversation, connection and community spirit.
Whether you are looking for support, hoping to meet new people, or thinking about giving volunteering a try, VolFEST is the perfect opportunity to explore what is happening locally and discover how you can get involved.
Visitors will have the chance to:
Find vital help and advice from trusted local organisations
Discover flexible volunteering roles to suit different interests, ages, skills and availability
Speak directly to charities about what volunteering is really like
Meet local people already making a difference in the community
Enjoy music, activities, demonstrations, charity items for sale and a welcoming festival atmosphere
From one-off events and practical outdoor projects to charity shop roles, befriending, fundraising, youth work, administration, community gardening and skilled volunteering, VolFEST showcases the huge variety of ways people can support causes they care about.
Meet the Charities Changing Chelmsford.
Since launching in 2019, VolFEST has grown into a major annual community event, attracting thousands of visitors and helping local organisations connect with new volunteers, supporters and service users.
This year’s event will feature a wide variety of charities and community groups, including organisations supporting health and wellbeing, young people, older residents, disability support, homelessness, community safety, animals, the environment and much more.
Well-known local organisations expected to attend include Broomfield Hospital, CHESS Homeless, Farleigh Hospice, Wilderness Foundation, and City of Chelmsford Mencap, alongside many more local groups making a huge difference behind the scenes every day.
Chelmsford CVS is grateful to Chelmsford City Council for supporting this year’s event.

You will work closely with the Board of Trustees, senior leadership team, staff, volunteers, partners, and supporters to ensure the organisation thrives operationally, financially, and culturally. Contract: Full-time, permanent

Strategic Leadership & Vision
Provide inspirational leadership and a clear, compelling vision aligned with the charity’s mission and values
Develop and deliver a long-term strategy that strengthens impact, reach, and sustainability
Lead organisational growth while safeguarding programme quality and ethos
Organisational Leadership
Lead, motivate, and support a skilled and passionate staff team
Foster a healthy, inclusive, and high-performing organisational culture
Ensure robust governance, risk management, and regulatory compliance
Finance & Sustainability

Drive income diversification through fundraising, partnerships, grants, and trading activity
Work closely with the Board on financial strategy and accountability
External Relations & Advocacy
Act as the principal ambassador and spokesperson for Wilderness Foundation UK
Build and maintain strong relationships with funders, partners, commissioners, and stakeholders
Represent the charity within the nature, conservation, wellbeing, and youth sectors
Programme & Impact Oversight
Ensure the delivery of high-quality, evidence-based nature and wilderness programmes
Champion innovation in nature-based education and therapy
Uphold strong monitoring, evaluation, and learning to demonstrate impact
Why Join Wilderness Foundation UK?
This is a rare opportunity to lead a respected and impactful organisation where nature is not a backdrop, but the catalyst for change. As CEO, you will shape lives, protect wild places, and guide a charity that stands at the intersection of wellbeing, education, and conservation.
If you are a leader who believes that nature can heal people and people can protect nature, Wilderness Foundation UK would love to hear from you.

https://rravs.org.uk/feed/.title: Free Online Training – Preventing Radicalisation
https://rravs.org.uk/feed/.text:
Prevent is part of the UK’s counter-terrorism strategy. It focuses on offering early support to individuals who may be vulnerable to radicalisation.  For the voluntary and community sector, Prevent is about noticing when someone might need help and connecting them with the right services before issues escalate. It is purely about safeguarding, early intervention, and support—not monitoring communities.   This training is available to all staff from Voluntary and Community Sector Organisations within the County Of Essex.
What will the training cover?
Background: An overview of CONTEST, The Prevent Duty, an understanding of Terrorism legislation and the current national picture. ·
Ideologies: What is meant by an extremist ideology, antisemitism and an overview of the ideologies behind and some of the symbols used by Islamist Extremists, Far Right Extremists and Emerging/Other Ideologies (Left-Wing, Anarchist & Single Issue, Incel, Fascination With Extreme Violence Or Mass Casualty Attacks, The Com Network).
Understanding Radicalisation: Four stages of radicalisation, influencing factors, what to look out for, online radicalisation, the ‘notice check share procedure’ and what happens when someone is referred to Prevent.
ACT Early: An introduction to ACT Early, outlining the support available, how it can assist you, and the appropriate channels for making contact.
When?
Wednesday 27th January, 10:00-12:00
Tuesday 27th April, 10:00-12:00
Where?
MS Teams

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Victorian Christmas Market raises £6k for charity
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Festive season begins with charity Christmas Market
MUSIC, performances, stalls and food ushered in the festive season with Tendring’s biggest charity Christmas market on Saturday.
Community Voluntary Services Together (CVST) hosted its annual Victorian Christmas Market at Clacton Town Hall on Saturday, 14th November.
Shoppers were welcomed in by festive music from the Salvation Army band and volunteers dressed in Victorian outfits on the door.
Inside there were 26 charity stalls selling Christmas decorations, fairtrade items, toys, jewellery, gifts and more – with all money raised on each stall kept by that charity.
More than £6,000 was raised on the day for charities and good causes.
Lisa Andrews, chief executive of CVST, said: “The Victorian Christmas market is our flagship event and not only does it support us as a charity, but it’s our way of supporting charities and good causes in Tendring at Christmas time too.
“It was such a lovely atmosphere and really got us all into the Christmas spirit.
“We had a scrooge, some amazing Victorian dresses, and truly beautiful stalls.
“Plus, the wonderful performances including those from Young Minds Dementia Choir, Kaleidoscope, SingalongaPen, Seated Dance, Princes Youth Theatre, the Panto stars, and more.
“Thank you to everyone for making such an effort with the decorations and costumes and really making the event so brilliant.”
Competition…
The winner of best costume was Kevin Burns from the Clacton branch of Parkinsons UK, while the winner of the best decorated stall was Grassroots charity – winners each won a free stall for next years’ event.
For more information about CVST’s events and activities visit the website at www.cvstogether.org.uk.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Hello from Mark
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Hello CVST!
from Mark Warwick (trustee)
The background…
Having spent many years visiting Clacton and the surrounding area, my wife and I decided to move from London to this lovely part of the country. We were confident that we were making the right decision and we have not been disappointed, spending lazy days on the beach, making new friends and discovering places that we never knew existed.
We felt at home straight away having found such a strong, friendly and welcoming community offering lots of different activities which has led to our foray into line dancing, bowling, yoga and singing!
Meeting CVST
One of the first places I came across when I moved to the area in April was Kennedy Way Community Gardens. I was so taken with the garden, which is a tranquil space near the Kennedy Way Surgery in Clacton with wildflowers and vegetable patches, seating and a Men’s Shed, I applied to be a volunteer. Now I spend time in the garden volunteering with some wonderful people and have helped at open day events showcasing the amazing space.
Mark in the polytunnel at Kennedy Way Community Garden
The gardens are an inclusive space for those who want to become part of the local community. It is also a safe space to help improve physical health and benefiting mental wellbeing.
I have enjoyed immensely being part of this community project, which in turn has given me the opportunity to become a Trustee for CVST.
Becoming a trustee
Having become a volunteer at the garden I began to learn more about CVST as a charitable organisation and learned about all the other wonderful projects and work it does across the district of Tendring. I couldn’t believe CVST did so much! Walks, befriending groups, craft clubs, dementia support, training, litter picking, allotments, networking, supporting other charities and community groups and more! So when the opportunity came to join the board of trustees I was excited to get involved. Communities thrive because of organisations like CVST and I’m so pleased to be able to be part of that now and help shape the future.
What I bring to the table
As well as being a Young Carer and more recently an Adult Carer, I have also worked in the health and social care sector for over twenty years in various roles, supporting vulnerable young people and adults with a wide range of disabilities and diagnosed conditions,
I have  worked on a number of projects in collaboration with organisations such as AgeUK, Mind, the NHS and various local authorities.
Although new to the post, of a Trustee I will bring my lived experience, skills and expertise to the role to complement the excellent work that the CVST volunteers, staff, senior management team and board have done over many, many years and help ensure our charity remains completely transparent and accountable, proving to our funders, volunteers, and local community exactly what a positive impact we are making.
Looking forward
I attended the 2026 CVST AGM – my first as a trustee, and loved seeing so many staff and volunteers and members of the local community. It’s a privilege to be part of such a fantastic charity.
I look forward to seeing those of you that I have yet to meet and working alongside my fellow trustees to support CVST in continuing to make a huge difference to residents in Tendring.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Kennedy Way Community Garden Celebrates 5 Years of Community Spirit
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
The Kennedy Way Community Garden 5th Anniversary Open Day was a beautiful sunny day of music, joy, networking, cake and importantly – togetherness.
More than 250 staff, volunteers, community groups, local representatives and members of the public came together to celebrate the fifth anniversary of CVST’s Kennedy Way Community Garden at a special Open Day filled with stories, performances, creativity and community spirit.
The event welcomed Susannah Dutton, High Sheriff of Essex; Councillor Ann Oxley, Chair of Tendring District Council; Bill Davidson, former Chair of Tendring District Council; Jane Taylor from the NHS Essex ICB; and Brenda Ellis BEM, Chair of CVST, alongside many others who have helped make the garden such a special place.
A dream brought to life
The day was an opportunity to celebrate five years of hard work, determination and community collaboration, and to recognise the people who have helped turn a vision into reality.
Lynn, who works at Kennedy Way and coordinates its groups, was among those celebrating the garden’s journey. Mo, a much loved and long serving volunteer, represented the dedication of the people who helped establish the project and continue to support it.
Jane Taylor brought the story of Kennedy Way to life in a delightful fairy tale about the dream of creating the garden, the villains of COVID and those who said no, and the heroes whose determination helped make it happen.
The High Sheriff of Essex, Susannah Dutton, also shared her appreciation for the garden. Having visited many places through her role, she explained that only a few really get under her skin and make her want to return; and Kennedy Way is one of them.
It was a fitting tribute to a place that means so much to the people who visit, volunteer and spend time there.
CVST Chief Executive Lisa Andrews thanked the staff and volunteers whose commitment has made the garden what it is today, expressing pride in everything they have achieved together.
More than a garden
Since opening in October 2021, Kennedy Way Community Garden has grown into a welcoming, inclusive space where people can connect with others, develop skills, enjoy the outdoors and support their wellbeing.
The project is a collaboration between CVST, NHS Property Services and the local NHS system. What began as a community garden has developed to include a Community Hub and Upcycling Hub, alongside the Men’s Shed, gardening activities and opportunities to get involved in creative projects.
There are raised beds, vegetable and flower gardens, wildlife-friendly areas, an orchard, a pond, accessible paths and outdoor fitness equipment. The sensory garden and quieter spaces offer further opportunities for visitors to enjoy the surroundings at their own pace. On this sunny Wednesday, the rosemary and lavender shrubs smelled incredible.
The garden also plays an important role in bringing people together. Its activities provide opportunities for people experiencing loneliness or isolation, people with disabilities and those looking to improve their physical and mental wellbeing to find connection, purpose and friendship.
CVST’s Impact Report recorded 3,900 attendances at the garden and over 500 community activities in a year. This is a remarkable reflection of how much the space has become part of local community life.
Celebrating local talent
The anniversary celebrations showcased the creativity and talents of the people who make Kennedy Way such a vibrant place.
Visitors enjoyed performances from African Families in UK , the Walton Feel Good Choir and Party Dance , a CVST group (funded by Active Essex) led by Sarah Kamara.
Craft stalls offered handmade items created by groups and volunteers, celebrating the skills people have developed and the things they make together. Visitors could also enjoy a tombola, raffle and the Guess the Acorns challenge to win a £20 Amazon voucher.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Celebrating Volunteer Managers
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
At CVST, we see every day how volunteering strengthens local organisations and brings people together. Behind every successful volunteer role is usually someone quietly making sure people feel welcomed, guided and encouraged often while juggling three conversations, a printer that has given up and a meeting that started five minutes ago.
As Volunteer Managers you are not just filling gaps on a rota. You are helping people feel at home and share what they have to offer. It is quiet, steady, important work and it makes a real difference in our communities.
For those of us who support volunteers, our role is about much more than keeping things ticking over. At its heart, volunteering is about people choosing to give a little bit of themselves to something that matters. It is the responsibility of everyone within our organisations to help make people feel that they are a welcome and useful part of the team.
Warm welcomes matter
We all know the difference a friendly face can make. A welcoming hello, a proper introduction and someone taking the time to explain things can help to turn first-day nerves into confidence. A cup of tea may not solve everything, but it is often a very good place to start!
People come through your door for all sorts of reasons. They may want to learn something new, support a cause close to their heart, or simply to meet others and feel useful again. If we take time to understand what has brought them to us, we are much more likely to help them find the right place in your organisation.
Not everyone volunteers in the same way
Some people can give a regular morning every week. Others can help now and again, from home or at an event. Or maybe they can help with that one small but very important task that somehow saves the day. What’s important is that the more flexible we can be, the more people we can include.
Volunteers usually bring far more than the role they first sign up for. They also bring with them their life experience and local knowledge, their kindness, practical skills and their ideas. Sometimes our job as Volunteer Managers is simply to spot those gifts and give people the confidence to use them.
Keeping people connected
Good volunteer management is as much about listening as leading. Checking in, saying thank you and being clear about expectations and being honest when something is not working all help build trust.
Life changes too. We know that work, health, caring responsibilities and family life can all affect how much time someone has to give. If we can keep the door open even when someone needs to step back, we show that they are valued as a person and not just for the hours they can offer our organisations.
So, to every Volunteer Manager quietly keeping things moving, thank you for all you do. You help people take that first step and get involved in their communities in ways that can change people’s lives… including their own.
Join us at our next Volunteer Managers Network at Imperial House, Rosemary Road, Clacton on 2 October at 8.30am , where we’ll be discussing how AI tools can support volunteer management by saving time and enhancing volunteer recruitment, engagement and recognition.
A great opportunity to connect with peers, share experiences and learn something new over a coffee. To book, click here for the booking page or email events@cvstogether.org.uk .

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Spotlight on Young Minds and how CVST helped it begin
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
By Karen Barber
The 10-Year Fight for Answers :
After 10 years of exemplary promotions and appraisals in the civil service, I was dismissed due to poor performance caused by a disease that took a decade to diagnose. It was a relief to finally get that diagnosis. Even though medical professionals told me it was all in my mind, I knew something was wrong.
Falling Through the Gaps :
After attending a cognitive therapy course at the Kingswood Centre in Colchester Hospital, I found there was no support out there for people of my age; I simply did not fit into the more senior groups. There is such a gap for people with young onset dementia, and it is unacceptable that we are just being forgotten. I decided to help others like myself who fell through the gaps without the support we needed.
Building a Vision with Community Partners :
I am so grateful for the community partners who understood the need. The Stroke and Wellness Foundation for hiring us a hall, and Sports for Confidence who designed our logo and poster when we had no funds. To CVST who when I contacted them believed in the project, my vision, p assion, and ambition, they are a true example of how a voluntary service should work by helping with advice, policies, and providing my excellent volunteers, who have worked tirelessly and with all this support we have made it a success. Together, we opened the Young Minds Dementia Group and secured grants from Grassroots, the Tudwick Foundation, and the Essex Foundation.
Speaking Out in Parliament and the Media :
Our group is steadily growing. I am speaking out not for myself, but for everyone out there who does not have a voice. I’ve raised awareness on ITV Anglia, in Alzheimer’s Magazine, and an upcoming Daily Mail article. In May, I was invited to speak in Parliament, where I made our message clear:
Dementia needs to be a medical condition not a social care issue… We will not be silenced, we are valued members of society, yet for far too long we have been forgotten. We are the nation’s untapped capital, not a burden to be managed.”
My Vision for the Future : It shouldn’t be on people like me to establish these groups to make our own support. Unless action is taken, the vacuum of care will only deepen into a social catastrophe. My vision is to get charity status and funding to see Young Minds Dementia Groups across Essex, rectifying this inequality so that we are finally seen, supported, and valued. I couldn’t do this without the support of my excellent volunteers and community support of CVST and so many organisations in Tendring. I thank you all for believing in my vision and for not letting those with young onset dementia be forgotten

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Volunteering Looks Like This
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Volunteers Week 2026: Volunteering Looks Like This
Volunteers Week is the time we pause, reflect and, most importantly, say a heartfelt thank you to all the people who give their time, skills and energy to support others across our community.
At CVST, we see every day the difference volunteers make – whether that is volunteering for us or for the many brilliant organisations across Tendring. From supporting weekly friendship groups, to helping teach others new skills, to bringing ideas, kindness and practical help where it’s needed most – volunteering is at the heart of a stronger, more connected Tendring.
‘Volunteering Looks Like This’
This year, our Volunteers Week campaign is called Volunteering Looks Like This , and it’s all about showing the true diversity of volunteering.
Volunteering doesn’t look just one way.
It looks like:
A volunteer trustee helping guide a local organisation
Someone giving a few hours a month to support a community group
A volunteer befriender offering time and compassion
People sharing professional skills, lived experience or simply a willingness to help
Individuals of all ages, backgrounds and abilities making a difference in their own way
Through our campaign, we’re celebrating real volunteers and real stories – highlighting that every contribution matters , whether it’s a little time or a long-term commitment.
Saying Thank You
To everyone who volunteers – whether through a charity, community group, or informally in your neighbourhood – thank you . Your generosity helps organisations survive and thrive, supports vulnerable people, and builds communities where people care for one another.
We’d also like to thank the organisations who support volunteers, create welcoming opportunities, and recognise the value of volunteering in all its forms.
Why Volunteering Matters
Volunteering matters because it changes lives.
For local charities and community groups, volunteers are often the difference between a service existing or not. They bring time, skills, passion and local knowledge that help organisations respond to real needs in their communities.
For individuals, volunteering can reduce loneliness, improve wellbeing, build confidence and open doors to new skills and opportunities. It allows people to connect and play an active role in shaping the place where they live.
And for communities, volunteering builds resilience and connection. It brings people together across generations and backgrounds, strengthens local networks, and helps ensure that support is there when it’s needed most.
That’s why at CVST, we believe volunteering isn’t just about giving time — it’s about creating stronger, kinder and more inclusive communities .
Get Involved
If you’re interested in volunteering, or if your organisation needs volunteers, CVST is here to help. We can support you to find opportunities, promote roles, and strengthen volunteering across the district.
Look at volunteering opportunities at
This Volunteers’ Week, let’s celebrate the people who make a difference — and show that volunteering really does look like this .

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: We provide the “hidden wiring” connecting Tendring
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Behind the people, the services, and the organisations in Tendring sits a layer of support that often goes unseen, the “hidden wiring” that keeps everything connected and working smoothly.
That hidden wiring is exactly the role CVST plays. Across Tendring, we work to bring people and organisations together. We help local groups navigate challenges and build their capacity to grow in ways that make them more sustainable. We advocate for the voluntary sector so that the voices of smaller and marginalised organisations are heard in the rooms where decisions are made. We help create the conditions where volunteering gives local people meaningful ways to contribute to the place they call home.
For our partners, this means having a trusted bridge into the community; an organisation that understands the local landscape and can convene the right people to help shape solutions that reflect real lived experience. For local groups, it means having someone in your corner offering the practical support that hopefully will help you to thrive rather than just survive.
.
Report highlights what makes good infrastructure
The National Association for Voluntary and Community Action’s (NAVCA) latest report on what good local infrastructure looks like really connects with CVST’s work as it talks about something that we see every day in Tendring… that when people have places to connect and services that genuinely understand their needs, the whole community becomes more healthy and confident.
https://www.navca.org.uk/news/what-does-good-local-vcse-infrastructure-look-like
What this NAVCA report highlights is that good infrastructure isn’t about a particular structure or model, it’s about relationships and collaboration. That’s why at CVST we invest so much time in listening to local groups and building strong partnerships with partners and funders. When those relationships are strong, it feels like everything else is more possible.
We run a number of different opportunities for groups and organisations to come together to share their skills, knowledge and experiences. For more information look around this website or email events@cvstogether.org.uk. If you’re a local partner, funder or voluntary sector organisations or community group who wants to work together to strengthen our area, we’re always ready for a conversation!
The NAVCA report makes a powerful point. When local infrastructure is recognised and properly resourced, the whole system benefits. Public services become more effective, voluntary and community organisations and groups become stronger, and local people feel more connected and able to take part in their communities. Who doesn’t want to be a part of that?
.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Proud to be a Trustee
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
What a journey I have had over the last two years. I have always ensured I have given something back to the community I live in and have had several different volunteering roles in the past including being a chair of governors for a primary school and an Ambulance Community First Responder.
My journey into trusteeship began at the CVST AGM in September 2023. A presentation was given about trusteeship and an offer from CVST’s Yvette Wetton to provide more of an insight into what being a trustee entails and to support me in finding an organisation that my skills would align with. Following a very fruitful conversation with Yvette, I went away with a renewed passion and very soon after I applied to be a trustee at the Youth Enquiry Service. Following a successful interview and completing the mandatory Trustee training provided by the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW) I formally became a trustee in April 2024.
I have found my first 18 months as a trustee very rewarding, working alongside my fellow trustees undertaking a skills audit and enabling each of us to be aligned to a head of section depending on our skills and background. This has been a very supportive way to enable a collaborative approach to the challenges around funding and working differently in this uncertain time across the sector. Being there to support the CEO, offering advice and support and understanding more about the service offerings has provided me with a sense of pride in being part of an amazing organisation which supports one of our most vulnerable cohorts across North East Essex, our young people.
The time commitment as a trustee is flexible, you can give as much or as little as you are able as long as you manage your statutory duties in reviewing board meeting documents such as budget papers, heads of service reports and provide constructive feedback as part of the regular board meetings, which are held bi monthly with an option of face to face and MS teams.
If you ever want to get more involved with a ‘special community voluntary sector faith enterprise group’ in your area please do so – we all have transferable skills that could make a real difference and a greater impact than you could imagine to many people in your community.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Why I became a trustee – and why you should too by Ali Blake
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Why I, Alistair Blake, became a Trustee (And why you should consider it too)
Eight years ago, I became a trustee, despite concerns I wasn’t qualified enough or have enough time. Today I chair the board.
How and why, I became a Trustee
My journey with Summit Services began in 2008. Having just finished a multimedia degree and struggling to find work the media sector, I took a receptionist position at what was then called ‘The Advocacy Service’ in Clacton, where I grew up. I didn’t know what advocacy was or have any understanding of mental health services. But I quickly fell in love with the work – largely driven by amazing mentors, the passion of the staff and witnessing first-hand the impact on people’s lives.
Over the next few years, I trained as an advocate and also used my skills in unexpected ways from developing interactive and accessible materials to running music groups and sports teams.
But I still dreamed of working in media, and in late 2011, an opportunity to work for a television company came up which I couldn’t refuse. So, I moved to London and spent the next few years doing exactly what I’d always planned.
Yet something was missing. And as I became more aware of my own mental health, I reflected on how critical Summit’s work was.
That’s when I thought about trusteeship. Despite concerns about what I could offer and whether I’d have enough time, I got in contact, went through the interview process, and was appointed to the board.
What does being a Trustee actually involve?
We meet formally every 6 weeks, with occasional sub-committee work between. Some months it’s just a few hours; others require more time when we’re navigating challenges or establishing new initiatives. But it’s manageable alongside full-time work and family.
As Trustees, we provide governance and strategic direction, ensure financial sustainability, and support the CEO and staff team. It’s not about doing day-to-day work; our excellent staff do that. It’s about acting in the best interest of our beneficiaries and ensuring the organisation can continue its mission effectively.
What Have I Learned?
In eight years as a trustee, now as Chair, I’ve seen enormous change. Leadership transitions, funding and service evolution, staff and trustees moving on. What hasn’t changed is our mission: Advocating Empowerment. Supporting Independence.
Clacton has the second-highest mental health need in the country and seven areas in Tendring are among the most deprived 10% in England. While the statistics are eye-opening, behind every statistic is a person – someone struggling to access support, someone feeling isolated, or someone simply trying to live a fulfilled and independent life. Which is why this work really matters.
What surprised me most about trusteeship is how much my perspective counts. My media and business experience has practical value, but the real contribution is diverse thinking. The board needs people who aren’t necessarily mental health professionals, people who ask different questions and represent the community we serve.
I still don’t feel I give enough time. I still sometimes question what I offer. But I’ve learned that’s okay and what really matters is showing up, having a voice, and bringing genuine commitment.
What do I get out of it?
There’s the satisfaction of contributing to meaningful work, staying connected to advocacy while pursuing my corporate career. But I’ve also developed skills in governance, strategic thinking, and leadership that I would not have gained otherwise. I’ve been part of decisions that genuinely changed outcomes for people in our community.
Why you should consider it
Tendring’s voluntary organisations need trustees. Not just people with medical, legal or financial backgrounds, but people with all kinds of experiences: project management, HR, marketing, IT, lived experience, or simply a passion for the cause and willingness to learn.
If you’re thinking you aren’t qualified or don’t have time – I thought the same.

A message from Eden, our Volunteer Co-ordinator
Last week I headed along to Thurrock Cares’ Warm Up for Winter event, this time hosted at Tilbury Community Association.

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Father and Son Cycle 500km From Plymouth to Southend-on-Sea in Aid of Local Hospice Care
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
A father and son have cycled 500km from Plymouth to Fair Havens adults’ hospice in Southend-on-Sea, raising over £4,000 in memory of their father-in-law and grandfather, Paul Wellsteed.
James (45) and Ted Warne (17) arrived at Fair Havens on 31st October after six gruelling days cycling from their home in Noss Mayo, a village near Plymouth.
The pair began their journey after the passing of Storms Austen and Boelo and faced mixed weather conditions, from heavy rain to misty mornings. They cycled around 80km per day and, after three days, took a day off to rest when they both fell ill. Despite the difficult setback, they continued to push on for a further three days and were welcomed at Fair Havens by family, close friends, and staff.
James has previously completed the London to Southend bike ride, but for Ted, this was his first long-distance cycling experience, making the achievement even greater.
Paul sadly died from stage four bile-duct cancer in June, having been cared for by Fair Havens. The money his son-in-law and grandson have raised will help Havens Hospices continue giving expert, compassionate care to people of all ages living with incurable conditions, and to families just like theirs.
When reflecting upon their experience, James said, “Ted and I decided to do this ride after seeing Grandad being cared for at Fair Havens. We wanted to take on a challenge in his memory, while also giving back to the hospice that cared for him and our family.
“We moved to Devon eight years ago from Leigh-on-Sea and it felt like a good idea to cycle from our new home to our old home.
“Spending quality time with Ted, taking in the scenery and seeing my wife, Amy, waiting for us at the end of three very long, difficult days – these are memories I’ll always remember.”
Susie May, Fundraising Officer at Havens Hospices, said, “All of our care and support is provided free of charge, and that’s only possible because of generous people like James and Ted. Cycling 500km in memory of Paul is a remarkable thing to do, and we’re so grateful they chose to support Havens Hospices in his memory.”
To support James and Ted’s cycling challenge, visit their JustGiving page: www.justgiving.com/page/tedandjamesplymouthtosouthend

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Chelmsford family’s tribute to the hospice that helped them make memories with baby son
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
A Chelmsford couple whose baby son died at Little Havens when he was just 36 days old are sharing their story to ensure other families have the same chance to make those precious memories together.
Michael and Sarah Fragnito’s son Elio spent the last two days of his life at Little Havens, the children’s hospice run by Havens Hospices. Now, the couple are supporting the hospice’s ‘Big “Yes!” Christmas Appeal’ so that other families have the same chance to hear “yes” when it matters most.
The idea behind its Big Yes! appeal is simple: the hospice’s nurses can only say “Yes!” to the people they care for if the community says “Yes!” to Havens Hospices.
“Our son Elio was just 36 days old when he died, peacefully in our arms at Little Havens,” they said. “Grief is awful, but love comes out on top. And Little Havens gave us the chance to fill Elio’s life with love.”
Elio was born after a straightforward pregnancy. “He was perfect,” said Michael and Sarah. “Everything felt normal.”
But within 36 hours, Elio became critically unwell. He was rushed into intensive care and then transferred to Great Ormond Street Hospital, where doctors found he had a rare and serious heart condition that hadn’t been picked up during pregnancy.
“The weeks that followed were filled with uncertainty, operations and hope that rose and fell daily,” they said. “For much of that time, we couldn’t hold him because he was connected to so many wires and machines. When we were finally able to cuddle our son again, it meant everything.”
Eventually, the family were told nothing more could be done, and Elio’s care would focus on keeping him comfortable. They were offered a choice: to stay in hospital, try to take him home, or go to Little Havens.
“At first, we didn’t want to go to a hospice. We wanted him at home. His bedroom was ready for him,” they said. “But we also knew what was coming. When we visited Little Havens, everything changed.
“You expect somewhere clinical and depressing, but it wasn’t like that at all. It was calm, peaceful… it just felt safe. Everyone spoke to us like human beings. It felt like they were living this with us, not just treating us.”
“In hospital everything feels urgent, but at Little Havens, time slowed down,” said Michael and Sarah. “And that’s when the Care Team started saying yes.”
The family carried Elio around the gardens, and the team arranged a photographer so they could have proper family photos, something the couple say they wouldn’t have thought to ask for.
“As the tubes and equipment were removed, it felt like we had our baby back,” they said. “We were able to do things that had felt impossible in hospital.”
They decorated Elio’s room with a piece of wallpaper from home and drawings from his big sister, and watched films together, lying on the bed as a family. The team brought a little bath into the room so they could bathe him for the first time, and afterwards they sat together and had lunch with him, the double doors open onto the gardens.
“These are things you dream about doing with your baby,” they said. “It had been really hot since Elio was born and then it started to rain. So, we took him outside to feel the rain on his face. It felt so important letting him experience the world, even for a little while.
“The two days we were at Little Havens were the most tragic days of our lives – but also two of the most beautiful. If we’d stayed in hospital, we probably would have just sat by his bed waiting. But at Little Havens, they encouraged us to live, to make memories, not just wait. They helped make something horrendous bearable. We have memories that make us smile, not just memories of panic and fear.”
“Elio spent most of his life in hospital, but we will always associate his life with Little Havens,” said Michael and Sarah. “There’s never been a single regret about our time there. https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Irene remembers husband Trevor with a robin, one year after he died on Christmas morning
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Irene remembers husband Trevor with a robin, one year after he died on Christmas morning.
Irene Paskins is remembering her husband, Trevor, this Christmas by dedicating a robin in his memory through Havens Hospices’ Robins of Remembrance appeal.
Trevor was cared for by Fair Havens for nearly three years after he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. This will be the family’s first Christmas without him, and Irene’s robin will hang on the Christmas tree outside the hospice that meant so much to him.
Irene said: “Fair Havens and the whole team held a special place in Trevor’s heart. They supported him wonderfully for nearly three years, and that is where he chose to spend his final few days.
“He passed away peacefully on Christmas morning last year, surrounded by our family and the care team who meant so much to him. We have donated in Trevor’s name to Robins of Remembrance. We remember him every day, with love and gratitude for his life, and especially on this coming Christmas Day.”
Following the success of last year when over 1,000 robin decorations filled the Christmas trees outside the hospices, Robins of Remembrance again invites the local community to remember loved ones this winter.
For £18, supporters will receive a limited-edition robin decoration to hang on their tree at home, while a matching robin will be displayed on the Christmas trees at either Fair Havens in Prittlewell or Little Havens in Thundersley. Each robin is dedicated to a loved one, creating a display that celebrates the lives of people who are missed. The trees will be for everyone to see from 1 December 2026 to 3 January 2027.
Robins are often seen as a sign that loved ones are near, making them a fitting symbol for this time of year. All proceeds from the appeal go towards expert, compassionate care and support for people of all ages living with incurable conditions across Essex.
Karen Summers, Individual Giving Fundraising Manager at Havens Hospices, said: “We were overwhelmed by the community’s response to Robins of Remembrance last year, with over 1,000 dedications on our trees. This appeal gives families a meaningful way to honour their loved ones while supporting the care we provide.
“We’re so grateful to Irene for sharing Trevor’s story. It’s a privilege for our teams to care for people like Trevor and their families, and knowing his robin will be on our tree this Christmas means a great deal to all of us.
“As they fly into their third year, our robins are displayed together on our hospice Christmas trees, each one representing a life remembered and a love never forgotten. Your matching robin can hang on your tree at home, or anywhere else that brings you comfort and peace, as a unique way to honour someone special to you.
“You don’t have to have experienced our hospice care to join us. Everyone in our community is welcome, and your kind donations help us provide free, compassionate and expert care for local people and their families, this Christmas and beyond.”
To dedicate a robin in memory of a loved one, visit www.havenshospices.org.uk/robins

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: TV Star Ferne McCann returns to Essex’s only children’s hospice
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
TV personality and Patron of Little Havens, Ferne McCann, has returned to her local children’s hospice this Christmas to spend time with families, as she lends her support to The Big Christmas “Yes!” Appeal.
On Tuesday 17 th November, in her role as Patron, Ferne McCann visited Little Havens in Thundersley, which provides expert, compassionate care to babies, children and young adults across Essex.
She spent the evening with families cared for by the hospice, reconnecting with those she had met previously and getting to know others for the first time. Each family got to share personal stories with Ferne, from their everyday life at home to the care and memories they’ve found at Little Havens.
Jenna Whyman, mum to twins Raffy and Siddy, talks of the importance of Little Havens, “It means so much to families like mine. Being a medical parent means living with constant worries about Raffy and Siddy, navigating overwhelming demands, making impossible decisions, anticipating the next hospital admission and always being in a high state of vigilance. Little Havens gives us something that is so often taken away by SMA. It gives us time to step away and simply be parents. The moment we walk through the door we are welcomed with open arms, made a cuppa and given the chance to sit down, take a breath and just be Mum and Dad.
“There are no expectations, no judgements, just people who understand, help and take over responsibility to give us a break. Hearing the laughter and giggles of our children says more than words ever could about how much Little Havens means. It’s a place where they get to just be children which means the world when our lives are filled with all things medical.
“By Ferne raising awareness it helps people see what really happens behind those doors and understand the difference Little Havens makes, not just to our children but to our whole family. It’s a place that gives us moments of normality in a life that is far from a typical childhood, and that is something truly precious.”
Ferne also learned more about the charity’s Christmas campaign, The Big Christmas “Yes!” Appeal, which asks the local community to get involved in fundraising and say “Yes!” to Little Havens so that their nursing team can say “Yes!” to every family who needs them this Christmas.
At the visit Ferne has the chance hear Elio’s story, who was just 36 days old when he died peacefully in his parents’ arms at Little Havens. Although those final days were some of the toughest of his parents’ lives, Little Havens was able to say “Yes!”, whether that was supporting Elio’s parents, Michael and Sarah, to give him his first bath, or giving him the chance to go outside and feel the rain on his face.
