Talking about her visit to Little Havens, Ferne said, “Coming back to Little Havens this year, I felt the same way I did the first time. As soon as you walk in, you’re filled with warmth from the happiness, smiles and laughter you see from the families and the Care Team.

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Havens Hospices Reuse Shop Celebrates Selling 100 Tonnes of Pre-Loved Goods
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Havens Hospices’ Reuse Shop at the Stock Road Household Waste Recycling Centre has reached a major milestone, selling 100 tonnes of reused goods since opening in May 2025.
The local charity joined forces with SUEZ and Southend-on-Sea City Council to open the shop, giving quality, unwanted items a new home instead of sending them to landfill.
Everything on the shelves, from electrical appliances and furniture to toys, games, homeware and seasonal goods, is kindly donated by the local community. Every purchase reduces waste and helps fund the free hospice care Havens Hospices provides to people living with incurable conditions.
Since opening its doors, the shop has sold over £127,000 worth of second-hand goods, which equates to over 4,000 hours of care at Little Havens Children’s Hospice in Thundersley or Fair Havens Adult Hospice in Prittlewell.
Laura Matthews, SUEZ Senior Community Liaison Manager, said: “We are incredibly proud to have supported Havens Hospices in reaching this remarkable milestone. Every item donated, purchased and reused through the shop helps reduce waste and keeps valuable resources in use for longer. At the same time, it raises vital funds for hospice care across our community. It’s a wonderful example of how sustainability and social value can go hand in hand.”
Mark Davies, Head of Trading at Havens Hospices, said: “We’re incredibly proud to reach this milestone. Every tonne of pre-loved goods we sell is a tonne kept out of landfill, and every pound it raises helps fund the expert, compassionate care we provide to local families at Fair Havens and Little Havens. Thank you to everyone who has donated, shopped and helped us get here.”
Located at Stock Road Household Waste Recycling Centre, the shop lets residents easily donate and buy pre-loved items while also disposing of other recyclable waste. The opening hours of the shop can be viewed here: havenshospices.org.uk/shops/stock-road-recycling-centre-reuse-shop

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Local Swimmers Cross the English Channel and Raise Over £9,000 for Havens Hospices
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
A group of five friends from Burnham-on-Crouch challenged themselves by embarking on an open water relay swim across the English Channel in aid of a local hospice charity.
James Cliff, Andrew Bell, Madeline Raymond, Clare Boston and Stuart Sargeant, also known as the Burnham Gang, finished their relay in 10 hours and 50 minutes whilst fundraising for Havens Hospices. So far, they have raised over £9,000 to support the charity in providing expert, compassionate care to local children and adults of all ages living with incurable conditions.
The route is around 21 miles long across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, with powerful tidal movements, strong currents and cold water at temperatures of around 18°C.
The group made the decision to take on this challenge after visiting Fair Havens and Little Havens, the charity’s hospices for adults and children, and learning about the care they provide to families within the local community.
James, who also fundraised for the charity in 2023 by swimming across the English Channel solo, said, “We are keen open water swimmers and after seeing the incredible work of hospices firsthand by visiting Havens Hospices, we decided to fundraise by setting a hard challenge that would also stay with us as an amazing group memory.
“Standout memories were certainly made. Seasickness, jellyfish stings, swimming in the dark and narrowly avoiding big tankers! We swam on the night of the Harvest Moon and as we got to Cap Gris-Nez, it shone out at us just by the famous lighthouse.
“We’re all so pleased to have completed this challenge and knowing it was making a real difference to families helped get us through the tough moments.
“To all first-time fundraisers, it’s never too early to start fundraising ahead of your challenge. Don’t be afraid to keep asking and be inventive.”
Lucy Lock, Community Engagement Manager at Havens Hospices, said, “We want to say a huge thank you to the Burnham Gang. Swimming the English Channel through the night, with jellyfish, seasickness and tankers to contend with, is an incredible achievement, and we’re so grateful they chose to do it in aid of Havens Hospices.
“All of our care and support is provided absolutely free of charge, and we rely on the generosity of our community to make that possible. The money the Burnham Gang have raised goes towards expert, compassionate care for local families, whether that’s in our hospices, in the comfort of their own homes or out in the community, making every day count for the people who need us.”
The Burnham Gang are now calling on the local community to support them in their quest to continue raising vital funds for Havens Hospices by making a donation to their JustGiving page. The charity must raise more than £225,000 a week to be there for everyone who needs them, so every donation, no matter how small, will make a difference in supporting the hospice charity.
You can support the Burnham Gang’s fundraising efforts by donating to their JustGiving page: https://www.justgiving.com/page/burnhamrelay
The post Local Swimmers Cross the English Channel and Raise Over £9,000 for Havens Hospices appeared first on Havens Hospices .

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Havens Hospices launches school Santa Run campaign
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Havens Hospices is calling on local schools to organise a Santa Run, encouraging pupils to don their best festive outfits and run, walk or skip to raise funds for its expert, compassionate care.
The Essex charity has launched its Santa Run campaign, asking schools to become festive fundraisers by picking a date in December, running a route of their choice and setting up a JustGiving page to raise sponsorship.
Participation is free, and each school will receive a downloadable fundraising pack when they sign up. Resources include a poster template, an assembly video explaining Havens Hospices’ care, a certificate for those taking part, and a letter to parents and carers explaining how schools’ support makes a difference.
The charity encourages pupils and teachers to get in the Christmas spirit by wearing Santa hats, Christmas jumpers, or festive fancy dress. To make the campaign sustainable and low-cost, Havens Hospices suggests using what pupils already have at home.
By taking part, schools can help Little Havens Hospice support more children like Teddy to make every day of their lives count.
Teddy was diagnosed with Dravet syndrome at four years old, and Little Havens has supported his family ever since.
Jasmine, Teddy’s mum, says, “Little Havens provides a safe space where all of Teddy’s needs are met. If we didn’t have Little Havens, our lives would be very difficult.”
Havens Hospices must raise more than £225,000 each week to support families like Teddy’s.
£31 could pay for an hour of expert care at Little Havens, providing care during a respite break, emergency stay or support at the end of a child’s/ or young person’s life.
£50 could provide a session of complementary therapy for someone we care for, helping them to relax, ease anxiety and even reduce pain caused by their condition.
£160 could provide a pool session at Little Havens with two of our Care Team, or a family swim session. Children can feel weightless and move more freely, while lights, floats, and bubbles offer rich sensory experiences, helping reduce stress and relax tense muscles.
Schools can find out more or sign up to the Santa Run campaign here: havenshospices.org.uk/christmas/santa-run

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: When Christmas brings heartbreak: New Essex business launches to help people navigate separation
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
After experiencing the breakdown of her own 21-year relationship just weeks before Christmas, Clacton based Ann Scott is turning personal experience into practical support for others facing separation.
Christmas is often portrayed as a time of family, happiness and togetherness. But for people facing the end of a relationship, it can be one of the loneliest and most difficult times of the year.
While the world seems to be preparing to celebrate, some people are quietly facing the prospect of a very different future. Questions about where they will live, how they will manage financially and how they begin again can feel impossible to answer.
It is against this backdrop that Essex entrepreneur Ann Scott is launching The Ember Path ; a separation navigation service designed to help people make sense of the practical realities of relationship breakdown with clarity, confidence and support.
The service is for people across Essex, married or unmarried, whether they are the person initiating the separation or the one coming to terms with it.
For Ann, this is far more than a business idea. It comes from a place of deeply personal experience.
“Less than two weeks before Christmas, I was faced with the devastating blow of discovering infidelity in my 21-year relationship. That, in itself, is hard to process, but then comes the realisation that the future you had planned is gone in just one conversation.
“When your partner of over two decades tells you that someone significantly younger that he’s known for just two months and her children are now his priority, it’s certainly a shock. Even more so when you learn they are planning to move them into your home! It felt like jumping out a plane – not only are you winded by the rush of air to your chest but you have no idea where you will land.
“While other people were thinking about presents, celebrations and family gatherings, I was facing a future I didn’t want and had never planned for. I had a seemingly endless list of practical questions and decisions to make; it was overwhelming as I didn’t know where to start and who I could trust or afford for advice.
“Thankfully, I work with small businesses across Essex in my full-time employment and had a network of trusted connections at my fingertips. They were able to guide and signpost me, so I felt more confident in the decisions I was making”.
It was this experience that planted the seed for Ann’s business.
Separation is one of the most stressful and financially consequential experiences a person can face. Yet while solicitors guide people through the legal process and therapists help them deal with their emotions, there is often a huge gap between the two.
That gap is where The Ember Path sits.
What paperwork needs completing? How do you separate your finances? What happens to the mortgage? What decisions need to be made about the family home? Who should you speak to, and in what order?
The Ember Path helps people make sense of these questions, breaking an overwhelming situation into manageable steps and introducing them to trusted professionals; including solicitors, mortgage brokers and conveyancers. Accessing the right support at the right time is vital, particularly when stress can cloud judgement and decisions can have lifelong consequences.
“This isn’t about someone telling you how to feel or what decisions to make, as every situation is unique and only you will know what feels right. But I know how important it is to have someone to help you understand the options available and get specialist advice.
“I found myself ploughing through the practicalities of separating two lives on a daily basis for months – household bills, property deeds, mortgages, loans, credit cards, joint bank accounts, equity calculations… It was exhausting and all consuming.
“If I’d had the type of support being offered by The Ember Path myself, it would have been that parachute I needed after being pushed out the plane”.

Winning Small Business of the Year 2026 at the Epping Forest Business Awards is an important milestone in my professional journey. It also reflects the philosophy behind my business: businesses should be concentrating on growing and thriving, not losing valuable time, money and human energy to avoidable disputes.
My background working within litigation teams showed me first-hand what happens when commercial relationships break down. The financial cost is only part of the story. Management time, damaged relationships, lost opportunities and the pressure on everyone involved can be far more difficult to quantify.
Even a court order does not necessarily bring the stress to an end. Compliance, enforcement and the practical implementation of an outcome can create further expense and uncertainty. The real measure of a solution is whether it works in practice.
That is why my approach places such importance on implementation. In mediation, I focus not simply on reaching an agreement, but on whether the proposed solution is realistic, workable and capable of being put into effect.
A different perspective on business risk
What distinguishes Schumann Strategic is the combination of my professional experience and technical knowledge. Alongside my legal background and mediation work, I hold Cisco cybersecurity accreditation and am a member of the British Computer Society (BCS).
I bring together an understanding of litigation, commercial relationships, governance, data protection and cybersecurity. This enables me to recognise how a weakness in a contract, an internal policy or an information-security process can become a commercial, legal or reputational problem.
Cybersecurity is not simply an IT concern. It has implications for contractual obligations, client confidentiality, data protection and business reputation. Understanding these connections allows me to approach business risks from both a commercial and technical perspective.
I provide independent commercial mediation and consultancy, helping businesses identify vulnerabilities, strengthen their arrangements and address issues before they become costly distractions. I am not a solicitor and do not provide reserved legal services. Where appropriate, clients can also access specialist legal representation through a Direct Access barrister.
For me, excellence is reflected not only in the positive Google reviews clients leave, but also in the disputes successfully de-escalated, the misunderstandings resolved and the situations that never need to become formal proceedings. Preventing a problem from escalating can be just as significant as resolving one that has already arisen.
My guiding principle is simple:
“We draft for the breakdown, not just the honeymoon.”
Is your business properly protected?
If you are a business owner, director or professional practice leader, ask yourself: are your agreements, governance and risk arrangements protecting the business you are building?
Don’t wait for a disagreement, data incident or contractual failure to expose the gaps. Let’s identify them before they become expensive problems.
I offer a 15-minute introductory conversation to understand your concerns and identify where strategic mediation or commercial consultancy could add value.
Start with a conversation. Protect what you have worked hard to build.

Peter Richardson, Publishing Editor at BusinessTime in Essex, gets the ball rolling on a new feature on Business Wire in Essex – My Life in Business.
MY working life started back in 1978 (yes, I know, it’s quite a while back now!) when, at the age of 19, I joined the East Anglian Daily Times as a junior reporter.
James Callaghan was Prime Minister and the winter of discontent lie just ahead. More pertinently, I was writing my stories on a manual typewriter. Younger readers might want to Google winter of discontent and manual typewriter!
I’d long wanted to be a journalist, but what I really wanted was to be the next Brian Moore or John Motson football commentator. A stint on a regional newspaper was a mere short-term stepping stone, I thought. First lesson in adult life learned – keep your dreams realistic!
Instead of creating my own, ‘they think it’s all over’ moment’, I spent 12 very happy years in regional journalism, firstly reporting on some great stories (I spent a wet November afternoon trapsing around a north Essex graveyard looking for, and finding, the grave of Jack the Ripper – I’ll give the details to anyone who’s interested!) before climbing the greasy pole of promotion. The top of the pole culminated in me being appointed Group Editor of a 22-edion group of newspapers covering Essex and Greater London.
It was a largely hugely enjoyable time, but the pay was not great. I was paid for working a 37-hour week, but my average working week soaked up twice those hours. With a mortgage and two young children, I decided if I was working 70+ hours a week, I might as well try getting paid for most of those hours. I had started doing a little freelance media relations/PR work on the side (well, the kids had to be fed!) and soon realised there was much more money to be earned in PR than there was being a Newspaper Group Editor.
So, at 3am one morning I sat bolt upright in bed and proclaimed to my startled wife I was going to quit my job and work for myself. The most important decision of my working life had been made.
Whenever I look back, it still scares me at the magnitude of the decision. As I said, I had a mortgage and two young children – yet something just told me at that moment, it was the right decision. Second lesson in adult life learned – follow your gut instinct.
So, PJR Communications was born (it’s still my actual business name today, trading as BusinessTime in Essex) and a very enjoyable chapter began offering my media relations knowledge and experience to all and sundry. At one point there was hardly a new homes development in north Essex I didn’t handle the media relations for. Then a really big chapter began when I started working for the NHS, handing the comms and media relations for NHS Trusts across Essex before one of my biggest challenges – handling the media relations for Care UK when it became one of the country’s largest initial providers of the NHS 111 service when it was rolled out nationally back in 2013, in something somewhat less than a blaze of glory!
This was still the time when if you wanted exposure to the masses, newspapers were the way to go. However, the shadow of social media was looming ever larger. Increasingly, my existing clients and potential new clients were moving more of their budgets away from mainstream media and into social media and their websites. For the first time since I launched my own business back in 1989, I started to feel vulnerable in terms of workload.
Partly because of this (and partly, if you listen to my long-suffering wife, as my midlife crisis) I had another sit bolt upright in bed moment and decided, of all things, I was going to open a pancake parlour – as you do of course at the age of 46 and with no restaurant experience whatsoever other than eating far too many meals in other people’s restaurants. https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: Buying Fitted Kitchens Online: What Should Homeowners Check Before Ordering?
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
From cabinet construction and accurate measurements to quotations and delivery, a useful kitchen-buying checklist looks beyond the headline price.
A better starting point for a major purchase
Buying a new kitchen is one of the larger decisions in a home renovation. The cost matters, but so does getting the layout right, understanding what is being supplied and knowing how the order will be checked before production.
Today, homeowners can browse kitchen ranges, experiment with layouts and obtain indicative prices without starting with a showroom appointment. That extra freedom is valuable, provided it comes with clear specifications and practical checks. Whether you are planning a kitchen in Essex or elsewhere in the UK, the same questions apply.
Measure the room before choosing the units
A kitchen design should begin with accurate wall lengths, ceiling height and the position of doors, windows and fixed services. Radiators, boilers, pipework and the direction in which a door opens can all affect which cabinets will fit.
Online planning software can help visualise these details, but a drawing is only as dependable as the measurements entered. Before ordering, homeowners should check the final dimensions and confirm any site-specific requirements with their installer. Awkward corners and out-of-square walls deserve particular attention.
Compare the cabinet, not just the door colour
Two kitchens may look similar in photographs while differing significantly in construction. Ask about cabinet material and thickness, edging, shelves, drawer runners, hinges and whether soft-close hardware is included.
Check whether units arrive flat-packed or fully assembled. Flat-pack can be sensible for buyers comfortable with assembly, while rigid cabinets may reduce the amount of assembly required on site. The best value depends on the total supply-and-fitting cost, access to the property and the time available, not a blanket claim that one system always wins.
Find out exactly what the quotation includes
A headline kitchen price does not necessarily include every item needed to finish the room. Check whether the quotation covers doors and fronts, hinges, drawer systems, end panels, plinths, fillers, worktops, handles and appliance housings where required.
Then look at delivery, VAT, appliances and installation. A supply-only quotation should not be compared directly with an installed price unless those differences are made explicit. An itemised specification is often more useful than a large headline discount because it shows what you are actually buying.
Ask who checks the plan before the order is final
Kitchen layouts involve more than fitting cabinets along a wall. Drawer and door clearances, tall-unit placement, appliance ventilation, worktop joins and access around an island can all affect everyday use.
Even when a customer creates the first design independently, it is sensible to ask what review is available before the final order is released. A competent fitter or relevant tradesperson should confirm on-site dimensions and installation requirements; digital planning is not a substitute for those checks.
Understand delivery, changes and aftercare
Before paying a deposit, clarify the expected delivery process, how access is arranged, what to do if a component arrives damaged and which terms apply to changes or cancellations. Keep copies of the approved plan, itemised quotation and order documents.
A cabinet guarantee is worth reading in full. Confirm what components it covers, how a claim is made and any conditions that apply rather than relying on the number of years alone.
Online-first can still include personal support
An online kitchen supplier should make information easier to access, not leave customers to guess. For example, Fitted Kitchens offers a free online planning journey, product pricing and nationwide kitchen supply, with optional design assistance when customers need help reviewing their layouts and selections.

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: What’s Changing in the World of  Ceremony
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
Jane Elizabeth is a celebrant working across Essex, Suffolk, Hertfordshire and London.
Ceremonies are changing. Families are choosing what feels right for them rather than following one fixed pattern, and the rules and services around those choices are shifting too.  Families realise there are options and no one size fits all .
Three things I’m talking about with families and local businesses right now;-.
Could marriage law change?
This year the government consulted on reforming wedding law, in what has been described as the biggest overhaul in 200 years. The proposals, which follow the Law Commission’s 2022 recommendations, would shift the focus from regulating buildings which can hold  wedding ceremonies to regulating the people who conduct weddings. In time, that could allow independent celebrants to conduct legally binding marriages, and give couples more freedom over where and how they marry.
The consultation closed in September, but it’s important to be clear:  as at the end of 2026 nothing has changed yet.
There’s no timetable, and any change would need an Act of Parliament. For now, a celebrant-led ceremony  sits alongside a short, separate legal register office appointment.
For Essex venues and wedding businesses, it’s one to watch.
The rise of direct cremations
A direct cremation is a cremation without a traditional  funeral service. The person who has died is cremated without mourners present, and the ashes are usually returned to the family afterwards. Independent funeral directors take the utmost care of the deceased in exactly the same way as a traditional funeral- there just isn’t a ceremony at the same time and location as the cremation service .
Arrangements vary between providers.
It has become much more common.  In November 2026 research from the insurer SunLife puts direct cremations at around one in five UK funerals, compared with just 3% in 2019. Cost is a big part of the increase: the average direct cremation costs around £1,600, considerably less than an attended funeral. For some families it also simply feels right, with no formality and no pressure.
But many families still want to gather and remember. That is where a celebrant can help: a celebration of life ceremony  held at a time and place that suits, with the people, music and stories that matter, whether that’s weeks later, in a garden.pub or hall or a favourite beauty spot, or during a quiet moment to scatter ashes.
Direct cremation isn’t better or worse than a traditional funeral. It’ simply a different starting point.
Naming ceremonies and the role of guide parents
A naming ceremony is a warm, non-religious way to welcome a child into a family and
community. One aspect that often prompts questions is the role of guide parents.
Guide parents (sometimes called supporting adults) are people the parents choose to stand beside their child and make heartfelt promises: to be a trusted friend, to listen without judgement, to celebrate milestones, and to share something they love.
It’s a role similar in spirit to godparents, but without the religion, and shaped entirely by the family.
The promises  made by guide parents to a child aren’t legally binding, and the role is not the same as legal guardianship; that’s a separate matter to discuss with a solicitor.
A family can choose one guide parent, several, or none at all. The naming ceremony can still be joyous and significant .   Choosing guide parents is  simply a  heartfelt way to include the people who matter most to the family.
If you work with families across Essex, whether as a venue,  party planner,  mother and baby or parenting  group or in another child and family facing role, and you’d like to talk about any of this, I’d be glad to hear from you.
Email me at info@celebrantjaneelizabeth.co.uk or visit www.celebrantjaneelizabeth.co.uk for further information.

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: Essex business support organisation ranks among UK’s top four most impactful programmes
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
The Consortium (East) Ltd has secured national recognition at the 2026 Institute of Economic Development Awards, demonstrating that local expertise and ambition can deliver impact on a national scale.
Essex-based business support organisation The Consortium (East) Ltd has been recognised among the top four most impactful economic development programmes in the UK, by the Institute of Economic Development (IED) Annual Awards 2026.
The Consortium was shortlisted in the Outstanding Impact category for its work delivering the Elevate Basildon Business programme, commissioned by Basildon Borough Council in 2025/26 and funded through the UK Shared Prosperity Fund. The programme exceeded its KPI targets by an impressive 294%, reaching 342 people, helping create 55 new enterprises and supporting the creation of 29 jobs. It also incorporated an innovative digital app to extend engagement and provide ongoing support, alongside youth entrepreneurship skills initiatives designed to help prevent young people becoming NEET (not in education, employment or training).
While first place was awarded to Greater Manchester Growth Hub, The Consortium is celebrating its position among the UK’s leading programmes, particularly given the significant difference in resources available. Its programme budget represented just 0.4% of the budget associated with Greater Manchester’s programme.
Consortium Founder and Director Graham Broughton (pictured) said: “We are absolutely delighted to have been recognised among the top four in the country. To achieve that alongside some of the UK’s largest economic development bodies is a fantastic endorsement of our work. We’ve always believed that impact isn’t simply about the size of the budget. It’s about understanding local businesses, building strong partnerships and making every penny count. We’re incredibly proud of what our team has achieved for Essex and the businesses we support.”
Over the past nine years, The Consortium has supported more than 4,000 businesses, delivering a diverse range of initiatives spanning business growth, start-ups, female entrepreneurship, return-to-work programmes, digital skills, investment readiness, support for emerging entrepreneurs and NEET prevention.
The organisation has built a reputation for combining experienced practitioners with a practical, locally focused approach to economic development, working alongside local authorities, education providers and business partners to create opportunities and support sustainable growth.
For The Consortium, the national recognition is not just an award milestone, but a celebration of the businesses, communities and partners that have been part of its journey.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Southend Reform celebrates 80 years with special service
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
Words by Simon Rothstein
Pictures by Ashley Jay Brent Photography ( ajbrent.com / visualsbyash.com )
Southend and District Reform Synagogue (SDRS) marked its 80th anniversary with a Shabbat service on Saturday 24 October, exactly 80 years after the community was founded. The occasion brought together synagogue members, civic leaders and guests from across the Jewish community to celebrate eight decades of Jewish life in Southend.
Among those attending were Southend East MP Bayo Alaba, Southend West MP David Burton-Sampson, Southend Council Leader Daniel Cowan, Councillor Donna Richardson, and representatives from the police, Jewish Joint Burial Society, Jewish Care and other local synagogues.
Chair Lewis Miller and the current SDRS Council were joined by past Chairs Sue Levitas and Fern Potter. Ninety-nine-year-old Synagogue President Irene Klyman, whose parents were among the founding members, took part via Zoom.
The service was led by Rabbi Warren Elf MBE, who has worked with the community since 2001, with the sermon delivered by Rabbi Josh Levy, Co-Lead of The Movement for Progressive Judaism.
Rabbi Warren said: “It was a pleasure to lead our 80th anniversary Shabbat morning service, which was a true celebration. It was wonderful to host both of Southend’s MPs, the leader of the city council and our other guests from religious and civic life.
“I have enjoyed working with this special community for 25 years and hope to continue for a few more!”
Rabbi Josh’s sermon, which can be read here , centred on a teaching traditionally attributed to the sage Yehudah ben Tema: “ Ben shmonim ligvurah ”, meaning “The age of 80 for strength”.
He explored what strength means for a community, and how it lies not only in resilience and an ability to overcome challenges, but in the pursuit of justice, peace, equality and making the world a better place.
Rabbi Josh Levy presents Southend and District Reform Synagogue’s Chair Lewis Miller and Rabbi Warren Elf with a certificate of recognition for its contribution to Progressive Jewish life in Essex
Rabbi Josh presented the community with a certificate of recognition and concluded: “May 80 be a year of special strength for you – may this community always have the strength to keep safe, the strength to persevere, and most of all the strength to be a beacon of Progressive Jewish values in Southend and beyond.”
Southend Council Leader Daniel Cowan praised the synagogue’s contribution to the city over eight decades.
Reflecting on Rabbi Josh’s “thoughtful and moving sermon”, he said: “The strength of a community is found in its people. In the friendships built across generations, the traditions passed from parents to children, and the determination to preserve identity, faith and belonging through changing times.
“Eighty years is more than a milestone. It is a testament to the resilience of a community that has continued to grow, support one another and enrich our city.”
The community began as Southend Liberal Synagogue in Leigh-on-Sea in October 1946, when a group of local Jews came together to establish a Jewish community to meet their religious needs. Initially meeting and praying in one another’s homes, the group began holding weekly Shabbat services in a hall above shops in Leigh Road in 1947.
The synagogue moved to its present building in Westcliff-on-Sea in 1961 and became known as Southend Progressive Synagogue. In 1972, following a decision to move from Liberal to Reform Judaism, it adopted its current name, Southend and District Reform Synagogue. Today, it is a member of the newly united Movement for Progressive Judaism.
The anniversary service was part of a series of events taking place throughout the year, culminating in a musical gala evening in November.
Participants in the Southend and District Reform Synagogue 80th anniversary Shabbat service

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Theatre review: By Royal Appointment
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
★★★★½
Review by Simon Rothstein
Pictures by Robert Day
“My clothes say what I can’t…”
So says Queen Elizabeth II in Chelmsford Theatre’s By Royal Appointment, and this fascinating play about the late monarch’s wardrobe reveals just how much she could communicate without saying a word.
The first thing to say is that the costume design is fantastic, recreating some of the Queen’s most memorable looks and bringing key moments in recent history to life through her eyes.
There is the blue-and-yellow hat worn for the State Opening of Parliament after the Brexit referendum, and the striking green outfit she wore on her historic visit to Ireland in 2011, when the colour itself carried a message of welcome and goodwill.
Other costumes have more personal associations, including those chosen for family weddings and funerals, or the brooch worn when meeting the infamous Mrs Simpson.
The attention to detail is wonderful, and the first thing you will do after leaving the theatre is look up photographs of the original events to see just how closely they match.
But what sets this play apart is that it is about so much more than what the Queen wore.
Daisy Goodwin’s writing takes us into the lives of the four very different central characters: Queen Elizabeth II (Jane Asher), her dresser (Laura Main), her designer (David Robb) and her milliner (Matthew Cottle).
As we follow their lives over several decades, we see them deal with love, infidelity, coming out, divorce, death, disability and the ageing process that finally catches up with us all.
Some of the story is based on real people and events, while other elements have been introduced for dramatic effect, but you become genuinely invested in all four lives.
The chemistry between the actors is excellent. Stage legend Jane Asher brings real presence to the Queen, capturing the person behind the familiar public image, while Call the Midwife’s Laura Main is superb as the dresser from Wigan who strikes up an extraordinarily close relationship with a woman from a background that couldn’t be more different.
David Robb and Matthew Cottle are equally impressive, bringing their own personalities and vulnerabilities to the designer and milliner. Together, the four create a convincing picture of people who work closely together, sometimes liking each other and sometimes not, but ultimately learning to respect and look out for one another.
Laura Matthews also does a great job as the fifth character in the show, the curator, introducing the exhibition that frames the story and helping to place the Queen’s outfits in their historical context before each is revealed.
The play has plenty of laughs, but is ultimately about something much more poignant.
Without wishing to spoil the narrative, there is a powerful sadness in the play’s exploration of what happens when someone who has devoted their life to a particular role is no longer needed. It is a message that goes well beyond the Royal household, and one that stays with you long after the final curtain.
Best of all, we get to enjoy all of this in the intimate surroundings of the gorgeous Chelmsford Theatre, where the story feels all the more personal.
As Daisy Goodwin puts it: “It is the greatest feeling in the world to come to a theatre like Chelmsford and see people really enjoying themselves. In London, audiences are spoiled, but in Chelmsford the audiences are so appreciative and it is a privilege to serve them.”
By Royal Appointment is funny, moving, beautifully costumed and full of fascinating historical detail.
Some of the descriptions of dresses and hats go on a little too long, although, as a middle-aged man, I may not be the target audience for that part of the show!
Ultimately, this is a play that offers a fresh perspective on a Monarch we have all seen depicted many times, while reminding us that behind the carefully constructed outfits and public image were real people with complicated lives, relationships and emotions.

Pat Lidiker reports on her memorable visit to Jewish Care’s Sugar & Ronson Campus
Resident Naomi with her husband Norman and daughter Nicole as she moves into to The Sugar Family Care Home
When the Essex Jewish News was invited by Jewish Care for an incredibly tasty salt beef lunch and personal tour of the charity’s new Sugar & Ronson Campus in Redbridge, both this paper’s editor Simon Rothstein and I thought we’d wandered into a five-star hotel by mistake.
I’m seldom at a loss for words, but trying to describe this incredible building leaves me in danger of running out of superlatives!
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Jewish Care as the “gold standard” for the adult social care sector, and it’s easy to see why.
First impressions are of spacious, welcoming, stylishly designed and decorated eating and meeting areas, café’s, lounges, wide corridors and sheer comfort for all who make this their home, or their home from home.
The Sugar & Ronson Campus brings together care, community and support services for the local Jewish community under one roof, continuing the legacy of more than 50 years of Jewish Care services on the site.
The 66-bed Sugar Family Care Home provides residential, nursing, dementia and end-of-life care, as well as respite stays.
Alongside it is The Ronson Community Centre, a vibrant hub offering a programme of activities including live entertainment, dancing, card games, exercise classes, bridge, yoga, table tennis and Jewish festivals and community events.
One resident, Corinne, had just had her hair and nails done in the ground-floor salon available to care home and community centre members.
“It looks like a hotel, never in a million years did I think I’d be in a place like this!” she beamed happily.
Michael, a resident at The Sugar Family Care Home, added: “The whole building is fabulous. There’s everything here, they’ve done a wonderful job and the garden’s gorgeous too.”
Social care coordinator Jacklin Stephenson with Michael who is a resident at The Sugar Family Care Home
Jewish Care continues to make the most of a unique opportunity to create a new hub for the whole new community in the heart of Essex.
At The Ronson Family Community Centre on-site café, members of the community can meet friends for breakfast, lunch or tea and join in a variety of different events.
People of all ages can come in simply for a coffee, or a meal with their relatives. And the Campus is designed as a gentle pathway to attend an activity, while also having access to services such as social work, Meals on Wheels, specialist dementia support and mental health services from Jami if and when they need them.
The Dennis Centre, specifically designed for people living with dementia, is also part of the campus. Dementia-informed design runs throughout this part of building – that has its own secure entry and exit – with furniture, flooring, lighting and colour choices helping to support orientation, safety and independence.
One regular member there, Rita, was blown away when she first arrived, saying, “It’s really wonderful and the staff can’t do enough for us.”
Our lunch was hosted in the excellent café, open to the wider community, and serving kosher meat meals, somewhere that it’s easy to meet, eat and socialise. This includes an incredibly tasty salt beef lunch which will be on the varied menu once a month and will also features at the legendary Salt Beef Suppers.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Building Jewish connections across Essex
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
By Peter Wynch
When I moved back to Woodford in 2021, after almost a decade in North West London, I saw there was a particular gap for Jewish people in their 30s, 40s and 50s to meet each other socially – especially singles.
After talking this through with Rabbi Odom Brandman at Chabad Buckhurst Hill, I decided to do something about it.
With his initial support, I organised a walk through High Beach in September 2024. Six of us turned up on a warm late-summer day. That was the start of Essex Jewish Socials.
Since then, the group has gradually evolved. We have visited cultural landmarks in London, walked around Fairlop Waters, taken part in quizzes, gone bowling and enjoyed L’chaims in and around north-east London and Essex.
The ethos is simple: openness, inclusivity and keeping things local. Most events cost very little and people can come and go as they please.
Although singles are an important part of the group, I was determined from the outset that it would not become a dating forum. Couples, including those with non-Jewish partners, have also joined us. Genuine friendships have emerged.
The King William IV in Chigwell has proved our most popular venue so far. As we move forward, I would like to organise more walks, as well as potentially introducing Friday night dinners, discussion events and film screenings.
There is certainly scope for the group to grow, but that depends on people getting involved. My advice to anyone considering coming along is simple: have no expectations and enjoy the event for what it is. Everything else can develop from there.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: A life well lived: A tribute to Manny Robinson
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
Manny Robinson – the wonderful Editor of this newspaper for more than 40 years – had a saying when somebody died in old age.
He’d tell his sons: “When it’s a life well lived, of course, you are going to be sad, but these things should also be more about celebrating a life than mourning someone lost.”
When we remember Manny – who died in May aged 93 – we remember his wonderful career in the media, his love for our Essex Jewish community and his amazing EJN columns that continued right up until his final days. It truly was a life well lived.
Emanuel Rabinovitch was born on April 11, 1933, the first child of Ray and Sidney. He was close throughout his life with his brother Jeffrey and sister Gilda, whose passing in January of this year, which left him ‘last man standing’, affected him profoundly.
They grew up in Whitechapel in a block of flats called Chelsea Buildings in Princelet Street. His father was a Hoffman presser, his mother a seamstress.
On the night of 19 April 1941, the Luftwaffe launched one of its heaviest attacks on London, dropping a bomb on St Peter’s Hospital in Stepney, where Manny was being treated for dysentery.
His mother wouldn’t know for four days whether he had survived the bombing or not, only then finding out that he, together with the other survivors, had been evacuated to the village of South Mimms. He retained a vivid memory of tulips in the fields outside where he was staying. He was evacuated to Tylorstown in the Welsh valleys for the rest of the war, even attending chapel every Sunday.
Back in the East End, as youngsters, they had nowhere really to go, other than to the local dance hall, the Lyceum or the Royal, or to the local cinema, though sometimes a lack of money meant he often couldn’t afford to go to either.
And so, he joined a new club for Jewish boys, Brady. The purpose of the club, he once said, was to instil some sort of character. To him, Brady was his university. It was a place where they learned how to speak, how to respect their elders, and how to develop loyalties. It was also where he learned to dance – a skill to be shown off at simchas for years to come.
He became the first boy to edit the club’s magazine, once writing about the visit of Princess Margaret to the Brady Girls’ Club. He also used to go to watch Brady teams at football matches and started to write reports about their games.
And then on a Sunday afternoon after the match, he would write a report and take it down to the local newspaper, the East London Advertiser, and was chuffed when they used his report in the paper without changing a word.
Manny during his time at the Evening Standard
That planted the seed in his mind that maybe he could become a journalist. Committing to this, he would spend his weekends in Fleet Street delivering photographs from picture agencies to national newspapers. It was his way of finding his way round, and from five o’clock in the afternoon until nine o’clock at night, he would be paid 10 shillings, but it gave him an ‘in’.
After National Service, he applied for work on the Stratford Express. The paper served the supporters of two professional football teams, West Ham United and Leyton Orient, and so he was given a job, on the heady salary of £4 a week.
Having told the Editor he liked football, he subsequently found out that none of the other journalists wanted to cover football because it meant working weekends. So he was appointed Sports Editor at the age of 21 and started sending snippets of news from the two clubs to the Evening Standard.
Journalism, at that time, wasn’t really a go-to career for a young Jewish guy from the East End of London. In fact, he became Manny Robinson when it was explained to him that his name needed to change if he wanted a by-line as Emanuel Rabinovitch was just too long to fit across a single column of type.
Eventually he was approached by the Evening Standard and offered a job there. And at 23, he became the youngest journalist at that point ever to get in

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Cable Street 90 festival to celebrate stories of courage and sacrifice
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
By Linda Newman
To mark the 90th anniversary of the historic clash at The Battle of Cable Street, the Board of Deputies of British Jews presents Cable Street 90 , a festival of Jewish culture, history, and solidarity in which a whole kaleidoscope of fascinating events will be taking place
As part of the festival, historian and AJEX archivist Martin Sugarman whose work we featured in our current issue (p 10 ) will be giving a talk on October 8 th titled  Jews Against Franco: The Jewish Contribution to the Spanish Civil War. Martin’s talk will explore the Spanish Civil War as one of the defining struggles against fascism of the 20th century – in which Jews played a remarkable part.
The Battle of Cable Street took place on October 4, 1936. Just months earlier, in July 1936, the Spanish Civil War erupted. For the Jewish youth of East London, Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts at home and General Franco’s fascists in Spain were the same enemy. Many of the very same young Jewish men and women who stood at the barricades shouting “No Pasarán” (They Shall Not Pass) at Cable Street went on to volunteer for the International Brigades in Spain to continue the fight.
Thousands of Jews from around 53 countries became involved in the Republican cause. Many joined the International Brigades and travelled to Spain to fight Franco; others supported the struggle through fundraising, political activism, refugee aid and humanitarian work. Some went openly as Jews, while others adopted aliases. Some fought alongside fellow nationals, while others joined different national units. Some were refugees from antisemitism and political persecution; others left relatively secure lives in democratic countries to fight fascism.
Martin’s talk uncovers these often-overlooked stories of courage, idealism, international solidarity and sacrifice – and asks why the Jewish contribution to the fight against Franco remains so little known.
CABLE STREET 90
Running from 1–11 October 2026, Events will be taking place across iconic East London and central venues (locations revealed upon booking); the varied programme includes discussions, artistic performances, films, live performances and tailored black cab history tours of Whitechapel, Spitalfields, and Brick Lane.
For further info and to book, please go to: https://bod.org.uk/cable-street-90/

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Theatre review – Operation Mincemeat
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
****
Review by Simon Rothstein
Photos by Matt Crockett
The wonderful Operation Mincemeat, now playing at the Cliffs Pavilion in Southend, probably never should have made the big stage at all.
A historical musical spy comedy set during World War II, with an ensemble cast who frequently swap roles and genders, it started life in an 80-seater studio not long before the pandemic hit and its plans were interrupted.
However, post-lockdowns and carried by word of mouth, momentum soon built, with awards and glowing reviews following not far behind – leading to it becoming a huge West End and Broadway hit.
Now touring theatres around the UK, and indeed the world, it opened right here in Southend-on-Sea, Essex. Future stops will include Chicago, Los Angeles, Boston and cities in China and Australia, as well as Norwich and Crawley a little closer to home.
While not the original cast, four of the five principal performers – Christian Andrews, Seán Carey, Charlotte Hanna-Williams and Holly Sumpton – reprise roles from the West End production, joined by new recruit Jamie-Rose Monk.
All are superb, mixing high comedy with thrilling spy escapes – while bringing a sweetness that makes you really care about their characters and the mission’s success.
That mission was the extraordinary true story of a 1943 British deception operation, in which a dead man was given a false identity and planted off the coast of Spain carrying fake military documents. The elaborate ruse helped convince Hitler that the Allies intended to invade Greece rather than Sicily, drawing German forces away from the real target.
The show is also a tribute to the hugely important role of our intelligence services, who often operate with no public thanks or glory until decades later.
One key reason to see the production, other than its great entertainment value, is therefore keeping this history alive for future generations!
Back to the stage and two things that stand out are the clever choreography, with genuine ‘how did they do that’ moments, and a set design that does a wonderful job of transporting you back to the era.
The five performers, swapping between multiple parts, mix song, farce and intrigue, with the tunes moving the story along and the fast pace rarely letting up.
Some of the songs went on a little too long and they aren’t the type you’re still singing the next day, while a few of the gags missed the mark.
But overall this is a show that is funny, thrilling and full of things to learn, culminating in a happy ending and a lovely tribute (I won’t say any more so as not to spoil).
Judging by the standing ovation in Southend, it is clear that Operation Mincemeat has lost none of its ability to win over an audience as it heads on tour.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Theatre review – Dial M for Murder
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
*****
Review by Simon Rothstein
Photos courtesy of Phil&Ben Productions
A true joy of being the Editor of the Essex Jewish News is travelling around our glorious county discovering its hidden gems.
One of those is undoubtedly the Palace Theatre in Southend where stepping through the doors is like stepping back in time.
A Grade II listed Edwardian building, first opened in 1912, it’s a truly beautiful venue with original features preserved – giving you the same layout, atmosphere and experience those watching plays there 100 years ago would have enjoyed.
Of course, any theatre is only as good as the shows it puts on – which is why I’m pleased to report that Dial M for Murder, which is playing all this week, truly is a classic thriller fit for a Palace.
Brought back to the stage for 2026 by Phil&Ben Productions, in association with PW Productions, it is showing in Southend until Sunday (16 August) before heading off to Harrogate, Blackpool, Coventry and Peterborough. It previously toured Eastbourne, Crewe, Fareham and Swindon.
For a Frederick Knott play that first premiered in 1952 – made famous by Alfred Hitchcock’s 1954 film version – it may seem strange of me not to want to give any spoilers, but with every twist and turn being so impactful, I’m keen not to ruin any of them.
The story, as fans of the film will remember, begins with English former tennis professional Tony Wendice plotting to kill his wealthy wife Margot after finding out she’d been cheating on him with Mark Halliday, an American crime-fiction writer.
Blackmailing an old classmate turned con man, Charles Swann, into doing the deed for him – Tony feels he has the perfect murder planned as he explains to Charles, and therefore us, in great detail.
Things, as you can imagine, don’t go as expected, leaving Charles to come up with a second dastardly plan. But is his web of lies and latch keys enough to fool Inspector Hubbard and get him the inheritance he wants?
The direction from Josh Mathieson is one of the best I’ve seen in a small theatre, adding moments of dramatic pause to the gripping script to really allow you to take everything in and wonder what happens next.
You, of course, hate the dastardly Tony (played masterfully by Pete Ashmore), but there’s a moment where Margot (Tanya-Loretta Dee) chooses to walk with Max (Simon Pothecary) instead of Tony that really makes you wonder where your sympathies lie – a credit to the acting and directing.
Phil Stewart may be having the most fun as the slightly hapless Charles Swann, while you never know how much Katy Dean’s Inspector Hubbard really knows – keeping you guessing until the end.
Dial M for Murder is a whodunnit where you know who did it, how they did it and why they did it… yet it remains gripping throughout.
There were a mix of ages in the theatre, including my own teenage children, and all were hanging on every word.
Listening to conversations afterwards, the audience was a combination of those who know and love the film – like us – those who have seen it but forgotten the twists and turns, and those coming to the material for the first time. All enjoyed it equally.
Not only was this a five-star show, right here on our doorsteps, but it is also part of an important effort to strengthen the future of touring drama in towns and smaller cities across the UK.
As Phil and Ben said: “We believe audiences in towns and smaller cities like Southend deserve regular access to outstanding live drama, and that the appetite for it remains strong.
“This is an exciting production in its own right, but it also stands for something larger: a commitment to restoring confidence in mid-scale touring theatre and building lasting partnerships with venues and audiences.”
So if you’re looking for a great night out at a very reasonable price, just Dial M and get to the Palace.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Local MP Wes Streeting takes on top Government job
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
By Pat Lidiker
Since joining the Essex Jewish News 10 years ago, I have become increasingly aware of the growing reputation of our local MP, Wes Streeting. I have met and interviewed him on many occasions, so I was delighted to offer him mazel tov on behalf of the paper on his recent appointment as Secretary of State for Defence.
A Christian, Wes has forged close relationships with members of the Redbridge Jewish community and is a familiar and welcome face at local shuls, schools and organisations. He has also been a vocal campaigner against the growing threat of antisemitism.
At 43, Wes has already held one of the most demanding jobs in government, serving as Secretary of State for Health and Social Care from 2024 until May this year, before returning to government as Defence Secretary in July.
He also laid bare much of his personal history in his autobiography, One Boy, Two Bills and a Fry Up, published last year. I found it impossible to put down and admired his willingness to confront his past so openly.
Wes continues to live in his Redbridge constituency with his partner Joe Dancey, a communications and public affairs consultant. How much time they will now have for weekends away in the area remains to be seen.
His new role comes at a challenging time, with responsibility for Britain’s defence, security and armed forces.
On receiving our congratulations, the new Defence Secretary replied: “It is a huge honour to be taking on this role. Keeping our country safe is the first duty of government and since my appointment, we’ve been straight to work speaking to allies, including Ukraine, to make clear that we will continue to stand steadfast alongside them. I am also absolutely committed to ensuring our armed forces have the resources they need.
“I would like to wish your readers a Shanah Tovah this Rosh Hashanah. Chag Sameach!”
Wes Streeting with the EJN’s very own Pat Lidiker and Phillip Leigh in 2023

Sir John Whittingdale MP has written to the Home Secretary calling for plans to accommodate up to six asylum seekers in Tillingham to be reconsidered.
He has raised concerns about the village’s isolated location and limited public transport, as well as access to essential services. He has also highlighted the potential for community tensions arising from the proposed accommodation.
The Maldon MP believes that Tillingham is an unsuitable location both for local residents and for the individuals who would be accommodated there.
Sir John has requested urgent discussions with the Government to raise these concerns and seek a reconsideration of the proposals.
The letter forms part of his efforts to represent the concerns surrounding the proposed asylum accommodation in Tillingham and its potential impact on the village.

https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.text:
Sir John raised concerns about Labour’s Autumn Budget, arguing that it fails to address the UK’s rising national debt, economic challenges and the urgent need to increase defence spending. He welcomed continued cross-party support for Ukraine but questioned the delay in reaching the Government’s 3% of GDP defence spending target, highlighting the need to address welfare spending. Sir John also drew attention to the pressures facing high street businesses, the gambling sector, family farms and rural households reliant on heating oil.
Watch his full contribution here:
Debate Highlights
Andrew Griffith Shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer
This Budget must be bewildering to members of the Prime Minister’s party. He promised them a “circuit breaker”, an end to “40 years of neoliberalism” and a “new political model”. Instead, it is all gherkins and aubergines. The Defence Secretary, who is sitting on the front bench, is probably wondering the same as everyone else: was that it? To be honest, he is probably thinking he would have done a better job, and he might be right. It is not too late: if he resigns again, he might get his chance to be the Chancellor.
All the while, Britain has a debt problem, Britain has a defence problem, Britain has a growth problem, and apparently, as we learned yesterday, there is nothing the Chancellor can do. On the big challenges, what has this Budget actually done? It does not reduce borrowing; total debt has gone up. It does not properly fund defence; the Government still have not set out how 3% will be funded. It does not cut taxes to get the economy growing; instead, they are putting up taxes again.
[…]
John Whittingdale Conservative, Maldon
Before I turn to the Budget, I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to Sue Holt, whose death Mr Speaker announced to the House this morning. I am a member and former leader of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly delegation, and I worked with Sue over quite a long period. She was always immensely cheerful and efficient, and her death came as a real shock to us all. I send my condolences.
At least there is one part of the Budget that I welcome: the continuing support being given by this Government to Ukraine. That was initiated under the last Government —indeed, over 10 years ago, long before the full-scale invasion by Russia—and we have continued to maintain it. It is a cross-party matter, so that support is very welcome. One of the reasons it is so important that we support Ukraine is that Ukraine is our frontline, and the threat to Ukraine is not just a threat to that country; it is a threat to all of us. That is why it is essential that we increase our defence expenditure now.
The Chancellor has recommitted to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, but that is still some way off, and we have heard from the Secretary of State for Defence about the immediacy of the threat. It is a matter of some concern that while we are still debating how we will get to 3%, allies such as Denmark, Estonia, Lativa, Lithuania, Norway and Poland are already exceeding that level and planning to spend more. Perhaps one of the reasons we have not yet been able to explain how we will meet the target is that the essential measures to fund it—in other words, addressing the welfare budget—have again been ducked by this Government. https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.title: Local Government Organisation
https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.text:
Sir John Whittingdale MP challenges the Government over delays and uncertainty surrounding local government reorganisation in Essex, following the decision to scrap the previous reform proposals and reconsider the plans. He warns that the lack of clarity is disrupting local decision-making and questions how elections can proceed in 2028 when voters and candidates may not know which authorities will be in place. The exchange highlights concerns about the timetable for Essex local government reform, democratic representation and the need for clear decisions from the Government.
Debate Highlights
John Whittingdale Conservative, Maldon
Six weeks ago, the Government announced that they were scrapping the local government reform proposals for Essex and going back to the drawing board. That announcement created yet more uncertainty and further paralysed decision making, yet the Minister has not even mentioned Essex, and he has provided no additional clarity whatsoever. How can he expect elections to go ahead in 2028, when we will not even know what authorities the candidates will be elected to until next year?
Jim McMahon Parliamentary Under-Secretary (Housing, Communities and Local Government)
I definitely accept the right hon. Member’s point that having an itinerary of areas, with a clear date alongside them, would do what he has asked, but that is not where we are. We have decided that we ought to confirm the decision for an area as soon as possible, rather than waiting for this to be patched up, in the way that may have happened previously. On whether elections should go ahead, I have made the point that these district councils will be in place until the vesting days of the new local authorities. We cannot have elections being cancelled, creating a democratic deficit. Councils must have representatives around the table, with a mandate given to them by the public.

https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.title: Falkland Islands Oil Reserves
https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.text:
Sir John challenged the Prime Minister to confirm the Government will oppose Argentina’s efforts to prevent oil exploration authorised by the United Kingdom around the Falkland Islands. Sir John pressed for a firm commitment to defend the UK’s position, drawing attention to concerns over sovereignty and the Government’s approach to the strategically important Chagos Islands. The Prime Minister did reaffirm the Government’s support for the Falkland Islanders’ right to self-determination and for keeping the islands British and Sir John will continue to hold the government to account on this matter.
Debate Highlights
John Whittingdale Conservative, Maldon:
Unlike the Government’s shameful attempts to hand over the sovereignty of the strategically important Chagos islands, will the Prime Minister confirm that this time the Government will strongly oppose the case being made by the Government of Argentina to the international tribunal to try to stop the exploitation of oil reserves around the Falkland Islands, which is authorised by the United Kingdom?
Andy Burnham Leader of the Labour Party, The Prime Minister:
Indeed we will, and I am happy to make that clear again today. We will take the firmest of action to support the Falkland Islands—the right to self-determination of the islanders, who chose to remain British not so long ago. The Defence Secretary has met his counterparts to reiterate that position, and the Foreign Secretary too. I raised the matter with President Trump. There is no diminution in our strong support to keep the Falkland Islands British.

What steps is the Government taking to support the wine production industry?
Stephen Morgan The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs:
The wine sector is a British success story and we want to grow it further. We are supporting innovation, ensuring that vineyards can access essential labour and helping British producers access new export markets through our global network of agrifood and drink attachés.
John Whittingdale Conservative, Maldon:
Is the Minister aware that Essex is now a centre of English wine production, with producers such as Danbury Ridge, Missing Gate, New Hall, Crouch Valley and Crouch Ridge all producing in my constituency? Gentleman mentioned, obviously, matters of duty relief are for the Treasury, but DEFRA recognises the growth potential of the wine tourism industry, including its contribution to rural jobs and rural communities.

https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.title: Saudi Arabia
https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.text:
Sir John supports the deployment of British forces in support of Saudi Arabian allies but questions the distinction between offensive and defensive military support. In Parliament, he asks the Government what assessment it has made of potential increased threats to British civilian and military personnel in the region, and what measures are being taken to address them.
Watch his full question and the Government’s answer below:
Debate Highlights
Thomas Tugendhat Shadow Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Developmental Affairs:
Will the Secretary of State make a statement on the deployment of RAF Typhoon aircraft to defend Saudi Arabia, and the extension of air-to-air refuelling support for the Saudi air operations, including those against Houthi targets in Yemen.
Calvin Bailey Parliamentary Under-Secretary (Minister of Defence) (Minister for Veterans and People):
I am grateful for the opportunity to update the House on the UK Government’s support for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia as it responds to increased Houthi aggression in Saudia Arabia and Yemen. The whole House will have seen images of the attacks on civilian airports in Riyadh and the hundreds of casualties that those Houthi attacks have caused. The Government fully support the right of Saudi Arabia and the legitimate Government of the Republic of Yemen to defend themselves. However, we know that there is no long-term military solution to this conflict. The support we have announced is designed to help our partners at this critical moment while supporting efforts to create the conditions for political resolution to the conflict.
Although many of our constituents may feel that this is happening far away, we must be clear about the direct consequences for the United Kingdom. The Red sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait are among the world’s most important maritime trade routes, and continued instability increases costs for British families and businesses while also undermining security across the middle east. Helping that part of the world to be more secure and stable is firmly in the United Kingdom’s national security and economic interests.
As the House will know, we have already been providing Saudi Arabia with air defence support and air-to-air refuelling from defensive Saudi Arabia air operations, and the Prime Minister has now authorised additional military support. We are extending the provision of air-to-air refuelling to 90 days, and RAF Typhoon aircraft will conduct defensive counter-air operations from Saudi Arabia; these aircraft will operate in a defensive role, and will not conduct offensive strikes. We will also make an RAF A400M aircraft available to support the movement of matériel within Saudi Arabia in support of defence.
We remain deeply concerned by the humanitarian situation in Yemen and the suffering experienced by civilians. Alongside military support, we continue our diplomatic efforts, humanitarian assistance and work to encourage political negotiations.
Finally, all partners receiving UK assistance must comply fully with their obligations under international law. We will continue to monitor and assess this compliance as part of our ongoing engagement.

John Whittingdale Conservative, Maldon:
I support the deployment of British forces in support of our Saudi Arabian allies, but, as has become clear, the distinction between “offensive” and “defensive” support is pretty fuzzy at best. Sir John celebrates the news that yesterday the Minister confirmed, in a debate in Parliament, the Government’s support for a new neighbourhood health centre in Maldon.
Speaking in Westminster Hall, the Minister for Secondary Care, Karin Smith, about the improvement plans for Mid and South Essex Hospitals, said:
“Better organisation across sites and stronger clinical integration should improve patient experience, reduce delays and raise quality for patients. The clinical strategy will make greater use of neighbourhood and community care in line with our 10-year plan and focus on maternity and planned care treatment. This is backed by £80 million for Southend hospital’s long-standing structural estate problems and support for a neighbourhood health centre in Maldon.”
Sir John looks forward to the Government’s announcement of further details soon, and he will continue to press for the new facility to provide a full range of health services including and beyond those currently available at St Peter’s. He is delighted that the long-promised and desperately needed new community hospital facility has now received Government support.
Thanks go to the Essex ICB and the Save Maldon Medical Services Group for all they have done to help persuade the government of Maldon’s case. Sir John will continue to work with these hardworking teams to bring the health hub project to fruition.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Call For Breast Cancer Screening Funding
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Essex Police Federation is calling for partners to help fund breast cancer screening for the force’s female officers and police staff.
Last year, Essex Police’s Women’s Forum ran a pilot scheme and was able to secure 37 breast cancer ultrasound screenings for officers and staff; this year the Federation is helping raise funds to do the same again. The scheme is aimed at women aged under 50, who may not be eligible for routine NHS screening.
One woman who was screened last year as part of the initiative was told that a breast implant had ruptured.
She had no symptoms that indicated this and she would not have known if she hadn’t taken part in the screenings. She has since been able to avoid referral waiting times because she was able to send the scans that the screening consultant provided straight to her doctor, and already has an operation booked in to remove the damaged implants.
Alfie McPhilimey, Federation Vice-Chair and Lead for Equality and Wellbeing, said: “It’s really important that the Federation supports this initiative, because otherwise it might not happen. We are here to support our members and our women in policing, so I think it’s vital that we get behind this. We have seen positive results from last year’s screening, and we want to see that rolled out further to more officers.”
Alfie said he was speaking to member services who he hoped would come on board as sponsors. Any organisations that are interested in getting involved can email Alfie.McPhilimey@polfed.org .

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Essex Police Federation Pay & Morale Survey 2026
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
93% of Essex Police officers do not feel fairly paid for the stresses and strains of the job, and 75% are dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with their overall pay and allowances, new figures show.
According to the 2026 Police Federation of England and Wales Pay and Morale Report, 26% of officers frequently cannot meet their household’s financial needs.
54% say their workload is too high or much too high, and 44% have had at least one rest day cancelled in the past 12 months.
22% say they are satisfied with their job, and 16% intend to resign from the service either within the next two years or as soon as they can.
The survey also showed that 75% do not feel valued in the police and 73% would not recommend joining the service.
70% of respondents are not confident in their force’s ability to resource appropriately for day-to-day operational demands, and 49% say their team has been fully staffed on very few or no shifts in the past three months.
73% say their force relies heavily on officer goodwill to meet routine operational demands, and 64% have felt unsafe on duty because of staffing levels in the past three months.
And 66% of officers who responded to the survey are too fatigued to carry out their duties. In Essex Police, 49% of officers have been physically attacked by a member of the public in the past 12 months, and 71% do not have access to double crewing at all times while on duty.
Essex Police Federation Chair Steve Martin said: “All ranks should be getting a fair pay for the work they do. We know how difficult it is as a police officer in this day and age, and we need the Government to stand up and actually start rewarding us properly.
“They need to listen to what we say in the pay surveys, they need to listen to what we say from a morale point of view in those surveys, and realise that we’re not just… the comment a number of years ago from Theresa May, we’re not crying wolf.
“This is a genuine crisis in policing. We’re struggling with retention in force, we’re losing lots of good people and actually there’s probably some easy things that we could do about it, some really easy wins and one of those is probably starting to look at pay properly.”
The survey also showed that 83% of respondents had experienced stress, low mood or anxiety in the past 12 months, and 40% find their job very or extremely stressful.
54% have sought help for stress, low mood, anxiety or other mental health difficulties, and 60% rate their force’s support for officers and their wellbeing as inadequate or requiring improvement.
The survey also showed the effect that policing has on officers’ personal lives. In Essex Police, 28% of officers often or always pressured to work long hours and 51% had annual leave requests refused.
73% of respondents say they have been so fatigued that it has interfered with their family or social life in the past month, and 62% have had to cancel personal plans due to last-minute work requirements in the past 12 months.
30% have worked during annual leave to catch up, 16% have had at least one free day cancelled in the past 12 months and 9% have had their roster changed more than 10 times in the past 12 months.
For the first time, the survey asked about how policing affects parents and carers, with 69% of mothers and 39% of fathers in Essex Police saying they have had to change job roles or teams to meet their obligations as a parent.
The survey is based on 419 responses received from Essex Police officers.
