https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Policing A Low Government Priority
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Policing is clearly low down the Government’s list of priorities, Essex Police Federation has said.
Chair Steve Martin was speaking at the Police Federation of England and Wales conference, which neither the Policing Minister nor the Home Secretary attended.
He said: “It is really disappointing that our current Government is not here to listen to the issues facing police. The current Prime Minister doesn’t appear to mention policing ever, which for me demonstrates where we sit on his order of priorities.
“It is really positive that we’ve had the Shadow Home Secretary and the Leader of the Opposition, but I think the lack of Government presence speaks volumes as to where policing is currently seen under the current government agenda.”
Steve was joined by Rep Amy Sage, who spoke about a powerful presentation by a former officer from West Midlands who spoke about her experience of sexual assault and misogyny in the workplace.
Amy said: “Actually seeing the impact of it and how it’s affected her, I think it’s very powerful and that’s something I’ll probably take with me for the rest of my career.
“It’s small stories like that that let you kind of sit down for a minute, pause and think you actually are changing lives, and how you are as a Federation Rep matters and impacts people.”
As a new rep, Amy added that it was a useful learning experience for her to come to conference: “I think in terms of learning about the pay, how the PIP procedure is changing, how Regs procedure is changing, I just find it really impactful because obviously this is my first couple of months being a rep.
“I’ve always heard the other side but actually being in the room I think it’s just really powerful how such a big group comes together, and obviously we’re all here because we care and actually seeing that the change is being made.”
Steve added: “Amy has not been a rep for long but she’s clearly demonstrating what, as Branch Chair, I expect to see from our reps. Someone that wants to come in, make a difference, help people where they can.
“I think it’s really important to come to conferences so that they can actually see different viewpoints. You can see that some of the problems that we talk about in our Branch are replicated across the country.
“We’re all fighting the same challenges, we’re all trying to be that one Federation and now we’re transforming and we’re doing some meaningful transformation, hopefully we’re going to be changing the Federation for the better.”

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Federation sets out six-point plan to combat the suicide crisis affecting policing
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
More than 100 police officers and staff died by suicide between 2022 and 2025. At least 70 police officers have died during that time and there have been more than 200 attempted suicides.
The Police Federation of England and Wales (PFEW) is today calling for the silent crisis of police suicide to end – as this new data reveals the devastating scale of this crisis killing officers.
47 of the 70 suicides and 173 of 236 attempted suicides are attributable to officers involved in misconduct or criminal investigations against them.
In 2025 the link was even stronger, with 12 of 13 police officer suicides that the Federation is aware of involving officers under investigation.
Police forces are not required to record suicide or attempted suicide, meaning the Federation’s data is likely to significantly undercount the real figures.
The lack of recording means that policing is not currently regarded by the Office for National Statistics as an “occupation at risk”.
The Federation has set out a six-point plan to combat the crisis:
• Chief Constables need to agree today to begin recording and reporting on suicide and attempted suicide in the workforce.
• Police conduct regulations need to mandate a 12-month limit for disciplinary investigations into police officers, whether that is by the IOPC or police forces.
• Health and Safety legislation needs to treat police suicide as an incident at work and therefore reportable and investigated under ‘RIDDOR’ rules.
• All forces should implement the STEP (Suicide Trauma Education Prevention) campaign, launched by Hampshire Police Federation. The campaign calls for the downloading by forces of the Stay Alive app and mandatory TRiM (Trauma Risk Management) interventions for any officer attending a suicide.
• The coronial system needs to reflect the unique aggravating or contributory factors of the role of police officers in suicide and ensure that the crisis is dealt with nationally rather than through a patchwork of “prevention of future deaths” reports after individual inquests.
• The Police Covenant needs to be funded to better support the welfare and wellbeing of police officers in the same way that the Armed Forces Covenant and Covenant Trust does.
For more information about the Stay Alive app, visit stayalive.prevent-suicide.org.uk. Officers and police staff members who are struggling should know that they are not alone, and that there are people there to help.
This includes, for immediacy: Samaritans: call 116 123 and Oscar Kilo’s Mental Health Crisis Line: call 0300 131 2789.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: More Police Officers Awarded Elizabeth Emblem
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
The families of 30 UK police officers who have died on duty have seen their loved one’s sacrifice be recognised by the King with the Elizabeth Emblem.
This includes the families of DC Mick Swindells, of West Midlands Police; PC Alan McMurray, of Lothian and Borders Police; and PC Sandra Edwards, of South Yorkshire Police.
Also receiving the award will be the families of fallen officers PC Laurence Brown, of the Metropolitan Police; PC Andrew Winterburn, of West Yorkshire Police; PC John Alcock, of Grampian Police; PC Kenneth Adams, of Hampshire Constabulary; and from Norfolk Constabulary PC Bernard Brown, PC David Protheroe Davies and DC Terence Glister.
The Elizabeth Emblem recognises the sacrifices made by public servants who have lost their lives as a result of their duty. It is the civilian equivalent of the Elizabeth Cross, which recognises members of the UK Armed Forces who died in action or as a result of a terrorist attack.
This is the third list of Elizabeth Emblem recipients to be published. The next of kin are awarded the national form of recognition.
The design of the Emblem incorporates a rosemary wreath, a traditional symbol of remembrance, which surrounds the Tudor Crown.
It is inscribed with ‘For A Life Given In Service’, and will have the name of the person for whom it is in memoriam inscribed on the reverse of the Emblem.
It includes a pin to allow the award to be worn on clothing by the next of kin of the deceased.
The full list of those to be awarded the Elizabeth Emblem is here:  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-elizabeth-emblem-application-guidance-and-eligibility/list-of-recipients-of-the-elizabeth-emblem-15th-january-2026

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Christmas and New Year Message from Essex Police Federation Chair Steve Martin
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
As Christmas fast approaches, I just wanted to take a moment to look back on what’s been a year of progress and teamwork for the Essex Police Federation team.
2025 has brought plenty of change and growth.
We welcomed lots of new faces to the Branch Council – all with fresh ideas and energy that will help shape the future and continue the support and representation of you, the members. At the same time, we said goodbye to our previous Chair and Secretary, Laura and Dean, who retired after years of dedicated service.
A huge thank you to them for everything they’ve done (and continue to do in their new roles).
Nationally, the Federation has continued to transform into a more professional organisation, and locally we’ve worked hard to make sure we’re more visible and accessible than ever.
Whether it’s advice, support, or representation, we’re here when you need us.
We’ve invested in training and development for our new reps and strengthened our relationships with other branches, staff associations, support networks and our external service providers – because working together makes us stronger.
Most importantly, we’ve kept doing what matters most: supporting colleagues, whether that’s helping with compensation for injuries, providing access to medical assistance, assisting with representation during misconduct or criminal matters, or just day-to-day advice.
This is the heart of what we do, and I am proud of the difference we make.
Sadly, this year hasn’t been without loss. We have said goodbye to friends and colleagues, and their absence is deeply felt. Over Christmas, please take a moment to remember them and their loved ones. And for those working over the festive period – please stay safe.
Looking ahead to 2026, I’m optimistic. We’ll keep building on what we’ve achieved this year, making sure every member gets the support they deserve.
From all of us at the Essex Police Federation, have a great Christmas and a peaceful New Year. Thank you for everything you do for Essex and for each other.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: 2026 subscription changes confirmed following conference vote
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Delegates at the Police Federation’s Annual Conference have voted to introduce a £2 per month increase in member subscriptions from 1 January 2026. This will take the gross monthly rate from £24.31 to £26.31.
In addition, the current student officer 50% discount will end, meaning that from 1 January 2026 all new members joining the Federation will contribute at a single standard rate from their first day of membership. There will be no change to the rate for current student officers.
Motions proposing the subscription fee increase and ending the student officer discount passed with heavy majorities after voting at the Federation’s AGM on 18 November.
We know cost of living pressures continue to bite, and no one welcomes paying more. But maintaining the current rate is no longer sustainable if we are to protect, represent and support members in the way they expect and deserve.
Subscriptions have only risen twice in the past decade. In that time, we’ve absorbed rising costs, delivered more than £1 million in annual savings through restructuring, and continued to secure significant outcomes for members.
Demand for our legal and welfare support continues to grow rapidly. Case volumes have risen by almost a third in three years, and this year alone we’ve secured more than £41 million in compensation for members. The cost of expert legal representation and specialist welfare services continues to increase at pace.
What the £2 increase will deliver
The increase is expected to generate around £3.36 million a year. This funding will help us to:
Ending the student officer discount
The discounted rate for student officers, while well-intentioned, generates less than 0.3% of our total income. Our data also shows that newer officers often rely most heavily on Federation support.
Moving to one fair rate for all ensures consistency, sustainability and equal access to the same level of protection and support from day one.
Our role is to stand beside you on your toughest days, in the moments that matter most, and in the national debates shaping the future of policing. These changes are about securing the Federation’s ability to do that, not just now but for the long term.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Better Support Needed On Suicide Prevention in Forces
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Forces need to step up to record the numbers of police suicides and provide welfare support to officers, particularly those who are under investigation, the Police Federation of England and Wales Annual Conference heard.
In the session, ‘Code Zero: Policing’s Suicide Crisis’, delegates heard from PFEW national Health & Wellbeing Leads Richie Murray and Paul Williams, and Hampshire Police Federation Chair Spencer Wragg, who spearheads the STEP (Suicide Trauma Education Prevention) campaign.
Tragically the conference was told there have been at least 10 suicides of police officers and staff around the country this year.
Richie said he wrote to all Federation branches asking how many of their officers had died by suicide between 2022 and 2024. Two large forces are yet to respond, but so far PFEW has been told about 55 officers who took their own lives in this period, of whom 34 were under investigation. In addition, 120 had reported attempting to take their own lives, 71 of whom were under investigation.
Richie said: “There is a huge causal link between officer suicides and investigations. And I think everybody in this room will say investigations are taking too long, and that it has to have an effect.”
Paul agreed, saying: “We arrest criminals, we send them through the Criminal Justice System. We prosecute, they go to court, they serve a sentence, potentially a prison sentence. Now that criminal could be released back on the street a lot quicker than a police officer who’s been served a basic misconduct form and put under investigation by their own force.”
In addition, forces should carry out a documented basic risk assessment on misconduct investigations and provide the officer with wraparound care, Paul said: “Allocating a welfare officer is sometimes just not good enough.”
Paul said that there needed to be “common minimum standards across the country”. He continued: “We heard yesterday that there’s a postcode lottery of wellbeing in forces: 43 different Chiefs, 43 different personalities.”
PFEW has been successful is getting a motion tabled with the House of Lords to amend the Police and Crime Act to mandate the recording of suicide and attempted suicide in forces.
Another proactive step is for forces to put the free Stay Alive app from Grassroots Suicide Prevention on all officers’ work phones, said Spencer. Spencer spoke about how he and the Martis Media team have promoted the STEP campaign around the country and succeeded in getting the Stay Alive app put on 8,000 officers’ phones in Hampshire and Thames Valley Police. He said: “We’re asking and pushing for Chiefs to put that on job mobile phones, which will cost them absolutely nothing.”
It is important for officers who are struggling to know they are not alone, and that there are people there to help.
This includes, for immediacy, the Mental Health Support line from Oscar Kilo 0300 131 2789.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: ‘Policing Becoming Unaffordable Profession’
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Policing risks becoming an unaffordable profession for officers as the cost of living goes up and officer pay and conditions continue to stagnate.
National Secretary John Partington told the 2025 PFEW conference that potential recruits risk being priced out of the job because pay and conditions are so inadequate for the role that officers carry out.
He also said that equal percentage pay rises are unfair as higher ranks end up taking home more than those on the front line because of their higher baseline salary. He said lower earners – who spend almost their entire income on essential costs – need higher awards to maintain real terms pay.
He said: “A superintendent and a constable face the same inflation, but not the same pressure. Identical percentages create inequality.”
He suggested that lower earners should get higher percentage pay rises to redress this balance.
John said: “Equal percentage pay awards might look fair on paper, but they’re not fair in practice. When everyone gets the same percentage rise, those on higher salaries keep far more of their income after the bills are paid, while those on the frontline see their disposable income vanish.
“Federated rank members today spend almost everything they earn just on living. Housing, energy, and fuel have risen far faster than pay, and what used to be a modest but secure income has become a financial struggle. Simple research for credible sources will show how rent has risen more than police pay.
“This isn’t about generosity – it’s about fairness. A superintendent and a constable face the same inflation, but not the same pressure. Identical percentages create real-terms inequality, not parity. Without correction policing risks becoming unaffordable to those who deliver it.
“That’s why the next pay settlement must recognise this truth: lower earners deserve a higher pay award. Because pay that protects buying power is what keeps people in the job, keeps policing professional, and keeps faith with those who hold the line every day.”
John explained that police conditions should also be improved – to mandate sufficient rest, recovery and resilience because of the unique demands of the job.
He told delegates: “This job affects your mental health, your family life, and your personal wellbeing like few others.
“The risk of assault, the threat of injury, the emotional toll, all of these are part of policing today. And they must be met not just with decent wages, but with conditions that support rest, recovery, and resilience.”
He also highlighted the urgent need to reform police recruitment, calling for mandatory psychological and psychometric testing for every applicant and throughout initial training.
He said: “This is about safeguarding the integrity of policing. Resilience, empathy and moral strength cannot be assumed – they must be tested and proven.”

https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.title: Takeaways from the European Transport Conference: ABMs, Crisis Resilience, Futures
https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.text:
This year’s European Transport Conference (ETC) provided a valuable showcase of where transport analytics, data science, and modelling are heading. From agent-based simulations to knowledge graphs and futures frameworks, here are the core technical insights from the sessions.
Agent-Based Models (ABMs) take centre stage
ABMs had a major presence at this year’s conference with BERTIE – Transport East’s Activity and Agent-Based Model – having contributed to or been the subject of five separate talks, four of which reflected innovation enabled by BERTIE and delivered with Arup for the Department for Transport, National Highways, as well as by researchers at University College, London.
Key analytical applications covered in these sessions included the challenges and opportunities for A2BMs in economic appraisal, and actionable insights for modal shift using BERTIE’s ‘VAMoS’ (Viable Alternative Mode Selector) tool. VAMoS leverages a granular understanding of the options and choices of agents, across different segments of the population, to help identify realistic opportunities for mode shift.
Practical application of this work was undertaken for Basildon Borough Council, where Arup applied BERTIE and VAMoS as part of a data-led and people-focussed approach to testing the Local Plan and potential interventions to support the plan’s equitable and sustainable credentials.
The increasing importance of crisis resilience
Resilience was another important theme across the conference. DfT and Arup presented on the Crisis Resilience Digital Twin, which is bringing together Agent-Based Models to test crisis scenarios with Knowledge Graphs to embed that knowledge and support crisis response capability.
Complementing this, TIS presented the RURAL framework – a recovery framework designed for post-disaster scenarios. Developed in response to increasingly frequent severe climate hazards in Portugal, RURAL addresses a common gap: isolated and rural communities are frequently the last to see critical transport infrastructure restored.
Transport futures in decision-making
It was encouraging to see a dedicated session on transport futures, featuring a joint presentation by DfT and Mott MacDonald on how DfT is embedding futures thinking directly into strategic planning and transport decision-making.
Targeted EV Investment and inclusion from Suffolk
Suffolk County Council’s Amy Rushton delivered an excellent session to close Day 2, focusing on targeted use of government funding allocations for EV charging.
The talk demonstrated how to make optimal use of funding, in a large and sparsely populated county like Suffolk, to improve mobility and the conditions for social inclusion in largely rural geographies.

https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.title: National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) published: what this means for vision-led planning in the East
https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.text:
The Government’s publication of the NPPF marks a major shift in planning. The new framework uses vision-led planning at the core of its decision making. This means transport and land-use planning should be integrated even further, so new homes and employment space are well-connected to existing communities, essential services and jobs. By linking transport to wider economic growth and prioritising good design, the NPPF supports the East to plan sustainable communities.
A key part within the new framework is the introduction of Spatial Development Strategies (SDSs). In our area, two SDSs are set to be established – one for Greater Essex and a combined SDS for Norfolk and Suffolk. As long-term strategic plans, SDSs will coordinate housing, transport, infrastructure, and economic growth across local authority boundaries.
Transport East is fully committed to collaborating with local authorities as they develop their SDSs and implement the NPPF. Our evidence can help our partners plan for the future of the East with a clear understanding of how our growing communities connect to each other, to our neighbours and the rest of the UK.

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: New E-bike network to transform onward travel across coastal connections
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
Greater Anglia customers can now benefit from a new network of e-bike hire hubs designed to make sustainable onward travel easier across Felixstowe, Harwich and the Shotley Peninsula.
Named Harwich Haven Eezybike Connect and developed by the region’s Industrial Strategy Zone, Freeport East, the project sees five e-bike pods installed at key rail and ferry locations, creating convenient links between train services, the Harwich Harbour Ferry and popular local destinations.
The scheme, which is funded with a grant from Greater Anglia’s Customer and Community Improvement Fund , provides passengers, visitors, residents and workers with easy access to e-bikes for onward journeys, helping to improve connectivity while encouraging more sustainable travel choices.
The locations include Felixstowe station, Harwich Town station, and ferry landing points in  Harwich and Shotley, creating an integrated transport network across the area.
The initiative supports ambitions set out in the Freeport East Transport Masterplan , which was developed in partnership with Transport East, the region’s transport planning body, which identified improved links between the coastal communities as a priority.
The area continues to experience housing growth, new employment activity and attracts significant numbers of visitors each year, including many from Europe making use of the daily ferry services from the Netherlands to Harwich.  Making better local transport connections is therefore seen as increasingly important. The pod locations have also been selected to align with local hotels and the Shotley Marina, giving visitors to the area ready access to the facilities and encouraging them to stay longer.
The project uses e-bike pods supplied by Eezybike, with secure docking, charging facilities and the ability to rent an e-bike. You can find your closest location and book here .
Scott Dolling, Greater Anglia’s Partnerships Manager, said:
“This project makes it easier for our customers to continue their journeys beyond the railway by creating convenient links between rail services, the Harwich Harbour Ferry and local destinations.
“This is a great opportunity for people to discover some of the hidden gems East Anglia has to offer, while keeping their carbon footprint low.
“The e-bike network has the potential to encourage more sustainable travel, support local tourism and improve connectivity for residents and visitors across the area.”
Steve Beel, Freeport East’s CEO, said:
“We are delighted to work with Greater Anglia to bring these facilities to the Harwich Haven.
The visitor economy is critically important for this region and attracting visitors all year round and getting them to stay longer is key to creating more stable employment and income for local businesses.
We are confident that the new network will strengthen the visitor experience as well as also give options for local people looking for a fun day out or a new way to access work or education.”
John Pipe, Manager at Shotley Marina, said:
“We are delighted to be part of this project and to continue our excellent working relationship with Freeport East, Eezybike and the wider project partners. Collaboration is key to delivering meaningful improvements for our local communities, and this initiative is a great example of organisations coming together to support sustainable travel and connectivity. As a gateway to the Shotley Peninsula, we are committed to enhancing visitor experiences while promoting environmentally responsible ways to travel. The new Eezybike facility will make it easier for people to access the marina, ferry services and surrounding attractions, helping to encourage active travel and support our wider sustainability ambitions.”

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Build on £6.4 billion investment: new report urges government to unlock Freeport growth and jobs
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
£6.4 billion invested, 6,000 jobs supported: UK Freeports have already attracted substantial private investment, according to the report.
Thousands more jobs forecast: Thames Freeport aims to create 21,000 jobs by 2045; Freeport East forecasts 11,350 new jobs.
Key lever to deliver Reindustrialisation: Freeports link Government ambition on industry and jobs with delivering growth in every postcode, especially coastal communities
15 recommendations for government action: strengthen investment incentives, align infrastructure funding and tackle grid and transport barriers to turn investor interest into projects.
Thames Freeport and Freeport East today publish Free to Grow: Unlocking the potential of England’s Freeports , calling on the UK Government to work with Freeports to deliver even greater impact through strengthening tax certainty, delivery powers and infrastructure funding.
Written by Jack Shaw of Groundwork Research, the report sets out 15 recommendations to turn investor interest into projects, jobs and lasting benefits for communities across England. Alongside Government, Freeports can deliver stronger multi-region investment propositions to international investors, go further on tackling skills deficits and use their unique public-private investment role to support Mayors and other local authorities deliver stronger regional growth.
UK Freeports are working.  They have attracted £6.4 billion in private investment and supported 6,000 jobs, according to the report, as well as delivering a range of wider benefits on new skills and innovation infrastructure, strengthening trade links and investing in local SMEs.
The opportunity is substantial: Thames Freeport aims to attract more than £4.5 billion and create 21,000 jobs by 2045; Freeport East forecasts 11,350 new jobs and a £5.5 billion contribution to its local economy. By primarily using investment incentives to encourage investment, Freeports are low cost – no investment means no cost to Government, while success delivers economic growth and new opportunities for local communities.  But factors outside the control of Freeport bodies, such as planning delays, limited electricity grid capacity, transport constraints and skills gaps risk holding back investment.
The report encourages ministers to solidify tax incentives and give Freeports greater flexibility to finance infrastructure and develop sites. Government, regulators and network operators must work together to tackle electricity and transport bottlenecks. Four priorities are:
Give investors certainty: extend existing tax incentives to 2040 to avoid cliff-edges and give investors the long-term certainty they need when commencing complex projects.
Allow flexibility on designating freeport sites together with funding for infrastructure: create mechanisms to support borrowing against future business-rate income retained locally, with safeguards, and agree changes to tax-incentive sites.
Use Freeports as a platform for wider Government action on productivity: align investment in grid connections, transport and access to innovation funding and allow Freeports to drive regulatory trials.
Deliver local benefits and attract investment: improve reporting on local jobs and job quality and promote joint investment opportunities through the UK’s overseas trade network.
In their joint foreword, Rt Hon Ruth Kelly, Chair of Thames Freeport, and Mark Lemmon, Chair of Freeport East, write:
“Freeports have an important role to play and the case for Freeports has become more compelling as the UK confronts a changing economic landscape.
Freeports should be given greater certainty over their future, greater autonomy to overcome barriers to investment and a more clearly defined role in the Government’s plans to ‘rewire the state’. With these changes, Freeports can build on what has already been achieved and realise their full potential. ”

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Freeport East backs Road to Logistics to strengthen Tendring logistics workforce
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
Freeport East is expanding its collaboration with the award-winning Road to Logistics through a new fully funded training and employment programme designed to help people in Harwich, Clacton and the wider area to develop new skills and access careers in transport, logistics and warehousing.
Building on an earlier pilot phase in Felixstowe, the programme will take more than 30 learners from Tendring through industry-focused training to prepare them for careers in logistics. Around two-thirds will aim to become HGV drivers with the remaining third pursuing roles as warehouse operatives.
Freeport East is a major hub for logistics and warehousing investment, based on trade passing through the regions ports, and many businesses need local people to fill key roles in the workforce.
Since 2020, Road to Logistics has supported more than 750 unemployed people through industry-focused training and employment support across the UK. Of those taking part, 89% have progressed into employment, with 94% remaining in work after 12 months. To date, supporting those currently out of work into roles in the HGV industry has created almost 3 million pounds of social value – working out as a £6.50 return for every £1 invested.
Connecting skills with economic opportunity
Developing a strong local skills base and helping local people access new job opportunities is central to supporting the growth of businesses and supply chains across the Freeport East region.
The programme builds on an earlier pilot delivered by Freeport East and Road to Logistics in Felixstowe, which supported people facing barriers to employment through a comprehensive training model to become newly qualified HGV drivers. This focused not only on driving skills but also on developing contextual awareness of the responsibilities and risks associated with professional driving, helping to create safer, more informed drivers and giving employers greater confidence in recruiting newly qualified individuals.
Successful participants from the pilot went on to secure roles with organisations including XPO, The Range, Maritime Transport and the Port of Felixstowe.  Since the pilot, Road to Logistics has gone on to establish a new HGV driver training academy with Suffolk New College , extending the benefits of this training approach to more jobseekers.
The first information, guidance and awareness day for participants in the new programme will be held at the Freeport East Harwich Innovation Hub in early October, focusing on training and career opportunities for warehouse operatives.
Bridging the gap between employers and learners
Employer engagement is a key part of the programme. Businesses have the opportunity to share the skills and behaviours they are looking for, while learners gain a better understanding of the sector, the workplace and the career opportunities available to them.
Freeport East and Road to Logistics are encouraging more employers to engage with the programme by offering interviews or employment opportunities, sharing suitable vacancies, engaging with learners during their training or providing insight into their workplaces.
Recruitment challenges in HGV driving and warehousing can make it difficult for businesses to access the skilled workforce they need, potentially increasing operating costs and constraining growth. By supporting people who are currently out of work into logistics careers, the programme aims to help address these skills gaps while ensuring local communities benefit from the region’s economic growth.
Steve Beel, CEO at Freeport East, said: “Economic growth has to be about more than investment and new development. It must create opportunities that people and communities can access and benefit from.

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: New scheme offers regional business funding to upgrade digital skills
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
Businesses across the region are set to get access to the artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity expertise of University of Essex researchers to support their long-term resilience thanks to an exciting new partnership with Freeport East and Mid Suffolk District Council.
The Cyber Innovate to Elevate (CItE) scheme has returned to offer small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Mid Suffolk and the wider Freeport area including South Suffolk and North Essex the chance to secure funding to explore innovations to make them more secure, efficient and competitive.
Participating firms will receive hands-on intervention from an Innovation Manager from the University of Essex and access to a team of highly qualified academics and research staff who can offer expertise across cyber and AI challenges. In addition, participating companies will get access to Mid Suffolk District Council’s newly opened Stowmarket Innovation Gateway.
It builds on highly popular and successful programmes previously run between Essex and its partners, Freeport East and Mid Suffolk District Council.
CItE will offer businesses funding to access a range of services and opportunities, including the chance to improve cyber resilience, identify practical ways to use AI and data automation, explore new product opportunities and upskill staff.
Dr Marta Fernandez De Arroyabe Arranz from Essex Business School at the University of Essex said: “Businesses across the region are navigating a rapid technological revolution, with both cybersecurity and artificial intelligence becoming essential to long-term success. Strong cyber resilience is now critical for maintaining customer trust and accessing major supply chains, while AI is helping SMEs improve efficiency and compete more effectively. However, these technologies also introduce new risks, particularly for smaller firms with limited resources.
Through Cyber Innovate to Elevate, the University provides a unique combination of cutting-edge academic expertise and hands-on business support, working directly within companies to develop practical, tailored roadmaps that help them adopt AI with confidence while embedding the cyber resilience needed to remain secure, productive and competitive.”
The previous programme was run in conjunction with Freeport East earlier this year, backed by Innovate UK. It saw 8 businesses in the region receive funding to work with Essex academics to review and bolster their cybersecurity measures. This followed a wider programme across Babergh and Mid Suffolk that supported 21 businesses over a 2-year period, many of whom have continued to work with the University and subsequently completed follow on innovation projects.
Among those who received support were Colchester-based Curtis Machine Tools and Portable Space in Suffolk, with the latter describing the partnership with Essex experts as “rewarding and straightforward”.
This time, CItE broadens its reach and expertise, with businesses in Mid Suffolk now eligible for support thanks to Mid Suffolk District Council joining the partnership, enabling AI assistance and resilience support to be provided alongside cybersecurity. It will also leverage the regions’ growing high-quality innovation infrastructure including the newly opened Stowmarket Innovation Gateway.
Steve Beel, CEO, Freeport East commented: “We are very pleased to be supporting another round of the CItE programme – cybersecurity and application of Artificial Intelligence are both key priorities for so many SMEs in our region.  As well as building on the deep expertise in digital technology at the University of Essex, the programme also helps strengthen the bonds between our local businesses and the University sector which are critical to driving greater productivity and economic growth in the region.”

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Freeport East pushes Green Freight Corridor with backing for electric truck hub at Port of Felixstowe
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
Freeport East has joined the push to decarbonise heavy goods vehicles travelling to and from the Port of Felixstowe by providing an initial £50k to support Maritime Transport’s plans for a new electric truck hub on a freeport site.
The proposed electric truck hub, led by Maritime and planned for a site on Anzani Avenue in Felixstowe, could see up to 6MW of high-speed, open-access charging made available for electric HGVs, as well as other heavy vehicles and buses. It could serve hauliers, logistics operators, transport firms, employment sites and major infrastructure projects in the Freeport East region, including Sizewell C and other major energy projects.
The financial contribution from Freeport East, which could increase in subsequent phases, will help Maritime Transport move the project through the next stage of planning and technical development, including preparatory work towards a future planning application to East Suffolk Council. If plans progress smoothly, the hub could be up and running in 2028.
The proposed facility would boost Freeport East’s broader Green Freight Corridor initiative, launched in partnership with East Midlands Freeport in May 2024, which aims to decarbonise freight transport and support skills and employment along one of the UK’s most important logistics routes. The Port of Felixstowe sees over 5,000 HGV journeys a day, of which only a small minority are currently electrified.
Steve Beel, CEO at Freeport East , commented: “Decarbonising freight is one of the biggest challenges facing logistics in our region, and access to reliable and high-capacity charging infrastructure is a critical part of the solution. It is also a key part of maintaining the Port of Felixstowe’s leadership position for international trade, with many of the leading shipping lines, logistics operators and freight customers wanting to see lower emissions in the sector. This facility, under the leadership of Maritime Transport, could help fill a real gap for hauliers and other operators. Anyone interested in how the project could support their decarbonisation objectives would be welcome to get in touch as the development evolves.”
Tom Williams, Deputy CEO at Maritime Transport , added: “This funding allows us to take the next step in assessing what a full-scale, open-access eHGV charging facility in Felixstowe could look like. We’re working closely with our specialist infrastructure partners and with Freeport East to test the case for the site, and we’re encouraged by the progress so far.”
The proposed hub reflects a wider need across the region to expand access to reliable, high-power charging infrastructure for freight operators as the sector moves towards electrification. Freeport East will continue to work with Maritime Transport as the project develops, and welcomes interest from hauliers, logistics operators and other stakeholders keen to learn more about the proposed facility and how it could support their own decarbonisation objectives.
To find out more about the hub, please contact enquiries@maritimetransport.com

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Freeport East supports the next generation of indoor farming with CropWorks
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
CropWorks
As the global demand for sustainable food production grows and the impacts of climate change on agriculture become ever more visible, finding new ways of growing crops is becoming increasingly important. One of the businesses leading that innovation is East of England-based start-up CropWorks, which is developing a new kind of indoor farm with the precision to manufacture high-value compounds in plants and the scale to deliver fresh produce at supermarket prices.
With support from the Freeport East Clean Growth Fund, CropWorks is pioneering research that could help reshape the future of agriculture, combining cutting-edge engineering, plant science and artificial intelligence to create highly efficient “plant factories”.
The future of sustainable plant production
CropWorks’ mission is to commercialise plant factories, developing large-scale vertical farming systems that combine the precision needed for molecular farming with the scale required to produce affordable fresh food.
Unlike many conventional indoor farms, CropWorks’ technology is designed to support two growing markets:
Fresh produce , with plans to supply pesticide-free leafy salads and herbs directly to supermarkets and food service providers.
Molecular farming, where plants are used to produce valuable compounds for cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and advanced materials.
A key part of the company’s approach is combining laboratory research with advanced AI modelling. Data collected from experiments is used to create high-fidelity digital simulations of future commercial farms, enabling designs to be tested and refined before construction begins.
Accelerating innovation through Freeport East
Support from Freeport East’s Clean Growth Fund has enabled CropWorks to carry out crop cultivation research for biomanufacturing that would otherwise not have been possible.
Still in the research and development phase, CropWorks is working with leading partners including Imperial College London, the Hartree Centre, the University of Cambridge, the University of Essex and biotechnology company LeafyColl to develop technologies that can be commercialised at scale.
Working from laboratories at the University of Essex, the team has developed and tested new cultivation technologies, collecting detailed data on how factors such as temperature, humidity and light influence plant growth. These insights are helping to optimise future commercial-scale systems while reducing development time and risk.
The research has already delivered promising results, with laboratory trials producing higher plant biomass than the team had previously achieved under comparable growing conditions. Future research will focus on increasing protein production while reducing energy consumption, helping improve both productivity and sustainability.
Leo Roubicek, Founder & CEO of CropWorks states: “ The support we’ve received from Freeport East has been instrumental in helping our research that is pioneering the next generation of indoor farming. The Clean Growth Fund has brought CropWorks a significant step closer to commercialising our technology and building a more resilient, sustainable food production system. ”
Next steps: Unlocking precision farming
CropWorks’ next major milestone is the construction of an integrated prototype cultivation system, planned for late 2026 and will be optimised during 2027. They aim to start commercial build-out on a pilot basis, supplying customers in late 2028 to raise funds for mass-market expansion.
To find out more about CropWorks please visit: https://www.cropworks.net/ .

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Royal Navy joins forces with Freeport East and Harwich Haven Authority to showcase region’s maritime resilience
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
Freeport East and Harwich Haven Authority (HHA) welcomed the Royal Navy to Harwich this week, bringing together senior figures from industry, local government and the maritime sector to showcase the future of regional resilience and security.
The event, Resilience in Harwich with the Royal Navy, took place on Wednesday 12 August at the Pier Hotel in Harwich and coincided with the docking of a Royal Navy River Class Offshore Patrol Vessel, HMS SEVERN, at Harwich – marking a rare visit that gave guests the opportunity to tour the ship.
Hosted jointly by Freeport East and HHA , and attended by a network of business, civic and industry leaders, the session brought the Royal Navy’s Naval Regional Command and Presentation team to Harwich to set out their vision for a ‘Hybrid Navy’, which would blend crewed platforms, autonomous systems and data and digital technology to deliver operational effect around the UK coastline.
Attendees heard directly from the Royal Navy about its plans for the region – including the county’s affiliation with the new Type 31 frigate HMS Venturer, formalised in 2024 and the first such link between Essex and a warship in 30 years. Currently under construction in Scotland and due to enter service later this decade, HMS Venturer connects more than 1.8 million people across Essex, from Colchester to Southend, with the Royal Navy’s next generation of frigates.
Freeport East’s Steve Beel addressed the strategic importance of Harwich to the UK’s maritime and defence footprint.
Steve Beel, CEO at Freeport East , said: “It has been our pleasure to host the Royal Navy here in Harwich today and to have the opportunity to bring local industry and political leaders together to hear about the future of maritime resilience in the region. Harwich has always punched above its weight when it comes to maritime activity, from the days of Christopher Jones, the Harwich-born captain and part-owner of the Mayflower, through to the Kindertransport in the Second World War and on to being a prime link for millions of passengers to the European continent.  Days like this are a reminder that this coastline still matters both strategically and economically to the whole United Kingdom.”
Dr Jo North, CEO at Harwich Haven Authority , added: “Harwich has always been a place where maritime expertise, innovation and collaboration come together, so it is a privilege to welcome the Royal Navy and so many partners to the Haven. As the organisation responsible for the safe navigation of one of the UK’s busiest and most strategically important waterways, Harwich Haven Authority know that strong partnerships and shared knowledge are at the heart of building a resilient and thriving maritime future.
“Bringing together industry, government and defence gives us the opportunity to share ideas, explore new technologies and strengthen the relationships that will support our region for years to come. By working together, we can unlock new opportunities for innovation, economic growth and skills, while ensuring our ports and coastal communities continue to play a vital role in the UK’s prosperity.”
Naval Regional Commander of London and Eastern England, Commodore Timothy Green CBE ADC said: “I am delighted to join HMS SEVERN in Harwich this week. This warship visit is an ideal opportunity to engage with the Maritime and Security communities in Essex and meet many Civic and Defence Industry leaders.
“Essex has a long and proud history of supporting the Royal Navy and this region remains a key maritime county with one of the largest coastlines in the UK. Furthermore, Harwich remains a strategically vital port for both the region and the whole of the UK.
“I know that HMS SEVERN’s visit will further strengthen the very strong bonds between the Royal Navy and Essex.”

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Freeport East-backed £18m Stowmarket Innovation Gateway officially opens
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
A transformational skills and innovation centre backed by £16.66 million of Freeport East funding has officially opened today in Stowmarket during an event attended by more than 100 local businesses, organisations and dignitaries, creating a new gateway to growth for businesses across Suffolk and the wider region.
Mid Suffolk District Council’s Stowmarket Innovation Gateway offers office spaces for high growth start-ups, collaboration and innovation areas, meeting rooms, a café and high-quality training spaces.
The Gateway is a key part of Freeport East’s ambition to ensure that the benefits of investment extend beyond its principal port and development sites. By connecting local firms, education providers and innovation specialists, the centre will help businesses across the region take advantage of opportunities in clean growth, digital technology and artificial intelligence.
A rolling programme of professional development courses – spanning AI, digital, leadership and creative disciplines – will be delivered on-site by West Suffolk College, Suffolk New College and the University of Suffolk and aim to address the skills gap in the region.
The workshops and courses are open to all adults with local employers receiving direct access to higher-level training that used to mean travelling outside the district.
Cllr Richard Winch, cabinet member for housing and property at Mid Suffolk District Council , said: “I am thrilled to see the doors of this exceptional centre officially open.
“The Stowmarket Innovation Gateway was designed with growing sectors such as the green economy and digital/AI technology at the heart.
“Its mission is to help ensure that businesses and individuals in the area are not left behind by the next wave of economic change but are instead equipped to shape and build it.”
Attendees at the event took part in a series of demonstrations, including robotic strawberry picking from Versatile RobotX, AV headsets with Space East, West Suffolk College’s SimVan, and a responsive AI avatar from 1956 Individuals.
Lisa Perkins, Chair of the Suffolk Business Board , who delivered the keynote speech at the event said:
“It’s great to see the Stowmarket Innovation Gateway officially open. I am a firm believer that innovation doesn’t happen in isolation, it needs the right environment. It needs to be a space in which businesses, founders, students and entrepreneurs can come together and this building allows for that and ultimately, is set up for success.
“Suffolk has some incredible assets which often don’t get the credit that they deserve – this centre is another fantastic addition to the county and a truly exciting opportunity for local businesses and budding entrepreneurs.”
Mark Lemmon, Chair at Freeport East , said:
“Just a month ago, we were celebrating the opening of the Assan Panel facility next door. Today, we’re welcoming another major investment that reinforces Gateway 14’s growing reputation as one of the UK’s leading locations for ambitious, forward-looking businesses.
Freeports exist to attract new forms of investment, create skilled jobs and drive long-term economic growth. This development shows that strategy delivering real results.
It’s also a testament to the ambition and determination of Mid Suffolk District Council, Gateway 14 and all the partners who have helped bring this project to life. Now the focus turns to the businesses that will make this facility their home, creating new opportunities for the local economy and helping cement this region’s position as a centre for innovation and investment.”
It will be operated by Hethel Innovation, which provides innovation growth support to hundreds of businesses across East Anglia and already manages three innovation hubs in Norfolk.

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Building a stronger digital defence: Curtis Machine Tools partners with Freeport East on cyber security programme
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
Curtis Machine Tools
Based in Colchester, Curtis Machine Tools’ advanced manufacturing expertise supports Freeport East’s focus on strengthening high-value supply chains in the region.
Staying ahead of the hackers
With cyberattacks on the rise across the UK, small businesses are increasingly concerned about getting caught out but for one engineering business a Cyber Innovate to Elevate partnership with the University of Essex and Freeport East has provided a roadmap for modernisation that is protecting their systems, staff and revenue.
A small business with a global presence
With a 50-year heritage building precision grinding machines used across a range of industries, Curtis Machine Tools helps companies worldwide create everything from dental drills to fuel injector parts.
When Ed Mayhew joined as Operations Director in 2025 however, he spotted a weakness, out-of-date cybersecurity processes and infrastructure.
Ed Mayhew, Operations Director, Curtis Machine Tools says: “It’s given me the evidence I need to get the funding to roll out fixes. In small businesses, cash flow is really important; we try to save money wherever we can. If I’ve got a strong business case, it makes it easier to find that money.”
Understanding the risks
After a cyberattack suffered by one of their suppliers left a client waiting for their delivery, Ed knew they needed to assess their own vulnerabilities.
The aim was to fully assess their IT processes, protections and infrastructure, to identify gaps, get expert support and strengthen the business. Improving security would also help them achieve Cyber Essentials certification, a requirement for businesses working in aerospace and defence.
The cyber challenges for SMEs
Professor Haris Mouratidis, Director of the Institute for Analytics and Data Science, led the Curtis Machine Tools cybersecurity audit.
Professor Haris Mouratidis, Director of the Institute for Analytics and Data Science says: “Cybersecurity is not a one-off. There were some quick wins but it’s about changing the organisational approach towards cybersecurity for the long term. It’s the kind of project that makes academics engage in research in the first place, because we want our work to have a practical impact.”
With colleagues, he conducted a review of documentation, technical assessments and interviews with key staff. They focused on IT systems, operational technology, external dependencies, and security policies and procedures.
It was a process Ed describes as “quick, easy and not at all time-consuming.”
Like most small and medium sized businesses, Curtis Machine Tools faced several challenges familiar to Professor Mouratidis. They had overcome the major challenge of recognising they needed cybersecurity but lacked knowledge and expertise within the business.
“Cybersecurity is fundamentally a socio-technical challenge – human behaviour and digital systems cannot be separated. When the latest research shows that between 75% and 90% of data breaches stem from human error, it becomes impossible to treat security as a purely technical problem. For SMEs navigating compliance obligations across complex supply chains, that reality adds yet another layer of difficulty.” Professor Mouratidis explained.
A framework for security
The audit identified three critical vulnerabilities that needed addressing immediately as well as a range of security gaps which the researchers triaged as high or medium priority issues.
The result was a comprehensive framework that prioritised risks and provided a roadmap for fixing them.
Ed has put in place processes to fix the critical issues, educate staff and implement changes that will build business resilience.
Today Curtis Machine Tools has a cyber framework to match the high-tech, high-value machinery it manufactures and is working towards gaining Cyber Essentials accreditation.

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Portable Space strengthens cyber resilience with Freeport East’s Cyber Innovate to Elevate programme
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
Portable Space
Based in Stowmarket, Portable Space is a key part of the regional business base that Freeport East is working to support. Its experience shows how targeted expert input can help growing companies turn cyber risk into practical actions and greater confidence with customers and suppliers.
Keeping up with the pace of growth
Rapid growth is what every business hopes for but when one company feared its IT systems weren’t keeping pace with the change, a Cyber Innovate to Elevate partnership with the University of Essex and Freeport East helped ensure they built resilience for the future.
Beyond a technical issue
Portable Space is a Suffolk-based SME supplying and customising portable buildings, modular units, and containers, with clients in construction, agriculture, education and defence.
Like all businesses in the 21st century, the company relies heavily on embedded digital systems, making cybersecurity a business resilience, trust and continuity issue as well as a technical one. After an exciting period of growth brought new colleagues, more systems and bigger projects, Sales Consultant Ryan Taber knew they needed more than just IT compliance. They needed to be sure the workforce expansion wasn’t outpacing cybersecurity governance.
Ryan Taber, Sales Consultant, Portable Space says: “Our biggest concern going into the project was that you can’t know what you don’t know. Working with an independent party like the University of Essex is a great way to assess where a business stands in terms of security. The process was incredibly straightforward and rewarding.”
Rising stakes for Portable Space
Early warning signs involving compromised accounts and attempted payment fraud highlighted the need not only to protect the business, but also its customers and suppliers. Despite constantly aiming to be as secure as possible, Ryan and his team were “wary that gaps could appear through complacency.”
As well as a technical review, the Portable Space cyber audit aimed to explore governance, access control, behaviour and cultural practices; identify risks; design training opportunities; build confidence; and develop practical policies the company could act on.
Mapping a positive culture
The audit took three months and was led by Dr Marta Fernandez De Arroyabe Arranz, Deputy Director of the Institute for Analytics and Data Science. Through a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods, the researchers mapped out the business’ position, identifying opportunities for improvement, behavioural risks and governance gaps.
Reassuringly, they found there was a positive internal culture and level of trust, that baseline technical safeguards were already in place and Portable Space colleagues were motivated to contribute to the business’ success thanks to a company-wide focus on efficiency, delivery and problem-solving.
Dr Marta Fernandez De Arroyabe Arranz, Deputy Director of the Institute for Analytics and Data Science says: “During the assessment, it was clear that employees communicate openly, collaborate closely, and generally feel comfortable raising operational issues. From a cybersecurity perspective, this type of culture can be very beneficial because it supports awareness, transparency, and willingness to report potential incidents or mistakes early.”
Formalising practices for success
The research team delivered a roadmap for improvement which is helping Portable Space move from reactive, informal security practices to clearly defined and consistently applied controls, responsibilities and processes.
New training programmes help colleagues understand why company leaders are making changes and Portable Space has earned a Cyber Essentials Plus certificate.
Strengthening cybersecurity isn’t just helping Portable Space protect itself, it’s giving the business the confidence to participate more fully in supply chains, to pursue new contracts, and grow sustainably in an increasingly digital economy.

About the Essex Community Foundation
Essex Community Foundation (ECF) is an independent charitable trust dedicated to improving the quality of life for people across Essex. We invest and distribute charitable funds on behalf of individuals, families, businesses and public agencies, ensuring long‑term support for local initiatives. Since launching in 1996, ECF has awarded more than £60 million in grants, distributing around £4 million each year to organisations that make a real difference across our county.
Our story began with a commitment to giving back. After selling their family sweet‑making business, Trebor to Cadbury in 1989, Ian and Angela Marks wanted their success to benefit the county their family had called home for generations. They believed a community foundation could bring people together to support charities and voluntary groups improving local lives and communities. Their vision became reality in April 1996, when ECF was launched with Ian as our first Chairman.
Today, we manage over 200 charitable funds, carefully investing donations to provide sustainable support year after year. Our experienced team matches donors’ wishes with the needs of local organisations, carrying out thorough due diligence to ensure every grant has meaningful, measurable impact.
You can explore this impact through our Community Spotlight, where we share the stories of people and projects strengthened by ECF funding.
Through our unique giving model, donors can support the causes that matter most to them. Anyone can be part of this work, our flexible Fundbuilder programme even allows you to start with small regular donations and grow your charitable fund over time, building a lasting legacy in Essex without needing a large upfront contribution.
There is a way for everyone to give back, whether that’s setting up a charitable fund, making a small one‑off donation, leaving a legacy, or sharing our work. Explore the different ways to Give to Your Community through ECF.

The CO postcode area, centred on Colchester and stretching across north east Essex, is one of the county’s most commercially varied areas. But how diverse is it really?
How Many Businesses Operate in the CO Postcode?
Across the wider CO postcode area, there are several thousand registered businesses operating across multiple districts, with Colchester itself accounting for the largest share.
Looking specifically at Colchester Borough, official business count data shows over 7,000 active enterprises. When including surrounding CO districts such as Tendring and Braintree fringe areas within the postcode boundary, the total number rises significantly.
Like much of Essex, the area is dominated by small and micro businesses . Over 85 percent of registered enterprises employ fewer than 10 people. This strong SME presence shapes the local commercial character.
Business Sectors in Colchester and the CO Area
Using national industry classifications and local authority data trends, the CO postcode sector profile broadly reflects the following distribution:
• Construction and property related businesses: approximately 18 to 20 percent
• Professional, scientific and technical services: approximately 15 percent
• Retail and wholesale trade: approximately 13 to 15 percent
• Health and social care: approximately 10 to 12 percent
• Hospitality and food services: approximately 8 to 10 percent
• Manufacturing and engineering: approximately 5 to 7 percent
• Education and training: approximately 4 to 6 percent
• Other services including automotive, logistics and personal services: remaining share
This balanced spread is significant. Unlike areas dependent on a single dominant industry, the CO postcode benefits from cross sector resilience. Construction supports housing expansion. Professional services support growing SMEs. Retail and hospitality serve both residents and visitors. Health and care services respond to population growth.
Why Sector Diversity Matters for the Local Economy
A broad business mix reduces risk and increases opportunity. If one sector slows, others continue trading. That stability protects employment, sustains supply chains and strengthens commercial property demand.
For business owners, it means a wider local client base. For suppliers, it creates multiple entry points into different industries. For investors and commercial landlords, it signals a healthy and varied demand profile.
What This Means for Essex Businesses
For readers of Business Time in Essex, the CO postcode represents more than just Colchester city centre . It is a commercial ecosystem that blends urban enterprise, coastal tourism, rural trade services and professional growth.
As we begin analysing other postcode areas across Essex, this data driven approach will highlight how each region contributes differently to the county’s overall economic strength.
The CO postcode stands out not because it is dominated by one industry, but because it is not. Its diversity is its advantage.

https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.title: Business National Emergency Briefing
https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.text:
Colchester Institute collaborated with Colchester-based PR and marketing consultancy Mosaic – The Conscience Marketing Agency to host a special screening of The People’s Emergency Briefing. The event brought local businesses together to learn more about climate change, share ideas and explore what they can do to make a difference.
Held on Wednesday 18th November, the event followed a debate in Westminster on Monday 16th November, where around 75 MPs came together to discuss calls for a government-led national emergency briefing on climate change and nature loss.
The debate received support from across political parties, with the Minister for Climate Transition, Katie White, agreeing to meet with the National Emergency Briefing organisers to discuss the next steps. However, the Government has not yet committed to delivering a national briefing.
Presented by wildlife presenter and environmentalist Chris Packham, The People’s Emergency Briefing looks at how climate change is affecting our everyday lives. From the impact on food supplies and public health to the risks to the economy and national security, the film highlights why acting now matters.
Following the screening, guests heard from a panel of local experts, chaired by Gemma Rawlinson, Managing Director at Mosaic. The panel included Becky Baines from Green Growth Ltd, Dr Jeremy Dagley from Essex Wildlife Trust and Marie-Ann Capps, Sustainability & Climate Change Officer at Colchester City Council.
The discussion focused on what the evidence means for Essex businesses and communities, and the practical steps organisations can take to reduce their environmental impact and become more resilient.
Gemma Rawlinson, Managing Director at Mosaic, said, “The debate in Westminster is encouraging, but businesses also need to think seriously about their own risks. If your business or a key supplier was affected by extreme weather, how would your organisation cope? We wanted to give people the opportunity to consider questions like this, share their experiences and learn from others who are already acting.”
The event also gave local businesses the opportunity to network and showcase their own sustainability efforts. Exhibition stands included Mosaic, Steven Eagell Toyota, Paddy & Scott’s, Fairfield’s Farm and Essex Wildlife Trust.
As North Essex’s largest vocational college, Colchester Institute plays an important role in the local community by building strong connections with businesses and providing students with the skills and knowledge they need for their future careers. Sustainability is an important part of this, with the College committed to reducing its environmental impact and helping to create a greener future.
The College is already making great progress. In the last academic year, Colchester Institute reduced its carbon emissions by an impressive 31%. This brings its total reductions to 55% since declaring a climate emergency and beginning to monitor emissions in 2020–21.
Gary Horne MBE, Deputy Chief Executive at Colchester Institute, said, “Climate change affects us all, but there are important questions that every business leader needs to be asking about how it could affect their organisation. Whether it’s extreme weather disrupting operations, rising costs or the impact on employees and customers, businesses need to understand the risks and think seriously about how they prepare.”
Further events are planned, including another in December.
More details on future events can be found at www.colchester.ac.uk/sustainability/ .

https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.title: CBeebies’ Mr Bloom Visits
https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.text:
Early Years students at Colchester Institute enjoyed a visit from CBeebies star Ben Faulks, best known as Mr Bloom, who visited the College alongside his wife Mimi to introduce their exciting educational initiative, Let’s Grow .
The visit was part of a new partnership between Colchester Institute and Let’s Grow, giving students the chance to discover creative ways to support young children’s learning and development.
During an interactive session, Ben and Mimi introduced students to their ‘nature and nurture’ approach, exploring how outdoor learning, play and active activities can help children build important skills while having fun.
Created in line with the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) curriculum, Let’s Grow offers a range of resources that encourage children to get curious about the natural world. The session gave students ideas and inspiration to take into their own future careers in Early Years.
Arcturus, a Level 2 Early Years student said, “The experience was really interactive. I enjoyed how we got to hold the fruits and vegetables and say hello to them all. I thought this was really good for children’s development, particularly their social skills. If a child feels nervous, they don’t have to immediately talk to another child; they can start by talking to the fruits and vegetables to help build their confidence.”
Summer, another Level 2 Early Years student who took part in the session, said, ““I can use what I’ve learnt in my placement to help me understand children’s emotions and personal development, while giving them something they can take responsibility for and look after.”
Colchester Institute is the second further education institution to adopt Let’s Grow, making the partnership an exciting addition to the College’s Early Years courses.
Joedean Boyle, Area Head for Early Years at Colchester Institute, said, “Let’s Grow brings a really engaging approach to early years education, and we’re excited to see how our students incorporate these ideas into their own practice. It’s a fantastic opportunity for students to explore sustainability and understand how these experiences can enrich the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) curriculum.”
Ben Faulks, co-founder of Let’s Grow said, “We’re so excited to begin this fantastic partnership with Colchester Institute, bringing over 25 years of creative practice together with the EYFS curriculum to provide innovative teaching resources for the next generation of practitioners. Partnerships like this are vital in equipping today’s students with the creative skills they need to become the inspiring teachers of tomorrow.”

https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.title: Ministerial Visit
https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.text:
On Thursday 29 October, Colchester Institute welcomed Baroness Smith of Malvern, Minister of State for Skills, and Colchester’s MP Pam Cox to their Colchester Campus to showcase their commitment to developing the skills needed for the future workforce supporting the regional economy.
Following discussions on the College’s recent achievements and ambitions, they toured the College’s Net Zero and Renewables Centre and the newly opened Sustainable Construction Centre, seeing first-hand how Colchester Institute is preparing students for careers in the growing clean energy and construction sectors.
The visit comes at an exciting time for Colchester Institute, which has been named one of five Clean Energy Technical Excellence Colleges (CETECs) in the UK. This recognition underlines the College’s important role in delivering technical education and supporting the transition towards a more sustainable future.
Over the coming years, thousands of new jobs are expected across the region as the UK transitions towards cleaner energy. As a CETEC, the College works closely with leading employers and industry partners to understand the skills needed now and in the future. Its Net Zero and Renewables Centre and Sustainable Construction Centre play a key role in delivering this training and preparing students for these opportunities.
Pam Cox, MP for Colchester, said, “Colchester Institute is leading the way in preparing the next generation for the skilled jobs that will power our clean energy future. I was delighted to join the Skills Minister in seeing these impressive new facilities and meeting the people helping to deliver this vital work. Being selected as one of just five Clean Energy Technical Excellence Colleges is a tremendous achievement and a real vote of confidence in the College, its staff and its students. As we create new opportunities in renewable energy and sustainable construction, it is essential that local people have access to the training they need to secure good jobs and rewarding careers. Colchester Institute is playing a central role in making that happen, and I am proud to support its ambitions for the future.”
Ali Davies, Deputy Principal at Colchester Institute, said, “We are responding to the initial findings of the Milburn review, particularly around supporting young people who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). Our focus is on making sure every learner has a clear pathway from education into employment, with the right support, training and opportunities to succeed. Having facilities like these allows us to deliver relevant learning that prepares students for the world of work, giving them a higher chance of success.”
While Colchester Institute has benefited from significant investment and improvements to its facilities over the past decade, college leaders recognise that continued capital funding will be essential to keep up with demand.
Gary Horne MBE, Deputy Chief Executive at Colchester Institute, said, “Our student numbers are growing rapidly, so it was a really good opportunity to set out our bold ambitions to renew some of our older buildings and create more capacity for the future.
We hope that the DfE’s new 10-year Education Estates Strategy will help us deliver on our strategic ambitions, providing more skills training capacity to support local people into the jobs on offer in the region”.

https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.title: 55% Carbon Reduction
https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.text:
Colchester Institute has reduced its carbon emissions by 31 per cent in the last academic year, and by 55 per cent since it declared a climate emergency and began monitoring in 2020-21, despite the number of 16-19 students rising by over 15% over the period.
Year-end data shows emissions of 760 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) for 2025-26, using location-based methodology, down 31 per cent on 2024-25. Since monitoring began in 2020-21, the College has cut emissions by 831 tonnes, a 55 per cent reduction over a six-year period.
The College has previously invested in 972 solar PV panels across both Colchester and Braintree Campuses to self-generate 15% of all the electricity it uses, with the remainder coming from renewable sources. In 2022 the College was also the beneficiary of a £3.7m grant from the Salix Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme to support a major £6m retrofit of principal buildings at the main campus. The results demonstrate that sustained investment in energy efficiency and sustainable practices can deliver real reductions, even as an organisation grows.
Sustainability is also increasingly shaping the College’s curriculum, not just how its campuses are run. Sustainable Development Goals have been mapped to ensure green skills are embedded across the curriculum, from low-carbon heating and building methods in construction and energy-efficient systems in engineering, to sustainable procurement in hospitality, and careful use of resources across all subject areas.
The College sees this as essential preparation for learners entering a job market where sustainability knowledge is increasingly expected, whatever the industry.
Gary Horne MBE, Deputy Chief Executive said, ‘We are thrilled to confirm we have achieved our near-term 50% carbon reduction target four years ahead of schedule, and this gives us confidence that we can make further strides over the coming years to ultimately become a net zero organisation. Sustainability isn’t a niche subject anymore, it’s relevant to every industry our learners will go into. By embedding good sustainability practices across our curriculum, from construction and engineering to art and design, we’re making sure our students have a high level of awareness that they will need in the workplace.’
As a further education provider, the College recognises its responsibility to lead by example as well as preparing learners for the green economy more broadly, and to accelerate sustainable development a new Environmental and Sustainability Strategy was approved by the College Corporation in 2025.
Aligned to the FE Climate Action Roadmap, action plans across 7 key areas ranged from Curriculum to Estates, Personal Development, Data/Tech, Procurement, Governance and Partnerships. Campaigns included:
Sustainable Education Campaign (Enhancing SDG curriculum content and Personal Development programme, developing new partnerships and green pedagogy through the Clean Energy TEC bid, launching formal staff training)
Carbon Reduction Campaign (Delivering on the 50-point plan for carbon reduction including new solar PV and EV charging, replacement vehicles and creating new initiatives such as the fossil fuel divestment plan)
Whole College Marketplace Campaign (Impactful departmental Climate Action projects devised on 24/10/25 CPD day, delivered through the year and showcased at 09/07/26 Marketplace)
External Awareness Campaign (Including Charity fundraising, and Sustainability Roadshows for school pupils, and the National Emergency Briefing Campaign for learners, staff and local residents – sessions are being delivered in college and in local communities)
Wild College Campaign (Rewilding campuses, and partnering with others to survey and deliver tangible gains for biodiversity on our Local Nature Reserve),
The results build on the Colleges 50 Point plan for carbon reduction, which sets out its ongoing commitment to reducing emissions across its campuses.
