https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.title: Sustainable Construction Centre Launch
https://www.colchester.ac.uk/feed/.text:
On Tuesday 29 th September, Colchester Institute officially opened a new Sustainable Construction Centre following a £5m building transformation project.
Part-funded through capital grants received from Department for Education and Essex County Council, the College has worked with a range of partners to successfully repurpose a 1960’s teaching block to create a modern construction training facility.  Supporting over 250 learners this year across three multi-purpose workshops, a large dedicated painting and decorating suite, there will also be three classrooms for theory and technical learning across a range of disciplines including plant driver training.
The project was seen as an essential step towards delivering additional capacity as a result of unprecedented growth in student numbers at the College over the past few years.
Gary Horne MBE, Deputy Chief Executive said “We are passionate about technical skills delivery, and we are delighted to realise another very important milestone in our Colchester Campus accommodation masterplan. As the largest provider of construction training in the region, this provides us with more scope to expand our offer further, and we are very grateful to our funders and sponsors for making this possible as we realise how critical it is from an economic growth perspective to be able to supply the skilled workers needed to deliver on local regional and national housebuilding and infrastructure plans.”
The launch was attended by local and regional construction companies, along with representatives from Essex County Council and other employers and stakeholders.
Councillor Peter Harris, Leader of Essex County Council said, “Essex County Council has invested £1.9 million in the creation of Colchester Institute’s new construction training facility. Combined with matched funding from private sector partners, this investment demonstrates the power of public and private organisations working together to address our skills needs and support economic growth in Essex.
The construction sector is critical to our economic growth. With demand for skilled construction workers continuing to grow, this centre will help train the workforce needed to deliver housing, infrastructure and development projects across the county. Our investment reflects our commitment to ensuring that residents have access to high-quality training so that they can secure good-quality local jobs. By investing in skills today, we are helping to build the workforce that will drive Essex’s future growth.”
The new facility will provide specialist learning, supporting continued local demand for construction training and helping learners develop the practical and technical skills required by employers
The new facility boasts a significant improvement on the operational efficiency as the design incorporates air source heat pumps, photovoltaic (PV) solar panels and a rainwater harvesting system supporting various plans underpinning the College’s sustainability strategy.
Stuart Cadman, Managing Director at Cadman Construction, the main project contractor said, “Colchester Institute are at the forefront of construction training in the Eastern region, and it gives Cadman’s the greatest of pleasure being involved with such a successful education provider. Our workforce is putting their skills gained at Colchester Institute, back into the College and therefore directly benefitting today’s construction students, who are the future of our industry.”

https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.title: First 276 Homes Approved in the Gilston Area
https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.text:
The first 276 homes in Village 7 of the Gilston Area have been approved by East Herts Council, marking a significant milestone for Harlow and Gilston Garden Town.
With plans for future residents to generate and share clean energy, grow their own food and enjoy restored historic buildings, the first 276 homes will include 39 for affordable rent and 26 for shared ownership.
The Village 7 layout, which will include 1500 homes in total, is designed to make walking, cycling and public transport practical alternatives to driving.
Measures include separate walking and cycling routes through Church Lane Green, connections to the planned public transport corridor and more than 1000 cycle parking spaces.
Secure cycle storage within homes and apartment buildings, alongside visitor parking near play areas and green spaces, will help make cycling convenient for everyday journeys.
Raised community growing beds will give residents opportunities to grow food together, including spaces near apartments where private outdoor space is more limited.
A foraging trail featuring fruiting plants will run through the neighbourhood, alongside a sensory garden offering a quieter place to sit and enjoy the surroundings.
A play area inspired by the area’s farming heritage will include references to rare British farm breeds. Five smaller ‘play-on-the-way’ spaces will provide opportunities for children to play along everyday walking and cycling routes.
Every home will also connect to a shared heating and hot-water network. The Community Heat Hub, approved as part of an earlier infrastructure application, will be operational before the first residents move in.
Village 7 is being delivered by Taylor Wimpey. Its masterplan, approved in April, also includes a new football hub and the restoration of listed barns for office and community use.
Councillor Maura Connolly, Executive Member for Planning and Growth at East Herts Council, said: “This is a major moment for Gilston.
“After years of planning, we have approved the first 276 homes, including 65 affordable homes, in a development that will shape this area for generations.
“But what makes Village 7 particularly exciting is how it brings people together, whether that’s growing food, sharing clean energy, playing sport or making use of historic buildings given a new purpose.
“These features matter. They help create a community, alongside the homes people need, and we want them to be central to how Gilston develops.”
Jonathan Locke, Head of Planning at Taylor Wimpey North Thames, said: “This approval is a big step forward for Village 7 and the Gilston area.
“We can now start work on what will become the gateway to a highly sustainable new community, with the first 276 homes being built at the same time as significantareas of new public green space that will allow people to relax, play and look after the planet.
“We have carefully designed our homes to be fit for the future. They combine attractive architecture and modern layouts with a range of eco-friendly features and construction measures to make them car bonnet-zero ready.
“We are going much further than the requirements in our outline planning permission on carbon reduction and sustainability, both to create the best possible homes for future residents and to make a positive contribution towards the climate emergency.”
Harlow and Gilston Garden Town brings together plans for new homes, jobs, transport links and community facilities in and around Harlow, across the Hertfordshire and Essex border.
The Gilston area will comprise seven new villages, with plans for 10,000 homes alongside schools, green spaces and other infrastructure.

https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.title: Delivering a Long-Term Vision for Gilston
https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.text:
The delivery of the Garden Town’s Gilston Area is much more than building homes, it’s about creating a thriving new place, maintaining trust with communities and managing a project that will span decades.
That was the message from East Herts Council’s Martin Plummer and Jenny Pierce, who were speaking at Epping Forest District Council recently and sharing lessons from one of the country’s most ambitious place-making programmes as part of the Planning Officers Society’s East of England network event.
The Gilston Area will deliver 10,000 homes across seven villages alongside new schools, transport links, community facilities and extensive green infrastructure.
Martin, Assistant Director for Place Delivery, explained that the scale of the challenge extends far beyond housing numbers: “We’re working with different developers across the Gilston Area, which means we’ve had to create a single vision that underpins everything alongside two planning permissions and a long-term regulatory system.
“It’s a 30-year plan and we were always thinking and looking at the future, not just short or medium term.”
The scale and complexity of the project is reflected in the number of organisations involved, the extensive infrastructure required and the need to coordinate delivery over several decades.
Jenny, Team Leader for the Gilston Area at East Herts Council, said collaborative working had been critical to progress, but stressed that local authorities still had to take responsibility for key decisions: “Collaborative governance can help to align some interests but it can’t obscure the roles and responsibilities of the statutory decision maker.
“We own that risk of accountability and delivery.”
Community engagement was another central theme of the presentation, with both Martin and Jenny stressing that successful place-making depends on building and maintaining trust with residents throughout the life of the project.
Jenny explained that East Herts has an objective of being a listening council, recognising it may not always be possible to reach a view that everyone shares.
Instead, it’s about ensuring people have the opportunity to be heard: “The whole point is that we put ourselves in a room with residents and stakeholders.
“We listen to people and their ideas and we encourage collaboration.
“Engagement mustn’t be treated as a one stop shop and it has to be more than just a single consultation event.”
They also highlighted the importance of maintaining a “golden thread” through every stage of the development process, ensuring commitments made to communities continue to guide decisions.
Concluding the session, Martin reflected on the importance of retaining knowledge within teams on long-term projects: “Memories can be quite short when it comes to Section 106 negotiations.
“Having someone who remembers what was discussed, and the reasons behind those decisions, is so important.
“We’ve been able to rely on Jenny, who has been involved with the project since 2012, to help maintain that institutional memory, and that’s been absolutely key.”
The lesson from the Gilston Area was clear: successful place-making depends not only on planning policy and infrastructure, but also on governance, collaboration, community engagement and a shared commitment to delivering a long-term vision.

https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.title: HGGT Wins Partnership of the Year
https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.text:
HGGT Chair, Cllr Ken Williamson, has congratulated the Garden Town’s five council partners and Homes England after the project’s Sustainable Transport Corridor won Partnership of the Year at the 2026 Essex Housing Awards last week.
Completed in March and funded by Homes England, the project, delivered by Essex Highways, Jacobs and Essex County Council, with Hertfordshire County Council serving as the accountable body, features enhanced routes for walking, cycling and bus travel in Harlow.
“I want to congratulate our five council partners, Homes England and everyone involved in delivering the Sustainable Transport Corridor on this fantastic achievement,” said Cllr Williamson.
“It recognises what can be achieved through partnership working and the shared commitment to delivering infrastructure that benefits existing and future communities.
“Harlow & Gilston Garden Town is one of the most ambitious regeneration and development projects in the country, a cross-border scheme where partnership working, from policy through to delivery, is key to its success.
“Our Sustainable Transport Corridor has seen that partnership come together to deliver infrastructure that’s not only unlocking future housing, but making walking, cycling and public transport easier and more attractive for day-to-day journeys.
“This is just the first step in a wider programme of infrastructure delivery across Harlow & Gilston Garden Town, and we’re committed to working together to support new homes, sustainable communities and future growth for the region.”
Part of the wider Harlow & Gilston Garden Town development, the Sustainable Transport Corridor runs from an upgraded junction at Burnt Mill, along the A1019 to the town centre.
It features new bus lanes, safer and more pleasant walking and cycling pathways, new public spaces, trees, signs, and lighting.
The improvements are part of the infrastructure that will eventually connect to the 10,000 homes built across the Essex-Hertfordshire border as part of the Gilston area of the Garden Town.

https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.title: Reliable Bus Journeys
https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.text:
The bus is a vital part of everyday life for many people in Harlow, from getting to work and heading into town to visiting friends and family.
It’s one of the reasons why our Garden Town partners at Harlow Council are upgrading the bus station as part of their exciting regeneration of the Town Centre.
When we talk about improving the route between Harlow Town Station and the Town Centre, one of the key aims on that North to Centre corridor has been simple.
It’s about making bus journeys more reliable, easier to use and improving day-to-day travel for residents and visitors.
One of the biggest challenges for buses is getting caught in the same traffic as everyone else.
That’s why the route now includes continuous bus lanes in both directions and fewer gaps where buses would previously have had to merge back into traffic.
In simple terms, this helps to keep buses moving, especially at busier times of the day.
You won’t notice it while you’re travelling, but behind the scenes there’s also technology helping buses along the route.
In some locations, traffic signals are being set up to give buses priority as they approach junctions.
That means less waiting at lights, smoother progress through junctions and more consistent journey times.
It’s a small change, but it can make a real difference to reliability.
Waiting for the bus is part of the journey too and that experience has been improved along the route.
There’s new and upgraded bus shelters plus some additions where there weren’t any before.
Improved seating and space at bus stops has been added as well and these updates are designed to make waiting more comfortable, whatever the weather and time of year.
One of the most useful changes for passengers is the introduction of real-time information screens at bus stops.
These will show when your bus is actually due to arrive and if there are delays, giving people more confidence in planning journeys.
Instead of guessing or checking multiple apps, you can see what’s happening right there at the stop.
These changes are all about making buses more accessible and there have been improvements to make getting on and off buses easier.
Stops have been upgraded with raised kerbs to allow easier boarding, helping people with mobility needs, parents with pushchairs, anyone who benefits from a smoother step onto the bus.
It’s all about aligning this new infrastructure with modern standards needed for regular travel.
When it comes to buses, reliability is everything.
If a journey feels unpredictable then it’s much harder to rely on it day-to-day.
But when services feel consistent, easy to understand and comfortable to use then they become a much more realistic option, especially for shorter trips into town or the station.
These bus improvements don’t sit on their own, they’re part of a wider set of changes along the route.
We now have better walking and cycling connections, safer crossings and improved links into neighbourhoods.
Together, they make it easier to combine different ways of travelling and give people choice.
For example, someone could have a foldup bike, cycle to the bus stop, catch the bus for their main journey and then cycle the rest at the other end.
We know the bus won’t be the right choice every time, but the option is there.
When services are more reliable and easier to use then decision making is easier when you do need them.
That might be on a busy weekday when the weather turns or when you just don’t want to drive.
If you haven’t taken the bus along this route for a while, it might be worth giving it another try.
With improved reliability, better stops, and clearer information, the experience is designed to feel simpler and more predictable for Harlow residents and visitors.

https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.title: Creating Safer Journeys
https://hggt.co.uk/feed/.text:
When people think about getting around Harlow and the local area, safety often plays a big part in the choices they make.
It might be deciding to walk into town after work, cycle to the station, or whether a route feels suitable for children and families.
A key aim of the recent improvements between Harlow Town Station and the Town Centre was to create journeys that feel safer and more comfortable, with a new walking and cycling route running through the tree-lined corridor between the two locations.
The wider route provides dedicated space for pedestrians and cyclists, giving everyone more room to move along the corridor.
For many users, having extra space and clearer separation makes journeys feel relaxed and enjoyable.
That might not sound like a major change, but it can make a big difference to how a journey feels.
Instead of walking or cycling alongside busy traffic for the entire route, people now have sections that feel calmer, greener and more welcoming to use.
The Essex County Council project team also worked to protect the established trees by using a permeable surface in certain areas.
This allows rainwater to continue reaching the roots while helping to preserve one of the route’s most distinctive features.
It’s a small example of how the project is not just about getting people from A to B, but about creating routes that people actually want to use and enjoy.
Busy junctions can often feel like a barrier, especially for less confident cyclists or families travelling together.
New signal-controlled crossings have been introduced at key locations, including Burnt Mill and Velizy Avenue.
These upgrades make it easier to cross busy roads and improve links between neighbourhoods, Harlow Town Centre and the station.
For many residents, this could mean choosing a route they may previously have avoided.
Lighting is another improvement people may notice, particularly as we approach the clocks going back and the darker winter months.
New and upgraded lighting has been installed along sections of the route, including areas that previously had little or no dedicated lighting.
Good lighting doesn’t just help people see where they’re going.
It can also make routes feel more welcoming to use throughout the day and evening.
A well-lit crossing, a clear route through a neighbourhood or a path that feels open and visible can all make the difference between choosing to make a journey or staying in the car.
The improvements have also helped replace some of the informal routes people had created over time.
In places, residents were crossing grass verges, walking through muddy areas or using routes that were less direct.
New links, including connections to The Hides and local amenities, provide clearer and more accessible routes for everyday journeys.
Perhaps most importantly, the improvements aim to help people feel more confident about choosing to walk or cycle.
For experienced cyclists, some journeys may have always felt straightforward.
But for families and people returning to active travel, confidence can make all the difference.
The aim isn’t to tell people how they should travel. It’s about making sure there are realistic options available when deciding the best way to make a journey.
Over time, that can help more people make shorter trips without relying on the car every time.
It also frees up space on the road network for those journeys where driving remains the best option.
Whether you’re heading to the station, visiting the town centre or simply enjoying a walk, the improvements have been designed to make your journey feel safer, greener and more pleasant.

https://tcbgardencommunity.co.uk/feed/.title: New website opens the door to the Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community
https://tcbgardencommunity.co.uk/feed/.text:
There is a fresh new way to follow one of Essex’s most ambitious place-making projects, as Colchester City Council, Tendring District Council and Essex County Council celebrate the launch of the new Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community (TCBGC) website.
The new site brings the story of the Garden Community together in one easy-to-use place. Residents, businesses and community groups can explore the vision, catch up on progress, find key documents and discover how to stay involved as plans move forward.
Visit the new website at www.tcbgardencommunity.co.uk.
The three councils will continue working together so that homes, transport, green space and community facilities are planned in a coordinated way.
Cllr Paul Dundas, leader of Colchester City Council, said: “This website gives everyone a simple, welcoming way to see how the Garden Community is taking shape. There is a lot happening, and we want local people to be able to follow the story, find the facts and stay connected.”
Cllr Mark Stephenson, leader of Tending District Council, said: “Launching the new site is a moment to celebrate how far the project has come — and to make the next steps easier to follow. We hope people will take a look around, keep checking back and continue to be part of the conversation.”
Cllr Peter Harris, leader of Essex County Council, said: “A successful new community needs the right infrastructure from the outset. The website will help people see the connections between transport, education, green space and the places where future residents will live, work and spend time.”
From plan to delivery
The project has reached an important stage. The Development Plan Document (DPD) for Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community was adopted in 2025 and went on to win the Best Plan category at the RTPI East of England Awards for Planning Excellence 2026. It provides the locally led planning framework for a well-connected, infrastructure and landscape-led new community in north Essex.
A hybrid planning application submitted by master developer Latimer by Clarion Housing was validated by Tendring District Council and Colchester City Council in spring 2026. The application proposes 7,750 homes across three mixed-use neighbourhoods, including 30% affordable housing, employment space, schools and community facilities, active-travel connections and 51% open space, including a new Salary Brook Country Park.
The statutory consultation closed on 22 May 2026, and the application is now being considered by the two local planning authorities. It will be assessed against the adopted Local Plans, including the DPD. A decision is expected in summer 2027 and will be made by the Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community Joint Committee. Until then, the proposals remain subject to the planning process and no decision has been made.  Full details of the application can be viewed on the Tendring District Council Public Access System using application number 26/00424/TCBGC.
Major enabling infrastructure is also progressing, including Colchester Rapid Transit System (RTS) which links key destinations in the city to the Garden Community and Phase 1 of the A1331 Link Road which was opened earlier this year and when completed will provide access onto the A120.
Whether you want the quick overview or the detail behind the plans, the new website is the place to start. Please visit www.tcbgardencommunity.co.uk and take a look.
Joint press release from Colchester City Council, Tendring District Council and Essex County Council

https://tcbgardencommunity.co.uk/feed/.title: Garden Community plan named national finalist in prestigious RTPI awards
https://tcbgardencommunity.co.uk/feed/.text:
The Councils are celebrating after the Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community Development Plan Document (DPD) was named a national finalist in the Best Plan category of the Royal Town Planning Institute (RTPI) Awards for Planning Excellence 2026.
The national recognition follows the DPD’s success as winner of the Best Plan category at the RTPI East of England Awards for Planning Excellence in June. It places the councils’ shared plan among the leading examples of planning practice from across the UK and beyond.
Adopted in 2025, the DPD provides the planning framework for a new 7,750-home Garden Community on the Tendring–Colchester border. It sets out an ambitious, long-term vision for a healthy, sustainable and well-connected place, with homes, jobs, community facilities, green infrastructure and transport planned together from the outset.
Reaching the national final is a major achievement for the officers from all three councils who worked with dedication, professionalism and creativity over several years to prepare the DPD, and for planning consultancy Hyas Associates, which provided specialist expertise and worked as an integral part of the joint team throughout its development. This close collaboration, informed by communities and stakeholders, produced a robust and locally led plan that will guide the Garden Community’s delivery for decades to come.
Cllr Carlo Guglielmi, Deputy Chair of the Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community Joint Committee, said: “To be named a national finalist is a tremendous honour and a proud moment for everyone who has helped shape this pioneering plan. It is a fitting recognition of the exceptional commitment, expertise and perseverance shown by officers across Tendring, Colchester and Essex, together with the specialist input and sustained support of Hyas Associates. Working as one team, they have turned a bold vision into a clear framework for delivery.
“The DPD puts quality of place, sustainability, infrastructure and the needs of future communities at its heart. Following our success in the East of England awards, we are delighted that this work is now being celebrated on the national stage, alongside the very best in the planning profession.”
The RTPI Awards for Planning Excellence showcase the positive contribution that planning professionals make to communities and quality of life. National winners will be announced at a ceremony in London on 3 December 2026.

Tendring District Council, Colchester City Council and Essex County Council are thrilled to announce that the Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community Development Plan Document (DPD) has won the Best Plan category at the Royal Town Planning Institute (RTPI) East of England Awards for Planning Excellence 2026.

DPD establishes a clear vision for place-making, infrastructure, movement and connections, economic activity, community facilities, green infrastructure and environmental quality, helping to ensure that growth is planned in a comprehensive, coordinated and locally accountable way.
The Best Plan category celebrates planning documents that demonstrate excellence in shaping high-quality places and providing a robust framework for sustainable development. Securing this award is a proud moment for everyone involved in the project and reflects the strength of the councils’ shared commitment to creating a new community that is well-connected, infrastructure-led and landscape-led, while supporting homes, jobs, services and lasting environmental enhancement.
Cllr Andy Baker – Cabinet Member for Housing and Planning at Tendring District Council, said: ““We are absolutely delighted that the Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community Development Plan Document has won the Best Plan category at this year’s RTPI East of England Awards for Planning Excellence. This is a fantastic achievement and a real tribute to the ambition, care and collaboration that has gone into producing a plan that will help shape sustainable growth and high-quality placemaking for years to come.”
Cllr Paul Dundas – Leader of Colchester City Council, said: “Winning this award is a wonderful achievement and a strong endorsement of the extensive work undertaken by the councils and partners in preparing a bold, locally led plan for the Garden Community. We are incredibly proud that the DPD has been recognised in this way, and that its clear and ambitious framework for new homes, infrastructure, green spaces and community facilities has been celebrated at a regional level.”

Colchester Borough Homes (CBH) has been awarded the Gold Award under the Defence Employer Recognition Scheme (ERS), the highest recognition given by the Ministry of Defence to organisations that demonstrate exceptional and sustained support for the Armed Forces community.
The award recognises employers that go above and beyond in supporting serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families, while actively upholding the principles of the Armed Forces Covenant.
CBH received the award at a ceremony aboard HMS Belfast on 12 November, having previously achieved Silver Award status in 2024.
Philip Sullivan, Chief Executive of Colchester Borough Homes, said : “A number of veterans and family members of serving Armed Forces personnel work for CBH and showing our commitment to the Armed Forces community is a priority for us.
“We’re proud of the military connections and traditions that come with Colchester being a garrison city, and we’re delighted to have been awarded Gold status under the Defence Employer Recognition Scheme.
“This recognition reflects the commitment of our colleagues and Armed Forces Champions, who help ensure we provide a supportive and inclusive workplace. We will continue to champion the Armed Forces community and uphold the commitments we have made through the Armed Forces Covenant.”
Colchester has a long-standing relationship with the Armed Forces through its historic garrison, one of the largest in the country. As a major local employer and social housing provider, CBH works to ensure members of the Armed Forces community are supported both as employees and residents.
The Defence Employer Recognition Scheme acknowledges organisations that have demonstrated outstanding support for defence and the wider Armed Forces community. Gold Award holders show long-term commitment through employment policies, advocacy and practical support for serving personnel, veterans and their families.
For more information about the Defence Employer Recognition Scheme, visit GOV.UK.

https://cbhomes.org.uk/feed/.title: Colchester Borough Homes recognised with national inclusion award
https://cbhomes.org.uk/feed/.text:
Colchester Borough Homes (CBH), which manages more than 7,000 council homes on behalf of Colchester City Council, has been awarded Pledge Pioneer status through the LGBTQ+ Housing Pledge.
CBH representatives received the award at a celebration event at the Pan Pacific Hotel in London on 18 September, alongside housing providers from across the country recognised for their work to make social housing more inclusive.
The national accreditation, delivered by Stonewall Housing, recognises housing providers that are taking practical steps to ensure residents feel respected, represented and supported in their homes and communities. The award reflects work carried out across CBH to engage residents, promote inclusion and provide learning and development opportunities for colleagues.
Supporting residents and listening to their views
The LGBTQ+ Housing Pledge is designed to help housing providers work closely with residents and ensure their experiences help shape services. To achieve Pledge Pioneer status, organisations must demonstrate action in resident engagement, visibility and staff training.
As part of its submission, CBH highlighted a range of activities aimed at giving residents a stronger voice and creating opportunities for people to get involved. These included an Equality, Diversity and Inclusion policy review involving residents, dedicated engagement activities held at Colchester Outhouse in December 2025 and work through the Resident Voice Panel to help ensure different perspectives are reflected in decision-making. The assessment panel praised the effort CBH had made to engage residents and gather feedback, noting the organisation’s willingness to keep learning and developing its approach.
Bringing people together
The award also recognises work to increase visibility and create welcoming communities where people feel they belong.
During 2026, CBH organised and supported a number of activities designed to bring residents together and celebrate diversity. In May, residents were invited to take part in a guided LGBTQ+ History Tour at Colchester Castle, led by Senior Curator Ben Paites. The tour explored LGBTQ+ stories from throughout history and was open to tenants and allies in a welcoming and inclusive environment.
In June, CBH attended and supported the Colchester Pride Summer Picnic, hosting a community engagement stall offering free sports, games and creative activities, alongside housing advice and information about tenancy services and support available to residents. The event provided an opportunity to engage with local people in an informal and welcoming setting while promoting inclusive housing services.
CBH also supported a Pride Banner Making Workshop, bringing residents together through a creative activity linked to local Pride celebrations.
The assessment panel welcomed these kinds of activities, recognising the importance of creating visible opportunities for residents and colleagues to engage with inclusion and community life. The panel also reflected positively on the impact of seeing an Essex-based housing provider actively demonstrating its commitment to inclusion and allyship.
Developing knowledge and understanding
Alongside resident engagement activities, CBH has invested in training and learning opportunities to help colleagues better understand the experiences and needs of different communities.
Earlier this year, specialist housing awareness training was delivered by Stonewall Housing for CBH colleagues, helping to increase understanding of the experiences and challenges some residents may face and supporting the delivery of inclusive services. https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: Harlow College students join forces with Essex Sexual Health Service to challenge harmful behaviours
https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.text:
Essex Sexual Health Service has partnered with Harlow College to deliver a creative, student-led campaign raising awareness of consent, healthy relationships and gender-based violence as part of the global 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence campaign.
Taking place annually from Wednesday 25 November to Thursday 10 December 2026, the international campaign aims to raise awareness, challenge harmful attitudes and encourage action to prevent violence against women and girls.
As part of their studies, Harlow College Media and Journalism students were given the opportunity to work with Essex Sexual Health Service on a real-life brief, developing creative and educational content that resonates with young people and encourages meaningful conversations around important and often challenging topics.
Working collaboratively with the service, students developed and pitched their own creative concepts before bringing their ideas to life through a series of four short educational videos, exploring:
The manosphere – challenging harmful online influences and stereotypes surrounding masculinity and relationships.
Unhealthy relationships – recognising the warning signs of domestic abuse.
Coercive control – understanding the difference between love, care and controlling behaviours.
Consent and peer pressure – highlighting the importance of personal boundaries, consent and feeling empowered to say no.
The videos will be showcased across Essex Sexual Health Service’s social media channels throughout the 16 Days of Activism campaign, as well as being hosted on their website , helping to reach young people through relatable, engaging and thought-provoking content created by their peers.
A spokesperson from Harlow College said: “Consent has become a pressing issue within society and it’s concerning to see the ramifications it is having. A movement is starting and I wanted our students to be part of a change. I hope our work, which I am proud of, creates a positive impact.”
Sophie Milner, Head of Outreach and Education at Essex Sexual Health Service, said: “It has been fantastic to collaborate with the media and journalism students at Harlow College and see the creativity, enthusiasm and thought that students have brought to this project.
“Giving young people a voice in the development of educational campaigns is incredibly important. By involving them directly in the creative process, we can help ensure that our messages are relevant, relatable and meaningful to the audiences we want to reach.
“We are proud to provide a platform for their work and hope these videos encourage important conversations around consent, respect and healthy relationships, while helping young people recognise harmful behaviours and feel confident accessing support.”
The collaboration reflects Essex Sexual Health Service’s ongoing commitment to working with local educational settings and empowering young people to make informed decisions about their sexual health, wellbeing and relationships.
Essex Sexual Health Service, commissioned by Essex County Council and delivered by Provide Community, offers free and confidential sexual health information, advice and support to people across Essex.
To watch the student-created videos, follow Essex Sexual Health Service on social media throughout the 16 Days of Activism campaign or view them on our website here .
For more information about sexual health, healthy relationships and accessing support, visit www.eshs.org.uk .

https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: Provide Community invited to help pilot the UK’s first nursing and midwifery public health framework
https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.text:
We have been invited to help pilot the UK’s first Nursing and Midwifery Public Health Practice Framework. The framework recognises how nurses, midwives and nursing associates help people stay well, prevent illness and reduce health inequalities through the care they provide every day.
In community services, that might mean spotting early signs that someone’s health is getting worse, making health information easier to understand or working with local partners to help people get the support they need closer to home.
Professor Lucy Wightman, Chief Executive of Provide Health and Group Chief Nurse, said, “A routine appointment may be the first time someone tells us they are struggling to manage a condition at home or explains what’s making it difficult to get help.
“Listening and acting on what they tell us can help prevent problems from getting worse. The framework recognises the skill involved in that everyday work and gives teams a way to share what works.”
Published on Monday 16 November 2026, the framework was developed with contributions from all four UK nations and endorsed by their Chief Nursing Officers. It gives nurses and midwives across the UK, and nursing associates in England, a shared approach to five areas of practice: promoting wellbeing, protecting people from harm, preventing ill health, working in partnership to reduce inequalities and supporting environmentally sustainable care.
Mark Heasman, Group Chief Executive of Provide Community, added, “Our teams see first-hand what helps people get the care they need and where they still face barriers. Taking part in the pilot would give us a chance to share that experience, learn from other organisations and use what we learn to make our own services easier to access.”
We are due to meet with the Florence Nightingale Foundation, which supports the pilot programme, to discuss how the pilot could work. Activity could begin in January 2027, subject to those discussions.
Click here to read the Nursing and Midwifery Public Health Practice Framework

https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: Employee owners help ten charities benefit from Provide Community grants

Taking Baby Steps CIC
Sanctus
Assure (Lighthouse Family Trust)
A further £2,000 each has been awarded to:
Breast Friends CIC
Footsteps Walking With You
The Pear Tree Fund
Open Country
Hackney Foodbank
The close voting reflected the strong support for causes across the shortlist. Extending the funding means every shortlisted organisation will receive a contribution towards its work.

https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: One year, extraordinary impact: Provide Community Equipment celebrates £18.5 million in equipment value retained
https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.text:
More than 119,000 items delivered, over 78,000 collected and £4 million being returned to council partners, Provide Community Equipment is celebrating a remarkable first year of helping essential equipment reach the people who need it.
Since launching in October 2025, the service, based in Greenford, West London, has demonstrated what a different approach to community equipment can achieve, combining increasingly reliable delivery with exceptional levels of equipment reuse to make public resources go further.
Behind every delivery is someone who needs equipment to support their daily life. Behind every collection is an opportunity to help someone else.
In its first 12 months, Provide Community Equipment delivered over 119,000 items of equipment, collected over 78,000 items and answered over 96,000 telephone calls, retaining more than £18.5 million in equipment value for its system partners.
By recovering equipment and returning suitable items to use, the service has reduced the need to purchase new stock, keeping valuable resources available to support communities.
Joe Coogan, Chief Operating Officer at Provide Community Equipment, said: “Equipment reuse has been central to the service’s success, exceeding the expectations set when the contract began delivering equipment into eight London Boroughs for North London Equipment Partnership.
“Together with wider operational efficiencies, this performance means £4 million is being refunded to the service’s eight council partner, a substantial financial benefit at a time when making the most of public funding matters more than ever.
“The results demonstrate the potential of a service designed around getting equipment to people efficiently, recovering it when it is no longer needed and helping it support someone else.”
Provide Community Equipment is part of Provide Community, an employee-owned community interest company, where social value and a focus on public benefit sits at the heart of the group’s approach.
Joe added: “Our one-year anniversary also marks an extraordinary achievement for the colleagues who built the service.
“Before mobilisation, there were no staff onboarded, no vans, no working IT system, no stock and no access to a warehouse. Within a year, the team had established an operation delivering more than 119,000 items of equipment, with on-time job completion performance at around 95% in recent months.
“Customer service has also strengthened, with calls now answered in less than 30 seconds on average, giving a better experience for prescribers and customers.
“Listening to customers continues to shape improvements. Following successful trials across six routes, guaranteed morning and afternoon appointment slots are being extended across the service, giving customers greater certainty about when to expect a visit.”
Jacqueline Garraway Commissioning Manager at North London Equipment Partnership, said: “The transformation across the Provide Community Equipment site this last year has been clear to see. Every area reflected strong teamwork, collaboration and a shared commitment to delivering an excellent community equipment service.”
Provide Community Equipment enters its second year with ambitions to build on this progress, strengthen service resilience and continue improving the customer experience.
Deliveries are forecast to reach 125,000 to 150,000 items during the second year, while the team’s experience is already attracting interest from other councils seeking to understand and learn from its approach.
For now, the first anniversary is an opportunity to recognise everyone who has made this progress possible: colleagues, commissioners and partners working together to help essential equipment support more people.
One year on, the results show the difference that commitment can make, for individuals, communities and the public resources they depend on.
Find out more about Provide Community Equipment on their website.

https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: Provide Community among first organisations to achieve Smokefree Employer Award
https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.text:
Provide Community has become one of the first organisations to achieve a new Smokefree Employer Award, recognising its commitment to supporting colleagues to stop smoking and improve their health and wellbeing.
The award was launched by Essex Working Well in April 2026 and recognises employers taking practical steps to prevent tobacco dependency and provide effective support for employees who want to become smokefree.
Provide Community achieved the award after demonstrating a range of measures already embedded across the organisation, including trained Very Brief Advice Advisors, regular workplace and digital health checks which record smoking status and clear pathways into specialist stop smoking support.
Importantly, the approach is already making a difference. Three Provide Community colleagues have so far successfully become smokefree with support from the organisation’s in-house NHS smoking cessation service.
The achievement has particular significance for Provide Community as the lead provider of Essex Wellbeing Service, which includes Essex Working Well and provides health and wellbeing support to employers across Essex.
Mark Heasman, Group Chief Executive at Provide Community, said: “Achieving the Smokefree Employer Award is a fantastic recognition of the work taking place across Provide Community to support the health and wellbeing of our colleagues.
“What matters most is the difference that support can make to individuals. We are particularly proud that three of our colleagues have already successfully become smokefree with support from our in-house service.
“As lead provider of Essex Wellbeing Service, we also have an opportunity to lead by example, putting into practice within our own organisation the preventative health and wellbeing approaches that we encourage and support other employers to adopt.”
The award supports wider national ambitions to create a smokefree generation and reduce the health impacts associated with tobacco use.
Provide Community will continue to build on its approach to workplace health and wellbeing, ensuring colleagues have access to information, advice and practical support to make positive changes to their health.
Organisations interested in working towards the Smokefree Employer Award or requesting a copy of the Smokefree Employer Toolkit can contact essex.workingwell@nhs.net .

https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: Essex Wellbeing Service and partners come together to make a difference along Clacton seafront

https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: Suffolk Sexual Health Service launches new learning offer for Sexual Health Week 2026
https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.text:
Suffolk Sexual Health Service is supporting Sexual Health Week 2026 (Monday 14 to 20 September), encouraging people across Suffolk to connect, communicate and feel more confident talking about sexual health and relationships.
This year’s theme, ‘Let’s Connect’, highlights the importance of meaningful human connection, from our relationships with others to understanding our own bodies, emotions and needs.
To mark the week, Suffolk Sexual Health Service will launch a new sexual health eLearning platform, providing an accessible and free way for professionals across Suffolk, including those working with young people and those in public facing roles where sexual health and relationships may be discussed to build their knowledge and confidence around all things Relationships, Sex and Health Education (RSHE).
The platform will consist of a variety of different courses and modules, with the first course available being ‘Sex, Consent and Confidentiality’. The service will then release a new learning course each month, including modules on areas such as ‘growing up in an online world, ‘pornography vs real life intimate relationships’ and ‘contraception and sexually transmitted infections.
The Outreach and Education Team will also be out and about across the county throughout the week engaging with students and young people to raise awareness of the week and ensure that people know how to access local sexual health and other relevant services.
Jessica Kirby, Outreach and Education Service Lead at Suffolk Sexual Health Service, said: “Sexual Health Week is a valuable opportunity to encourage more open conversations about sexual health and relationships and to remind people that support is available.
“Connection can mean many different things, from communicating with a partner and understanding our own needs, to feeling confident asking questions or reaching out for support when we need it.
“We want people across Suffolk to know that sexual health is an important part of our overall health and wellbeing, and that our team is here to provide confidential, non-judgemental advice and support.”
During Sexual Health Week, the service will be sharing information and resources across its digital channels, helping to challenge stigma and make conversations about sexual health and relationships feel more normal.
Suffolk Sexual Health Service is commissioned by Suffolk County Council and delivered by Provide Community, an employee-owned Community Interest Company delivering health and social care services.
To find out more about Suffolk Sexual Health Service and the support available, visit suffolksexualhealthservice.org.uk . To access the eLearning Platform please click here.

“Sexual health is about much more than preventing sexually transmitted infections. It’s about consent, communication and how these support healthy relationships and self-confidence, as well as having the skills and knowledge to make informed choices that are right for you.”
Essex Sexual Health Service is commissioned by Essex County Council and delivered by Provide Community, providing sexual health support including STI testing and treatment, contraception, education, outreach and health promotion across the county.

https://providecommunity.org.uk/feed/.title: Provide Carecall247 launches London Borough of Hackney Technology Enabled Living Service

24-hour monitoring

Alarm response
Technology-enabled support to promote independent living

https://cmsm.co.uk/feed.title: CMSM Wins Visit England Hidden Gem Accolade
https://cmsm.co.uk/feed.text:
Lady Victoria Borwick, Chair of Visit England Advisory Board presented the accolade to  Julie Miller and Alex Pitts of CMSM
On 10 November Visit England revealed the recipients of its 2025-2026 Visitor Attraction Accolades.
Combined Military Services Museum in Maldon, Essex was awarded the Hidden Gem accolade, given to smaller specialised attractions that deliver an outstanding visitor experience. Curator Julie Miller said:
“We are proud and delighted to receive this accolade on behalf of the team of trustees, staff and volunteers who keep the museum running, with immaculate standards of artefact presentation and customer service. We really are a hidden gem, it is wonderful to be nationally recognised and hope this accolade will put us on the map at a time when military museums are having a tough time.”
The accolades, presented to 73 attractions across England, recognise all aspects of the visitor experience and are awarded in five categories including ‘Hidden Gem,’ ‘Best Told Story,’ ‘Quality Food and Drink,’ ‘Welcome,’ as well as ‘Gold’ for customer experience excellence.
VisitEngland Director Andrew Stokes said:
“England’s visitor attractions are first-class, and these accolades highlight why they deserve this recognition. From stadium tours and water parks, castles, cathedrals and museums to wildlife reserves and wetlands these attractions provide outstanding customer service, going above and beyond to make visitor experiences extra special and spreading the economic benefits of tourism across communities in England.”
Attractions have received accolades based on the scores they obtained following their annual VisitEngland Visitor Attraction Quality Scheme assessment.
Participating attractions are supported by a network of highly trained and experienced independent assessors who deliver advice and guidance on improving and promoting the quality, accessibility and sustainability of their offer.
The VisitEngland Visitor Attraction Accolades 2025-2026 were presented at a celebratory lunch at the British Motor Museum in Warwickshire on 10 November.
Tourism is one of England’s largest and most valuable industries, supporting more than two million jobs, sustaining hundreds of thousands of small and medium-sized businesses, and generating £127 billion annually for the economy.
For more information please contact Julie Miller at Julie.miller@cmsm.co.uk

https://cmsm.co.uk/feed.title: Zeppelins Over Essex: The Night the L32 and L33 Fell
https://cmsm.co.uk/feed.text:
Marking the 110th Anniversary of 23 rd and 24 th  September 1916
On the night of 24 September 1916 , the skies over Essex were lit by searchlights, tracer fire, and the glow of burning hydrogen. Two German airships — Zeppelin L32 and Zeppelin L33 — crossed the county on what would become their final missions. Today, 110 years later, their story still echoes across the villages where these giants of the air came down.
Combined Military Services Museum is marking the 110 th anniversary of the L32 and L33 Zeppelin crashes which took place over the night of 23 rd and 24 th September 1916 with a special display of  artefacts and souvenirs from these events, which led to the deaths of one crew, and the capture and imprisonment of the other, in the only known example of an enemy military force marching through England, during either world war.
Why Zeppelins Came to Britain
By 1916, the First World War had reached a brutal stalemate. Germany sought new ways to strike at Britain’s morale and industry. Under Korvettenkapitän Peter Strasser , the Imperial German Navy deployed long‑range Zeppelins to bomb towns and cities across the country. These “super‑Zeppelins” were extraordinary machines:
650 feet long ,
built from lightweight duralumin ,
lifted by millions of cubic feet of hydrogen ,
capable of flying above most British defences.
They were intended to be unstoppable.
The L32: Shot Down Over Great Burstead : A Mission Interrupted
The Zeppelin L32, commanded by Oberleutnant zur See Werner Peterson, crossed the Channel aiming for London. Searchlights and anti‑aircraft fire forced it off course, and it dropped bombs near Aveley and South Ockenden.
The Attack
Two Royal Flying Corps aircraft intercepted the airship. Second Lieutenant Frederick Sowrey fired into the mid‑section, igniting the hydrogen. The L32 became a blazing fireball, falling near Snail’s Hall Farm, Great Burstead. All 22 crew members were killed.
Local resident Frederick Rayner saw the burning airship pass low over Billericay High Street. He reached the wreckage first, helping to lay out the bodies in a nearby barn — later known as Dead Men’s Barn . The crew were buried at Great Burstead Churchyard, later reinterred at Cannock Chase German Military Cemetery.
The L33: Crash Landing at Little Wigborough: A Damaged Airship Over Essex
The L33, commanded by Kapitän‑Leutnant Alois Bocker, carried out a separate raid over Upminster, Hornchurch, Woolwich, and West Ham. Damaged by ground fire and losing gas rapidly, the crew threw out ballast, equipment, and weapons — many later found in gardens across Essex.
The Crash Landing
Shortly after midnight, the L33 crash‑landed near Little Wigborough, blocking the lane to the church and narrowly missing nearby homes. The crew set the airship alight to prevent British capture.
A Remarkable Surrender
In an extraordinary moment in British history, Bocker and his 21 crewmen marched in formation through local lanes seeking a boat. They were intercepted by Special Constable Edgar Nicholas, joined by other officers including PC Charles Smith, who later received a medal for his handling of the situation.
The crew were held overnight in West Mersea Church Hall — believed to be the only time a hostile force marched in formation on British soil during either World War.
Local Memories and Lasting Impact
The crash sites drew thousands of visitors. Children picked blackberries beside the fallen airship; families retrieved small souvenirs; and one local doctor even suggested naming a newborn baby “Zeppelina.”
For Essex communities, the events of that night brought the global conflict directly into quiet rural parishes. For Britain, the destruction of L32 and L33 marked a turning point: improved aircraft and defences made Zeppelin raids increasingly dangerous and ultimately unsustainable.
Further Reading
British Airships 1903–1930 — Ian Castle
The End of Zeppelin L33 — Douglas J. Gurton
The Last Flight of the L32 — R. L. Rimell
The Fate of Zeppelin L32

This month the museum received a new particularly large artefact, a 25-Pounder Artillery piece! Originally from the Imperial War Museum Duxford, it has kindly been given to us as to add to our outside display, alongside our other artillery pieces and various other interesting historical pieces.
Come and see the 25-Pounder and our other new items at the museum today.

https://cmsm.co.uk/feed.title: Combined Military Services Museum Secures Rare Replacement Victoria Cross Linked to Maldon Hero
https://cmsm.co.uk/feed.text:
The Combined Military Services Museum is proud to announce the acquisition of a rare replacement Victoria Cross believed to have been made for Maldon-born VC recipient Frederick Corbett, also known by his birth name, David Embleton. The medal, now sits alongside Corbett’s Snider Mk III cavalry carbine, purchased by the museum in 2017, bringing together two remarkable artefacts from a turbulent and extraordinary life.
David Embleton was born in Maldon on 17 September 1853, one of thirteen children. By the age of seventeen he had joined the 23rd Essex Rifle Volunteers, and in 1872 he enlisted in the Royal Regiment of Artillery. Although his conduct was described as “very good,” his health deteriorated rapidly. After only five years he was pensioned off with chronic bronchitis and a persistent cough, later labelled tuberculosis. Yet this diagnosis may have been mistaken, as Embleton soon re-enlisted under a false identity: Frederick Corbett of the 60th Rifles, later the King’s Royal Rifle Corps.
It was under this assumed name that Corbett earned the Victoria Cross. During the 1882 Egyptian campaign, at Kafr Dowar, he displayed exceptional bravery when Lieutenant Howard Vyse fell mortally wounded under heavy fire. Corbett remained beside him, attempting to stem the bleeding, and later helped carry him from the field, an action that earned him Britain’s highest award for gallantry.
Health problems again interrupted his service, and as a decorated soldier he was transferred to the newly formed Military Foot Police and promoted to corporal. But after leaving the Army in 1883, Corbett’s life began to unravel. Struggling financially, he sold his Victoria Cross for just 15 guineas. Within months he re-enlisted once more, this time accepted as a Driver in the Royal Horse Artillery. He returned to Egypt in 1884, and earned further campaign honours. Known to wear a replacement VC, he may have crafted the replica himself, drawing on his training as a tinsmith, or it may have been made by his ironmonger brother Joseph.
Corbett’s later years were marked by repeated disciplinary issues, imprisonment, and eventual medical discharge in 1891. Today his behaviour might be recognised as consistent with PTSD, but in the nineteenth century such conditions were poorly understood. Returning to Maldon under his birth name, he drifted into destitution, repeatedly appearing in court for minor offences. In 1904 he was jailed for breaking a window at the War Office in an apparent attempt to reclaim his lost VC. He died in Maldon Workhouse in 1912 and was buried in a pauper’s grave, receiving a military headstone only in 2004.
Corbett’s original Victoria Cross is now held by the Royal Green Jackets (Rifles) Museum, though questions remain about its authenticity. Another copy was once recorded in the Royal Artillery collection.
Bringing this piece home to Maldon allows the museum to honour a local man whose courage was undeniable, even as his life took a tragic and troubled path.

CMSM has been proud to take part in a new series on Sky History, Battle Treasures with our patron Bruce Crompton, and SAS hero Jason Fox.
Battle Treasures tells the stories behind some of the rarest and most remarkable military artefacts ever discovered. Hosted by Jason Fox and Bruce Crompton, each episode explores three extraordinary items – revealing their provenance, the battlefield stories behind them, and little-known facts to bring each object to life. Bruce brings his encyclopaedic knowledge to each item while Jason draws on his experience as one of Britain’s most elite soldiers to offer vivid, first-hand context. The series also delivers world firsts, revealing artefacts never seen by the public.
This week’s episode featured our 10th Century Maldon Sword, found locally and believed to be a relic from the famous Battle of Maldon in 991.

https://saffronscreen.com/feed/.title: Saffron Screen needs your help.
https://saffronscreen.com/feed/.text:
You may not know that Saffron Screen is a charity. We’ve been one since 2006, run from a school hall by a small team of part-time staff and nearly 50 local volunteers.
This year, we’ve been celebrating 20 years of Saffron Screen .
From our earliest screenings to our birthday celebrations this summer, thousands of people have come through our doors to enjoy great films, live performances and the shared experience of cinema.
DONATE NOW
But 2026 has also been a tough year for us.
Our day-to-day costs have continued to rise and, in the middle of it all, our projector failed. It was 15 years old and we had no choice but to replace it. It was the only decision we could make, but it has left us with a hole that ticket sales cannot fill.
It costs us around £800 to put on a single film, our screenings aren’t always full and a high percentage of every ticket sold goes directly to the film distributor.
Ticket sales matter enormously, but they aren’t enough on their own. That’s why we depend so heavily on the support of our wonderful community and supporters to keep us going.
So, we’re asking for your help to raise £50,000.
£5 could help us switch the lights on
£10 could help bring a big-screen experience to our community
£25 could help us maintain our projection equipment
£50 could help us design, print and distribute our monthly programme and posters
£200  could help towards specialist equipment such as captioning glasses, making our cinema more accessible
£800 could cover the average cost of putting on a film at Saffron Screen.
It’s an ambitious target, but every donation will take us closer.
If you are a UK taxpayer, Gift Aid adds 25p to every £1 you donate, at no extra cost to you.
We have a plan to maintain Saffron Screen’s future, but we need our community behind us to put it into practice.
Donate. Every contribution makes a difference.
Come to the cinema. Every ticket matters.
Become a Member. Regular support helps us plan ahead
Spread the word. Tell your friends and family that Saffron Screen is a charity and share our appeal.
DONATE NOW
Thank you in advance,
From all of us at Saffron Screen
The post Saffron Screen needs your help. appeared first on Saffron Screen .

https://metalculture.com/feed/.title: The Unlonely City and Ten Years Since Olivia Laing’s The Lonely City
https://metalculture.com/feed/.text:
The Unlonely City , Metal’s programme of gatherings, celebrations and citizen-led initiatives, was born from the belief that we need ways to come together.
So far, it’s involved 20 artists and 70 local people shaping what matters to them, plus nine initiatives to disrupt loneliness across Liverpool, Peterborough and Southend.
Ten years ago, Olivia Laing wrote The Lonely City , an exploration through art of the loneliness they found in New York City. This month, to mark the launch of the book’s tenth-anniversary edition, Olivia Laing will join writer and curator Charlie Porter to discuss art, solitude and the relevance of the book ten years on. You can get tickets here .
“Loneliness is personal, and it is also political. Loneliness is collective; it is a city.” Olivia Laing
The title The Lonely City inspired the name of our programme, and it still resonates. Loneliness isn’t just an individual feeling; it’s shaped by the conditions we live in – housing, work, inequality, technology, public space and the loss of places where people can gather and belong.
We recently read Octavia Butler’s The Book of Martha in our anti-racist book club, where the idea of utopias, and the challenges of creating a universal utopia, sit at the heart of the story. We came away asking: What is your utopia? Could it work? Who would it work for? Who wouldn’t it work for?
An ‘unlonely’ city in Liverpool, Peterborough and Southend, where Metal is based, is one of our utopias. So far, we’ve had fun making scouse with a scouser, uncovering the magic left behind in art lockers, sharing banquets of hope, spinning yarns and watching a photography series develop among strangers. These moments of laughter, connection and unexpected joy, remind us that even small, surprise acts of gathering can begin to disrupt loneliness.
“A sense of lingering like the feeling of those conversations you have by the front door, when one of you is about to leave and you stay there for ages, and it means the most because it wasn’t meant to be a special moment but it really was and now it’s gone and you’ve hugged goodbye and closed the front door and one of you walks away smiling and the other pauses behind the front door savouring the moment.” – Luca Rutherford, The Unlonely City Power and Cultural Democracy Commission
We look forward to more moments like this.

https://metalculture.com/feed/.title: 10 Years of Connect & Create: Celebrating Creativity, Connection & Wellbeing
https://metalculture.com/feed/.text:
May marks both Mental Health Awareness Week and Dementia Action Week, making it a fitting time to reflect on 10 years of  Connect & Create   –   our creative wellbeing programme.
Since launching in 2016,  Connect & Create  has reached  more than 2000 people  across Southend, including people living with dementia, survivors of trauma, and those experiencing mental health challenges, through inclusive therapeutic arts practice, nurturing healing, confidence and joy through creativity.
Image credit: Anna Lukala
Image credit: Anna Lukala
A Decade of Impact
Over the last ten years, Connect & Create has delivered more than  25,500 hours of support , across over  100 groups , reaching  2,194 people .
This year alone,  49% of participants said they had reduced the use of crisis teams  or NHS and GP mental health services, with visits falling from 175 total visits before participation to 90 total visits afterwards.
Reflecting on the programme’s impact, Warren Harper, our Director of Southend said:
“Over the last decade, people in our community have been facing growing and complex mental health challenges. During this time, Connect & Create and its legacy has shown how the arts can play a crucial role in strengthening mental wellbeing at a time when such resilience is needed most.
We’re proud to be working with Southend City Council to provide free, safe and accessible sessions to strengthen connection and community, and it is much needed work I hope we can continue doing for the next ten years.”
Reflecting on the Programme
At its heart, the programme aims to be a welcoming space for people facing a wide range of challenges. As part of this anniversary year, we invited participants to reflect on what creativity and connection mean to them.
Mental Wellbeing Coordinator Emma Mills and Class Facilitator Ian Wilson spoke with some of the  Connect & Create  participants about how creative spaces can help people feel understood, valued and connected.
Connections through Creativity
Participants described the programme as a place where they can connect, feel safe and a sense of community.
“Connect & Create is like a big day out for me. It makes me feel a part and included, and like I am an artist rather than a person with ‘issues’. People talk about what’s important to them, and other times it goes very quiet as we get into our artwork. It makes me feel whole.”
“It makes me feel exposed but not in a bad way. I feel like I’m showing parts of myself that I would normally keep hidden and growing in confidence. I don’t have to hide here.”
Creativity without Pressure
Participants spoke passionately about the freedom and encouragement they experience through making art together in the sessions.
“What I like most about the art I create is that it doesn’t have to be ‘perfect’, but it’s appreciated.”
“It connects art, nature and local history to create a true sense of place and connection with others.”
Emma Mills, Art Psychotherapist, Mental Wellbeing Facilitator and our Connect & Create Coordinator said:
“We warmly welcome anyone facing mental health challenges—whether you’re feeling anxious, low, lonely, or simply in need of a safe space to breathe. Through the therapeutic power of creativity, we offer opportunities to reconnect with yourself, create meaningful artwork, build new friendships and enjoy the moment.”
Thank you to everyone who has been part of  Connect & Create  over the last decade and everyone who has supported the programme. A special thank you to the participants who generously shared their experiences with us.
If you’re interested in joining us or referring someone, we’d love to hear from you. Learn more  here .

https://clactonairshow.com/feed/.title: Clacton Airshow dates revealed for 2027
https://clactonairshow.com/feed/.text:
Clacton Airshow will return to the skies in 2027, with organisers confirming the dates as Thursday 26 and Friday 27 August.
The announcement follows another spectacular year for the seafront show, which once again brought fast jets, historic warbirds, twilight pyrotechnics and family entertainment to the Essex Sunshine Coast.
This year’s event marked Clacton Airshow’s 33rd year and celebrated the very best of aviation, entertainment and community spirit along Clacton’s seafront.
From the precision of the RAF Red Arrows to the sight and sound of Sally B, Spitfire MH434, the MiG-17F ‘Fresco’ and the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, the 2026 flying programme delivered memorable moments for every generation of airshow fan.
The popular twilight display also provided a dramatic finale to the first day, while the West Greensward Airshow Village added to the festival atmosphere with exhibitors, traders, activities and attractions for visitors on the ground.
Organised by Tendring District Council (TDC), the free event remains one of the district’s biggest summer attractions and is estimated to be worth more than £12million to the local economy.
Councillor Ivan Henderson, TDC Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Economic Growth, Regeneration and Tourism, said: “Clacton Airshow has just given us another brilliant reminder of what makes this event so special for our district.
“For two days, the seafront was full of people enjoying world-class flying displays, family entertainment and the atmosphere that only Clacton Airshow can create.
“It brings visitors into the heart of the Essex Sunshine Coast, supports businesses, showcases our seafront and creates shared memories for residents, families and visitors.
“That success is down to a huge team effort, and I would like to thank everyone who helped make this year’s show happen, from council staff and emergency services to sponsors, partners, traders, volunteers and everyone who supported the event.
“With the dates now confirmed for 2027, we can start looking ahead to welcoming people back for another unforgettable two days on Clacton seafront.”
Clacton Airshow 2027 will take place on Thursday 26 and Friday 27 August. To help keep the show in the skies, donations are welcomed via the official website at clactonairshow.com.
