https://greatdunmow-tc.gov.uk/feed/.title: COUNCIL TAX SUPPORT SCHEME CONSULTATION
https://greatdunmow-tc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Uttlesford residents can have their say on how much support should be given to people who might struggle to pay their Council Tax bill.
The Local Council Tax Support scheme (LCTS), or Council Tax Reduction (CTR), is designed to help the most vulnerable.
For 2027/28, Uttlesford District Council (UDC) are proposing to maintain the current schemes on the same basis as this year.
This means that UDC are proposing to:
Freeze the contribution rate so that the minimum amount that LCTS claimants pay towards their Council Tax bill will be kept at 12.5%. This remains the lowest contribution rate in Essex.
Continue to protect pensioners, vulnerable and disabled residents and their carers on a low income. Their minimum contribution rate will remain at 0%.
UDC want to know what you think of the proposals.
The easiest way to do this is via the online questionnaire which can be found on the Uttlesford District Council website or by emailing any comments to consultation@uttlesford.gov.uk
For people who do not have access to the internet, paper copies of the questionnaire are available by calling 01799 510510 .
The consultation closes at 5pm on Monday 14th September.

https://writtle-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Oak Processionary Moths
https://writtle-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
You may have noticed some of our oak trees on the Green have been fenced off.  This is due to oak processionary moths.  The Oak Processionary Moth (OPM) is a quarantine pest and is under official control and must be reported.  Although any tree can be infected they prefer mature oak trees.  The moths are becoming more common.
Why does it matter to me?
OPM caterpillars and nests contain hairs which cause itchy rashes, eye and throat irritations and can cause breathing difficulties in people and animals.  The caterpillars can shed hairs when they are disturbed.  The nests and the caterpillars should not be touched.  The greatest risk is between May to July when the caterpillars are most active.
What do they look like?
The nests are web like structure and are located on the boughs and branches of predominantly oak trees.  The hairy caterpillars process in formation when they are moving, hence their name.
What action have the Parish Council taken?
We have had our oak trees reviewed by tree professionals.  This years nests have been removed.  The Forestry Commission has determined Writtle is located in the buffer zone.  Currently they are actively treating sites in the buffer zone by spraying trees.  We have reported the trees we can see have nests to the Forestry Commission and the trees will be sprayed in the spring.  We will, as a precaution, relocate the two benches from under the large oak tree on the Green.
What action do I need to take?
Be vigilant.  If you have large oak trees in your garden check them.  If you spot a nest report it on Tree Alert – https://treealert.forestresearch.gov.uk/ .  Please do not touch the nests or caterpillars.  If you or your pet comes into contact with them, please seek medical advice.  The Forestry Commission have produced a useful leaflet with further information – https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6278d2a98fa8f5206c75d3ed/FC_OPMoth_Leaflet.pdf

https://www.ingatestone-fryerningpc.gov..text:
Free entry – open most Friday and Saturday mornings, 10 am–12 noon. Please check website for details: ingatestonemuseum.org.uk
Ingatestone Museum is situated next to the railway crossing on Station Lane, in a restored Victorian railway gatekeeper’s cottage dating from the 1840s. The cottage has been brought back from a state of serious dilapidation and water damage.
Visitors can enjoy their latest main exhibition, Ingatestone High Street: Past to Present, and admire the art display by the Ingatestone Meet and Paint group.
The museum showcases life as it was when the cottage was last occupied, in the late 1950s, and highlights the history of the parish, from the sarsen stones and Roman villa to the stagecoach and railway eras. Visitors can also follow the trail of Ruffles the railway cat!
Free visits for small groups of around 6 to 16 people are very welcome and can be arranged for a suitable date and time. To arrange a visit, contact imt.secretary@gmail.com .
Would you like to help?
The museum currently has a vacancy for a Treasurer . The role mainly involves dealing with running costs and occasional grant expenditure, with around 10 Zoom meetings a year.
They are also looking for volunteers to welcome visitors, ideally for around one session a month. Two volunteers are welcomed per session, and full training is provided.
Anyone interested in helping can contact the secretary at imt.secretary1@gmail.com

https://www.ingatestone-fryerningpc.gov..title: Housing Applications: IFPC Agrees Further Action
https://www.ingatestone-fryerningpc.gov..text:
Two major housing proposals are currently raising concerns for Ingatestone and Fryerning, particularly regarding their potential impact on the village and whether the policies in our adopted Neighbourhood Plan are being given sufficient consideration.
Application 26/00224/OUT proposes up to 32 homes on land opposite Seymour Field, to the south-east of the High Street and north of Docklands Avenue. At the time of writing this article, the application had been withdrawn from Brentwood Borough Council’s planning agenda while further reports and objections are considered.
For application 26/00769/OUT, proposing up to 216 homes behind Woodfield Cottages, councillors agreed to object at the Planning & Highways Committee meeting on 22 October. IFPC is also seeking an extension from Brentwood Borough Council to allow sufficient time to prepare its response.
At a subsequent Extraordinary Full Council meeting on the same day, councillors approved funding for an independent planning consultant to review both applications. For the 216-home proposal, the consultant will carry out a detailed assessment, including a site visit, with the resulting report forming the basis of the prish council’s objection. For the 32-home proposal, the consultant will review existing documents, identify any gaps and recommend whether further evidence or a report should be submitted. The parish council hopes this work will help ensure that our Neighbourhood Plan and the interests of our community are properly represented. Updates will be shared on our website and social media channels.

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: Marine scientist unlocks secrets of the deep for BBC’s Blue Planet III
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
A marine biologist whose pioneering research has uncovered some of the ocean’s most elusive creatures has helped shine a light on the mysteries of the deep for the BBC’s Blue Planet III.
Dr Michelle Taylor , from the School of Life Sciences , advised producers behind the Sir David Attenborough-fronted smash hit.
Dr Taylor helped shape Sunday’s episode, which ventures into the depths of the oceans to explore what has been described as “the last great frontier on earth”.
The Senior Lecturer, who is also Head of Science at Ocean Census , reviewed the science and connected the production team with other experts.
Her expertise was sought following pioneering research that has led to the discovery of coral reefs in Antarctica and helped capture the only confirmed footage of a colossal squid in the wild .
She has also had a species of coral , seaspider, and sea cucumber named in her honour.
Dr Taylor said: “It’s always a pleasure to work with the BBC Natural History unit and I’m thrilled that Blue Planet III is being aired – the cinematography and story-telling when applied to the deep-sea animals brings that relatively unknown realm to life.
“The deep-sea is the largest habitat on Earth and has a plethora of ecosystems that this episode highlights. I’m thrilled that so many exciting animal stories of the deep will be shown to the world.”
Explore the gallery below to relive some of Dr Taylor's exciting expeditions
Dr Michelle Taylor and Oenone Scott on board
The episode, which airs on November 29, and is live on iPlayer , explored the Pacific and Arctic ocean basins. It showcases a range of creatures, including the ‘flying spaghetti monster’, a young female argonaut, and forests of hidden coral.
This is the second time Dr Taylor has worked with producers, helping the team behind Blue Planet II in 2017 as well.
Away from the series national treasure Sir David is no stranger to Essex, having been awarded an honorary degree in 1987 .
Professor Terry McGenity , Head of the School of Life Sciences, said: “The deep ocean has a remarkable array of different habitats.
“Its inhabitants are vital for life on Earth, from abundant microbes, recycling nutrients, controlling climate, providing medicines and underpinning food webs, to the amazing and enigmatic animals that Dr Taylor and her team are discovering.
“It is hoped that Blue Planet III will inspire the current and next generation of leaders to create joined-up policy that better recognises the connectedness of all habitats on Earth, and that considers both biodiversity and climate.
“In the School of Life Sciences, we share our excellent research with students, the wider world and policy makers. "Dr Michelle Taylor’s expert contributions help to shed light on the (mostly) dark, deep ocean in an entertaining and thought-provoking way.”

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: UN Special Rapporteur helps shape new housing laws
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
United Nations Special Rapporteur Dr Koldo Casla has helped shape new housing laws in Spain following a high-profile homeless case which sparked nationwide protests and triggered a national election.
Dr Koldo Casla , a Senior Lecturer at Essex Law School and the Human Rights Centre, engaged constructively with government ministers in the wake of 87-year-old, Maricarmen Abascal’s eviction from her home.
A decree-law that aims to give better protections to vulnerable tenants has since been passed, with the Minister for Housing, Isabel Rodriguez, highlighting Dr Casla’s contribution to the new law in Parliament.
Dr Casla’s intervention came in his capacity as the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Adequate Housing.
Dr Casla was appointed Special Rapporteur by the UN Human Rights Council in March 2026.
He has the responsibility of assisting the United Nations and Member States in implementing laws and policies to satisfy the right to housing.
As well as numerous high-profile media appearances in Spain, Dr Casla engaged with the authorities to push for legal changes to ensure there is no repeat of the Maricarmen case.
His representations included the urgent need for new legislation to protect the vulnerable from eviction, the introduction of mandatory proportionality tests in all evictions, and tighter anti-speculation measures in Spain’s housing market.
Dr Casla said: “Maricarmen’s case was a painful reminder that Spain’s law had significant shortcomings in relation to the right to housing.
"I am determined to continue collaborating with whatever future government after the election of 29 November to fulfil the promise of article 47 of the Spanish Constitution, which proclaims the right to housing.”
Alongside his work in Spain, Dr Casla made an official 12-day visit to Ghana in October as Special Rapporteur, where he urged the government to introduce stronger protections for tenants, put an end to forced evictions, set realistic targets for affordable housing, and encourage the use of locally sourced materials in construction.
Dr Casla is also preparing his first thematic report for the UN Human Rights Council on a topic that resonates with Human Rights Local, a project of Essex’s Human Rights Centre, which he launched in 2020.
The report will explore best practices from local governments and community-led initiatives around the world to make the human rights to housing real and effective at the local level.
Dr Casla’s work at the United Nations is informed by his research on the social function of housing, including his most recent book The Social Right to Property.

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: Scientist using AI to detect skin cancer named top 50 UK innovator
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
A computer scientist who is using AI to detect skin cancer has been named in a top 50 power list of innovative researchers in the UK.
Universities UK (UUK) has highlighted Dr Haider Raza’s work in its 50 Future Innovators list, which celebrates the groundbreaking innovations and scientific breakthroughs that are reshaping industries such as healthcare and engineering.
UUK, which represents more than 140 universities, has launched the list as part of a campaign to push for further investment into higher education research.
Dr Raza, a Senior Lecturer in the University of Essex’s School of Computer Science and Electronic Engineering, has worked with Check 4 Cancer through a Knowledge Transfer Partnership (KTP) to create SKINTEL, a diagnostic tool that determines if suspicious lesions are malignant.
The tool, which is 99 per cent accurate, uses 22 patient characteristics and image analysis to deliver a diagnosis.
SKINTEL, designed to support clinicians and doctors rather than replace them, will speed up skin cancer diagnoses, reduce waiting times, and save lives by detecting the most dangerous skin lesions at the earliest opportunity.
Dr Raza said: “I'm honoured to be recognised as one of Universities UK's Future 50 Innovators.
“This recognition reflects the collaborative work undertaken with colleagues at the University of Essex, Check4Cancer and other partners to develop SKINTEL.
“What excites me most is the opportunity to demonstrate how trustworthy and explainable AI can deliver real-world impact in healthcare, helping clinicians and patients alike.”
UUK hopes its power list will inspire the next generation of innovators and secure more funding. It wants to see external investment in university innovation double to £100bn by 2035.
Professor Noam Lubell, Essex’s Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research, said: “Dr Raza has deservedly been recognised for his dedication to using AI in healthcare and is a wonderful example of the power of research at Essex.
“His work with Check 4 Cancer has the potential to transform skin cancer diagnostics around the world and ensure interventions are made at the earliest opportunity.
“Investment in Essex’s research has allowed our academics to work with businesses and organisations to come up with innovative ideas like Dr Raza’s. It is this kind of investment that is driving change in industries and allowing universities to make a real impact in people’s everyday lives.”
Alongside his work on SKINTEL, Dr Raza is the co-founder of Seniswise AI, which helps organisations assess their AI readiness and build custom, ethical AI and agentic systems for measurable business impact.
He has also advised UK policymakers on the use of AI in healthcare, as well as trained National Emergency Department professionals in emerging technologies.
Dr Raza is able to share his expertise and knowledge with students at Essex, where he teaches Data Science and decision-making. He also mentors postgraduate researchers.
Dr Raza added: “Beyond healthcare, this recognition also highlights my broader mission through Sensiwise AI to support organisations in adopting AI responsibly and effectively. Whether working with clinicians, businesses or policymakers, my goal is to ensure that AI remains transparent, accessible and focused on delivering meaningful societal benefit.”
Malcolm Press, President of Universities UK, said “UK universities sit at the cutting edge of the breakthroughs that define our age, from life-saving treatments and clean energy to artificial intelligence. The innovations coming out of our world-leading universities anchor Britain’s leadership in the industries that will power the global economy.
“These 50 future innovators, supported by universities the length and breadth of the UK, are just the tip of the iceberg. By celebrating these individuals and their innovations we hope to inspire the next generation of founders right across the country.”

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: The gut protein that could help prevent bowel cancer
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
A protein in the gut may hold the key to why bowel cancer affects men and women differently so an international research team is investigating to see if it could unlock better treatment.
Professor Patrick Varga-Weisz from the University of Essex is leading the four-year £1.2m project, which is jointly funded by the São Paulo Research Foundation and the UK’s Medical Research Council.
The work centres on a specific protein that helps package DNA inside our cells and decides which genes are switched on or off.
Professor Varga-Weisz said: “We’ve found that this protein acts as a kind of master switch for genes in the bowel that are controlled by sex hormones.
“If we can understand how it links gut bacteria to those genes and helps limit inflammation, we open up a genuinely new way of thinking about preventing cancer.”
Bowel cancer is more common in men than women, with around 26,800 new cases in men and 21,400 in women in the UK each year, according to Cancer Research UK.
Once differences in age are taken into account, men are also around one and a half times more likely than women to die from the disease.
The researchers believe the protein sits where three major influences on gut health meet: the bacteria living in our intestines, the chemicals those bacteria produce and the body’s own hormones.
Their theory is that it helps protect the gut lining, stopping the build-up of damaged cells that could later turn into tumours.
The team will investigate how the protein does this and why its effects differ between the sexes, with the aim of opening up new routes to drugs, diets or supplements that could lower cancer risk.
While the study will focus on the gut, the protein is also active in other tissues, so the findings could matter well beyond bowel disease.
Professor Varga-Weisz, from the School of Life Sciences at Essex, is working with researchers at Quadram Institute, Queen Mary University of London and the University of Campinas in Brazil.
He added: “This work brings together expertise from different fields across two continents, and we hope it has a real prospect of improving health.”
Quadram Institute, on the Norwich Research Park, specialises in food, gut health and the microbiome, while the University of Campinas is one of Latin America’s leading universities.
The São Paulo Research Foundation supports science in Brazil’s São Paulo state, and the Medical Research Council is part of UK Research and Innovation.

VR could help helicopter crews prepare for life-or-death rescues
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
Virtual reality could help helicopter rescue crews safely prepare for life-or-death emergencies that are too dangerous to recreate in the air, new research suggests.
Researchers from the Department of Psychology worked with Air Rescue UK to investigate how virtual and mixed reality technology could complement traditional training for helicopter hoist operators.
These highly skilled crew members operate the helicopter hoist during rescues, directing pilots while simultaneously monitoring weather, obstacles, aircraft movement and the safety of people being rescued.
Live-flight training is expensive and carries inherent risks, while some extreme situations, including severe weather, equipment failures and dangerous sea conditions, cannot safely be deliberately recreated.
Researchers found immersive simulation could offer a safe and cost-effective way for crews to repeatedly practise these rare but critical emergencies without putting people or aircraft at risk.
Dr Claire Oakley , Research Associate on the project, said: “What is exciting about virtual reality is that it allows us to study decision-making under pressure in a safe and controlled way.
“Better understanding these processes in this environment could help us design more effective training for rescue crews.”
The project, supported by the University of Essex Innovation Fund , evaluated Air Rescue UK’s mixed-reality simulator alongside a comprehensive review of existing research.
The technology combines a virtual environment with physical equipment, including a hoist cable that recreates the tension and movement operators experience during real missions.
It means trainees can practise emergencies including runaway winches, fouled cables, engine failures and emergency hoist cuts, as well as challenging environmental conditions.
Feedback from operators was overwhelmingly positive, with up to 92 per cent of post-training evaluations showing trainees felt they had learned something new or refined existing skills.
Researchers also found the level of mental challenge experienced during simulations was linked to how much operators felt they learned.
This suggests training could eventually be tailored to experience, with novices gradually introduced to increasingly complex situations while experienced operators face more demanding, time-pressured emergencies.
A spokesperson for Air Rescue UK said: “Air Rescue UK are pleased with the early results from this partnership with University of Essex which has laid the groundwork for the future in developing training processes within helicopter hoist simulation that meet the needs, firstly of the individual student or experienced hoist operator, and also of the helicopter operators, industry and the regulator.
“By applying academic rigour to simulation training, to get the best out of users, will translate directly to operational performance.”
The next phase of the partnership will explore how simulator training can be personalised, objectively measure stress and mental workload, and assess whether skills developed during simulation translate into live operations.
The project was led by Professor Miroslav Sirota , in collaboration with Dr Claire Oakley and Professor Marie Juanchich at the University of Essex, as well as Dr Motonori Yamaguchi, now at Shimane University, Japan, alongside Ian Bonthrone MSc of Air Rescue UK.

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: Open letter urges place-based focus in mental health strategy
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
An open letter to the government signed by close to 150 researchers, health chiefs and charities is calling for the new Mental Health Strategy for England to focus more on the places most affected by inequality.
Signatories, including the chief executives of Mind, YoungMinds, Place2Be and the Centre for Mental Health, are concerned the strategy will not fully reflect the challenges faced by coastal, rural and former industrial communities.
They warn that research, expertise and lived experience from these areas are being underrepresented in national policy discussions.
The letter to Social Care and Mental Health minister Alison McGovern MP is being coordinated by Professor Susan McPherson and Professor Victoria Bird from the Institute for Public Health and Wellbeing at the University of Essex.
Their research shows young adults in the most deprived coastal areas are three times more likely to experience undiagnosed mental distress than those in equally deprived inland areas.
Professor McPherson said: “Our research at Essex has shown that young people growing up in deprived coastal communities face particular disadvantages compared with their inland peers, highlighting that geography, as well as deprivation, can shape mental health outcomes.
“Excellent mental health research is taking place right across the country, and national policy should reflect that diversity of insight.”
The letter warns that mental health inequalities are shaped not only by individual characteristics and deprivation, but by access to local jobs, transport, housing, education, community infrastructure and other services.
It also notes that, based on publicly available affiliations, seven in ten contributors to the government’s Independent Review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism were based in London, Oxford or Cambridge.
The letter’s signatories include more than 60 professors from universities across England, many of them leading experts in health inequalities.
Professor McPherson added: “To reduce inequalities effectively, England’s mental health strategy must draw on the full breadth of expertise, evidence and lived experience across the country, rather than being disproportionately influenced by a small number of places and institutions.”
The researchers are asking government to recognise geographical inequalities in the strategy and to consider insight from a more diverse range of research leaders, local partners and people with lived experience from the areas most affected.
They are also calling for funding for local authority public health teams to invest in community-led mental health work, and for the Prevention Concordat for Better Mental Health to be revived and refreshed.
Other signatories include former Minister for Care and Support Sir Norman Lamb and leaders from universities, councils and Healthwatch organisations across England.
The team, alongside Dr Emily Murray , Director of the Centre for Coastal Communities at Essex, also set out evidence on mental health in coastal areas in a response published in the BMJ this month.
Their research found that among young people in the most deprived fifth of areas in England, those who grew up on the coast reported mental functioning scores 3.7 points lower than their inland peers.

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: Statement: Exploring the use of surplus accommodation
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
The University of Essex is currently considering a potential arrangement with the Ministry of Defence and Colchester Garrison regarding the use of a small section of our Colchester Campus. This would provide accommodation at The Houses for Ministry of Defence personnel for two years.
Due to lower student numbers, the University has surplus accommodation on its Campus so is looking at a variety of appropriate alternative uses.
Any revenue would be reinvested to support the University’s educational and research missions.
Deputy Vice-Chancellor Professor Chris Greer said: “No decision has been made on whether to proceed. Further work is being undertaken to understand its potential implications, practical requirements and suitability for the University community. As part of this process, we will continue discussions with the Ministry of Defence, the Students' Union and other relevant stakeholders.
“We have a proud history of working with civic and local partners, and this is one of several options we are exploring for the future use of surplus accommodation capacity. In doing so, we are seeking to balance our responsibilities to students and staff, our role as a civic institution, and the need to generate sustainable income to support our education and research activities.
“Any decision would be subject to careful consideration. We would only proceed if we were satisfied that the arrangement was in the best interests of the University community and will keep staff and students informed as these discussions progress.”
An Army spokesperson said: “We are committed to looking after our soldiers and will always strive to provide the best quality accommodation available. Colchester Garrison is exploring options to provide housing that delivers best value for money and relieves pressure on the local housing market. Discussions are being held with the University of Essex about the use of surplus student accommodation, but no agreement has been reached.”

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: Two scientists named among the most influential researchers in the world
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
Two scientists whose work spans how crops cope with drought and how emotions shape learning have been named among the world’s most influential researchers.
Professor Tracy Lawson features on Clarivate’s Highly Cited Researchers list for the seventh year running, while Professor Reinhard Pekrun has been named in every edition since 2024.
Clarivate estimates that around one in every 1,000 scientists and social scientists worldwide is recognised on the annual list.
Professor Lawson, from the School of Life Sciences , develops ways to measure how plants photosynthesise and use water.
Her work helps researchers understand how crops respond to heat and drought and identify traits that could make them more resilient.
Earlier this year, she received the Innovation Award from the International Society of Photosynthesis Research .
Professor Lawson said: “I am delighted to be included in this list for another year - this is only possible due to the hard work and dedication of everyone in the lab and the support of colleagues and collaborators.”
Professor Pekrun, from the Department of Psychology , has pioneered research into the role of emotions in learning. His work explores how feelings such as enjoyment, anxiety and boredom affect students’ motivation and performance.
Professor Pekrun said: “I feel deeply honoured by receiving this recognition again. The recognition is based on teamwork and attests to the invaluable support I received from colleagues, students, and professional staff at Essex in pursuing our research on human emotions.”
Professor Noam Lubell , Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research, said: “Having two academics named among the world’s Highly Cited Researchers is a brilliant achievement.
“Both Professor Lawson and Professor Pekrun are helping to shape what other researchers investigate and where their fields go next.
“They exemplify what makes the University of Essex so special and their work showcases our global reputation, reach and impact.
“I’m delighted to see both colleagues get the international recognition they deserve.”
Clarivate looks at how often other researchers cite their work, drawing on papers published between 2015 and 2025, and considers the breadth of their influence and the integrity of publication and citation patterns.
This year, Clarivate awarded 7,090 Highly Cited Researcher designations to 6,802 individuals from more than 1,200 institutions across 62 countries and regions. Some researchers were recognised in more than one field.

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: Can fungus solve the British river water quality crisis?
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
The cleansing power of fungus is being trialled in a pioneering project which could help tackle Britain’s river water quality crisis.
Researchers from the School of Life Sciences are testing whether mycelium, the root-like network of Fungi can support wetlands in filtering polluted water before it flows into rivers and other systems.
The study could offer an environmentally friendly way to tackle water pollution, helping protect aquatic wildlife and people enjoying Britain's waterways.
PhD researcher Lucinda Robinson , has helped create a 'living lab' at the University's Colchester Campus to put the natural filtration system to the test.
The sacks packed with mycelium used in the experiment
Lucinda Robinson testing water quality in the 'living lab'
Six experimental wetlands, known as mesocosms, were constructed to investigate whether adding mycelium to constructed wetlands can remove harmful bacteria, including E. coli, and excess nutrients that contribute to damaging algal blooms.
Over 12 weeks, the wetlands were subjected to controlled contamination, with researchers regularly monitoring water quality across a series of experiments.
Lucinda said: "Everyone deserves to be able to swim in natural water ways and enjoy nature without the risk of getting ill.
"This natural filtration method could help to improve water quality in our waterways.
"This is an exciting project that could have real benefits on the environment and really highlights how versatile and useful mycelium could be.
"Wetlands can help with this, and we want to know whether by adding mycelium we can support them to further enhance safety for recreational users, restore currently damaged aquatic habitats, all while creating new wetland habitats where wildlife can thrive."
Looking to the future - Lucinda hopes her work will have real impact
As part of her research Lucinda has also tested river water quality
Previous laboratory studies suggest mycelium can remove pollutants and neutralise bacteria without the need for synthetic treatments.
The Essex project aims to establish whether these promising findings can be replicated in real-world conditions, potentially paving the way for wider use of the natural treatment.
Lucinda is now analysing the results to assess how effectively the mycelium-treated wetlands remove pollutants compared with conventional constructed wetlands.
If successful, the approach could eventually be scaled up to help tackle water pollution across the country.
Professor Tom Cameron , who is supervising the project, said: “It’s a very exciting area of research, where increasingly we find that the natural world already has the capacity to provide functions and services that let us live healthier lives, if only we give it room to do so.
“It may mean living differently and accepting more of nature on our doorstep so that it can provide for us.”

https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.title: Uncovering legacy of influential textile designer
https://www.essex.ac.uk/news.text:
A unique project exploring the life and legacy of one of Britain's most influential twentieth-century designers is being launched thanks to a partnership between the University of Essex and the Warner Textile Archive in Braintree.
The University’s School of Philosophical, Historical and Interdisciplinary Studies is seeking applicants for a fully funded doctoral studentship which will support a researcher to uncover the remarkable life and work of pioneering textile designer Marianne Straub, who worked for Warner & Sons in Essex for two decades from 1950 onwards.
Straub’s innovative designs helped shape everyday life in post-war Britain, appearing in London Underground trains, buses, airports, public buildings and homes nationwide, reflecting her belief that high-quality design should be accessible to everyone.
The successful applicant will become the first to study the Archive’s collection of design records, textile samples and business archives alongside her personal diaries and correspondence, helping to shed new light on the role of women, migration, industry and innovation in post-war Britain.
Dr Alix Green, who is lead supervisor alongside Dr Matthew Grant, said: “We’re delighted to be able to offer a studentship focused on a designer whose iconic fabrics furnished post-war Britain but whose life and work have been largely lost from view. It’s a project built on years of collaboration between historians at the University of Essex and the Warner Textile Archive – and one that will set Straub’s legacy within the county’s long weaving and design heritage.”
The new project, titled Fabric of Everyday Life: Marianne Straub, Textile Innovation and Design, 1950-1970, is supported by a prestigious Collaborative Doctoral Award and will give a doctoral researcher unprecedented access to a nationally significant collection of materials held by the Warner Textile Archive, alongside newly acquired personal papers that are yet to be fully catalogued.
As part of the project, the doctoral researcher will work closely with the Warner Textile Archive , the UK's largest publicly accessible archive of a single textile manufacturer. Located in Braintree, the archive preserves more than 150 years of textile manufacturing history and holds over 100,000 records, designs and artefacts linked to Warner & Sons and the wider British textile industry.
Straub's impact as a designer, innovator and educator will be explored through the project which will also examine wider themes of industrial decline and renewal, sustainability, globalisation, women's work, mass consumption and the changing nature of British identity after the Second World War.
Dr Sam Woodward, Digital Threads Project Manager at the Warner Textile Archive, said: “We are delighted to be working with the University of Essex to offer this postgraduate Collaborative Doctoral Award. As the first doctoral research project to explore the Marianne Straub Collection in such depth, it presents an exciting opportunity to generate new insights into the life and work of one of the twentieth century’s most significant, yet often overlooked, industrial designers.”
The research project forms part of Digital Threads, an ambitious programme at the Warner Textile Archive that is creating a comprehensive digital archive collection. The programme aims to transform access to the Archive’s collections, establish a nationally significant resource for design, education and research, and widen participation to help ensure their long-term sustainability.
Alongside their research, the doctoral candidate will gain hands-on professional experience in archival cataloguing, digitisation, conservation, public engagement and exhibition development. They will also contribute to educational and outreach activities designed to bring Straub's story to new audiences.
The deadline for applications is 10 February 2027.

https://hashtagunited.co.uk/feed/.title: A New Era Begins:Meet The Caretaker
https://hashtagunited.co.uk/feed/.text:
As part of our summer reshuffle, today we’re announcing that our founder, Spencer Carmichael-Brown, is stepping into a new temporary role known as The Caretaker . This role has been created to help guide us through an exciting period of change as we continue shaping the next chapter of Hashtag United. It’s all about making sure the direction we’re taking as a club is properly implemented across everything we do, while bringing our football and content teams even closer together. Our ambition is simple: to make football fun again. Every decision we make, from the football we play to the content we create and the experiences we deliver, will be driven by one thing: putting our fans first. As we announced earlier this summer, we won’t have a traditional men’s first team manager this season. Instead, Sammy Knott will lead the football side as Head Coach, taking responsibility for the team’s performances on the pitch while working closely with Spencer, and our Head of Football Jay Devereux, on areas such as recruitment, philosophy and the continued development of the squad. The Caretaker role will sit between football and content, helping ensure both departments work together with a clear identity and shared purpose. Spencer will also personally deliver a range of new innovations throughout the season, all designed to bring our fans closer to the action and maximise the entertainment, enjoyment and overall Hashtag United experience. From exclusive behind-the-scenes access to fresh content and new matchday ideas, there are plenty of exciting things to look forward to. Spencer takes up the role with immediate effect. As part of these changes, Joe Gorman will also be leaving his role as CEO. Joe joined us with some hugely important objectives: helping secure a permanent home for the club, overseeing the redevelopment of our new facilities and building our in-house commercial operation. He leaves the club in a much stronger position than when he joined us, and we’d like to thank Joe for everything he has done during his time with us and wish him every success in his new role. Above all, these changes are about making Hashtag United even more entertaining, accessible and enjoyable for our fans. With Spencer stepping into The Caretaker role, we’re looking forward to bringing new ideas to life throughout the season and creating even more ways for you to get closer to the club than ever before. This is just the headline. There’s much more to this than a new role. Read A Letter from The Caretaker to hear why. Want to meet The Caretaker? https://hashtagunited.co.uk/feed/.title: Jay Devereux appointed as Hashtag United’s first-ever head of football
https://hashtagunited.co.uk/feed/.text:
We’re delighted to confirm that Jay Devereux, our very own Devs, has agreed terms to become Hashtag United’s new Head of Football, becoming the first person in the club’s history to take on the role.
As many of you will know, Devs recently stepped aside as Men’s First Team manager. But that certainly doesn’t mean he’s going anywhere. Hashtag United has always been built on people, and when someone has given as much to this club as Devs has, you do everything you can to keep them involved.
This appointment is a reflection of exactly that.
In his new role, Devs will oversee football operations and strategy across the entire club, including the Men’s and Women’s First Teams, recruitment, the pathway programme, and our youth teams. It’s a hugely important position within our structure, and one that will play a key role in shaping the future of football at Hashtag United.
There really is nobody better placed to take it on.
A New Role For A Club Legend
If anyone needed reminding of what Devs means to Hashtag United, his induction into the Hashtag United Hall of Fame in 2026 says everything.
For years, he has been at the heart of this football club. Through promotions, challenges, memorable moments and historic milestones, Devs has played a major role in helping build Hashtag United into what it is today. His understanding of our identity, values and ambitions is unmatched.
Moving into the Head of Football role feels like a natural progression.
His passion for the club is clear, his standards are high, and his knowledge of the game across every level of our football pathway makes him the ideal person to help drive the next stage of our journey.
This is not a farewell wrapped up in a new job title. It is an opportunity for Devs to make an even greater impact across the whole football club, helping support and develop every area of the game under the Hashtag United banner.
Word From Our Founder
Here’s what Spencer Owen had to say:
“As stressed when we announced his departure from the Men’s manager role, I’ve been very keen to keep Devs at the club, which is why I’m delighted he’s agreed to become our first ever Head of Football. This is a role that will see Devs oversee football operations and strategy across our Men’s, Women’s and Youth teams.
“He’s perfect; his passion for our club is undeniable, his understanding of our history and future runs very deep, and his knowledge, ethics and diligence are the exact traits we want spearheading our new-look structure. I’m over the moon that we get to continue our partnership working together.”
Word From Devs
And from the man himself:
“Although it’s the right time for me to step aside as manager, I really don’t feel ready to walk away from something I care so deeply about. This club, and being part of it, is incredibly important to me, which is why I’m delighted to have been asked to stay involved.
“I’m excited to be able to build on my involvement beyond the Men’s 1st Team, and I’m looking forward to supporting the management and their teams across the men’s, women’s and youth sections of our club.”
This appointment marks an exciting new chapter for Hashtag United.
As the club continues to evolve both on and off the pitch, strong foundations are being put in place to support long-term success across every level of the football programme. Bringing everything together under a clear football structure is an important step forward, and having someone with Devs’ experience, commitment and understanding of the club leading that process is invaluable.
Few people embody what Hashtag United is all about in the way Devs does.
Having a Hall of Famer with his passion, experience and deep connection to the club at the heart of our football operation is exactly the sort of move that demonstrates our ambition for the future while staying true to who we are.
Please join us in congratulating Devs on his new role.
Welcome to the role, Devs.
Let’s get right behind him.
Let’s go.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/24.title: Housing Targets and Green Belt: Castle Point | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/24.source: Rebecca Harris MP (Castle Point) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/24.text:
Absolutely—100%. Housing targets do not mean that houses get built automatically. They may be built, or we may just be planning a large number of sites on a map. If we build the level of housing being asked for in Castle Point on the sites that are potentially available to us, I do not think that many people will want to live there in 20 years’ time, because they will not be able to get anywhere. It will not make sense. We cannot build extra road capacity there—it is just not an option. Well, there is one place where we could do so, but I will come to that later.
I extend an offer to the Minister to visit my constituency, although I fear that he may not be comfortable with coming to Castle Point due to the live local plan. If he did, he could sit in traffic with me and explain how he thinks our road network will accommodate the residents of nearly 12,000 new homes. We would have ample time to discuss it, because we would be stuck in congestion.
The Government’s formula can produce a housing number, but it cannot widen the A13, create another route off Canvey or add capacity to our antiquated drainage network. Those are real-world problems that my constituents have to live with. Castle Point borough council’s own evidence to the examination says that, even with its lower proposed figure of 6,196 homes and the proposed mitigation measures, the traffic conditions will dramatically worsen. The council expects capacity to be exceeded on Canvey Way, parts of the A13, the A129 and roads on Canvey itself.
In August, the chief executive of Essex county council wrote to me to confirm that the highways authority had not yet received the revised transport assessment that it needed to satisfy itself that even those 6,196 homes could be accommodated in terms of capacity and, critically, safety, yet my council is being pressured to accommodate thousands more. Before deciding how many more houses Castle Point can take, surely somebody should establish whether our roads can safely take the traffic. The economic impact of the current levels of congestion should be enough of an argument on its own to reduce the number of houses in the Government’s target.
Of course, the traffic does not stop at the borough boundary. Our neighbouring authorities are also being asked to accommodate an enormous amount of development. Many residents in those new developments will use exactly the same stretches of road and exactly the same junctions as my constituents. The Minister cannot reasonably expect councils to plan for thousands of additional homes in isolation from one another, given that they all rely on the same incredibly overstretched infrastructure along the Thames estuary.
I am particularly concerned about the infrastructure on Canvey Island, which is home to 40,000 people. It is a strong and proud community, but it faces circumstances that very few other communities in this country have to contend with; indeed, I would say it is absolutely unique. Much of the island lies below sea level. It relies on extensive sea defences and a very complex network of pumps, ditches, culverts and drainage channels. The island has two roads to the mainland, both of which start at the same roundabout and then feed into the same heavily congested wider road network.
Canvey Island is also home to major industrial installations, including two top-tier control of major accident hazard sites, subject to stringent safety regulations, that are part of our national critical infrastructure. If the gas, and road and jet fuel, cannot leave the island because of traffic or an accident—one year, a tanker burst into flames, closing a road—it will have a genuinely wider impact on the energy resilience of the whole south-east of England and beyond. That has not received anywhere near enough consideration by the Government and has possibly been overlooked by the inspector, as he waded through reams of evidence.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/24.title: Housing Targets and Green Belt: Castle Point | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/24.source: Rebecca Harris MP (Castle Point) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/24.text:
I have always thought that it is for local people to make decisions. Even the most highly qualified planning inspector does not always have as good an understanding of the issues in a local area as the local residents do, which is why it is so important that those residents have a say. I hope I made that broad point when I talked about how my borough might look on a map; the lived experience—as is the current buzz phrase—is a different matter. I do not think it is sensible national planning policy to leave brownfield sites in urban areas undelivered and then have to build out on the green belt. I would be very grateful if the Minister can explain some of the justice or logic of that today to my constituents, who feel that, in effect, an injustice is being perpetrated.
There is also the small matter of how people are expected to live in these thousands of new homes. How are they going to get around the borough? I recently participated in an examination of Castle Point’s local plan and made extensive representations about the capacity of our road network. Castle Point is dependent on just three principal road routes in and out of the borough for 100,000 residents—eastward along the A13 and towards Southend, westward through Sadlers Farm, and northward through Rayleigh Weir. All three of those routes already suffer from chronic congestion. If there is an accident, a broken-down vehicle or a set of temporary traffic lights on just one of them, very large parts of my constituency pretty much grind to a halt, because there are no alternatives. We are on the estuary; people cannot just hang a right and take another road. That is just not an option.
Earlier this year, planned gas works at Tarpots resulted in some residents experiencing delays of up to two hours for incredibly short journeys. People were struggling to get to work and to appointments. It took them hours just to get home after a hard day’s work, and residents of neighbouring communities such as Bowers Gifford suffered enormously. That was not the result of thousands of new homes being built; it was down to the road network that we have today. I would happily invite the Minister to visit my constituency, and I would suggest that he comes during the morning rush hour. I could take him to Sadlers Farm, through to Tarpots, along the A13, up to Rayleigh Weir and, if we have any time left in the day, back through Canvey Way.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/24.text:
I thank my hon. Friend for his intervention, and I think a lot of us have had the same thought about urban areas that have brownfield land available. We all know there are vast swathes of brownfield land in places such as London and Birmingham that also have good connectivity—road infrastructure, good bus services and, in London, good prospects of people getting home and to work when the tubes are not on strike. Especially in Castle Point and other coastal communities like mine, it is incredibly congested and difficult, and the local communities as originally developed were never intended to have the level of housing they have. It would be entirely different if we were starting from scratch.
Research by the Campaign to Protect Rural England last year identified capacity for nearly 60,000 homes on brownfield sites with planning permission in Birmingham alone. I do not begrudge Birmingham getting a housing figure that reflects its circumstances, if that is the case, but I would quite like the same consideration to be given to my constituents. I do not know how it can possibly make sense to reduce housing targets in cities with vast amounts of brownfield land available while doubling them in places where the only realistic way of accommodating growth is to build on the countryside.

I wish to thank Mr Speaker for granting me this debate and for allowing an extremely rare exception to the usual convention under which I, by virtue of my constitutional position as Opposition Chief Whip, do not normally speak in this Chamber. I am particularly grateful to him for recognising the exceptional importance of this issue to my constituents.
Although I have the great privilege of serving as Chief Whip of His Majesty’s loyal Opposition, my first duty in this House is clearly to the people of Castle Point. Protecting the green belt that my residents treasure and tackling the problems caused by our already overstretched local infrastructure are the two biggest issues facing Castle Point, and they have been for many decades. Such is the strength of feeling among my constituents, and such are the potentially devastating consequences of the Government’s planning changes in the communities I represent, that it is my duty to have sought this debate.
For more than 16 years, I have fought alongside my residents to protect the precious little countryside that we have left in Castle Point. I have done so regardless of which political party has been in government and regardless of who has been in control of my local council. I have never believed that protecting the fields, farmland and woodlands that separate our communities should be a party political issue.
However, the changes that the Labour Government have made to the national planning policy have put those much-loved spaces under greater threat than at any point during my time in Parliament. Let me explain to the Minister why Castle Point is so particularly badly affected by his Government’s policies, why I believe that the housing numbers being imposed on us are wholly unrealistic and what I believe can be done to try to limit the damage.
I will start by explaining a little bit about my constituency. Castle Point is a tiny borough on the Thames estuary, comprising the towns of Benfleet, Hadleigh and Thundersley and the community of Canvey Island—a true island in the Thames estuary. We have just 17.4 square miles of land and a population density of nearly 5,000 per square mile. However, those figures do not tell the whole story.
Ministers and officials in Whitehall looking at a map of Castle Point could be forgiven for thinking that we have an abundance of underdeveloped land. They will see some great expanses of green on a map, but they will not necessarily appreciate that most of that land is tidal marshland, mudflats, protected nature reserves and land subject to extremely serious flood risk. Some of the largest green spaces in my constituency provide excellent accommodation for lapwings, but they are rather less suitable for accommodating the Minister’s housing targets.
We have internationally protected wildlife habitats, six sites of special scientific interest, ancient woodlands and an important historic landscape, including the setting of Hadleigh castle, made famous by John Constable. Approximately half of our borough is affected by tidal flood risk. Once those constraints are properly taken into account, the amount of land on which people can realistically live is considerably smaller than a map of the borough might suggest.
That is why the remaining fields around and between our towns are so incredibly precious to my residents. They are the lungs of our highly urbanised communities. They are where people walk their dogs, take their children and grandchildren, and enjoy some respite from the very busy and congested towns in which they live. They are also what prevent Benfleet, Thundersley, Bowers Gifford and Hadleigh from becoming one great, sprawling urban mass. Yet the Government have chosen to almost double the housing figure for Castle Point to 686 new homes and flats a year, amounting to nearly 12,000 new dwellings over the period of our emerging plan. https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Child Sexual Offender Data - [Dame Siobhain McDonagh in the Chair] | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Nigel Farage MP (Clacton) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
While this debate is very welcome, it is on the broad range of sexual offences against children and the gathering of data about the perpetrators. I suggest, and certainly my constituents in Clacton suggest, that there is something uniquely evil and awful about mass-rape gangs. That is not in any way to diminish sexual abuse committed in the home or elsewhere by trusted people, but there is something uniquely evil about what is going on.
I certainly speak for many of my constituents in saying that there is a feeling that for a couple of decades the authorities at all levels have not done the job of genuinely pursuing justice because of racial sensitivities. I was unaware of the problem, its scale and the cover-up until the Rotherham by-election in 2012, when the current hon. Member for Rotherham (Sarah Champion) was elected. In the intervening years she has spoken out more bravely on the issue than most Members of this House. I was genuinely shocked by the stories I was told by families who came forward, and stunned that the police, social workers and local councillors had received multiple reports of what had happened. When I say mass rape, in some cases we are talking about individual girls being raped by hundreds of men over a period of time. Something genuinely shocking had happened.
In the intervening years, we have had the Jay report, the Casey report, attempts by Home Secretaries and current attempts to find out the truth about what has gone on. While a handful of people have been held to account, the truth is that the vast majority have not. I was surprised that during 14 years of Conservative Government, we did not have a proper judicial inquiry with the necessary powers. I have done my best to encourage the current Prime Minister to do the same, but sadly to no avail.
There are two things that it strikes me would be helpful. First, we ought to get published, with redacted names, all the reports of police and social services over the past 40 years, across the whole country, as a public record that everybody can read. But the thing that really surprises me is the reluctance of Members of Parliament to realise their own powers. We are in the Palace of Westminster, in this remarkable historic building, and we are all privileged to be here. We have enormous powers. They were last effectively used back in 2011 by the Public Accounts Committee, which in the wake of the global financial collapse of 2008 used the powers of this Palace to turn Committees into courts. That means that they have powers of subpoena; it means that people can be brought into Committee Rooms like this, under oath, and could face charges of perjury if they do not tell the truth.
My suggestion is this: rather than waiting for this Home Secretary or the next one, who may come soon—who knows?—to act with full judicial power and the ability to subpoena, why don’t we, as Members of Parliament, forget party affiliation, recognise the upset, concern and fear of our constituents that we are increasingly living in a two-tier justice system in this country, come together and force the Government to have a powerful Committee in this place? Let us call the heads of social services, let us call senior police officers and let us call former or serving councillors, or even former or serving MPs, and get to the truth.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Power to Cancel Local Elections - [David Mundell in the Chair] | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Nigel Farage MP (Clacton) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
No taxation without representation is quite a powerful political adage, and it has worked well over the years. What people were facing in many parts of the country was paying their council tax, but not being able to have a say and, in certain cases, elected county councillors staying in position for a full seven years.
However, it was not just the Minister that did this. It was done with the connivance of the Conservative party, which did everything it could to deny the vote in Norfolk, Suffolk, East and West Sussex, and initially in Surrey—doing its best to stop people voting for two consecutive years. And the Lib Dems got in on the act in Cheltenham, although, granted, in slightly different circumstances.
Talking of the Lib Dems, I have been having a very good chat with a prominent Liberal Democrat who I get on rather well with, Sir Bob Russell, who represented Colchester for many years. He made the point that there was last fundamental local government reorganisation in England 50 years ago, but no one suggested that elections should be cancelled, delayed or postponed. In fact, the debate about the shape of local government reorganisation became part of the campaigns and an issue upon which people voted.
I am proud of the fact that 153,000 people signed the petition, but I am even prouder that 4.6 million people will get the vote on 7 May because of the judicial review that I took against the Government. I am proud of that, and Reform will go on fighting for proper, open democracy.
It is clear that section 87 of the Local Government Act 2000 delegates way too much power to a Minister of any Government, and that elections are completely fundamental to liberty and freedom in our country. We need to change section 87—I ask the Government to support this—to make sure that, in the future, any delays to elections, for whatever reason, must be the subject of primary legislation, open debate and a vote by all Members of Parliament. If we do that, we will never finish up in this awful mess and with this lack of trust in politics again.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Pam Cox MP (Colchester) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
The law exists to uphold our rights and freedoms and to protect the public interest, but the law can be used by bad actors against the public interest. As we have heard today, some use legal action or the threat of it to silence, exhaust and bankrupt their critics, who seek to expose their wrongdoing. We have heard powerful testimonies relayed by the Chair of the Justice Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Derby North (Catherine Atkinson) , from victims who have been shamefully silenced, shut down and financially ruined when they have sought to speak out. Strategic lawsuits against public participation—SLAPPs—use the law in bad faith, and the private Member’s Bill before us would make it much harder to bring such suits.
I am very pleased that this important Bill, brought forward by my fellow Essex MP, the right hon. Member for Maldon (Sir John Whittingdale) , has received Government support. The right hon. Gentleman is extremely well placed to lead on these matters, given his long experience of speaking out on them. As a Minister and as the Chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, he played a pivotal part in exposing the phone-hacking scandals of the early 2000s and challenging those who sought to use legal means to conceal them, and I pay tribute to him.
The Bill will tackle SLAPPs and provide effective protections for defendants where such claims are still raised. It will help to reduce exposure to disproportionate legal costs, allow early dismissal of cases and prevent litigation from being used as a tool of delay, pressure or intimidation. By doing that, it will rebalance a system that is currently stacked in favour of those with wealth and power, and empower those who lack both.
This Bill will also strengthen the rule of good law in the UK and further afield. The right hon. Member for Maldon and I have shared commitments that stretch beyond Essex; we are both involved in the Inter Parliamentary Union, a body that seeks to spread good parliamentary practice at a global level. Through its co-operation with UNESCO on freedom of expression and digital governance, the IPU has hosted events examining the misuse of the judicial system to attack freedom of expression, including defamation laws and SLAPPs, and has made recommendations to legislators to reform defamation laws and protect journalists and parliamentarians from retaliatory legal pressure.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Chris Vince MP (Harlow) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
It is a pleasure to speak in this debate. I promise I will not go on too long. [Hon. Members: “More!”] Cross-party support already! I draw the House’s attention to the fact that my father-in-law, Professor Robin Bloomfield, is a professor of system and software dependability at City and St George’s University—I finally got his title correct. Also, the Kao data centre is in my constituency of Harlow. I thank the Minister for his opening statement, and particularly for his commitment to looking at increasing the scope of the Bill. We had conversations across parties in Committee on the scope of the Bill, and whether it could be extended to other potentially vital infrastructure.
We live in uncertain times, and bad state actors, used by foreign powers, will seek to undermine our national infrastructure and our democracy using the internet and AI. We need to be alive to that. I rise to speak against Lords amendment 107. Although I am sure that it is well-meaning, I am concerned that it could have unintended consequences. It would require the Secretary of State to conduct an annual review of the effectiveness of the national infrastructure and security systems regime, and to lay that review in front of Parliament once it was complete.
As you will know, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am always a huge supporter of parliamentary scrutiny, not least because it allows me to give a matter scrutiny. However, it is very likely that the foreign powers that we have concerns about are observing said debates and said scrutiny, so if the report highlights any potential weaknesses in the network and information systems, those powers will be aware of those weaknesses, which could put us at risk when they seek to exploit those weaknesses.
Finally, Madam Deputy Speaker—I promised I would be short—I reiterate the concerns expressed by Members from across the House about the Hugging Face incident that the hon. Member for Exmouth and Exeter East (David Reed) mentioned. How does the Minister see Lords amendment 33, or other Bills in this place, being able to look at OpenAI’s potential liability for that incident, and what can this Government put in place to protect systems in the wake of that? We need to be aware of the emerging threats around cyber-security and AI. I welcome the fact that this Bill seeks to address those threats. Bad state actors controlling AI is worrying, but AI controlling AI is truly terrifying.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Chris Vince MP (Harlow) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I thank my hon. Friend for his intervention. I was just about to say that although bereavement does not end at 18 months, bereavement support payment does and, as has been touched on, many people do not realise that they are eligible for it. I recognise that the BSP is not taxed and does not count towards the benefit cap, but may I ask the Minister, on behalf of my constituent and his daughter and granddaughter, to consider further—I know that the BSP is reviewed annually—whether we might better support those who suffer a bereavement, either by extending the BSP beyond the current 18 months, as my hon. Friend just suggested, or through additional support?
I want briefly to mention the support that local authorities give to those who are bereaved. I have heard from constituents in Harlow about a number of cases in which people lost a loved one who was a council tenant and the council demanded the keys to the council house straightaway, without taking into account that the person was grieving. We need to think about how services that are there to support those in our community can better respond to and better treat people who are themselves suffering from bereavement.
Will the Minister also look at what she can do to ensure that everyone who is entitled to BSP is aware of that? As many Members across the House will know, one of the many campaigns that I support is about supporting young carers. Clearly, when the loved one a young carer has been providing support to passes away, there is a transition in that young person’s life. Will she relay that to the Department for Education to think about how we can better support young carers who lose the loved one they have cared for?
Finally, may I put on the record my thanks to all those who support people who are grieving in my community of Harlow? I pay tribute to the volunteers who run the Grieving Friends Support Network in Wych Elm, as well as those at St Clare Hospice, Mind in West Essex and Butterfly Effect.
Ultimately, as many Members from across the House have described so eloquently this evening, when we lose a loved one, it is a tragic loss. For many of us, it will be a loss that we never get over. The right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) spoke about his parents; I think about the loss of my grandparents every single day. I looked at a photo of me sitting on my grandad’s lap over the weekend and it was like he was there, or had only been gone for a short period. He has actually been gone for 23 years, but I miss him every single day. There are things we can do to support people suffering bereavement, and I ask the Government to see what they can do to make that just a little bit easier.

To pick up on the point made by the right hon. Member for Dwyfor Meirionnydd (Liz Saville Roberts) , what national or public interest is served by retaining these documents in secret? That is what the Minister has to answer. I notice she has been listening intently to everything that is being said, and I hope she will take the opportunity, if she has not done so already, to greet the former Welsh Guards in the Public Gallery and listen to their testimony. [Interruption.] She has already done so—let us put that on the record—or she will.

Incidentally, the Welsh Guards should be honoured for their contribution to winning the campaign, just as much as any other battalion or military formation. They played their part. We lost ships and we lost men, who died in battle because war means taking losses. What happened to them does not detract from them, and the blame heaped on them tells us there is something to be uncovered. Some people are hiding things for their own interests, not for the national or public interest.
I knew Johnny for many years before I understood what he had been through, and I met my good friend Crispin Black many times before I understood what he had been through. It was only because I was shadow Defence Secretary and met Surgeon Commander Rick Jolly, who was there in the field hospital at Ajax bay and treated so many of the casualties on the day, that I understood the reality of what happened and the trauma it left. That is why I am a vice-president of Combat Stress. The unresolved nature of the trauma makes it so much worse. They are unable to explain to themselves, the public, their friends or their military comrades why what happened happened.
A new book, the next edition of “Too Thin for a Shroud”, is coming out. If anyone has not read the book that is already out, it does not take long to read. It is absolutely shocking. Many things happened that should not have, and the bombing of Sir Galahad was just one of them. The new book will reveal so much more because a lot of the witnesses to the inquiry have released their testimony voluntarily. Good on them.
But what about the people who refused to do so? I attach no blame to them because reputations are at stake. It is in the public interest for this information to come out, because it is evident— the hon. Member for Llanelli (Dame Nia Griffith) touched on this—that a system failure was at fault. The amphibious taskforce and the land and maritime components were all separately commanded from Northwood—very long screwdrivers and communication chains. Nobody in theatre was individually or jointly responsible for the whole operation.
Others have testified to me casually and in writing, including Admiral Chris Parry, whose last job was at the Development, Concepts and Doctrine Centre at Shrivenham.
