https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Bayo Alaba MP (Southend East and Rochford) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I welcome this Bill, because I know from experience how important it is. Before becoming the Member of Parliament for Southend East and Rochford, I was fortunate enough to be involved in the London 2012 Olympic games, the Euro 2020 football championships and the 2022 FIFA world cup. I have seen at first hand what it takes to make a major sporting event a success and the benefits it can have for the wider community. These events have taught me that while venues, organisation and promotion are all important, the most crucial factor is support from Government and local authorities. Unfortunately, that support is not consistent across the country. While some areas have the relationships, expertise and capacity to help sporting events thrive, others start from scratch each and every time. That is why the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee has called for a national strategy for major events, and I welcome the Government’s commitment to publish one.
The Committee has also called for responsibility for major events to be moved from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport to the Department for Business and Trade. That move would highlight the role of events in driving investment, tourism and growth. The importance of major sporting events is not just their financial contribution, but their ability to create and celebrate community. We also see that in grassroots events, such as Rochford Hundred’s Remembrance Day fixture, which recently brought the community together in an extraordinary way. That event was not a global spectacle, but it showed the true power of sport in building community. I commend the club’s president, Ray Stephenson, and its chairman, Steve Maguire, who made that match happen.
I finish by encouraging colleagues to think back to the successful sporting events of the past few decades, and specifically their ability to make the whole country feel united. In these times, we all know how important it is to stay united. This Bill strengthens our ability to deliver those moments and ensures that the benefits reach every community in the country.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Clause 1 - Introduction | Northern Ireland Troubles Bill | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Bayo Alaba MP (Southend East and Rochford) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I am pleased to be able to participate in today’s debate. I did not serve in Northern Ireland, but I did spend time as a Parachute Regiment reservist—an experience that laid the foundations of my path to becoming the Member of Parliament for Southend East and Rochford. It afforded me opportunities I would never have otherwise experienced, and I know the same is true for countless others.
Paratroopers served alongside members of our armed forces and the Northern Irish security forces throughout Operation Banner, often in the most dangerous situations. They were asked to do an immensely difficult job in the hope of delivering lasting peace. Many of those soldiers, now in their 70s and 80s, have spent decades fearing a knock at their door. The unjust reality is that most who are fearful of historical prosecutions are largely working-class men who served in their late teens or 20s.
I want to speak to the point made by the hon. Member for Foyle (Colum Eastwood) about justice for victims and civilians, which I fully understand. What I would say is those young service personnel are victims, too. They saw and experienced things that they cannot unsee. They were deployed to Northern Ireland on the instructions of the British Government and fulfilled their duties as commanded by their chain of command. That is why I feel so passionately about the Bill and the protections it must offer.
For more than a quarter of a century, the job of properly addressing the legacy of the troubles has been kicked down the road by successive Governments. This legislation is an attempt to end that unwillingness and to deliver justice to all those affected. What it is not is an attempt to unfairly target British soldiers with legal proceedings or to reopen wounds that are barely healed. The truth is that if this legislation is not passed, those who served in Operation Banner would be completely exposed to spurious prosecution and would lack the immunity that they were falsely promised.
This legislation will offer veterans new protections, including strict guidelines on what can be considered new and compelling evidence, measures to adequately recognise the context in which soldiers were operating, and the explicit rejection of equivalence between service personnel and insurgents. That is why, despite my concerns about certain details of the Bill, I have worked extensively with the veteran community, most notably the Parachute Regimental Association, throughout this process. I commend it for the good-faith nature in which it has engaged.
This Bill is not perfect, but it is a marked improvement on the flawed legislation passed in 2023. The consequences of not getting this Bill right are very real, and while the failure of the process would belong to us all, its impact will be felt hardest by those we claim to support. If we are unable to talk, listen and make good-faith compromises, we risk repeating the mistakes that this legislation seeks to correct. No one here wants to see our children and our grandchildren patrolling the streets of Belfast again. We have a duty to prevent that cycle of violence from reigniting. I want this Bill to go even further in protecting our veterans, and I will keep working with the veteran community and the Government to make that happen. We do need justice, we need closure, and families need answers, but, most of all, we need long-lasting peace.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Sir David Amess Summer Adjournment | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Bayo Alaba MP (Southend East and Rochford) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I am deeply honoured to have the opportunity to speak in the Sir David Amess debate. Sir David’s life was defined by public service, including the 24 years he spent representing the constituency of Southend West. Indeed, it was in Sir David’s memory that Southend was granted city status in 2022.
That passion for our stretch of south-east Essex coastline is something I share, and something that makes sense when we consider what it has to offer. From Wallasea Island and Shoebury east beach to Southend pier and the Kursaal, there is plenty to shout about along our shores. Yet although the coast is crucial to Southend East and Rochford’s character, it also poses its own unique set of challenges. Bordered by water on three sides, we are physically isolated, an obstacle compounded by a single century-old link road and our location at the end of the railway line. I regularly hear from local residents, business owners and farmers about the impact that regular cases of standstill traffic has on their daily life and work. The cost of that, however, is felt most acutely by our young people. Teenagers in coastal areas like ours suffer worse adult health than their inland counterparts, achieve below-average GCSE results in maths and English, and go on to earn lower wages.
There is, however, good reason to be hopeful. Southend is one of the country’s fastest-growing seaside resorts, with more than 7 million visitors choosing the city for their seaside day trips each year. That is unsurprising when you consider the regeneration efforts of recent years, which I have been proud to play a part in. It is a particular pleasure to see the steps being taken to return our iconic Kursaal to public use.
Coastal communities are also beginning to feel the benefit of the turning economic tides generated by this Labour Government. The promise of local government reorganisation and devolution is also set to pave the way for greater community control of spending. In Southend and Rochford district, we know what the solutions to our problems are. We know how to unlock the huge potential for growth that exists along our coast, and in our towns and in our rural areas.We recognise the impact that a new link road would offer, and the opportunities that would be created by improved access to high-tech skills training. That is why I am proud to be reigniting the mission to secure a new link road into south-east Essex, and why I am working to attract new industries and investment into our area.
As I believe Sir David Amess understood, the success of south-east Essex is defined by our spirit of hard work and self-improvement. If our communities are given the tools to succeed, I have no doubt that we can achieve incredible things.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Northern Ireland Troubles Bill (Carry-over) | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Bayo Alaba MP (Southend East and Rochford) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
This debate is deeply personal for me, because, in addition to being the Member for Southend East and Rochford, I am a proud former paratrooper.
For me and countless others with military backgrounds like my own, the legacy of the troubles is not a distant memory but something that our community continues to carry the weight of. Back in November, I brought members of the Parachute Regimental Association, together with officials from the Northern Ireland Office and the Ministry of Defence. I had one simple aim: to ensure that veterans had a voice and their concerns about the Bill were heard clearly and directly. I thank those officials for their attendance and engagement.
Let me be clear: the legislation passed by the Conservative Government must be updated. This is not myth or fallacy; indeed, even some Conservative Members have acknowledged that the current legislation is inadequate. It troubles me when colleagues from this House head over to Parliament Square, as they did this afternoon, not to engage with former colleagues or members of their local military associations, but to “virtue signal”, as my teenage daughter would put it. Our duty as parliamentarians is to lead, make difficult decisions and speak with honesty and sincerity. It is not to spew negative and dangerous rhetoric, as some across this Chamber seem intent on doing. They parade around with lapel badges larger than some solar panels and bearing the slogan, “Proud of my country, ashamed of this government.” That does not help or resolve this issue, and it is certainly not why the public voted us into this special place. It is dangerous and unproductive noise.
However, I must be equally clear that, as it stands, the Bill leaves many questions unanswered and needs additional work. We cannot afford to rush it. Although justice must be delivered, we must also take the time to ensure that the legislation delivers the protections that our veterans need and deserve. Those who served in Northern Ireland followed orders and put their lives on the line to defend our country, and they cannot be an afterthought in this process. So I say to the Government that we should take the time to get this right, to continue our engagement, to listen to those who serve and the families who lost loved ones, and to ensure that before the Bill moves to its next stage veterans can have full confidence that it will deliver what is intended without creating serious unintended consequences that cannot be later undone.
In conclusion, I say that, to every member of our armed forces community who has served and those who continue to serve, we owe a debt that cannot be repaid. And to those watching from the Gallery today, I say thank you: thank you for standing up for the memory of those we have lost and for standing together to protect those who are yet to serve.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge) | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: David Burton-Sampson MP (Southend West and Leigh) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I start by thanking my right hon. Friend the Chancellor for the measures that he laid out in his Budget last week, and for his focus on giving my constituents breathing space as we navigate through tough global headwinds. Like him, I pay tribute and offer my thanks to the former Chancellor, my right hon. Friend the Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves) . It is clear that through her work and clear focus on fiscal discipline, she helped to stabilise the economy, despite the significant headwinds, and to create the headroom that has enabled us to take the positive actions set out in this Budget.
I am lucky to have my office on Leigh Road in Leigh-on-Sea. Along with Leigh Broadway, it is a thriving high street, full of small independent shops and hospitality businesses, including Tiny, a sandwich shop, Juice Bay, which does fantastic smoothies and juices, and Float On Records. They are all new businesses and it is great to see so many new businesses opening despite the challenges we have faced of late. That shows me that there is confidence in our economy and belief in our country. And it is not just in Leigh: Mez, a delicious Turkish restaurant, recently opened in Westcliff—I can vouch for that as I had my dinner there on Saturday.
However, I have listened to businesses in my constituency that tell me that sometimes things can be challenging. That is why I am delighted by the Government’s announcement that more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses will be completely exempt from business rates, meaning that around 52% of those types of business in the east of England will pay absolutely no business rates whatsoever. That is help for businesses. An additional 484 businesses in my constituency will have their business rates frozen in real terms until 2029, giving business owners time to plan ahead, while many others will see their business rates reduced.
When my constituents get home from their days out shopping, they will know that they have support with paying their bills. In addition to extending the 0% rate of VAT on electricity, an enormous 39,520 households in my constituency will benefit from the £100 payment to combat rising energy costs. I know that will help many people, from young families through to pensioners.
Speaking of pensioners, I welcome the excellent news that pensioners on low incomes will not have to pay income tax on their state pension. I am glad to hear the announcement that pensioners who rely solely on their state pension income will get to keep all of it. The Budget also provides the security that comes with knowing that pensions will continue to rise in line with earnings, while the adjusted triple lock will mean we can focus on providing a high-quality national care service.
Finally, I was really glad to hear that self-employed fathers and partners will now get statutory paternity pay. I have personally championed that, alongside many colleagues, and I pay particular tribute to my hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) for her work in this area and in championing this cause.
This Budget shows that the Government are listening to people in my constituency and taking action to fix the issues they have raised. The constituents I spoke to at the weekend know that the times that we are in and that we face are difficult, and they are grateful for everything this Government are doing to support them.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: David Burton-Sampson MP (Southend West and Leigh) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
My hon. Friend makes a fantastic point. The CWU, too, is deeply concerned about the differences in contracts, and it is working with Royal Mail towards contract harmonisation. Royal Mail has shown some desire to move towards that, but, like many others, I am concerned about the speed with which that will happen—and whether it will happen at all.
Royal Mail faces challenges on several levels. Through better employment practices, a more efficient delivery model and, most importantly, listening to their posties, the unions and residents, I am hopeful that for the first time in a while, there is a possible route to improvement in Southend. I thank Ministers, past and present, for working with me and other Members across the House on the issue and for the continued focus on holding Royal Mail to account. I will continue to work on this issue as hard as I can to ensure that my residents are getting the service that they are paying for and, to speak frankly, the service that is absolutely essential to so many.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Performance of Royal Mail | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: David Burton-Sampson MP (Southend West and Leigh) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Redditch (Chris Bloore) for securing the debate and my hon. Friends the Members for Lichfield (Dave Robertson) and for Corby and East Northamptonshire (Lee Barron), and many other hon. Members across the House, for their work on this matter. My constituents in Southend West and Leigh, like those of so many other hon. Members, have been rightfully disappointed in the service provided by Royal Mail. I concur with much of what I have heard.
Southend was the original pilot area for the optimised delivery model, so we have been experiencing these issues locally for well over a year. It was deeply concerning that the clear indications that the ODM was not working in Southend did not prevent it from being rolled out nationwide. It is increasingly frustrating for my constituents, who feel that they are not getting the service they are paying for. For many people, the poor service has been not just inconvenient but disastrous, and we have heard many stories tonight about how it has been replicated across the country.
NHS letters are not the only urgent post not being delivered. One constituent lost a job opportunity when a Disclosure and Barring Service certificate failed to arrive in time and another man, who was terminally ill, experienced unacceptable delays in receiving the paperwork he had requested to arrange his own funeral. I heard many such stories at a public meeting I held back in April, which gave residents the chance to put their concerns directly to Royal Mail’s regional management. Improvement was promised at the meeting, but guess what? It never came.
In July, I held a consultation, which received 122 responses in just a couple of days. I am sorry to say that the feedback was overwhelmingly negative. Of those 122, 102 said that they were “dissatisfied” or “very dissatisfied” with the postal service. Only one person considered the current standard of service acceptable.
Throughout this time, I have regularly met the CWU—the union that represents postal workers—and heard from it that postal workers in my constituency have been overworked, under immense pressure and unhappy with the standard of service they have been able to provide. They are equally unhappy at the massive variations between the old and new contracts, but I do not have time to talk about that.
I was heartened to hear—a bit of positivity—that after a visit in August, having requested my fourth visit to the depot, Southend sorting office, in partnership with CWU reps, was ready to trial a new system that would rebalance the round loads and help reinforce the local link between the postie and their area in an amendment to DM26 that is about to be rolled out. Posties are much more efficient when they know the layout of their rounds, so it is clearly not rocket science to have them on a dedicated round.
The trial took place in Leigh-on-Sea in my constituency. A month later, I was glad to visit the sorting office again and see the racks empty—but this time the CWU assured me that things had worked well and that, in that particular round, they were back in control. As of 19 October , the new system has been rolled out across our whole sorting office area. I will be keeping a watching brief, but it is showing real positive signs. I hope that those at Royal Mail will look at the success of the local pilot and roll it out across the rest of the country. If it is working, why would they not?

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I beg to move,
That leave be given to bring in a Bill to make provision about the marketing, advertising and offering for sale of wet wipes; to make provision about the labelling of wet wipes; and for connected purposes.
The city of Southend has 7 miles of beautiful beaches, and Leigh-on-Sea is well known as a picturesque fishing village that still has a vibrant cockling industry. My constituency is also home to many wild swimming groups such as the Bluetits, who find that the refreshing waters of the Thames estuary provide great exercise as well as benefits to their mental and physical wellbeing—although I have to say that when I took a dip in December for charity, I did not find it too relaxing.
All of this might help the House to understand why water quality is so important to my constituents and to me. Like so many, my constituents were rightfully outraged at the sewage dumps that sadly had become routine during the years of the former Conservative Government, so the people of Southend West and Leigh did what they so often do: they came together to make a difference on something they care about. They worked together to form quarterly water summits in 2024, giving residents the opportunity to hold water companies directly to account and to collaborate with the council, Ofwat, the Environment Agency and many more to find solutions to our water problems in Southend. It was the first summit of its kind in the country, and those summits continue to this day. I thank my constituent Daniella Boon, who is in the Gallery today, for her leadership on those summits and in this area.
It was through chairing those water summits as a newly elected MP that I came to learn just how complex the issues affecting water quality and sewage discharges are. Certainly, water companies play the most important role, and I welcome the work being done by this Government to hold them to account. However, sewage discharges happen when the water system fails on so many different levels. Councils, the community, planning decisions, green spaces, and even whether or not a person chooses to pave their driveway all come together to influence outcomes.
Last year, when spending time at our local sewage treatment plant, I learned that blockages are a leading cause of sewage discharges. When the sewers block, there are only two places for sewage to go—in Southend, it will be out into the estuary, or back up into people’s homes and toilets. We will all have seen in the media that those blockages are often caused by fatbergs. The pictures can be very shocking. The Guinness world record belongs to the fatberg found in Whitechapel in London in 2017, which was 250 metres long—longer than Tower bridge.
With blockages of that size, it is no wonder that our sewerage system sometimes struggles to cope, and alongside grease and fat, those bergs are mostly made up of wet wipes. In Anglian Water’s network alone, around 500,000 wet wipes are flushed every single day. Instead of breaking down, many wet wipes remain largely intact. They snag on roots, pumps and rough surfaces within sewers, and they combine with fats, oils and grease to create these large blockages. In my constituency alone, Anglian Water dealt with 610 blockages last year, all caused by unflushable items.
This Government have brought in legislation to ban plastic in wet wipes, a measure that my constituents and I welcome. It is an incredibly necessary step, as it reduces the harmful microplastics that poison wildlife and enter the food chain. However, biodegradable does not necessarily mean flushable, and even plastic-free wipes are made of tougher fibres that do not break down in the toilet in the same way that paper does.
At our water summits, Anglian Water will often remind us that there is no such thing as a flushable wipe. When I visited Anglian Water’s water treatment plant on Stock Road I got to see a whole skip—yes, an entire skip—filled with long stringy fibres from wet wipes that have been fished o

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Highways (Financing) Bill | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Jen Craft MP (Thurrock) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I am grateful to my hon. Friend for his intervention. It is a bit like “Beetlejuice”—you mention ferries and he appears; it summons him. He is absolutely correct that ferries should prove a vital part of public transport infrastructure.
Let me turn to the huge and important role that the Tilbury ferry played in our public transport infrastructure locally. It ran continually until 2022 when, unfortunately, due to historic bankruptcy by the then Conservative council, it was unable to pay the subsidy needed to keep the ferry running, and it came to a close. That was an absolute tragedy for my area. Not only did the ferry provide a vital commuter route for a number of people, but a number of my constituents used it to attend schools in Kent, for example—they are now having to make a journey that is about an hour and a half each way, and they are encountering problems at the Dartford crossing that could have been avoided by a quick 10-minute hop across the water.
Gravesend High Street in Gravesham used to lead directly on to the ferry terminal, and those businesses have been hit so hard by the loss of this vital transport link. In my patch, there are fond memories of the ferry, not just for myself and my family but for so many of my constituents. I put a call out for people to share their memories of the Tilbury ferry and to sign my petition, and the numbers hit the thousands within a couple of days. People are desperate to see it return.
The main issue with the return of the ferry is the cost of the subsidy for running it. There is public will to get it back, and there is will from businesses in the area—the Port of Tilbury, Forth Ports, DP World and a whole host of others really want to see it, because they know it provides that link and enables them to encourage people to come and work for them from both sides of the river. Furthermore, if we are trying to get people off our road networks, a large number of people who use the Dartford crossing are projected to use the lower Thames crossing for short hops either side of the river, and the ferry would allow them an alternative, so that they could make that journey in a much more sustainable way, which is much better than adding to the congestion that already exists. It is a much greener way of travelling.
I ask the Minister to seriously consider putting aside a very small proportion of the tolls to be paid on the lower Thames crossing—I am talking about 0.01%, which is less than a penny—to enable the Tilbury ferry to be funded in perpetuity. There is precedent: the Dartford crossing used to fund the subsidy for the Tilbury ferry, until that was given over to the two local authorities at the time, Kent county council and Thurrock council. A levy on the lower Thames crossing would allow the Tilbury ferry to be insulated from potential shocks, such as we saw with the bankruptcy of Thurrock council. It would allow the ferry to keep running well into the future, so that it can serve my children and my grandchildren. It would take people off the already overloaded road network. It would bring life back to Gravesend High Street. It would make sure that people on my side of the river can visit their relatives, go to their hospital appointments, go to work, go to school and just enjoy a really nice day out, and it would prove to people in my patch that we can have nice things and we do deserve them.
This ferry is a crucial part of our infrastructure, and given that people in my patch will be bearing the brunt of the construction and operation of the lower Thames crossing, I believe that they deserve this. I ask the Minister to seriously consider allowing this piece of infrastructure to fund a critical part of the local transport infrastructure and to help me bring back the Tilbury ferry for good.

https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.title: Saffron Walden Sparkles as Christmas Lights Switch On Brings Festive Cheer to the Town
https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Saffron Walden was filled with festive cheer on Friday 20 November as residents and visitors gathered in the town centre for the annual Christmas Lights Switch On, organised by Saffron Walden Town Council.
The much-loved event marked the official start of the festive season, bringing the community together for an evening of Christmas celebrations, entertainment and seasonal magic, with host Stuart Vant.
The town centre was buzzing with excitement as families and friends enjoyed the festive atmosphere, culminating in the eagerly anticipated moment when Saffron Walden’s Christmas lights were switched on by the Mayor and Father Christmas himself, illuminating the town with a wonderful seasonal glow.
Saffron Walden Town Council would like to extend a heartfelt thank you to everyone who attended and helped make the evening such a success. A huge thank you to Stuart Vant from InXpress Cambridge, SWTC’s compere and DJ throughout the event.
Saffron Walden Town Council would like to extend a heartfelt thank you to everyone who attended and helped make the evening such a success. Special thanks go to all those involved in organising and supporting the event, including performers, volunteers, food vendors, local businesses and everyone who contributed to the celebrations.
SWTC would like to thank all its sponsors and supporters, said a SWTC spokesperson, “we appreciate the support from our business sponsors and event partners in helping to bring exciting Christmas events and activities to the community – special thanks also to; Town Crier David Razzell, volunteer stewards from Saffron Hall, Christmas Pudding mascot costumes from Saffron Hall – worn by Anna Kelly and Father Christmas himself!”.
The Mayor of Saffron Walden, Cllr Jeanette Curtis, said, “It was wonderful to see so many people coming together to celebrate the start of Christmas in Saffron Walden. Thank you to everyone who joined us and helped make the evening so special and for your support with my charity tombola. I wish you all a very happy festive season!”
The celebrations are far from over, with a fantastic programme of festive activities still to come, including Lantern Making Workshops taking place this Friday 27 November (2pm – 7pm) and on Saturday 28 November (10am – 2pm).  Families are welcome to join us in The Jubilee Hub, CB10 1EH – no booking required, just drop in.
Saffron Walden Town Council looks forward to welcoming residents and visitors to these upcoming events and wishes everyone a wonderful Christmas season.
Keep up to date on social media or www.visitsaffronwalden.gov.uk/events .  And if you have any feedback regarding the event, please email events@saffronwalden.gov.uk
Photo by Walden Local
The post Saffron Walden Sparkles as Christmas Lights Switch On Brings Festive Cheer to the Town appeared first on Saffron Walden Town Council .

Food, party and dancing will be taking place in the Market Place from 3pm and into the evening until 7.30pm.  Stuart Vant will again be hosting the event and Saffron Hall’s cast of Sleeping Beauty will be joining in with the fun. Said Stuart Vant, “I am very excited to be hosting the ‘Light Switch On’ once more.  Each year we have built on the success of the last – this will be my sixth year, and I am delighted to be invited back to spread some cheer and give back to the community.”
Arrive from 3pm for a selection of music and entertainment to include; free facepainting, performances from LP Chorus Collective and Somewhere 2 Sing, dancing and show choir songs from Tempo’s Performing Arts, and an exciting build up to the Light Switch on with cast members from Saffron Hall’s Pantomime, Sleeping Beauty.  Food options from 3pm include; delicious bagels from Beats & Beigels, wood fired pizzas from Optio Pizza, Greek cuisine from The Greek Man – and there will be confectionery treats from The Candyfloss Stall, amazing cakes from Just Baked by Sophie, hot drinks and Baileys hot chocolate from the Giddy Up Bar and a fully licenced bar from High Spirits. A SWTC spokesperson said, “we endeavour to provide a fun vibrant events for families which also encourages footfall into the town centre, supporting all local businesses”
At 6pm the Christmas lights will be switched on by Father Christmas, with host Stuart Vant taking you through the afternoon and into the evening with some party tunes to get you dancing!  Said a SWTC spokesperson, “we appreciate the support from our business sponsors and event partners in helping to bring an exciting schedule of Christmas events and activities to the community.  A special thank you to Stuart Vant who is giving his time to our Christmas events”.  Angela Dixon, Chief Executive of Saffron Hall added: ‘We’re delighted to once again partner with Saffron Walden Town Council, this time bringing some panto magic to the town this Christmas. This is yet another example of our collaborative approach to creating free arts experiences for our community.’
Mayor’s Tombola
Visit the Mayor, Cllr Curtis’ fundraising stall from 3pm, where you can have a go at the Tombola! Said the Town Mayor, “I will have some fabulous prizes on my stall this Friday some of which have been kindly donated by local businesses. Come along, take your chance, and support my very worthwhile local charities: Together in Sound, The Garden Youth Music Project and Teenage Kicks”
Indoor Christmas Markets
The first of Saffron Walden’s Indoor Christmas Markets takes place this Friday 20 (12 noon -7.30pm) and Saturday 21 November (9am – 4pm) at The Town Hall, CB10 1HR.
It is a perfect chance to start your Christmas shopping and get into the festive mood  – each market will be showcasing a fantastic selection of unique, handmade gifts.
A SWTC spokesperson said, “With something to suit all ages and tastes, you’re sure to find something special for all the family. From gifts to keep little hands busy, handmade children’s clothes and wooden toys – to beautiful artwork, Christmas decorations, jewellery, delicious jams, soaps and gorgeous room fragrances.  There really is something for everyone! Drop in and browse the stalls; shop local, discover unique gifts and support talented local creatives”

https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.title: SWTC Awarded J9 Domestic Abuse Awareness Accreditation
https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Saffron Walden Town Council is delighted to have been awarded its J9 Domestic Abuse Awareness Accreditation.
On Monday, representatives of Uttlesford District Council Community Safety Partnership, training provider Alpha Vesta and the Policing Chief Inspector Martin Richards attended to formally present Saffron Walden Town Council with the accreditation certificate.
Both staff and councillors of Saffron Walden Town Council have completed the online awareness training – enabling members to offer safe, discreet support for victims of domestic abuse.
District Councillor Sutton, Portfolio Holder for Communities and Local Partnerships at Uttlesford District Council, said: “We are thrilled to congratulate Saffron Walden Town Council on achieving J9 accreditation and becoming a recognised Safe Space. Together with the Uttlesford Community Safety Partnership and other J9 Safe Spaces across the district, we are helping to create a stronger, more connected network of support, ensuring that anyone who needs help knows they are not alone.”
Said a Saffron Walden Town Council representative: “We are delighted to have received the J9 Accreditation, marking the training completed by our staff and councillors further reflecting our commitment to offering safe, discreet support to anyone affected by domestic abuse.”

https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.title: Saffron Walden War Memorial
https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.text:
It may have come to your attention that the Saffron Walden War Memorial has developed a build-up of dirt and atmospheric staining over time.  While this may be noticeable, it is entirely normal for historic stone memorials exposed to the elements.
War memorials are intended to endure for generations, and there are strict conservation guidelines governing when and how they can be cleaned. Excessive or inappropriate cleaning can damage the stone and accelerate deterioration. In line with professional conservation advice, the Town Council undertook a light clean of the memorial plaque in 2025.
Saffron Walden Town Council takes its responsibility for the care and preservation of the War Memorial very seriously. Dedicated reserves are maintained to fund future conservation works, which must be carried out in accordance with recognised heritage and war memorial conservation standards. As a Grade I listed structure, any significant cleaning or restoration work would also require the appropriate permissions and specialist expertise.
At present, the memorial remains in good condition and does not warrant the level of intervention that would justify more intensive cleaning. Conservation best practice is to minimise intervention wherever possible to protect the long-term integrity of the monument.
We are extremely proud of Saffron Walden’s strong military heritage and of the sacrifices made by members of our community in service to the nation. Our priority is to ensure that the memorial is preserved with dignity and respect for future generations.
Put simply, a memorial with some natural weathering is preferable to one that has suffered irreversible damage through unnecessary cleaning!

https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.title: Mayor of Saffron Walden Launches Christmas E-Card Design Competition
https://saffronwalden.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Calling all young artists!
The Mayor of Saffron Walden, Cllr Jeanette Curtis, invites children aged 4 – 11 who live or go to school in Saffron Walden to design her Christmas E-Card celebrating the wonderful Christmas spirit in Saffron Walden!
The winning design will be chosen by the Mayor and used as the Mayor’s official e-Christmas card for 2026, which will be sent out via email to Dignitaries, schools, community groups and local organisations. The winner will also receive a £20 voucher to spend at a local shop of their choice!
Your Challenge:
Create a Christmas card design inspired by Christmas in Saffron Walden !
You could include some of our town’s famous landmarks such as the Town Hall, the Market Square or Bridge End Gardens with a Christmas twist. Perhaps you could imagine Saffron Walden covered in snow, decorated with Christmas lights, or filled with festive cheer!
Competition Details:
Design: Create an original, colourful Christmas card design inspired by Christmas in Saffron Walden, with the message ‘Merry Christmas’.
All submissions must be on A4 paper. Please keep the design flat and do no use any 3D materials.
Scan and Send: Scan your design and send as a JPEG or PDF via email to the Mayor’s Secretary at mary@saffronwalden.gov.uk . Alternatively, physical entries can be brought to the Tourist Information Centre, CB10 1HR, for the attention of Mary.
All submissions must include : Your child’s full name, age, primary school name, parent or guardians full name, telephone number and email address.
Deadline for entries is Monday 30 November at 9am. The winner will be notified that week.
The Mayor said, “I’m always inspired by the imagination of young people in our town, and I can’t wait to see their Christmas ideas come to life.”
Have fun and good luck!

https://essexcdp.com/feed/.title: A Town Like Diss: Film festivals, nominations and awards
https://essexcdp.com/feed/.text:
Last year Moving House Films worked with residents of Diss to create a participatory film A Town Like Diss, as part of a commission entitled The Changing Faces of Diss. The film was a celebration of the town through stories and memories of those who live there. It was launched at a red carpet premiere at Diss Corn Hall and accompanied by a two-day multi-venue exhibition featuring its props co-created by the community at the Corn Hall, No.8 Market Place and DesignerMakers21.
Since the film’s ‘world premiere’ in Diss last Summer, it has been touring to various film festivals, accruing awards, accolades and nominations.
These include:
OffBeat Folk Film Festival in London: nominated for the Community Award
Castine Film Festival in Castine, Maine USA: won Best Documentary
Sunrise Film Festival, Lowestoft, Nominated for Community Award
Fakenham Film Festival, Norfolk
Greenwich Film Festival, London: won Best Folk Film
The film will be going online soon for all to enjoy, so keep an eye on our website and socials for more details!
The Changing Faces of Diss is made possible through a commission from Essex Cultural Diversity Project supported by Arts Council England, in partnership with Diss Corn Hall, DesignerMakers21, and No 8 Market Place.

https://essexcdp.com/feed/.title: Celebrating Women in Sport on the Streets of Chelmsford
https://essexcdp.com/feed/.text:
This Summer we celebrated Women in Sport in Chelmsford with a new mural, an empowering street art workshop, a motivational chat with a Paralympian, and a Global Village Procession to welcome Women’s International T20 Cricket teams to the city.
We worked in partnership with Chelmsford City Council, Essex Cricket and Chelmsford For You to organise three outdoor events, taking inspiration from the new mural in Market Square created by 7th Pencil as part of Concrete Canvas , the street art festival taking place across the city in May. The piece is a bold and vibrant celebration of women in Sport, capturing the energy, diversity and achievement of women athletes from across Essex. It was commissioned by Chelmsford For You, Chelmsford City Council and Essex Cricket.
The Global Village Procession took place on the day of the England vs India Women’s International T20 Cricket match. After an afternoon of dancing, performances and pop-up cricket related activities in front of Shire Hall on Tindal Square, we walked with communities to the Cricket Ground. The procession was led by Bhangra drummers and dancers, so shoppers, our international guests and cricket lovers alike were welcomed to the city by a festival of colour and noise!
Street artist 7th Pencil hosted an afternoon of drop-in workshops for young people to make their own wearable art in the form of giant medals, to celebrate themselves, their achievements and inspirations.
This was followed by a motivational chat with Paralympian Anne Wafula Strike MBE , who features on the mural. Anne was on Market Square in conversation with Claire Gevaux, CEO of Culture Chelmsford. The event also brought in voices championing women across the city, with shout-outs from 7th Pencil, The Feminine Way, Ideas Hub Chelmsford, SPARK! and Dose Festival. The event was part of our Stand Up For Diversity programme which brings people together to celebrate diversity across the East of England.
The post Celebrating Women in Sport on the Streets of Chelmsford appeared first on Essex Cultural Diversity Project .

https://essexcdp.com/feed/.title: Celebrating Constable250 at Flatford
https://essexcdp.com/feed/.text:
On 11 June 2026 the National Trust at Flatford welcomed visitors, partners and the local community for a special celebration marking the 250th anniversary of the birth of John Constable, as part of a wider programme taking place across Suffolk and Essex.
We’ve been working with the National Trust, commissioning artists Tom Hobden and Phoebe Stapleton on a new project The Rivers and Skies , which invites audiences from across the generations to tell or imagine their life stories through the metaphors of rivers and sky, drawing a parallel with John Constable’s way of seeing landscape as an emotional record.
The Rivers and Skies : Meet the artists
20 June & 19 July 12-3pm
The artists will be in residence at Flatford in June, July and August; they are inviting all drop in and chat to them about their work on 20 June & 19 July. Find out more here.
A message from our partners
National Trust Flatford Celebrates Constable’s 250th Birthday
as Part of Regional Constable250 Programme
On the 11 June, Flatford, which is on the Suffolk and Essex Border, welcomed visitors, partners and the local community for a special celebration marking the 250th anniversary of the birth of John Constable, as part of the wider Constable250 programme taking place across Suffolk and Essex.
Despite typically unpredictable English weather, the event proved a great success, bringing together people from across the region to celebrate the life, work and legacy of one of Britain’s most influential landscape painters. The day showcased the unique connection between Constable and the landscapes of Flatford and East Bergholt that inspired many of his most famous works.
The celebrations were made possible through the collaboration of numerous organisations, partners and volunteers. The National Trust team at Flatford worked alongside colleagues from across Essex, national curatorial teams and delivery partners to create a memorable programme of activities for visitors. Special thanks were extended to East Bergholt Parish Council, Essex Cultural Diversity Project and artist-in-residence Tom Hobden, whose contributions helped bring the anniversary celebrations to life.
The event also attracted significant media attention, helping to share the Constable250 story with audiences far beyond the Stour Valley. Coverage from BBC Essex Radio, BBC Suffolk Radio and BBC Look East highlighted the importance of the anniversary and the continuing relevance of Constable’s artistic legacy. The support of those involved in media activity, including local partners and community representatives, played a key role in extending the reach of the celebrations.
Constable250 is a year-long programme commemorating the artist’s 250th birthday through exhibitions, events and community projects across the region. At Flatford, the anniversary provides an opportunity not only to celebrate Constable’s remarkable contribution to British art, but also to recognise the enduring beauty of the landscapes and communities that inspired his work and continue to attract visitors from around the world.
Look out for the #Constable250 events and exhibitions happening across the region and head to Flatford’s website to find out more: https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/suffolk/flatford

Essex Cultural Diversity Project is delighted to announce that we have received funding from The National Lottery Environment Fund to work in partnership with RAMA (Refugee, Asylum & Migrant Action), AFIUK (African Families in the UK) in Colchester, and Old Hall Community in East Bergholt.
Visits will be organised from culturally diverse communities in Colchester to Old Hall, an intentional community and organic farm in a rural location close to the River Stour where 50 people live and work together sustainably.
By connecting people to the environment through workshops and activities, increasing access and engagement for diverse communities to rural areas, and building connection to nature, this project will foster cultural exchange, learning about local biodiversity, taking part in river walks, growing food and planting trees together.
The project will include relaxed social activity in the countryside, sharing knowledge and experiences, making friends, and understanding intentional community living.
We would like to thank the National Lottery Environment Fund for giving us the opportunity to work with RAMA and AFiUK who are two brilliant charities in Colchester, and with Old Hall Community, who are generously hosting the project.

https://essexcdp.com/feed/.title: Celebrating the winners of the Coalhouse Fort Ghost Story Competition
https://essexcdp.com/feed/.text:
For their commission at Coalhouse Fort, artist and writer Laura Trevail has been engaging with Thurrock residents to help foster a sense of local pride and ownership, and help all value and invest in the future of the Fort, an important cultural asset on their doorstep.
Over the last few months, Laura has been bringing together people who love, seek out, or stumble upon Coalhouse Fort in the creation and sharing of ghost stories, and recently launched the Coalhouse Fort Ghost Story Competition .
This March the winners were announced, and invited to the Fort to celebrate their writing.
Introducing the winners:
Vienna Moon , winner of the ‘Family Friendly Spooking Around’ category, with Little Gloria and the shadow man . A properly frightening story for both adults and children, rich in modern-historical and ghostly detail.
“My name is Vienna Moon. I am a 28 years old female who lives in Corringham, Essex. I am Autistic and I love being creative! I love Halloween so much that I get really excited about it and end up getting into the spooky spirit from the end of August every year. I also love visiting Coalhouse Fort on occasions as it is refreshing to walk around and be out in nature and around history.” Vienna Moon
Leanne Drain , winner of the “Scare the Grown-Ups” category, with her story The three shadows of my bad dreams . A claustrophobic dream-state short, flinging us helplessly and viscerally around in time.
“I have always enjoyed writing since the age of 12 my granddad was my inspiration behind all my journey I loved him dearly he was my world and I am proud that he got to see 12 years of my life writing has always been a great part of my life I write with passion and It’s something I hold dear.” Leanne Drain
The winners’ stories will be now be recorded by professional actors to haunt the Fort for years to come.
The artist and writers were welcomed by Roxie Curry, representing co-commissioners Start Thurrock and Essex Cultural Diversity Project; Kevin Diver, Coalhouse Fort’s new Engagement Manager; Allen Jones, Chair of the Coalhouse Fort Advisory Group; and Kirsty Riches, representing the Engine Tearoom, who presented each writer with a £25 voucher for the tearoom.

https://essexcdp.com/feed/.title: Epping Forest: Tai Chi and Qigong-Ba Duan Walks
https://essexcdp.com/feed/.text:
A day of walking to mark the start of the Year of the Horse took place on Sunday 8 March 2026 in Epping Forest with Chinese communities from Colchester, Chelmsford and Epping, as part of Essex Cultural Diversity Project’s Creative Health Programme .
The session began with light warm up exercises including Tai Chi and Qigong-Ba Duan, a foundational Chinese qigong often called the Eight Pieces of Brocade or Eight Silken Movements , consisting of eight gentle, flowing movements that integrate mind, body, and breath to improve overall health, balance energy flow, and strengthen the body, functioning as a form of medical qigong for wellness. It’s known for its simplicity, effectiveness, and ability to enhance flexibility, strength, and respiratory function, with each movement targeting specific meridians and internal organs, making it popular for general wellbeing and as a warm-up before exercise or walking.
The walks were led by Community Ambassador Simone Xue from the Colchester Chinese Cultural Society, who took part in our Active Essex funded Tendring Coastal Walks project recently in January 2026. The Tendring Coastal Walks demonstrated that diverse community groups who attended highly benefited through the project, which supported wellbeing, mental health and physical fitness. The funding gave community groups the confidence to independently continue their weekly walks for the long term in the natural environment.
The Epping Forest Walks took place after Global Village Presents Chinese New Year Celebrations at Harwich Arts Centre in February 2026, and were part of the Chinese community’s celebrations to welcome in the Year of the Horse.

https://essexcdp.com/feed/.title: From Essex to Amritsar: After the Partition exhibition in India
https://essexcdp.com/feed/.text:
From Essex to Amritsar
Punjabi diaspora’s UK journey documented in an exhibition at the Partition Museum, India
With the aim to celebrate and preserve cultural heritage, this month Essex Cultural Diversity Project launched a 30-day exhibition featuring community memories at the Partition Museum in Amritsar, entitled After the Partition: A Shared Cultural Heritage in Essex .
The exhibition is a legacy following on from the Heritage Lottery Fund project of the same name, highlighting the journey of the Punjabi Diaspora in the United Kingdom, through oral history narratives, preserved cultural materials, and visual archives spanning three generations.
Developed in collaboration with elderly Punjabi community members living in East England, the exhibition presents powerful memories of the 1947 Partition capturing the shared memories, reflections, and legacy passed down through generations, offering a moving tribute to resilience, identity, and cultural continuity.
The exhibition also incorporated ‘Re-rooted’, a collection of work by Suman Gujral, and artist and poet based in Harlow, Essex. At the centre of Suman’s practice is the exploration of Indian history, in particular Partition when India was divided and many communities displaced; she explores the effect this had on her own family, and more broadly on India itself. She is interested in how the cycle of displacement and division of families is still happening today in places all around the world.
Strengthening International Connections
One core aim of Essex Cultural Diversity Project is to develop connections with international partners, to build bridges and create new opportunities for creative organisations and practitioners based in the East of England.
Stating that this cross-cultural collaboration is set to further strengthen ties between heritage institutions in Punjab and the UK, Punjab State Information Commissioner, Harpreet Sandhu inaugurated the exhibition and said that such initiatives play a vital role in promoting one of Punjab’s key tourism landmarks – The Partition Museum, Amritsar – while also showcasing the state’s rich cultural heritage to diverse communities across the UK.
Indi Sandhu, CEO of Essex Cultural Diversity Project said, “We work strategically with creative practitioners, culture and heritage sectors, diverse communities, and the voluntary sector to help develop skills, build sustainable networks and infrastructures, alongside creating new opportunities to enhance diverse artists’ work.”
Indi Sandhu from Essex Cultural Diversity Project and Essex based artist Suman Gujral were joined by renowned artists and ECDP Patrons The Singh Twins, Prof Jagjit Singh, Rajwinder Kaur, Malwinder Singh Ahluwalia and Ravinder Singh Chamak.

After the Partition: Chelmsford Heritage Open Days
12 – 21 September 2025
For Heritage Open Days, the pop-up exhibition After the Partition: A Shared Cultural Heritage in Essex will be shown at the Meadows Shopping Centre in Chelmsford.
Over half a million Sikhs, Hindu’s and Muslims came to Britain because of the upheaval of Partition, the promise of economic opportunities and a safer life. This exhibition, curated by Sikh historian Simran Bance, captures seven decades of their families’ lives, exploring experiences, challenges, successes, and social change since 1947. This is a rare chance to focus on lived experiences since Partition, rather than on the experience of Partition itself, opening opportunities to explore this unique cultural context within and between communities. As time passes and memories fade, it is important for Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslim communities to capture what shaped their modern heritage for posterity, and to reflect on wider issues of migration and colonialism today.
Find out more about the project and listen to oral recordings at essexcdp.com/project/afterthepartition
Chelmsford Heritage Open Days
Heritage Open Days was established in 1984 and is a countrywide festival each September celebrating heritage in many ways. The main idea for events is to allow access to buildings which are not usually available to the public along with talks and tours about our local heritage – and every event has to be free! Each year has a theme and for 2025 it is ‘architecture’. Chelmsford Heritage Open Days has been organised by Chelmsford Civic Society since 2013

Nurturing Creatives in East Anglia
ECDP’s Community Engagement Lead in Norfolk and Suffolk
A funding uplift as part of our National Portfolio Organisation programme funded by Arts Council England has given us the opportunity to explore new opportunities and make connections with communities, local authorities, and arts and cultural organisations in Norfolk and Suffolk, led by Daisy Lees, our Community Engagement Lead.
Over the last two years we have been forging new partnerships, working with new friends and partners to host Salons, events and commissions across the region.
We have also been supporting creatives to develop projects and funding applications, offering match funding to help uplift their bids. £9000 in seed funding across six projects levered a total of £118,383 worth of investment into the region.
Projects we’ve supported so far include For the Benefit of Pablo Fanque by Ashton Owen , Goodnight Maharajah by the ŚŪNYA Co , Brave Art Unlimited by Suffolk Art Link , Cultural Influence of African American Airman in the East of England by Elma Glasgow , a project by Dulce Duca; and Kabir Hussain ‘s new project Walnut Works which includes bronze casting community workshops at care homes and primary schools led by Vicky Hussain, eight artist residencies at Butley Mills Studios near Woodbridge, and three exhibitions with artist talks across Suffolk and Norfolk.
We have also been forging new partnerships, working with new friends and partners to host Salons, events and commissions across the region. We’ve made connections with other NPOs in the region including Snape Maltings and Firstlight Festival, and are seeking new opportunities with Counterpoints Arts as part of their Platforma Festival in October.
Much of this strategic work and investment is coming to fruition and starting to shape our current and future programmes. More about the some of the projects we’ve supported is below:
Walnut Works: Artists in Residence and Community Bronze Casting Workshops
Walnut Works was recently awarded an Arts Council Project Grant, supported by Essex Cultural Diversity Project and The Arts Society Woodbridge. The award enabled Vicky Hussain and Foteini Araka from Creative Mojo to lead wax modelling workshops with residents from three Woodbridge care homes; Cavell Manor, Haughgate House and Highlands Care Home, Woodbridge Chinwags – an over-60’s meeting group and pupils at Orford Primary School.
In September 2025, artists Kabir and Vicky Hussain opened an exhibition of bronze works at Butley Mills Gallery which included an Artists Panel moderated by Norwich University of Arts Senior Lecturer BA (Hons) Fine Art Desmond Brett.
Community workshop participants made 92 works in wax which were cast in bronze by Kabir Hussain and displayed in the exhibition. Kabir and Vicky also led an artist residency programme at Walnut Works which developed ideas and technical skills for the exceptional bronze work created by Denise Cordova, Clare Jarret, Juliet Lockhart and Laura Wilson. Unusual, highly lyrical and figurative pieces by experienced artists sit side by side with works created in community settings.

https://essexcdp.com/feed/.text:
After the Partition:
A Shared Cultural Heritage in Essex
Launching a New Pop-up Touring Exhibition
Over half a million Sikhs, Hindu’s and Muslims came to Britain because of the upheaval of Partition, the promise of economic opportunities and a safer life. In 2024 Essex Cultural Diversity Project was awarded funding from the National Lottery Heritage Fund for Sikh, Hindu and (Pakistani) Muslim communities living in Essex to reflect on seven decades of their families’ lives, to explore experiences, challenges, successes, and social change from 1947 to today.
With few original settlers surviving, this is the last chance to bring three generations together to document the fortunes of settlers and their families who can trace their migration directly to Partition between India and Pakistan. This is a rare chance to focus on lived experiences since Partition, rather than on the experience of Partition itself, opening opportunities to explore this unique cultural context within and between communities. As time passes and memories fade, it is important for Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslim communities to capture what shaped their modern heritage for posterity, and to reflect on wider issues of migration and colonialism today.
Through the project we have captured people’s memories through oral history recordings, films and interviews. The project has created a touring pop-up exhibition by emerging Sikh female historian Simran Bance. The exhibition was launched at a special event at Essex Record Office on Saturday 1 February, and was on display along with the oral history interview recordings. There were also talks and a panel discussion with interviewees, who shared their memories.
Find our more about the project and listen to the oral history accounts at  After the Partition: A Shared Cultural Heritage in Essex

https://www.discoveruttlesford.co.uk/fee.title: Walks in Uttlesford
https://www.discoveruttlesford.co.uk/fee.text:
This article was submitted by GPS Cycle and Walking Routes. Their website features nearly 1,000 cycling routes and over 3,000 walking routes, including National Trails, long-distance paths, canal walks, coastal routes and countryside adventures. Each route includes downloadable GPS files, Google Maps and Ordnance Survey mapping, making it easy to plan your next outing. You can also use the handy “near me” tools to find routes close to your location.
Whether you’re exploring Uttlesford on foot or by bike, GPS Routes is a great way to discover new places and enjoy the outdoors! For more walks in the area, see their Essex Walks page.
Uttlesford is a largely rural district in north-west Essex, known for its historic market towns, grand country houses, ancient woodland and quiet countryside footpaths. From exploring the medieval streets of Saffron Walden to walking through the historic parkland of Audley End and following former railway lines, there are plenty of varied routes to enjoy.
Saffron Walden
Saffron Walden is one of Essex’s most attractive historic towns, with a wealth of medieval buildings, narrow streets and traditional market-town character. A walk through the town takes you past historic landmarks, including the parish church of St Mary the Virgin and the remains of the medieval castle, while the picturesque streets and old buildings provide plenty of interest along the way.
The circular walk tours the countryside around the Essex town of Saffron Walden. You’ll visit the ruins of the 12th century Walden Castle and one of the highlights of the area at Audley End.
Audley End
Audley End is one of Essex’s most impressive historic estates, centred on a grand Jacobean mansion near Saffron Walden. The surrounding grounds offer attractive walking through landscaped parkland, with views across open lawns, mature trees and the River Cam. The house was built on the site of a former Benedictine monastery and is now managed by English Heritage.
The estate’s parkland provides a peaceful setting for a walk, with historic features and sweeping views adding to the scenery. Nearby Saffron Walden is worth exploring too, making it easy to combine a countryside outing with a visit to one of the area’s most characterful towns.
Hatfield Forest
Hatfield Forest is an ancient royal hunting forest near Takeley, with a distinctive landscape of old pollarded trees, open grassland, woodland and seasonal ponds. The forest has a long history stretching back many centuries and is now a National Trust property, providing a valuable habitat for wildlife as well as an atmospheric place to walk.
The network of paths allows you to explore the woodland and open areas at your own pace. Look out for veteran trees, wildflowers and birds, while the lake known as the Shell House Pond adds further interest. The changing scenery makes Hatfield Forest particularly appealing in spring and autumn.
Flitch Way
The Flitch Way follows a former railway line between Braintree and Bishop’s Stortford, providing a largely level route through the Essex countryside. The old railway has been converted into a long-distance walking and cycling trail, passing through farmland, woodland and small rural settlements. Its traffic-free sections make it a good option for a relaxed walk away from busy roads.
Along the way, remnants of the railway’s past can still be seen, including old stations and structures. The route also provides opportunities to enjoy local wildlife and the changing countryside, with different access points allowing you to choose a shorter section or explore further along the trail.

Every September, Heritage Open Days celebrates England’s history and culture with thousands of free events, giving people the chance to explore fascinating places, uncover local stories and experience traditions that have shaped our communities.
This year, residents and visitors can enjoy a fantastic range of events across Uttlesford, from medieval churches and historic bellringing traditions to windmill heritage and family-friendly cultural activities.
Parish Lives at St Mary’s Church, Stebbing
For more than 700 years, St Mary’s Church has been at the heart of community life in Stebbing. This year’s programme celebrates the people, skills and stories that have shaped the church over the centuries.
Highlights include:
Saturday 12 September : Ride and Stride welcome stop and Cornerstone Café (10am to 3pm)
Monday 14 September : Medieval Churches Talk with historian and archaeologist Matthew Champion (1.30pm to 2.30pm)
Tuesday 15 September : Organ recital by Professor David Rowland (12.30pm to 1.30pm)
16 to 18 September : Have a go at stitching a traditional church kneeler and explore the Parish Lives exhibition (9.30am to 4.30pm)
Thaxted Windmill: More Than a Restoration
Discover the story behind one of Uttlesford’s most recognisable landmarks. This exhibition explores the history of Thaxted Tower Mill, the people connected to it and the important role windmills played in the local economy during the Georgian period.
Visit at The Guildhall, Thaxted:
Friday 18 September : 10.30am to 2pm
Saturday 19 September : 1pm to 4pm
Sunday 20 September : 10am to 2pm
The Bells That Brought Him Home: St Mary’s Church, Saffron Walden
Follow the story of Thomas Turner, who is said to have found his way home by following the sound of Saffron Walden’s bells in 1623. Four centuries later, this remarkable bellringing tradition continues.
Visitors can:
Climb the church tower
Learn about centuries of bellringing heritage
Try ringing a bell on the mini-ring
Explore the largest parish church in Essex
Enjoy refreshments during their visit
Event times:
Saturday 19 September : 10am to 12.30pm and 2pm to 4pm
Sunday 20 September : 2pm to 4pm
Ukrainian Traditions Family Festival at Saffron Walden Museum
Join a local Ukrainian family for an afternoon celebrating Ukrainian heritage through crafts, music, dance and storytelling. The festival offers a welcoming opportunity for families to learn about Ukrainian culture while enjoying free access to the museum.
Saturday 19 September
1.30pm to 4.30pm
There will also be a collection in support of Ukrainian medical aid.

https://www.essexlgrhub.org/rss.xml.text:
How changes will be implemented
Mikaela
Mon, 07/27/2026 - 17:12
Learn how LGR changes in Greater Essex will be implemented gradually and who will be responsible for the transition
Elections for the five new unitary councils will take place in May 2027. After the elections, a shadow authority will be set up. A shadow authority is a temporary body made up of the newly elected councillors. Its role is to:
prepare for the official launch of the new councils
agree budgets, policies, and governance arrangements
ensure everything is ready for the transfer of services from 1 April 2028
Until 1 April 2028, all day-to-day services will continue to be run by the 15 county, unitary, district, city and borough councils in Greater Essex.
After 1 April 2028, the new unitary councils will align services, systems and ways of working. Alignment won’t happen all at once. Instead, they will introduce changes gradually over time to make sure they are:
well planned
practical
easy for residents to adapt to
Behind the scenes, some services will be brought together sooner to improve efficiency and create a smoother experience overall.
Stay updated
Keep checking this website to see what has been done as each key deadline approaches. You can also sign up to your local council newsletters and follow them on social media for further updates.

Key words and phrases explained
Mikaela
Thu, 04/16/2026 - 16:12
A glossary of key words and phrases relating to Local Government Reorganisation in Greater Essex
Show all sections
Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)
Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)
The process by which the structure and responsibilities of local authorities are reconfigured.
Find out more about what LGR is and what it means for Greater Essex.
Aggregation
Aggregation
The process of combining data, resources, services or functions from multiple councils into a new authority.
Devolution
Devolution
The transfer of powers and funding from national to local government. It is separate to LGR, although they are both included in the English Devolution White Paper.
Find out more about devolution on the Essex County Council website.
Disaggregation
Disaggregation
The process of separating and redistributing services, functions and resources from one larger council into multiple smaller authorities.
English Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill
English Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill
A piece of legislation designed to transfer powers from central government to local leaders. The bill aims to drive regional growth and empower local communities by:
establishing a standardised statutory devolution framework
creating new Strategic Authorities
introducing local powers, including a community right to buy
English Devolution White Paper
English Devolution White Paper
The government’s statement of their plans to reform local government. This includes proposals on devolution, wider plans for LGR and changes to local audit.
Read the full English Devolution White Paper on gov.uk.
Essex Leaders and Chief Executives (ELCE)
Essex Leaders and Chief Executives (ELCE)
Chief Executives and leaders of all 15 councils in Greater Essex leading the LGR transition.
Greater Essex system or system-wide
Greater Essex system or system-wide
This is a reference to the range of different partners delivering services or shared outcomes for residents across Greater Essex. It includes public sector organisations, such as councils, the NHS and Police, Fire and Rescue, as well as voluntary and community sector organisations (VCS).
Implementation plan
Implementation plan
A document required by legislation. It must contain detailed plans and timetables showing how the new unitary authorities will be delivered effectively.
Implementation team
Implementation team
A dedicated officer-led group responsible for the transition from the existing 15 councils to the five new ones. This includes the day-to-day management, design, and delivery of the transition.
Joint Committee
Joint Committee
A formal governing body established to manage the LGR transition in advance of shadow authorities being elected. Detail of the Joint Committees will be outlined in the Structural Changes Order.
Lead authority model
Lead authority model
This is where one authority provides a lead role in hosting a shared service on behalf of other authorities in the system.
Minded To Decision
Minded To Decision
The government's decision on its preferred model of LGR. This includes the geography and number of unitary councils.
The minded to decision for Greater Essex was announced on 25 March 2025.
Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG)
Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG)
The government department responsible for LGR and devolution.
Section 24 Direction
Section 24 Direction
This refers to Section 24 of the Local Government and Public Involvement in Health Act 2007. It allows the Secretary of State to restrict the financial and contractual activities of councils that are to be dissolved. This is to ensure that they do not make significant commitments that could affect the future authorities' ability to manage their resources effectively.
Shadow Authority

Changes coming to Greater Essex
Mikaela
Wed, 03/25/2026 - 14:06
Find out about the new unitary councils in Greater Essex and how changes will be carried out
Essex is a special place with a proud past and a bright future. To help Essex grow and do even better, we are making changes to how it is run. These changes will make things easier to understand and help decisions get made faster.
There are currently 15 county, unitary, city, district and borough councils in Essex. Some look after things like bins and parks. Others look after schools and care for children and older people. It’s hard to know who does what.
Following a formal consultation, the government have decided that these 15 existing councils will be replaced by five new unitary councils.  Read the government's decision statement on the UK Parliament website.
Your new unitary council will deliver all the services you rely on, including:
waste collections
roads
housing
planning
play areas, parks and green spaces
leisure centres
education
children’s services
adult social care
This will make it easier for everyone - including local people, businesses, the NHS, and the police - to know who is responsible for what and how we can work together to make Essex even better.
Find out more about why these changes are happening and how decisions were made.
The five new unitary councils
Services currently provided by your local unitary, city, district and borough council will be taken over by the new unitary council for that area.
Services currently provided by Essex County Council will be split between all five new unitaries.
Visit gov.uk to find out which council, or councils, currently provides your services.

If any future changes affect how you access a service, these will be consulted on in the usual way.

Other changes happening in Essex
We’re also working with government on plans for devolution. Devolution means transferring more power and money locally, instead of the government making all the decisions. It means local councils can make choices about things like transport, housing and jobs.

This website is managed by Essex County Council on behalf of all of Greater Essex's 15 local authorities.  We want as many people as possible to be able to use this website.  For example, that means you should be able to:
change colours, contrast levels and fonts
zoom in up to 400% without the text spilling off the screen
navigate most of the website using just a keyboard
navigate most of the website using speech recognition software
listen to most of the website using a screen reader (including the most recent versions of JAWS, NVDA and VoiceOver)
We’ve also made the website text as simple as possible to understand.
AbilityNet  has advice on making your device easier to use if you have a disability.
How accessible this website is.
We know some parts of this website are not fully accessible:
some page headings are used incorrectly and could confuse users as to the pages purpose
some page titles are not clear as to the pages content
some link text is not descriptive of the destination
some pages have text that does not meet the minimum contrast requirements
some pages have focus styles which are difficult to see

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) is responsible for enforcing the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 (the ‘accessibility regulations’). If you’re not happy with how we respond to your complaint,  contact the Equality Advisory and Support Service (EASS) .

Content that’s not within the scope of the accessibility regulations.
PDFs and other documents

share any of the data we collect about you with others, or

Frequently asked questions about Local Government Reorganisation
Show all sections
Why are Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and devolution happening?
Why are Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and devolution happening?
The government believes that devolution over a large area, at the same time as LGR, can boost the economy and deliver better public services.
They think that simpler local government structures will:
make it easier for residents to know who delivers their services
make it easier for residents to know who deals with local issues
result in better services for the local community
Where can I find explanations for words or phrases I don't understand?
Where can I find explanations for words or phrases I don't understand?
There are a lot of official words and phrases relating to LGR. Our LGR glossary explains what some of the key words and phrases mean so that you can better understand the changes happening in Greater Essex.
What is Greater Essex?
What is Greater Essex?
Greater Essex refers to the combined area represented by Essex County Council, Southend-on-Sea City Council, and Thurrock Council.
How is LGR different from devolution?
How is LGR different from devolution?
Devolution is about transferring powers and funding from government to local areas. This gives them powers and funding that they don't currently have.
LGR aims to simplify and reduce the number of councils across the country. It will create larger unitary councils, which means:
a more streamlined and effective system
better value for money
Unitary councils are responsible for all council services in an area. Southend-on-Sea and Thurrock are examples of a unitary council.
Visit the Essex County Council website to find out more about devolution in Greater Essex , including information about a Mayoral Combined Authority.
What will LGR mean for Greater Essex?
What will LGR mean for Greater Essex?
From 1 April 2028, five unitary councils will replace:
Essex County Council
the Southend and Thurrock unitary councils
the 12 city, borough and district councils
All the same council services will still be provided, but by a single unitary authority in each area.
How does this impact residents now?
How does this impact residents now?
