Why changes are happening
Ella
Tue, 07/08/2025 - 15:41
The government has written a plan called the English Devolution White Paper. It explains how local councils can be changed and improved by Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). Read the full English Devolution White Paper on gov.uk.
The government wants to:
help local areas have more say in their future
make councils work better and more efficiently
help people know who is responsible for services
The plan also gives more power and money to mayors in England, so they can help make big decisions for their areas. This is called devolution. Find out more about devolution on the Essex County Council website.
In Greater Essex, we recognise that LGR will lead to better, more efficient services and stronger local leadership. It will mean that:
services can be easier to use and understand
councils can work together and stop doing the same jobs twice
we can save money in the long run by running things more simply
bigger councils can speak up more for their areas
bigger councils can deal with problems better
people in Essex can have more say in what happens in their area
Find out why Local Government Reorganisation is happening and how decisions were made
Engagement
During June and July 2024, councils across Greater Essex talked with many different people to understand what they thought. This included residents and stakeholders from different areas, backgrounds, organisations and businesses. One method of engagement was a survey of 1,400 residents, completed by the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen).
All the feedback gathered helped councils think about how a new unitary council could:
better support residents and local services
work more closely with partners
make things simpler and more joined-up for everyone
Visit the NatCen website to find out more about their research.
Consultation
The government ran a formal consultation between Wednesday 19 November 2025 and Sunday 11 January 2026. Thousands of people took part to help shape the future of local government in Greater Essex.
Visit gov.uk for more information about the consultation.
(opens in a new window)
Proposals
Each council in greater Essex has their own unique local priorities, challenges, and opportunities. This led to councils in Greater Essex submitting four different proposals to government in September 2025.
These proposals reflected a shared commitment to finding the best solution for everyone. They were created using shared data from across Essex and views from:
residents
partners
businesses
community organisations
Find out more about the four proposals submitted to government.
(opens in a new window)
The government’s decision
On 25 March 2026 the government announced their decision for five unitary councils in Greater Essex.
Find out what the five unitary councils will be.

https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.title: Wooden spires and atmospheric graveyards
https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.text:
The Epping Ongar Railway was not the only Essex location to play a starring role in the magical blockbuster  Practical Magic 2 .
When producers began searching for locations that could double as small-town America, Essex was once again called into action. Their search for a traditional American churchyard eventually led filmmakers to the picturesque village of Abridge near Lambourne.
Grade I listed  St Mary and All Saints Church  is one of the oldest churches in the district and holds exceptional historical significance. Dating back to the 12th century, the church offers a stunning insight into medieval parish life and Norman architecture. Its beautifully preserved Norman doorway a particular highlight. Nestled among a peaceful churchyard and ancient trees, it offered the atmosphere and charm the filmmakers needed.
When the Essex Film Office learned the production team needed a church that could double as an American church, the team instantly knew that Essex had the ideal spot.
The churchyard was not the only local site to experience a touch of Hollywood magic. Large productions need a big support operation. This includes crews, vehicles, equipment, and welfare facilities. The Essex Film Office teamed up with the local parish council to find a good nearby spot for the production’s unit base.
Gary Kinch, Film Officer at Essex Film Office said:
” Productions like this need a lot of space for unit base and support vehicles, and we were able to find secure and discreet locations nearby. Privacy is very important for productions like this. It was great that we could provide everything they needed close to the filming location.
We’re often the fixers behind the scenes, using our local knowledge and connections to make things happen. For this project, we worked closely with the parish council, who were fantastic and incredibly keen to help. They opened up local facilities and residents even baked cakes for the cast and crew. It’s that community spirit that makes Essex such a great place to film.”
You can visit  St Mary and All Saints Church  as part of the  Abridge Country Walk , a three-mile route through the ancient woodlands and countryside surrounding Lambourne. Find out more at:  https://www.visiteppingforest.org/things-to-do/abridge-country-walk-p1729191
And if you’d like to discover more film and television locations across the county, explore the  Essex Film Office Movie Map  to see what else has been filmed in Essex and plan your own screen-inspired adventure.

https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.title: From commuters to celebrities: visit the Essex railway that cast a spell on Hollywood
https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.text:
The Epping Ongar Railway has been part of Essex history for more than 160 years. Now, thanks to its starring role in  Practical Magic 2,  the heritage line has added another chapter to its remarkable story
On a rainy spring afternoon in 2025, deep in the Essex countryside, the telephone rang in the office of one of the country’s best-preserved heritage railways.
Picking up the receiver, Epping Ongar Railway Operations Manager Robert Bentley answered a call he certainly wasn’t expecting.
On the other end of the line was a location manager searching for a very specific railway carriage to feature in the sequel to one of Hollywood’s most beloved films of the 1990s.
Practical Magic 2 , released this autumn, reunites screen legends Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman in the follow-up to the cult classic about a family of witches navigating love, loss and a centuries-old family curse. Filmed across locations in the United States and at the world-famous Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden in Hertfordshire, the production also found some of its most atmospheric backdrops much closer to home, right here in Essex.
Filming took place during the spring and summer of 2025, and as production arrived in Essex, Robert and the team at Epping Ongar Railway prepared to welcome the vast operation that accompanies a major Hollywood film.
The film sees the reunion of sisters Sally and Gillian Owens as they embark on another magical adventure. This time, part of their journey takes them through the English countryside by train.
“I didn’t really know what to expect at first,” explained Robert.  “ We’ve had a fair bit of filming here on the railway over the years, but nothing quite as big as this production.”
Moving history for the movies
While scenes were filmed on the railway itself, the production also required the controlled environment of a studio for interior filming.
One of the railway’s heritage carriages was carefully lifted onto a low-loader and transported to Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden, where it was reassembled on set and became a key part of the production.
For Robert, who accompanied the carriage on its journey, it was a once-in-a-lifetime experience.
“It was the first time I’d ever been on a film set in a studio,” he said. “It was an amazing experience. Everyone was incredibly friendly and focused on working together to create something special. It felt odd to see the carriage outside its usual setting, but I was proud that our heritage railway could contribute to such a big Hollywood film.”
Perhaps the most exciting part for visitors is knowing they can still experience a piece of movie history for themselves.
“What’s really cool is that you can sit in exactly the same seats where the stars sat in the film,” said Robert. “I’m watching the trailer thinking, that’s our train.'”
Epping Ongar Railway has gained popularity among film and TV producers in recent years. Its beautifully preserved stations, vintage rolling stock and authentic period atmosphere make it one of Essex’s most versatile filming locations.
An Essex star of the screen –  Epping Ongar heritage railway
The railway has welcomed productions from across the television and film industry. In 2025, it featured in Netflix’s festive comedy Man vs Baby, the four-part Christmas special starring Rowan Atkinson. The station at Ongar became ‘Tring’ railway station where Trevor Bingley rushed to catch a train for an important house-sitting interview. providing the perfect backdrop for the opening scenes.
The heritage line also appeared in the BBC’s Death in Paradise Christmas Special the same year. For the production, North Weald Station was transformed into the fictional station of “Swindon East” for scenes set back in the UK, showcasing once again the railway’s remarkable ability to double for a number of locations.

https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.title: CAMA AssetStore, Southend: Supporting craft and legacy within the Film and TV industry
https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.text:
CAMA AssetStore, a Southend based storage company, has established itself as one of Essex’s standout partners for film and TV. Family run and with over 100 years of experience in the industry, CAMA is a trusted and sustainability driven leader in entertainment storage. Their location in Essex offers a perfect balance of services, situating them close enough to London’s major studios, while remaining rooted in a vibrant local community that’s becoming increasingly attractive for filmmakers.
CAMA works closely with both independent creatives and larger production teams, supporting titles including Doctor Who , Slow Horses and most recently, Downton Abbey: The Grand Finale . CAMA was responsible for storing and tracking many of Downton Abbey’s iconic costumes, props and set pieces, safeguarding and preserving their legacy. Using their asset management platform AssetFlow , they tracked each item, ensuring distinctive pieces of design were monitored after wrap.*
High security, climate control and photographic records ensure that assets are ready for the next stage of their journey – whether that be exhibition, use in a new production or auction. In fact, many of the Downton Abbey pieces that CAMA were responsible for safeguarding were later sold at Bonhams auction, where all proceeds went towards Together for Short Lives , a UK charity supporting children and families facing life limiting conditions.*
A defining part of CAMA’s mission is its commitment to sustainable and responsible practices across the film and television sector. Their flagship warehouse in Southend-on-Sea is powered by clean energy, and, through their AssetCycle software they have collaborated with over 150 UK charities and social enterprises, ensuring items are repurposed to benefit local communities. By developing regional hubs in key locations such as Cardiff, Manchester and Liverpool CAMA is strengthening production ecosystems across the UK, supporting regional businesses in Essex and beyond.
Did you know?
Downton Abbey: A New Era features several filming locations in Essex including the elegant Belchamp Hall in Belchamp Walter, where Tom Branson and Lucy Smith’s wedding was shot. The beautifully preserved Electric Palace Cinema and nearby King’s Quay Street in Harwich were also transformed into 1920’s sets, with the town’s waterfront providing a charming backdrop for the film.
Learn more about these locations here .

https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.title: Essex Church Lands Starring Role in New Knives Out Film
https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.text:
Essex has long been a favourite location for filmmakers, but now it’s taking centre stage in one of Hollywood’s biggest franchises. Holy Innocents Church in High Beech, Epping Forest is the star location for the third instalment of the Knives Out series, Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery .
The blockbuster, featuring Hollywood A-listers Daniel Craig, Glenn Close, and Josh Brolin , hits UK cinemas this week and will stream on Netflix from 12 December . Although the story is set in upstate New York, the filmmakers chose Holy Innocents Church for its stunning Gothic architecture and woodland backdrop—perfect for recreating the American setting.
Essex Film Office’s Role
The Essex Film Office, part of Essex County Council, played a key role in making this happen. Our team secured filming permissions, coordinated with local authorities, and even arranged a road closure to ensure smooth production. We also supported the crew with logistics near a second filming location for the rectory.
Holy Innocents beat a number of churches to the top spot, offering the perfect combination of gothic style architecture and even the tree in the church yard – which matched the director’s vision for how the church yard needed to look.
Erica Gilson, Manager of Essex Film Office, added:
“In recent years we’ve welcomed productions like Slow Horses, Spiderman, and The Essex Serpent. Wake Up Dead Man was a major moment for us—it showed how Essex can stand out on the global stage. The filmmakers considered over 100 churches across the UK, and Essex delivered the perfect setting.”
Why Essex?
From historic architecture to sweeping countryside and coastal views, Essex offers filmmakers a wealth of options. This latest success reinforces our reputation as a prime filming destination for major productions.
Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery is in cinemas now and streaming on Netflix from 12 December .
Interested in filming in Essex?
The Essex Film Office is your central point of contact for filming activity in the county. We work with local authorities, location owners, and production companies to attract filming into Essex and support future investment.

https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.title: Tales of the unexpected: Essex Chocolate maker becomes a supply chain star in new Frankenstein show.
https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.text:
From horror chocolatier to Netflix collaborator—how Essex craft talent is powering the film supply chain
When Netflix and Guillermo del Toro’s production team needed chillingly realistic props for their Frankenstein adaptation they turned to a rather unusual supplier— Sarah Hardy , Essex-based “horror chocolatier” and founder of The Edible Museum in Sible Hedingham. This fascinating corner of the creative supply chain is making waves, even landing a feature on BBC News!.
Essex craft talent
Rather than opting for digital effects, del Toro insisted on authentic, handcrafted props. That’s where Sarah’s skill and artistry came in. The production’s Action Props Buyer contacted Sarah to craft “jewel-like” chocolate beetles in a precise palette, with colour coding tied to the narrative and specific characters (for instance, red hues reflecting Frankenstein’s mother).
Sarah delivered a stock of anatomically accurate pieces made of milk, dark and white chocolate, combining her sculpting background and mould-making techniques to achieve hyper-realistic results. The crew loved them—and ordered more, immediately. To meet tight filming timelines, Sarah and her team worked throughout the weekend to ship the props to Glasgow and meet the productions deadline.
Essex Creativity Within the Film’s Supply Chain
This isn’t just chocolate—it’s Essex-made chocolate! The Edible Museum is a perfect example of a local business stepping up as a specialist supplier in a high-stakes film production pipeline.
Sarah’s craft reflects years of experience in artisanal sculpting and mould-making, earning recognition from Guillermo del Toro himself, who chose her authentic craftsmanship over CGI and AI for this project.
Colour played a vital role in the visual narrative underpinning the storytelling in this adaptation of Mary Shelley’s gothic novel. By working closely with Sarah the production team achieved the precise aesthetic they needed.
Film schedules move fast, and not only was Sarah’s work exceptional in quality, but as an independent supplier, she was able to be agile, working through the weekend to deliver the props on time.
Helping to put Essex on the Global Stage
Sarah’s edible creations gained national attention when BBC News spotlighted her as a “horror chocolatier” – highlighting how carving out a niche can help to attract new opportunities for creative businesses.
Essex suppliers, prop specialists, artisans and creative makers like Sarah are becoming an important part of the film and TV supply chain – proving that local skills bring big productions into the county.
For small businesses or budding creative enterprises in Essex, collaborations like this prove that mastering a craft remains a highly valued selling point, even in an era of increasing AI use.
The Essex film and production supply chain is open to opportunities. If you offer a craft or provide a unique service, keep your phone close—you never know, the next call could be from a major production!.
If you work with film and TV production, let us know about – we want to help Essex’s creative supply chain to shine even brighter!
You can find out more about Sarah Hardy’s work and The Edible Museum

https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.title: Where Heritage Meets Hollywood
https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.text:
From Historic Docks to Cinematic Triumph
Essex’s Marine Heritage Specialists – Powering the Film Industry
When audiences marvel at sweeping maritime scenes in blockbuster films, few realise the craftsmanship and expertise behind the camera. One of Essex’s best-kept secrets, Heritage Marine Ltd , plays a pivotal role in bringing these cinematic visions to life—quietly anchoring the global film industry from the historic Downs Road Boatyard in Maldon.
From Maldon Shipyard to Silver Screen
Founded and led by marine engineer Jim Dines, Heritage Marine has evolved from a traditional shipyard into a specialist provider for film and television. Jim’s career spans decades—from serving as an Engineer Officer in the Royal Fleet Auxiliary working on the design and build of two 40,000-ton tankers for the Ministry of Defence. Today, his passion for maritime heritage fuels a unique enterprise that blends engineering precision with creative artistry.
Heritage Marine doesn’t just restore historic vessels; it builds entire worlds for film. From authentic WWII landing craft to fantastical flying ships, Heritage Marine’s expertise has supported some of the most ambitious film projects in recent years:
For Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein (2023), produced by Netflix, the team designed and shipped the rig for a full-size 120ft rigged vessel to Canada, then flew out to spend 5 weeks rigging the ship, standing by as specialist advisers on the shoot.
In Paddington III: Paddington in Peru (2023), produced by StudioCanal and Heyday Films, the Heritage Marine team rigged and supplied maritime props and set decoration for gimbaled boat sets, built rope bridges, and provided marine training for cast and crew.
For Paramount’s A Quiet Place: Day One (2023), directed by Michael Sarnoski, Heritage Marine supplied and operated a 1914 steel coaster as the hero ship for dramatic dockside scenes.
Their work on Netflix’s Shadow and Bone involved designing and rigging three full-size fantasy sailing ships, training actors and stunt performers, and ensuring marine authenticity throughout production.
And for The Last Voyage of the Demeter (2021), produced by DreamWorks and Universal, the Heritage team   designed the rig, then flew out  to   Malta where on location they rigged the ship and operated a three-masted schooner and multiple gimbaled sets, delivering the eerie authenticity that brought Bram Stoker’s tale to life.
And that’s just a glimpse of a portfolio that spans Game of Thrones, Wonder Woman, Death on the Nile, and many more!.
A Skilled Crew Behind the Scenes
Heritage Marine’s strength lies in its people—a dedicated team of shipwrights, riggers, and sailors who understand both traditional craftsmanship and the demands of modern film production. Their expertise covers everything from set design and prop creation to marine coordination and safety on location.
Training the Next Generation
Through the Heritage Marine Foundation, Jim and his team are passing on these rare skills to young people, ensuring the preservation of maritime heritage while creating pathways into the film industry. These skills—rigging, engineering, navigation—are not only vital for historic vessels but also highly sought after in cinematic production.
Why Heritage Marine Matters
Film is a collaborative art form, and Essex’s cultural economy thrives on partnerships like this. Heritage Marine exemplifies how local businesses can contribute to global storytelling while sustaining traditional skills. Their work positions Essex as a film-friendly region with deep creative roots.

https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.title: Starring Essex! – The Essex Film Office launch new interactive map showing where top film and TV shows were filmed
https://essexfilmoffice.co.uk/feed/.text:
The county’s film office has launched a new movie map to encourage film buffs and tourists to visit top TV and film locations.
Ever wondered what the big trucks are parked up in a disused carpark? Or why there are people in Hi-Viz jackets directing traffic when there aren’t any road works? It is more than likely that you are witnessing a little bit of movie magic being made.
Essex has long been a destination of choice of film and TV productions looking for the perfect location to shoot their latest movie or show.
On screen, Essex has been host to spies, superheroes and gothic romances and has been the location for TV shows which have inspired social change. The county has welcomed some of the biggest names in film and TV, including Tom Cruise, Cate Blanchett, Tom Holland, Claire Danes and Tom Hiddleston.
This summer the Essex film office has teamed up with Visit Essex to launch an interactive movie map which allows users to view where top films and TV shows were made and to follow in the footsteps of their favourite actors and superheroes.
A new campaign ‘Starring Essex’ has revealed the top spots across the county that have hit the screen. From the gritty streets of the ever-popular spy thriller series ‘Slow Horses’ to the star-studded historical romance of ‘The Essex Serpent’, Essex has taken centre stage.
Screen tourism is growing; the latest figures reveal 7 in 10 UK visitors have sought out a film or TV location¹. Over recent years Essex has also seen an exponential growth in TV and film productions. In 2024/25 the Essex Film Office recorded over £3m in economic impact from film and TV production activity in Essex. Due to these figures, the tourism sector is now looking forward to benefit.
Thanks to the launch of the new movie map, film fans can follow in the footsteps of their favourite actors and superheroes. The map includes locations for ‘The Crown’, which was filmed in Chelmsford at Hylands House. Visitors can recreate a pose from ‘Wonderwoman’ at Tilbury Fort, or imagine being Lady Mary from ‘Downton New Era’ at the Electric Palace, Harwich. It also details locations for much-loved historic TV shows, such as Porridge, which was filmed in Chelmsford prison. The city was also the backdrop for one of the UK’s biggest groundbreaking dramas, ‘Mr Bates vs The Post Office’, which was filmed at Chelmsford’s Shire Hall. Tom Hiddleston and Claire Danes’ fans can retrace their steps by following The Essex Serpent trail.
Since 2021, the Essex Film Office has been helping production crews find their perfect filming locations, promoting the county’s natural and urban landscapes and securing permits for private and commercial locations, ensuring that Essex is a film -friendly county.
To follow in the footsteps of Tom Cruise, Helena Bonham Carter, Lady Mary and more, view the movie map at:

https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.title: From Harlow to the World: How Charles K. Kao's Fibre Optic Breakthrough Changed Global Communications
https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.text:
In 1966, a young researcher working in a Harlow laboratory published a paper that would transform global communications forever. Charles K. Kao, then head of the electro-optics research group at Standard Telecommunication Laboratories in Harlow, demonstrated that glass fibres could carry light signals over long distances. This discovery laid the foundation for the fibre optic networks that power today's internet.
The Laboratory on the Edge of Town
Standard Telecommunication Laboratories (STL) had moved to Harlow from Enfield in 1959, becoming one of the new town's first major technology employers. The research centre, owned by Standard Telephones and Cables (STC), employed hundreds of scientists and engineers working on cutting-edge telecommunications technology.
Charles K. Kao joined STL in 1963 and was appointed head of the electro-optics research group that same year. When his supervisor Antoni Karbowiak left in December 1964 to take a university chair in Australia, Kao took over the optical communications programme. He was working towards his PhD at University College London whilst conducting his research in Harlow, earning his doctorate in 1965.
Kao met his wife Gwen Wong May-Wun at STL; they married in London in 1959 and raised two children in Harlow, both born during the 1960s whilst the family lived in the town.
The 20 dB/km Threshold
At the time Kao began his work, optical fibres suffered from severe light loss; commonly as high as 1,000 decibels per kilometre. This made them impractical for anything beyond very short distances. Kao and his colleague George Hockham, who had joined STL Harlow in 1961, set out to determine whether the problem was fundamental to glass itself or could be overcome.
In 1965, Kao and Hockham concluded that the fundamental limitation for glass light attenuation was below 20 dB/km, a figure that became the crucial threshold for optical communications to become viable. Kao demonstrated that impurities in the glass material, not fundamental physical effects like scattering, caused the dramatic loss of light transmission. Such impurities, he argued, could be removed.
He identified fused silica (SiO₂) as an ideal candidate for optical communication due to its high purity. In 1969, Kao and M. W. Jones measured the intrinsic loss of bulk-fused silica at 4 dB/km, providing the first evidence of ultra-transparent glass.
Publication and Initial Scepticism
The results were first presented to the Institution of Electrical Engineers in London in January 1966. The paper, titled "Dielectric-fibre surface waveguides for optical frequencies," was published in the Proceedings of the IEE in July 1966. It established the electromagnetic theory and performance parameters still used in fibre optic communications today.
Initial reception was far from enthusiastic. Kao's proposal that glass fibre could be used for long-distance information transfer was widely disbelieved. Professor Charles Midwinter of UCL later told the BBC that "a lot of people just openly laughed at the paper."
Kao himself recounted telling his wife that the project could be "world shaking," only to be met with absolute disbelief. It was not until 1970 that Corning Glass Works finally broke the 20 dB/km barrier, proving Kao's theory correct. By 2017, fibre optic losses had fallen to as low as 0.1419 dB/km.
The Birthplace of a Revolution
STL Harlow is now recognised as the birthplace of optical fibre communications. David Devine of Harlow Museum stated: "What Kao did in Harlow transformed the world and provided a backbone for the internet. He was the father of fiber optics."
Kao's work became the foundation for the internet and World Wide Web. He became known as the "godfather of broadband," the "father of fibre optics," and the "father of fibre optic communications."
Recognition and Return
Kao's contributions earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009, awarded "for groundbreaking achievements concerning the transmission of light in fibers for

https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.title: Harlow Town Park: 164 Acres of Post-War Vision
https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.text:
Harlow Town Park stands as one of the most significant legacies of Britain's New Town movement. Spanning 164 acres, it opened in 1957 as a central element of Sir Frederick Gibberd's masterplan for Harlow, designated under the New Towns Act 1946. In August 2020, Historic England added the park to the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens at Grade II, one of only 12 post-war parks to receive this recognition.
A Pioneering Collaboration
The park's design emerged from a collaboration between Gibberd, the master planner of Harlow New Town, and Dame Sylvia Crowe, one of the 20th century's most influential landscape architects. They refined the masterplan between 1947 and 1953, with construction beginning in 1956 under the direction of Welsh architect John St. Bodfan Gruffydd.
Gibberd conceived the park not as a formal garden but as an oversized village green, accessible on foot from surrounding homes. In a departure from contemporary practice, he chose to preserve existing woodlands and the hamlet of Netteswell Cross rather than clear the site. This early conservationist approach integrated historic landscape features into the modern design.
From Watercress Beds to Water Garden
The park contains several distinct gardens and features, each with its own history. The Water Garden, established in 1964 on the site of former watercress beds, features three cascading pools with waterfalls. The 1973 sculpture Pisces by Jesse Watkins remains a focal point.
The Sensory Garden opened in 1984 as the "Scented Garden for the Blind," dedicated to Milicent Bach. It was renamed in 2014 to reflect its broader accessibility. The Walled Garden, formerly a plant nursery, now houses community beehives and the Harlow Men's Shed. The Newfoundland Garden, planted in 1997, commemorates both Harlow's 50th anniversary and Newfoundland's 500th.
Spurriers House, built as a private villa in 1868, now operates as a café and community hub. The bandstand, constructed in 1973, was destroyed by fire on 19 September 2025 in a suspected arson attack. Harlow Council has confirmed plans to rebuild.
A Park That Evolves
The park has undergone significant additions and changes across seven decades. Lookout Hill was created in 1965 from surplus material generated by New Town construction. A 21-acre riverside walk along the River Stort was added in 1988. The 650-square-metre skatepark opened in August 2008 following a £357,500 investment, part-funded by Sport England.
Between 2014 and 2016, a £2.8 million regeneration project restored the park's heritage features. Funded by the Heritage Lottery Fund (£1.8 million) and council match funding, the work included restoring Spurriers House, renovating gardens, and refurbishing the bandstand.
Management of the park passed from the Harlow Development Corporation to Harlow District Council in 1959. The council has maintained the park's Green Flag Award for multiple consecutive years, and in 2019 it placed among the top 10 parks nationally in the Green Flag People's Choice Award.
Community and Heritage
Harlow Town Park continues to serve as a venue for community events. The annual fireworks display attracts up to 15,000 people, and parkrun events operate every weekend. Guided walks, volunteer sessions, and educational programmes run throughout the year.
Several historic buildings stand within the park's boundaries, including Grade II listed properties on School Lane and at Marshgate Farm, ranging from the 16th to the 19th centuries. These structures predate the New Town by centuries and demonstrate the park's layered history.
The Grade II listing in 2020 specifically recognised the "high quality landscape architecture by Gibberd and Crowe" and the park's significance as an example of post-war public space design. Historic England noted its importance as a demonstration of how New Town planners integrated green infrastructure into residential development.
Ongoing Investment

https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.title: Anne Lister: The 'Gentleman Jack' Diarist Who Put Halifax on the UNESCO Map
https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.text:
The Woman Behind Five Million Words
Anne Lister was born on 3 April 1791 in Halifax and lived at Shibden Hall from 1815 until her death in 1840. She left behind what UNESCO has described as one of the most important documents in British history: twenty-six volumes containing approximately five million words, written across her lifetime.
Shibden Hall and the Lister Legacy
The Lister family had owned Shibden Hall since 1619. Anne inherited the estate in 1826 upon the death of her uncle, James Lister, though she did not assume full control until 1836. The hall dates from around 1420 and sits in the Shibden Valley; it is now Grade II* listed.
Anne commissioned substantial renovations to the property. In 1830, she engaged York architect John Harper and landscape gardener Samuel Gray. She added a Gothic tower in 1838 to house her private library, constructed a south terrace, installed new bay windows, and rebuilt the east side with kitchens and servant quarters. The Housebody was recreated with a grand staircase and gallery in what is termed "Jacobethan" style. She also had tunnels and cellars dug beneath the building so staff could move about without disturbing her.
The Diaries and the Code
Lister began keeping her diary in 1806, initially on scraps of paper, and continued until her death. Approximately one-sixth of the text, amounting to the equivalent of twenty-six volumes, was written in a code combining Greek letters, zodiac symbols, punctuation marks, and mathematical symbols.
The code was deciphered in the late nineteenth century by the last Lister to inhabit Shibden Hall, John Lister, working with his friend Arthur Burrell. In the late 1980s, researchers at Birmingham University, including Dorothy Thompson and Patricia Hughes, translated much of the remaining code. Helena Whitbread published decoded volumes in 1988 and 1992, followed by Jill Liddington's biography in 1994.
The diaries contain graphic accounts of lesbian relationships, details of seduction methods, and observations on weather, social events, national affairs, and business interests. They are considered the earliest comprehensive record of lesbian life in English.
UNESCO Recognition
In 2011, Anne Lister's diaries were inscribed on the UK Memory of the World Register. UNESCO's citation noted the "comprehensive and painfully honest account of lesbian life" contained within them. The register places the diaries alongside documents such as the Domesday Book, Magna Carta, and Shakespeare's First Folio as items of outstanding national importance.
Ann Walker and the York Marriage
Anne Lister met Ann Walker in the 1820s. By 1832, Walker had inherited the Crow Nest estate and become a wealthy heiress. On Easter Sunday, 30 March 1834, the two women took communion together at Holy Trinity Church on Goodramgate in York. They considered themselves married, though the union had no legal standing.
The women lived together at Shibden Hall from 1834 until Lister's death in 1840. A commemorative rainbow plaque was installed at Holy Trinity Church in 2018. Walker's own journal, covering June 1834 to February 1835, was discovered in 2020.
A Life of Travel and Business
Anne Lister was a businesswoman with interests in coal mining, canal and railway shares, stone quarries, and property. She dressed entirely in black and participated in ventures typically reserved for men. She was a chief investor in the Calder and Hebble Navigation, with her family holding significant canal shares.
She was also a mountaineer. On 7 August 1838, she completed the first tourist ascent of Vignemale, the highest peak in the French Pyrenees at 10,820 feet. She had earlier ascended Monte Perdido, which stands at 11,007 feet.
In June 1839, she departed with Ann Walker on a journey through France, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Russia. They reached St Petersburg in September 1839 and Moscow in October 1839. The pair travelled south along the frozen Volga River toward the Caucasus. Anne Lister died of fever on

https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.title: Sir Frederick Gibberd: The Architect Who Built a Town
https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.text:
Sir Frederick Gibberd's vision transformed open countryside into a planned community that became a model for post-war Britain. Appointed consultant architect-planner for Harlow New Town in 1946, he spent the next four decades shaping a town that balanced modernist architecture with landscape preservation and community-focused design.
The Man Behind the Masterplan
Frederick Ernest Gibberd was born in Coventry on 7 January 1908, the eldest of five children. After articled training in Birmingham and study at the Birmingham School of Art, he established his private practice in 1930. His early career brought success with projects such as Pullman Court in Streatham and the BISF prefabricated house design that would influence post-war council housing.
Gibberd was appointed consultant architect-planner for Harlow in 1946, shortly before the town received formal designation as a new town on 25 March 1947. He would remain involved with Harlow until his death in 1984, having lived locally for most of his later years.
A Radical Vision for Living
Gibberd approached Harlow with a clear philosophy: a new town should respect existing landscape whilst embracing modernist design principles. He collaborated with landscape architect Sylvia Crowe to create Green Wedges; corridors of green space that separated neighbourhoods and preserved woodlands whilst providing wildlife habitats and recreational areas. These wedges now cover 23 per cent of the district.
Each neighbourhood was designed as a self-contained community with its own shopping precinct, pubs, and facilities. Gibberd insisted that 20 to 30 per cent of housing be built as flats rather than traditional two-storey houses with gardens, a position that frequently put him at odds with the Development Corporation's preferences.
Pioneering Firsts
Harlow under Gibberd achieved several British firsts. The town opened Britain's first pedestrian precinct and, most notably, constructed Britain's first modern residential tower block. The Lawn, completed in 1951, featured a distinctive butterfly-shaped design that preserved existing oak trees. Rising nine storeys and containing 36 flats, it won a Ministry of Health Housing Medal and influenced the construction of 440,000 high-rise flats across Britain by 1975. The Lawn was Grade II listed in 1998.
Buildings That Shaped the Town
Gibberd personally designed numerous structures that defined Harlow's character. The Town Hall, completed in 1958 and officially opened by Lord Attlee in 1960, featured a nine-storey concrete tower in a striking modern style. Cost constraints prevented Gibberd from realising his preferred 15-storey design, and the building was demolished in 2002.
The Water Gardens, established in 1964, were landscaped around three connected pools with waterfalls and featured Jesse Watkins's sculpture Pisces from 1973. The gardens were later listed by English Heritage. Gibberd also designed the Orchard Croft housing estate, which won a British Housing Award in 1951, and the Harvey Centre, one of Britain's earliest purpose-built indoor shopping malls.
Gibberd's collaborative approach brought leading contemporary architects to Harlow, including Powell and Moya, Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew, and Gerard Goalen, creating a diverse architectural landscape across the town.
Gardens and Legacy
Gibberd created his own sanctuary at Marsh Lane, developing The Gibberd Garden between 1972 and 1984 with his wife Patricia. The garden contains architectural elements salvaged from his reconstruction of Coutts Bank and is now owned by the Gibberd Garden Trust, open to the public from April to September.
His contributions were recognised with a CBE in 1954 and a knighthood in 1967. Several of his Harlow designs now carry listed status, including The Lawn (Grade II), St Paul's Church (Grade II), and Harlow Town Park (Grade II). The Mark Hall neighbourhood, the first neighbourhood developed, is designated as a conservation area.

https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.title: How Harlow Became Britain's Unexpected Sculpture Capital
https://harlowmagazine.com/feed.xml.text:
When Harlow New Town was designated on 25 March 1947, few could have predicted that this planned community in Essex would eventually house one of Britain's most significant public art collections. More than seven decades later, the town boasts over 60 documented sculptures by internationally renowned artists, earning its official designation as "Harlow Sculpture Town" in 2009.
The Vision of Frederick Gibberd
The foundation of Harlow's sculpture heritage lies in the vision of Sir Frederick Gibberd, the architect and town planner who created Harlow's masterplan in 1947. Gibberd believed that art should not be confined to galleries but integrated into the daily lives of residents. In the 1950s, he established the Harlow Art Trust to acquire and display public sculpture throughout the town.
Working alongside Sir Philip Hendy, then Director of the National Gallery, Gibberd secured works that would have been unattainable for most local authorities. Their collaboration brought masterpieces to Harlow that today would command museum-quality status anywhere in the world.
Masterpieces in Public Spaces
Harlow's collection includes works by some of the most celebrated sculptors of the twentieth century. Henry Moore's "Family Group," commissioned in 1954 and unveiled on 17 May 1956, stands as one of the artist's first major public commissions. The bronze was originally displayed outside the Harlow Playhouse before weathering necessitated its relocation indoors to the Civic Centre foyer.
Auguste Rodin's "Eve" (1882), acquired from the Musée Rodin in 1960, sits in the Water Gardens as testament to the Trust's ambitious acquisition policy. Elisabeth Frink's "Wild Boar" (1970), a Grade II listed bronze, shares the Water Gardens with Henry Moore's "Upright Motive No. 2" (1955-56), creating an outdoor gallery of international significance.
Barbara Hepworth's "Contrapunctal Forms" (1951), originally created for the Festival of Britain and resited to Harlow in 1953, is another Grade II listed work. The collection extends to pieces by Lynn Chadwick, F.E. McWilliam, Ralph Brown and numerous other significant British sculptors.
Democratic Access to Art
The placement of these works reflects Gibberd's belief in democratic access to art. Sculptures appear in shopping centres, housing estates and public squares rather than being confined to museums. The Water Gardens themselves, listed by English Heritage, serve as a focal point for the town's artistic heritage, featuring William Mitchell's 1963 concrete reliefs alongside major sculptural works.
This approach created what the BBC described in 2005 as "one of the most exceptional sculpture collections of any town in Britain." The Art Newspaper characterised Harlow in 2020 as "Essex's unlikely sculpture town," acknowledging both the quality of the collection and its unexpected location.
Gibberd Garden: A Personal Legacy
Beyond the public collection, Sir Frederick Gibberd's personal contribution to Harlow's artistic landscape continues at the Gibberd Garden. Created by Gibberd and his wife Patricia from 1972 until his death in 1984, the Grade II listed garden spans more than nine acres of landscaped grounds containing an eclectic collection of sculptures and architectural elements. The garden, now owned by the Gibberd Garden Trust, opens to the public on Wednesdays, Sundays and Bank Holiday Mondays from April to October.
Official Recognition
On 26 March 2009, Harlow Council voted to approve the Harlow Art Trust's proposal to rebrand the town as "Harlow Sculpture Town." The designation, intended to emulate Hay-on-Wye's reputation as "Booktown," appears on council and tourist publications. The Trust aims to make Harlow as readily associated with sculpture as its Welsh counterpart is with literature.

https://www.centraleast.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Get your flu vaccine now to help protect yourself and your loved ones this Christmas
https://www.centraleast.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
NHS organisations across the East of England are jointly urging anyone eligible for a free flu vaccination to get it now if they have not yet had it this winter. The call comes ahead of spending time with family and friends this Christmas.
The flu vaccine can take up to two weeks to build protection. NHS Essex, NHS Central East and NHS Norfolk and Suffolk are encouraging residents to get vaccinated by Friday 11 December to give the vaccine time to work before Christmas Day.
Christmas is a time when families and friends come together, and flu can spread easily through close contact. Getting vaccinated helps reduce your risk of serious illness. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to family members, including those at greater risk of becoming seriously unwell.
Older people, pregnant women and people with certain long-term health conditions are particularly at risk of serious illness from flu. Getting vaccinated helps reduce that risk.
Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex, said:
As you make your Christmas plans, please make time for your flu vaccination too. Flu can make anyone unwell, but for some people it can lead to serious complications, a hospital stay and, in some cases, death. If you’re eligible for a free vaccine and haven’t had it yet, book an appointment now rather than leaving it until the festive rush.
If you’re a parent or carer, please also check whether your eligible child has had their flu vaccine. If they’ve missed it, make arranging their vaccination part of your Christmas preparations.
If you can only get an appointment after 11 December, please still take it. Flu can circulate well beyond Christmas, and vaccination can help protect you through the rest of winter.
Dr Katherine Rowe, Deputy Clinical Director at NHS Central East, said:
Christmas brings different generations together, including older people, pregnant women and those with certain long-term health conditions, for whom flu can be particularly serious.
If you’re eligible, taking up your free flu vaccine is an important step in reducing your risk of serious illness. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to family members. Please make vaccination part of looking after yourself and your loved ones this Christmas.
Lisa Nobes, Executive Director of Nursing, NHS Norfolk and Suffolk ICB, said:
If you’re eligible for a free NHS flu vaccination, a participating pharmacy can help you get protected ahead of Christmas. Some pharmacies offer walk-in vaccinations, so you may not need to book an appointment.
Please check with your local pharmacy about availability before travelling. The chances are, there’s one near you offering the vaccination.
It’s a busy time of year for most of us, but our health and wellbeing is worth making a bit of time for, alongside all our Christmas preparations. I want people to be able to enjoy the festive season and not be in bed, or in hospital, with flu.
Dr Eleanor Powers, Head of Public Health Commissioning (immunisation) for NHS England – East of England, said:
Last year, around 104,000 hospitalisations were avoided through people getting their jabs and protecting themselves, their loved ones, our communities and helping the NHS prepare for winter.
So far this season, over 2 million people in the East of England have already had their flu jab, which is great news, but there are plenty more appointments available.
The flu jab really is your best defence against winter illness. It takes just a few minutes, but it can protect you for months, helping to prevent serious illness, avoid hospital admissions and keeping the most vulnerable people safe.
Now is also a great time to get your 2- and 3-year-olds vaccinated; little ones can get really unwell with flu. Many people don’t know that whilst school age children get their offer in their schools, younger children age 2 and 3 are also entitled to a nasal spray vaccine and they can get it at their GP or at a participating local

https://www.centraleast.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: New crisis text service launches across East of England to provide round-the-clock mental health support
https://www.centraleast.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
A new NHS-funded Crisis Text Support Service has launched across the East of England, making reaching out for mental health support easier by providing free, confidential support via SMS, WhatsApp and online chat, 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
The service offers an alternative for people who feel more comfortable communicating through text rather than speaking on the phone or in person, connecting them directly with trained mental health professionals when they need support. Available to children, young people and adults, it can help people experiencing anxiety, loneliness, overwhelming thoughts or those who simply need someone to listen.
People can access support through:
SMS: Text ‘SOS’ to 80899
WhatsApp: 0800 884 0655
Webchat: https://nxgthrive.co.uk/crisis-text-service
Commissioned by the NHS Central East, NHS Norfolk and Suffolk and NHS Essex Integrated Care Boards, and delivered by NXG Thrive, the service is available to people living in Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Essex, Hertfordshire, Luton, Milton Keynes, Norfolk, Peterborough and Suffolk.
Dr Andrew Rochford, Executive Medical Director for NHS Norfolk and Suffolk Integrated Care Board (ICB) said:
The launch of the East of England Mental Health Crisis Text Service gives people another way to access mental health support when they need it most. The service is designed to complement existing NHS mental health services, including crisis lines and local support available across the region, helping to ensure people can access the right support in the right way.
“We know that reaching out for help takes courage. For many people, especially younger people, sending a message can feel far less daunting than making a phone call or speaking face-to-face. That’s why we’re pleased to offer a service that meets people where they are and allows them to seek help in a way that feels comfortable to them.
“With no minimum age and support available around the clock, we hope this service will make it easier for more children, young people and adults to reach out early and access the support they need.
The service is entirely staffed by registered health and care professionals. When a person reaches out, they are connected to one of the Crisis Text Responders – all of whom are qualified and experienced mental health professionals from backgrounds including psychology, counselling, social work and mental health nursing. They are trained in safeguarding, crisis intervention and evidence-based therapeutic approaches and can support people in distress, assess risk, develop safety plans and connect individuals to appropriate local services.
The web chat option also includes real-time translation tools, so responders can communicate in the sender’s first language.
The service is integrated with local mental health services, helping people access timely support and signposting to local services and specialist care if needed.
Alfred Bandakpara-Taylor, Director of Commissioning – Adult Mental Health and Neurodiversity for NHS Essex ICB, said:
As we move into the autumn and winter months, we know that many people can find this a particularly challenging time of year. Shorter days, social pressures, feelings of loneliness and worries about work, money or family circumstances can all have an impact on mental wellbeing.
“This service provides a free source of support at any time of day or night, ensuring people have somewhere to turn whenever they need help or simply someone to talk to.
“There’s lots of other support on hand too to help people through winter. We encourage residents to visit their local ICB and council websites to explore the advice, services and practical support on offer to help them stay warm, well and connected.
Dr Fiona Head, Medical Director for NHS Central East ICB said:
