https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: Some more serendipity in the Searchroom!
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
You know how much Archive Assistant Neil Wiffen loves a bit of serendipity – well here’s some more,a Neil explores a serendipitous discovery, that revealed more about Essex’s role in the Great War!
When we have new visitors to the Searchroom, I always warn them that it’s a dangerous business coming in, as you never know what you’ll come across. You might think you’ll do a bit of family history, take a look at a record or two but before you know it, six months have passed and you stagger out from being interested in so many things and going down so many rabbit holes!
Well, it’s the same for the staff as well – what will we see today? You might be working quietly away, getting on with the task allotted to you but sometimes fate comes looking for you – especially if we have our wonderful volunteers in who might have a question to ask or an item to share.
It was the latter in this case. Volunteer Annette, who has been beavering away listing a large collection of postcards and ephemera over the last few years, came up to the Searchroom enquiry desk clutching an aerial photo of a trench system labelled ‘Chelmsford’, dated 1917. Well, that certainly piqued our interest – who wouldn’t be interested in this unidentified location within ‘Chelmsford’?
Image of trench network at Chelmsford (A15840 Batch 3)
The first thing, looking at this photo, is that the landscape is distinctly ‘heathy’, with patches of scrub. This marginal land would have been actively sought out by the military for their exercises, as they always tried to use areas of poor soil, which was of little value to the locals apart from rough grazing or for cutting furze or heather from. So where in ‘Chelmsford’ was this practice trench system located? First thoughts turned to Little Baddow and Danbury, the latter the site of an important Napoleonic camp. Was it Galleywood Common, once the location of a major Napoleonic defensive line? Scouring Ordnance Survey maps drew a blank so we spread the net wider. It came when Edward Harris was looking at a combination of maps on the National Library of Scotland website ( Ordnance Survey Maps – Map Images – National Library of Scotland ) and our trusty A to Z from the early 2000s – it was Mill Green, Ingatestone – huzzah!
So, we now knew where it was, but what was it for? Reaching out to our archive community, ERO regular Robert Fletcher told us that it was the Southern Area Bombing School SABS) – he had undertaken some research on this in previous years. In fact, it had been mentioned by a Miss Christy of Ingatestone who had a sketch map of the site. Robert also gave us some other references, one of which was to a notebook kept by a member of the Durham Light Infantry, Charles Edward Shaw.
Front page of Charles Shaw’s notebook (D/DLI 7/959/1. Reproduced by courtesy of the Trustees of the Durham Light Infantry and The Story, Durham)
Our friends at The Story in Durham ( The Story ), took a look at Charles’s notebook for us, but, apart from the rather attractive title page, and although it does contain details about grenades, there is nothing on his time in Ingatestone. Do any of you know anything about SABS as it would be great to find out more.
And just when you think you’ll never need to think about bombs and bombing schools again, an interesting video comes along which explains all about them including some of the set-up which you can see in our aerial photo:
So, on this Armistice Day we can remember all those who had to undertake a course at the bombing school, be grateful that it does not exist now, but also thankful that on one day in 1917 a photograph was taken of this long-forgotten relic of World War One.

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: ‘An Oyster Feast Beneath the Waters of the Colne’
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
This year’s Colchester Oyster Feast takes place on 23 rd October, and we thought it would be a great opportunity to showcase some of the programmes that have been created to accompany the event in the past.
Colchester Oyster Feast programme, 1895 (LIB/E/COL 341.5)
These programmes were all designed and illustrated by W. Gurney Benham. Benham was a prominent local figure, being mayor of Colchester three times (1892/93, 1908/09, 1933/34), as well as editor of the Essex County Standard newspaper from 1884 to 1944. He also served as part of Essex County Council between 1925 and 1940, and was knighted in 1935. He was responsible for a variety of publications during his career, including his books of quotations and transcriptions of documents. He clearly was also a keen cartoonist and illustrator.
Colchester Oyster Feast programme, 1896 (LIB/E/COL 341.6)
Colchester shares a long history with oysters. The first Royal Charter was granted to the people of Colchester for a fishery in the River Colne by Richard I in 1189 and a fishery still exists there to this day.
Colchester Oyster Feast programme, 1897 (LIB/E/COL 341.7)
The Oyster Feast originally coincided with the St. Dennis Fair, which was held every year on 9 th October. The St. Dennis Fair dates back at least to a Charter of 1318 which declared that the fair should begin on 8 th October, the day before St. Dennis’ Day. In addition, the annual oyster dredging licences were issued in October of each year, and by the 1790s it had become tradition for a gift of oysters to be given to the Corporation lunch of the Mayor and councillors which was held after the proclamation of the St. Dennis Fair. Thus, the connection between oysters and the fair at the beginning of October was firmly established. Following the calendar adjustment in 1752 the date of the fair moved to 20 th October.
Colchester Oyster Feast programme, 1900 (LIB/E/COL 341.10) – one of the more sinister examples!
In 1845 Colchester’s new mayor, Henry Wolton, made the Oyster Feast a large affair for the first time – inviting 200 people – to dine at the town hall, covering the cost himself. Previously the Feasts were for members of the council, but in 1845 the Feast was extended to the public more generally for the first time, albeit by invitation only.
Colchester Oyster Feast programme, 1907 (LIB/E/COL 341.16)
The Feast grew in popularity throughout the late 19 th century and early 20 th century and over the years has been attended by royalty, dignitaries and celebrities.
The St Dennis fair has not taken place since 1938, but the Oyster Feast is still held on one of the last Fridays of October.
Colchester Oyster Feast programme, 1930 (LIB/E/COL 341.33)

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: Curiosity Cabinet – A river cruise to Dagenham
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
The Ford factory at Dagenham opened on 1st October 1931, with its first vehicle (a Ford AA Van) being produced the same month. At its peak in 1953, around 40,000 workers were employed there. The factory ceased vehicle production in 2002, but engines are still built on site.
In 1938, members of the public could go on a river cruise aboard the ‘luxuriously appointed’ M. S. New Dagenham. The boat could accommodate up to 300 passengers who would depart from Westminster Pier at 11:30, being provided with a running commentary by a Ford official during the cruise to Dagenham, with the option of lunch included. Once there, they were treated to a two-hour guided tour of the factory by specially trained guides, before their return cruise to Westminster.
On display we have an advertising leaflet (LIB/E/DAG36) for this day trip, published by Ford Motor Company Ltd in 1938.

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: The serendipity of the Searchroom (oh, and Waltham Forest!)
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
Archive Assistant Neil Wiffen writes:
Regular readers of this Blog will know how much we at the Record Office enjoy using our venerable 1933 edition of the Oxford English Dictionary, and recently I had cause to consult it once more to check a meaning.
One of the joys (there are so many!) of working at ERO is the instances of serendipity occurring – be it the documents being looked at or the happy coincidence (serendipity) of working in the Searchoom on a particular day and meeting new researchers. The summer brings all sorts of exotic things across the globe to our own shores; often they will have drifted here via the Gulf Stream or blown over the ocean by contrary winds. Some visitors though, have a premeditated reason to travel thousands of miles to reach us, and quite often, even here, in the Searchroom we have our own long-distance travellers descending on us. The reasons can be legion: perhaps they are here from the other side of the world tracing their Essex family history containing an ancestor who might have been given free passage to Australia, against their will, for some nefarious crime. Or maybe it is tracing the medieval history of one of our villages or the treatment of the aged in early-modern Essex. We never know who will be walking through our door and what they will want to look at.
A month or two ago we had just one such visitor who came to us from the University of Wisconsin-Madison (which according to the ‘measure’ tool in Google maps is about 3,970 miles away!), Dr Emily Spunaugle. Emily was over here researching early nineteenth century Wanstead, which was once in the historic county of Essex. After almost a day with us and having looked at many documents, Emily came across a book from our library that she had been waiting a long time to see: Rambles in Waltham Forest: a stranger’s contribution to the triennial sale for the benefit of the Wanstead Lying-in Charity from 1827.
Our particular copy of the book also, entirely unexpectedly, answered an important question for which Dr Spunaugle had long been seeking an answer.
Rambles in Waltham Forest: a stranger’s contribution to the triennial sale for the benefit of the Wanstead Lying-in Charity 1827 (LIB/634.9 BLE)
There was much excitement and a photo was demanded
Dr Emily Spunaugle
It is lovely to be able to help researchers to make the most of their visits and being a regular using of archives myself, I know what it feels like to have that ‘moment’ when your research falls into place. Emily has subsequently contacted us to say that
As an academic, I’ve conducted research in countless libraries, local museums, and record offices around the United Kingdom during my career, and none have been so welcoming and helpful as the Essex Record Office. During my visit, workers expressed appropriate and genuine interest in researchers’ topics, including my own, and consulted with their colleagues for additional expertise when needed. From the wayfinding information on the website to the friendly service of the in-person visit itself, it’s apparent that the ERO wants researchers to come and use their collections, and actively sees this as their mission. Here’s hoping my next research project also involves Essex!
So, whether you are planning on visiting us from near or far (and we do want you to visit to look at the documents we car for), we look forward to seeing you and hope that you have as successful a visit as Emily did. Thinking about it, Emily experienced some serendipity in the Searchroom, as much as we did in being able to help her: serendipity squared – now that’s something powerful in this day and age!

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: Curiosity Cabinet – Back to School
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
For many families children have returned to school after the long summer break. We thought it an excellent opportunity to display some school related items from the Collections.
On display we have a school exercise book of John G Freeman from 1888 (D/DGs/F91), when he was in the Upper Fifth form, and a copy of his school report from July 1887 (D/DGs/F89).
John was from Southend and attended Dame Alice Owen’s School in Islington. The type of lessons John had is reflected in his exercise book –  trigonometry, algebra and composition for example, complete with feedback on his work from the Form Master. References to the neatness of margins might be familiar to teachers and parents alike!
On viewing John’s school reports, it appears he was on the whole a good student and impressed his Form Master.
John later went on to become an electrical engineer, an emerging profession at that time.

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: “The one that got away!” Survey and Valuation of the Estate of the Earl of Essex in Parishes of Stebbing, Saling, Raine and Bocking (D/DU 3713/1)
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
The vast majority of the records preserved at the Essex Record Office have been donated or loaned freely for the benefit of the public. We, and generations of researchers and residents, are grateful for the generosity of donors and owners of records who help to ensure these documents are safely preserved and widely accessible to the public.
However, from time to time the Record Office is alerted by The National Archives to documents coming up for auction. If it is something significant enough and suitable to acquire for the archive, we seek external funding for the full cost of the purchase. Our first approach is usually to the Friends of Historic Essex , the charity that supports ERO. For relatively small amounts, the Friends are generally more than happy to finance the purchase of documents themselves, which are then added to our holdings for all researchers to access.
Occasionally the documents we are told about are more expensive than the Friends on their own can fund, so we may need to apply to other awarding bodies to help build a bigger pot of cash. The Essex Heritage Trust , the Essex Society for Archaeology and History and other local organisations have kindly provided grants for this. But for higher value documents it is often the support of the Friends of the Nations’ Libraries (FNL), with their generous contributions, that has allowed us to successfully acquire the item in question.
However, this is not always the case and just recently we were delighted to be directly approached by a vendor who had just purchased a document which we unsuccessfully bid for in 2019 – the ‘Survey and Valuation of the Estate of the Earl of Essex in Parishes of Stebbing, Saling, Rayne and Bocking’, which we remembered as ‘the one that got away’!
In 2019 we were alerted that this volume was about to be auctioned and the then Chair of the Friends, Dr Chris Thornton contacted FNL, who gave a promise of funding, and the Stebbing Local History Society (SLHS) to see if they might be willing to contribute as well.
The very active SLHS were excited with the possibility of this volume being acquired for the ERO, as they have a long-running research programme with American academic Prof Lawrence Poos of the Catholic University of America, looking at the landscape history of their parish.
For many of our parishes, the earliest complete map showing individual plots of land detailing ownership, tenancy and land use can often be that created (with the accompanying ‘Award’) for the Tithe Commutation Act of 1836, with the resulting maps dating from the late 1830s into the early 1850s. While there will almost always be earlier estate maps, these can often be of only limited areas rather than an entire parish. Therefore, this volume which contains many maps of areas across Stebbing, as well as adjoining parishes, would be very useful as it shows the area 40 or so years earlier than would have been surveyed on the Stebbing tithe map (D/CT 332B).
All was progressing nicely: a member of SLHS had visited the auction house to examine the volume to give it the once over and had given the ‘thumbs up’; a decent sum of money had been pledged and our bid was made. Come the day of the auction, we waited with bated breath to see if we were successful – and we were not! SLHS passed on their details to the auction house, for forwarding to the successful purchaser, in the hope that they might be permitted to photograph it for academic purposes – nothing was heard. Chris Thornton counselled us to keep an eye out for it appearing again in the future, for you never know …
Fast forward six or so years and ERO were approached early in 2026 by someone who had been attending an antiques fair and had come across the very same volume of maps on a stall and being retailed for much less than we had lost it for. Realising its importance, he purchased it and got in contact to offer it to the Record Office for what it had cost him. ERO sprang into action and approached the Friends

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: Tracing lives through allotment records
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
Once you’ve explored the main family history sources, it’s worth investigating the records that survive for the towns and boroughs where your ancestors lived. Local records can reveal a lot about their lives, documenting their trades, involvement in community affairs, notable achievements or misdemeanours, and even the allotments they cultivated.
The records for the Borough of Saffron Walden contain a fascinating insight into allotments in the 1830s and 1840s. As with many places across the country, “spade husbandry” was introduced as a form of poor relief, with unemployed men being offered a piece of land to grow food for their families and provide an income at a reasonable rent. The 1830s was a period of instability in rural communities with poor harvests and increased mechanisation meaning food prices and unemployment rates were high and wages were low. This led to the Swing Riots where arable workers in the south and east of England destroyed threshing machines and set fire to haystacks in protest of these conditions. Saffron Walden’s Justices of the Peace were concerned enough about disturbances to call upon certain householders “to act as Special Constables for the prevention and suppression of any tumult, riot or felony” in the area (catalogue ref: D/B 2/QSS5/34 ).
Front cover of Register of proceedings in matters relating to Spade-Husbandry and Allotments’ [title page], recording minutes of committee relating to provision of allotments for poor labourers, 1829-1834 ( D/B 2/PAR9/5 )
Saffron Walden set up an Allotment Committee in 1829 and the surviving records include committee minutes ( D/B 2/PAR9/5 and D/B 2/PAR9/6 ), allotment rent accounts which record the names of people cultivating plots ( D/B 2/BRL5/71 ), and maps of the fields with allotment plots marked out and numbered so they can be linked to the rent accounts, allowing individual plot holders to be identified ( D/B 2/BRL5/72 ). The minutes also contain maps of the allotments and have been digitised so can be viewed on Essex Archives Online.
Plan of Turners Field with numbered plots and named plot holders in Register of proceedings in matters relating to Spade-Husbandry and Allotments’ [title page], recording minutes of committee relating to provision of allotments for poor labourers, 1829-1834 ( D/B 2/PAR9/5 )
The Allotment Committee managed several fields provided by local landowners and charities such as Lord Braybrooke, and the banker and philanthropist Wyatt George Gibson among others. Two such fields were Turners Field and Warners Field. Both fields have been identified on Saffron Walden’s tithe map of 1848 ( D/CT 378B ) – marked in green with Turners Field on the left. Turners Field is recorded as “Next Windmill Hill Road” on the tithe apportionment, but the owner is the Trustees of the Turners Charity and the shape of the plot corresponds to the shape of Turners Field as drawn in the account books and allotment plan. There are still allotments on this site.
Section of the Tithe Map for Saffron Walden, 1848, showing Turners Field on the left and Warners Field on the right ( D/CT 378B )
Allotments were primarily assigned to men such as John Cornell who is recorded in a rent account book as working a 30-rod plot in Turners Field and a 40-rod plot in Warners Field, however, there is a note that he died in 1838 and that the plots were taken on by his widow. In Warners Field, John Auger had a 20-rod plot and there is a note that he was killed in 1840 with the plot being taken over by his widow, so women and children were likely involved in cultivating the plots. The fact that widows took on the plots shows how important they were to the household.
Entry for Widow Cornell’s plot in Turners Field in the allotment account book 2, 1838-1887 ( D/B 2/BRL5/71 )
In Warners Field, Charles Byatt had a plot until 1840 when he is recorded as a “rate payer” and the plot was taken over by Richard Barker. At one point the plot was “all potatoes” which went against the rul

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: Grounds for Appeal at the Essex Record Office
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
Archive Assistant, Neil Wiffen, introduces Essex Record Office’s part of the “Grounds for Appeal” project, made possible with the support of The National Lottery Heritage Fund.
Here at the Essex Record Office (ERO) we are pleased to be taking part in the national Grounds for Appeal (GfA) project . While there are not a huge number of surviving records at ERO in comparison to some of our project partners, it is still great to be able to participate in the GfA project and contribute the data from our records to the national database that is being constructed. We are particularly pleased to be taking part in this project as we are sure that the Project Officer will be well known to many of you – Hannah Salisbury who undertook various roles at ERO over many years in the 20teens including starting this very blog!
It is only in the last few weeks that we have got our volunteers to start work on the surviving records. In the first instance they will be concentrating on the 700 or so surviving applications (and their associated supporting paperwork) for medical re-examinations to Essex Appeal Tribunal, which date from the end of 1917 into 1918.
C/DC 14/5/1. The application form for medical re-examination from E.W.G. Bagshaw of Leytonstone, 16 November 1917.
The first job that we decided to undertake was to re-package and label the documents associated with each application. While they are in generally good condition, despite being over a century old, we needed them to be ready to be inputted into the GfA database when that stage was reached. Each set of documents (which might comprise just the application form but, more usually, this and several supporting documents) were checked and re-packaged into an acid free paper wrapper and then ten document filled wrappers were put into an acid free manilla folder. Several of these completed folders are then stored in an acid free box thus ensuring their long-term preservation.
The first day of re-packaging in the Conservation Workshop. (L-R) GfA volunteers Kim, Lucy and Ashley.
Volunteer Ashley says:
“It was great fun learning what conservators have to do to protect these documents and getting a chance to clean some of them with smoke sponges .”
Folders in green Lydamore box.
The crucial piece of information to give each application at this stage was a unique catalogue reference number so that in the fullness of time, the descriptions of each application can be loaded onto our Essex Archives Online catalogue , making these documents searchable and available to researchers.
Some of our regular conservation volunteers taking a welcome break from flattening and cleaning architectural plans. (L-R) Julie, Pat, Jacky, Sue and Ann.
Once the re-packaging had got underway, the next task was to start inputting the data from the documents into the GfA online data collection form. This is slightly trickier and more involved than the re-packaging as the volunteers have to contend with handwriting from a century ago as well as various medical terms. However, they have been tackling it with great enthusiasm. Each case is different and the documents shine a light on the process of recruitment during the last year of the First World War.
Volunteer Karishma inputting data into the online GfA data collection form.
Volunteer Kim says:
“ It has been very interesting working through the data collection form as it has allowed me to look in more detail at the medical examination process. It gives a great insight into the issues affecting men at that time .”
That’s all for now, the volunteers are carrying on re-packaging and listing and on behalf of ERO and GfA I would like to say how grateful we are for their enthusiasm and dedication to this project. Reading the application forms makes you realise how lucky we are to live in a country which does not need to recruit to a mass citizen army at a time when many hundreds of thousands of men had already been killed.
And remember, further details can be found at Grounds f

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: Of Gallows
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
Here at the Essex Record Office our Archive Assistant (and events wrangler) Neil Wiffen has been looking at things again, specifically the 1777 Chapman and André map of Essex. Here he explains all:
Extract from the Walker Map of Chelmsford 1591 (D/DM P1).
Hopefully you are all aware of the wonderful Chapman and André map of Essex. If not, you can view it in incredible detail on Tim Fransen’s excellent website (I dare you not to be amazed and to lose hours of your life by exploring the late eighteenth century landscape of Essex: you have been warned!)
So, I was preparing an event listing for our 2027 season of talks, where we will be discussing the (spoiler alert!) witchcraft statutes of 1563 and 1604. To accompany the text there is always a need to have an illustration or two and, thinking outside the box, I thought that showing the Chelmsford gallows, as shown on John Walker’s 1591 map (above) would be a suitable image, albeit well known. There are not many images of gallows and the couple of other instances I could think of where those depicted by Chapman and André.
Chapman and André sheet 21. Showing the gallows/gibbets along the river Thames between Barking Level and Dagenham Marsh.
The first was of one of the sites along the river Thames and either shows gallows or a gibbet (could they be both?) and the other was those just to the north-east of Romford on the common, what we now know as Gallows Corner.
Chapman and André sheet 17. The gallows/gibbets on Romford Common.
As interesting as these are, I thought I would check out the site of the Chelmsford gallows to see what Chapman and André show. Well, you could knock me down with a feather! There, it was in a semi-circular enclosure – what a view it must have been to the surrounding properties. I had never ‘looked’ before and it was hiding in plain sight, albeit at quite a small scale!
Chapman and André sheet 12. Chelmsford gallows.
This might not be news to any of you out there, it might just be me not looking! Do let me know though if this is news to you and, do let me know what else you have found surprising/delightful on the Chapman and André map. And the funny little field of ampersands opposite the gallows – well I’m fairly sure they are hops. Take a look at the big field in Castle Hedingham!
Neil
If you would like to discover more about witchcraft in Essex, come to our talk and book launch for “Witchland” with Marion Gibson on the 29th September , we are running it twice! Once in the morning at 10:40 and once in the afternoon at 18:40.
Tickets available through our website!

https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.title: A House History Case Study: ERO Search Service
https://www.essexrecordofficeblog.co.uk/.text:
In this blog post, Archive Assistant Robert Lee explores a previous example of how the ERO Search Service can assist with property history.
One such case was a search request from Mr. Ben Parker of Great Braxted. The purpose of which was to help establish a general history of a farm called “Brick House” (or Brickhouse), south of Kelvedon near the River Blackwater.
Indeed this now comprises modern dwellings, but the farm encompasses three buildings which are Grade II listed 1 with Historic England. The individual listings contain abridged architectural descriptions (e.g. timber frame, thatched or tiled roof, if any later alterations are apparent) which work towards establishing an approximate biography of the building in question. Indeed, the three entries for Brick House cite “C17 or earlier”; “C16 origin”; “C18”, respectively. Clearly, then, a farm which spans several eras: a wide net for historical inquiry.
It is difficult to determine with complete accuracy, but there does look to be a farmhouse, stables, and perhaps a barn on the 1777 Chapman & Andre Map of Essex. It is just across from A Corn Mill – a mill still stands on this site in Great Braxted.
‘A map of the county of Essex from an actual survey taken in MDCCLXXII:LXXIII & MDCCLXXIV by John Chapman & Peter André’. ( MAP/CM/37/4 Plate 13 )
This is also the case on the Gt. Braxted Tithe Map [ D/CT 48B ], with the accompanying apportionment suggesting that the farmlands were occupied by a Thomas Brown and owned by Peter Du Cane III. Now, properties tend to be allusive in archives due to changing house names, street re-numbering, et cetera. “Brown’s Farm” is the given name of Brick House in 1839, presumably on account of Thomas’ occupancy. This is inferred by simply overlaying a modern street map onto the tithe plan, but this was also evidenced by W.A. Gimson’s local history work Great Braxted, 1086-1957 [ LIB/E/BRAXG1 ], which helpfully correlates the tithe apportionment with modern place-names.
Great Braxted Tithe Map 20 inches to 1 mile [72″ x 63″]. Dated 1839. ( D/CT 48B )
‘Great Braxted, 1086-1957’ by W.A. Gimson. ( LIB/E/BRAXG1 )
We can see Thomas Brown’s payments in an 1838 tithe survey as well [ D/DDC E11 ]. The accounts for Brown’s farm are broken down into more detailed plots than the tithe apportionment, and include House, Garden, Yards; Cart Lodge Field; and Barn Meadow Field – which correlate with the three Historic Building listings.
Survey of Great Braxted, dated 1838. ( D/DDc E11 )
It is clear, however, that Peter DuCane III was the principal landowner within Great Braxted. The DuCanes were prominent cloth merchants, the family having descended from Hugenot ancestry. Peter DuCane purchased Braxted Park from the Darcy family in 1745; an estate which includes Braxted Lodge, a Georgian Mansion. Given Peter DuCane’s ownership, and its proximity to Braxted Park, it seemed plausible that Brick House Farm was formerly an aggregate of the whole estate. This was confirmed by a 1923 Sale Catalogue for Braxted Park [ SALE/A62 ] which includes Lot 5, A Desireable Dairying and Corn Granary Farm known as Brickhouse farm .
Sale catalogue for Braxted Park, Great Braxted. Includes photographs and plan. Dated 20 July 1923. ( SALE/A62 )
For the remainder of the search, we looked at establishing more historical occupants. Maldon district’s electoral registers show an Anthony Patten residing here from 1891-1902. The 1910 Finance Act records show a John Melson residing at the farm. On the 1911 National Census, Thomas Goodwin and his family reside here – as is the case in the 1912 & 1914 Essex Trade Directories. In the 1926 and 37 Trade Directories, Ralph Goodwin lives here.
If you would like us to look into the history of your house in Essex, contact us for details of how to get started.
Grade II indicating “particularly important buildings of more than special interest” ︎

https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.title: Castle Park Boating Lake is to be restored and reopened
https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.text:
We’re delighted that Colchester City Council have confirmed that the historic Victorian Boating Lake in Castle Park is to be restored and reopened.
The announcement from the City Council came after our high profile campaign generated a public outcry that the council seemed to be sitting on their hands and continuing to let the lake stand empty and to deteriorate to the point where there were rumours the council wanted to fill it in.
Using it as  a hard standing backstage area for portaloos and portacabins during the recent Summer Series of Concerts was, at best, insensitive.
Jo Edwards, Chair of Colchester Civic Society said:
‘The lake has been a much loved feature of the Grade ll listed park since it first opened back in 1892. We’re thrilled that future generations will be able to enjoy the lake as much as previous generations have done’
‘Many people were saddened that  the lake  was allowed to fall into such a sorry state of disrepair and the length of time it has been  standing empty.  We’re grateful to everyone who supported our campaign for its restoration, to those who contacted their councillors, and MPs, wrote letters to the press, posted to social media, asked searching questions and made clear that the lake was an important and much loved part of Colchester’s heritage and history.
See recent Gazette Report
See the City Council Press Release

https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.title: Civic Society Calls for Immediate Restoration and Reopening of Boating Lake
https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.text:
“
Colchester Civic Society are calling on Colchester City Council to ‘stop dithering’ and make an immediate public commitment to restore and reopen the Victorian Boating Lake in Castle Park and to  ‘firmly and quickly scotch rumours’  that the lake is to be permanently decommissioned.
The lake has stood empty, neglected and decaying since the council drained it after the collapse of the Middle Mill Weir in December 2023.
We are concerned that the City Council has not yet committed to restore and reopen the much-loved Victorian Boating Lake in Castle Park.
We’ve heard various rumours, one of which is that the boating lake is to be permanently de- commissioned and call on the council to firmly and quickly scotch this worrying possibility’
The boating lake is an integral part of Castle Park – it’s been there as long as the park itself and is included in the park’s grade ll listing and the supposed protection such a listing offer.
Generations of Colcestrians have incredibly happy memories of the boating lake which dates back to the 1800’s and is an important part of Colchester’s Victorian heritage.
No doubt, after standing empty and neglected for the last three years the lake – which dates back to the 1800’s – will now need some major restoration and repair. Presumably the brickwork and cement will need quite a bit of attention. No doubt that will cost money.
But frankly, that’s money the council will just have to find and have to spend. Grants are no doubt available. Have the council spent any time over the last three years looking at potential sources of funding?
If they haven’t, then perhaps they should commit now, to using some of the profits from this years Summer Concert Series to fund the restoration, repair and reopening of the park’s cherished boating lake?’
For our part, Colchester Civic Society stands ready and willing to help in any way we can…
More:

https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.title: New Blue Plaque Marking Colchester’s Napoleonic Barracks
https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.text:
A new blue plaque will be unveiled at the Artilleryman public House in Artillery Street on June 18th at 10,45 to mark Colchester’s forgotten Napoleonic barracks. This will be unveiled by Colchester Garrison commander Lieutenant Colonel ED Rankin DL
The barracks, built from 1794, were designed to house troops during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.
Project lead Paul Knappett explains “Colchester is the nation’s oldest garrison city with a significant military history spanning 2,000 years. Today, Colchester remains home to 16 Air Assault Brigade Combat Team which includes the Parachute Regiment and 7th Parachute Regiment Royal Horse Artillery.
It should be noted that 7th Parachute Regiment Royal Horse Artillery carried out the Royal Gun Salute in Lower Castle Park for The King’s Official Birthday on Saturday, June 13. Their predecessors were I Troop Royal Horse Artillery who were formed in Colchester on February 1, 1805 under Captain Robert Bull. They were affectionally known as Bull’s Troop and earned a strong reputation during the Napoleonic Wars.
By 1805, the barracks housed more than 7,000 officers and men -about half the borough’s population at the time – along with around 500 horses.
Following the Duke of Wellington’s victory at the Battle of Waterloo, eight ships carrying wounded soldiers arrived at the Hythe. Many of them were treated at a 450-bed military hospital located opposite the barracks, on the present-day site of Colchester Adult Community Centre. The hospital was later demolished, with its materials reused in building the Essex and Colchester Hospital.
The Napoleonic Barracks played a vital role at a time when Britain faced the threat of invasion. The blue plaque will ensure this important site is remembered and recognised as part of Colchester’s remarkable military heritage.

But the BID team also do all they can to promote our City businesses both large and small; for example, they recently produced the Colchester Chronicles – a mini series focusing on the people behind six independent businesses. They support the evening and night-time economies too, doing everything they can to ensure the safety and wellbeing of both staff and customers, working closely with Colchester Pubwatch, which won the National Pubwatch of the Year Award this year. https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.title: East Hill Cycle Lanes
https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.text:
Colchester Civic Society Highways Group are attempting to persuade Essex County Council to review the design for the East Hill Cycle Lanes before the scheme is given the go ahead. There are very serious concerns over this scheme, which will divert cyclist from the downhill cycle onto the footpath right outside the front door of the GP Surgeries.
A form of this letter has gone to Pam Cox MP, to David King (leader of Colchester City Council), Kevin Bentley (as leader of Essex County Council), County Councillors Simon Crow and Lee Scordis and ward Councillors Mark Goacher, Amy Kirby Taylor, Kemal Cufoglu.
Dear…
I am enclosing a copy of the letter I am about to send to Tom Cunningham on behalf of the Colchester Civic Society Highways group. We are requesting a review of the current design for the East Hill cycle lanes before final approval is given. Will you please consider supporting this request?
We have very serious concerns over the current scheme. This was substituted for the original floating bus stops design when a temporary pause was imposed on ‘Bus Boarder ‘ and ‘Floating Bus Stops’ last year during the passage of the 2025 Bus Services Bill no.2. The ban on floating bus stops has now been lifted, but the East Hill Design Team are continuing to plan for the implementation of this ‘shared use scheme’, which we consider to be seriously flawed.
Colchester Civic Society Highways Group has been set up to look closely at proposals such as the ‘Walking and Cycling Improvements for East Hill with a view to helping to produce the best possible design without passing judgement on the overall merits of the scheme under consideration.  Our members include people with special interests in cycling, walking and public transport and we have worked directly with the Essex Highways Colchester Design team to assist with their development of plans for both St. Botolph’s Circus and East Hill.
Our aim is to assist in the delivery of the best possible scheme for East Hill and we are convinced that this current scheme is not good enough. The following letter to Tom Cunningham provides a full account of our reasoning. Please give it serious consideration.
Best regards
John Salmon
Ps. The attached drawing is a detail of the shared use scheme. It focuses on the design for the Surgeries Bus Stop.
This letter was sent to Tom Cunningham as portfolio holder for Highways. However there has been a change of roles on the Essex County Council Cabinet. A  copy has therefore also been sent to the new portfolio holder Mark Platt, along with an explanation similar to the one sent to our councillors and MP.
Dear Mr. Cunningham,
I wrote to you in September last year regarding the current proposals for the East Hill Cycle Lanes in Colchester, requesting that the scheme be reviewed once formal guidance has been issued regarding the use of bus bypasses. This guidance has now been issued and does allow for the use of bus bypasses once more, but does not allow the use of the bus boarder type stops, where people getting on and off buses have to step into an active cycle lane.
The East Hill Design Team tell me that they will be continuing with the current shared use scheme, rather than reverting to the original plan for fully segregated cycle lanes. I recognise that the uphill bus stop at the bottom of East Hill must remain as a shared use area in order to be seen to be in compliance with the guidance. I also accept that given this bus stop does not see a lot of use and cyclist will be beginning their ascent of the hill, this compromise arrangement (and circumvention of the rules)  might be seen to present an acceptable level of risk.
However the risk of conflict and injury to both cyclists and pedestrians is of very a different order at the other east Hill bus stops.

https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.title: Looking Up At Colchester
https://www.colchestercivicsociety.co.uk.text:
Posted below is the information to accompany the Looking Up At Colchester page which came with the December 2024 Newsletter.
If you wish to view the Looking Up At Colchester page then follow this link    20240724-LOOKING-UP-AT-COLCHESTER-__-revision-4-1.pdf
Looking Up: information on places
Site of the Roman and later North Gate, North Hill
This was originally a Roman gate built as part of the town wall circuit in late 1st century AD. From Speed’s 1610 map it appears as if the gate was rebuilt in the Medieval period as it is shown with a square headed gateway. The top of North Gate was taken off in 1774, but the sides were incorporated into the adjoining houses, which were not demolished until 1823.
Marquis of Granby Inn, North Hill
Here is an important early C16 building (circa 1520) with exceptionally fine carved detail. Built as a high-status house, it has been an inn for much of its history. Most of the building – the façade in particular – was extensively restored in 1914, as it had been heavily Georgianised.
North Hill Hotel
The North Hill Hotel and Green Room occupies a C19 brick building with a C15 cottage and barn to the rear.
Fire insurance mark, North Hill
These little metal signs on older buildings, known as firemarks, served a practical role in the early days of fire insurance. At that time there was no fire service as we know it – insurance companies maintained their own fire engines, which would only attend buildings insured with them. Colchester had no pressurised water supply until the C19, and the risk of fire was a major concern.
St. Peter’s Church, North Hill
St Peter’s Church was probably an Anglo-Saxon foundation, but was substantially rebuilt at least twice, with further major alterations in the Georgian period. The fine clock was added to the tower in 1866.
Former Boots The Chemist store High Street / Head Street corner
This was built in 1935 as part of the company’s expansion in the interwar period. It was the main Boots store in the town until the store moved to Lion Walk in 1975. On this site, the pharmacy, cosmetics and toiletries counters were on the ground floor whilst much of the first floor housed the local branch of the Boot’s Book Lovers Lending Library, which sadly closed in 1966.
Fire Office, High Street
The Essex and Suffolk Fire Office occupied an early C19 Corn exchange in neo-classical style by David Laing. The third story was added later.
Bank Building, High Street, south side
This was originally the Provincial Bank and is now a Waterstone’s bookshop. The building has a frontage admired by Pevsner in his Essex guide – describing it as a “fine example of 1920’s bank architecture”.
High Street, south side
This shop and offices date from circa 1870 and have a late C20 shopfront, featuring brick with stucco dressings. The roof is behind the parapet. Shop space is on the ground floor and possibly utilises the floor above. Offices are at the top. The building is an example of high Victorian Venetian style.
High Street, south side
This commercial building was originally the Capital Counties Bank, by Baker; May, 1901.A  20th century shopfront is on the ground floor. The two upper storeys are faced in stone.
Fenwick’s Department Store, High Street
Here is one of two sculptures by Sean Henry which have been permanently installed on Colchester High Street. Standing near the Town Hall and Fenwick’s new department store, Man with Cup is located on a ledge 4m above ground, while the 7ft high Walking Woman is at ground level, striding west along the line of the High Street.
Lloyds Bank, High Street south side
This commercial building was built for Lloyds Bank in stripped ‘Wrenaissance’ style in 1926. It is a good example of bank architecture of its date, as it was designed to create an impression of stability and tradition. H. Munro Cautley (architect), W.H. Ross (builder).

https://hornchurchfc.com/feed/.text:
Hornchurch Football Club are delighted to announce the signing of Ernie Weaver on a short-term loan from Sheffield Wednesday.
The young defender joins the club on loan from the Owls until 3rd January 2027. Born in Sheffield, he began a two-year scholarship with Sheffield Wednesday ahead of the 2023–24 season, captained the U18 side, and signed his first professional deal in July 2025. He debuted in the EFL Cup against Bolton Wanderers on 13 August 2025 and made his senior league bow three days later against Stoke City.
Since then, made further first team appearances this season, making four appearances this term in League One.
Speaking on the move, manager Daryl McMahon said;
“Ernie is a young defender coming from Sheffield Wednesday, with good experience already for a youngster having played last season with some appearances in the Championship with Sheffield Wednesday and this season in League One.
We’re delighted to get him on board. We tried to sign him earlier on this season but we couldn’t get it done due to some injuries at Sheffield Wednesday.
We’re delighted Sheffield Wednesday have trusted us to take him on loan and we look forward to working with him.
He is a committed, hard working defender who has qualities on the ball as well. We look forward to welcoming him to our enviornment. It’s another youngster to get in the building and will hopefully show the promise in the coming months.”
Ernie is available for selection for Saturday’s home fixture against Solihull Moors. He has been allocated a squad number of 29.
Welcome to the club Ernie!

By Bailey Howard
Hornchurch shared the spoils with Sutton United on Tuesday evening as the Urchins played out a goalless draw at Bridge Avenue in the Enterprise National League, with neither side able to find a breakthrough in a closely contested encounter.
The hosts produced a disciplined defensive display to keep Sutton at bay, with Arthur Nasta and the Hornchurch backline dealing comfortably with the majority of the visitors’ attacking efforts. However, despite creating a number of opportunities of their own, the Urchins were unable to find the decisive goal as both sides settled for a point.
Daryl McMahon made five changes to his side following Saturday’s 4-0 defeat at Wealdstone, as Hornchurch looked to respond positively at Bridge Avenue.
The game kicked off and the Urchins made a bright start to the contest, with both sides looking to establish themselves early on, but Sutton’s Archie Stevens looked lively in the opening stages and was involved in one of the first notable incidents of the evening, going to ground inside the penalty area under a challenge from Harry Taylor. However, referee Alan Young judged the Sutton forward to have simulated the contact and showed him a yellow card in the seventh minute.
Hornchurch looked to make the most of their defensive organisation, with Sam Ling’s long throws providing a regular source of pressure for the Urchins’ backline. The hosts dealt well with the deliveries, preventing Sutton from creating any clear-cut opportunities from the dangerous situations.
At the other end, Henry Sandat looked particularly lively in a deeper role, working hard to create opportunities for the hosts and offering an attacking threat throughout the first half.
Sutton’s best opportunity of the opening period came through Stevens, who collected a neat lay-off from Emmanuel Osadebe before striking a low effort from around twenty yards. The shot was well struck but straight at Nasta, who dealt comfortably with the attempt.
Osadebe then had an opportunity of his own for Sutton shortly before the interval, meeting a free-kick from Joe Knight with a volley that flew over the crossbar.
Hornchurch continued to work hard defensively, limiting the visitors to efforts from distance and preventing them from finding a way through as the first half drew to a close.
Both sides continued to battle for control of the midfield, with clear-cut opportunities remaining difficult to come by as the contest developed into a tight and physical encounter.
Half-Time – Hornchurch 0-0 Sutton United
Hornchurch returned for the second half looking to build on their defensive performance and find a way through the Sutton backline.
The Urchins looked to threaten going forward, with Sandat seeing an effort fly well wide before forcing a save from Spike Brits early in the second half. The forward’s shot took a slight deflection on its way towards goal, but Brits was able to get down and make the save.
The visitors made an early change, with Jermaine Francis replacing Stevens in the fifty-fifth minute.
Sutton began to enjoy more possession as the half progressed, but the Urchins remained organised and continued to frustrate the visitors, with Nasta rarely called into serious action.
Hornchurch looked to make the most of their opportunities on the counter-attack, with Sandat continuing to offer a threat in the attacking areas. However, Sutton’s defence remained difficult to break down, with both sides struggling to create a clear opening.

https://eppingforest.foodbank.org.uk/fee.title: Chrismas Match Funding Campaign
https://eppingforest.foodbank.org.uk/fee.text:
Local residents can double the impact of their donations to Epping Forest Foodbank this Christmas, as a new match funding campaign launches from 1–8 December 2026.
For the first time in its history, Epping Forest Foodbank is launching a Christmas match funding campaign, giving local residents an opportunity to make their donations go twice as far in the fight against food poverty.
Between 1 and 8 December 2026, every donation made through the campaign will be doubled , meaning that a £10 donation will provide £20 of support for local people facing financial hardship.
Behind the quiet residential roads and bustling shopping parades of the Epping Forest District, thousands of local people are struggling to afford the essentials. On average, around 700 people each month are driven to seek support from foodbanks across the district.
Epping Forest Foodbank, which operates as part of the nationwide Trussell network, provides emergency food and practical support to people referred in crisis. Every household receives a nutritionally balanced supply of food designed to last a minimum of three days.
However, providing this guaranteed support comes at a cost. Each year, the Foodbank spends approximately £30,000 purchasing food to supplement public donations and ensure that no household goes without because of a shortage of supplies.
The need for support continues to grow
During the 2025/26 financial year, Epping Forest Foodbank provided support to 7,501 people, including 3,793 children under the age of 16. This represents a significant increase on the previous year’s total of 6,079 people, including 2,091 children.
Alongside emergency food provision, the Foodbank works to tackle the underlying causes of poverty. Benefits and debt advisers are available across all its hubs, helping people access financial support, manage debt and work towards greater long-term financial security.
This work has already helped secure approximately £200,000 in additional income for local households, making a lasting difference to people’s lives and, in some cases, helping them avoid needing to return to the Foodbank.
Jacob Forman, Director of Epping Forest Foodbank, said:
“Behind every statistic is a person, a family or a child who is facing the reality of not having enough money to put food on the table. We want to make sure that nobody in Epping Forest has to go hungry because they cannot afford the essentials.
“Our Christmas match funding campaign is a fantastic opportunity for the community to make an even bigger difference. Every donation made between 1 and 8 December will be doubled, helping us provide emergency food to those who need it while also supporting our wider work to tackle the causes of poverty.
“We know that Christmas can be an especially difficult time for families already struggling financially. We would encourage everyone who is able to give, however much, to consider supporting the campaign.”
A community working together
Epping Forest Foodbank began as a single church-based foodbank at St Mary’s Church in Loughton. Since then, it has grown into a district-wide service operating across four locations, supported by an incredible network of volunteers, churches, community groups, businesses and local residents.
Its work is underpinned by four core values: Compassion, Justice, Community and Dignity. The Foodbank believes that everyone deserves access to the essentials, and that building a fairer society requires communities to work together.
Our vision is simple: an Epping Forest where no one needs to go hungry.
To donate and have your contribution doubled, visit:  Christmas Giving Challenge – Big Give
For further information about Epping Forest Foodbank, volunteering opportunities or ways to support its work, visit www.eppingforest.foodbank.org. uk or contact the team on 0300 102 9808 or info@eppingforest.foodbank. org.uk .

https://eppingforest.foodbank.org.uk/fee.text:
The Foodbank exists to support people experiencing crisis. We define a crisis as a situation where there is not enough money in the household to afford sufficient food for everyone living there.
In recent months, we have seen a significant increase in longer-term use of the Foodbank, with some clients requiring support over extended periods. Our model has always been to provide emergency food provision alongside appropriate advice and signposting. The food support we offer is intended as a short-term emergency measure rather than a long-term solution.
Please be aware. At the point of first referral, we will ensure that clients are offered a full signposting conversation so they can access additional support where needed.
Inside our hubs are professional advisors in the Benefits system and Debt relief. As well as full access to the Frontline system to give all our clients the best chance of moving away from needing the Foodbank.
Without engaging in these additional services, there will be a limit of 3 vouchers per 6 months per client.

Baby Loss Awareness Week (BLAW) 9-15 October is a time for people across the pregnancy and baby loss communities, and beyond, to come together, remember much-loved and missed babies, reflect on experiences of loss in whatever way feels right and raise awareness of pregnancy and baby loss.
The parish council will be supporting this event. There will be an area in our community space for reflection, with a memory book to record your thoughts. Rainbow coloured heart notelets will also be available to write your message and pop on the window.

https://siblehedingham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Book Your Flu Vaccination
https://siblehedingham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Have you had your flu vaccination yet?
People eligible for a free NHS flu vaccination are being encouraged to book their appointment if they have not yet done so, to help protect themselves ahead of winter.
Flu is much more than a heavy cold and can lead to serious illness, hospital treatment and, in some cases, can be life-threatening. Older people, pregnant women and those with certain long-term health conditions are at greater risk of becoming seriously unwell.
If you are eligible, you can book your vaccine through the NHS website or the NHS App, or alternatively most chemists offer this service for those not eligible.
It can take up to 14 days for the vaccine to provide full protection, so please book as soon as you can. www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/news/flu-vaccination-bookings-essex-2026/

https://siblehedingham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Keeping Warm this Winter: Help with Heating and Energy Bills
https://siblehedingham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Getting help and support with energy costs
If you’re finding it difficult to keep up with your energy bills, you’re not alone. There are organisations that can offer advice, practical support and help you access financial assistance.
Here are a few examples:
Winter Fuel Payment – eligible households can receive a one-off payment of between £250 and £600 to help with energy costs during the winter months.
Essex County Council’s Energy and Fuel Support services , which can help residents find available grants and support schemes.
The Warm Home Discount Scheme , which may provide eligible households with a reduction on their electricity bill.
Your energy supplier , as many providers offer hardship funds, payment plans and additional support for vulnerable customers.
Green Doctor Service – this scheme is delivered by Groundwork East and is a free service offering personalised energy-saving advice, practical support, referrals to additional assistance and free energy-saving measures where available.
Don’t wait until bills become unmanageable, and seeking advice early can help you access support and reduce financial pressure.
www.braintree.gov.uk/advice-environment/energy-efficient-homes/2
There are lots of simple ways to reduce energy use and often small changes can add up to make a noticeable difference to your energy bills.
Save energy by reducing your bills
You could try:
Turning thermostats down by just 1°C, which can help reduce heating costs.
Only heating the rooms you use most often.
Switching lights off when leaving a room.
Unplugging appliances that are left on standby.
Using draught excluders around doors and windows.
Closing curtains at dusk to keep heat indoors.
Avoiding blocking radiators with furniture or curtains.
These simple habits can help keep your home warmer while reducing energy consumption.
Keeping your home warm for less
Making a few changes to your home can help reduce heat loss, lower energy bills and make your home more comfortable during the colder months.
Here are some ideas which might work for you:
Improve loft insulation – this can significantly reduce heat escaping through the roof.
Install cavity wall insulation where suitable.
Draught-proof doors, windows and letterboxes – this will prevent cold air entering the home.
Upgrade old boilers or heating systems to more efficient models.
Install smart heating controls – this may help you manage energy use better.
Switch to energy-efficient lighting and appliances – this will help to reduce overall energy costs.
Some households may also qualify for grants or free energy-saving improvements through local and national schemes
www.braintree.gov.uk/advice-environment/energy-efficient-homes/3
Find a local Warm Space and save on energy bills
With colder weather arriving and many households feeling the pressure of rising energy costs, Warm Spaces continue to provide welcoming places where residents can keep warm, meet others and access support within their local community.
As well as offering a warm environment, many venues provide refreshments, opportunities to socialise and information about services and activities available in the area.
There are a range of venues available to suit different needs and locations, so take a look at the directory below for a warm space near you.

Community Lottery marks 2 successful years
The Epping Forest Community Lottery has marked its 2nd anniversary, celebrating another successful year of supporting local good causes across the district.
Representatives from local organisations came together on 12 October to celebrate 2 years of the lottery, which was launched on 3 August 2024 to help community groups, charities and voluntary organisations raise vital funds. All proceeds received through the lottery’s central fund are reinvested into the local community.
Since the first draw in August 2024, the central fund has grown significantly, enabling £8,450 in grants and bonus awards to be distributed to local organisations on top of the regular funding received by participating good causes each month.
The funding is supporting a wide range of projects, from youth activities and community groups tackling isolation to family support services, digital inclusion programmes and opportunities for local athletes.

How residents use Community Transport services.
Levels of awareness of services available locally.
User experiences and satisfaction.
Barriers to accessing services.
Unmet transport needs.
The wider impact Community Transport has on independence and wellbeing.

Calling the children of Stock!
Come and decorate the Village Christmas Tree at the 2026 Stock Christmas Fayre and you could win a prize from Santa!
The 2026 Christmas Fayre will take place on Saturday 5 December between 12noon and 6pm, organised by Stock Parish Council and supported by Stock Cricket Club.
This year, we are inviting the children of Stock to create your own Christmas decoration, with a loop to hang it by, to hang on the Village Christmas Tree.
Write you name, age and contact number on a slip of paper or card and attach it too, and Santa will judge all the decorations and award prizes to the best in all age ranges!
You can collect your decoration at the end of the Fayre to hang on your own tree at home, too.
With cold and wet weather affecting the event in recent years, the 2026 Fayre will be held undercover in three marquees on the Common.
The Christmas Fayre will feature 20 arts and craft and 10 food and drink stalls run by villagers and local businesses, and children’s activities, with an emphasis on it being an occasion for all the family.
Father Christmas will be visiting, carol singers and live musicians will be performing, while Stock Cricket Club bar will be open to serve drinks and snacks.
If you are interested in finding out more, please email info@stock-pc.gov.uk

https://stock-pc.gov.uk/?feed=rss2.text:
Stock Parish Council held its latest monthly meeting on Monday 9 November at which a wide range of important issues regarding the village were discussed and voted upon.
Mill Lane Sports & Leisure Facility
The £500,000 goal for the purchase of the former football ground in Mill Lane has nearly been met.
Stock Parish Council has, to date, received promissory notes totalling £489,419.00 and we would like to thank all of those parishioners who have made donations.
Would those who haven’t as yet contributed to the fund please consider a donation by way of a promissory note.
Stock Parish Council can then proceed with completion of the purchases of the plots and start planning the development of the sports and leisure facility.
The charity has been set up as STOCK FOOTBALL AND LEISURE GROUND – CIO. The registered charity number is 1219741.
Stock Parish Council is waiting for the opening of the bank account for the charity so that all donations being paid into this account will qualify for Gift Aid. This increases each donation by 25%.
Christmas Fayre
Stock’s biggest-ever Christmas Fayre will take place on Stock Common on Saturday 5 December between 12noon and 6pm . To protect visitors from the winter weather, this year’s event will be held under-cover!
Marquees will host Santa’s Grotto, children’s entertainment, live music, arts and crafts stalls and hot and cold food refreshments, while Stock Cricket Club will serve drinks from the pavilion bar.
S-Type Security
Villagers are reminded that Stock Parish Council employs S-Type Security to provide regular mobile patrols in and around Stock.
S-Type Security provide a presence to deter criminal and antisocial activity in the village and rapid response officers to answer villagers’ calls and alerts.
If you are aware of any potential criminal and antisocial behaviour, please report it to S-Type Security by phone on 01245 931598 or email at info@s-typesecurity.co.uk
Parking
Stock Parish Council is committed to improving road safety across the village for all users.
In 2025, the Parish Council withdrew an application for parking restrictions following feedback from stakeholders.
However, it is still strongly felt that a number of very dangerous junctions would be made safer by the introduction of parking restrictions.
As such, the Parish Council intends to discuss the issue with residents and business owners at a public meeting before any agreed proposals are submitted to the South Essex Parking Partnership (SEPP) in the New Year.
Speeding
Stock Parish Council was disappointed to be informed that the Essex County Council Local Highways Panel (LHP) has been abolished by the new administration.
This means the LHP applications submitted and pursued by the Parish Council since 2023 are now obsolete.
These applications covered reductions in speed limits on Stock Road, Downham Road and minor roads, improvements and upgrades to pedestrian crossings, moving the bus stop on Stock Hill and the potential installation of average speed cameras in the High Street.
Essex Highways have suggested that a number of the above could go ahead if they are self-funded, and the Parish Council is now awaiting a response from the Essex County Council Cabinet Member for Highways and Infrastructure, Councillor Mark Webster.
In the meantime, the Parish Council continues to hold regular Community Speedwatch patrols.
Maintenance
The Parish Council has commissioned and completed a host of works across the village.
A number of serious pot holes have been repaired in the High Street, the ponds in Mill Road and Austen Drive have been cleared and the four timber village noticeboards have been refurbished.
Councillors have commissioned a survey of the children’s playground on the Common with a view to improving the facilities.
The Parish Council will hold its final monthly meeting of the year at Stock Cricket Club pavilion on Monday 7 December 2026 at 7.30pm . All are welcome.

https://stock-pc.gov.uk/?feed=rss2.title: Stock Parish Council Update
https://stock-pc.gov.uk/?feed=rss2.text:
Stock Parish Council held its monthly meeting at Stock Cricket Club pavilion on Tuesday 8 September.
Parish Councillors were joined by Essex County Councillor Mike Steel and Chelmsford City Councillors Gillian Bonnett and Roy Whitehead, who each gave a report regarding local authority matters and the recent withdrawal of plans to replace existing councils with unitary authorities.
New Parish Councillors Jo Charnley and Graham Kingston attended their first meeting, making up our allocated quota of nine Councillors following the departure of Sophie Clark resigned. Sophie had served the Parish Council for over ten years and made a major contribution. Councillors thank her for her service and wish her every success for the future.
The main topic of Parish Council discussion was the ongoing plans to purchase six plots that form the previous football ground in Mill Lane, which have been pursued by travellers to purchase.
Stock Parish Council has been appealing for donations by way of promissory notes to raise £500,000 for the purchase the six plots and return them for the use of sports and leisure.
Any surplus funds would go toward the construction of a sports pavilion on the site.
The purchases of the plots would be undertaken through a Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO), which has been set up, but waiting for registration.
The use of the site would be for football, cricket, padel, plus indoor leisure activities. This would be for perpetuity.
Should you wish to make a donation, a promissory note can be downloaded from the Stock Parish Council website. These notes have also been delivered on the reverse of leaflets which have been delivered to homes in the Parish.
A villagers-only meeting will be held at Stock Village Hall on Saturday 3 October between 11am and 1pm to provide residents with full details and an update on this project.
The Parish Council can also report that Essex Rangers have cleared all the footpaths in the Parish and other repairs are underway.
Six Memorial Trees have been planted. Residents can have a Memorial Tree planted for their loved ones at a cost of £500 which includes the choice of one of four species of tree, a plaque and ongoing care. Details can be found on the Stock Parish Council website.
Lastly, the 2026 Stock Christmas Fayre poster will be held on the Common on Saturday 5 December between 12noon and 6pm, supported by Stock Cricket Club.
This year, for the first time, the Fayre will be held under cover in three marquees, including one for children’s activities, Father Christmas and an entertainer, one for food and refreshments, and one for local crafts. There will also be a band entertaining villagers with live music.

https://ashingdonparishcouncil.gov.uk/fe.title: Rochford’s community decides Rochford’s future
https://ashingdonparishcouncil.gov.uk/fe.text:
Rochford’s community decides Rochford’s future
Home
This is an update on the Local Plan.
Rochford's community decides Rochford's future
The Government has directed Rochford District Council to begin the final pre-submission public consultation on its draft Local Plan on 7 December 2026.
The Minister of State for Housing and Planning, Matthew Pennycook MP, set out the intervention decision in a letter to the Leader of the Council, Cllr Adi Malviya, on 23 November 2026. According to the letter, the consultation must be on the 'option 1' version of the Plan presented to Full Council on 23 September 2026, before the changes agreed at that meeting.
The letter also directs that Rochford District Council:
Must not take any step to withdraw the Plan
Must report monthly to officials from the Ministry for Homes, Communities and Local Government on the Plan’s progress
Must progress the Plan to the end of the examination process
Can make minor modifications to the plan after the consultation, but any significant changes must be set out for consideration by the Secretary of State.
Cllr Adi Malviya, Leader of Rochford District Council, said, “Many people in our district feel strongly about the Local Plan. We are considering next steps in how we respond to this letter from the Government and will update residents in the coming days.”
Read more about the Local Plan at www.rochford.gov.uk/newlocalplan

NEW UNITARY AUTHORITIES ANNOUNCED
Home
The government has announced its decision on Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) in Greater Essex, confirming the county will move to five new unitary councils, subject to parliamentary approval.   The creation of five unitary councils -    West Essex Council
North East Essex Council
Mid Essex Council
South West Essex Council
South East Essex Council
means that from April 2028, these unitary authorities will replace the current 15 councils across Greater Essex, who will have responsibility for delivering all services in one area including waste collections, planning, adult social care, highways, children’s services and more.   The new unitary authorities will be:   Rochford
Castle Point
Southend-on-Sea
Brentwood
Chelmsford
Maldon
Epping Forest
Harlow
Uttlesford
Braintree
Colchester
Tendring
Basildon
Thurrock
LGR aims to simplify council structures by creating new, more streamlined local councils that work better, making it easier for residents to access and navigate services.   Government has also confirmed their commitment to repayment in-principle of £200m of Thurrock Council debt.   Elections for the new shadow unitary authorities in Greater Essex are scheduled for May 2027, with new authorities expected to become operational in April 2028.   The latest updates and information about local government reorganisation in Greater Essex is available on the Essex LGR hub website   https://www.essexlgrhub.org/ stronger-greater-essex

https://hawkwellparishcouncil.gov.uk/fee.title: Minor Injuries Move – Orsett Hospital to Thurrock
https://hawkwellparishcouncil.gov.uk/fee.text:
A Minor Injuries Unit (MIU) supporting patients across Thurrock, Basildon, Brentwood, south east Essex and surrounding areas will move from Orsett Hospital to Thurrock Community Hospital from Monday 2 November 2026.
The Minor Injuries Unit, run by North East London NHS Foundation Trust (NELFT), will move to upgraded premises at Thurrock Community Hospital in Grays.
The MIU at Orsett Hospital will close permanently from 12noon on Friday 30 October . If you need minor injury support from then until the Thurrock Community Hospital MIU opens at 10am, Monday 2 November:
Contact NHS111 by phone or online 111.nhs.uk
Visit Basildon Hospital A&E, Basildon Road, Basildon
NHS Essex has secured nearly £1 million of national funding to support the move and improvements to the John Tallack Centre at Thurrock Community Hospital, where the MIU will be based. Being located alongside the Community Diagnostic Centre (CDC), will help people access faster diagnosis and treatment.
From its new location, the MIU will continue to provide the same seven-day walk-in service between 10am and 7.30pm for minor injuries such as wounds, bumps, sprains, broken bones, minor eye injuries and minor burns. It will be provided by the same staff who currently provide the MIU at Orsett Hospital.
As well as more streamlined patient care, the upgraded MIU will offer a better environment for patients and staff. A larger waiting area will provide space for patients to sit indoors after booking in, improving the overall experience.
NHS Essex is working with Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT), which operates the Thurrock Community Hospital site, to ensure adequate parking, access and signage for patients and staff.
NHS Essex aims build on the upgraded service by developing it into an Urgent Treatment Centre from April 2027. This would expand the service to include minor illnesses as well as minor injuries, with longer opening hours.
For more details, including getting to Thurrock Community Hospital, go to the NHS Essex website: Minor Injuries Service moving to Thurrock Community Hospital – NHS Essex Integrated Care Board

From Monday 16 th March, users of the bridlepath in Magnolia Nature Reserve may see some ground works going ahead. These works will be carried out by Essex County Council (ECC) Highways and they will re-route part of the existing bridlepath through the Reserve. These works are necessary due to heightened badger activity along this stretch of the bridlepath, where now some of the path is no longer fit for use. (The badgers have been extremely busy digging away in their setts!) As many are aware, badgers are protected by law and so ECC and HPC are working to both protect the badgers’ home and allow a better, more secure route for all users of the bridlepath.
Especially during these works, please can users remember to keep their dogs on leads in the Nature Reserve.
HPC and ECC apologise for any inconvenience this work may cause.
If anybody would like any more information, or has any questions during works, please do get in touch with the office and/or ECC Highways Officer, Roy Read on 07545 756009 or roy.read@essexhighways.org

https://hawkwellparishcouncil.gov.uk/fee.text:
Neighbourhood Plan Feasibility Working Group – FURTHER UPDATE
Hawkwell Parish Council agreed to undertake a feasibility study into a Neighbourhood Plan in July. Since then, it has called for community volunteers to join the Working Group. The Terms of Reference (ToR) for the Neighbourhood Plan Feasibility Working Group (NPFWG) have been agreed and can be found by clicking on the link at the bottom of this page.
It is important to emphasise that Neighbourhood Plans are community led. Currently, there are still insufficient numbers of community volunteers to enable it to get up and running. Eight community volunteers are required; to date Council has five volunteers. Therefore, Council needs at least three more residents to come forward before it can kick off this important project.
The work undertaken by the NPFWG is key, see the ToR for detail. The group expect to meet weekly for an hour; members will need to undertake research (potentially for a minimum of 2 hours per week) and bring back findings to the group. The initial due-diligence scoping exercise is estimated to take 2-4 months.
It is expected members of the NPFWG will also be prepared to form part of a future Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group, should Council proceed with a Neighbourhood Plan. If a Neighbourhood Plan does go ahead, then the commitment from the Steering Group members, together with the wider community, will likely need to extend beyond two years.
No particular skills are required to join the NPFWG. However, volunteers will need to have a high level of passion, commitment, teamwork and resilience.
Council has agreed a final deadline for residents to volunteer their services of 31st December 2025. Please get in touch by contacting the Parish Clerk on info@hawkwellparishcouncil.gov.uk
