https://hawkwellparishcouncil.gov.uk/fee.title: Neighbourhood Plan Feasibility Working Group (NPFWG) – Update
https://hawkwellparishcouncil.gov.uk/fee.text:
Following residents’ demand for a Parish Poll asking that Hawkwell Parish Council undertake a Neighbourhood Plan, the result was that over 700 (7.8%) of Hawkwell residents voted ‘yes’.  Council have since agreed to undertake a feasibility study, in the first instance.  At its recent Full Council meeting, Hawkwell Parish Council set out the Terms of Reference (ToR) for the Neighbourhood Plan Feasibility Working Group (NPFWG).
It is important to emphasise that Neighbourhood Plans are community led.  Currently, there are sufficient Councillors willing to join the NPFWG, but there are insufficient numbers of community volunteers to enable it to get up and running.  Eight community volunteers are required; to date, Council has two volunteers, with two more expressing interest.  Therefore, Council needs at least four more residents before it can kick off this important project.
The work undertaken by the NPFWG is key:  the group aim expect to meet weekly for an hour; members will need to undertake research (potentially for a minimum of 2 hours per week) and bring back findings to the group.  The initial due-diligence scoping exercise is estimated to take 2-4 months.  It is expected members of the NPFWG will also be prepared to form part of a future Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group, should Council proceed with a Neighbourhood Plan.  If a Neighbourhood Plan does go ahead, then the commitment from the Steering Group members, together with the wider community, will likely need to extend beyond two years.
No particular skills are required to join the NPFWG.  However, volunteers will need to have a high level of passion, commitment, teamwork and resilience.
If you are able to support these efforts, please get in touch by 26 th September 2025 .    Contact the Parish Clerk on info@hawkwellparishcouncil.gov.uk

https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.title: New national rules change how planning applications are decided
https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.text:
New Government rules governing who decides planning applications are now in force  across the country following the introduction of the National Scheme of Delegation on 31 October 2026 of the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 and the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026.
The scheme of delegation replaces some of the locally determined arrangements with national rules setting out which applications must be decided by planning officers and which may be referred to a planning committee. The Council is required to follow these rules.
Many routine applications must now be determined by officers. Other applications may be considered by a committee where the national referral requirements are met and the nominated officer and councillor agree.
Councillors can no longer require a planning application to go to committee through the previous local call-in arrangements. Additionally, the number of objections to a planning application received does not automatically trigger a committee hearing.
The new scheme of delegation changes ‘who’ makes the decision, not whether an application should be approved or not. Residents can still submit comments, and relevant planning concerns must still be considered. Each application must be assessed against the development plan, national planning policy and other material considerations, including its possible harm.
At its meeting on 22 October 2026, the Council agreed arrangements to implement the national scheme of delegation but also decided to increase public speaking time for concerned residents to five minutes for applications considered by committee. This gives residents more time to explain any planning concerns directly to councillors.
Cllr Simon Morgan, Leader of Maldon District Council said: “I recognise that residents want to understand how these changes affect planning decisions in their area. While the Council must follow the new national rules on who decides applications, residents can still comment and relevant planning concerns must be considered.
“The changes do not alter the planning policies against which applications are assessed. For applications considered by committee, increasing public speaking time to five minutes gives residents more time to explain their concerns directly to the committee”

https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.title: National housing policies limit Council’s scope to refuse village developments
https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.text:
Maldon District Council is explaining why national housing requirements and planning policies can mean developments are approved despite strong local objections, following concerns about decisions affecting Tollesbury, Great Totham and Latchingdon.
Changes to the Government’s housing calculation in December 2024 increased the district’s annual housing need figure from 310 to 586 homes per year. The Council has written to the Government to raise concerns about the implications for rural districts made up predominantly of small villages.
Planning decisions must be made in accordance with the development plan unless material considerations indicate otherwise. The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) is an important material consideration. Its revised policies, published in August 2026, introduces a more supportive approach to certain forms of housing development outside settlements where there is evidenced unmet need, subject to requirements including the site’s relationship to an existing settlement and whether infrastructure can accommodate the development.
This means that being outside a village’s settlement boundary, or attracting substantial opposition, is not in itself sufficient reason to refuse an application. Where national policy supports a proposal and the evidence does not justify refusal, the Council may have little scope to withhold permission. This is not a requirement to approve every application: the relevant policy tests, environmental protections and site-specific evidence still apply.
Cllr Simon Morgan, Leader of Maldon District Council, said: “I recognise the strength of feeling about recent planning decisions in Tollesbury, Great Totham and Latchingdon. Residents are understandably concerned about the impact of new homes on roads, schools, healthcare and the character of their villages.
“The Council does not set the national housing calculation or national planning policy. We must assess applications within that framework, even where the outcome is not what residents want. We cannot refuse an application simply because it is unpopular: any reasons for refusal must be supported by sound planning evidence.”
The Council considers evidence about infrastructure and local services, including consultee advice from Essex County Council on highways and education and from NHS bodies on healthcare. Where consultees raise no objection, or identify measures that would address a development’s impacts, a refusal on those grounds would need clear supporting evidence. Applicants can appeal against a refusal, and unreasonable decision-making can result in an award of costs against the Council.
Cllr Morgan added: “An approval does not mean residents’ concerns have been ignored. It means the Council has assessed the proposal against the relevant policies and evidence and concluded that permission should be granted. Your views remain an important part of that assessment, and every application must be considered on its own merits.”

https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.title: Dengie Peninsula Energy Park
https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.text:
Maldon District Council has been asked to comment on what environmental studies are needed for the proposed Dengie Peninsula Energy Park.
Low Carbon is developing plans for a large solar park with battery storage near Bradwell-on-Sea, Dengie and Burnham-on-Crouch. The plans also include the equipment and connections needed to supply electricity to the National Grid.
This early consultation is not a planning application, but is part of the pre-application process,  it asks what environmental studies should be included with any future planning application. These studies form an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). It is not a consultation on whether the park should go ahead, and it does not give permission to build it.
Cllr Simon Morgan, Leader of Maldon District Council, said: “Because of its size, any planning application that comes forward would be considered through the national planning process by Government and the Secretary of State, rather than decided by Maldon District Council.
“The Council would still have an important role: giving planning and technical advice, identifying how the project could affect the local area and representing our communities throughout the process.
“It would be the Planning Inspectorate who would examine any future application for permission to build the park. The Secretary of State would make the final decision, not Maldon District Council .”
The proposed park could generate up to 1 gigawatt (1,000MW) of electricity. The developer estimates it could produce enough electricity to power around 250,000 homes.
More information about the plans is available on the developer’s Dengie Peninsula Energy Park website .
What this consultation covers
Low Carbon has asked the Planning Inspectorate to agree which environmental issues need to be studied. This is called an EIA Scoping Request. The Planning Inspectorate is now asking for comments on what those studies should cover.
This stage is about what needs to be investigated, not whether the project should go ahead. It helps identify possible environmental impacts and local concerns early on.
The studies would look at changes to the landscape and views, effects on wildlife and habitats, loss of farmland, and traffic when the park is built and later taken down. They would also consider how power lines and other grid connections would look. Noise, effects on aircraft and sunlight reflected from solar panels may also need to be studied. Listing these issues does not decide how important they would be when an application is considered.
The Council must send its comments to the Planning Inspectorate by 24 November 2026. The consultation documents are available on the Planning Inspectorate’s project documents page.
Next steps
Council officers are reviewing the documents and preparing a response. They will check whether the planned environmental studies cover the issues that matter to the District.
Discussions with Essex County Council will help both councils agree how to work together and make the best use of their expertise.
The developer has said it plans a separate, wider public consultation in early 2027. Residents, councillors and others with an interest would have another chance to comment before a formal application for permission, called a Development Consent Order, is submitted.

https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.title: New Livewell Grants to Support Healthier Communities in the Maldon District
https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.text:
Local organisations with ideas to improve health and wellbeing are being encouraged to apply for funding through the Maldon District Livewell Partnership small grants programme.
The programme brings together Public Health grants and Active Maldon grants, providing funding for projects that can make a positive difference to the health and wellbeing of residents across the Maldon District.
Public Health funding is available for projects that address at least two of three local health priorities: physical activity and obesity, social isolation, and mental health. Projects should be new and innovative, although previously run activities may be considered where applicants can show their success and explain how further funding would build on it.
Through the Public Health grant, eligible organisations can apply for up to £2,000 per project, with no minimum grant amount. Applications are open to a range of UK-registered organisations, including voluntary and community organisations, Charitable Incorporated Organisations, not-for-profit companies limited by guarantee, Community Interest Companies, educational settings, and statutory bodies.
Cllr Simon Morgan, Leader of Maldon District Council, said: “We know there are organisations across the Maldon District with great ideas for helping people live healthier, happier and more connected lives.
“These small grants can help turn those ideas into action, whether that means encouraging people to be more active, helping people make new connections or supporting better mental health and wellbeing.
“I’d encourage local organisations with an idea that could make a difference to take a look at the guidance and see what support may be available.”
The grants form part of the work of the Maldon Livewell Partnership Board, which brings together delivery partners to help address the health and wellbeing priorities of residents across the district.
There are different requirements for the Public Health and Active Maldon funding streams, so applicants should read the relevant guidance before applying.
Applications are open until 14 December 2026.
Funding is limited and the programme will remain open while funding is available.
For more information about the grants, eligibility and how to apply, visit https://www.maldon.gov.uk/livewellgrants .

https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.title: Major changes coming to Maldon District Council car parks this November
https://southminsterparishcouncil.gov.uk.text:
Maldon District Council is modernising its parking machines and going paperless in its car parks this November, with 12 new payment machines being installed in Maldon’s town centre and Promenade Park. The work will take place during November and is due to be completed by 20 November. The new machines will accept contactless payments only and will not print a paper ticket.
Drivers will need to enter their registration number when paying to park, and an email payment receipt can be requested on the machines.
RingGo will remain available in all council car parks, giving people the option to pay using the app. The Council Offices Car Park and Promenade Park Coach Park will move to RingGo-only payments due to low levels of payment machine use at these locations.
RingGo was first introduced to Maldon car parks in 2018 and has grown steadily in popularity since. It is now used for 63% of parking sessions at Promenade Park and 30% in town centre car parks. As more people choose to pay using RingGo, the Council has taken the decision to reduce the number of payment machines in its car parks.
Moving to paperless parking will help the Council run its car parks more cost-effectively, reduce administration and machine maintenance demands, cut its carbon footprint by removing the need for paper tickets, as well as making it easier for residents and visitors.
Cllr Simon Morgan, Leader of Maldon District Council, said: “More people are choosing digital ways to pay for many things these days including parking, so we’re updating our car parks to reflect how people are using them today.
“The new machines will make paying simple, while going paperless will help us cut waste, reduce maintenance, and run our car parks more efficiently. We know changes like this can take a little getting used to, so we’ll make sure clear information, and guidance is available to help people.”
The Council will be sharing more information about the changes on their social media channels and putting up signs in the car parks to help people understand the new system. For more information, including frequently asked questions, visit https://www.maldon.gov.uk/paperlessparking .

https://wethersfield-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Essex County Fire and Rescue Service Article
https://wethersfield-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Be ready for whatever the weather brings.
There’s been plenty of conversation recently about being prepared for emergencies, with the Government’s new Be Ready campaign encouraging households to think about how they would cope if everyday services were disrupted for a few days.
But what does being prepared actually look like, particularly if you live in a rural community?
At Essex County Fire and Rescue Service (ECFRS), we know that living in the countryside can bring its own challenges when extreme weather strikes. From flooding and storms to prolonged dry spells and wildfires, severe weather can affect our homes, roads and the services we rely on.
We want to encourage residents to take a few simple steps to help keep themselves, their homes and their neighbours safe.
A few things you can do today:
Think ahead: Keep a torch, spare batteries, a charged power bank, essential medication and some long-life food and bottled water at home in case of a power cut or disruption to supplies.
Know your local risks: Check whether your property or nearby roads are prone to flooding. Think about alternative routes if roads become impassable.
Reduce fire risks: During dry weather, keep grass and vegetation around your property under control. Take extra care with barbecues and never leave them unattended.
Prepare for storms: Check gutters, drains, fences and roof tiles, and secure garden furniture and other items that could be blown around in strong winds.
Look out for neighbours: If you live in a more isolated location, agree how you could check in on elderly or vulnerable neighbours if bad weather affects power, phone signal or road access.
A little preparation goes a long way
Being prepared doesn’t mean expecting the worst or buying lots of extra equipment. It’s about thinking ahead, knowing what to do and looking out for one another.
Rural communities are often well placed to support each other, and a little local knowledge and preparation can make a real difference when an emergency happens.
For more advice on staying safe in rural areas, visit www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rural .

Regulation 19 – Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012.
The Submission Draft Local Plan represents the final version of the Plan that Braintree District Council intends to submit to the Secretary of State for independent examination. It sets out the vision, strategy, site allocations and development management policies to guide development in the Braintree district to 2043.
How to View the Consultation Documents:

Braintree District Council Offices, Causeway House, Bocking End, Braintree (during usual working hours)
Public libraries across the District (during usual working hours)

• Legally compliant, and
• Sound (i.e. positively prepared, justified, effective, and consistent with national policy)
Guidance is available on what makes a Local Plan ‘sound’ or ‘unsound’.
Consultation responses are strongly encouraged directly via the Councils online consultation system.
Online: www.braintree.gov.uk/localplanreg19
For those unable to respond online:
A response Form can be downloaded, completed and returned
Paper response forms are available at Braintree District Council Offices, Causeway House, Bocking End, Braintree and from public libraries.

Wednesday 23rd September to 5pm Friday 6th November 2026. Late responses will not be accepted.

Duly made representations received by 5pm on Friday 6th November 2026 will be submitted to the Secretary of State alongside the Local Plan for independent examination.

A summary leaflet to accompany the consultation is available.  Government guidance requires that sound evidence is required to support a Local Plan. Our Evidence Base Documents can be found on the Council’s website.

https://kelvedonhatch-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: The MIU at Orsett Hospital – information about closure
https://kelvedonhatch-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
A Minor Injuries Unit (MIU) supporting patients across Thurrock, Basildon, Brentwood, south east Essex and surrounding areas will move from Orsett Hospital to Thurrock Community Hospital from Monday 2 November 2026.
The Minor Injuries Unit, run by North East London NHS Foundation Trust (NELFT), will move to upgraded premises at Thurrock Community Hospital in Grays.
The MIU at Orsett Hospital will close permanently from 12noon on Friday 30 October . If you need minor injury support from then until the Thurrock Community Hospital MIU opens at 10am, Monday 2 November:
Contact NHS111 by phone or online 111.nhs.uk
Visit Basildon Hospital A&E, Basildon Road, Basildon
NHS Essex has secured nearly £1 million of national funding to support the move and improvements to the John Tallack Centre at Thurrock Community Hospital, where the MIU will be based. Being located alongside the Community Diagnostic Centre (CDC), will help people access faster diagnosis and treatment.
From its new location, the MIU will continue to provide the same seven-day walk-in service between 10am and 7.30pm for minor injuries such as wounds, bumps, sprains, broken bones, minor eye injuries and minor burns. It will be provided by the same staff who currently provide the MIU at Orsett Hospital.
As well as more streamlined patient care, the upgraded MIU will offer a better environment for patients and staff. A larger waiting area will provide space for patients to sit indoors after booking in, improving the overall experience.
NHS Essex is working with Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT), which operates the Thurrock Community Hospital site, to ensure adequate parking, access and signage for patients and staff.
NHS Essex aims build on the upgraded service by developing it into an Urgent Treatment Centre from April 2027. This would expand the service to include minor illnesses as well as minor injuries, with longer opening hours.
For more details, including getting to Thurrock Community Hospital, go to the NHS Essex website: Minor Injuries Service moving to Thurrock Community Hospital – NHS Essex Integrated Care Board

https://feeringparishcouncil.gov.uk/feed.title: Be ready for whatever the weather brings
https://feeringparishcouncil.gov.uk/feed.text:
There’s been plenty of conversation recently about being prepared for emergencies, with the Government’s new Be Ready campaign encouraging households to think about how they would cope if everyday services were disrupted for a few days.
But what does being prepared actually look like, particularly if you live in a rural community?
At Essex County Fire and Rescue Service (ECFRS), they know that living in the countryside can bring its own challenges when extreme weather strikes. From flooding and storms to prolonged dry spells and wildfires, severe weather can affect our homes, roads and the services we rely on.
Thy want to encourage residents to take a few simple steps to help keep themselves, their homes and their neighbours safe.
A few things you can do today:
Think ahead:  Keep a torch, spare batteries, a charged power bank, essential medication and some long-life food and bottled water at home in case of a power cut or disruption to supplies.
Know your local risks:  Check whether your property or nearby roads are prone to flooding. Think about alternative routes if roads become impassable.
Reduce fire risks:  During dry weather, keep grass and vegetation around your property under control. Take extra care with barbecues and never leave them unattended.
Prepare for storms:  Check gutters, drains, fences and roof tiles, and secure garden furniture and other items that could be blown around in strong winds.
Look out for neighbours:  If you live in a more isolated location, agree how you could check in on elderly or vulnerable neighbours if bad weather affects power, phone signal or road access.
A little preparation goes a long way
Being prepared doesn’t mean expecting the worst or buying lots of extra equipment. It’s about thinking ahead, knowing what to do and looking out for one another.
Rural communities are often well placed to support each other, and a little local knowledge and preparation can make a real difference when an emergency happens.
For more advice on staying safe in rural areas, visit www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rural .

https://feeringparishcouncil.gov.uk/feed.title: Diary of a Chair – From 10 November
https://feeringparishcouncil.gov.uk/feed.text:
You might be interested in what your Parish Councillors do, so we hope to fill you in on our activities from time to time. I have been very busy with one thing and another.  If you want more information about any of this, please contact the Clerk and she’ll help.
The Chair’s Fortnight From 10 November
Hello Everyone.
The weather has definitely turned Autumnal.  We have reminded our handyman/greenkeeper team to sweep paths where lots of leaves have fallen.  If you spot anywhere that needs attention, let us know.   10 Nov.  I went to the Rural Community Council for Essex (RCCE) offices, conveniently located at Threshelfords, and joined in a networking meeting on the subject of Community Led Housing.  As a result of our Housing Needs Survey last year, we know that there are local people looking to stay in the village, or move back here, but they can’t afford market rents or purchase prices.  As a direct result of that, the Parish Council has decided to investigate the exciting possibility of providing some houses specifically for people with a local connection.  At this meeting I was able to talk to providers and to groups who have already done this in their village.  This directly lead on to our meeting on 19 Nov (see below).
11 Nov.  Remembrance Day.  I was privileged to join in with many others from the village to remember those who have given their lives for the country in conflict since 1914.  As ever, the children from the school read out the names and laid crosses.  Afterwards, we hosted the Royal British Legion at the Community Centre for an informal get-together which was welcomed by all. 12 Nov.  The councillors, plus Lisa and Cathy got together to discuss Health and Safety management for the Parish and for the Community Centre.  This is one of those things that go on in the background to make sure that our employees and everyone using the Centre facilities are protected and supported.
15 Nov.  Indoor Boot Sale.  This is a fun fundraiser.  Lisa and Cathy had done all of the planning and arranging and then provided the teas and coffees.  Councillors Evans and Spencer and I staffed the FCC Bric-a-brac stall to raise money for the Community Centre.  There were 2 halls of stalls and people were enjoying selling and buying a whole range of items.
17 Nov.  Full Parish Council Meeting.  As ever, we discussed a range of topics related to the village, including replacing the rabbit fencing along the railway embankment, the Community Living Rooms and various planning applications affecting the village. 18 Nov.  Christmas Fayre planning meeting.  I play a very small part in this.  Cathy has organised stallholders, the singing group, the volunteer rota and a myriad of other things that have to be done to enable the event to run smoothly.  Much of the rest of the organisation is done by Lisa and our brilliant volunteers, Paula, Kathy, and Mark, whose legendary mulled wine always goes down a storm.  Councillors and their families are also key to making the day magical.
19 Nov.  Today the Councillors met Laura, the Rural Housing Enabler from RCCE together with a representative of a registered provider of rural housing to find out exactly what we have to do to meet the needs of local people for local housing.  Over 80% of respondents to our Housing Needs Survey approved of the idea of community housing in the village.  We are hoping to make this a reality.
Over the last fortnight, Councillors have been active all over the place.  I hope you’ll soon be able to read their news here too.  Watch this space!
Cllr Pamela Carlaw Councillor Feering Parish Council

https://feeringparishcouncil.gov.uk/feed.text:
Proud to Support Our Athletes
Feering Parish Council was approached by Stephanie Longmore, Club Administrator of Arena Karate for a grant to help send two amazingly talented athletes to Italy to complete in the 2026 Championships.
Feering Parish Council were thrilled to be able to support our local athletes Ben and Oliver and they WON!
Both Ben and Oliver had a fantastic competition in Italy, returning home with some brilliant results.
In a message to Lisa, The Feering Parish Clerk, Stephanie writes:
“Oliver, aged just 11, achieved an incredible milestone, becoming a WTKA World Champion after winning gold in Sanbon Kumite and Kumite Point. He also secured two silver medals:
Gold – Sanbon Kumite
Gold – Kumite Point
Silver – Traditional Korean Forms (Kata)
Silver – Open Traditional Forms (Kata)
Ben also had a fantastic competition, bringing home a silver medal in Sanbon Kumite . Competing on an international stage and representing Arena Karate and his country was a huge achievement in itself, and it was wonderful to see his hard work and commitment rewarded with a place on the podium. His contribution to the team and the experience of competing alongside the other squad members made the trip particularly special.
The wider Arena Karate squad also enjoyed an incredibly successful competition, bringing home an impressive collection of medals across a range of events. Every member of the team worked exceptionally hard to reach this stage, and it was wonderful to see their dedication and commitment rewarded on the international stage.
For Ben and Oliver, the opportunity to travel to Italy, compete internationally and represent Arena Karate and their country was an experience they will never forget. For Oliver in particular, returning home as a WTKA World Champion is an extraordinary achievement and something he should be incredibly proud of.
It took an enormous amount of fundraising and community support to get our team to Italy, and contributions such as yours made a genuine difference. Your generosity helped provide Ben and Oliver with an opportunity to compete internationally, gain invaluable experience and create memories that will last a lifetime.
We really cannot thank Feering Parish Council enough for believing in our athletes and helping make this opportunity possible. Your support meant a great deal to Ben and Oliver, their families and everyone at Arena Karate.
We are more than happy for you to share this news with the wider Parish Council and on your socials if you should wish.
Thank you once again for being part of their journey”
We at Feering Parish Council are very proud of you all!
Follow Arena Karate on Facebook for all of their latest updates

Updates to waste and recycling collection routes mean no printed calendar
Chelmsford City Council is updating its kerbside bin collection routes to help ensure residents continue to receive the best possible waste and recycling service as the city grows and more homes are added to existing collection rounds.
While this work is underway, the city council won’t be issuing printed recycling calendars. The new collection routes are currently being reviewed, with changes expected to be introduced in early 2027.
Around 10% of households may see a change to their collection day, although it is not yet known which addresses will be affected. There are no plans to change how often collections take place or what materials are collected. The only potential change is the collection day or round.
Residents can still check their collection days online at any time, ensuring they always have access to the most up-to-date information. Simply visit Chelmsford City Council’s bins and recycling page to view your collection schedule. Alternatively, download the free Loci app to receive collection reminders straight to your phone.

https://www.boreham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
New strategy aims to help eliminate road deaths in Essex
Residents are being invited to help shape a new strategy which aims to eliminate road deaths and make Essex a safer place for everyone.
In 2025, 60 people lost their lives on the county’s roads – the highest number since 2016. Almost half of the deaths were related to speed.
Essex County Council has now launched a public consultation on the new draft Essex Safer Speeds Strategy.
The strategy has been developed with the Safer Essex Roads Partnership, including Essex Police. It will help introduce safer speeds across Essex, with recommended speed limits decided based on how different streets are used.
The strategy is designed to be flexible and there will not be a blanket approach. Speed limits will instead be decided on a case-by-case basis, where there is demand for change by local communities.
Find out more and have your say before the consultation closes on Sunday 26 April 2026.
For more information about the strategy and to take part in the consultation, please visit:  https://consultations.essex.gov.uk/essex-highways/essex-safer-speeds-strategy

https://www.boreham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Beaulieu Park Station construction update
https://www.boreham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Weekend engineering work for the construction of Beaulieu Park station will continue this autumn to integrate the new transport hub for Chelmsford into the existing railway network.
Construction of the new Beaulieu Park station has been progressing well over the recent months. The new station building structure has been completed and topped off with a wooden laminated roof to provide a visually striking environment for passengers.
The main station footbridge was installed in May to connect the station building to the island platform and will have lifts installed to provide step free access. The platform structures have also been constructed with partial canopies to provide weather protection for future passengers.
Major work has also been taking place to upgrade the overhead wire electrification systems along the main line, install new track, update the signals, power systems, telecoms and ancillary systems that will support the new station once opened. This work will continue over the following autumn weekend dates which will affect rail services for Greater Anglia passengers:
Sunday 29 September: Buses replace trains between Witham/Southend Victoria and Newbury Park tube station & between Southminster and Wickford.
Sunday 6 October: Buses replace trains between Witham and Ingatestone.
Sunday 13 October: Buses replace trains between Witham and Ingatestone.
Sunday 3 November: Buses replace trains between Witham and Ingatestone.
The work focusses on getting the rail systems complete and in place by the time for the Christmas period when the signalling control centre at London Liverpool Street (LST) will be updated with the new three track layout and Beaulieu Park Station will be included on the signalling network.

Hello, and welcome to the October edition of our newsletter.
The last month has seen important developments in the future direction of regulation for both the rail and road sectors.
First, we saw the publication by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade of the independent review of the Office of Rail and Road led by Dr Richard Judge. The review recognises the value of our independence, expertise and unique role across economic and safety regulation. It also identifies opportunities to build on these strengths, many of which align with work already under way through our transformation programme.
Second, we saw the publication of the Highways (Financing) Bill which was laid in Parliament on 10 September. Once enacted this will enable us to take on the economic regulation for the Lower Thames Crossing (LTC) which will connect Kent and Essex through a tunnel beneath the River Thames.
With the importance of changes in the regulatory landscape – including for rail – I was delighted to speak at the Regulatory Policy Institute annual conference in Oxford earlier in September, sharing a panel with senior representatives from the rail freight sector and Network Rail.
As well as engaging with the regulatory and legislative changes afoot, we have also continued our important work of holding Network Rail to account. Just today, we have published reports on the economic and financial performance of Network Rail and on cost benchmarking .
Our analysis here shows how, despite above target efficiency performance, a number of factors have nevertheless led to overall cost increases. Network Rail delivered £614 million of efficiency improvements in the second year of CP7, covering April 2025 to March 2026, but inflationary pressures, maintenance of ageing assets and train performance issues placed additional pressure on Network Rail’s financial performance in the last year.
Another report featured this month is our 2026 open access monitoring report . This provides an update on open access passenger services, including an overview of new open access services and open access decisions; market outcomes since our 2025 report (such as punctuality, service growth and passenger experience); and a summary of what international market participants are saying.
And today we have published the conclusions of our work on rail investment . Originally commissioned by HM Treasury, this work has been a key focus for us as we seek to support investment and resilience in the rail sector.
We are delighted to have been able to bring forward improvements to the risk fee funds to support investors and improve service standards, while ensuring that risk is allocated appropriately and achieving value for money to enable further investment, ensuring the railway delivers the maximum economic benefit for the country.
Finally, yesterday we announced that ORR has appointed Paul Smith as our new Chief Executive . Paul brings extensive regulatory leadership experience spanning the UK's aviation, energy and payments sectors. We all look forward to welcoming Paul to ORR in January.
Following an open and fair competition, the ORR Board has appointed Paul Smith as our new Chief Executive. Paul brings extensive regulatory leadership experience spanning the UK's aviation, energy and payments sectors, as well as having senior roles in Australia, and joins ORR from Fingleton, the strategic regulatory and competition advisory firm. He will take up the role on 4 January 2027, with Feras Alshaker continuing as Interim Chief Executive until then. Read the full announcement .

Welcome to the September edition of ORR’s stakeholder newsletter.
A pressing focus for us as a regulator is ensuring a safer railway for passengers, workers and the general public. We were therefore deeply concerned by August’s derailments at Lewes and Wickford. Our thoughts are with those affected and we are investigating the circumstances of the incidents.
Such incidents are thankfully rare, but maintaining that record depends on continual vigilance, learning, and improvement. ORR's role is to ensure that investigations are thorough, that the industry's response is evidence-based, and that any lessons needed to manage future risks are identified and acted upon.
Alongside our investigative and regulatory work, ORR's legal team plays a vital role in protecting the public and supporting a railway and road network that works for everyone. Their expertise helps ensure that safety obligations are properly understood and enforced, that operators and infrastructure managers are held to account where necessary, and that regulatory decisions are fair, robust and capable of withstanding scrutiny.
Whether supporting prosecutions, advising on complex regulatory issues, or helping to shape the framework within which industry operates, our work is fundamental to achieving better outcomes for passengers, road users and freight customers.
That contribution was evident again in August when Network Rail was fined £1.2million after it pleaded guilty to an offence under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 following the collapse of a wall in September 2022 near Rugby station.
The boundary wall beside a car park at the station collapsed onto 81-year-old pedestrian Edward Hanlon, as he walked along the adjacent path. Although Network Rail owned the wall and remained responsible for its repair and maintenance, undocumented redevelopment of the station car park by a previous tenant led to the mistaken assumption that responsibility lay elsewhere.
ORR's investigation found that the wall had therefore been omitted from Network Rail's inspection regime. The organisation had failed to identify both the discrepancy in its boundary records or the wall's deteriorating condition. These failings meant the risk the wall posed to members of the public went unidentified. Mr Hanlon passed away in January 2025 from lymphoma. A statement from his daughter indicated he never fully recovered from his injuries.
We will continue to use the full range of our regulatory and legal powers where it is in the public interest to do so.
Through this work, and through our broader regulatory activities, we remain committed to protecting people while enabling safe, reliable and efficient rail and road systems that serve everyone.
We have pre-approved a new framework track access agreement between HS1 Limited (London St. Pancras Highspeed) and Virgin Trains, supporting economic growth and international travel.
Virgin Trains will be able to operate up to 20 daily return international services between London and Paris, and Brussels and Amsterdam from 1 October 2030 through to 31 December 2040.
Network Rail has been fined after a boundary wall it owned at Rugby railway station collapsed onto and seriously injured an 81-year-old member of public who was using the adjacent alleyway in September 2022.
Our detailed investigation and decision to prosecute followed Network Rail’s failure to inspect or maintain the wall after undocumented redevelopment work by a previous tenant led to a mistaken assumption over the station boundary. These failings led to the wall’s deteriorating condition going unidentified and the consequences that followed.

https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.title: Hartismere homes make the move to smart meters
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.source: Northumbrian Water Group releases (Essex & Suffolk Water)
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.text:
The milestone comes as Essex & Suffolk Water continues its smart metering programme across the area, helping customers use water more efficiently and protect local resources for the future.
Now, the water firm’s community engagement team is heading out across the area to meet customers face-to-face, answer any questions about the smart metering programme and share practical water-saving advice.
The team will be holding a series of local sessions at village halls and community spaces, many of them alongside the Rural Coffee Caravan, a free service that helps rurally isolated people in Suffolk access services and information.
Happening throughout November and December, customers will be able to drop in for a chat over a cup of tea or coffee, find out more about smart meters and pick up simple tips to help reduce water use at home.
Smart meters send readings to Essex & Suffolk Water automatically which customers can keep track of, helping them to understand how much water they use and highlighting changes in usage that could indicate a leak.
This can help households avoid wasting water and identify problems sooner, saving money on bills in the process.
Since the hosepipe ban began in August, households on a smart meter in Hartismere, have saved 64 litres of water per day – equivalent to about five large buckets full of water - helping to reduce demand on local water supplies.
Dominic Butcher, Head of Metering at Essex & Suffolk Water, said: "Most customers in Hartismere have already made the move to smart metering and we’re really grateful to customers for their support as the programme continues.
"For many people, seeing their water use can help them spot simple ways to save water, which is good for both the environment and their household budget too.
"We know some people still have questions about smart meters, so these community events are a great opportunity to come along, meet the team and find out more about metering and water-saving.”
Residents can meet the team at the following sessions:
All Saints Church, Rishangles Road, Thorndon, IP23 7JR
St James & St Nicholas Village Hall, St James Sth Elmham, IP19 0HP
Bedfield & Monk Soham Community Hub (Pavilion), Bedfield, IP13 7JE
Westhorpe Village Hall Church Road, Stowmarket, IP14 4SY

https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.title: Northumbrian Water Group achieves world first for customer service excellence
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.source: Northumbrian Water Group releases (Essex & Suffolk Water)
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.text:
The company, which operates in the North East as Northumbrian Water and in Essex and Suffolk as Essex & Suffolk Water, has been officially awarded the Service Excellence Kitemark™ by the British Standards Institution (BSI).
Recognising organisations that consistently put customers at the heart of everything they do, the independent assessment looked at how the company listens to customers, resolves problems and continually improves its services based on customer feedback.
It also considered the support it has available to customers who may need extra help, including through the company’s Priority Services Register and affordability schemes.
The achievement builds on Northumbrian Water Group’s existing BSI Kitemark™ for Inclusive Service, which it received in 2023 for its efforts supporting vulnerable customers across the region.
Northumbrian Water Group is now the first water company globally to hold both the Service Excellence and Inclusive Service Kitemarks™ together, and sees these external benchmarks as strong evidence of its ambition to provide world-class services to customers across its operating regions.
Together with its recently achieved Innovation Management Kitemark™, which measures practices for using innovation to deliver results for customers, communities, and environment, the latest certification means Northumbrian Water Group has also become the first organisation in the world, across any industry, to hold these three BSI Kitemarks™ at the same time.
The accreditations follow a strong track record in customer service, with Northumbrian Water Group ranking as the top performing water company in Ofwat's Customer Measure of Experience (C-MeX) for the past two years and recently being again named the most trusted water company in England and Wales.
Dawn Creighton, Head of Customer Strategy and Experience at Northumbrian Water Group, said: “Our customers are at the heart of everything we do, and we aim to deliver an unrivalled customer experience every single day, so this certification is something we're incredibly proud of.
"But it all starts with our people. We live and work in the communities we serve, and we all care about the services we provide because our customers are our friends, neighbours and family members too.
"We’re genuinely passionate about listening to our customers, understanding what's important to them and making sure it's as easy as possible for them to get the help and support they need.
"This achievement reflects the hard work and dedication of colleagues right across our business who go above and beyond every day to do the right thing for our customers."
The certifications recognise the company's commitment to delivering great customer service, making support accessible to all and continually improving the services it provides.
Shahm Barhom, Managing Director, Product Certification, BSI, said: "Putting customers first is more important than ever, and the Service Excellence Kitemark is a rigorous, independent benchmark for organisations that do this consistently well.
"Northumbrian Water Group's achievement in becoming the first water company in the world to gain this certification, and the first organisation globally to hold the Service Excellence, Inclusive Service and Innovation Management Kitemarks together, shows a genuine commitment to its customers and sets a strong example for the water sector."

https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.title: How much does it need to rain before the temporary use hosepipe ban is lifted?
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.source: Northumbrian Water Group releases (Essex & Suffolk Water)
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.text:
There is no specific amount of rainfall that would allow the temporary use hosepipe ban to be lifted. Decisions are based on a range of factors, including reservoir levels, river flows, groundwater levels, soil moisture and the wider environmental impact of drought.
In Essex and Suffolk, rainfall in July was just 3% of the long-term average, and only 34% in August. The Environment Agency is also monitoring soil moisture, which shows the ground is currently around 30% drier than normal.
After months of hot and dry weather, the ground is very dry and compacted, meaning rainfall cannot easily soak into the soil. Steady, damp and prolonged rainfall conditions allow water to slowly soak into the ground, replenishing soil moisture and groundwater.
This recovery process typically takes place over autumn and winter. As rivers and groundwater recover, reservoirs can also begin to replenish, helping build water supplies for the following year.
While the recent rainfall has been welcome, sustained periods of wetter weather will be needed before drought conditions ease and restrictions can be reviewed.
Kieran Ingram, Water Director, said: “ After a prolonged period of hot and dry weather, the ground, rivers and groundwater sources all need time to recover. Recent rainfall has helped, but much more is needed before we see a significant improvement in water resources.
"Nature will take time to recover, and while the recent rainfall is encouraging, we will need sustained wetter weather over the coming months before drought conditions ease and restrictions can be reviewed."
Drought recovery happens in stages. Rainfall first needs to restore moisture levels in the soil, which have been depleted by months of hot and dry weather. Once the ground has recovered, water can more easily reach rivers and groundwater sources to enable the recovery of reservoir levels and a return to more normal water resource conditions.
Customers can help protect water resources by using less water at home and in the garden.
To find out how you can help nature, visit our website and use our water saving calculator for hints and tips on how to bring down your water usage: Save Water | How to Help With Water Conservation

https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.title: Explaining the month’s water - July
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.source: Northumbrian Water Group releases (Essex & Suffolk Water)
https://www.nwg.co.uk/news-and-media/new.text:
At the end of last month, the Environment Agency declared a drought in more than half of the country, including in Essex and Suffolk where temporary use bans (hosepipe bans) were introduced.
On Monday 3 August, Essex & Suffolk Water introduced a temporary use ban, meaning that customers are being asked to use watering cans and buckets instead of hosepipes for watering plants and washing cars.
Each month, the water company release an infographic packed with statistics to demonstrate to customers what local water supply looks like.
The data from Essex & Suffolk Water shows that there was just 2mm of rain during the month, causing reservoir levels to drop by 18%.
It showed that the highest day for water demand was Thursday 9 July, when 596 million litres of water were used, the equivalent of 238 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
The statistics also showed that a total of 4,158 leaky pipes have been fixed since 1 January 2026, with 625 of these being repaired in July.
By keeping customers updated on the monthly information, customers will be able to see how water-saving efforts across the operating areas can impact reservoir levels. The data is available across social media and on the Essex & Suffolk Water website.
Katie Davis, Head of Water Service Planning, said: “By sharing these four key statistics, we want to give our customers a clear view of the factors affecting water resources across our region.
“There is a close relationship between rainfall, the amount of raw water available in our reservoirs and groundwater sources, and overall demand for water, including leakage and customer use.
“Making this information available helps customers see how conditions are changing and the part we can all play in using water wisely.”
Customers can see the infographic, here; Water Resources .
For more information about the temporary use ban, visit our website: Temporary Use Ban .

After months of dry weather and three successive heatwaves, Suffolk has experienced temperatures of up to 31°C in recent days and received just 0.3mm of rainfall since 1 July.
The hot weather has had a significant impact on demand for water, with an extra seven million litres needed per day in Suffolk since Wednesday 1 July.
That’s the equivalent of supplying a town the size of Lowestoft, on top of our normal supply areas.
While a temporary usage ban, often referred to as a hosepipe ban, is not currently being introduced, Essex & Suffolk Water is closely monitoring water resources and preparing for all eventualities.

"We're asking customers to help by using water wisely wherever possible. Small changes can make a big difference and could help reduce the likelihood of restrictions being needed later in the summer.
"We're continuing to tackle leaks and bursts and are doing everything we can to manage supplies, but we also need customers' help.
“If a temporary water use ban becomes necessary, we’ll work closely with local communities to provide the right support. But by making wise choices now, our customers can help lower the risk of such restrictions being needed.”

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Funding to help prevent workplace sexual harassment
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) have secured almost £250,000 in Government funding to accelerate the development of a pioneering digital platform designed to help organisations prevent sexual harassment and sexual assault in the workplace before serious incidents occur.
The Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Auditing Service (SASHAS) has received UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) Proof of Concept funding to support its transition from a validated research prototype into a market-ready tool for organisations in the UK and internationally.
Developed by Professor Matt Fossey and Dr Ashley Perry at ARU, SASHAS is a comprehensive digital intelligence platform designed to measure and monitor workplace sexual harassment and sexual assault. It captures employee experiences and perceptions and transforms them into actionable insights through advanced analytics and real-time data visualisation.
By providing metrics at organisational, departmental, and team levels, SASHAS analyses data to identify where inappropriate behaviours are occurring and, crucially, highlights emerging risk areas before they escalate into more serious incidents.
Traditional reporting systems often rely on formal complaints being made after harm has already occurred. Instead, SASHAS is designed to help organisations recognise cultural vulnerabilities and warning signs earlier, allowing leaders to take preventative action and strengthen safeguarding measures.
The project comes amid heightened national attention on workplace culture. Research suggests that many incidents continue to go unreported because victims fear negative consequences or lack confidence in reporting processes.
SASHAS emerged from a NATO research programme examining sexual misconduct across militaries, where estimates suggest that military sexual trauma can affect over 20% of serving personnel. Researchers identified a need for tools capable of assessing not only incidents of misconduct, but also the organisational conditions that can allow harmful behaviours to occur and remain hidden.
Having been rigorously tested and piloted across multiple organisations, the platform is now entering its next phase of development. The new funding will support enhanced analytics, expanded user testing, readying for procurement and the development of sustainable commercial pathways for wider adoption.
“Sexual harassment and sexual assault are often understood through formal reports and investigations, but these only represent a fraction of what people experience. Organisations need better ways of understanding workplace culture, barriers to reporting, and emerging risks before harm escalates. SASHAS has been designed to provide that insight, helping organisations move from reactive responses towards prevention.”
“We are incredibly pleased that UKRI has recognised the potential of this work. SASHAS has emerged from years of research into organisational culture, safeguarding, and wellbeing. This funding will help us transform a validated research innovation into a practical tool that can support organisations, improve workplace safety, and strengthen trust in institutions.”
The research has been led by ARU’s Veterans and Families Institute for Military Social Research (VFI) in collaboration with the International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute (IPPPRI) and the Centre of Excellence for Equity in Uniformed Public Services (CEEUPS) .

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Can NAD+ supplements help us age more healthily?
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
By Justin Roberts , Anglia Ruskin University
Anti-ageing supplements are everywhere, from advertising campaigns to social media feeds. Promising everything from increased energy to a longer life, they come in many forms, from powders containing multiple ingredients to single-nutrient capsules.
One molecule in particular, NAD+ , has attracted growing interest, with claims it can boost energy, improve vitality, slow ageing and even help us live longer.
But does the science support these claims? And can NAD+ supplements really help us age more healthily?
NAD+ (short for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is found in every cell in our bodies. It plays an essential role in helping our cells turn food into energy . Without it, many of the processes that keep us alive would be unable to function.
NAD+ also supports numerous enzymes and proteins, including sirtuins, which help regulate inflammation, DNA repair and the function of mitochondria , the structures responsible for producing much of the energy our cells need.
Research suggests that NAD+ levels decline as we get older . This is partly because damage to our DNA accumulates over time, activating enzymes that use up NAD+ more quickly. Another enzyme, called CD38, also becomes more active with age and inflammation, increasing NAD+ use. Meanwhile, our cells may become less efficient at producing it .
The extent of this decline varies between people and different tissues, with some studies suggesting that NAD+ levels may fall by between 10% and 80% as we age.
Lower NAD+ levels have been linked to reduced energy production in cells, slower DNA repair and other changes associated with ageing.
Animal studies suggest that increasing NAD+ levels may improve muscle function and metabolism and even cognitive function , encouraging researchers to investigate whether similar benefits are possible in humans.
There is limited evidence that taking NAD+ itself as a supplement effectively increases NAD+ levels, as it is broken down during digestion . A potential solution to this could be liposomal NAD+, where the molecule is enclosed in tiny fat-based structures designed to improve absorption.
A 2026 study involving 14 people found that taking 1,000mg of liposomal NAD+ daily for two weeks increased NAD+ levels inside cells by more than 64%. However, larger, carefully controlled studies are needed to confirm this finding.
Most human research has instead focused on NAD+ precursors: substances the body uses to make NAD+. These include two compounds derived from vitamin B3, nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
There is good evidence that both can increase NAD+ levels in the blood.
In one randomised, placebo-controlled study involving 140 overweight but otherwise healthy adults aged 40–60, NR supplementation increased blood NAD+ levels over eight weeks. The greatest increase occurred among those taking 1,000 mg (milligrams) daily, whose levels rose by 142% after two weeks and remained elevated throughout the study.
Another study involving 30 healthy adults found that taking 250 mg of NMN daily increased blood NAD+ levels by around 50% after four weeks, with levels remaining elevated throughout the 12-week trial.
High doses of vitamin B3 may also increase NAD+ , although these can be poorly tolerated over longer periods.
Together, these findings suggest that NAD+ precursors can successfully raise blood NAD+ levels. However, whether this also increases levels in other tissues, such as muscles and organs, remains unclear .
Animal studies have produced encouraging results, with NAD+ precursors improving physical performance, insulin sensitivity and the way cells produce energy . One study found that giving older mice NR for six weeks increased their lifespan by an average of 39 days , equivalent to around 5%.
However, results from human studies have been less convincing.
A recent systematic review examined 33 human studies and found inconsistent effects on physical function,

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: ARU is using creativity to drive economic growth
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) is a key partner in a new £6.75 million initiative that aims to harness the power of creative industries to accelerate economic growth in the East of England.
The programme, called CreateSci, will connect the region’s creative businesses with major tech partners including BT, ElevenLabs and industrial software company AVEVA – providing access to new technology, expertise and potential markets.
More than 250 creative businesses will benefit from the new programme, led by the University of East Anglia (UEA), helping create up to 500 skilled jobs across the region.
CreateSci is being funded by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and delivered by the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC). It is one of only a handful of creative clusters being funded across the UK , and the first of its kind in the East of England.
The programme will be led by UEA alongside ARU, Norwich University of the Arts and the University of Suffolk, with the University of Cambridge as a project partner.
At the heart of the programme is the development of the Creative Clinic, where creative businesses and arts and humanities researchers work alongside scientists, the NHS and major employers to tackle real world challenges in relating to health, wellbeing and the environment.
It will showcase how creativity, storytelling, design and community engagement are vital to ensure scientific breakthroughs are understood, trusted and used. Using creative expertise to drive innovation, the programme will help businesses access research, build new skills, and turn ideas into products, while forging new connections with investors and partners.
CreateSci is also expected to attract further public and private investment into the region, creating new opportunities across towns, cities, rural areas and coastal communities – strengthening the East of England’s reputation as a place where creativity drives growth.
“The creative industries are one of the UK’s greatest economic strengths, and vital to the Government’s Industrial Strategy ambitions for national growth, but that growth depends on having the right skills, talent and opportunities in place in all regions.
The East of England has a strong and growing creative sector but has historically attracted less investment than many other regions.
“This cluster is unique because growth goes way beyond creative industries – into the East’s other key sectors of clean energy and life science.
“CreateSci will help businesses across the East of England develop the expertise needed in a rapidly changing sector, supporting them to innovate, grow and attract investment.
<p“We are delighted to be working alongside Norwich University of the Arts, Anglia Ruskin University, the University of Suffolk, Cambridge, industry partners and the Arts and Humanities Research Council on this shared ambition.
“Together, we are investing in the people, skills and ideas that underpin the Government’s Modern Industrial Strategy and strengthen the region’s long-term economic future.”
“Across Cambridge and the wider East of England, we have world-class scientific and technological research alongside creative businesses and communities. CreateSci provides a platform to connect this knowledge.
“At ARU, through DesignLab, one of the specialist labs within the Centre for Media, Arts and Creative Technologies (MACT) , we are particularly interested in how design-led approaches can connect research with real-world challenges, ensuring that innovation is grounded in the needs, knowledge and experiences of communities.
“Our ambition is to help build a more connected, collaborative, and resilient regional economy, generating lasting value and benefits that extend well beyond the lifetime of the programme.”

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Denise enjoys much calmer second graduation day
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
Denise Erica Da Costa Silva at her graduation ceremony at Peterborough Cathedral this week after completing a Master's Degree in International Business Management at ARU Peterborough
A mother-of-four who fled domestic abuse in her home country to build a new life in the UK is celebrating her second graduation from ARU Peterborough – which was considerably less eventful than the first.
After completing her undergraduate studies with ARU Peterborough in 2025, Denise Erica Da Costa Silva went straight from Peterborough Cathedral to hospital to give birth to her fourth child.
Last September, she began her postgraduate course in International Business Management , and she celebrated her second ARU Peterborough graduation at Peterborough Cathedral this week.
Denise had moved to the UK in 2019 with her oldest three children after making the difficult decision to leave an abusive relationship and start again. Determined to create a safer and more secure future for her family, she arrived in Peterborough ready to rebuild her life from scratch.
Denise had previously studied Portuguese and Communication at university and built a career in banking, customer services and marketing in Angola. As she qualifies as a Portuguese citizen through her mother, she was able to settle in the UK but found that the qualifications she had gained earlier in her life were not fully recognised here.
“When I moved here it was very challenging to find work. My first job was as a part-time cleaner which made it very challenging to juggle work and childcare.”
She decided to gain UK qualifications, starting with Level 3 studies and then a Foundation course in London, but the opening of ARU Peterborough offered a life-changing possibility to gain qualifications closer to home. Being able to study locally enabled Denise to balance family responsibilities with her academic ambitions.
She successfully applied to study for an undergraduate degree in Business and Management, graduating in 2025, and has now graduated from her postgraduate studies while preparing a future PhD proposal exploring challenges within human resource management.
Denise was heavily pregnant on the day of her undergraduate graduation, but made it through the ceremony before heading straight to hospital, where she gave birth to baby Zlatan a few days later.
“I came for the ceremony and I started feeling the pain but to be honest I was so focused. I rushed from the Cathedral to the hospital straight afterwards.
“I was in considerable pain, but there was no way I was going to miss that milestone!”
Denise began her postgraduate course when Zlatan was just two months old. She added: “It was a very hard time. It was just me and the kids but because I had a lot of support from ARU Peterborough, the lecturers and my personal tutor, they gave me a lot of strength and in the end I made it.”
Denise is now pursuing a PhD qualification and hopes her story will encourage others facing adversity to pursue their ambitions. Her eldest daughter Lourdes is considering following in her footsteps by studying Business Management at ARU Peterborough next September.
“When I first started studying in the UK, I could never have imagined reaching this point. Balancing motherhood, employment and studying has not always been easy.
“My advice to others is don't allow barriers to stop you from pursuing your ambitions. Whether it is language, family commitments or a lack of confidence, there are tools and support available to help you overcome those hurdles.”

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Most dog attacks are preventable – new research
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
A new analysis focusing on dog attacks on humans in the UK suggests that most incidents are preventable and committed by a wide variety of breeds rather than solely by highly publicised ‘dangerous dogs’ – and owners have a key part to play in prevention.
The new report, entitled Safety Around Dogs: A Process Analysis of Dog Bites , was commissioned by Battersea Dogs and Cats Home and carried out by Anglia Ruskin University (ARU), and examined court records, hospital admission, policy and survey data.
The report analysed 130 dog bite incidents from court data between 2020 and 2025 and found that the circumstances behind dog attacks are highly variable. Of the court data, owner failure to control a dog was the single most common cause, blamed for 32% of cases. The report describe these as unprovoked attacks where a dog jumps up and bites a passer-by in a public place.
A total of 24 cases were a result of the dog escaping either from a property or being tethered and then biting, suggesting that the dog was not appropriately secured by its owner.
All data sets analysed within the report showed that dog attacks involve a wide variety of breeds and that bites are not confined to dogs covered by breed-specific legislation.
Researchers also found that adults account for the majority of victims in both court cases and hospital admission data, despite public concern often focusing on attacks involving children. A notable 14% of people who completed the survey had been bitten three or more times.
As a result of the findings, the report urges both dog owners and policymakers to use similar situational crime prevention measures that are deployed in most other antisocial behaviour scenarios to reduce the risk of attack.
Recommendations set out in the report include better education about safe interactions with dogs, keeping dogs on a lead in higher-risk public settings, and better “dog-proofing” of homes to protect visitors, postal workers and delivery drivers.
The researchers also call for consideration of measures such as enhanced dog registration, stronger links between registration and microchipping, and a mandatory code of practice for dog owners.
According to the report, policies aimed at reducing dog attacks should focus on the situations in which bites occur and the actions owners can take to minimise risk, rather than focusing solely on breed.
“Public debate often focuses on labelling certain breeds as ‘dangerous dogs’, but our analysis shows that a wide range of dogs are involved in attacks and that many are preventable. The evidence suggests that dog attacks do not have a single cause and cannot simply be explained by the breed involved.
“Across the data we examined, we repeatedly found examples of dogs being off leads, escaping from homes or gardens, or being placed in situations where an attack was both foreseeable and preventable. Owners have a role to play in preventing incidents alongside use of accepted crime prevention techniques. Greater awareness, better training and prevention approaches linked to situations where dog attacks are likely to occur all have the potential to reduce many of these incidents.
“The focus should be on understanding the circumstances that lead to attacks and implementing practical measures that help owners manage risks before injuries occur.”
“Every dog bite is a reminder that more must be done to keep people and dogs safe. This research shows that many incidents can be prevented by helping owners better understand and reduce risks through effective behaviour training and secure home environments.
“This report reinforces what Battersea and other animal welfare organisations have long known: dogs involved in bite incidents come from a wide range of breeds, not just the small number of banned types targeted by current dangerous dogs legislation.
