https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Identical twins ready to deliver after graduation joy
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
Twin sisters Freya Ward, pictured left, and Ella Ward at their ARU graduation ceremony in Chelmsford
Two identical twin sisters are ready to deliver after graduating from the Midwifery course at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU).
Ella and Freya Ward, from Benfleet, have journeyed together through school, college and university and will now go on to work as midwives at Basildon Hospital after graduating at Chelmsford Cathedral this week.
The 21-year-olds attended Appleton School in Benfleet before going to nearby USP College to study health and social care. They then applied to ARU where they both underwent hospital placements at Basildon Hospital.
They even passed their driving tests three days apart, and for a while shared a car to travel into university and to placements.
Freya said: “We’re very similar in lots of ways. We share the same friends and the same interests. We both liked the idea of becoming midwives so it seemed a natural path to take for us both.
“My mum was the person who first gave me the idea to become a midwife when I was 15, and I have never looked back since. My parents and wider family have been amazing throughout my training and have always been there to encourage me during moments when I doubted my abilities.”
While going through life together as identical twins has been fairly seamless, the situation has sometimes thrown up unusual challenges for others.
Freya added: “One of the most memorable moments was on the delivery suite when Ella had finished a day shift and I had just started the night shift. A patient I was caring for asked if I was feeling alright after such a long day. I immediately realised she had mistaken me for my sister and had to explain I'd only arrived a few hours earlier. We all laughed and it became a bit of a joke among the midwives.”
Ella said: “We’re used to it but we do get quite a lot of people interested in how it works and asking us questions. They usually want to know who has delivered the most babies, or whether the patients and other midwives get confused.”
Their hospital placements also confirmed they had chosen the right profession. Both sisters vividly remember delivering their first babies during her first year of training.
Remembering that first delivery, Freya said: “I was lucky enough to be working with an amazing midwife who took the time to explain things to me and made me feel included in the experience. It is a really nice memory and reminds me that even throughout the busy, more stressful moments, birth can be calm and empowering. I will always remember and be grateful to that family.”
Ella said: “I remember being excited about the first birth. An amazing midwife helped me deliver the baby and they called the baby Freya which I thought was funny and obviously I told my sister straight away!”
Although the similarities between Ella and Freya are clear, they both had different strengths while studying.
Ella added: “I was stronger with coursework and Freya was better with exams. When it came to revising for exams, Freya helped me with revision notes and preparation for those. Everyone has those high and low moments but we helped each other through.”

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Five ways to enjoy fashion without overconsuming
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
By Cathrine Jansson-Boyd , Anglia Ruskin University
Fashion lovers are generally associated with bursting wardrobes and chasing the latest trends. But that reputation is beginning to shift.
In the last few years, market surveys have found that around a third of shoppers are now buying second hand clothing . For gen Z, this figure increases to just under half. Giant hauls from fast fashion brands were once the trend – but an eye for vintage bargains and pre-worn fits is now more on point.
Though buying used is far preferential to buying new, overconsumption can still be a problem with second-hand clothing. That’s because buying used often supplements, rather than replaces, fast fashion habits.
If you love fashion, but want to indulge in your hobby without falling into the trap of overconsumption, here are five tips.
“Shopping your closet” – creating new looks with the existing pieces in your wardrobe – has been trending online for a while. Putting some thought into how you can restyle existing pieces will help you to shift your focus from buying something, to becoming creative.
Research has shown that a small and versatile wardrobe that can easily be mixed and matched into several outfits fosters creativity as your brain must solve styling puzzles with limited items. It also generates feelings of satisfaction and enjoyment. This is important as being content with your clothing choices is linked to general wellbeing.
It can be helpful to schedule a dedicated wardrobe date and treat styling your closet like a fun puzzle rather than a chore. Creativity tends to flow better when under less pressure, so don’t try to build your creative cognitive styling muscles when you are in a rush.
To get inspiration flowing, try searching sites like Pinterest. Type in exact terms like “oversized blazer outfit” to discover fresh styling ideas for pieces sitting in your closet. Set yourself a challenge for 10 days not to wear any combination you have worn before.
And just so you don’t forget: snap quick mirror photos of any outfit combinations that work well so you have a personal outfit catalogue ready for busy mornings.
Having too many clothes can lead to choice overload , when the difficulty of decision exceeds our cognitive ability to make a choice.
Generally, people tend to find it easier to make a choice when they have less to choose from. If you have two T-shirts, your brain can decide in seconds. But if you have 18 T-shirts, wardrobe paralysis kicks in.
Treat sorting through your clothes as an interactive styling project. Reorganising by colour or silhouette can help you to rediscover forgotten favourites and appreciate the craftsmanship of items you already own, as well as making it easier to choose.
Try buying clothing as a collector or curator. This means that you should select unique, high-quality pieces based on your personal preference and their long-term value. Look past trends by evaluating fabric weight, seam stitching, lining quality and natural fibres (like wool, linen, or silk) before buying, ensuring each addition to your wardrobe is built to last.
Keep a running list of missing baseline pieces or specific archive designs. Planning ahead limits the likelihood of making an impulse purchase, which may lead to regret . Taking 48 hours to think it over also reduces the chances of making the wrong decision.
Craft a clear vision of your personal aesthetic focusing on your favoured silhouettes, colour palettes and textures, so that every prospective purchase must earn its place alongside your existing collection.
Building a wardrobe based on your specific personal taste allows you to treat your personal style as a fine art rather than a fast-fashion race. You’ll also probably keep your garments for longer as items people care for tend to become tangible extensions of their identity .

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Volunteering delivers purpose - but also anxiety
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
New research has found that people who volunteer have a greater purpose in life, but it comes at a cost, with volunteering also linked to higher levels of anxiety.
The study was led by psychologists from the Research Centre for Better Living at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) and involved data from 7,146 adults in England who participated in the Taking Part Survey, carried out by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.
Volunteering is regarded as a net benefit to society, often focusing on the unmet needs of individuals and communities, and the economic contribution of volunteers is substantial, with the UN estimating it accounts for around 2.5% of global GDP.
Published in the journal Behavioral Sciences , the new research found that any form of volunteering in the previous 12 months was associated with participants reporting a stronger sense that their lives were worthwhile.
After controlling for variables linked to subjective wellbeing and loneliness outcomes – gender, age, level of deprivation, health and employment status – the effect of volunteering on people reporting that their life was worthwhile was more than 1.5 times greater than the effect of being in employment.
The researchers believe this could be because unlike employment, volunteering usually involves activities that are chosen because they are personally meaningful. It is often in charitable or not-for-profit sectors, and being able to help a particular cause may strengthen feelings of purpose.
However, the study also found that volunteering was not linked to greater happiness, higher life satisfaction or lower levels of loneliness, despite volunteering often suggested as a form of ‘social prescribing’. And crucially, it found that volunteering predicted significantly higher levels of anxiety.
The findings that volunteering is associated with a greater sense of meaning (eudaimonic wellbeing) but not positive feelings such as happiness (hedonic wellbeing) could be because meaningful activities come with emotional costs as well as benefits.
The researchers suggest people might gain a stronger sense of purpose through volunteering precisely because it involves commitment and effort, sometimes in sectors that involve emotionally distressing situations, which may explain the relationship with anxiety.
"Volunteering is often promoted as something that boosts wellbeing, and our findings partly support that idea. However, the picture is more complex.
“We found evidence that volunteering was linked to greater purpose, but not to greater happiness. In fact, volunteers reported slightly higher anxiety. That doesn't mean volunteering is harmful, but it does suggest that meaningful activities may come with emotional costs as well as benefits.
"Volunteers provide enormous benefits to society, and our findings should not be interpreted as a reason to volunteer less. Instead, they highlight the importance of supporting volunteers properly and recognising that people who give their time to help others may also need support themselves.
"As a society, we often focus on whether an activity makes people happy. Our findings suggest that volunteering may offer something different: a sense that life matters and has purpose. That may be one of the most important contributions volunteering makes, even if it is not always accompanied by greater happiness.
"Perhaps our most unexpected finding was that volunteering was a stronger predictor of a sense that life is worthwhile than being in employment. Employment provides income, structure and social connection, but volunteering may offer something different: an opportunity to choose work that reflects personal values and directly helps others.”

https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.title: Ceremony sees new ARU Chancellor formally invested
https://www.aru.ac.uk/news.text:
ARU's new Chancellor Professor Lady Sue Black
The formal investiture of Professor Lady Sue Black as the new Chancellor of Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) took place this week during graduation celebrations for hundreds of students in Chelmsford.
One of the world's leading forensic scientists, Professor Lady Black is an internationally respected academic, author and public servant whose career has been distinguished by excellence in education, research and civic contribution.
Since graduating from the University of Aberdeen in Human Anatomy, Professor Lady Black has made an exceptional contribution to forensic science. Her work for the UK Government and international agencies has taken her across the world, including investigations in Iraq, Sierra Leone and Grenada, and she served as lead forensic anthropologist during the international war crimes investigations in Kosovo.
Alongside her academic achievements, she has been recognised through numerous honours, including her appointment as Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2016, election as a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2023, appointment to the Most Ancient and Most Noble Order of the Thistle in 2024, and her service as a Crossbench member of the House of Lords.
Professor Lady Black is currently the 37th President of St John's College, Oxford, and previously served as Pro Vice Chancellor for Engagement at Lancaster University.
Among her many media appearances, Professor Lady Black has featured as the guest on The Life Scientific and Desert Island Discs on BBC Radio 4. She is also the author of three books, the most recent of which, An Expert Witness , was published in July.
ARU’s autumn graduation ceremonies in Chelmsford, Cambridge and Peterborough this month will see 3,140 students formally receive their degrees, ready to take the next step in their lives.
“It is a tremendous honour to stand before you today as the new Chancellor of Anglia Ruskin University. I feel enormously privileged to be taking on this role and I do so with a genuine sense of excitement, humility and I hope a healthy dose of Scottish Highland determination.
“Universities have always held a special place in my heart. They are extraordinary places full of extraordinary people. They are where curiosity is encouraged, where conventional thinking can be challenged, where ideas are born, and where people are given the opportunity to discover not only what they can achieve, but who they might become.”
“Professor Lady Sue Black is a passionate advocate for widening opportunity through education and for ensuring that universities make a meaningful contribution to the communities they serve. In accepting her appointment as Chancellor, she spoke of her commitment to supporting and championing Anglia Ruskin University's work across research, education and civic engagement, and of the importance she places on transforming lives and widening opportunity through social mobility.
“Her values, her commitment to public service, and her belief in the power of education align closely with the mission of Anglia Ruskin University: transforming lives through innovative, inclusive and entrepreneurial education and research.”

https://www.heritagefund.org.uk/news.title: Seven historic buildings we’re funding to become community hubs
https://www.heritagefund.org.uk/news.text:
We’ve awarded grants to over 300 projects since 1994 that have transformed historic buildings and natural heritage spaces into dedicated hubs for public activities supporting learning, training and wellbeing.
Our local teams fund communities to restore and reuse the historic places that matter to them, and achieve their potential to make a difference to people's lives and local economies.
Community hubs provide social, mental health and shared learning benefits for all and, critically, give new life to formerly redundant buildings.
Eilish McGuinness, Chief Executive of The National Lottery Heritage Fund
Our £402,000 grant is supporting plans to reinvigorate a community hub and wayfinding centre for visitors that will share the history of the Essex town. Shoeburyness was used for testing guns and ammunition for the army and navy from 1850 and as a military base during both world wars. It’s also where dogs were trained as messengers, sentries and for patrolling there during the First World War.
Two 18th-century buildings on the high street of this coastal town are being restored and refurbished as part of an expansion of its community-focused local museum. Dr Nic Wright from the project spoke to us recently about overcoming challenges and how on-the-ground engagement has created a buzz in the town for the £2.1m project.
This Georgian building is already a valued centre for delivering community services across Kendal, Westmorland and Furness. Our £4.6m grant will restore the building and upgrade its accessibility so it can better serve local charitable, voluntary and community sector needs.
Activities benefitting local people will be at the heart of the project, following conservation and enhancement of this unusually grand place of worship in rural Norfolk, thanks to our £475,000 grant. Working with HoltYouth Project, which serves around 200 local young people, the project will run cookery lessons and provide respite meals for young carers.
Our grant of £2.65m starts a new chapter in the 1,000-year history of Colchester’s oldest building. Urgent conservation will remove the Grade I listed building from Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register and repurpose it as a welcoming community space open daily to the public for the first time since 2017.
Our £1.2m funding will help refurbish and expand this centre – which tells the story of the people of the Outer Hebrides – and support more family tree and heritage research and Gaelic language learning.
We’ve awarded Bolton Council and Lancashire Wildlife Trust £4.4m to renovate this derelict Grade II listed historic building. It’ll be turned into a centre for celebrating local heritage through creative interpretation, exhibitions and event programming.
By restoring the old rather than building new, these projects will have a lower environmental impact and support traditional heritage skills while retaining the individual character of their areas, neighbourhoods or towns. And as useful spaces for local people and visitors to learn and have fun, they will help people connect with each other and the past.
Eilish McGuinness, Chief Executive of The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said: “Heritage has a unique role in building pride in place and connection to the past, bringing people together where they live, work and visit.
“Community hubs provide social, mental health and shared learning benefits for all and, critically, give new life to formerly redundant buildings.”
Browse snapshots of projects we’ve funded across the UK that are valuing, caring for and sustaining heritage for everyone’s future.

https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.title: Steve’s Volunteering Story
https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.text:
From Rock Bottom to Purpose: How Helping Others Helped Me Heal
Steve has been volunteering for 20 years. Here’s his story:
There was a time in my life when everything I’d built—my home, my business, my sense of direction—collapsed under the weight of addiction. When the dust settled, I was left searching for the cheapest accommodation I could find, feeling sorry for myself and convinced that my situation was as bad as it could get.
That’s how I ended up at a hostel. What I didn’t expect was how quickly my perspective would change. I soon realised that the people around me were facing challenges far greater than my own – mental health struggles, alcohol dependency, drug addiction.
Before long, I found myself stepping up. I began helping run the hostel, working closely with housing officers, and supporting residents who were navigating some of the darkest chapters of their lives. It wasn’t glamorous, but it was real. It mattered.
During that same period, I spent six years volunteering with Crisis during Christmas week, running the barbering department. People really open up and tell you their life stories.
Those experiences changed me. It has made a massive difference in my life.
They inspired me to educate myself as a therapist, to understand people more deeply, and to continue supporting those who need it.
The truth is, the rewards you get from volunteering and helping others are priceless. I genuinely believe everyone should, at some point in their life, devote themselves to helping others. It makes you a more loving and compassionate human being.
Inspired by Steve’s story? Why not give volunteering a go. You’ll find a range of volunteering roles to suit. Click on the ‘Search for Opportunities’ button at the top and find your volunteering role now!
Are you Volunteering? Would you like to share your Volunteering Story? Tell us what you enjoy about volunteering by completing our  Volunteer Story form .

https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.title: How to Start Volunteering
https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.text:
A Beginner’s Guide to Making a Difference in Essex
Volunteering is more than giving your time – it’s about making a difference in your community, meeting new people, and gaining valuable skills. Whether you’re looking to support a local charity, help young people, or simply give back, Essex offers countless opportunities through Volunteer Essex.
1. Think About What You Want to Give
Before you search for a role, reflect on:
Your interests
Do you enjoy working with people? Animals? Historic sites? Outdoors?
Your skills
Are you good at organisation, communication, technology, caregiving, or fundraising?
Your availability
How much time can you offer—weekly, monthly, or occasionally?
Understanding these helps you choose opportunities that you’ll enjoy and stick with.
2. Explore Volunteering Opportunities in Essex
The easiest way to find a role that fits your interests is to browse local listings. Volunteer Essex provides a searchable directory of volunteering opportunities across the county, making it simple to find roles based on location, time commitment, and cause.
As you explore opportunities, consider:
Whether the role suits your schedule
What training or experience is required
If you prefer remote or in-person volunteering
If the organisation aligns with your interests
Use the search tool to filter by postcode, interests, or activities.
3. Register an Account / Your Interest
If it’s the first time you’ve visited our website, you’ll first need to ‘register an account’. Once this is done you can register your interest for any volunteering roles that appeal to you.
We recommend you register for no more than three roles at a time.
4. Contact from Organisation
Your details will be passed on to the organisation and they will be in touch directly. They will go through the volunteer recruitment process as well as answer any questions you may have such as:
What will the regular duties be?
Is training provided?
What is the expected commitment?
Are there any requirements (e.g., DBS checks)?
If you have any questions whilst you’re waiting to be contacted, or if you’ve not heard anything after a couple of weeks, then contact your local Volunteer Centre .
5. Get Started!
Once you’ve gone through their volunteer recruitment process, and you and the organisation decide you’re a fit, and you’ve completed any necessary training and induction process then you’re ready to get started!
Volunteering is a rewarding experience. You’ll meet new people, gain experience, and make a positive impact in Essex.
Want to inspire others to volunteer? Tell us your Volunteer Story by completing this form .

https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.title: How Volunteering Can Help Your Career
https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.text:
Build Skills, Confidence, and Connections
Volunteering isn’t just about giving back – it’s a smart career move.  Whether you’re looking to gain experience, grow your network, or discover your passion, Volunteer Essex is here to help you discover a variety of volunteering roles that can help your career.
Gain Real-World Experience
Volunteering offers hands-on experience in a variety of areas, which help to build a portfolio of work to showcase to future employers. By getting involved with local charities, community projects, or social enterprises in Essex, you can build a strong track record of teamwork, leadership, and problem-solving.
Develop Transferable Skills
Volunteering helps you develop transferable skills that employers love, such as:
– Communication and teamwork
– Organisation and time management
– Leadership and initiative
– Problem-solving and adaptability
Many roles also offer training, giving you a chance to learn new tools and systems, all of which can be transferred to almost any career path.
Build/Expand Your Professional Network
One of the biggest benefits of volunteering is the opportunity to meet people. Volunteering connects you with individuals from different industries, backgrounds, and experiences. These relationships can lead to job referrals, recommendations, and even job offers.
Boost Your CV and Stand Out
Employers appreciate candidates who go the extra mile. Volunteering highlights your initiative, social awareness, and community spirit. Including your volunteer work on your CV can set you apart from other candidates.
Boost Your Confidence and Wellbeing
Volunteering gives you a sense of purpose and achievement, which can greatly improve your confidence. If you’ve been out of work for a while, it can help you ease back into a routine and refresh your skills – all while making a positive difference in your community.
Plus, studies show that helping others reduces stress and improves mental wellbeing -something that benefits both your personal and professional life.
Explore New Career Paths
Thinking of switching careers? Volunteering offers a low-risk way to try something new. From marketing and administration to animal care and environmental projects, Essex has a wide range of volunteer roles to explore.
At Volunteer Essex , we connect people with meaningful volunteer opportunities across the county. Whether you want to develop your skills, gain experience, or make a difference, there’s a role that’s perfect for you. Click on the ‘Search for Opportunities’ button at the top of the page.
Ready to boost your career while making a difference? Start your journey with Volunteer Essex today.

https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.title: Why Charities Need Volunteers
https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.text:
The Vital Role of Volunteers in Essex Communities
Charities play a crucial role in supporting local communities — but behind every successful charity, there’s often a team of passionate volunteers making it all possible. Volunteers are the unsung heroes behind many of the UK’s most impactful charities. From offering time and skills to raising awareness, volunteers are the heart of charitable work.
At Volunteer Essex, we believe that volunteering isn’t just helpful—it’s essential.
What Volunteers Bring to Charities:
Energy, Passion, and People Power
Charities depend on volunteers to deliver services, run events, and support day-to-day operations. With limited funding, many charitable organisations wouldn’t be able to operate without the dedication of volunteers.
From helping in charity shops to supporting fundraising campaigns, volunteers bring energy, creativity, and enthusiasm that can also inspire others to get involved too. They help charities stretch their resources further — meaning more money goes directly to the causes that matter most.
Skills and Expertise
Not all support comes in the form of donations — sometimes, time and knowledge are even more valuable. Volunteers come from all walks of life—retirees, students, professionals—and they bring with them a wealth of experience in areas like administration, marketing, IT, or finance, helping charities become more efficient and effective helping charities to grow and innovate.
By connecting through Volunteer Essex , local charities can find volunteers with specific skills to strengthen their work and deliver even greater community impact.
Community Engagement
Volunteers are often local residents who care deeply about their communities. When people volunteer locally, they help build stronger, more connected communities. Their involvement strengthens ties between charities and the people they serve, building trust and fostering long-term support.
Advocates and Ambassadors
One of the biggest benefits of volunteering is the ripple effect it creates. Volunteers don’t just work—they talk. They act as ambassadors, spreading the word about causes and helping charities reach new audiences both online and offline.
This organic advocacy is invaluable for raising awareness and attracting new supporters. When people see volunteers giving their time to make a difference, it inspires others to do the same.
Low Costs and High Impact
Charities often operate on tight budgets. Volunteers make it possible for these organisations to deliver essential services without the financial strain of hiring additional staff. This allows charities to allocate more of their funds directly to their mission — whether that’s supporting vulnerable people, protecting the environment, or promoting education and wellbeing, volunteers make more possible.
Volunteering doesn’t just benefit charities — it’s also incredibly rewarding for the volunteers themselves. It’s a great way to gain new skills, meet new people, boost confidence, and make a positive difference in the community.
Whether you’re looking to enhance your CV, explore a new career path, or simply give back, there’s a volunteer role in Essex that’s perfect for you.
If you’re ready to make a difference, Volunteer Essex connects you with hundreds of local charities and volunteering opportunities across the county. Whether you can give a few hours a week or just a day every now and then, your time truly matters.
Find volunteering opportunities near you at www.volunteeressex.org and be part of something bigger.
Together, we can strengthen communities, support local causes, and make Essex an even better place to live.

https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.title: The Power of Micro-Volunteering
https://www.volunteeressex.org/feed/.text:
Small Actions Give Big Impact
Would you like to give back to your community and make a difference? Like the idea of volunteering, but feel you don’t have the time to commit? That’s the power of micro-volunteering – a flexible, accessible, and incredibly impactful way to give back in small, manageable ways.
At Volunteer Essex, we have various one-off, irregular volunteering roles across the county helping you to get involved, no matter how busy life gets.
What is Micro-Volunteering?
Micro-volunteering refers to ad hoc, one-off or irregular volunteering roles, where regular, ongoing commitment isn’t needed, meaning you can volunteer in your local community without it impacting too much on your daily routine. This makes it ideal for busy individuals who still want to contribute to meaningful causes, but don’t have a lot of time to spare.
These activities typically:
Don’t take long to complete
Require no long-term commitment
Can often be done from home or on the go
Still contribute to real, measurable change
Why Micro-Volunteering Matters
It’s Accessible to Everyone
You don’t need special skills, lots of free time, or sometimes even to leave your house. Whether you have 5 minutes or an hour, there’s something you can do to help.
Micro-volunteering empowers everyone to contribute, including:
Students juggling studies and part-time jobs
Parents with unpredictable schedules
Retirees looking for flexible ways to stay active
Professionals who want to give back during lunch breaks
Small Tasks Add Up
When many people contribute small efforts, the collective impact is significant. Imagine hundreds of volunteers each spending 10 minutes a day supporting a cause—that’s thousands of hours of help every week!
Encourages Civic Engagement
Micro-volunteering makes it easy for more people to participate in community work, particularly those who may have felt excluded from traditional volunteering due to time, mobility, or location constraints.
Great for First-Time Volunteers
If you’re new to volunteering, micro-tasks are a low-pressure way to get involved. They allow you to try different causes and roles before committing to something long-term.
How to Get Started with Micro-Volunteering in Essex
Identify Your Interests
Just like traditional volunteering, micro-volunteering is most meaningful when it aligns with your values. Do you love education, the environment, animal welfare, or mental health advocacy?
Explore Local Opportunities with Volunteer Essex
Volunteer Essex is a great place to discover micro-volunteering roles tailored to your interests. Browse listings by cause or location, and find both in-person and remote tasks that suit your schedule. Search on the opportunities button above to find current opportunities.
Set Your Own Pace
Start small. You don’t need to do everything at once. Even one act a week can create impact.
Share Your Efforts
By sharing your micro-volunteering experiences, you inspire others to get involved. Tag @VolunteerInEssex on Facebook or share your story through our Volunteer Story form .
Volunteering doesn’t have to be a big commitment to be meaningful. With micro-volunteering, you can be part of something bigger—one small act at a time. It’s a flexible, rewarding way to stay engaged with causes you care about.
In a world where time is limited but the need for compassion is great, micro-volunteering offers a powerful solution. Start small, act often, and watch how even the tiniest efforts can lead to big change—right here in Essex.
Explore micro-volunteering today!

https://braintreemuseum.co.uk/feed/.title: Toddler Time
https://braintreemuseum.co.uk/feed/.text:
Toddler Time
Toddler Time welcomes children aged one to four to share new experiences, create memories and connect with others at Braintree District Museum. Each session provides stimulating sensory and educational sessions for families to participate in, with every other week being a messy play session! Every week has a unique theme, which has included exploring our current exhibition, investigating the museum garden and things the children have suggested like beach activities. Our most popular sessions so far have been:
·         Garden Explorers – We used magnifying glasses to search for plants and insects in the Museum Urban Garden. We learnt that many insects like to come out in the warm weather and then created a snail picture to take home.
·         Roar Roar Dinosaur – This activity engaged us by using archaeological dig boxes to search for dinosaurs. We then counted them, sorted them into different colours and reburied them to repeat!
·         Transport Time – Families participated in group parachute games to engage movement and coordination skills. One session we were lucky enough for a local police officer to see our fun and stop and join in! Another popular transport session was the ‘Car Wash Station’. Toddlers took cars that had been covered in ‘mud’ and washed them off in soapy water. This was very messy but a lot of fun!
Toddler Time starts at 10am every Friday morning. The session runs from 30 minutes to an hour, but families are welcome to stay and play as long as they like.
We receive funding to make Toddler Time FREE. We recommend booking to avoid missing out! To book, please call 01376 328 868
Feedback:
Feedback from families has highlighted that they valued ‘the well thought out activities’, ‘the many things to do inside the museum’ and ‘engaging with other families’.

https://braintreemuseum.co.uk/feed/.title: NEW EXHIBITION: Art Deco & Beyond – Innovation and Design in Braintree 1925-1935
https://braintreemuseum.co.uk/feed/.text:
NEW EXHIBITION: Art Deco & Beyond – Innovation and Design in Braintree 1925-1935
17 th January – 27 th June 2026
Art Deco and Beyond explores how Braintree, Essex paved the way in manufacturing innovations and textile design during the 1920s and 1930s. Featuring Crittalls and the centenary of the unique village of Silver End. Courtaulds, innovators of artificial silk and esteemed textile manufacturers Warner & Sons.
More about the exhibition
This colourful and interactive exhibition, filled with never before displayed plans, objects and design, steps back into the vibrant world of the 1920’s and 1930’s.
The interwar period in Braintree saw a general improvement in the quality of life for the majority of people, as significant successes of local companies kept them in employment despite the Depression. It was a period of freedom of expression in art and architecture, fashion and music. It really was a new age!
Crittalls introduced the first modernist housing to Britain with the creation of Clockhouse Way in 1919. They went on to develop the Art Deco and Modern Movement – styled village of Silver End, which celebrates 100 years this year.
Courtaulds changed washing day and fashion forever with artificial silk. They also changed how we access and appreciate art.
Warner & Sons led the way in fabric design and production.
The Bardfield artists started settling in Essex, developing their innovative and playful vision of art and print.
During this period there were two particularly influential exhibitions; the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley in 1924-1925, and the International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts in Paris in 1925. The Paris exhibition gave the name ‘Art Deco’ to the emerging modern style. Textile giants Courtaulds and Warner & Sons attended these exhibitions and Crittalls were also present. They all showcased modern alongside traditional styles, reflecting the diversity of output and techniques developing in the mid-1920s and this exhibition explores and displays the colours, patterns and materials defined by these companies during this iconic decade.

https://www.tiptreeparishcouncil.gov.uk/.title: What is the New Colchester Local Plan?
https://www.tiptreeparishcouncil.gov.uk/.text:
The New Local Plan is our blueprint for how Colchester will grow over the next 15 years. It sets out where new homes, jobs and community facilities could go, how we protect green spaces and heritage, and how we plan for transport and climate-friendly development. It guides decisions so growth is sustainable and benefits local people.
What is this consultation aiming to achieve?
We’re asking residents, businesses, parish councils and community groups to review the draft proposals and tell us what they think. Feedback will help shape the final plan – what gets built, where it goes, and the standards new development must meet. Every response matters. The consultation runs 26 November to 14 January .
Short explainer
Regulation 18 Consultation is Live
• Purpose: Gather views on the emerging Preferred Options Local Plan.
• Deadline for responses: 14th January 2026
Why It Matters
• Influences future development, housing, and infrastructure in your area.
• Opportunity for local voices to shape policy.
How Residents Can Get Involved
• Review the Preferred Options document online.
• Town Hall events • Submit comments – preferred method via the JDi consultation portal.
What Feedback Should Cover
• Support or objections to proposed policies and sites.
• Suggestions for alternative sites or policy wording.
• Evidence-based comments (e.g. local data, infrastructure needs).
How Does This Fit With Our Neighbourhood Plan?
The major site policies of the Local Plan meet the needs of extending our Neighbourhood Plan to complete the proposed link road between Colchester Road and Kelvedon Road and provides a country park that acts as a dividing line between the parishes of Tiptree and Messing and Inworth.
The Colchester Local Plan acts as a framework for local development. Following the current Preferred Options consultation the plan will amended for further consultation. Once approved and adopted, developers of the indicated sites will still be obliged to submit planning applications where the full details of local needs will be built into the decision following the guidance of the new Local Plan and our Neighbourhood Plan.
Please see our neighbourhood plan.

https://news.cityoflondon.gov.uk/feed/.title: Historic east London landmark saved from Heritage at Risk Register after careful restoration
https://news.cityoflondon.gov.uk/feed/.source: City of London Corporation newsroom (Epping Forest)
https://news.cityoflondon.gov.uk/feed/.text:
[Full image gallery below]
Wanstead Park’s Grade II listed Grotto removed from Heritage at Risk Register
Trustee of the Epping Forest charity secures future preservation of historic structure
18th-century landmark no longer considered at risk
Wanstead Park's Grade II listed Grotto has been removed from Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register.
It follows years of conservation planning and specialist restoration, led by the City of London Corporation and its Epping Forest charity, to stabilise the structure, preserve its historic fabric, and secure its future.
Built in 1761, the Grotto is a remarkable surviving fragment of the former Wanstead House estate, once among the grandest country houses and formal designed landscapes in Britain. Positioned beside the Ornamental Water, it was designed as a boathouse and elaborate place for entertainment with its interiors originally decorated with shells, crystals, mirrors and stones.
Although much of the structure was destroyed by fire in 1884, its ruins remain one of the most distinctive landmarks in Epping Forest.
A public consultation on potential work to the Grotto and other historic features is expected to begin next year, giving local communities the opportunity to help shape the park's future.
Work to secure future funding for improvements across Wanstead Park is also underway, helping the Epping Forest charity enhance visitors’ experience and celebrate the park’s unique heritage.
Chair of the City Corporation's Epping Forest & Commons Committee, Caroline Haines, said:
“The Grotto is one of Wanstead Park’s most recognisable landmarks. Generations of local people have walked past it, photographed it and wondered about the stories it could tell.
“Thanks to years of careful conservation work, investment and partnership, the future of this important piece of local history – that very nearly disappeared altogether – has been saved.”
Christopher Laine, Landscape Architect at Historic England, said:
"The removal of the Grotto from the Heritage at Risk Register is a fantastic achievement. It is testament to years of dedication by the City of London Corporation and its partners that a once-vulnerable ruin is now stable and well-maintained.
“I hope this restoration will inspire people to continue to learn about the Grotto's history and its place as an evocative vestige of one of the country's grandest – and now largely lost – designed landscapes."
David Bloxam, Head of Architectural Projects, Cliveden Conservation said:
"It has been a privilege to help secure the future of Wanstead Grotto. An important part of the conservation project was creating discrete novel connections through the structure to the supporting steel frame.
"By carefully matching handmade bricks and stone, and re-using original materials found on site, our team has made these repairs almost invisible, so the historic fabric remains the focus. We’re very proud of the result.”
Cliveden Conservation was commissioned by the City Corporation to help remove the Grotto from the Heritage at Risk Register. The main scope of works was to install a galvanised steel frame, fixed to new concrete foundation trenches, to stabilise the principal façade and secure the surviving structure for the future.
Wanstead Park has been managed by the City Corporation as Conservators and Trustee of the Epping Forest charity since 1880.
Today it is recognised as a nationally important heritage landscape and wildlife site, designated as a Grade II* Registered Park and Garden, a Site of Metropolitan Importance for Nature Conservation, an Archaeological Priority Area and forms the most part of the Wanstead Park Conservation Area.
Covering more than 300 acres, the park attracts hundreds of thousands of visits each year and contains historic lakes, veteran trees, acid grassland, woodland and important remnants of the former Wanstead House estate including the nearby Temple.
The City Corporation is the sole trustee and largest funder of eight open spa

https://www.takeley-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Household Support Fund Allocation
https://www.takeley-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
This year’s support package for Essex (through the Household Support Fund), which will provide over £16m of support to households in need over the next year.
ECC has now allocated the £16,631,626 received from the Department for Work and Pensions’ Household Support Fund – this will support residents from young to old with over £6 million allocated to help feed thousands of children eligible for free school meals, and £1 million for pensioners, which will be incredibly valuable over the winter as a result of changes to the government’s winter support allowance. The funding runs until March 2026. It aims to ease financial pressure for families, pensioners, and vulnerable residents across the county by supporting with food, household bills and essential items.
The allocations include:
£8,900,926 to the Essential Living Fund for those in need of support with household bills, food and essential items. (including £1m targeted at pensioners.)
£5,605,200 for supermarket food vouchers to support families with children eligible for free school meals.
£500,000 for foodbanks, food support groups, and food pantries to stock groceries for residents in need.
£200,000 for organisations supporting groups such as unpaid carers with the cost of energy, food, essentials items.
£140,000 for the 14 Community Supermarkets in Essex that provide affordable food to local residents.
£100,000 for Essex Citizens Advice to provide direct financial support and advisory services to struggling households.
£75,000 for supermarket vouchers for food and essential items to support Young Carer households in need.
£67,500 in supermarket vouchers for care leavers.
£63,000 to provide food for children and young people attending the holiday activities and food programme.
£50,000 to Essex Citizens Advice to fund training for frontline workers to support people affected by benefit cuts.
£10,000 for Essex Libraries “Winter Warm Welcome” over October 2025- March 2026.
The Household Support Fund was introduced by the previous government and provides crucial aid to vulnerable families and communities.
With taxes on the increase and the cost of living continuing to rise, this fund ensures that support reaches those who need it most across Essex. More information on help with the cost of living is available at https://www.essex.gov.uk/help-cost-living .
If you are contacted by residents in need, please remember that they may be able to utilise/apply for these valuable support services/funds.
Kind regards, Louise
Councillor Louise McKinlay BA (Hons) MSc, Prince II Certified Practitioner
Deputy Leader of Essex County Council
Cabinet Member for Communities, Economic Growth and Prosperity
County Councillor for Brentwood Hutton Division

https://finchingfield-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Neighbourhood Plan Regulation 16 Public Consultation Now Open
https://finchingfield-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Neighbourhood Plan Regulation 16 Public Consultation Now Open
Braintree District Council has now formally opened the Regulation 16 Public Consultation for the Finchingfield and Wethersfield Neighbourhood Plan, marking an important milestone in the formal planning process.
What is a Neighbourhood Plan?
A Neighbourhood Plan is a community led planning document that helps shape how the local area develops in the future. Once adopted, it becomes part of the statutory Development Plan used when planning applications are considered. It can help guide matters such as housing location and design, protection of valued community assets and green spaces, support for local businesses, transport improvements, and wider local priorities.
What is Regulation 16?
Regulation 16 is the formal statutory public consultation stage in the Neighbourhood Planning process. At this stage, the submitted draft Plan is published by the local planning authority, allowing residents, businesses, statutory consultees, and other interested parties to make final formal representations before the Plan proceeds to independent examination.
This consultation follows substantial work by the Neighbourhood Plan Team, including review of comments received during earlier consultation stages and refinement of the draft Plan.
The consultation is open until 5.00pm on Wednesday 1 July 2026 .
Please note that this consultation is being administered entirely by Braintree District Council , and all formal comments must be submitted directly to them.
The draft Plan can be viewed online via:
• Braintree District Council consultation portal
• Finchingfield & Wethersfield Neighbourhood Plan website
Hard copies are available at:
• Wethersfield Shop
• Freshwell Health Centre, Finchingfield
• Braintree District Council Offices
What happens next?
Once the consultation closes, the draft Plan and all submitted representations will be reviewed by an independent examiner, who will assess whether the Plan meets the necessary legal requirements and planning policy standards.
If successful, the Plan will proceed to a local referendum , where eligible local electors will be invited to vote on whether the Plan should be adopted. If supported by a majority vote, it will formally become part of the planning framework for the area.
Alongside the formal Neighbourhood Plan process, both Parish Councils continue progressing wider actions identified through the Plan’s broader community work, including matters such as community assets, local business support, public transport, footways, and local safety improvements.

https://barlingmagna-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Extraordinary meeting of the Full Council – 21st August 2026
Wildlife Reserve 2026 – Green Flag Award Presentation
https://barlingmagna-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Today we had the pleasure of presenting our Wildlife Reserve volunteers with their 14th Green Flag award – an incredible achievement that reflects their dedication, commitment and countless hours of hard work.
The green flag award is an internationally recognised quality mark that celebrates well-managed parks and green spaces. Receiving this award for the 14th time is something the whole parish can be proud of.
Our volunteers work tirelessly throughout the year to care for the reserve, maintaining paths, habitats and facilities, while creating a welcoming space for wildlife and for everyone in our community to enjoy. Their passion, enthusiasm and willingness to give up their own time make the Wildlife Reserve the special place it is today.
On behalf of Barling Magna Parish Council, we would like to say a huge thank you to everyone of our volunteers. Your dedication does not go unnoticed, and we are incredibly grateful for everything you do for the parish.
Congratulations on your 14th Green flag award – a fantastic achievement that is thoroughly deserved. Here’s to many more years of protecting and enhancing our wonderful wildlife reserve.

https://cadentgas.com/news-media/news.text:
Ageing gas pipes are being replaced in Wivenhoe by engineers from Cadent – the UK’s largest gas distribution network.
The project will see more than 1,200 metres of ageing gas pipes originally laid in 1952 replaced in The Avenue, Spring Lane, Tower Road, Heath Road, Valfreda Way, Broome Grove, Cappillar Close, Spring Chase, Vanessa Drive, Chaney Road, Sonell Court, Bobbits Way, Phillip Road and High Street. The tough new pipes are designed to last for decades, helping to future-proof the local network.
Work gets underway on Monday 25 January 2027, with permits in place for 25 weeks.
Cadent has worked with Essex County Council to plan the essential work and minimise disruption as far as possible.
Traffic management will be needed during the works, but access will be maintained for residents. The arrangements include:
A public event will be held between 11am and 1pm on Thursday 26 November on the green at the corner of Grasby Close and Broome Grove, Wivenhoe, Colchester, CO7 9QU. It is an opportunity for residents and businesses to learn more about the scheme and ask any questions. There is no need to book an appointment – just turn up and chat with a member of the team.
Gas stays ON for the duration of the works. The only interruption to supply will be to properties that take a direct feed from the pipes being replaced (in the immediate local area). Supply to these properties will be disconnected for a short while (it will be back on the same day it goes off), as the property gets connected into the new pipe. Advance notice will be given, and more information will be provided to these properties.
If you smell gas, always ring the National Gas Emergency Service immediately on 0800 111 999*, day or night. Do not assume it is related to these works; it may not be and needs to be checked.

The cleansing power of fungus is being trialled in a pioneering project which could help tackle Britain’s river water quality crisis.
Researchers from the School of Life Sciences are testing whether mycelium, the root-like network of Fungi can support wetlands in filtering polluted water before it flows into rivers and other systems.
The study could offer an environmentally friendly way to tackle water pollution, helping protect aquatic wildlife and people enjoying Britain's waterways.
PhD researcher Lucinda Robinson , has helped create a 'living lab' at the University's Colchester Campus to put the natural filtration system to the test.
The sacks packed with mycelium used in the experiment
Lucinda Robinson testing water quality in the 'living lab'
Six experimental wetlands, known as mesocosms, were constructed to investigate whether adding mycelium to constructed wetlands can remove harmful bacteria, including E. coli, and excess nutrients that contribute to damaging algal blooms.
Over 12 weeks, the wetlands were subjected to controlled contamination, with researchers regularly monitoring water quality across a series of experiments.
Lucinda said: "Everyone deserves to be able to swim in natural water ways and enjoy nature without the risk of getting ill.
"This natural filtration method could help to improve water quality in our waterways.
"This is an exciting project that could have real benefits on the environment and really highlights how versatile and useful mycelium could be.
"Wetlands can help with this, and we want to know whether by adding mycelium we can support them to further enhance safety for recreational users, restore currently damaged aquatic habitats, all while creating new wetland habitats where wildlife can thrive."
Looking to the future - Lucinda hopes her work will have real impact
As part of her research Lucinda has also tested river water quality
Previous laboratory studies suggest mycelium can remove pollutants and neutralise bacteria without the need for synthetic treatments.
The Essex project aims to establish whether these promising findings can be replicated in real-world conditions, potentially paving the way for wider use of the natural treatment.
Lucinda is now analysing the results to assess how effectively the mycelium-treated wetlands remove pollutants compared with conventional constructed wetlands.
If successful, the approach could eventually be scaled up to help tackle water pollution across the country.
Professor Tom Cameron , who is supervising the project, said: “It’s a very exciting area of research, where increasingly we find that the natural world already has the capacity to provide functions and services that let us live healthier lives, if only we give it room to do so.
“It may mean living differently and accepting more of nature on our doorstep so that it can provide for us.”

A computer scientist who is using AI to detect skin cancer has been named in a top 50 power list of innovative researchers in the UK.
Universities UK (UUK) has highlighted Dr Haider Raza’s work in its 50 Future Innovators list, which celebrates the groundbreaking innovations and scientific breakthroughs that are reshaping industries such as healthcare and engineering.
UUK, which represents more than 140 universities, has launched the list as part of a campaign to push for further investment into higher education research.
Dr Raza, a Senior Lecturer in the University of Essex’s School of Computer Science and Electronic Engineering, has worked with Check 4 Cancer through a Knowledge Transfer Partnership (KTP) to create SKINTEL, a diagnostic tool that determines if suspicious lesions are malignant.
The tool, which is 99 per cent accurate, uses 22 patient characteristics and image analysis to deliver a diagnosis.
SKINTEL, designed to support clinicians and doctors rather than replace them, will speed up skin cancer diagnoses, reduce waiting times, and save lives by detecting the most dangerous skin lesions at the earliest opportunity.
Dr Raza said: “I'm honoured to be recognised as one of Universities UK's Future 50 Innovators.
“This recognition reflects the collaborative work undertaken with colleagues at the University of Essex, Check4Cancer and other partners to develop SKINTEL.
“What excites me most is the opportunity to demonstrate how trustworthy and explainable AI can deliver real-world impact in healthcare, helping clinicians and patients alike.”
UUK hopes its power list will inspire the next generation of innovators and secure more funding. It wants to see external investment in university innovation double to £100bn by 2035.
Professor Noam Lubell, Essex’s Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research, said: “Dr Raza has deservedly been recognised for his dedication to using AI in healthcare and is a wonderful example of the power of research at Essex.
“His work with Check 4 Cancer has the potential to transform skin cancer diagnostics around the world and ensure interventions are made at the earliest opportunity.
“Investment in Essex’s research has allowed our academics to work with businesses and organisations to come up with innovative ideas like Dr Raza’s. It is this kind of investment that is driving change in industries and allowing universities to make a real impact in people’s everyday lives.”
Alongside his work on SKINTEL, Dr Raza is the co-founder of Seniswise AI, which helps organisations assess their AI readiness and build custom, ethical AI and agentic systems for measurable business impact.
He has also advised UK policymakers on the use of AI in healthcare, as well as trained National Emergency Department professionals in emerging technologies.
Dr Raza is able to share his expertise and knowledge with students at Essex, where he teaches Data Science and decision-making. He also mentors postgraduate researchers.
Dr Raza added: “Beyond healthcare, this recognition also highlights my broader mission through Sensiwise AI to support organisations in adopting AI responsibly and effectively. Whether working with clinicians, businesses or policymakers, my goal is to ensure that AI remains transparent, accessible and focused on delivering meaningful societal benefit.”
Malcolm Press, President of Universities UK, said “UK universities sit at the cutting edge of the breakthroughs that define our age, from life-saving treatments and clean energy to artificial intelligence. The innovations coming out of our world-leading universities anchor Britain’s leadership in the industries that will power the global economy.
“These 50 future innovators, supported by universities the length and breadth of the UK, are just the tip of the iceberg. By celebrating these individuals and their innovations we hope to inspire the next generation of founders right across the country.”

A unique project exploring the life and legacy of one of Britain's most influential twentieth-century designers is being launched thanks to a partnership between the University of Essex and the Warner Textile Archive in Braintree.
The University’s School of Philosophical, Historical and Interdisciplinary Studies is seeking applicants for a fully funded doctoral studentship which will support a researcher to uncover the remarkable life and work of pioneering textile designer Marianne Straub, who worked for Warner & Sons in Essex for two decades from 1950 onwards.
Straub’s innovative designs helped shape everyday life in post-war Britain, appearing in London Underground trains, buses, airports, public buildings and homes nationwide, reflecting her belief that high-quality design should be accessible to everyone.
The successful applicant will become the first to study the Archive’s collection of design records, textile samples and business archives alongside her personal diaries and correspondence, helping to shed new light on the role of women, migration, industry and innovation in post-war Britain.
Dr Alix Green, who is lead supervisor alongside Dr Matthew Grant, said: “We’re delighted to be able to offer a studentship focused on a designer whose iconic fabrics furnished post-war Britain but whose life and work have been largely lost from view. It’s a project built on years of collaboration between historians at the University of Essex and the Warner Textile Archive – and one that will set Straub’s legacy within the county’s long weaving and design heritage.”
The new project, titled Fabric of Everyday Life: Marianne Straub, Textile Innovation and Design, 1950-1970, is supported by a prestigious Collaborative Doctoral Award and will give a doctoral researcher unprecedented access to a nationally significant collection of materials held by the Warner Textile Archive, alongside newly acquired personal papers that are yet to be fully catalogued.
As part of the project, the doctoral researcher will work closely with the Warner Textile Archive , the UK's largest publicly accessible archive of a single textile manufacturer. Located in Braintree, the archive preserves more than 150 years of textile manufacturing history and holds over 100,000 records, designs and artefacts linked to Warner & Sons and the wider British textile industry.
Straub's impact as a designer, innovator and educator will be explored through the project which will also examine wider themes of industrial decline and renewal, sustainability, globalisation, women's work, mass consumption and the changing nature of British identity after the Second World War.
Dr Sam Woodward, Digital Threads Project Manager at the Warner Textile Archive, said: “We are delighted to be working with the University of Essex to offer this postgraduate Collaborative Doctoral Award. As the first doctoral research project to explore the Marianne Straub Collection in such depth, it presents an exciting opportunity to generate new insights into the life and work of one of the twentieth century’s most significant, yet often overlooked, industrial designers.”
The research project forms part of Digital Threads, an ambitious programme at the Warner Textile Archive that is creating a comprehensive digital archive collection. The programme aims to transform access to the Archive’s collections, establish a nationally significant resource for design, education and research, and widen participation to help ensure their long-term sustainability.
Alongside their research, the doctoral candidate will gain hands-on professional experience in archival cataloguing, digitisation, conservation, public engagement and exhibition development. They will also contribute to educational and outreach activities designed to bring Straub's story to new audiences.
The deadline for applications is 10 February 2027.

Two scientists whose work spans how crops cope with drought and how emotions shape learning have been named among the world’s most influential researchers.
Professor Tracy Lawson features on Clarivate’s Highly Cited Researchers list for the seventh year running, while Professor Reinhard Pekrun has been named in every edition since 2024.
Clarivate estimates that around one in every 1,000 scientists and social scientists worldwide is recognised on the annual list.
Professor Lawson, from the School of Life Sciences , develops ways to measure how plants photosynthesise and use water.
Her work helps researchers understand how crops respond to heat and drought and identify traits that could make them more resilient.
Earlier this year, she received the Innovation Award from the International Society of Photosynthesis Research .
Professor Lawson said: “I am delighted to be included in this list for another year - this is only possible due to the hard work and dedication of everyone in the lab and the support of colleagues and collaborators.”
Professor Pekrun, from the Department of Psychology , has pioneered research into the role of emotions in learning. His work explores how feelings such as enjoyment, anxiety and boredom affect students’ motivation and performance.
Professor Pekrun said: “I feel deeply honoured by receiving this recognition again. The recognition is based on teamwork and attests to the invaluable support I received from colleagues, students, and professional staff at Essex in pursuing our research on human emotions.”
Professor Noam Lubell , Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research, said: “Having two academics named among the world’s Highly Cited Researchers is a brilliant achievement.
“Both Professor Lawson and Professor Pekrun are helping to shape what other researchers investigate and where their fields go next.
“They exemplify what makes the University of Essex so special and their work showcases our global reputation, reach and impact.
“I’m delighted to see both colleagues get the international recognition they deserve.”
Clarivate looks at how often other researchers cite their work, drawing on papers published between 2015 and 2025, and considers the breadth of their influence and the integrity of publication and citation patterns.
This year, Clarivate awarded 7,090 Highly Cited Researcher designations to 6,802 individuals from more than 1,200 institutions across 62 countries and regions. Some researchers were recognised in more than one field.

The University of Essex is currently considering a potential arrangement with the Ministry of Defence and Colchester Garrison regarding the use of a small section of our Colchester Campus. This would provide accommodation at The Houses for Ministry of Defence personnel for two years.
Due to lower student numbers, the University has surplus accommodation on its Campus so is looking at a variety of appropriate alternative uses.
Any revenue would be reinvested to support the University’s educational and research missions.
Deputy Vice-Chancellor Professor Chris Greer said: “No decision has been made on whether to proceed. Further work is being undertaken to understand its potential implications, practical requirements and suitability for the University community. As part of this process, we will continue discussions with the Ministry of Defence, the Students' Union and other relevant stakeholders.
“We have a proud history of working with civic and local partners, and this is one of several options we are exploring for the future use of surplus accommodation capacity. In doing so, we are seeking to balance our responsibilities to students and staff, our role as a civic institution, and the need to generate sustainable income to support our education and research activities.
“Any decision would be subject to careful consideration. We would only proceed if we were satisfied that the arrangement was in the best interests of the University community and will keep staff and students informed as these discussions progress.”
An Army spokesperson said: “We are committed to looking after our soldiers and will always strive to provide the best quality accommodation available. Colchester Garrison is exploring options to provide housing that delivers best value for money and relieves pressure on the local housing market. Discussions are being held with the University of Essex about the use of surplus student accommodation, but no agreement has been reached.”

An open letter to the government signed by close to 150 researchers, health chiefs and charities is calling for the new Mental Health Strategy for England to focus more on the places most affected by inequality.
Signatories, including the chief executives of Mind, YoungMinds, Place2Be and the Centre for Mental Health, are concerned the strategy will not fully reflect the challenges faced by coastal, rural and former industrial communities.
They warn that research, expertise and lived experience from these areas are being underrepresented in national policy discussions.
The letter to Social Care and Mental Health minister Alison McGovern MP is being coordinated by Professor Susan McPherson and Professor Victoria Bird from the Institute for Public Health and Wellbeing at the University of Essex.
Their research shows young adults in the most deprived coastal areas are three times more likely to experience undiagnosed mental distress than those in equally deprived inland areas.
Professor McPherson said: “Our research at Essex has shown that young people growing up in deprived coastal communities face particular disadvantages compared with their inland peers, highlighting that geography, as well as deprivation, can shape mental health outcomes.
“Excellent mental health research is taking place right across the country, and national policy should reflect that diversity of insight.”
The letter warns that mental health inequalities are shaped not only by individual characteristics and deprivation, but by access to local jobs, transport, housing, education, community infrastructure and other services.
It also notes that, based on publicly available affiliations, seven in ten contributors to the government’s Independent Review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism were based in London, Oxford or Cambridge.
The letter’s signatories include more than 60 professors from universities across England, many of them leading experts in health inequalities.
Professor McPherson added: “To reduce inequalities effectively, England’s mental health strategy must draw on the full breadth of expertise, evidence and lived experience across the country, rather than being disproportionately influenced by a small number of places and institutions.”
The researchers are asking government to recognise geographical inequalities in the strategy and to consider insight from a more diverse range of research leaders, local partners and people with lived experience from the areas most affected.
They are also calling for funding for local authority public health teams to invest in community-led mental health work, and for the Prevention Concordat for Better Mental Health to be revived and refreshed.
Other signatories include former Minister for Care and Support Sir Norman Lamb and leaders from universities, councils and Healthwatch organisations across England.
The team, alongside Dr Emily Murray , Director of the Centre for Coastal Communities at Essex, also set out evidence on mental health in coastal areas in a response published in the BMJ this month.
Their research found that among young people in the most deprived fifth of areas in England, those who grew up on the coast reported mental functioning scores 3.7 points lower than their inland peers.

A protein in the gut may hold the key to why bowel cancer affects men and women differently so an international research team is investigating to see if it could unlock better treatment.
Professor Patrick Varga-Weisz from the University of Essex is leading the four-year £1.2m project, which is jointly funded by the São Paulo Research Foundation and the UK’s Medical Research Council.
The work centres on a specific protein that helps package DNA inside our cells and decides which genes are switched on or off.
Professor Varga-Weisz said: “We’ve found that this protein acts as a kind of master switch for genes in the bowel that are controlled by sex hormones.
“If we can understand how it links gut bacteria to those genes and helps limit inflammation, we open up a genuinely new way of thinking about preventing cancer.”
Bowel cancer is more common in men than women, with around 26,800 new cases in men and 21,400 in women in the UK each year, according to Cancer Research UK.
Once differences in age are taken into account, men are also around one and a half times more likely than women to die from the disease.
The researchers believe the protein sits where three major influences on gut health meet: the bacteria living in our intestines, the chemicals those bacteria produce and the body’s own hormones.
Their theory is that it helps protect the gut lining, stopping the build-up of damaged cells that could later turn into tumours.
The team will investigate how the protein does this and why its effects differ between the sexes, with the aim of opening up new routes to drugs, diets or supplements that could lower cancer risk.
While the study will focus on the gut, the protein is also active in other tissues, so the findings could matter well beyond bowel disease.
Professor Varga-Weisz, from the School of Life Sciences at Essex, is working with researchers at Quadram Institute, Queen Mary University of London and the University of Campinas in Brazil.
He added: “This work brings together expertise from different fields across two continents, and we hope it has a real prospect of improving health.”
Quadram Institute, on the Norwich Research Park, specialises in food, gut health and the microbiome, while the University of Campinas is one of Latin America’s leading universities.

Virtual reality could help helicopter rescue crews safely prepare for life-or-death emergencies that are too dangerous to recreate in the air, new research suggests.
Researchers from the Department of Psychology worked with Air Rescue UK to investigate how virtual and mixed reality technology could complement traditional training for helicopter hoist operators.
These highly skilled crew members operate the helicopter hoist during rescues, directing pilots while simultaneously monitoring weather, obstacles, aircraft movement and the safety of people being rescued.
Live-flight training is expensive and carries inherent risks, while some extreme situations, including severe weather, equipment failures and dangerous sea conditions, cannot safely be deliberately recreated.
Researchers found immersive simulation could offer a safe and cost-effective way for crews to repeatedly practise these rare but critical emergencies without putting people or aircraft at risk.
Dr Claire Oakley , Research Associate on the project, said: “What is exciting about virtual reality is that it allows us to study decision-making under pressure in a safe and controlled way.
“Better understanding these processes in this environment could help us design more effective training for rescue crews.”
The project, supported by the University of Essex Innovation Fund , evaluated Air Rescue UK’s mixed-reality simulator alongside a comprehensive review of existing research.
The technology combines a virtual environment with physical equipment, including a hoist cable that recreates the tension and movement operators experience during real missions.
It means trainees can practise emergencies including runaway winches, fouled cables, engine failures and emergency hoist cuts, as well as challenging environmental conditions.
Feedback from operators was overwhelmingly positive, with up to 92 per cent of post-training evaluations showing trainees felt they had learned something new or refined existing skills.
Researchers also found the level of mental challenge experienced during simulations was linked to how much operators felt they learned.
This suggests training could eventually be tailored to experience, with novices gradually introduced to increasingly complex situations while experienced operators face more demanding, time-pressured emergencies.
A spokesperson for Air Rescue UK said: “Air Rescue UK are pleased with the early results from this partnership with University of Essex which has laid the groundwork for the future in developing training processes within helicopter hoist simulation that meet the needs, firstly of the individual student or experienced hoist operator, and also of the helicopter operators, industry and the regulator.
“By applying academic rigour to simulation training, to get the best out of users, will translate directly to operational performance.”
The next phase of the partnership will explore how simulator training can be personalised, objectively measure stress and mental workload, and assess whether skills developed during simulation translate into live operations.
The project was led by Professor Miroslav Sirota , in collaboration with Dr Claire Oakley and Professor Marie Juanchich at the University of Essex, as well as Dr Motonori Yamaguchi, now at Shimane University, Japan, alongside Ian Bonthrone MSc of Air Rescue UK.
