United Nations Special Rapporteur Dr Koldo Casla has helped shape new housing laws in Spain following a high-profile homeless case which sparked nationwide protests and triggered a national election.
Dr Koldo Casla , a Senior Lecturer at Essex Law School and the Human Rights Centre, engaged constructively with government ministers in the wake of 87-year-old, Maricarmen Abascal’s eviction from her home.
A decree-law that aims to give better protections to vulnerable tenants has since been passed, with the Minister for Housing, Isabel Rodriguez, highlighting Dr Casla’s contribution to the new law in Parliament.
Dr Casla’s intervention came in his capacity as the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Adequate Housing.
Dr Casla was appointed Special Rapporteur by the UN Human Rights Council in March 2026.
He has the responsibility of assisting the United Nations and Member States in implementing laws and policies to satisfy the right to housing.
As well as numerous high-profile media appearances in Spain, Dr Casla engaged with the authorities to push for legal changes to ensure there is no repeat of the Maricarmen case.
His representations included the urgent need for new legislation to protect the vulnerable from eviction, the introduction of mandatory proportionality tests in all evictions, and tighter anti-speculation measures in Spain’s housing market.
Dr Casla said: “Maricarmen’s case was a painful reminder that Spain’s law had significant shortcomings in relation to the right to housing.
"I am determined to continue collaborating with whatever future government after the election of 29 November to fulfil the promise of article 47 of the Spanish Constitution, which proclaims the right to housing.”
Alongside his work in Spain, Dr Casla made an official 12-day visit to Ghana in October as Special Rapporteur, where he urged the government to introduce stronger protections for tenants, put an end to forced evictions, set realistic targets for affordable housing, and encourage the use of locally sourced materials in construction.
Dr Casla is also preparing his first thematic report for the UN Human Rights Council on a topic that resonates with Human Rights Local, a project of Essex’s Human Rights Centre, which he launched in 2020.
The report will explore best practices from local governments and community-led initiatives around the world to make the human rights to housing real and effective at the local level.
Dr Casla’s work at the United Nations is informed by his research on the social function of housing, including his most recent book The Social Right to Property.

A marine biologist whose pioneering research has uncovered some of the ocean’s most elusive creatures has helped shine a light on the mysteries of the deep for the BBC’s Blue Planet III.
Dr Michelle Taylor , from the School of Life Sciences , advised producers behind the Sir David Attenborough-fronted smash hit.
Dr Taylor helped shape Sunday’s episode, which ventures into the depths of the oceans to explore what has been described as “the last great frontier on earth”.
The Senior Lecturer, who is also Head of Science at Ocean Census , reviewed the science and connected the production team with other experts.
Her expertise was sought following pioneering research that has led to the discovery of coral reefs in Antarctica and helped capture the only confirmed footage of a colossal squid in the wild .
She has also had a species of coral , seaspider, and sea cucumber named in her honour.
Dr Taylor said: “It’s always a pleasure to work with the BBC Natural History unit and I’m thrilled that Blue Planet III is being aired – the cinematography and story-telling when applied to the deep-sea animals brings that relatively unknown realm to life.
“The deep-sea is the largest habitat on Earth and has a plethora of ecosystems that this episode highlights. I’m thrilled that so many exciting animal stories of the deep will be shown to the world.”
Explore the gallery below to relive some of Dr Taylor's exciting expeditions
Dr Michelle Taylor and Oenone Scott on board
The episode, which airs on November 29, and is live on iPlayer , explored the Pacific and Arctic ocean basins. It showcases a range of creatures, including the ‘flying spaghetti monster’, a young female argonaut, and forests of hidden coral.
This is the second time Dr Taylor has worked with producers, helping the team behind Blue Planet II in 2017 as well.
Away from the series national treasure Sir David is no stranger to Essex, having been awarded an honorary degree in 1987 .
Professor Terry McGenity , Head of the School of Life Sciences, said: “The deep ocean has a remarkable array of different habitats.
“Its inhabitants are vital for life on Earth, from abundant microbes, recycling nutrients, controlling climate, providing medicines and underpinning food webs, to the amazing and enigmatic animals that Dr Taylor and her team are discovering.
“It is hoped that Blue Planet III will inspire the current and next generation of leaders to create joined-up policy that better recognises the connectedness of all habitats on Earth, and that considers both biodiversity and climate.
“In the School of Life Sciences, we share our excellent research with students, the wider world and policy makers. "Dr Michelle Taylor’s expert contributions help to shed light on the (mostly) dark, deep ocean in an entertaining and thought-provoking way.”

The UK's busiest online shopping period is almost here. From Black Friday and Cyber Monday through to Christmas shopping and January sales, millions of parcels will be delivered to homes across the country over the coming months.
For many households, these deliveries contain gifts, electronics, clothing and other high-value purchases. But the surge in online shopping also creates opportunities for opportunistic thieves targeting unattended parcels left on doorsteps, driveways and communal entrances.
This autumn, Crimestoppers and Ring are encouraging people to think about parcel security as part of their wider approach to staying safe at home. Our partnership is focused on helping communities feel safer, sharing practical advice and reducing opportunities for crime.
Parcel theft can be more than a financial inconvenience. For many people, deliveries contain important items, gifts for loved ones, medication or purchases that have been carefully saved for.
After ordering several Christmas presents during Black Friday sales, Amy returned from work to discover a delivery had disappeared from her doorstep.
"The cost was frustrating, but it was the feeling that someone had come onto my property and taken something that really stayed with me," she says.
Following the incident, Amy arranged for parcels to be delivered to a secure collection point when she wasn't home, asked neighbours to accept deliveries and installed a video doorbell to help her keep track of visitors.
Whilst fictional, Amy's experience reflects concerns many households share during the festive shopping season.
Community awareness also matters. Neighbours looking out for neighbours can help deter opportunistic offending and create a stronger sense of security across a street. This is a key message at the heart of partnership work, promoting practical community action to help make neighbourhoods safer.
The excitement of seasonal shopping should be about finding the perfect gift, not worrying about whether it will arrive safely. By taking a few simple precautions, households can reduce risk and enjoy the festive season with greater peace of mind.
Anyone with information about theft, criminal activity or repeat offending in their area can contact Crimestoppers anonymously, online here on our website or by calling 0800 555 111.

As autumn arrives and we prepare for the clocks to go back, millions of people across the UK will find themselves travelling to and from work, school and social activities in darkness. Shorter days and longer nights can affect how safe people feel, both at home and within their local communities.
October also marks National Home Security Month, an annual opportunity for households to review how they protect their homes, possessions and loved ones. As many families prepare for the darker months ahead, it's an ideal time to think about simple steps that can help reduce opportunities for crime and increase peace of mind.
That's why Crimestoppers and Ring are launching a new partnership focused on helping people protect what matters most: their families, homes and neighbourhoods. While our organisations have different roles, we share a common goal of helping people feel safer and more connected to their communities.
As an independent charity, Crimestoppers gives people the power to speak up about crime anonymously, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. We also provide practical crime prevention advice to help people stay safe and reduce opportunities for crime.
The partnership builds on the success of Safe Street, our community safety campaign which encourages neighbours, charities, businesses and local organisations to work together to help make communities safer.
Criminals often look for easy opportunities, such as poorly lit entrances, unlocked doors, visible valuables or homes that appear unoccupied.
When Hannah, a teacher from Nottingham, started arriving home after dark every evening, she became increasingly concerned about the poorly lit alleyway beside her property. After speaking with neighbours, she installed additional outdoor lighting, secured a rear gate and joined a local online neighbourhood group.
"It wasn't about being fearful," she says. "It was about feeling prepared. We all started talking more as neighbours and keeping an eye out for one another."
While Hannah's story is fictional, the actions she took reflect practical measures that experts regularly recommend.
According to Neighbourhood Watch, homes combining good locks, indoor timer lights and external security lighting can significantly reduce burglary risk.
As we move into the darker months, keeping communities safe is something everyone can play a part in. Whether that's improving security around your home, checking in on vulnerable neighbours or sharing information about crime anonymously, small actions can make a meaningful difference.
If you have information about crime and want to remain anonymous, contact Crimestoppers online, here on our website , or call 0800 555 111 . In an emergency, always call 999 .

You might have received an email claiming to be from a bank or someone claiming to have an urgent unpaid invoice. Other scams may look as though they come from one of your social networks.
So how do you avoid being scammed? How can you protect yourself from becoming a victim of phishing?
If money has been lost or financial information has been provided as a result of a phishing scam, tell your bank immediately and report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or by calling 0300 123 2040 . In Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101 .

Despite this, unscrupulous vendors will continue to sell these products illegally, likely in cash-only transactions at convenience stores, market stalls, online platforms, and even in places like barbershops and phone repair kiosks. These products pose serious health risks – they are unregulated, untested, and may contain dangerously high levels of nicotine and harmful substances such as lead and nickel.
Shops found to be flouting single-use vape ban
Criminal gangs are increasingly involved in the illicit vape market, using these illegal sales to fund other serious crimes, including drug trafficking, human trafficking, and money laundering. Disturbingly, vulnerable individuals, especially minors, are being exploited through coercive practices, with some children being pressured into buying or selling illicit vapes in exchange for money or favours.
Crimestoppers is committed to protecting communities by encouraging the public to stay alert and provide anonymous information about illegal vape activity. Your tip-off can help prevent harm and dismantle criminal networks.

Residents across the North East are being encouraged to take some simple steps to protect their homes from costly burst pipes, as temperatures swing between chilly spells and milder weather.
After a spell of cold conditions, with milder weather forecast early next week before dipping again, Northumbrian Water is reminding households that changes in temperature can put extra pressure on pipes, both inside homes and across the wider network.
When temperatures drop below freezing, water inside pipes can freeze and expand. As temperatures change again and the ice thaws, pipes and the ground around them can move, increasing the risk of cracks, leaks and bursts.
To help prevent burst pipes at home, the water company is encouraging residents to:
Alongside helping customers protect their homes, Northumbrian Water’s teams work across the region finding and fixing leaks, repairing nearly 10,000 leaks so far this year.
With thousands of kilometres of water mains to look after, customers can also play an important part by reporting any water they spot where it shouldn’t be.
Carly Gray, Head of Water Networks at Northumbrian Water, said: “Cold weather can be tough on pipes, particularly when temperatures start moving up and down, and a burst at home is the last thing anyone wants.
“Taking a few simple steps now to wrap exposed pipes and check your stop tap works can help save a lot of stress and costly damage later.
“Our teams are also keeping a close eye on conditions and working around the clock to respond to leaks and bursts across our network as quickly as we can.
“If you’re out and about and spot any puddles or running water where it shouldn’t be, please let us know so we can investigate.”
Customers can report leaks online at www.nwl.co.uk/leaks or by calling Northumbrian Water on 0800 393 084.
Once a leak is reported, teams prioritise repairs based on customer impact, traffic management and how much water is being lost.
Urgent bursts in the network affecting customers’ supplies or safety must come first, while smaller leaks can take a little longer, especially if roadworks are needed.
For more winter weather advice, visit www.nwl.co.uk/winter .

Northumbrian Water completes £2.6m investment at Seahouses Sewage Treatment Works
The significant investment was completed at Seahouses Sewage Treatment Works by the water company's delivery partner Mott MacDonald Bentley (MMB) earlier this month (NOV).
The vital work is now helping to maintain resilient wastewater services for the Northumberland coastal community, while also supporting the long-term protection of the local environment and water quality.
A key part of the project involved refurbishing the site’s central distribution chamber. The chamber receives incoming flow and divides it equally across the treatment units on site.
To allow the work to be carried out safely, flows through the treatment works were transferred onto a temporary over pumping system, allowing the chamber to be isolated and drained while remaining fully operational. Damaged concrete was then removed and the structure refurbished.
Joe Williamson, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said:
“It’s great to reach the end of this important investment at Seahouses.
“Carrying out significant refurbishment within a live sewage treatment works takes careful planning and teamwork, and throughout the project our priority has been to complete the improvements safely while keeping the site fully operational.
“The work we have delivered will help make the treatment works more resilient and ensure it can continue providing an essential service for Seahouses and the surrounding area, while supporting the long-term protection of the local environment."

The project will see approximately 3km of new water main installed near Waren Mill Caravan Park, helping to provide a more resilient water supply for customers in the area.
Work is currently scheduled to begin on Monday 30 November 2026. Northumbrian Water’s delivery partner, United Infrastructure, will carry out the work.
The investment is targeting an area of the existing network which has experienced water pressure and capacity challenges in the past. The new water pipes will strengthen the network, improve resilience, and help support future demand.
Rach Graves, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said:
“This is an important investment at Waren Mill that will help improve water pressure for customers and businesses.
“We understand how important access is for local residents and businesses, and we’ll be working closely with our delivery partner to minimise disruption wherever possible.
“We would like to thank the community in advance for their patience and understanding while we carry out these essential improvements.”
Local traffic management will be required when the work is carried out.
A clearly signposted diversion route will be in place to minimise disruption to residents, businesses and road users throughout the project. Follow project updates on Northumbian Water's community hub page: Waren Mill Belford | Northumbrian Water

The water company is reminding customers its free leaky loo repair service is available, as part of its ongoing work to save water this winter.
A single leaking toilet can waste up to 215 litres of clean water every day – adding around £200 a year to water bills for those on a water meter.
To help households save water and money, Northumbrian Water’s technicians are offering free home visits across the region to fix leaking toilets.
Marked annually on 19 November, the United Nations’ World Toilet Day highlights the importance of safe toilets and sanitation, and protecting precious global resources.
While millions around the world still lack access to basic facilities, leaky loos are one of the most common, and easily fixable, causes of wasted water in UK homes.
Olivia Marsh, Water Efficiency Analyst at Northumbrian Water, said: “World Toilet Day is a great reminder of just how vital clean water and decent sanitation are, yet many of us take our loos for granted.
“Leaky loos are huge water wasters and because the water usually trickles silently from the cistern into the back of the pan, they can go unnoticed for months, wasting hundreds of litres of water a day.
“We’re pleased to bring back our free leaky loo repair service to make fixing them as easy as possible for our customers. Taking two minutes to do a quick check at home could save a lot of water and knock hundreds of pounds off your annual bill.”
Leaking toilets are often silent, but customers can spot a leak using the tissue test. Simply place a piece of toilet paper on the back of a dried toilet bowl, just below the rim. If it remains dry, it’s ok. If it sticks or is wet, then there could be a leak.
Customers who spot a leak can book their free repair visit online at www.nwl.co.uk/leakyloos or by calling Northumbrian Water’s dedicated team on 0800 953 0130 .
Those unsure whether their toilet is leaking can even send the company a short video of their toilet from their smartphone via the website for a quick assessment.
Businesses and other non-household customers can also get help to identify and repair leaking toilets, by emailing savingwater@nwl.co.uk

Network Operations Manager, Ian Wade, from Crook, was just 17 when he joined the company as a plumber’s mate on 15 November 1976, beginning a career that would span 50 years.
Back then, Northumbrian Water’s main depot was just across the road from his family home in Bearpark, meaning Ian was able to walk to work on his very first day.
He collected his allocated vehicle and headed to the team’s sub-depot on North Road in Durham – now The Water House pub - to meet his new boss and colleagues.
But while getting to work was usually easy, getting from there to some of the day’s jobs could be a little less straightforward.
If there wasn’t a vehicle available, Ian and plumber Gordon Dazzley would just gather up the kit they needed, leave the North Road depot and catch the bus.
Ian said: “ I always remember sitting on the front seat of the bus with my arm cradled around a toilet bowl, heading off to a job.
“We’d have pipes at our feet and all sorts. We’d hop off the bus, do the plumbing and repairs, then get on another bus and make our way to the next job.
“We must have looked a sight, but we didn’t think much of it, it’s just what we did. You certainly wouldn’t see that these days.”
Ian’s interest in the water industry began at an early age, after watching a crew lay a major new water main from Auton Style reservoir to Durham City right past his childhood home.
After a short stint as a heating engineer straight from school, Ian began his career at Northumbrian Water Authority as it was then, moving from plumbing into repairs and excavation, learning the different sides of the job as he went.
He even taught himself to operate a JCB during his lunch breaks. He said: “Things were different in the early days, if there was something you wanted to learn, you’d get stuck in and learn it.
“I wanted to get my head around driving a JCB, so when the crews were stopped for their dinners, I’d just hop on and teach myself – you couldn’t do that now!”
Over the decades, Ian worked his way from the crews into operational and management roles. Today he is Network Operations Manager, overseeing a team of 92 employees helping to keep the water flowing across the region.
Among his many memories is being bussed up to Kielder in 1982 to watch Queen Elizabeth II officially open the reservoir.
However, Ian says his greatest source of pride has always been serving the communities where he and his colleagues live.
He said: “Over the years, many things have changed. But a pipe is still a pipe and what is inside it is something that people need every single day.
“We drink the same water as our customers and we're part of the communities we serve. That's always mattered to me.
“There are people working incredibly hard behind the scenes, often in difficult conditions, to make sure customers have clean, wholesome water when they turn on the tap and I’ve always been very proud to be part of that.”
Ian admitted that deciding to retire after half a century hadn’t been easy, but he has plenty of things to keep him busy, including finishing a long-running house-build project.
His advice to someone just starting their career today is simple. He said: “Don’t expect everything to happen overnight. Build your experience, build your knowledge and build relationships with people. Take the opportunities that come along and keep learning.”
Kieran Ingram, Water Director at Northumbrian Water, said: “Fifty years with one company is an extraordinary achievement!
“Ian has been part of an enormous amount of change during that time but more importantly he’s built up a huge amount of knowledge and experience which he’s shared with people around him.
“We’re incredibly grateful for everything he’s done over the last 50 years and wish him all the very best for his retirement.”
Ian retires 19 November, 50 years and four days after starting his Northumbrian Water career.

The milestone comes as Essex & Suffolk Water continues its smart metering programme across the area, helping customers use water more efficiently and protect local resources for the future.
Now, the water firm’s community engagement team is heading out across the area to meet customers face-to-face, answer any questions about the smart metering programme and share practical water-saving advice.
The team will be holding a series of local sessions at village halls and community spaces, many of them alongside the Rural Coffee Caravan, a free service that helps rurally isolated people in Suffolk access services and information.
Happening throughout November and December, customers will be able to drop in for a chat over a cup of tea or coffee, find out more about smart meters and pick up simple tips to help reduce water use at home.
Smart meters send readings to Essex & Suffolk Water automatically which customers can keep track of, helping them to understand how much water they use and highlighting changes in usage that could indicate a leak.
This can help households avoid wasting water and identify problems sooner, saving money on bills in the process.
Since the hosepipe ban began in August, households on a smart meter in Hartismere, have saved 64 litres of water per day – equivalent to about five large buckets full of water - helping to reduce demand on local water supplies.
Dominic Butcher, Head of Metering at Essex & Suffolk Water, said: "Most customers in Hartismere have already made the move to smart metering and we’re really grateful to customers for their support as the programme continues.
"For many people, seeing their water use can help them spot simple ways to save water, which is good for both the environment and their household budget too.
"We know some people still have questions about smart meters, so these community events are a great opportunity to come along, meet the team and find out more about metering and water-saving.”

The Power Resilience programme focuses on sewage treatment works and pumping stations considered particularly vulnerable to power interruptions, mainly located in rural areas. The investment is designed to reduce the risk of disruption leading to pollution incidents or issues with the performance of treatment sites.
The need for greater resilience has been highlighted by severe weather in recent years including Storm Eowyn (2025) and Storm Dave (2026), which brought strong winds and disruption to electricity supplies in the North East.
As part of the programme, the company is introducing back up power solutions for critical wastewater sites so key processes can continue during an unplanned loss of mains electricity.
This work complements other significant investments being delivered to strengthen wastewater infrastructure across the North East in rural areas such as Seahouses, in Northumberland.
Chris Clark, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said:
“Our wastewater sites provide an essential service around the clock, so building greater resilience into them is really important.
“Power interruptions can put additional pressure on treatment works and pumping stations, particularly during severe weather, and this investment is about making sure we’re better prepared when those situations arise.
“We’re looking at the right solution for each site, helping our teams keep vital wastewater processes operating while reducing the risk of disruption and protecting the environment.
“This investment is part of our wider commitment to make our wastewater infrastructure stronger and more resilient for the communities it serves.”

Work is expected to begin on Monday 9 November until May 2027 and will help reduce the number of storm overflow spills and improve water quality in the River Wansbeck.
The project will see new underground stormwater storage installed near the existing pumping station at Sheepwash Road, alongside associated pipework and chambers.
The new storage will provide additional capacity within the wastewater network. This means that during periods of heavy rainfall, pressure will be eased on the system, helping to reduce storm overflow discharges to the environment.
The work will be carried out by Northumbrian Water's delivery partner Avove.
Rachael Clifford, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said:
“This is an important investment for the area, which will provide additional capacity in our wastewater network and help reduce storm overflow spills - supporting our wider work to protect and improve the River Wansbeck.
“We know the field at Cleasewell Hill is valued and used by local people, so we understand there will be some inconvenience while we carry out this essential work.
“Once the project is complete, we will reinstate the affected area and continue to keep the community informed as the work progresses.
“We have already had the opportunity to speak directly with residents about the project, and their feedback has been really valuable. We will continue working with the community as the project progresses and look at opportunities to create a positive legacy from our work.”
Project updates are available on Northumbrian Waters community hub page: Project: Cambois Environmental Improvements

This Talk Money Week (2-6 November), Northumbrian Water is encouraging customers who may be struggling financially to check what help is available, with support ranging from discounted tariffs, flexible payment plans, payment breaks and independent advice.
Some customers could be eligible for discounts of up to 50% off their annual water bill if their household has a total income of less than £30,000.
Meanwhile, the company’s WaterSure tariff may help metered customers who have high essential water use due to a medical condition or larger family.
More than 126,000 customers across the region are already receiving help with their water bills, backed by a £100 million support package set aside by the firm through to 2030.
Mark Wilkinson, Head of Income for Northumbrian Water, said: "We know money can be a real worry, particularly as we head into the colder months when household costs can increase.
"But some customers could be missing out on support simply because they don’t realise they’re eligible. That’s why Talk Money Week is a good opportunity to check what help is available.
“No one should be worrying about paying their water bill and we'd encourage anyone who is concerned to get in touch and talk to us.
“We have lots of schemes available and many people are often surprised to find out they qualify for help.”
For more information about the support available and to check eligibility, visit: www.nwl.co.uk/bill-help

The start of work on upgrades at a sewage treatment works (STW) marks the latest milestone in more than £100m of investment to protect and improve the River Wear in the South West of County Durham.
Northumbrian Water is investing £20m in enhancements to the treatment processes at Bishop Auckland STW, building on similar work that has already started at sites in nearby Low Wadsworth and Willington.
Additional projects are also being planned in all three areas to reduce spills from storm overflows, adding further protection and improvements to the river.
Upgrades at Bishop Auckland STW will see the treated water that’s returned to the environment via the river improved even further, with the introduction of processes that will increase the site’s ability to remove phosphorous and ammonia.
Work at Bishop Auckland STW is being carried out by Northumbrian Water’s partner, Costain, and is expected to run until early 2028.
Dean Thompson, Northumbrian Water’s Project Manager, said: “Investment to protect and improve the River Wear is part of a £2bn programme of work to benefit the environment, and reflects our ambition for the North East to have the best coasts and rivers in the country.
“The treatment works will take place within our site, but as our plans to reduce spills from the storm overflows take shape, we will work to help the community know what to expect from those works when they take place.”
Customers can follow progress on the Bishop Auckland works at Project: Bishop Auckland Wastewater Treatment Works | Northumbrian Water – or navigate to the Willington and Low Wadsworth projects to see updates from that work.

A North East business leader has become the first person ever to achieve a new qualification designed to help organisations deliver better services for customers.
Louise Hunter, Director of Customer and Corporate Services at Northumbrian Water, has been awarded the Institute of Customer Service's (ICS) Mini-MBA in Strategic Service Leadership.
The first-of-its-kind in the UK, the qualification is aimed specifically at senior customer service leaders and has been designed to strengthen leadership, improve customer experiences and ensure customers remain at the heart of decision-making.
Northumbrian Water was one of ten organisations involved in helping ICS to develop the programme, as well as shaping the content and developing the new online learning platform, Portis, which hosts it.
Louise said: “I’m really pleased to have achieved this qualification, and especially to be the first person to do so.
“It has been a stretching and hugely valuable learning experience, giving me the opportunity to share best practice in customer service with other leading companies like First Direct and Hays Travel.
“The programme assignments have given me the luxury of the time and the tools to reflect on how Northumbrian Water can continue to deliver an unrivalled customer experience every single day.
“I feel very fortunate to work for an employer who invests in the skills and knowledge of its people by supporting programmes like the ICS mini-MBA and I’m delighted that I could be involved in helping to shape the programme via my role on the steering group.
“I hope the programme goes on to inspire and support other future customer service leaders.”
Louise was presented with her award at a prestigious ceremony at the House of Lords in London on Monday 19 October, where ICS also launched Portis.
Her achievement reflects Northumbrian Water's commitment to supporting its employees to develop throughout their careers and helping to ensure customers continue to receive the best possible service.

The company offers a range of support for any customers who may need a little extra help, including a password scheme designed to provide reassurance for homeowners when answering the door.
The password service allows customers to choose a unique password which Northumbrian Water employees will provide when they visit, helping to protect themselves from bogus callers posing as water company workers.

A gruelling climb up the UK’s highest mountain by Northumbrian Water volunteers has helped provide life-saving equipment for a North East bereavement therapy service.
Eleven water workers took on the challenge of climbing Ben Nevis in July, raising more than £1,240 for the Stephen Carey Fund, a charity that provides defibrillators, first aid equipment and emergency training to local communities.
Their efforts have now helped buy a defibrillator for Elemental Occupational Therapy, which provides outdoor bereavement support for children and adults.
The device will be carried by occupational therapist Cath Darling, whose work often takes place in nature-based settings, where access to emergency medical equipment can be limited.
She said: "My work often takes me into forests, riversides and remote trails - beautiful places that offer peace and healing, but they're often far from immediate medical support.
"I had been looking at ways to purchase a defibrillator, as sudden cardiac arrest can happen to anyone, and having a defibrillator on hand can increase survival rates dramatically.
“The donation from the Stephen Carey Fund came as a real surprise and has been incredibly gratefully received. It will now travel with me to every session, workshop and group activity, giving my clients reassurance that their wellbeing is always my priority."
The idea for the challenge came from Northumbrian Water’s Scott McEwan, who volunteers with the Stephen Carey Fund and wanted to support the charity through the water company’s Just an Hour volunteering scheme.
He said: "We set ourselves the target of raising enough money for the Stephen Carey Fund to purchase a defibrillator for a community or good cause. We needed a challenge big enough to help achieve that goal and when Ben Nevis was suggested, everyone jumped at the opportunity.
"The hike was enjoyable but definitely challenging, especially towards the summit as the weather changed and tired legs started to kick in. It was a fantastic experience and we're hugely grateful to everyone who supported us.
"To see the money turned into something that could genuinely help save a life is really special. We're proud to be able to support the amazing work Cath carries out helping children and adults through bereavement."
Some members of the fundraising team recently met Cath to hand over the defibrillator and hear how their efforts could make a real difference to people accessing bereavement support across the North East.

New eel screens to boost wildlife protection on Northumberland River
The £11.8 million project will protect the local wildlife and the safe migration of European eels by preventing them from entering the pumping station.
The project is being carried out by the water company’s partner, Mott Macdonald Bentley (MMB) and will be complete in December 2028.
The screens, which will be installed at the site’s water abstraction point, support the safe passage of eels as they move through the River North Tyne, helping to protect local populations and meet environmental requirements.
European eels are listed as critically endangered, with numbers having declined significantly in recent decades due to a range of factors including habitat loss, barriers to migration, climate change and overfishing. Installing eel screens is an important measure that helps to support the eel population’s recovery by reducing the risk of injury at water abstraction sites.
The work forms part of Northumbrian Water's ongoing investment in environmental improvements across the region, helping to protect local waterways and the wildlife that depends on them.
Graeme Ridley, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said: "Protecting and enhancing the environment is a key part of what we do, and we're pleased to be carrying out this important project at Barrasford. While much of the work takes place behind the scenes, the new eel screens will play a vital role in helping to protect migrating eels and support the long-term health of the River North Tyne.
"Projects like this demonstrate how we can continue to provide reliable water services for our customers while also delivering meaningful environmental benefits for the communities and environments we serve."
You can follow the project on the community hub page - Project: Barrasford Eel Screens | Northumbrian Water

The 2026 Environmental Monitoring & Measurement Achievement (EMMA) Awards, held in Birmingham, celebrate innovation and excellence in environmental monitoring and measurement.
Pipebot Patrol, which uses robotic technology to detect the signs of early-build ups in sewer pipes before they cause floods, was recognised in the ‘Innovative Sensor or Instrumental Deployment’ category.
Developed in partnership with the University of Sheffield, Cura Terrae Water, Minicam and Spring Innovation, Pipebot Patrol is helping to protect the environment from sewer flooding, reduce the need for emergency callouts and improve health and safety by minimising human exposure to sewers.
Meanwhile, a project delivered in partnership with FIDO Tech won the ‘Real-Time Monitoring & Control Project of the Year’ award for its AI-powered approach to leak detection.
More than 1,000 acoustic smart sensors were deployed across 149km of water network, helping teams identify and respond to leaks more quickly.
This helped save around 6.4 million litres of water per day during the cold winter period, when temperature changes can increase the risk of bursts and leaks.
Angela MacOscar, Head of Innovation at Northumbrian Water, said: “We're delighted that these projects have been recognised at the EMMA Awards.
“Innovation plays a vital role in helping us tackle the challenges facing the water industry, from reducing leaks to preventing sewer flooding, and improving how we monitor and manage our networks.
"By working closely with our partners and embracing new technology, we're able to find smarter ways to improve our environmental performance, protect our water resources and continue delivering benefits for our customers and communities."

A £2.2 million investment to strengthen wastewater treatment in East Cleveland is entering its second phase.
Northumbrian Water is carrying out proactive maintenance and upgrades at Marske Sewage Treatment Works.
This includes the cleaning, inspection and refurbishment of key treatment tanks, alongside the renewal of aeration pipework and diffusers. The investment will improve the site's resilience and help ensure treated water continues to meet strict environmental standards before being returned to the environment.
The water company is using regional suppliers and subcontractors, led by Washington-based United Infrastructure, to carry out the work.
Two of the site's four large treatment tanks, known as Sequence Batch Reactors (SBRs), have already been replaced, with work on the third tank due to start in the next few months. All four tanks are expected to be completed by the end of March 2027.
SBRs play a key role in the wastewater treatment process, and the renewal of critical components, including aeration pipework and associated diffusers, will help improve efficiency, resilience and regulatory compliance at the site.
The new pipework is being manufactured by Middlesbrough-based Donoghue Tees Valley Engineering, while Redmarshall-based Mantank Environmental Services is carrying out cleaning and tankering work. Earlier phases of the project were delivered by Washington firm Gowland & Dawson.
Northumbrian Water Project Manager Glen Campbell said: "This is a significant investment that will help ensure Marske Sewage Treatment Works continues to operate reliably and maintain the high environmental standards expected of us.
"We're also proud to be working with our local supply chain on this work, supporting local jobs and skills while delivering essential improvements to our assets. It reflects our commitment to the regional economy and our ambition for 60p of every £1 we spend to remain within the region."

It also considered the support it has available to customers who may need extra help, including through the company’s Priority Services Register and affordability schemes.
The achievement builds on Northumbrian Water Group’s existing BSI Kitemark™ for Inclusive Service, which it received in 2023 for its efforts supporting vulnerable customers across the region.
Northumbrian Water Group is now the first water company globally to hold both the Service Excellence and Inclusive Service Kitemarks™ together, and sees these external benchmarks as strong evidence of its ambition to provide world-class services to customers across its operating regions.
Together with its recently achieved Innovation Management Kitemark™, which measures practices for using innovation to deliver results for customers, communities, and environment, the latest certification means Northumbrian Water Group has also become the first organisation in the world, across any industry, to hold these three BSI Kitemarks™ at the same time.
The accreditations follow a strong track record in customer service, with Northumbrian Water Group ranking as the top performing water company in Ofwat's Customer Measure of Experience (C-MeX) for the past two years and recently being again named the most trusted water company in England and Wales.
Dawn Creighton, Head of Customer Strategy and Experience at Northumbrian Water Group, said: “Our customers are at the heart of everything we do, and we aim to deliver an unrivalled customer experience every single day, so this certification is something we're incredibly proud of.

"We’re genuinely passionate about listening to our customers, understanding what's important to them and making sure it's as easy as possible for them to get the help and support they need.
"This achievement reflects the hard work and dedication of colleagues right across our business who go above and beyond every day to do the right thing for our customers."
The certifications recognise the company's commitment to delivering great customer service, making support accessible to all and continually improving the services it provides.
Shahm Barhom, Managing Director, Product Certification, BSI, said: "Putting customers first is more important than ever, and the Service Excellence Kitemark is a rigorous, independent benchmark for organisations that do this consistently well.
"Northumbrian Water Group's achievement in becoming the first water company in the world to gain this certification, and the first organisation globally to hold the Service Excellence, Inclusive Service and Innovation Management Kitemarks together, shows a genuine commitment to its customers and sets a strong example for the water sector."

Tees Cottage Pumping Station, a remarkable example of Victorian engineering and local heritage owned by Northumbrian Water, is inviting visitors to enjoy a fun-filled day out while exploring one of the region's most important industrial heritage sites.
Built in 1849 to help transform public health by providing clean drinking water to Darlington and surrounding areas across Teesside, the pumping station remained operational until being converted into a museum in 1980.
Visitors attending the Teddy Bears' Picnic will have the opportunity to bring along their favourite teddy bear and enjoy a day packed with fun. Guests can see the station's impressive pumping engines and water pumps in action, watch traditional ironwork demonstrations in the historic smithy, take a ride on the miniature railway and relax in the cafe with a range of refreshments available.
Vicky Cairns, Partnerships Consultant at Northumbrian Water, said: "We are immensely proud of our historic monument but most importantly of the longstanding partnership with the dedicated museum volunteers, who make public steaming weekends possible and work hard with us helping to preserve this important heritage site for generations to come.
“Giving back to our local communities is something we are passionate about and do in lots of different ways. Whether that’s through in-kind donations of equipment, community grants, sponsorship or through our national award-winning employee volunteer programme, Just an Hour.”
The volunteer-run museum is home to two original pumping engines, including one of the largest preserved rotative beam engines of its type in Europe. The site remains a fascinating example of Victorian architecture and engineering ingenuity.
Trevor Sheard, Museum Chairman at Tees Cottage Pumping Station, said: "The volunteers are working hard behind the scenes to get the museum ready for opening the doors and our Teddy Bears' Picnic is always a wonderful event that brings together families, history lovers and the local community for a memorable day out.
"There is so much to see and do around our wonderful site, from the steam-powered machinery and miniature railway to our demonstrations and exhibits. We look forward to welcoming visitors through our doors and sharing the local story of this unique heritage site.”

There is no specific amount of rainfall that would allow the temporary use hosepipe ban to be lifted. Decisions are based on a range of factors, including reservoir levels, river flows, groundwater levels, soil moisture and the wider environmental impact of drought.
In Essex and Suffolk, rainfall in July was just 3% of the long-term average, and only 34% in August. The Environment Agency is also monitoring soil moisture, which shows the ground is currently around 30% drier than normal.
After months of hot and dry weather, the ground is very dry and compacted, meaning rainfall cannot easily soak into the soil. Steady, damp and prolonged rainfall conditions allow water to slowly soak into the ground, replenishing soil moisture and groundwater.
This recovery process typically takes place over autumn and winter. As rivers and groundwater recover, reservoirs can also begin to replenish, helping build water supplies for the following year.
While the recent rainfall has been welcome, sustained periods of wetter weather will be needed before drought conditions ease and restrictions can be reviewed.
Kieran Ingram, Water Director, said: “ After a prolonged period of hot and dry weather, the ground, rivers and groundwater sources all need time to recover. Recent rainfall has helped, but much more is needed before we see a significant improvement in water resources.
"Nature will take time to recover, and while the recent rainfall is encouraging, we will need sustained wetter weather over the coming months before drought conditions ease and restrictions can be reviewed."
Drought recovery happens in stages. Rainfall first needs to restore moisture levels in the soil, which have been depleted by months of hot and dry weather. Once the ground has recovered, water can more easily reach rivers and groundwater sources to enable the recovery of reservoir levels and a return to more normal water resource conditions.
Customers can help protect water resources by using less water at home and in the garden.
To find out how you can help nature, visit our website and use our water saving calculator for hints and tips on how to bring down your water usage: Save Water | How to Help With Water Conservation

The £493,000 investment forms part of the company's ongoing programme to maintain and improve the region's water network, helping to ensure that customers continue to receive high-quality drinking water for years to come.
To enable the work to be carried out safely and efficiently, a number of temporary traffic management measures will be in place throughout the project.
From Monday 24 August 2026 to 14 September 2026, multi-way temporary traffic lights will be in operation on the A696 between The Beeches and Belsay Road.
Between Tuesday 1 September 2026 and 14 October 2026, a temporary road closure will also be in place on the U9049 Road to West Newham.
And from Monday 5 October 2026 to 23 October 2026 a temporary road closure will be in place between Highlander Junction and March Burn Junction.
Brian Hardy, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said: "We're investing in our water network in Ponteland to help ensure customers continue to receive a reliable, high-quality water supply both now and in the future."
"We know customers in this area have experienced a number of bursts on the existing water main over recent years, and we've listened to the feedback they've provided.
"We appreciate that work of this nature can cause some disruption and we'd like to thank local residents and road users for their patience while we carry out these essential improvements. We've carefully planned the programme and will work to keep any inconvenience to a minimum while the new water main is installed."
Last week, the water company hosted its busiest ever Local Action event in Ponteland, with 74 customers attending to talk to experts about our infrastructure projects, river quality, water bills, and so much more.
In the feedback, customers commented that their local “plans seem well constructed”, are “needed and welcome”, and that they have a “record of responsible resource and environmental management”.

The project forms part of the water company's wider investment in improving the region's wastewater network and helping to protect local rivers and watercourses. The scheme will deliver upgrades designed to reduce the number of storm overflow spills into the Ouseburn, while improving the resilience of the sewer network during periods of heavy rainfall.
The first phase of work will take place at Killingworth Lake, where Northumbrian Water is working in partnership with North Tyneside Council to support wider efforts to address surface water flooding in the area. This is part of the wider storm overflow improvements that feed into the Ousebrurn.
The project will then progress to Grassholme Place, Benton Lane and Salters' Lane.
The work is being carried out by the water company’s partner, Esh-Stantec and delivering the work in phases will allow teams to carry out the improvements in a planned and coordinated way, while keeping local communities informed as the project progresses.
The improvements will create additional capacity within the wastewater network and help better manage rainwater entering the system during storm events. This will help reduce pressure on the network, lower the frequency of storm overflow activations, and support improved water quality in the Ouseburn.
Stef Chester, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said:
"We're pleased to be bringing this important project forward and starting work earlier than anticipated. This £6 million investment will help improve the performance of the local sewer network, reducing the number of storm overflow spills into the Ouseburn and supporting healthier watercourses for the future.
"We're working closely with North Tyneside Council to carefully plan and deliver these improvements, while keeping disruption to local communities to a minimum. We would like to thank residents and businesses in advance for their patience and understanding while the work takes place."
Northumbrian Water will continue to provide updates throughout the project and share information about upcoming works with local residents and stakeholders.

At the end of last month, the Environment Agency declared a drought in more than half of the country, including in Essex and Suffolk where temporary use bans (hosepipe bans) were introduced.
On Monday 3 August, Essex & Suffolk Water introduced a temporary use ban, meaning that customers are being asked to use watering cans and buckets instead of hosepipes for watering plants and washing cars.
Each month, the water company release an infographic packed with statistics to demonstrate to customers what local water supply looks like.
The data from Essex & Suffolk Water shows that there was just 2mm of rain during the month, causing reservoir levels to drop by 18%.
It showed that the highest day for water demand was Thursday 9 July, when 596 million litres of water were used, the equivalent of 238 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
The statistics also showed that a total of 4,158 leaky pipes have been fixed since 1 January 2026, with 625 of these being repaired in July.
By keeping customers updated on the monthly information, customers will be able to see how water-saving efforts across the operating areas can impact reservoir levels. The data is available across social media and on the Essex & Suffolk Water website.
Katie Davis, Head of Water Service Planning, said: “By sharing these four key statistics, we want to give our customers a clear view of the factors affecting water resources across our region.
“There is a close relationship between rainfall, the amount of raw water available in our reservoirs and groundwater sources, and overall demand for water, including leakage and customer use.
“Making this information available helps customers see how conditions are changing and the part we can all play in using water wisely.”
Customers can see the infographic, here; Water Resources .
For more information about the temporary use ban, visit our website: Temporary Use Ban .
Rainfall helps environments to flourish, refills reservoirs and replenishes groundwater levels. This is important because reservoirs collect and store 'raw water', ready for the treatment works to process and make drinkable. The more it rains, the more raw water there is.
Essex is relatively flat, so when it rains, there is limited natural run-off into the reservoirs and only small gains from rain falling directly onto the reservoir itself. Most water is pumped in from nearby rivers.
This is important because the reservoirs are the main storage for ‘raw water’.
In summer, when the weather is hot and dry, the teams at Essex & Suffolk Water work incredibly hard to make sure the water in reservoirs across the region is carefully managed, to meet customer demand and support the environment.
It’s a balancing act that the teams are equipped for, but it becomes more challenging each year with climate change.
The bar chart shows the overall number of leak repairs the company carry out on a monthly basis, revealing the number of completed jobs so far this year. This includes emergency and planned repairs, and is important because it helps to make sure as much treated water as possible reaches our customers.
The company is the top performer for leakage – but the teams can only respond to the leaks that they know about, which is why customers are asked to report any leaks they see. There are also specialist teams of analysts and leakage technicians who work tirelessly every day seeking out the majority of leaks which aren't visible.
There are certain days of the week when there is more demand for water than others.
Sunday is the day of the week when customers typically use more water, perhaps because they will do their laundry, wash their car, do some gardening, cook a roast dinner with lots of dishes, or maybe enjoy a soak in the bath.
The weather also has a huge impact on demand, because when it is hot, people use water to stay cool and hydrated. Millions of litres are used across our region every day, but simple water savings habits can bring this figure down.

Northumbrian Water expands 24/7 Regional Control Centre with 13 new recruits
Acting as the eyes and ears of the water company, the RCC, which is based in Washington, monitors the networks around the clock to keep the water flowing for customers.
The team, which will include 13 new network controllers, respond to alarms and manage flows to ensure water is delivered where it is needed most.
The expansion marks a major upgrade in how Northumbrian Water manages it’s infrastructure and responds to incidents at any time of day or night.
The new recruits bring a wide range of experience from demanding, high-pressure environments, like the fire service and ambulance - which is helpful when reacting under pressure or when dealing with concerned customers who sometimes call out of hours.
Cheryl Squires, who joined Northumbrian Water as a Network Controller after previous roles in the police service and housing sector, said: “Before joining Northumbrian Water, I worked as a police control room operator, dealing with emergency situations where you have to think quickly and stay calm.
“Having previously worked as a housing officer, I've seen first-hand how distressing property emergencies can be. When customers call us overnight with a burst pipe or leak, they're not just reporting a problem, they're looking for reassurance. Understanding their situation and helping them feel supported is incredibly important.”
Cheryl, who started in the control room at Leat House earlier this year, said she was made to feel welcomed as soon as she stepped through the doors.
She added: “There isn’t a ‘typical’ shift, the weather alone can change everything in minutes. We’re trained to deal with all sorts of conditions and system issues.
“You don’t realise how complex it is until you’re in the role, but what we’re doing ensures people can turn on the tap or flush the toilet, something we all take for granted. It sounds simple, but it really isn’t, there is so much work that goes into having essential services in our homes and that’s what makes the job so rewarding.”
Andrew Lineham, Head of Regional Control Centre at Northumbrian Water, said: “Providing an around the clock control room function is essential to us, keeping those systems and processes working for our customers is of paramount importance.
“We’re very pleased to have 13 new members in the team and believe that their experience is going to really help deliver a quality service.”
In 2025, the control room took an important step forward, expanding its responsibilities beyond water to include wastewater network management.
The team’s skills and experience will help shape the future of how Northumbrian Water protect our networks, support customers and deliver for the environment.

The investment, being made by Northumbrian Water, will add long-term resilience to the site’s ability to support water treatment for customers in Teesdale and beyond.
Earlier this year, work was carried out to establish elements of the site, ready for work to start in earnest following the nesting season, for up to 18 months.
The work will include renewing the site’s pipework and related infrastructure, enhancing the management of water flows that are passed forward for treatment at Lartington Water Treatment Works.
During the course of the work, a compound will be in place on the main car park, with visitors directed to alternative parking on site. Access across the dam will remain open for most of the work, although there may be times when temporary closures are required.
The work is being carried out by Northumbrian Water’s partner, Esh-Stantec.
Northumbrian Water’s Project Manager, Sophie Hudspeth, said: “This investment will help to ensure Selset Reservoir continues to serve our customers across Teesdale and the wider County Durham area for years to come. Selset Reservoir was constructed 65 years ago, and will be a part of the area’s water supply network for many more.
“Along with our other reservoirs, Selset is also a part of what draws many visitors to Teesdale to enjoy leisure time and take advantage of the welfare benefits of spending time in the great outdoors. We’re pleased that people will still be able to enjoy visits to Selset during this work, with access restrictions being kept to a minimum.”

The company’s colourful creation, named Patchwork Peter, will be one of 43 large sculptures featuring in Peter Rabbit™: Tales on the Tyne, a free family art trail which launched across Newcastle and North Tyneside this week (15 July).
Organised by St Oswald’s Hospice, the attraction will see sculptures popping up in streets, parks and public spaces across the region, encouraging families to explore the area, all while raising vital funds for the charity.
Northumbrian Water, which provides water and sewerage services to 2.7 million people across the North East, is sponsoring Patchwork Peter – a colourful design created by artist Daniel Weatheritt, alongside pupils from Hilton Primary Academy.
The design celebrates the importance of water in the natural environment, how it supports wildlife and plants, and uses vibrant blues and greens inspired by rivers and nature.
As part of its support, the water company is also the trail's official Learning Programme Partner, which includes 53 smaller sculptures, inspired by Beatrix Potter’s famous character, decorated by schools, nurseries and community youth groups.
To help inspire the young artists, Northumbrian Water provided participating schools and groups with a design guide based on its Ripple Effect education programme, encouraging children to explore saving water through the story of Peter Rabbit.
Jennie Collingwood, Head of Corporate Affairs at Northumbrian Water, said: "We're delighted to be supporting St Oswald's Hospice once again and especially proud to see the creativity and imagination of the children from Hilton Primary Academy brought to life through our very own Patchwork Peter.
"The children worked closely with artist Daniel Weatheritt to design a sculpture that celebrates the importance of water in nature, and the finished design just looks fantastic.
"As Learning Programme Partner, we're pleased to have the opportunity to help young people learn more about water, while supporting a trail that will excite families and raise money for a fantastic local charity."
Andrew Cowan, Principal at Hilton Primary Academy, said: “We’re very proud of what our pupils have achieved through this project. While we’re always focused on helping them achieve their best academically, this exciting project demonstrates their strength in the arts too.
“Thanks to the support of our Arts Lead, Miss Stevens, the children have helped create something special while linking it to recent learning about protecting our planet, saving water and looking after the environment.

Patchwork Peter will be displayed alongside dozens of other sculptures, located across Newcastle and North Tyneside until 14 September. At the end of the trail, most of the large sculptures will be auctioned to help raise funds for St Oswald's Hospice.
The trail marks the fourth time Northumbrian Water has supported one of St Oswald's Hospice's popular art trails, following Great North Snowdogs, Elmer’s Great North Parade and Shaun on the Tyne.
For more information about Peter Rabbit™: Tales on the Tyne, visit www.talesonthetyne.co.uk and for updates on Patchwork Peter, follow Northumbrian Water on social media.

Investigations progress into Cullercoats bathing water quality
Northumbrian Water, North Tyneside Council and the Environment Agency have been working together to try to identify and fix the source of contaminated groundwater at Cullercoats beach to improve the area’s bathing water quality.
Extensive investigative work done by the organisations over the years has shown that contamination is likely coming from several different sources in the local area, rather than a single issue.
Detailed survey and excavation work done by Northumbrian Water in the last few weeks, suggests that polluted groundwater may be travelling through the ground and onto the beach and sea via the cliffs and caves.
A lot of corrective work has already been undertaken, and this has identified a number of potential contributing factors including damaged pipework, likely to have been caused by previously unknown land drainage systems and misconnected private drains feeding into a culvert around the John Street and Beverley Terrace areas.
Northumbrian Water has been fixing wrongly connected customers’ waste connections, including repairing, and diverting connections. This work has stopped waste flows getting into the old land drainage systems which are connected to the culvert.
Further work is planned in the area by North Tyneside Council and Northumbrian Water in the coming months, as well as regular water quality monitoring and testing by the Environment Agency.
Richard Warneford, Wastewater Director at Northumbrian Water, said: “Recent work has found some historic and unrecorded land drains in the areas around John Street and Beverley Terrace.
“We think there’s a strong possibility that these old systems have caused damage to sewers and allowed water from misconnections and damaged pipes to pass through ground in the area and into the cave and cliff systems and then down to the beach, causing poor bathing water quality.
“We’ve done a lot of excavation work in those streets and where we’ve found misconnected properties we’ve immediately fixed any issues and correctly connected homes to our sewage networks, so that the waste can be taken away safely and treated properly. We are hopeful that these actions will make a positive difference to the bathing water at Cullercoats – which is something we all want to achieve.
Sam Dand, Director of Environment at North Tyneside Council, added: "Everyone wants to see excellent bathing water quality at Cullercoats, and we're committed to working with Northumbrian Water and the Environment Agency to understand and tackle what is a complex issue.
“These investigations are helping to build a much clearer picture of the causes, and it's encouraging that practical improvements have already been made.
“We'll continue to play our part by supporting further investigations and works, while keeping residents informed as this long-term programme of work progresses.”
Rachael Caldwell, Area Environment Manager for the Environment Agency said: “Improving water quality takes time and involves everyone including water companies, farmers, transport operators, local councils and communities to play a part and work together.
“A site’s bathing water quality is impacted by a whole range of factors from mis-connected drainage to agricultural run-off. We investigate and work closely with local partners at priority sites, such as Cullercoats, to tackle all factors influencing water quality.”

Northumbrian Water has invested in the work in the Ashby Street area of Hendon.
Work has been carried out by the water company’s partner, United Infrastructure, over the last five months, constructing a total of 3.4km of new water pipes.
The £1m project is part of a wider £74m investment in the water network across five years, which will see a total of more than 360km of older pipe replaced across the North East.
Brian Hardy, Northumbrian Water’s Project Manager, said: “This investment will help protect the quality and resilience of water supplies for customers in Hendon.
“The project has involved working within the community, up and down streets and back lanes, making the team a visible local presence since November. We’re grateful for the patience and understanding of our customers while we’ve been working near their homes.”

The scheme will protect the bankside adjacent to Dunstanburgh Road and the Craster wastewater pumping station, which plays an important role in delivering reliable wastewater services for the local community. Following severe winter storms in 2025/26, erosion along the coastline accelerated, increasing the need for long-term protection of the site and surrounding infrastructure.
The work is being carried out by the water company’s delivery partner, Esh-Stantec and the work should be completed in November 2026.
The work involves installing a "rock armour” embankment along the affected stretch of coastline. This involves large natural stone, sourced locally, being carefully placed to stabilise the eroded bankside, protecting exposed infrastructure and helping reduce the risk of future storm damage. The project will also include reinstatement of the bankside and vegetation restoration to help blend the scheme into its coastal surroundings.
The project has been designed in collaboration with environmental specialists and key stakeholders to ensure it is delivered sensitively within Craster’s unique coastal setting, while protecting a key piece of infrastructure for the future.
To help minimise disruption, Northumbrian Water has planned deliveries carefully, limited the size of the working area, and will continue to work closely with residents, local businesses and the community throughout the programme. Access arrangements have also been considered to reduce the impact s on visitors and those using the popular coastal routes around Craster and Dunstanburgh Castle this S ummer.
Joe Williamson, Project Manager at Northumbrian Water, said
"These works are essential to protect the Craster embankment from further coastal erosion and ensure it continues to provide a reliable wastewater service for the community for many years to come.
"We recognise that carrying out construction work during the busy summer season is not ideal and we would like to thank residents, businesses and visitors for their patience and understanding. We have worked closely with the local community and partners to carefully plan the project, keeping disruption to a minimum wherever possible while making sure this important infrastructure is protected before future winter storms."

Northumbrian Water is carrying out a project at the site over five years, working in phases to avoid bird ground nesting periods, while also taking advantage of drier months to make best progress.
The work will include the installation of pipework into the dam structure and connecting with Waskerley Beck, which will enhance the safety of the site by increasing the ability to reduce water levels more quickly, if needed.
The reservoir sits on Muggleswick Common in the North Pennines, between Stanhope and Edmundbyers, and Northumbrian Water has been working with Natural England and ecological experts to ensure the project is delivered in a way that protects the area’s flora and fauna. This has included adding two years to the phased delivery programme, to take the nesting seasons into account.
Work being delivered between now and November 2026 will be at a low level, helping prepare for the next element of work, in 2027, which will take place to the east of the dam. Phases three and four, planned for 2028 and 2029, will involve working on and around the dam itself, which will require temporary restrictions on visitors’ rights of way.
Currently scheduled for 2030, the fifth phase will largely involve restoring the working areas to ensure the site is restored to its normal condition.
Work will be carried out by Northumbrian Water’s partner, Esh-Stantec.
Mike Foster, Northumbrian Water’s Project Manager, said: “This work is part of a series of investments across our reservoirs to support the continued and enhanced resilience and safety of our sites.
“We’ve worked closely with ecological experts and the Natural England team to make sure we plan this work in a way that is sensitive and protective of species that call Waskerley home, and the project has been phased to take this into account.
“Work in the first two years will be visible, and we are liaising with local residents to keep them informed, and we would like to thank the site’s neighbours and visitors for their patience while this work takes place. We do not anticipate requiring any access restrictions for visitors until at least 2028, and we will work to help people understand these at the appropriate time.”

Northumbrian Water will this month (July) complete work on the first of two projects in Pelton, near Chester-le-Street, ready to start on the second in August. The work will reduce the frequency of spills from local storm overflows, protecting and improving water quality in the Chester Burn and Cong Burn, as well as watercourses downstream.
On land next to Pelton Community Primary School, new sewer pipes and underground stormwater storage have been constructed. This adds capacity to the local combined sewage and rainwater network, reducing the chances of it over-filling during periods of heavy rainfall.
Now, similar upgrades will be installed in land south of The Wynd, with work expected to be completed by the end of March 2027.
Northumbrian Water’s partner, Avove, is carrying out both projects, helping to reduce spills from each of the two storm overflows to less than ten a year.
Storm overflows act as relief valves in the combined sewage and surface water network. This protects homes and businesses from sewer flooding at times of heavy rainfall.
Christopher Bond, Northumbrian Water’s Project Manager, said: “This is an important double investment in the local environment at Pelton, reducing spills and contributing to better water quality in the area. Completing the work near the school is a huge milestone and we’re really looking forward to getting going with the work near The Wynd.
“We’re investing £1.7bn across five years to protect and enhance the environment, and reducing storm overflow spills is a big part of that. The progress we are making here at Pelton is a great local example of this, and we are grateful to the community here for their patience and understanding while we’re carrying out this work.”
Dean Wallace, Senior Project Manager at Avove, added: “Reaching this milestone is a significant step forward for the project and reflects the strong collaboration between Avove and Northumbrian Water. Together, we are delivering improvements that strengthen the local network and reduce the impact of storm overflows on nearby watercourses, particularly during periods of heavy rainfall.
“As we move into the next phase, we will continue working closely with Northumbrian Water, our partners and the local community to complete the remaining upgrades safely and efficiently.”
You can follow progress on the work at Pelton at: www.communityhub.nwl.co.uk/pelton .

After months of dry weather and three successive heatwaves, Suffolk has experienced temperatures of up to 31°C in recent days and received just 0.3mm of rainfall since 1 July.
The hot weather has had a significant impact on demand for water, with an extra seven million litres needed per day in Suffolk since Wednesday 1 July.
That’s the equivalent of supplying a town the size of Lowestoft, on top of our normal supply areas.
While a temporary usage ban, often referred to as a hosepipe ban, is not currently being introduced, Essex & Suffolk Water is closely monitoring water resources and preparing for all eventualities.
Kieran Ingram, Water Director, said: " It takes a great deal of effort to turn rainwater into clean, safe drinkable water for everyday use, and the recent spell of hot, dry weather has led to a significant increase in water demand across Suffolk.
“Because of this, we need to formally appeal to our customers to show restraint with their water use and ask them to help us by considering how they use water.
"We're asking customers to help by using water wisely wherever possible. Small changes can make a big difference and could help reduce the likelihood of restrictions being needed later in the summer.
"We're continuing to tackle leaks and bursts and are doing everything we can to manage supplies, but we also need customers' help.
“If a temporary water use ban becomes necessary, we’ll work closely with local communities to provide the right support. But by making wise choices now, our customers can help lower the risk of such restrictions being needed.”
To try and help avoid any restrictions the water company is asking its customers in the Suffolk areas to consider using less water.
Advice on how to do this is here: Water saving tips .

Part of the Wild Ouseburn initiative, Northumbrian Water worked with Wild Intrigue to install the structure last year, funded through a community crowdfunding campaign and support from Northumberland & Tyneside Bird Club, after the birds were first spotted in the area in 2023.
Earlier this year, following observations from other urban colonies, some slight improvements were made to the nesting chambers ahead of the birds' return in spring.
Shortly afterwards, the first pair of sand martins took up residence and successfully raised five chicks.
The youngsters have now been ringed by a licensed expert from Northumbria Ringing Group, helping researchers learn more about the birds as they make their incredible 4,000km migration between the North East and Africa each year.
Ian Cole, Conservationist at Northumbrian Water, said: “We’re absolutely delighted to welcome the first chicks to the nesting bank.
“This partnership project is a great example of how organisations, communities and wildlife experts can work together to help nature thrive.
“Seeing five young birds successfully raised and take flight is a brilliant result and we’re excited to see the colony grow in future.”
Cain Scrimgeour, Co-Director of Wild Intrigue, said: “Our cities are full of urban wildlife and projects like this show that through collaboration, community support and a little bit of vision, we can make real impacts for our wild neighbours. The Ouseburn Sand Martin colony is now a new wild spectacle right in the heart of the city.
“This year, the Ouseburn Sand Martin colony is the largest we’ve seen it since the birds arrived in 2023. They can also be spotted feeding on insects over the recently created City Stadium Wildflowers Meadows.”
The Ouseburn sand martin bank will continue to be monitored and maintained as part of the Wild Ouseburn initiative.
The installation of the nesting bank forms part of Northumbrian Water's five-year migratory birds programme, which is creating new nesting opportunities for species including swifts, swallows and sand martins across the region.
