Hello, and welcome to the October edition of our newsletter.
The last month has seen important developments in the future direction of regulation for both the rail and road sectors.
First, we saw the publication by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade of the independent review of the Office of Rail and Road led by Dr Richard Judge. The review recognises the value of our independence, expertise and unique role across economic and safety regulation. It also identifies opportunities to build on these strengths, many of which align with work already under way through our transformation programme.
Second, we saw the publication of the Highways (Financing) Bill which was laid in Parliament on 10 September. Once enacted this will enable us to take on the economic regulation for the Lower Thames Crossing (LTC) which will connect Kent and Essex through a tunnel beneath the River Thames.
With the importance of changes in the regulatory landscape – including for rail – I was delighted to speak at the Regulatory Policy Institute annual conference in Oxford earlier in September, sharing a panel with senior representatives from the rail freight sector and Network Rail.
As well as engaging with the regulatory and legislative changes afoot, we have also continued our important work of holding Network Rail to account. Just today, we have published reports on the economic and financial performance of Network Rail and on cost benchmarking .
Our analysis here shows how, despite above target efficiency performance, a number of factors have nevertheless led to overall cost increases. Network Rail delivered £614 million of efficiency improvements in the second year of CP7, covering April 2025 to March 2026, but inflationary pressures, maintenance of ageing assets and train performance issues placed additional pressure on Network Rail’s financial performance in the last year.
Another report featured this month is our 2026 open access monitoring report . This provides an update on open access passenger services, including an overview of new open access services and open access decisions; market outcomes since our 2025 report (such as punctuality, service growth and passenger experience); and a summary of what international market participants are saying.
And today we have published the conclusions of our work on rail investment . Originally commissioned by HM Treasury, this work has been a key focus for us as we seek to support investment and resilience in the rail sector.
We are delighted to have been able to bring forward improvements to the risk fee funds to support investors and improve service standards, while ensuring that risk is allocated appropriately and achieving value for money to enable further investment, ensuring the railway delivers the maximum economic benefit for the country.
Finally, yesterday we announced that ORR has appointed Paul Smith as our new Chief Executive . Paul brings extensive regulatory leadership experience spanning the UK's aviation, energy and payments sectors. We all look forward to welcoming Paul to ORR in January.

Network Rail charges fees to cover the risks it takes on when a third-party, funds or delivers work on the rail network. ORR’s deep dive review found that there is scope to reduce fees to ensure the risk fee funds are set closer to the break-even level. Today (30 September) ORR has published new rates for the relevant fees, setting out how much third parties will save.
Of the 11 relevant industry agreement types, fees for nine of them are being reduced. For example, for basic asset protection agreements using the Network Rail Fee Fund, where a customer leads straightforward, low risk delivery of works on the railway, the fee is being reduced from 5.0% to 2.4%. For development services agreements, which cover development and design work undertaken by Network Rail for a customer, the third parties will pay one tenth of the current fee (0.1%).
Taken together, the Government Actuary Department (GAD) who carried out an independent actuary review of the funds for the ORR estimates that, if relevant investment levels remain at 2025/26 levels, third parties could save £2-3 million per year. The new fees will be effective from 1 November.
Graham Richards, director, planning and performance, said:
“These cuts to fees will have a tangible, positive impact on investment decision making into Great Britain’s rail network. This is a core example of how smart regulation can boost growth by making investment more attractive, while ensuring a good deal for the taxpayer."

Billions of pounds are spent on operating, maintaining and renewing Great Britain’s mainline railway each year. One of our core functions is to regulate, monitor and report on the financial performance of Network Rail, which has responsibility for managing the mainline railway infrastructure. Passengers, freight users, taxpayers, and the supply chain all have an interest in ensuring Network Rail’s financial performance is strong.
Our annual efficiency and finance assessment (AEFA) , and cost benchmarking report , shed light on Network Rail’s financial performance so far in control period seven (CP7). Our analysis shows how, despite above target efficiency performance, a number of factors have led to overall cost increases.
Network Rail delivered strong efficiencies in the last year, at £614 million, exceeding its target by 4%. Network Rail also expects to exceed its efficiency targets during the remainder of this control period.
Network Rail’s funding set at the start of the control period accounts for its efficiency targets, meaning it must meet its targets to remain within its funding envelope without having to make savings elsewhere, for instance by cutting renewals. At the same time, this means that exceeding its efficiency target, as Network Rail is doing, reduces the need to cut spending in other areas.
That’s one of the reasons why it’s so important that Network Rail maintains its focus on delivery of efficiencies and why ORR has an official growth goal to ensure Network Rail remains on track to deliver this regulatory target.
Across net expenditure, Network Rail spent £490 million more for what was delivered than originally planned in the last year. This is significantly, but not exclusively, due to higher-than-expected inflation and input prices.
Our analysis also suggests that over the full five-year control period Network Rail could face around £2.3 billion of additional pressures compared with the inflation and input prices underpinning the periodic review (PR23) that set its current five-year funding. With approximately one quarter of Network Rail’s risk fund remaining (but with three fifths of the control period still to go), the company has significant choices to make about reprioritising expenditure within a more constrained budget.
Therefore, strong efficiency delivery alone will not be enough to offset all the financial pressures facing Network Rail, with the company already revising planned activity due to rising costs. The challenge over the remainder of the control period will be ensuring that short-term affordability pressures do not undermine the long-term condition, reliability and sustainability of the railway.
Faced with rising costs Network Rail has pushed back some renewals work and delivered approximately 12% less renewals activity than originally planned for Year 2 of CP7. This lowers expenditure in the short term but increases reliance on maintenance and is likely to have additional cost implications down the line.
Our separate cost benchmarking report outlines how cost increases are not a short-term trend. For example, after accounting for inflation, maintenance expenditure has increased by 56% to £2.5 billion over the ten years to 2024-25 and this cannot be explained by changes in network scale, usage and complexity. Factors such as changes in asset management strategies (from reduced renewals to increased maintenance), initiatives to improve track worker safety and vegetation management, and input prices above general inflation may also be contributing to the continued increase in maintenance expenditure. However, controlling for those factors does not explain some of the large variations we see between regions and between maintenance delivery units.

There were 11,289 reported workforce assaults on the mainline railway, up 12% compared with the previous year.
This total comprised 6,390 incidents of verbal abuse, 2,487 physical assaults and 2,412 threats. This is the first time ORR’s annual rail safety release has published workforce assaults across these three categories.
There were also 13,464 reported assaults against passengers and members of the public on the mainline, an increase of 36% and the highest number recorded since the series began in 2004. Harassment increased by 52% and common assaults by 30%.
On London Underground, assaults against passengers and members of the public increased 20% to 5,534 in the latest year, while reported workforce assaults fell 3% to 3,525.
Reflecting on the statistics, Richard Hines, ORR’s Chief Inspector of Railways, said:
"The increase in reported assaults is concerning. No-one on the railway should be subjected to violence, threats or abuse.
"We're working with industry and our trade union colleagues to address work-related violence and harassment, including through recent guidance which sets out what we expect from rail employers. This includes understanding where the risks are, putting effective controls in place, encouraging staff to report incidents and providing appropriate support afterwards. Our inspectors will continue to check how these risks are being managed."

We are often asked what effect open access rail services have on the passenger experience and the wider railway.
Until Great British Railways (GBR) is stood up, ORR is responsible for regulating access to the rail network and deciding, where appropriate, whether operators can secure rights to run new services.
ORR is responsible for decisions on both domestic and international applications, which attract significant interest from industry, government and passengers. By monitoring how services perform and how passengers respond, we can provide evidence that helps operators, investors, policymakers and ORR better understand how rail markets are developing and where future opportunities may emerge.
That is why ORR publishes an annual open access monitoring report . By tracking market outcomes over time, we can build a clearer picture of how rail markets are evolving and how passengers experience the services that operate within them. This evidence helps inform future regulatory decisions and contributes to wider discussions about the future shape of the railway.
This year’s report has a significant focus on the international open access market, following our decisions to grant access for Virgin Trains to Temple Mills International depot, and the High Speed 1 network, unlocking the prospect of international rail competition for the first time since the Channel Tunnel was opened.
Since these decisions were taken, interest from a number of prospective operators has continued, reflecting the opportunities many businesses see in international passenger rail. To better understand both those opportunities and the challenges that remain, ORR spoke with infrastructure managers, existing operators and prospective entrants during summer 2026. Participants were broadly optimistic about the potential for increased competition and growth in international rail, while highlighting a number of interconnected challenges around access to key facilities, financing, and investment planning.
Open access operators remain a very small part of the overall rail market, accounting for around 0.5% of passenger journeys on the GB rail network. On average, open access operators performed slightly better than comparable long-distance contracted operators on measures of punctuality and reliability during 2025-26, with significantly lower cancellation rates. Passenger demand has also recovered strongly since the pandemic, particularly amongst domestic open access operators, although some of this growth reflects the introduction of new services in recent years.
Passenger experience presents a more nuanced picture. Overall passenger satisfaction was generally higher amongst open access operators, with all domestic open access operators recording satisfaction scores around or above the industry median. At the same time, complaints per journey remained higher for open access operators than for comparable contracted operators and increased more quickly during the latest year. As in previous years, punctuality and reliability remained amongst the most important drivers of passenger complaints.
The rail market in Great Britain will undergo significant changes over the coming years with the creation of GBR, and ORR as the independent regulator will continue to monitor domestic and international passenger services with a focus on whole system outcomes. We have issued more than 29,000 train driving licences (TDL) since the licensing regime was introduced, with drivers continuing to be medically assessed throughout their careers. This means doctors regularly consider a wide range of medical conditions and treatments, making informed decisions regarding the drivers' fitness to drive.
To better support them, we, along with the recognised doctors, Department for Transport (DfT) and Rail Safety and Standards Board (RSSB) are working together on a pilot Medical Advisory Panel (MAP), recently established, comprising of medical professionals recognised by the ORR to provide TDL medicals.
The concept for the panel followed the 2023 Post Implementation Review of the Train Driving Licences and Certificates Regulations (TDLCR) 2010 and engagement with our recognised doctors. They told us they wanted more opportunities to share experience and discuss the medical issues they encounter in practice. The panel gives them a structured forum to do that, bringing together experienced ORR-recognised doctors from across the industry.
The panel is advisory only. It will not provide second opinions or overrule another doctor, and responsibility for individual medical decisions remains with the doctor carrying out the assessment.
It will look at how the application process for becoming an ORR-recognised doctor can be improved, as well as developing best-practice guidance on medical issues that regularly arise in train driver assessments, including cardiac conditions, diabetes, sleep apnoea and the use of off-label or unlicensed medicines. The panel's experience will also be helpful as we work together to consider further reform of TDLCR.
The pilot will run until 31 March 2027. Over that period, we want to see how bringing recognised doctors together in this way can improve consistency, strengthen professional support and help keep railway medical guidance up to date.
We also expect the panel to contribute to our work with DfT and RSSB on future reform of TDLCR, including considering where the regulations could be made less prescriptive while continuing to maintain appropriate safety standards.
The pilot will be assessed against six key areas of work. The panel will report its findings to RSSB, which will bring together the evidence and outputs for stakeholders. ORR, DfT and RSSB will then jointly assess the success of the pilot and consider what should happen next.

Welcome to the September edition of ORR’s stakeholder newsletter.
A pressing focus for us as a regulator is ensuring a safer railway for passengers, workers and the general public. We were therefore deeply concerned by August’s derailments at Lewes and Wickford. Our thoughts are with those affected and we are investigating the circumstances of the incidents.
Such incidents are thankfully rare, but maintaining that record depends on continual vigilance, learning, and improvement. ORR's role is to ensure that investigations are thorough, that the industry's response is evidence-based, and that any lessons needed to manage future risks are identified and acted upon.
Alongside our investigative and regulatory work, ORR's legal team plays a vital role in protecting the public and supporting a railway and road network that works for everyone. Their expertise helps ensure that safety obligations are properly understood and enforced, that operators and infrastructure managers are held to account where necessary, and that regulatory decisions are fair, robust and capable of withstanding scrutiny.
Whether supporting prosecutions, advising on complex regulatory issues, or helping to shape the framework within which industry operates, our work is fundamental to achieving better outcomes for passengers, road users and freight customers.
That contribution was evident again in August when Network Rail was fined £1.2million after it pleaded guilty to an offence under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 following the collapse of a wall in September 2022 near Rugby station.
The boundary wall beside a car park at the station collapsed onto 81-year-old pedestrian Edward Hanlon, as he walked along the adjacent path. Although Network Rail owned the wall and remained responsible for its repair and maintenance, undocumented redevelopment of the station car park by a previous tenant led to the mistaken assumption that responsibility lay elsewhere.
ORR's investigation found that the wall had therefore been omitted from Network Rail's inspection regime. The organisation had failed to identify both the discrepancy in its boundary records or the wall's deteriorating condition. These failings meant the risk the wall posed to members of the public went unidentified. Mr Hanlon passed away in January 2025 from lymphoma. A statement from his daughter indicated he never fully recovered from his injuries.
We will continue to use the full range of our regulatory and legal powers where it is in the public interest to do so.
Through this work, and through our broader regulatory activities, we remain committed to protecting people while enabling safe, reliable and efficient rail and road systems that serve everyone.

The incident happened on 16 September 2022, when a boundary wall beside a car park at Rugby railway station collapsed onto 81-year-old pedestrian Edward Hanlon, who was using the adjacent alleyway.
Mr. Hanlon suffered several fractured ribs, a punctured lung and a blood clot in his lung, and spent two weeks in hospital. The incident had a lasting impact on him both physically and mentally, leaving him in persistent pain, restricting his mobility and preventing him from returning to many of the activities he had previously enjoyed. Mr. Hanlon died in January 2025 following a diagnosis of lymphoma.
Network Rail owned the wall and remained responsible for its repair and maintenance. However, undocumented redevelopment of the station car park by a previous tenant, including the installation of a fence in front of the wall, led to the mistaken assumption that the fence marked the station boundary.
ORR's investigation found that the wall was consequently omitted from Network Rail's inspections and that it failed to identify either the discrepancy in the boundary records or the wall's deteriorating condition. These failings meant the risk the wall posed to members of the public went unidentified.
Richard Hines, ORR’s HM Chief Inspector of Railways, said:
"Our thoughts remain with Mr Hanlon’s family and friends. The sentence imposed by the court reflects the seriousness of Network Rail’s failings and the devastating consequences when infrastructure is not managed effectively.
“Duty holders must know which assets they are responsible for, carry out appropriate inspections, and take timely action to address defects before they pose a risk to people. This prosecution sends a clear message that ORR will not hesitate to take enforcement action where failures to manage safety expose workers or members of the public to serious harm.”
The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) is the independent economic and safety regulator for Britain's railways and regulates the performance and efficiency of England's strategic road network.
Network Rail pleaded guilty to a single breach of section 3(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.
Network Rail was fined £1.2 million and ordered to pay ORR's costs of £27,320.01. Network Rail will also pay a £2,000 victim surcharge.
Network Rail was sentenced at Birmingham Magistrates' Court.

Two nuclear industry companies have been fined a combined total of £140,000 after safety failings led to a container of radioactive uranium powder being dropped and rupturing open at a nuclear fuel enrichment site.
Urenco ChemPlants Limited and Babcock Critical Services Limited were sentenced today at South Sefton Magistrates Court following a prosecution brought by the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR).
The incident happened at the Urenco site in Capenhurst, Cheshire, inside the Tails Management Facility, which is run by Urenco ChemPlants Limited.
Workers at the facility process a by-product of uranium enrichment and pack the resulting powder into large steel containers, each weighing at least 11 tonnes when full, ready for long-term storage.
On 5 February 2024, a forklift truck driver was moving a full container when he mistakenly tilted the forks forward instead of lowering them, causing the container to slide off, hit a metal guard rail and split open, releasing a quantity of uranium powder.
A banksman had been checking underneath the full containers for any radiological contamination before the container was dropped, and was put at significant risk of harm should the container had fallen during that task.
At least 3.3kgs of the uranium powder were released and radiological surveys carried out later, revealed widespread, low levels of contamination across the room.
The dispersed triuranium octoxide powder is a hazardous radioactive material and various long-term and serious health effects can potentially arise from inhalation, ingestion or absorption through the eyes.
Thankfully, nobody was harmed on this occasion. Tests on the two workers closest to the incident showed no internal radiation exposure, and there was no risk to the public or the environment.
However, ONR's investigation found that this was largely down to good fortune rather than good safety management.
ONR found that Urenco ChemPlants Limited were responsible for basic safety failings and had exposed their employees to avoidable risk for a number of years.
The investigation found that the company failed to adequately assess and manage risks, and that safety shortcomings in both the Tails Management Facility and the operation of the forklift truck contributed to the incident.
Urenco ChemPlants Limited’s working practices required its employees to stand close to forklift trucks. This is a recognised danger in industry, and free guidance on managing the associated risks is widely available.
The company also did not have dedicated kits to deal with uranium powder spills, so employees had to improvise and gather items themselves including a vacuum cleaner, bags and wipes.
Babcock Critical Services Limited provides the site's emergency response service, including fire, medical and security teams.
ONR found multiple basic failings on their part, including the company having no radiation risk assessment in place for its work at Capenhurst, having no registration for radiological work, not consulting or appointing a radiation protection adviser, and having no radiation protection supervisors; all of which are legal requirements.
Emergency responders had inadequate training for an incident at the facility and did not have the right equipment to seal the damaged container.
Two of Babcock Critical Services Limited’s employees had not been issued with personal radiation monitoring devices, despite being expected to attend incidents involving radiation on site.
Both companies cooperated with ONR's enquiries and have since made significant improvements in safety procedures following the incident.
Urenco ChemPlants Limited has removed the need for workers to stand close to forklift trucks - introducing a three-metre exclusion zone and they are no longer required to check underneath full containers for radiological contamination.

Sellafield Ltd has strengthened its control and supervision arrangements at the Cumbrian site following an improvement notice issued by the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR).
A health and safety incident occurred in April 2025 when contractors operating under the supervision of Sellafield Ltd were replacing steel ropes on an overhead crane when they became loose and fell to the ground.
Sellafield Ltd has now complied with the ONR enforcement action by making the Technical Oversight role clearer, which supports examination, inspection, maintenance and testing activities, and integrating it into the site wide arrangements for supervision.
Supervisors now have an improved way of getting subject matter expert assistance when they need it, supported by updated arrangements and better training.
ONR issued the notice to Sellafield Ltd under Regulations 7(1) and 7(5) of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, in relation to the provision of health and safety assistance (specifically, supervision).

A landmark agreement will strengthen international cooperation on nuclear safeguards and security while supporting the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear technology.
The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) and the Australian Safeguards and Non-Proliferation Office (ASNO) marks an important step in the relationship and reflects the growing value of international regulatory cooperation.
The MoU, signed at the International Atomic Energy’s (IAEA) Safeguards Symposium in Vienna, is ONR's first ever dedicated framework for collaboration on nuclear safeguards and security.
As the UK and Australia expand their nuclear programmes, prepare for emerging reactor technologies, civil maritime nuclear applications, and expand safeguards capability, the agreement creates timely opportunities for ONR and ASNO to share expertise, build capability and strengthen regulatory approaches.
Through joint research, technical collaboration, staff exchanges and training, both organisations will be better equipped to address the emerging challenges and support the evolving nuclear sector.
The partnership will deliver clear benefits for both organisations. ASNO will gain from ONR's experience in developing safeguards capability, inspector competencies and professional development through the ONR Academy.
In turn, ONR will benefit from ASNO's internationally recognised expertise in safeguards, non-proliferation and support for the global safeguards regime.
Alan Homer, ONR's Head of Profession for Nuclear Material Accountancy and Safeguards, said: “International collaboration is vital to ensuring nuclear technology and nuclear material continues to be used safely, securely and for peaceful purposes.
“Through closer collaboration, we can enhance safeguards and security outcomes in both countries and support the safe, secure and sustainable growth of the nuclear sector.”

The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman (LGSCO) has presented its Annual Report and Accounts to Parliament for the period April 2025 to March 2026.
The Ombudsman continued to see a large increase in the number of new complaints registered, like all other UK public Ombudsman services.
In 2025-26, despite the Ombudsman increasing the number of complaints and enquiries it dealt with (23,293) by 12%, this did not outstrip the 32% more cases it received (29,013) on the previous year.
Of the 23,293 cases dealt with, the Ombudsman closed 9,422 cases at its first stage because the organisation complained about had not been given the chance to properly consider the issue, or the matter was very clearly outside the Ombudsman’s jurisdiction.
The Ombudsman closed 9,424 cases at its Assessment stage because the law does not allow it to investigate or there were good reasons not to do so. For example, there was a more appropriate appeal route, such as a Tribunal, or there was insufficient injustice to warrant an investigation.
The Ombudsman investigated 4,447 cases, finding fault in 3,788 (85%) of those. It maintained an excellent compliance rate, with 99.9% of the Ombudsman’s recommendations carried out to its satisfaction.
The significant increased demand for the Ombudsman’s service has resulted in increased numbers of cases waiting to be allocated to its investigators, meaning longer case times than it would like, particularly at its Assessment stage. However, once allocated, case decision times remain very efficient, and 88% of all cases were completed within 26 weeks over the year.
Amerdeep Clarke, Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, said:
"Demand for our service has risen steeply for the third year running, and we are not alone in this. Every other public service Ombudsman in the UK is seeing a similar picture.
The sheer scale of the increase in complaints means people are waiting longer for a decision, and so we have continued to look at how we explain our processes better to people. While we appreciate a great many people come to us at a time of distress, with high expectations of what we can do for them, giving people a firm – but empathetic – steer on whether we are likely to help, is vital.”
Julie Odams, Chief Executive and Accounting Officer, added:
"Alongside our casework, we remain committed to getting the maximum public value from what we learn. Our reports on planning enforcement and on housing for Disabled people are great examples of this – where we can give constructive support and help councils to make practical changes that will benefit many people in their areas."
The Ombudsman continued to prioritise using the learning from its cases to help improve local services. It published seven thematic reports in 2025-26, including a focus report on planning enforcement, Losing Control, which warned that under-resourced enforcement teams risk undermining public confidence in the planning system, as well as a campaign on housing for Disabled people, including the report Access Denied. The LGSCO also published a good practice guide on supporting children out of school.

A non-verbal Autistic boy was left without the specialist education support he needed to help him communicate for more than a year because of faults by City of York Council, a Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman report has found.
The boy uses a sign, symbol and speech system called Makaton to communicate with the world around him, along with other methods such as pointing to objects and gestures.
The Ombudsman's investigation into a complaint from the boy’s family found the council failed in its legal duty to make sure the boy's teaching staff were properly trained in Makaton. His Education, Health and Care (EHC) Plan states it was necessary for every member of staff in his classroom be trained to levels three and four.
For more than a year, the Ombudsman found either no staff member, or at most one, held the level of qualification required. Training was patchy and slow, with staff still learning Makaton while they were teaching the boy.
The council argued the impact was reduced because staff were using other approaches, including gestalt language processing, as part of a broader "total communication" method. The Ombudsman did not agree.
The Ombudsman also had concerns about the way the council handled the family's complaint. It took too long to issue a formal response, and the mother was repeatedly left chasing for updates, at one point even being asked by the council to confirm herself whether the problems had been fixed.
When the boy’s mother complained, the council arranged and paid for Makaton training and offered the family a substantial financial remedy. The Ombudsman welcomed this but said it still did not reflect the significance of what the family had been through and recommended a further payment.
Julie Odams, Chief Executive at the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, said:
“A legal duty to a disabled child is not something a council can work around. If an EHC Plan says a child needs Makaton to communicate, finding other ways to navigate the school day is not good enough. That duty was non-delegable and absolute.
“I recognise City of York Council had taken steps to put things right before the family approached us. Unfortunately that doesn't change the fact that for more than a year, a little boy who relies on Makaton to be understood was left without it.
“Every council holding an EHC Plan should check provision is in place when the plan starts, check it every year, and act quickly when someone raises a concern. That is how councils can be sure a child is getting the support their EHC Plan expects."
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman remedies injustice and shares learning from investigations to help improve public, and adult social care, services. In this case the council has agreed to apologise and make a payment to the mother to reflect the missed educational provision.
The Ombudsman has the power to make recommendations to improve processes for the wider public. In this case the council will review its procedures for checking that provision specified in an EHC Plan is in place from the start of a new or amended Plan, create an action plan to reduce delays in Makaton training and increase its commissioning of trainers.

A Lancashire homecare provider failed to follow its own procedures after a service user expressed suicidal intent, the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman has found, in a decision that highlights lessons for the wider care sector on recognising and responding to risk.
The Ombudsman investigated a complaint against Promedica24 (Lancashire) Limited after a live-in care worker did not escalate concerns when a man in their care expressed an intention to take his own life. The man later took an overdose and died in hospital a short time later.
The investigation found the care worker failed to follow the provider's own Self-Harm and Suicide Awareness Policy, which required staff to treat any expression of suicidal intent as an emergency, contact the emergency out-of-hours line, and notify family members. The care worker also demonstrated a lack of understanding of medication risk, having casually told the man's daughter that he would have had to “eat the whole package” of the medication involved to “finish him off”.
The Ombudsman found the care provider's actions amounted to a breach of regulations requiring providers to assess and mitigate risks to people's health and safety, and to treat people with dignity, respect and compassion.
The care provider subsequently refused to investigate a complaint from the daughter after her father's death, on the grounds that a coroner's inquest had already considered the circumstances. The Ombudsman found this was inconsistent with the provider's own complaints policy and amounted to a further breach of regulatory standards on complaint handling.
While the Ombudsman could not say whether the outcome for the man would have been different had staff acted correctly, the failure to escalate his concerns meant his daughter lost the opportunity to be involved in decisions about her father's care, causing her avoidable distress.
Amerdeep Clarke, Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, said:
"This is a deeply distressing case, and I want to extend my sympathy to the family for their loss. When someone in a carer's charge expresses thoughts of taking their own life, that must always be treated as an emergency. Providers have clear policies for exactly this reason, and it is vital that staff are trained and confident enough to follow them under pressure.
"Equally concerning is that when the family sought answers through a complaint, they were turned away. A coroner's inquest and a complaint investigation serve very different purposes, and providers should not use one as a reason to avoid the other. Families deserve to have their concerns heard and properly investigated.
"I hope this case prompts all care providers to reflect on how confident their staff are in recognising and escalating risk, and how robust their complaints processes are, so that families are not left with unanswered questions at the worst possible time."
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman remedies injustice and shares learning from investigations to help improve public, and adult social care, services. In this case the care provider has agreed to apologise to the daughter for the distress caused by its failure to escalate her concerns and to properly investigate her complaint.
The Ombudsman has the power to make recommendations to improve processes for the wider public. In this case the care provider has agreed to remind relevant staff of the need to accept and investigate complaints in line with its own complaints policy, reinforcing how staff should respond sensitively to bereaved families. It will also arrange refresher training for staff on recognising and responding to suicide risk, understanding medication risks, and communicating sensitively with service users and their families.
Anyone affected by the issues raised in this case can contact Samaritans free, any time, on 116 123, or the Campaign Against Living Miserably (CALM) on 0800 58 58 58.

Complaints about adult social care in England rose by 22% last year, according to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman's (LGSCO) Annual Review of Adult Social Care Complaints 2025-26 , published today.
The LGSCO received 3,938 complaints and enquiries about adult social care in general in 2025-26, up from the previous year.
In the independent sector, complaints from people who fund their own care also rose by 10% to 368. The Ombudsman said this reflects a welcome increase in public awareness of the right to complain, though it remains concerned that too few people who fund their own care come forward given the scale of privately arranged care across the country.
Of the 904 cases investigated, 77% were upheld. The high rate of compliance with Ombudsman recommendations was maintained, with 99.8% of cases being completed to the Ombudsman’s satisfaction.
Positively, around a third (33%) of upheld complaints about private social care providers had already been suitably remedied by the organisation before the Ombudsman investigated, a 13-percentage-point rise on the previous year.
Amerdeep Clarke, Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, said:
"We are seeing welcome signs of improvement in how councils and care providers handle complaints, but there is still more to be done. My message to the sector is simple: use the learning in this report to improve services now, rather than waiting for wider changes to the care system that are currently under discussion.
"Councils should ensure the care providers they commission have current policies in place that reflect best practice, including clear signposting to us as the final step in the complaints process.
“And for care providers, dealing with complaints properly isn't just the right thing to do, it i fundamental to fostering excellent relations with your clients, families, and the wider communities in which you operate. Handling a complaint well protects your reputation, and where you have already investigated and appropriately remedied an issue, this can mean a full Ombudsman investigation isn't needed.
"Behind every one of these numbers is a person, a family or a carer trying to get things back on track after something has gone wrong. Getting the fundamentals right: clear records, honest explanations and proper signposting to our service, protects everyone: the people who rely on care, and the organisations providing it."
The Ombudsman offers a free online toolkit for care providers ( asctoolkit.lgo.org.uk ) to help them become "complaints confident", alongside guidance and training for councils on managing complaints and reviews.
The report and associated data tables can be downloaded from the Ombudsman’s website at www.lgo.org.uk/ascreview

Householders who think their council tax bill is wrong may be entitled to challenge it through a free tribunal, but new guidance suggests many are never told this option exists, and can lose the right to use it by the time they find out.
Last year the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman received more than 1,600 complaints about council tax. Many, it says, should never have needed to reach it at all, because the person involved had a straightforward right to take their case to the Valuation Tribunal, a free and independent service, rather than going through a council's own complaints process.
The problem is not being told by the council of the cost free right of appeal to the tribunal and timing. Appeals to the tribunal come with strict deadlines, typically one to two months, and anyone who spends that time going through a council complaints process instead can lose their right to appeal altogether, even with a strong case.
Real cases highlighted by the Ombudsman show the consequences: one man's appeal window closed after his dispute was wrongly treated as a customer service complaint; another was pursued through the courts, with bailiffs and threats of bankruptcy, without ever being told he could challenge the decision itself for free; a tenant who queried her bill found a bailiff at her door months later, still unaware she had a right to appeal.
What you can challenge, and how long you have:
If your council hasn't decided within two months of you first contacting it, you can still appeal, but you then have four months from your original contact to do so.
The tribunal is free and doesn't require legal representation. The Ombudsman is urging councils to signpost this right clearly, at the point a decision is made, rather than leaving people to find out too late.
Amerdeep Clarke, Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, said:
"If you think your council tax bill is wrong, you may have a free and independent way to challenge it, and you shouldn't have to find that out by accident, or too late to use it. Too many people come to us having lost that right simply because no one told them it existed. Councils should be telling people about their right to appeal at the point a decision is made, clearly and in writing, not leaving them to stumble across it on a website, or not find out at all. A single line in a letter can make all the difference."

The family also discovered the woman's Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR) document scrunched up in a cupboard, its details unknown to the care workers responsible for her.
The Ombudsman’s report also highlights failures of oversight by Portsmouth City Council. When safeguarding concerns were first raised in April 2024, the council opened an enquiry. Its own local policy sets a 28-day completion target, but this was not completed till October 2024 - six months later.
The Ombudsman found the council had treated Radis' internal investigation as if it discharged its own statutory duty, without putting in place independent scrutiny - despite Radis already being subject to a separate Large Scale Safeguarding Enquiry at the time. The Ombudsman found the failings engaged the woman’s Human Rights under Articles 3 and 8, relating to degrading treatment, dignity and private life.
Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, Amerdeep Clarke said:
"This is a truly shocking case, with abysmal failures. In this case, a vulnerable woman's care deteriorated over many months while a statutory inquiry drifted without proper oversight. It is a stark reminder that a council's safeguarding duty does not end when a contract is signed. Councils must actively scrutinise the care they commission - especially where concerns already exist about a provider.
“For care providers, the message is equally clear: robust care planning, clear escalation, and accurate record keeping are not administrative niceties, they are the foundations of safe care. I urge every organisation working in adult social care to look carefully at the lessons from this case."
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman remedies injustice and shares learning from investigations to help improve public, and adult social care, services. In this case Portsmouth City Council has accepted the Ombudsman's findings and has agreed to apologise to the family, refund the woman's care fees for the period April to July 2024, and make symbolic payments totalling £1,000 to recognise the distress caused.
The council no longer commissions services from Radis.

Many of us will face the moment when someone we love needs end of life care - whether in a care home, at home with support, or in a council-funded placement. How that care is delivered does not just affect the person who is dying: it shapes how their family grieves, and how they remember those final days, for years to come.
Mistakes made at the end of a loved one’s life cannot be corrected. But unlike almost any other public service failure, there is one chance to get it right, and the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman (LGSCO) is today calling on councils and care providers to take that opportunity, every time.
The report, No Second Chances: What Complaints Teach Us About End of Life Care , sets out the most common failures seen in the complaints it receives: poor communication with families, inadequate care plans, services not working together, insensitive handling of death notifications, difficulties around visiting, and unfair charges after death.
Real cases drawn from the ombudsman’s work illustrate the human cost of these failings - families not called in time to say goodbye, a daughter learning of her mother's death before anyone offered condolences, and a woman who discovered her cousin had died over a year earlier, her grave unmarked and overgrown.
The report sets out what families have a right to expect: to be kept informed as a loved one's condition changes; to be treated with warmth and honesty; to have the person they love cared for as an individual, with their own wishes and preferences respected. And when the worst happens, to receive the news with the sensitivity and compassion it deserves.
These things do not require significant extra resources or investment. They simply need more compassion and a human touch. These are acts of basic humanity, and they shape how families grieve for years to come.
Amerdeep Clarke, Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, said:
"Most of us will face the death of someone we love. How that experience unfolds – whether we feel informed, included and treated with kindness, or left confused and shut out – becomes part of how we remember that person and how we grieve them. Those memories do not fade.
"We know that the people working in care homes and councils want to do their best for the people they look after. This report is for them. It is a practical guide to help them ask honestly: could every family we work with look back on this time with as much comfort as possible?
"The changes we are asking for do not require significant new investment. They require compassion, good planning, and a genuine commitment to treating every dying person as a human being with people who love them. There is only one chance to get this right. We want to help the sector take it."
The report includes practical guidance and self-review questions for councils and care providers on end of life care.
The Ombudsman also has a free toolkit, to help care providers strengthen their complaints handling more generally. The toolkit can be downloaded from asctoolkit.lgo.org.uk .

The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman has welcomed PM Andy Burnham's announcement about the need for adult social care reform.
"We welcome the government's commitment to reforming adult social care, and the recognition that this is a problem too important to keep putting off. Every year, our casework reveals the human cost of a system under strain: people left uncertain about what care they'll need to pay for and how much it will cost them, vulnerable people treated without the dignity and respect they deserve, and families bounced between health and care services while no one takes responsibility for putting things right.
"In September, we will publish our annual review of social care complaints, looking at what people have told us about local authority and private social care services in 2025/26, and we hope this will add further weight to the case for reform. We look forward to engaging with the Big Conversation on Care, and would urge the government to ensure that the experiences of people who have been let down by the current system, including those who come to us for redress, are heard.
"Meaningful reform is not just about a fairer way of paying for care, but building a system where people know what to expect, are treated with dignity, and can get things put right when they go wrong."

Local authority leaders have an historic opportunity to rebuild public trust in local services through local government reforms, says the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman.
New figures, showing a 33% rise in complaints made to the Ombudsman about English authorities over the past year, suggest the case for change is more urgent than ever.
The Ombudsman’s annual review of complaints argues the sweeping programme of local government reorganisation and devolution underway across England is a chance to break down the barriers that have held back joined-up delivery of public services for decades.
The LGSCO received 27,625 complaints in 2025-26, more than doubling the 16% rise recorded the previous year, across every service area from housing and adult social care to special educational needs and children's services. The scale of the increase is striking:
Ombudsman, Amerdeep Clarke said the figures reflect not just individual service failures, but a broader and deepening crisis of public confidence - a pattern visible across all UK public sector Ombudsman bodies.
"A 33% rise in complaints is not a statistical blip. It is a signal. When people cannot get the help they need, and feel they have no other recourse, they come to us. That so many are doing so tells us something important: there is a serious and growing gap between what residents expect and what they are receiving from their local authorities.
"The once-in-a-generation programme of local government reorganisation and devolution now underway presents a genuine opportunity to redesign services, break down the silos that have frustrated joined-up delivery for decades, and find locally-driven solutions to problems that have persisted through successive waves of national reform.
“New authorities should not inherit old failures: they should inherit the learning that comes from them. That intelligence, if left uncaptured, cannot be recovered.
"The problems documented here are serious. But they are not insurmountable. And the opportunity to address them, at pace and at scale, has rarely been greater."
The report also gives reason for optimism. When someone brings a complaint, the Ombudsman first assesses whether it needs a full investigation. In a growing number of cases - up 20% this year - the Ombudsman found that the authority had already dealt with the complaint properly through its own process. This suggests authorities are improving how they handle complaints. When the Ombudsman does make formal recommendations, local authorities act on them in 99.9% of cases, though in more than 750 instances, agreed actions were carried out later than required.
The review also highlights independent University of Manchester research, funded by the Nuffield Foundation, which found many of the problems driving complaints are rooted in national systemic failures, including inadequate funding and chronic shortages of educational psychologists among them. That research concluded that how seriously local authorities engage with learning from complaints makes a measurable difference to residents' lives.

Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) have secured almost £250,000 in Government funding to accelerate the development of a pioneering digital platform designed to help organisations prevent sexual harassment and sexual assault in the workplace before serious incidents occur.
The Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Auditing Service (SASHAS) has received UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) Proof of Concept funding to support its transition from a validated research prototype into a market-ready tool for organisations in the UK and internationally.
Developed by Professor Matt Fossey and Dr Ashley Perry at ARU, SASHAS is a comprehensive digital intelligence platform designed to measure and monitor workplace sexual harassment and sexual assault. It captures employee experiences and perceptions and transforms them into actionable insights through advanced analytics and real-time data visualisation.
By providing metrics at organisational, departmental, and team levels, SASHAS analyses data to identify where inappropriate behaviours are occurring and, crucially, highlights emerging risk areas before they escalate into more serious incidents.
Traditional reporting systems often rely on formal complaints being made after harm has already occurred. Instead, SASHAS is designed to help organisations recognise cultural vulnerabilities and warning signs earlier, allowing leaders to take preventative action and strengthen safeguarding measures.
The project comes amid heightened national attention on workplace culture. Research suggests that many incidents continue to go unreported because victims fear negative consequences or lack confidence in reporting processes.
SASHAS emerged from a NATO research programme examining sexual misconduct across militaries, where estimates suggest that military sexual trauma can affect over 20% of serving personnel. Researchers identified a need for tools capable of assessing not only incidents of misconduct, but also the organisational conditions that can allow harmful behaviours to occur and remain hidden.
Having been rigorously tested and piloted across multiple organisations, the platform is now entering its next phase of development. The new funding will support enhanced analytics, expanded user testing, readying for procurement and the development of sustainable commercial pathways for wider adoption.
“Sexual harassment and sexual assault are often understood through formal reports and investigations, but these only represent a fraction of what people experience. Organisations need better ways of understanding workplace culture, barriers to reporting, and emerging risks before harm escalates. SASHAS has been designed to provide that insight, helping organisations move from reactive responses towards prevention.”
“We are incredibly pleased that UKRI has recognised the potential of this work. SASHAS has emerged from years of research into organisational culture, safeguarding, and wellbeing. This funding will help us transform a validated research innovation into a practical tool that can support organisations, improve workplace safety, and strengthen trust in institutions.”
The research has been led by ARU’s Veterans and Families Institute for Military Social Research (VFI) in collaboration with the International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute (IPPPRI) and the Centre of Excellence for Equity in Uniformed Public Services (CEEUPS) .

By Justin Roberts , Anglia Ruskin University
Anti-ageing supplements are everywhere, from advertising campaigns to social media feeds. Promising everything from increased energy to a longer life, they come in many forms, from powders containing multiple ingredients to single-nutrient capsules.
One molecule in particular, NAD+ , has attracted growing interest, with claims it can boost energy, improve vitality, slow ageing and even help us live longer.
But does the science support these claims? And can NAD+ supplements really help us age more healthily?
NAD+ (short for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is found in every cell in our bodies. It plays an essential role in helping our cells turn food into energy . Without it, many of the processes that keep us alive would be unable to function.
NAD+ also supports numerous enzymes and proteins, including sirtuins, which help regulate inflammation, DNA repair and the function of mitochondria , the structures responsible for producing much of the energy our cells need.
Research suggests that NAD+ levels decline as we get older . This is partly because damage to our DNA accumulates over time, activating enzymes that use up NAD+ more quickly. Another enzyme, called CD38, also becomes more active with age and inflammation, increasing NAD+ use. Meanwhile, our cells may become less efficient at producing it .
The extent of this decline varies between people and different tissues, with some studies suggesting that NAD+ levels may fall by between 10% and 80% as we age.
Lower NAD+ levels have been linked to reduced energy production in cells, slower DNA repair and other changes associated with ageing.
Animal studies suggest that increasing NAD+ levels may improve muscle function and metabolism and even cognitive function , encouraging researchers to investigate whether similar benefits are possible in humans.
There is limited evidence that taking NAD+ itself as a supplement effectively increases NAD+ levels, as it is broken down during digestion . A potential solution to this could be liposomal NAD+, where the molecule is enclosed in tiny fat-based structures designed to improve absorption.
A 2026 study involving 14 people found that taking 1,000mg of liposomal NAD+ daily for two weeks increased NAD+ levels inside cells by more than 64%. However, larger, carefully controlled studies are needed to confirm this finding.
Most human research has instead focused on NAD+ precursors: substances the body uses to make NAD+. These include two compounds derived from vitamin B3, nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
There is good evidence that both can increase NAD+ levels in the blood.
In one randomised, placebo-controlled study involving 140 overweight but otherwise healthy adults aged 40–60, NR supplementation increased blood NAD+ levels over eight weeks. The greatest increase occurred among those taking 1,000 mg (milligrams) daily, whose levels rose by 142% after two weeks and remained elevated throughout the study.
Another study involving 30 healthy adults found that taking 250 mg of NMN daily increased blood NAD+ levels by around 50% after four weeks, with levels remaining elevated throughout the 12-week trial.
High doses of vitamin B3 may also increase NAD+ , although these can be poorly tolerated over longer periods.
Together, these findings suggest that NAD+ precursors can successfully raise blood NAD+ levels. However, whether this also increases levels in other tissues, such as muscles and organs, remains unclear .
Animal studies have produced encouraging results, with NAD+ precursors improving physical performance, insulin sensitivity and the way cells produce energy . One study found that giving older mice NR for six weeks increased their lifespan by an average of 39 days , equivalent to around 5%.
However, results from human studies have been less convincing.

Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) is a key partner in a new £6.75 million initiative that aims to harness the power of creative industries to accelerate economic growth in the East of England.
The programme, called CreateSci, will connect the region’s creative businesses with major tech partners including BT, ElevenLabs and industrial software company AVEVA – providing access to new technology, expertise and potential markets.
More than 250 creative businesses will benefit from the new programme, led by the University of East Anglia (UEA), helping create up to 500 skilled jobs across the region.
CreateSci is being funded by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and delivered by the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC). It is one of only a handful of creative clusters being funded across the UK , and the first of its kind in the East of England.
The programme will be led by UEA alongside ARU, Norwich University of the Arts and the University of Suffolk, with the University of Cambridge as a project partner.
At the heart of the programme is the development of the Creative Clinic, where creative businesses and arts and humanities researchers work alongside scientists, the NHS and major employers to tackle real world challenges in relating to health, wellbeing and the environment.
It will showcase how creativity, storytelling, design and community engagement are vital to ensure scientific breakthroughs are understood, trusted and used. Using creative expertise to drive innovation, the programme will help businesses access research, build new skills, and turn ideas into products, while forging new connections with investors and partners.
CreateSci is also expected to attract further public and private investment into the region, creating new opportunities across towns, cities, rural areas and coastal communities – strengthening the East of England’s reputation as a place where creativity drives growth.
“The creative industries are one of the UK’s greatest economic strengths, and vital to the Government’s Industrial Strategy ambitions for national growth, but that growth depends on having the right skills, talent and opportunities in place in all regions.
The East of England has a strong and growing creative sector but has historically attracted less investment than many other regions.
“This cluster is unique because growth goes way beyond creative industries – into the East’s other key sectors of clean energy and life science.
“CreateSci will help businesses across the East of England develop the expertise needed in a rapidly changing sector, supporting them to innovate, grow and attract investment.
<p“We are delighted to be working alongside Norwich University of the Arts, Anglia Ruskin University, the University of Suffolk, Cambridge, industry partners and the Arts and Humanities Research Council on this shared ambition.
“Together, we are investing in the people, skills and ideas that underpin the Government’s Modern Industrial Strategy and strengthen the region’s long-term economic future.”
“Across Cambridge and the wider East of England, we have world-class scientific and technological research alongside creative businesses and communities. CreateSci provides a platform to connect this knowledge.
“At ARU, through DesignLab, one of the specialist labs within the Centre for Media, Arts and Creative Technologies (MACT) , we are particularly interested in how design-led approaches can connect research with real-world challenges, ensuring that innovation is grounded in the needs, knowledge and experiences of communities.
“Our ambition is to help build a more connected, collaborative, and resilient regional economy, generating lasting value and benefits that extend well beyond the lifetime of the programme.”

Denise Erica Da Costa Silva at her graduation ceremony at Peterborough Cathedral this week after completing a Master's Degree in International Business Management at ARU Peterborough
A mother-of-four who fled domestic abuse in her home country to build a new life in the UK is celebrating her second graduation from ARU Peterborough – which was considerably less eventful than the first.
After completing her undergraduate studies with ARU Peterborough in 2025, Denise Erica Da Costa Silva went straight from Peterborough Cathedral to hospital to give birth to her fourth child.
Last September, she began her postgraduate course in International Business Management , and she celebrated her second ARU Peterborough graduation at Peterborough Cathedral this week.
Denise had moved to the UK in 2019 with her oldest three children after making the difficult decision to leave an abusive relationship and start again. Determined to create a safer and more secure future for her family, she arrived in Peterborough ready to rebuild her life from scratch.
Denise had previously studied Portuguese and Communication at university and built a career in banking, customer services and marketing in Angola. As she qualifies as a Portuguese citizen through her mother, she was able to settle in the UK but found that the qualifications she had gained earlier in her life were not fully recognised here.
“When I moved here it was very challenging to find work. My first job was as a part-time cleaner which made it very challenging to juggle work and childcare.”
She decided to gain UK qualifications, starting with Level 3 studies and then a Foundation course in London, but the opening of ARU Peterborough offered a life-changing possibility to gain qualifications closer to home. Being able to study locally enabled Denise to balance family responsibilities with her academic ambitions.
She successfully applied to study for an undergraduate degree in Business and Management, graduating in 2025, and has now graduated from her postgraduate studies while preparing a future PhD proposal exploring challenges within human resource management.
Denise was heavily pregnant on the day of her undergraduate graduation, but made it through the ceremony before heading straight to hospital, where she gave birth to baby Zlatan a few days later.
“I came for the ceremony and I started feeling the pain but to be honest I was so focused. I rushed from the Cathedral to the hospital straight afterwards.
“I was in considerable pain, but there was no way I was going to miss that milestone!”
Denise began her postgraduate course when Zlatan was just two months old. She added: “It was a very hard time. It was just me and the kids but because I had a lot of support from ARU Peterborough, the lecturers and my personal tutor, they gave me a lot of strength and in the end I made it.”
Denise is now pursuing a PhD qualification and hopes her story will encourage others facing adversity to pursue their ambitions. Her eldest daughter Lourdes is considering following in her footsteps by studying Business Management at ARU Peterborough next September.
“When I first started studying in the UK, I could never have imagined reaching this point. Balancing motherhood, employment and studying has not always been easy.
“My advice to others is don't allow barriers to stop you from pursuing your ambitions. Whether it is language, family commitments or a lack of confidence, there are tools and support available to help you overcome those hurdles.”

A new analysis focusing on dog attacks on humans in the UK suggests that most incidents are preventable and committed by a wide variety of breeds rather than solely by highly publicised ‘dangerous dogs’ – and owners have a key part to play in prevention.
The new report, entitled Safety Around Dogs: A Process Analysis of Dog Bites , was commissioned by Battersea Dogs and Cats Home and carried out by Anglia Ruskin University (ARU), and examined court records, hospital admission, policy and survey data.
The report analysed 130 dog bite incidents from court data between 2020 and 2025 and found that the circumstances behind dog attacks are highly variable. Of the court data, owner failure to control a dog was the single most common cause, blamed for 32% of cases. The report describe these as unprovoked attacks where a dog jumps up and bites a passer-by in a public place.
A total of 24 cases were a result of the dog escaping either from a property or being tethered and then biting, suggesting that the dog was not appropriately secured by its owner.
All data sets analysed within the report showed that dog attacks involve a wide variety of breeds and that bites are not confined to dogs covered by breed-specific legislation.
Researchers also found that adults account for the majority of victims in both court cases and hospital admission data, despite public concern often focusing on attacks involving children. A notable 14% of people who completed the survey had been bitten three or more times.
As a result of the findings, the report urges both dog owners and policymakers to use similar situational crime prevention measures that are deployed in most other antisocial behaviour scenarios to reduce the risk of attack.
Recommendations set out in the report include better education about safe interactions with dogs, keeping dogs on a lead in higher-risk public settings, and better “dog-proofing” of homes to protect visitors, postal workers and delivery drivers.
The researchers also call for consideration of measures such as enhanced dog registration, stronger links between registration and microchipping, and a mandatory code of practice for dog owners.
According to the report, policies aimed at reducing dog attacks should focus on the situations in which bites occur and the actions owners can take to minimise risk, rather than focusing solely on breed.
“Public debate often focuses on labelling certain breeds as ‘dangerous dogs’, but our analysis shows that a wide range of dogs are involved in attacks and that many are preventable. The evidence suggests that dog attacks do not have a single cause and cannot simply be explained by the breed involved.
“Across the data we examined, we repeatedly found examples of dogs being off leads, escaping from homes or gardens, or being placed in situations where an attack was both foreseeable and preventable. Owners have a role to play in preventing incidents alongside use of accepted crime prevention techniques. Greater awareness, better training and prevention approaches linked to situations where dog attacks are likely to occur all have the potential to reduce many of these incidents.
“The focus should be on understanding the circumstances that lead to attacks and implementing practical measures that help owners manage risks before injuries occur.”
“Every dog bite is a reminder that more must be done to keep people and dogs safe. This research shows that many incidents can be prevented by helping owners better understand and reduce risks through effective behaviour training and secure home environments.

Twin sisters Freya Ward, pictured left, and Ella Ward at their ARU graduation ceremony in Chelmsford
Two identical twin sisters are ready to deliver after graduating from the Midwifery course at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU).
Ella and Freya Ward, from Benfleet, have journeyed together through school, college and university and will now go on to work as midwives at Basildon Hospital after graduating at Chelmsford Cathedral this week.
The 21-year-olds attended Appleton School in Benfleet before going to nearby USP College to study health and social care. They then applied to ARU where they both underwent hospital placements at Basildon Hospital.
They even passed their driving tests three days apart, and for a while shared a car to travel into university and to placements.
Freya said: “We’re very similar in lots of ways. We share the same friends and the same interests. We both liked the idea of becoming midwives so it seemed a natural path to take for us both.
“My mum was the person who first gave me the idea to become a midwife when I was 15, and I have never looked back since. My parents and wider family have been amazing throughout my training and have always been there to encourage me during moments when I doubted my abilities.”
While going through life together as identical twins has been fairly seamless, the situation has sometimes thrown up unusual challenges for others.
Freya added: “One of the most memorable moments was on the delivery suite when Ella had finished a day shift and I had just started the night shift. A patient I was caring for asked if I was feeling alright after such a long day. I immediately realised she had mistaken me for my sister and had to explain I'd only arrived a few hours earlier. We all laughed and it became a bit of a joke among the midwives.”
Ella said: “We’re used to it but we do get quite a lot of people interested in how it works and asking us questions. They usually want to know who has delivered the most babies, or whether the patients and other midwives get confused.”
Their hospital placements also confirmed they had chosen the right profession. Both sisters vividly remember delivering their first babies during her first year of training.
Remembering that first delivery, Freya said: “I was lucky enough to be working with an amazing midwife who took the time to explain things to me and made me feel included in the experience. It is a really nice memory and reminds me that even throughout the busy, more stressful moments, birth can be calm and empowering. I will always remember and be grateful to that family.”
Ella said: “I remember being excited about the first birth. An amazing midwife helped me deliver the baby and they called the baby Freya which I thought was funny and obviously I told my sister straight away!”
Although the similarities between Ella and Freya are clear, they both had different strengths while studying.
Ella added: “I was stronger with coursework and Freya was better with exams. When it came to revising for exams, Freya helped me with revision notes and preparation for those. Everyone has those high and low moments but we helped each other through.”

By Cathrine Jansson-Boyd , Anglia Ruskin University
Fashion lovers are generally associated with bursting wardrobes and chasing the latest trends. But that reputation is beginning to shift.
In the last few years, market surveys have found that around a third of shoppers are now buying second hand clothing . For gen Z, this figure increases to just under half. Giant hauls from fast fashion brands were once the trend – but an eye for vintage bargains and pre-worn fits is now more on point.
Though buying used is far preferential to buying new, overconsumption can still be a problem with second-hand clothing. That’s because buying used often supplements, rather than replaces, fast fashion habits.
If you love fashion, but want to indulge in your hobby without falling into the trap of overconsumption, here are five tips.
“Shopping your closet” – creating new looks with the existing pieces in your wardrobe – has been trending online for a while. Putting some thought into how you can restyle existing pieces will help you to shift your focus from buying something, to becoming creative.
Research has shown that a small and versatile wardrobe that can easily be mixed and matched into several outfits fosters creativity as your brain must solve styling puzzles with limited items. It also generates feelings of satisfaction and enjoyment. This is important as being content with your clothing choices is linked to general wellbeing.
It can be helpful to schedule a dedicated wardrobe date and treat styling your closet like a fun puzzle rather than a chore. Creativity tends to flow better when under less pressure, so don’t try to build your creative cognitive styling muscles when you are in a rush.
To get inspiration flowing, try searching sites like Pinterest. Type in exact terms like “oversized blazer outfit” to discover fresh styling ideas for pieces sitting in your closet. Set yourself a challenge for 10 days not to wear any combination you have worn before.
And just so you don’t forget: snap quick mirror photos of any outfit combinations that work well so you have a personal outfit catalogue ready for busy mornings.
Having too many clothes can lead to choice overload , when the difficulty of decision exceeds our cognitive ability to make a choice.
Generally, people tend to find it easier to make a choice when they have less to choose from. If you have two T-shirts, your brain can decide in seconds. But if you have 18 T-shirts, wardrobe paralysis kicks in.
Treat sorting through your clothes as an interactive styling project. Reorganising by colour or silhouette can help you to rediscover forgotten favourites and appreciate the craftsmanship of items you already own, as well as making it easier to choose.
Try buying clothing as a collector or curator. This means that you should select unique, high-quality pieces based on your personal preference and their long-term value. Look past trends by evaluating fabric weight, seam stitching, lining quality and natural fibres (like wool, linen, or silk) before buying, ensuring each addition to your wardrobe is built to last.
Keep a running list of missing baseline pieces or specific archive designs. Planning ahead limits the likelihood of making an impulse purchase, which may lead to regret . Taking 48 hours to think it over also reduces the chances of making the wrong decision.
Craft a clear vision of your personal aesthetic focusing on your favoured silhouettes, colour palettes and textures, so that every prospective purchase must earn its place alongside your existing collection.
Building a wardrobe based on your specific personal taste allows you to treat your personal style as a fine art rather than a fast-fashion race. You’ll also probably keep your garments for longer as items people care for tend to become tangible extensions of their identity .

Christmas shoppers will be able to pick up unique festive gifts, enjoy seasonal treats and try their hand at a range of games and activities when Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) students bring their annual Elevate Winter Market to Cambridge and Chelmsford next month.
The free event, open to the public, will take place on Tuesday, 1 December in the Helmore and Lord Ashcroft buildings at ARU's Cambridge campus on East Road, before moving on to the Michael Ashcroft building at ARU's Chelmsford campus on Thursday, 3 December, with shoppers invited to browse stalls created and run by student entrepreneurs.
The market, which runs from 10am until 3pm on both days, is organised by students taking part in ARU’s Elevate programme, which gives aspiring entrepreneurs hands-on experience of developing, funding and running a business. After pitching for seed funding and creating their festive ventures, students will be selling directly to members of the public while supporting charities across the local community.
