The response to the sessions from the schools has been overwhelmingly positive.
At Westcliff High School for Girls, students were ‘fully engaged and visibly moved by the session.’ School staff noted a clear improvement in awareness and suggested including tips on behaviour in stations and trains, as well as PSHE topics like mental health and respect for others.
Harold Wood Primary pupils asked thoughtful questions about electrified tracks and station safety. Teachers praised the session’s impact.
At The Willows Primary school, children engaged well and showed a good understanding of existing safety rules, while staff felt the video clearly communicated the dangers.
Recently, c2c Head of Revenue Protection and Security, Iain Palmer, became a Rail Safe Friendly Ambassador – making him the first RSF Ambassador to come from a UK Train Operating Company (TOC).
c2c Head of Revenue Protection and Security, Iain Palmer, said:
“I’m really proud to be a Rail Safe Friendly Ambassador. Having sponsored 100 schools last year – and another 150 up and coming this year to reach ‘Gold Standard’ – this partnership sees tens of thousands of students in our local communities educated in railway safety. That can only be a good thing and I urge any interested companies to get involved as well.”
“I’d like to congratulate Iain on becoming the first RSF Ambassador to come from a UK TOC. Iain’s dedication to ensuring children and young people stay safe when using the railway typifies the core values everybody here at c2c has.”

Local rail company c2c has teamed up with Colegrave Primary School in Stratford to celebrate Better Transport Week, and to raise awareness amongst pupils, parents and staff of the benefits of taking the train and making more sustainable travel choices.

“It is great to be partnering with Colegrave Primary School to both celebrate and highlight Better Transport Week, and how train travel can help improve air quality and reduce social isolation, while connecting people with work, education and leisure opportunities.

Local rail operator Trenitalia c2c is proud to have honoured rock ‘n’ roll icon, Essex native and co-founder of the legendary band Dr. Feelgood, Wilko Johnson, with a specially commissioned train nameplate at a ceremony at Southend Central station today (Monday 9 June).
The nameplate, which can be seen on unit 357316, reads ‘Wilko Johnson 1947-2022 – He did it right,’ and plays tribute to the legendary Dr. Feelgood song ‘She Does it Right.’ It was unveiled by Wilko’s son Simon Johnson on platform 4 at Southend Central station. He said:
‘’It is very touching that c2c are honouring my father in this way. I am told this is a tribute usually only reserved for poets and royalty. As an aspiring poet, I know he would be well chuffed.”
The event was attended by a host of special guests including fellow Dr. Feelgood bandmate John B Sparks as well as Wilko’s brother Malcolm Wilkinson and many friends including Kursaal Flyers frontman, Will Birch and Blockheads bassist Norman Watt-Roy.
The event also featured a live musical performance both on the platform and on board the charter train from cast members of ‘Wilko: Love and Death and Rock and Roll’. The critically acclaimed production is heading to London’s West End in July – written by Jonathan Maitland, who also attended the ceremony – celebrating Wilko’s life and music.
Performers Johnson Willis, John House and Georgina Field delivered a special rendition of R&B classic ‘Route 66’ – with lyrics adapted to celebrate Southend and the Essex coastline. The ‘Wilko Express’ – as the train has been affectionally named – departed Southend Central on its maiden voyage to London Fenchurch Street, calling at key ‘Wilko’ locations along the route including Westcliff, Benfleet and Barking.
“We are delighted to have been able to honour Wilko with the ‘Wilko Express,’ it was artists like him and his bandmates in Dr. Feelgood that had such an amazing impact on the punk scene in the 1970s that it inspired the likes of Roger Daltrey and Paul Weller to follow in his footsteps.
“Away from the fame, he was a dedicated member of our local community throughout his life and used our line often when travelling across Essex. He travelled the world yet always came home to Essex and c2c. We are proud to recognise his inimitable contribution to British music and our local communities by having his family and friends turn out to celebrate this honour.”
“Wilko was a hugely significant cultural figure, nationally and internationally, but he was above all a proud Essex man, so we are delighted that c2c has chosen to honour him in this way. I can’t think of anyone who’s had the honour of a train naming ceremony and then, three weeks later, been the subject of a West End play. But then Wilko was unique.”
Born in Canvey Island, Wilko Johnson was famed for his electrifying stage presence and unique guitar style. As one of the driving forces behind Dr. Feelgood, he helped shape the foundations of punk rock, earning praise from music legends including Roger Daltrey, Paul Weller, the Ramones and the Sex Pistols.
The tribute comes at a celebratory time for fans, with the stage play ‘Wilko: Love and Death and Rock and Roll’ heading to London’s iconic West End, opening at the Leicester Square Theatre this July following sold-out performances in Hornchurch and Southwark. Meanwhile, 2025 marks the 50th anniversary of Dr. Feelgood’s landmark debut album ‘Down by the Jetty’- a record that continues to inspire generations of musicians.
Wilko’s legacy also features prominently in Scene by the Sea, an ongoing exhibition at Southend’s Beecroft Gallery exploring the area’s musical and cultural history.

Trenitalia c2c is delighted to announce its membership of the Employers’ Initiative on Domestic Abuse (EIDA), a leading business network that supports employers to take action on domestic abuse.

Susan Bright, CEO of the Employer’s Initiative on Domestic Abuse, added:

Local rail operator Trenitalia c2c has welcomed a new cohort of trainee drivers to the team as part of its ‘Street to Seat’ recruitment programme, following unprecedented interest in the position.
The eight new trainee mainline drivers are the fifth group to join c2c the training scheme – which is open to individuals with little or no rail experience – with the latest programme attracting more than 5,000 applicants in just two weeks!
The new team, aged between 22 and 54 years old, have been dubbed ‘Team Delta’ and come from all walks of life, bringing a range of experience.
The c2c ‘Street to Seat’ course is available to individuals with little or no rail experience to become fully qualified mainline train drivers. Applicants must pass a competitive application process, including an assessment centre with psychometric testing, panel interviews and a full medical.
Rob Mullen, c2c’s Managing Director, said:
“We’re very proud of c2c’s Street to Seat programme, as it gives people from all backgrounds the chance to become fully-fledged mainline drivers. It is an immensely popular scheme, as evidenced by the incredible over 5,000 applications we had in response to the roles being made available.
“Personally, I want to wish all of our new trainee drivers the best of luck with their training, and I look forward to hearing more about their progress!”
Team Delta includes a familiar face to c2c customers in Alex Bossom, a former British Transport Police Officer (BTP) who has been working alongside the c2c team since 2017, where he was a core part of the BTP’s c2c policing team. Alex has solidified great working relationships with so many c2c colleagues already and will now forge even more, as he starts a brand-new career path to becoming a driver.
Iain Palmer, c2c Head of Revenue Protection and Security, said:
“I have known Alex since he first began working with us for the BTP and I have always seen the amazing effort he’s put in. So, now that he has come from the thin blue line to the c2c magenta one, I am very pleased that we will have such a reliable and safe pair of hands transporting our customers to their destinations.”

Furthermore, all our new trainee drivers are aged between 22-54-years-old – showing that anybody can retrain to become a train driver with c2c.
Training is already well underway with the course including weekly exams, followed by a minimum of 240 hours of on-the-job training with a mentor, three interim assessments and a final five-day assessment. Those that successfully compete the training will typically become qualified drivers in around 9-11 months.
Once qualified, all drivers undergo continuous, frequent assessments to maintain c2c’s high safety and performance standards.

Local rail company Trenitalia c2c has announced it is installing British Sign Language (BSL) screens at locations across the route to provide the latest, up-to-date passenger information for customers, fostering a more accessible environment on the railway.
The trial consists of BSL totems at Fenchurch Street and Southend Central stations which, if successful, could be rolled out to further stations after the three-month trial.
The trial of BSL totems is designed to give customers greater confidence to travel with c2c, with the default display set to playing upcoming departures in sign language. As the totems are interactive, there is the opportunity for customers to use the journey planner, check onward travel from the station and see the local area maps with places of interest.
c2c Accessibility and Integrated Travel Manager, Steve Scutt, said:
“From research, 40 per cent of d/Deaf people whose first, or preferred language is BSL, don’t feel confident using the train.
“There is a common misconception that all d/Deaf people can read, write or understand text based or written information but for most Deaf people who are sign language users and have been deaf all of their lives, English is a second language and as such they may have a limited ability to read, write or understand the text or written information displayed to them.
“We are proud to have installed these screens, which will give customers who use BSL real-time departure information and allow them to travel with confidence.”
The new totems are pre-loaded with standard messaging and timetable information and are also interactive in providing customers with information during periods of unexpected disruption.
The screens also offer journey planning and onward travel functionality, meaning that customers can view local area maps and the next direct trains. An NFC (near field communication) pad on the side of the totem also allows customers to wirelessly transfer information to their phone or device by touching the pad, meaning that the benefit of the machines extends far beyond the station concourse.
Additionally, c2c has also installed the ‘Recite Me’ assistive toolbar to make its website more accessible and inclusive to all. This can be found at www.c2c-online.co.uk
The tool is a web-friendly solution, which provides a range of tools that help users navigate, read and interact with web content more effectively. This includes customers who may have decreased vision, speak or read English as a second language or have a learning difficulty.
Customers simply click on the ‘accessibility tools’ button at the top of the c2c website and the text-to-speech software will help understand the digital content by reading aloud website text.

We are very sorry for the disruption our customers experienced yesterday afternoon and evening.
At approximately 14:40 yesterday, a signalling fault was reported in the Southend area. As a result of this failure, services from Southend East to Chalkwell in both directions were suspended. This severely restricted the number of trains we could operate.
Upon confirmation of the signalling failure, arrangements were made for c2c tickets to be accepted on Greater Anglia services and First Buses between Leigh-on-Sea and Shoeburyness.
Network Rail dispatched a team of engineers to the area who had to manually install heavy clips to eight sets of track points, which were repaired at approximately 17:30. However, the fault caused knock-on delays and cancellations to our services, which continued into the evening.
Unfortunately, at 21:30, a driver reported having hit an obstruction in the West Horndon area. This meant we had to suspend trains in both directions to allow specialist train crew and the emergency services to inspect the site.
On inspection, it was discovered the train had hit an animal and the line was opened at 23:00. Again, this caused knock-on delays and cancellations to our services.
Rob Mullen, Managing Director of c2c, said: “I am sorry to our customers who were caught up in the disruption on our route during yesterday’s evening peak.
“We know this will have caused extensive delays to your journeys especially as it happened at the worst possible time during the evening peak. We worked closely with our Network Rail colleagues to try and get our services up and running as quickly as possible, but we know this will have impacted many of your journeys last night.”
Katie Frost, Network Rail Anglia’s Route Director said: “I’m really sorry to all the passengers who were affected by the disruption yesterday. We had a very rare failure of several signalling modules, which meant we couldn’t run trains.
“While we had our response teams on site quickly, for us to be able to get trains running again safely, we needed to manually install heavy clips to eight sets of track points, which took around three hours.
“I have launched an immediate investigation with our signalling equipment supplier to understand what went wrong and prevent this from happening again. Once again, I’m sorry to everyone involved.”

Trenitalia c2c is currently undertaking a significant project to repaint its entire Class 357 train units with the first units now in service.
With an approximate 35.8 million journeys being made on c2c services every year, the work will extend the longevity and reliability of the 357 fleet as well as enhancing t he customer experience and maintaining the highest standards of service.
The project is being carried out in collaboration with rolling stock manufacturer Alstom at its depot based in Ilford, which is a centre of excellence and employs over 120 people working on a range of train classes.
c2c’s iconic 357 fleet were introduced into service between 1998 and 2002 and comprise a total of 74 units. The units are on lease until 2029 and run across the c2c route alongside the 720 fleet, which came into service in 2023.
Each 357 unit will receive a complete external re-paint to protect them and ensure they have a successful future on the route.
Each train takes approximately 20 days to complete, and the work involves stripping back the cars, including exterior fittings, undertaking minor repairs and restoration and comprehensively re-painting, a layer at a time, to prevent corrosion and rust. A waterborne hydro topcoat is used, which is an eco-friendly paint system with the lowest VOC content.
This protects against wear and tear and will enable the trains to operate as successfully for the second half of their life, as they have done for the first. With advances in paint technology the newly painted trains are finished as well, or better, than when they were first introduced.
c2c’s Head of Engineering Jeff Baker said: “We are delighted with the progress of the 357 repaint project. We know that this work, led by our partners at Alstom, will both improve the longevity of our 357 fleet and will benefit our customers for years to come.”
Alstom’s Portfolio Director – Commuter Fleets, Peter Keighron said: “We are very proud of the job we are doing with this repaint project. The trains were orginally built at our Litchurch Lane site in Derby and we now maintain them at East Ham depot, therefore Alstom has all the knowledge to work on these units.
“The 357 units are the workhorse of the c2c fleet and this repaint will allow them to continue serving the millions of passengers they carry every year.”
The project will take 24 months to complete, and the first unit ( 357207) is already operational on the c2c route. The second unit (357005) will be released onto the c2c route next week.

We are very sorry for the disruption our customers experienced yesterday and during this morning’s peak on the c2c route.
Yesterday, at approximately 06:00 a signal failure was reported between Dagenham Dock and Barking. As a result of this failure, we had to run trains at a reduced speed.
Network Rail dispatched a team of engineers to the area, which involved a line possession for 30 minutes, but they were unable to resolve the fault at this time. This meant we had to run trains through the affected area at a reduced speed, which caused a knock-on effect to the entire c2c route. The signalling fault was fixed by Network Rail engineers at 10:30.
Unfortunately, at 10:20, a train unit fault in the Becontree area caused further delays to the service. This train was moved back to Barking station where passengers were able to alight the faulty unit.
The service returned to normal running during the early afternoon.
Upon confirmation of the signal damage, arrangements were made for c2c tickets to be accepted on Greater Anglia and London Underground services.
This morning (Tuesday 14 January), at approximately 06:45 a train at West Ham station developed a technical fault, which meant it was unable to move from the station. Again, this caused knock-on delays and cancellations to our services. We returned to normal service running at 10:30.
Rob Mullen, Managing Director of c2c, said:
“I am sorry to our customers who were caught up in the disruption on the c2c route yesterday and earlier today.
“I know this will have caused extensive delays to your journey, especially as the disruption hit our peak services on both days. We worked closely with our Network Rail colleagues to repair Monday’s signalling fault and thanks to their hard work our service recovered in time for yesterday’s peak evening service.”
Lawrence Bowman, Network Rail Anglia Route Director, said:
“I am really sorry to any passengers who had their journey disrupted on Monday. We had a loss of signalling on the network which, even once fixed meant we had to cancel and delay a number of services on what is usually a very punctual line.”

Local rail operator Trenitalia c2c recouped a record-breaking £596,493 from ticketless travel in 2024, after clamping down on fare evasion through a variety of operational and data-led tactics.
By expanding the Revenue Protection team, c2c has ramped up deployment and coverage across the network, with the significant sum representing an 88% increase on 2023’s total of £317,000.
The result showcases the increasing use of data to identify fare evasion activity, as well as the focus and commitment of c2c’s Revenue Protection and Security teams on reducing and eliminating fare evasion across the network.
From January 1, 2024, to 31 December 2024, c2c handed out over 8,863 penalty fares to passengers that did not have a valid ticket for travel, representing a substantial increase from the 3,542 penalty fares issued in 2023 – with the total sum collected from penalty fares being £337,068.
Across the course of 2024, the team had great success with investigating fare evaders, with thousands owed by some for historic unpaid tickets.
c2c’s Head of Revenue Protection and Security, Iain Palmer, said, “I’m delighted that c2c has recouped such a significant sum across 2024, as ticketless travel is an issue that blights the entire rail network in the UK.
“Our Revenue Protection and Security teams work incredibly hard under sometimes difficult circumstances to ensure that all our passengers have a valid ticket to use the c2c line. So, to achieve this record-breaking year is a testament to their hard work and determination to ensure that all passengers use the network fairly.
“At c2c, we are committed to ensuring that our passengers have a safe and reliable journey and work in close partnership with The British Transport Police to achieve this. We know from historic evidence that ticketless travel is linked to ASB (anti-social behaviour), and our front-line teams work very hard to ensure that we catch as many of these people that feel they are exempt from the rules as possible,” he added.
In November 2024 c2c launched its ‘Don’t Take the Gamble’ campaign, which highlights the repercussions of travelling without a valid ticket, in order to ensure that passengers understand the risk they are taking if they choose to evade their fare.
The criminal implications of ticketless travel are central to the campaign, fronted by TV presenter, Ortis Deley, and highlights the risks and impacts of being caught without a valid ticket. For the full details of the campaign, please click here.
To discover more about how c2c is tackling ticketless travel, visit www.c2c-online.co.uk/gamble .

Engineers have completed track and station improvement works on the c2c route to help boost reliability and the passenger experience.
Over a series of weekends in November and December, Network Rail replaced more than 3,800 metres of worn-out rail between Leigh-on-Sea and Southend Central stations. Having first been installed in 1967 and 1968, the old rail needed to be replaced to minimise the chance of defects that can cause delays. The newly-installed rail is expected to last for another 50 years.
Engineers also fixed faulty drainage pipes alongside the platforms at Chalkwell station. If the pipes had not been fixed, excess water could have affected the quality of the track, potentially causing a bumpy ride and the need for speed restrictions on trains.
At the same time, c2c engineers and station colleagues took the chance to carry out essential improvement works at key locations across the network, including Shoeburyness, Southend-on-Sea and Westcliff.
These delivered vital upgrades which are crucial to maintaining the safety and efficiency for c2c customers across the route.
Most c2c services will be running normally over Christmas and the New Year, but there will be earlier last train times on Christmas Eve, no trains on Christmas Day and Boxing Day and other timetable changes. Find out more here.
Laura McEwen, Operations and Engineering Director for c2c, said, “We appreciate that for customers these works have caused disruption, but the benefit is projected to last for another five decades and ensure the safety of our railway for all.
“While Network Rail caried out the work, we made the most of the time to carry out a huge variety of improvements. These encompassed everything from cutting back trees in customer car parks, painting ticket halls, resurfacing platforms and ensuring the structural durability of station canopies.
“Some of these will of course be more apparent to customers than others, but we hope that this work behind the scenes gives our passengers confidence that we are using our resources as wisely as possible.”
Simon Milburn, infrastructure director for Network Rail Anglia, said, “Our work over November and December was vital to keeping trains running safely and reliably in future. Thank you to c2c passengers for bearing with us while our engineers got out on track and got these jobs done.”
c2c is the award-winning train operator running services between Fenchurch Street and Shoeburyness, serving 26 stations in East London and South Essex. Owned by Trenitalia, c2c is one of the UK’s most punctual and popular train operators and nearly 35.8 million journeys are made on its services every year. Italian-based Trenitalia is one of Europe’s leading rail operators and the passenger rail arm of FS Italiane Group. For more information email mediaenquiries@c2crail.net

The team from local train operator c2c Trenitalia welcomed 13-year-old Rainham-resident Bowie to Fenchurch Street station ahead of International Day of Persons with Disabilities 2024.

Fay, Bowie’s mum, said,“I have always championed Bowie to believe he can do whatever he sets his heart on, autism isn’t a barrier – it’s his superpower!
“One of his dreams in life is to be a Station Announcer and c2c made this happen. We cannot thank them enough for the kindness they showed us. The team and the station staff were so autism aware that Bowie felt right at home.
“We have made lifelong friends with the team at Fenchurch Street and will always make sure we say hello when passing through!”
Femi Oyetunji, c2c Customer Delivery Manager managing London stations, hosted Bowie’s visit and said, “We were honoured to welcome Bowie to Fenchurch Street station and were really happy to be able to show him some behind the scenes railway action. “I know he was practicing the announcement script at the weekend and this really showed in his word-perfect delivery. He is very welcome to come back to see us any time.”
c2c is committed to making its route as accessible as possible and within the business we are driving accessibility improvements across our east London and south Essex network.
Looking ahead, customers will start to see some of these improvements in the new year, with Grays station soon to be fully accessible with the addition of two new lifts, delivered as part of the Department for Transport’s ‘Access for All’ scheme.
Paul McGunnigle White, c2c’s Diversity and Inclusion Manager, said, “It is really important for us as an industry to adapt so we attract and welcome more autistic and neurodiverse customers.
“At c2c, we are committed to ensuring our network is accessible for everyone and we have an ongoing programme of work which develops colleagues’ awareness of how autistic people or other neurodiverse passengers might behave or act during their journey.

He explains: “It’s a criminal offence to travel on a train without the right ticket, so this is a serious issue. c2c offers so many ways to buy a ticket, passengers can purchase a ticket from the station, our app or online, making it easy for passengers to have the right ticket before they travel.”
He continued: “Our revenue protection officers are everywhere, uniformed and undercover. We use intelligence to ensure we have enough evidence to take long term fare evaders to court and we’ve been very successful at finding those that fare evade. If we don’t get you today, we’ll get you tomorrow or the day after, it’s really not worth the risk.”

Play Their Way has been developed by the Children’s Coaching Collaborative , of which we are one of 17 partner organisations.
The campaign’s aim is to build a ‘child-first’ coaching movement and it was launched this morning with a special event at Peckham BMX Club, which is already changing the lives of young people through their child-first approach to coaching.
With the campaign aligning so closely with the goals of our strategy, it’s no surprise our chief executive Tim Hollingsworth has welcomed its launch.
“Positive experiences for children and young people are at the heart of Uniting the Movement – and child-first coaching is an important part of this,” he said.
“Our research tells us that for children, ‘fun’ is the primary reason for taking part in sport and activity. They will want to take part if they enjoy it.
“It’s vital that we put fun and enjoyment at the centre of sport and activity and give our children and young people the chance to shape their sporting experiences to boost activity levels.
“We look forward to working with our partners and supporting the amazing coaches across the UK. We want to give all children the chance to have their say – and play their way.”
Our latest Active Lives Children and Young People survey found that of those who regularly exercise, 47% strongly agree that they enjoy taking part in sport and physical activity – down from 51% prior to the coronavirus pandemic.
A child-first approach to coaching champions the child’s voice, choice and journey in sport and physical activity.
The same survey also showed that 53% of children and young people don’t get the recommended average of 60 minutes of physical activity a day.
This knowledge has driven Play Their Way to ensure children have the best possible experience in sport and activity through the people who know them best – their coaches.
The campaign will work with England’s 2.6 million coaches to build a grassroots movement aimed at increasing and improving child-first coaching in communities across the nation.
It’s hoped that by putting the child first, it will help them enjoy being active their own way and allow great coaching to inspire children into staying active for life.
Which for Heather Douglas, head of coaching and policy at UK Coaching , is what the campaign is all about.

“Our goal is for all children and young people, regardless of age, background or ability, to have a voice, choice and decide their journey when participating in sport and physical activity, so they develop a genuine and lifelong love for being active.”
The campaign has been developed using insight and engagement from a network of grassroots coaches, along with children and young people through a series of focus groups and workshops.

Our chief executive Simon Hayes has welcomed the announcement of a landmark ambition to drive opportunities for one million more girls to play, watch and lead in sport.
The vision, set out by the government today, will see women and girls guaranteed the same access to all funded grassroots facilities as men and boys by the time the UK hosts the FIFA Women’s World Cup in 2035.
Furthermore, sports will only be able to unlock public funding if they commit to structural equality – with the needs of women and girls given equal consideration to the needs of men and boys at every step.
It follows the launch of The Equal Sport Project earlier this month, when we and UK Sport committed to working with our funded partners to ensure their governance is designed by men and women, for men and women.
"Women and girls should have an equal say in how sport is run, as well as equal opportunities to take part," Simon said. "Linking public funding to equal governance is an important step towards making that a reality.
"This gives further momentum to The Equal Sport Project. Our focus will be on working with funded partners to ensure women’s and girls’ experiences help shape the decisions they make, creating more opportunities to be active in environments where they feel welcome and supported."
Women’s sport in England has enjoyed huge recent growth, boosted by the success of the Lionesses and Red Roses in football and rugby union respectively.
Participation in football among women and girls has risen by 2.3 million since the UEFA Women’s European Championship was held in England in 2022.
However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions. Just a quarter of CEO, chair and performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women, while only 12% of sports federations are led by a female president.
By 2035, the ambition is for girls to see women not only on the pitch, but on the touchline, in the boardroom and making the big decisions.

"But this can't just be about one summer nine years from now. That's the legacy we're going to build, and it starts now."

New research from our campaign reveals that more than half (55%) of women feel unsafe exercising outdoors alone after dark, compared to only a third (33%) of men.

In a bid to change that, the Let’s Lift the Curfew movement is back for a fourth year, bringing together women, community groups, sports clubs, organisations and allies to raise awareness of the fears and barriers many women face at this time of year.
Our director of marketing, Kate Dale, said the latest research shows there is still much work to do if we’re to drive meaningful change – not least eradicating the increasing amount of anti-women sentiment online.
“Every year when the clocks go back, countless women find their worlds getting smaller, and many change or step away from exercise altogether because of fear,” Kate said.
“Women’s fears are growing, with more concern about harassment and intimidation than we saw three years ago; many women believe rising online misogyny is making them feel even less safe exercising after dark.
“Police have warned violence against women and girls is reaching epidemic levels, so it's more important than ever that we understand women's experiences and address the rising safety concerns.
“We’re here to help more people understand the everyday reality many women face and raise awareness of what women need to feel safer.”
The new research comes as Let's Lift the Curfew returns for a fourth year.
Since it launched in 2023, thousands of women have mobilised around the movement to challenge the safety concerns that continue to shape women’s ability to be active in autumn and winter.
This year, This Girl Can is again working with England Athletics and Good Gym to help clubs, community groups and individuals turn awareness into action by hosting walks, runs and other activities.
Organisers can register their activity on a national map , helping women find opportunities near them, and access practical guidance on creating welcoming, inclusive and supportive experiences.

We’ve signed a long-term agreement with York & North Yorkshire Combined Authority and North Yorkshire Sport to improve health, wellbeing and economic growth by using the power of movement, activity and sport.

Our chief executive Simon Hayes was in York to sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Mayor of York and North Yorkshire , David Skaith, and the chief executive of North Yorkshire Sport, David Watson.
Simon explained how the link-up will blend the partners’ national, regional and local leadership, knowledge and networks to make physical activity more accessible to everyone.
"Community sport has a vital role to play in creating healthier, happier communities and stronger local economies," Simon said.
"This partnership is about making that a reality for people across York and North Yorkshire, particularly those who face the greatest barriers to being active.
"Local people know their communities best. Their needs, experiences and ambitions should help shape where we invest and how we work.
"By bringing together our national expertise, the combined authority’s leadership and North Yorkshire Sport’s local knowledge and relationships, we can make a real difference to people's health and happiness.
"This agreement is a strong example of that joined-up approach in action – bringing organisations together, tackling inequalities and making it easier for more people to enjoy the benefits of an active life."
The agreement also aims to improve links between health services and activity opportunities, and to create safer, more welcoming places for children and young people to walk, cycle and play.
It builds on existing investment in the movement, activity and sport workforce in the region, including around £400,000 from Mayor Skaith to strengthen skills, capacity and leadership across the sector.
"Coming together with Sport England lets us bring our regional ambition together with their national vision," said the Mayor.
"Our ambitious Moving Forward campaign is backed by £7m Mayoral funding to support people to move more and live healthier, happier lives.
"Working closely with Sport England, we’ll be able to maximise the impact of this investment and support more people right across York and North Yorkshire."

Two regional mayors are joining our Board as advisors, strengthening the connection between local leadership and our work to help more people get active.
David Skaith, Mayor of York and North Yorkshire, and Helen Godwin, Mayor of the West of England, will bring their experience of leading places and understanding of local communities to our national discussions.
We’ve invited them to help shape our thinking on how sport and physical activity can improve lives, tackle inequalities and build stronger communities.
Our chair, Chris Boardman, said their arrival marks an important step in how we work.
"I’m delighted to welcome David and Helen as advisors to the Sport England Board. This is more than two new appointments. It’s an important step in how we work," he explained.
"Sport England has long championed place-based working. Now we’re taking that principle further, bringing two leading Mayors directly into our national thinking.
"This is devolution in action, with regional leaders helping shape national priorities and ensuring more communities benefit from the power of sport.
"Sport has a remarkable ability to bring people together across social divides, creating connections and strengthening communities.
"That makes it a powerful tool for local leaders who want to improve the places they represent."
David welcomed the opportunity to bring the experiences of York and North Yorkshire to those conversations, while championing the contribution of regions across the country.
He said: "Mayors are at the centre of driving the change in their regions, so I'm delighted to take on this role and make sure that their voice is heard at the top level of Sport England.
"Here in York and North Yorkshire, we've seen how investment in sport, physical activity and active lifestyles can improve health and strengthen communities.
"I'll be proud to bring those experiences to the table while helping ensure all regions have a strong voice in shaping national priorities."
Helen Godwin, Mayor of the West of England, added: "As mayors take on more powers to deliver for our communities, I’m excited to be working with Sport England to help champion the transformative power of sport and investment in places for people to play.

"From encouraging healthier and more active lifestyles to building confidence and self-esteem, sport can be an amazing thing for people of all ages and abilities - as the football team that I set up found!"

We’re building on this approach through increasingly locally led investment, giving communities greater influence over priorities and how funding is used, supported by our national evidence, expertise and accountability.
Our focus remains on the people and places facing the greatest inequalities.
David and Helen’s advisory roles will support this direction by bringing regional experience directly into our national discussions.

In August, Sport England, Sport Wales, sportscotland, Sport Northern Ireland and UK Sport confirmed that the Transgender Inclusion in Domestic Sport Guidance will be reviewed .
This is to ensure that the guidance aligns with the updated context that sports are operating within.
The contractual requirements for the review of the Transgender Inclusion in Domestic Sport Guidance have now been published and are available to view here .
The invitation to tender will close on 16 November.
After procurement is completed, the review of the guidance is expected to begin in early 2027.
The revised guidance is estimated to be published later in the year.
Transgender Inclusion in Domestic Sports Guidance Review
In April 2025, the Supreme Court Ruling (For Women Scotland Ltd vs. The Scottish Ministers) ruled that, under the 2010 Equality Act, the protected characteristic of ‘sex’ means a person’s biological sex.
The updated Equalities and Human Rights Commission Statutory Code of Practice for services, public functions and associations became legally binding on 5 August 2026 and provides guidance as to how the Equality Act 2010 should be applied. The updated legal context means that a review of TIDS is necessary.
Additionally, a commitment to review TIDS in light of new scientific or medical evidence was made when it was published in 2021.
In April 2026, the sports councils commissioned an independent and impartial review of peer-reviewed scientific and medical evidence - spanning physiological and psychosocial literature - related to transgender inclusion in sport since the publication of the TIDS guidance.
It also concluded that a full review of evidence would provide a more nuanced narrative around key issues emerging which may enable sports councils and national governing bodies to revise policies accordingly.
Please note that this Code of Practice does not apply in Northern Ireland. The Northern Ireland Equality Commission is asking the High Court to clarify how the Supreme Court’s judgment should be applied in Northern Ireland, given its different equality law framework, and the implications of Article 2 of the Windsor Framework for how that equality law should be interpreted.
The guidance is jointly owned by the four home country sports councils (Sport England, Sport Wales, Sport Scotland and Sport NI) and UK Sport.
The external context we are operating in has changed.
As a result, the 2021 guidance has been withdrawn and new guidance will be published to replace this.
We will continue to support governing bodies through any questions or queries they have.
The tender is open for any organisation to bid and shared on the Sport England tender portal.

Historic England has published its Heritage at Risk Register 2026 , giving a snapshot of the health of England’s historic buildings and places.
This year, 85 heritage sites have been rescued and their futures secured. Many of them have been revived with the help and commitment of local people, communities, charities and owners.
The following sites have been restored and revived with our support, thanks to National Lottery players.
St Peter’s is a 10th-century church most notable for its impressive Saxon round tower. The project was awarded £580,000 to urgently repair weather-induced damage and develop activities and resources with the community to celebrate the church’s architectural and ecological heritage.
In Haringey, part of a pair of Georgian terraced houses has been saved from dereliction. Awarded £2.6million from us, it is now a creative hub featuring artists’ studios, galleries and a café run by Sarabande Foundation, which was established by the late Lee Alexander McQueen.
Grade II* listed Severn Wharf Building is a large former warehouse on the north bank of the River Severn, which is now part of the Ironbridge Gorge Museum – a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Built by the Coalbrookdale Company in the Gothick style between 1838 and 1847, it suffered flood damage in 2020. Following a grant of £9.9m from the National Heritage Memorial Fund , the building has been repaired and reopened and is now managed by the National Trust.
Almost exactly 90 years after the Crystal Palace burned down, the Italian Terraces that once led up to the Palace have been saved. We contributed £5m to the restoration project, which included restoration of the stonework, improved drainage, planting of wildflower meadows, two new step-free routes and the reinstatement of staircases.
The Temple of Vaccinia at Dr Jenner’s House in Berkeley, recognised as the birthplace of vaccination, received a £221,508 grant following its addition to the register in 2025. The project carried out critical repair work to its thatched roof, rear wall and chimney and the site reopened to the public in May 2026.
The register helps raise awareness of heritage sites to ensure they can be safeguarded for the future. Over the past year, 197 sites have been added to the register, as Historic England believes they are at risk of neglect, decay or inappropriate development.
Eilish McGuinness, our Chief Executive, said: "These are inspiring examples of what can be achieved when organisations and communities come together to save the heritage that matters to their community. Their removal from the Heritage at Risk Register is a testament to the dedication of everyone involved in these projects. The benefits of these will be felt for generations to come."

The award, previously known as Sustainable Project of the Year, is free to enter and open until 29 January 2027.
This work is more relevant than ever, and we can't wait to celebrate the exciting sustainability projects that the sector has delivered in the past year.
Alistair Brown, Head of Museums, Libraries and Archives Policy at The National Lottery Heritage Fund
The award helps to shine a light on creative approaches that can also inspire others to embed sustainability at the heart of what they do.
The award is open to all museums, galleries and archives as well as digital, cultural, natural and built heritage organisations and visitor attractions.
Entries must be based in the UK and the project or exhibition must have been delivered in 2026.
The award commends outstanding environmentally sustainable projects or exhibitions that demonstrate best practice in managing or communicating environmental impacts.
Entries may have used, for example, energy efficiency measures, green visitor travel planning or unique approaches to engaging audiences with the climate crisis. You should also identify any wider economic, social or environmental benefits to the organisation or community that have come from ‘thinking sustainably’.
For inspiration, take a look at some of our previous winners including Lambeth Palace and Gloucestershire Archives in 2026 and Stourbridge Glass Museum and Railworld Wildlife Haven in 2025.

Saved through dedicated community action, the Grade II listed landmark opened on 5 September following a dramatic physical transformation.
The arcade has been restored to its former 19th-century elegance while also being made fit for the future as a modern hub for independent businesses and local creators. It’s now home to 16 affordable small shops, artists’ studios and an event space.
Jenny Holden-Stokes, Arcade Manager, said: “Our fantastic local traders are ready to bring the buzz back to Dewsbury.”
First opened in 1899, the arcade reflects the changing story of high streets and town centre shopping, from its golden years in the 1950s and 1960s to its decline as shopping habits changed in the early 2000s. Its last shop tenants left in 2016.
Our 2023 grant has funded the restoration of some of the building’s finest features, including timber shopfronts, ornate ironwork and the glass canopy roof – replaced by local heritage glazing specialists to once again flood the central thoroughfare with natural light.
Reopening the arcade is the first project in Kirklees Council’s 10-year town centre investment plan to make improvements that benefit local people, encourage more visitors and boost trading opportunities.
After the arcade was bought by Kirklees Council, local residences and businesses formed The Arcade Group, a community benefit society, to lease and manage the building. They aimed to bring it back into use as a place for people to meet, shop and feel pride in where they live.
Dewsbury Arcade is just one example of a project we’ve funded that’s helping a community take ownership of a heritage site that matters to them.

Cadent, the gas distribution network for the region, uses state-of-the-art robotic technology called STASS for the first time in Rochdale to repair a gas pipe nearly 130 years old.
Installed at the start of the twentieth century and buried more than four metres beneath Dane Street, it is one of the earliest pipes to provide gas to Rochdale town centre.
Developed by Synthotech, STASS (The System Two Assess Survey and Seal) is a robotic vehicle that travels through pipes, locates joints and applies a sealant to the inside of the pipe to prevent leaks.
At Dane Street, STASS entered each end of the 30-inch cast iron pipe - roughly the width of a household doorway - and travelled 100 metres in each direction (200 metres total), applying a long-lasting sealant to the joints.
Chris Campbell, Customer Operations Area Manager for Cadent in the North West, said: “This technology allows us to work on hard-to-access pipelines, including those that are wide, deeply buried or particularly old. The pipe beneath Dane Street is an example of all three challenges.
It enables us to carry out delicate, precise repairs that protect our pipe, maintain a reliable gas supply and limit emissions, while keeping colleagues safe and improving the technology we use.
Using STASS supports Cadent’s ongoing efforts to reduce emissions and deliver a gas network that keeps people safe and warm while protecting the planet.
In 2026 alone, Cadent has invested £90 million to upgrade pipes across the North West, safeguarding gas supplies and supporting the transition to cleaner, greener gases – like biomethane.
This year, 12,500 metres of pipeline will be upgraded in Rochdale, supporting local authorities’ ambition to achieve carbon neutrality by 2038.

A search is under way to trace descendants or relatives of six Liverpool gas workers who were killed during the First World War.
More than a century after their deaths, Cadent – which manages the gas network today – is hoping to find relatives of Samuel Corfe, James Hitchmough, Richard Ireland, Alexander McDonnell, Allan Prophet and John Williams.
They are named on two memorials which are now housed at the company’s base in Huyton – and Cadent is keen to make sure their relatives know these exist and have opportunity to pay their respects, particularly on Armistice Day.
Every year, modern-day employees of Cadent gather at the memorial on 11 November, to pause for a moment of reflection and silence.
In more recent years, they have been joined by the great-niece of Thomas Thompson, to whom one of the two memorials is dedicated.
Thomas was 24 when he was killed as his unit advanced into Belgium in October 1918. Before the war, he worked at Caryl Street gas works, which at that time was a huge gas production site close to what is now Brunswick train station.
His father, Robert, was a foreman at the site and – at some point soon after Thomas died – a memorial stone was engraved and added to the wall at the site.
Fast-forward more than 100 years and this site is today a much smaller gas pressure management station, accessed by only a handful of workers.
A decision was taken several years ago to move the memorial to a location where more people can see it, and it now sits outside the headquarters for Cadent’s Merseyside operations, which is in Huyton. A plaque was placed on the exterior, public-facing wall of the original location of Thomas’s memorial.
The original was merged with another memorial dedicated to ‘the men employed at the Garston gas works … who gave their lives for their fellow countrymen’.
Now Cadent is keen to make sure the descendants of the six men named on that memorial know it exists and can join them in paying their respects.
Nick Jerman, Head of Safety and Engineering, and the regional lead for the Cadent Military Community, said: Cadent is proud to have a history that dates back to the early 1800s here in Liverpool.
Thousands of Merseyside gas workers served in both of the world wars, and many were killed. As a company, we pause every year to remember that.
It has been wonderful to welcome Thomas Thompon’s great-niece to join us every year and we want to extend the opportunity to all descendants.

Cadent, the UK’s largest gas distribution network, has – for the second year in a row – achieved a perfect score of 100/100 in the globally-recognised GRESB Infrastructure Asset Assessment, retaining both its 5-star rating and Sector Leader status for 2026.
The result reflects the maturity of Cadent’s approach to sustainability, with the assessment praising strong performance across areas including climate risk, governance, emissions reporting, employee and stakeholder engagement, and customer performance.
GRESB, a global ESG benchmark for real assets, is used by investors and stakeholders to assess the sustainability performance of infrastructure assets. The assessment recognises organisations that demonstrate excellence in sustainability management, operational performance, governance and social impact.
For 2026, Cadent achieved the highest possible overall score and retained the 5-star rating, alongside its Sector Leader status, which it first obtained in 2025.
Cadent achieved a first-place Management Score, securing full marks across leadership, governance, risk management, reporting and stakeholder engagement.
It also recorded a strong Performance Score, including full marks in energy, greenhouse gas emissions, health and safety, and customer categories.
Dave Garner, Chief of Health, Safety and Engineering at Cadent, said: “Retaining a perfect score of 100/100, our 5-star rating and Sector Leader status is an excellent result, and one that reflects the contribution of colleagues right across Cadent.
Achieving these results for a second consecutive year demonstrates the strength and maturity of the approach we have built to sustainability. It recognises not just our governance and reporting, but the work happening throughout the business on areas including climate risk, emissions, health and safety, our customers and engagement with our stakeholders.
We are incredibly proud of this recognition, but sustainability is about continuing to improve. This provides another strong benchmark for us as we continue to develop our approach and deliver responsibly for our customers, communities and the environment.
The recognition also builds on a broader track record of strong ESG performance. Cadent is rated AAA by MSCI and is ranked among the top-rated gas companies globally by Sustainalytics, providing further independent validation of its approach to sustainable business.
Each year, GRESB assesses and benchmarks the ESG performance of real assets worldwide, providing information to financial markets on material performance factors that can influence long-term value. The assessments are informed by issues considered material by investors and industry and are aligned with international reporting frameworks, goals and emerging regulations.
A GRESB 5-Star Rating is awarded to entities in the top 20 per cent of the benchmark, while its Sector Leader awards recognises infrastructure and real estate organisations demonstrating leadership within their peer groups.

Engineers from Cadent – the UK’s largest gas distribution network – will be starting work in Hitchin next month to replace 250 metres of ageing gas pipes, which were installed in 1946, with modern plastic pipes that will help future-proof the local network for decades to come.
The mains replacement work will take place in Lancaster Avenue, Brampton Park Road and York Road, starting on Monday 9 November, with permits in place for five weeks until Friday 11 December.
The project is part of a £123million investment this year, which will see more than 395km of pipes upgraded across the East of England.
Following consultation with Hertfordshire County Council, Cadent has agreed traffic management arrangements to keep engineers, residents and road users safe while the essential work is carried out.
Road closures will be in place on Brampton Park Road from Monday 9 November to Friday 27 November, Lancaster Avenue on Monday 23 November, and York Road from Monday 23 November to Friday 11 December.
A diversion route will be clearly displayed while the closures are in place.
Access will remain available for residents living within the work area, although some journeys may take longer than usual.
Gas stays ON for the duration of work. The only interruption to supply will be to properties that take a direct feed from the pipes being replaced (in the immediate local area). Supply to these properties will be disconnected for a short while as the property gets connected into the new pipe. Advance notice will be given, and more information will be provided to these properties.

Cadent, the UK’s largest gas distribution network, has launched its annual Energy Diaries insights alongside Thinks Insight & Strategy, revealing that customers want to ensure technological progress in the energy sector does not come at the expense of choice, trust and human support.
As digital technology continues to influence how energy networks operate, the latest report – Energy Diaries: Gas in a digital age – explores how different groups in society feel about managing their energy digitally. And while many people believe that the UK is a digitally confident nation, the insights from Energy Diaries has found a more diverse picture.
The study found that although 94 per cent of the public can go online as much as they want, only two thirds (68%) feel confident to do most things they need to online. If a digital device fails, almost one in five (18%) cannot afford to repair or replace it. This figure rises to two in five (40%) when considering the findings from those living in fuel poverty.
Nearly three quarters of people (72%) say that greater reliance on digital services, or technology for heating, would require additional support for some people. One third believe they would require help themselves, while two in five (41%) say a family member would.
The report also highlights the importance of multi-channel experiences in the context of the energy transition. As the energy transition becomes more complex, and people are being asked to make decisions about how they heat their homes and use energy, the research identifies customer concerns.
Four in five (81%) of people, for example, are worried about misinformation or fake news online, while three quarters are calling for better online services. Over three in five (62%), meanwhile, are concerned about the use of AI in customer service, such as chatbots.
Dr Angela Needle, Director of Strategy at Cadent, said: Our latest Energy Diaries show that not only are people worried about the spread of misinformation, but there is a wariness of the use of AI and digital technology in public services and Government. It is clear, therefore, that communications must not digitally exclude people. Communications must be multi-channel for important operational work updates, vital safety campaigns, as well as signposting support for vulnerable households.
Cadent has a number of different routes to support its customers. This includes more than 250 Centres for Warmth, where customers living in vulnerable situations can access support with bills and energy efficiency, as well as learning about important gas and carbon monoxide safety advice. It has also expanded its fleet of Mobile Advice Centres to help rural communities and areas without a nearby centre, access the support.
Energy Diaries is Cadent’s flagship insight platform, delivered in partnership with Thinks Insight & Strategy. Each year, Cadent surveys over 2,000 members of the UK public to uncover their attitudes towards energy, fuel poverty and sustainability, helping to inform thinking and shape Cadent’s future strategy and decision-making.
This year’s focus – gas in a digital age – coincides with Cadent’s ambitions to consider the growing role of digital technology in its customers’ lives.
Dr Angela Needle said: Digital technology is influencing how Cadent operates, from managing increased demand to using robotics, smart sensors and advanced leak detection technology to improve safety, efficiency and customer service. Digital innovation is also enabling more biomethane and other green gas producers to connect to the network, supporting the transition to a lower-carbon energy system.
It is crucial, however, that customers have a choice, and we are committed to ensure everyone can access and manage energy services in a way that suits them. Whether that is what system they use in the energy transition, or how they choose to engage with us, we must ensure there are multiple options available.

The UK may have inadvertently locked itself out of one of the most cost-effective routes to delivering net zero, according to a new report published today by Cadent.
The report finds that the Government’s carbon capture and storage (CCS) allocation processes have unintentionally excluded much of the UK's biomethane sector from participating in greenhouse gas removals (GGRs), despite the sector having the potential to generate one of the country's lowest-cost sources of carbon removals.
The findings are significant because achieving net zero will require more than simply reducing emissions. While renewable energy and energy efficiency will continue to play a critical role, some sectors, including aviation and industrial processes, are expected to retain emissions that are prohibitively expensive or technically difficult to eliminate entirely.
These industries will increasingly need to purchase greenhouse gas removals to offset remaining emissions.
According to the report from Cadent, the UK's largest gas distribution network, which has 47 biomethane production plants connected into its network in North West England, the Midlands, Yorkshire, East of England and North London, biomethane production offers a unique opportunity to help meet this demand.
Biomethane is produced from organic wastes such as food waste and agricultural residues. During the production process, a high-purity stream of biogenic carbon dioxide, known as bioCO2, is also created. If that carbon dioxide is captured and permanently stored, in Carbon Capture and Storage clusters - like HyNet and East Coast Cluster - it removes carbon from the atmosphere and can generate greenhouse gas removals that can be sold to companies seeking to offset residual emissions.
Analysis contained within the report suggests that when bioCO2 from multiple biomethane producers is aggregated and transported to carbon storage infrastructure at scale, the resulting greenhouse gas removals could become one of the lowest-cost removal pathways available to the UK.
The report also finds that revenues from selling these removals could provide biomethane producers with an additional income stream worth up to £20 per MWh of biomethane produced, potentially reducing the current subsidy requirement for biomethane production by around one-third.
At the sector's full potential of 120 TWh of biomethane production per year, the UK could generate approximately 17 million tonnes of bioCO2 annually. This is equivalent to around half of UK international aviation emissions. Even if only half of that potential is realised, the report suggests biomethane could provide around a quarter of the Climate Change Committee's engineered greenhouse gas removals target for 2050.
The report identifies several reasons why this opportunity is not taken up widely now, including that carbon capture infrastructure is still under construction and that policy development has historically focused on large industrial emitters.
However, it highlights that previous CCS allocation processes have also unintentionally excluded much of the biomethane sector by favouring large projects connected directly to pipelines, setting minimum scale thresholds that many biomethane producers cannot meet individually and preventing the use of non-pipeline transport solutions.,
This is a particular challenge because most biomethane plants are located in rural areas where direct pipeline connections are impractical. Instead, captured bioCO2 is expected to be transported by road to aggregation facilities before entering carbon transport and storage networks, a process known as non-pipeline transport (NPT).
The report says recent Government action is beginning to address the issue through the launch of the Non-Pipeline Transport Pathfinder process, which will enable a CCS cluster to source non-pipeline CO2 for the first time and could open the door to participation from hundreds of biomethane producers across the UK.

A gas main that has supplied homes and businesses in Shropshire for more than 60 years is set to be replaced as part of a major investment in the local gas network.
Cadent will begin work on Monday 26 October to replace around 750 metres of ageing gas pipe on the A49, starting at Bridge Farm and continuing approximately 750 metres northbound.
The existing metal gas main has been serving local communities since the 1960s and has quietly delivered gas to homes and businesses across three generations.
As part of Cadent's ongoing Mains Replacement Programme, the 750-metre stretch of pipe will now be upgraded with modern plastic pipework designed to keep the network safe, reliable and fit for the future.
The replacement forms part of a nationwide programme to modernise older sections of the gas network. Once complete, the new pipe will continue supplying customers for decades to come while reducing the need for future maintenance.
To carry out the work safely, temporary two-way traffic lights will be used along the route as the project progresses. The works are expected to take place between 26 October and 20 November, with a planned pause from 9 to 13 November while another utility company undertakes separate works in the area. Weekend working will also be utilised where possible to help reduce the overall duration of the project.
Customers' gas supplies will not be affected during the works.
Phil Carmichael, Head of Operations at Cadent said: The gas main we're replacing has served local communities for more than 60 years, meaning it has provided gas to generations of families, businesses and customers throughout its lifetime.
Our engineers will be replacing around 750 metres of this ageing pipe as part of our ongoing investment in a safe and reliable gas network. While most people never see the infrastructure beneath their feet, it plays a vital role in everyday life.
By replacing older metal pipes with modern plastic alternatives, we're helping ensure the network continues to serve local communities for many years to come.
We appreciate this work may cause some disruption for people travelling through the area, and we'd like to thank everyone for their patience while we complete these essential upgrades as quickly and safely as possible.
Access for residents, businesses and landowners will be maintained throughout the scheme wherever possible.

Newly released photographs show engineers working against the clock to repair a 114-year-old gas pipe above an electrified railway line in Manchester.
The complex operation by Cadent, which manages the local gas network, took place at Cornwall Street in Clayton, where a cast-iron gas main is attached to a railway bridge and runs directly above the Manchester Piccadilly to Sheffield route.
Installed in 1912, the pipeline supplies around 8,000 properties.
While the repair required specialist engineering expertise, safely reaching the pipe presented the biggest challenge.
Because the gas main sits above an electrified railway, Cadent first had to secure a tightly controlled overnight possession of the route, during which the electricity supply to the railway could be safely switched off.
Months of planning and close coordination involving Cadent, Network Rail, specialist contractors, arborists and access teams were needed to create the short window in which the repair could take place.
Once the line had been de-energised and handed over, engineers had only a matter of hours to access the pipe, complete the repair and clear the railway. This had to be achieved with enough time remaining for the line to be safely re-energised before passenger services resumed at 8.30am.
The pressure intensified when a late-running train from Glossop delayed the start of the operation. Although the possession window had been scheduled from 12.30am until 8.30am on a Sunday morning, the team could not begin work until around 2am. This reduced the available repair window to approximately five hours.
Marc Chester-Lees, Technical Specialist at Cadent and authorising engineer for the work, said: Because the pipe is positioned directly above an electrified railway, we could only carry out the repair when power to the line had been switched off. Securing that access took months of planning, and once the railway was handed over to us, every minute counted. We had one opportunity to complete the repair and safely return the route for the start of passenger services.
The pipe is situated around five metres above ground level, while nearby trees further restricted access. The presence of overhead electrical equipment meant traditional scaffolding could not be used, so the team brought in a specialist mobile elevated working platform to lift engineers safely above the tracks.
Once lifted into position, the Cadent engineers completed the repair in four hours. The work was finished and the site cleared by 6am, allowing the railway to be safely re-energised before the morning timetable began.
Engineers used an external injection technique to complete the repair, avoiding the need to add further weight to the ageing structure through encapsulation.
The successful operation means the gas network is continuing to safely supply around 8,000 properties while longer-term plans progress to divert the pipeline away from the railway corridor entirely.
Phil Hendrick, Head of Operational Delivery (North West), Cadent: This was a very challenging repair operation, delivered brilliantly. We made sure everyone was safe – our team and the public – and kept an uninterrupted supply of gas to local homes.

Engineers from Cadent – the UK’s largest gas distribution network – will be starting work in Hitchin later this month to replace ageing gas pipes with modern plastic pipes which will help future-proof the local network for decades to come.
The mains replacement work will take place at the roundabout junction of Verulam Road and Nightingale Road, starting on Friday 23 October, with permits in place until Sunday 1 November.
The project is part of a £123 million investment this year, which will see more than 395km of pipes upgraded across the East of England.
Following consultation with Hertfordshire County Council, Cadent has agreed traffic management arrangements to keep engineers, residents and road users safe while the essential work is carried out.
The roundabout at the junction of Verulam Road and Nightingale Road will be closed for the duration of the work. Instead, traffic lights will be in place in Nightingale Road and Florence Street so traffic can continue to flow.
Verulam Road will be closed at the junction of Wimbush Road, with clearly signed diversion routes in place.
Access will remain available for residents throughout the work, although some journeys may take longer than usual.

Gas engineers from Cadent are preparing the local network for winter by carrying out essential work to replace gas pipes in Hatton, Warwickshire.

Work will be delivered in three phases. Phase one will begin on Hockley Road before continuing onto Birmingham Road and ending at the Canal Road junction. Phase two will cross Birmingham Road and continue into Brownley Green Lane, followed by the final phase on Brownley Green Lane.
Temporary traffic lights will be required throughout the project to enable the work to be completed safely.
To ease delays, Cadent will also use REMOS technology for the first time in the West Midlands. This advanced traffic management system allows trained operators to monitor live traffic conditions and manage the temporary signals remotely to help reduce unnecessary delays. Drivers should still allow extra time for journeys, particularly during peak periods.
A Cadent spokesperson said: We are carrying out this work after identifying increased leakage in this part of the gas network and want to replace the affected pipes before colder weather increases demand.
These upgrades will help improve the reliability of the local gas network and ensure we can continue to deliver gas safely to homes and businesses in Hatton for many years to come.
We appreciate that temporary traffic lights on this busy route will cause some disruption and would like to thank residents and road users in advance for their patience while we complete this important project.
We are working closely with Warwickshire County Council, Hatton Parish Council, local residents and businesses, including The Hatton Arms, to minimise disruption wherever possible. Access will be maintained wherever it is safe and practical to do so, and customers directly affected by the work will be kept informed throughout the scheme.
To help reduce unnecessary delays, we will be using live traffic monitoring technology alongside advance warning signs and regular updates. However, drivers should still allow extra time for journeys, particularly during peak periods.
Gas supplies are expected to remain on during the work. If any interruption is required, affected customers will be contacted directly in advance and given further information.

For Gas Safety Week (14 – 20 September), Cadent, the UKs largest gas distribution network, is shining a light on one of the industry’s most unusual but vital roles - a specialist team trained to ‘smell gas’ to ensure the odourant levels are correct for public safety.
In 2025, Cadent received more than 67,000 calls to the national gas emergency number from people reporting a smell of gas across its North West network alone – equalling one call every 8 minutes - showing the importance of people recognising the smell and knowing what to do in an emergency.
Natural gas has no smell of its own, so a specially made chemical (mercaptan) is added to give it the distinctive odour people associate with gas. This acts as an important warning sign to let people know a leak may be present and to immediately call the national gas emergency number on 0800 111 999* .
Cadent’s rhinologists are trained to detect whether the right level of mecaptan is present in the gas supply. Getting the balance right is critical, if the odour is too strong, a small leak could be mistaken for a major incident; if it is too weak, people may not detect a gas escape at all.
James Dyson is one of four Lead Rhinologists at Cadent in the North West responsible for ensuring the correct levels of mercaptan are maintained across 34,000km of pipeline in the region.
Across the North West, odourant is injected at gas pressure control sites and entry points. The rhinologists test levels at several different locations, as well as carrying out additional checks at many district governors, where gas pressure is reduced before it reaches homes and businesses.
James Dyson said: It’s a serious job with potentially life-threatening consequences if we get it wrong. To ensure we are fully competent, we test ourselves rigorously, completing checks every quarter and before every site visit. We also attend external training every year.
To cross-check our results, we use a portable device known as an odorimeter that presents a controlled mixture of gas and air to the human nose, helping us ensure we meet strict standards.
While the smell of gas remains an important safeguard for customers. Cadent is also investing in advanced technologies alongside its specialist teams to identify gas escapes even earlier.
Picarro, a ‘gas-sniffing’ device fitted to specialist vehicles, is now used across Cadent’s networks to help detect gas escapes before the odour is noticeable to the human nose. In the North West alone, over half of the gas pipeline have been surveyed using the technology.
Nick Jerman, Head of Engineering and Safety at Cadent North West, said: Innovating our detection processes has safety and environmental benefits, while also helping us prioritise work for our repair and replacement teams.
The device has accurately identified gas escapes in rural areas where it is unlikely residents would have noticed a smell of gas.
By helping the public understand what gas smells like, and by using technology to identify gas escapes before they become noticeable, we can find leaks quicker, reduce disruption and help keep people safe and warm every day.

Gas mains and cable replacement works were co-ordinated into a single programme of roadworks to save weeks of disruption for Wigan residents.
Cadent and Wigan Council’s highways department have completed their first collaborative streetworks project.
Carried out by PGL Pipelines and Pegasus Utilities, the single project saved six weeks of disruption for people in and around Goose Green, as well as reducing carbon emissions.
The work on Warrington Road and Little Lane included replacing more than 1,300 metres of gas pipeline with new, more durable pipe that supports the transition to cleaner, greener gases, like biomenthane.
With the work now complete, the traffic management measures needed to carry it out safely have been removed.
Coun Paul Kenny, Wigan Council’s portfolio holder for planning, environmental services and transport, said: It's encouraging to see innovative approaches being used to deliver this work in our borough.
By adopting modern construction techniques and collaborative planning, the project has been completed more efficiently, helping to reduce disruption for residents and road users whilst ensuring essential infrastructure improvements are delivered effectively.
The works were carefully scheduled during the summer to help minimise disruption as much as possible and will help to maintain a safe and reliable gas network for the future.
I'd like to thank residents, businesses, and road users for their patience and understanding while these essential gas maintenance works were carried out over the summer holidays.
Both Cadent and Wigan Council are delivering major long‑term investment across the area and are already looking at further projects to work together on.
This forms part of Cadent’s five-year programme to upgrade more than 2,000 kilometres of pipes in the North West, with 21,000 metres scheduled for replacement across Wigan in 2026 alone.
Lucy Sterry, head of work management for Cadent (North West), said: Combining two major upgrades into one set of roadworks is a big step forward for how we plan our essential gas mains upgrades.
Where it is possible, and where we can safely co-ordinate, we are working closely with utility partners and councils to find opportunities to join up our activity. It means less digging, fewer teams on site, less disruption for residents and a lower overall carbon impact.

Engineers from Cadent – the UK's largest gas distribution network - will be getting to work in Peterborough to replace gas pipes that have been underground since the 1960s.

These upgrades also have big environmental gains, as they reduce methane emissions and enable a move to more renewable gases like biomethane. This is essential for a cleaner future - the UK will need energy to come from a range of sources to meet demand and be sustainable.
